Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic and fibroblast cells resulted in increased colony formation, activation of downstream signaling and acceleration of xenograft tumor growth in mice. The CBL Q367P alteration was found to reduce the ubiquitination activity of wildtype CBL, leading to increased stabilization of target proteins such as JAK2, FLT3 and c-KIT (PMID: 19620960).

The CBL L399V mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in decreased EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, likely leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 26676746).

Deletions in CBL have been identified in patients with myeloid malignancies, often affecting the RING domain of the protein (PMID: 19901108, 22315494). Studies investigating CBL deletions demonstrated that these alterations lead to growth factor-independent proliferation and autophosphorylation of the FLT3 kinase, causing activation of the STAT5 and AKT signaling pathways (PMID: 19276253).

The CARD11 E134G mutation lies in the coiled-coil domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human cell lines demonstrated it is activating, as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype CARD11 (PMID: 25352053, 28628108).

The CBL C381A mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in decreased EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, likely leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 26676746, 25178484).

The CBL G375P mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain of the CBL protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in decreased EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, likely leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 26676746).

The CBL Y371H mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells results in increased phosphorylation of CBL protein leading in enhanced cell growth, as evidenced by proliferation assays. The CBL Y371H mutant protein phosphorylates the GM-CSFR receptor and activates downstream signaling including JAK2 and MAPK pathways (PMID: 23696637). HEK293T expressing the CBL Y371H mutation have decreased EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, likely leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 26676746).

The CBL V391I mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in a modest decrease of EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, likely leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 26676746).

Truncating mutations in CBL have been identified in patients with myeloid malignancies, often located within the RING domain of the protein. These alterations are predicted to confer dominant-negative effects on the wildtype CBL protein (PMID: 20694012, 22315494, 20508043). Experimental studies in human cell lines suggest that these mutations produce hypersensitivity to interleuken-3 (PMID: 22315494).

The CBL H94Y mutation occurs in the protein's tyrosine kinase domain and was found to co-occur with CBL S80N in a patient with non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 20126411, 26676746). Expression of this mutation in epithelial cells, in combination with CBL S80N, resulted in increased cell viability and cell motility, as compared to wildtype CBL (PMID: 20126411). However, the CBL S80N and H94Y combined mutations do not effect EGFR ubiquitination, therefore, the mechanism by which this mutation alone or in combination with CBL S80N leads to transformation is unknown.

The CBL S80N mutation occurs in the protein's tyrosine kinase domain and was found to co-occur with CBL H94Y in a patient with non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 20126411, 26676746). Expression of this mutation in epithelial cells, in combination with CBL H94Y, resulted in increased cell viability and cell motility, as compared to cells with wildtype CBL (PMID: 20126411). However, the combination of these CBL mutations did not effect EGFR ubiquitination, therefore, the mechanism by which this mutation alone or in combination with CBL H94Y leads to transformation.

The CBL V430M mutation occurs in the protein's RING domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells did not impact the ubiquitination of EGFR, suggesting that this mutation does not effect CBL E3 ligase activity (PMID: 26676746).

The CBL P417A mutation occurs in the protein's RING domain. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells results in transformation, as evidenced by cytokine independent growth. The CBL P417A mutation results in reduced ubiquitination of the tyrosine kinase receptor FLT3, likely leading to stabilization of the FLT3 protein and enhanced activation of downstream signaling (PMID: 19387008).

The CBL H398Y mutation occurs in the protein's RING domain. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells results in transformation, as evidenced by cytokine independent growth. The CBL H398Y mutation results in reduced ubiquitination of the tyrosine kinase receptor FLT3 compared to wildtype CBL, likely leading to stabilization of the FLT3 protein and enhanced activation of downstream signaling (PMID: 19387008).

The CBL M374V mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells did not impact the ubiquitination of EGFR, suggesting that this mutation does not effect CBL E3 ligase activity (PMID: 26676746).

The CBL W802* occurs in the C-terminal domain of the CBL protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small lung cancer (PMID: 20126411). In vitro studies in A549 and H358 cells expressing this mutation demonstrated that CBL W802* is inactivating as measured by the loss of apoptosis and EGFR signaling regulation leading to increased cell viability, cell proliferation and cell motility in wound healing assays compared to wildtype CBL (PMID: 20126411). In vitro studies in HEK293T cells expressing CBL truncations mutations also demonstrate the CBL W802* mutation is likely inactivating as measured by loss of CBL signaling function in other downstream CBL truncation mutations (PMID: 23744067).

The CARD11 F97Y mutation lies in the CARD domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is activating, as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype CARD11 (PMID: 26711259, 23149938).

The CBL Q249E occurs in the C-terminal domain of the CBL protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small lung cancer (PMID: 26676746). In vitro studies in A549 and H358 cells expressing this mutation demonstrated that CBL Q249E is inactivating as measured by the loss of apoptosis and EGFR signaling regulation leading to increased cell viability, cell proliferation and cell motility in wound healing assays compared to wildtype CBL (PMID: 20126411).

The CBL P428L mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells did not impact the ubiquitination of EGFR, suggesting that this mutation does not effect CBL E3 ligase activity (PMID: 26676746).

The CBL D390Y mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in COS-7 cells resulted in decreased EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 25178484).

The CBL K382E mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in decreased EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, likely leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 26676746, 25178484).

The CBL R420Q occurs in the protein's RING domain (PMID: 17446348). Biochemical assays demonstrated that CBL R420Q cannot ubiquitinate the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT3, EGFR, or KIT. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic or epithelial cells results in increased cellular growth and transformation in cells that overexpress EGFR, FLT3 or KIT, leading to increased MAPK signaling (PMID: 17446348, 19387008, 19734451, 25178484). Mice engineered to express this mutation develop a hematopoietic disorder (PMID: 19734451).

The CBL S376F mutation occurs in the protein's RING domain. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells results in transformation, as evidenced by cytokine independent growth. The CBL S376F mutation results in reduced ubiquitination of the tyrosine kinase receptor FLT3 compared to wildtype CBL, likely leading to stabilization of the FLT3 protein and enhanced activation of downstream signaling (PMID: 19387008).

The CBL N454D mutation occurs in the protein's RING domain. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells does not result in transformation or changes in FLT3 ubiquitination, suggesting that this mutation is not oncogenic (PMID: 19387008).

CDC73 truncation mutations typically result in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in hyperparathyroidism-with-jaw-tumors syndrome and parathyroid carcinoma (PMID: 28774260). Truncating mutations of CDC73 are likely inactivating as measured by loss of parafibromin expression in CDC73-null parathyroid carcinomas compared to wildtype (PMID: 30926677). CDC73 truncating mutations have been identified to be enriched in sporadic parathyroid carcinomas compared to sporadic non-carcinomas (PMID: 12960210, 15531515).

The loss of CDC73 is an event identified in hyperparathyroidism-with-jaw-tumors syndrome and parathyroid carcinoma (PMID: 29755684, 28774260). In vivo studies with CDC73-deficient mice models demonstrated that CDC73 deletion is inactivating as measured by loss of parafibromin expression, increased cellular proliferation and development of parathyroid tumors in CDC73 deletion models compared to wildtype (PMID: 28288139).

The CBL H398Q mutation occurs in the protein's RING finger domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in decreased EGFR ubiquitination due to loss of CBL E3 ligase activity, likely leading to stabilization of EGFR and activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 26676746).

The CDH1 D257N mutation is located in the calcium-binding pocket of the protein. Structural analysis of this mutation demonstrates that it is inactivating by disrupting calcium-binding and dimerization (PMID: 24690483).

The CDH1 A298T mutation is located in the calcium-binding pocket of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in gastric cancer (PMID: 15235021). Expression of this mutation in a hamster ovary cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased cell aggregation and increased invasion compared to wildtype. Structural analysis suggests that this mutation may inhibit dimerization (PMID: 15235021, 24204729).

The CDH1 T340A mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in gastric cancer (PMID: 12588804). Expression of this mutation in a hamster ovary cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased cell aggregation and increased cell invasion and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 12588804).

The CDH1 D254N mutation is located in the calcium-binding pocket of the protein. This mutation has been found in intestinal and stomach cancer (PMID: 28481359, 24816255). Expression of this mutation in a hamster ovarian cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased protein stability and cell invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 26123647).

CDH1 deletions result in the loss of the protein. This mutation has been found in hereditary gastric cancer (PMID: 24037103, 23812922, 23341533, 19168852). CDH1 loss in a transplant mouse model demonstrated increased genomic instability and increased disease burden compared to wildtype (Abstract: Ishizawa, et al. ASH 2013, Abstract# 602 https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/122/21/344/83783/Loss-of-Function-of-The-Cell-Cycle-Regulator-Cdh1).

The CDH1 A634V mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in gastric cancer (PMID: 12588804). Expression of this mutation in a hamster ovary cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased cell aggregation and increased cell invasion and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 12588804).

The CDH1 G239R mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein and results in the loss of 29 bases within the gene. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial gastric cancer (PMID: 17545690; 23264079, 17221870). This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

The CDH1 R732Q mutation is located in the cadherin domain 2 of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial gastric cancer (PMID: 17545690). Expression of this mutation in a hamster ovary cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased cell aggregation and increased invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 15235021).

The CDH1 A617T mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in gastric cancer (PMID: 12588804). Expression of this mutation in a hamster ovary cell line demonstrated that it is neutral as measured by no change in cell invasion or migration, despite having decreased cell aggregates, compared to wildtype (PMID: 12588804).

CDH1 truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated CDH1 proteins. These mutations have been found in breast cancer and as germline mutations in familial gastric cancer (PMID: 8934538, 17522512). CDH1 loss in a transplant mouse model demonstrated increased genomic instability and increased disease burden compared to wildtype (Abstract: Ishizawa, et al. ASH 2013, Abstract# 602 https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/122/21/344/83783/Loss-of-Function-of-The-Cell-Cycle-Regulator-Cdh1).

CDH1 epigenetic silencing results in decreased expression of the protein. This alteration has been found in gastric cancers (PMID: 11313896). CDH1 loss in a transplant mouse model demonstrated increased genomic instability and increased disease burden compared to wildtype (Abstract: Ishizawa, et al. ASH 2013, Abstract# 602 https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/122/21/344/83783/Loss-of-Function-of-The-Cell-Cycle-Regulator-Cdh1). Over half of the cases harboring CDH1 mutations also had CDH1 epigenetic silencing suggesting that complete loss of CDH1 is favorable to gastric cancer cells (PMID: 11313896).

The CDKN2A P48L mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in vitro or in an osteosarcoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by reduced ability to inhibit CDK4/6 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 10491434).

The CDKN2A Q50* mutation results in a truncated variant of the p16/INK4A protein that partially lacks the ankyrin repeats. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and failure to inhibit the cell cycle compared to wildtype (PMID: 8668202).

CDKN2A truncating mutations form several forms of C-terminally truncated CDKN2A proteins. These mutations have been found in germline mutations in families with squamous cell cancer of the oral cavity (Abstract: Fostira et al. JCO PO, 2018. http://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00022). Expression of a truncation mutation in vitro demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and failure to inhibit the cell cycle compared to wildtype (PMID: 8668202). Additionally, expression of several C-terminally truncated CDKN2A proteins demonstrated that truncations upstream of residue 131 were inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 (PMID: 8603820).

The CDKN2A D74N mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in thyroid and esophageal cancer (PMID: 27519597). Expression of this mutation in osteosarcoma cells demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by reduced protein activity and the inability to induce cell cycle arrest compared to wildtype (PMID: 10491434).

The CDKN2A D108Y mutation occurs in the ANK3 domain of the protein and likely confers loss of function to this tumor suppressor. The CDKN2A D108Y mutation is associated with loss of cell cycle arrest whereas expression of wildtype CDKN2A induces cell cycle arrest, as determined by DNA content measured by flow cytometry when expressed in the CDKN2A-deficient U2OS cell line,(PMID: 12606942).

The CDKN2A D153H mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. This mutation has not yet been experimentally characterized although residue D153 is located at a splice junction suggesting that this mutation likely disrupts p16/INK4A splicing (PMID: 12853981).

The CDKN2A G35V mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062).

The CDKN2A D84Y mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by structural modeling and decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 compared to wildtype (PMID: 10498896).

The CDKN2A D108V mutation is located within the second Ankyrin repeat of the protein, and is a statistically significant hotspot. In silico analysis suggests that CDKN2A D108V is inactivating as measured by CDKN2A D108 mutations causing discordant cell cycle arrest function as compared to wildtype (PMID: 12606942).

The CDKN2A G65S mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p14/ARF protein (encoded by the CDKN2A locus). This mutation has been identified as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 25370744). In vitro studies in melanoma cells with a p53-proficient/ARF-deficient background expressing the G65S mutant demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating, resulting in increased superoxide levels and decreased cellular senescence compared to wildtype (PMID: 25370744).

The CDKN2A R87L mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID:10491434). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma and fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and the inability to induce cell cycle arrest leading to increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 10491434, 9607312).

The CDKN2A G23D mutation is located at the N-terminus of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A D108G mutation is located within the second Ankyrin repeat of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 30602096). In silico analysis suggests that CDKN2A D108G is inactivating as measured by CDKN2A D108 mutations causing discordant cell cycle arrest function as compared to wildtype (PMID: 12606942).

The CDKN2A G65R mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p14/ARF protein (encoded by the CDKN2A locus). This mutation has been identified as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 25370744). In vitro studies in melanoma cells with a p53-proficient/ARF-deficient background expressing the G65R mutant demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating, resulting in increased superoxide levels and decreased cellular senescence compared to wildtype (PMID: 25370744).

The CDKN2A P72L mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p14/ARF protein (encoded by the CDKN2A locus). This mutation has been identified as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 25370744). In vitro studies in melanoma cells with a p53-proficient/ARF-deficient background expressing the P72L mutant demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating, resulting in increased superoxide levels and decreased cellular senescence compared to wildtype (PMID: 25370744).

Deletion of CDKN2A results in loss of the p16/INK4A and p14/ARF proteins. CDKN2A deletion has been found in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, glioma, bladder carcinoma, leukemia and melanoma and is often associated with poorer clinical outcomes (PMID: 15495191, 26516359, 10999737). Deletion of CDKN2A in mouse models of malignant mesothelioma resulted in accelerated tumorigenesis compared to wildtype (PMID: 21526190). In addition, knockdown of CDKN2A in an HRAS G12V mouse model resulted in the induction of high-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma (PMID: 28982163).

The CDKN2A D108H mutation is located in exon 2 of the gene. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma, laryngeal cancer and squamous cell carcinoma, and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28467829, 19690981, 34663923). In silico analysis suggests that CDKN2A D108H is inactivating as measured by CDKN2A D108 mutations causing discordant cell cycle arrest function as compared to wildtype (PMID: 12606942).

The CDKN2A D74Y mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 compared to wildtype and computational modeling indicated impaired protein function (PMID: 19260062).

The CDKN2A V59G mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 12700603, 22841127, 25780468, 10874641, 21893440). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in fibroblasts demonstrated that is it inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 12700603).

The CDKN2A N71I mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A S56I mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062).

The CDKN2A A68T mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID:9036865). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line or in a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A Q50R mutation is located within the second ankyrin repeat of the protein. This mutation has been identified in ductal carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). Although not functionally characterized, in vivo studies with yeast expressing CDKN2A Q50P suggest that CDKN2A Q50R is inactivating as measured by CDKN2A Q50P disrupting CDKN2A and CDK4 interaction and ablating cell cycle transition inhibitor function as compared to wildtype (PMID: 14508519).

The CDKN2A D108N mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation was found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in fibroblasts demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 12417717).

The CDKN2A R87W mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma and fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and the inability to induce cell cycle arrest leading to increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062).

The CDKN2A R24P mutation is located at the N-terminus of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma and pancreatic cancer (PMID: 15146471, 9516223; 9425228; 15235029, 11556834, 9699728, 9328469). Expression of this mutation in vitro or in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 9328469).

The CDKN2A N71S mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471, 7987387, 11556834, 11807902, 12072543, 16905682, 18363633). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A Q50P mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 compared to wildtype (PMID: 14508519).

This CDKN2A A148T mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation was found as a germline variant in families with melanoma or breast cancer (PMID: 15879498). Expression of this mutation in vitro suggests that it may be neutral as measured by no change in the ability to inhibit CDK4 kinase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 8603820).

The CDKN2A G35A mutation is located at the N-terminus of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062).

The CDKN2A G67R mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062).

The CDKN2A A36P mutation is located at the N-terminus of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A H83Y mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID:21462282). Expression of this mutation in an osteosarcoma cell line demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by the inability to induce cell cycle arrest leading to increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype. However, this mutation had more subtle effects compared to other CDKN2A variants and could still bind to CDK4 and CDK6 and inhibit their kinase activity (PMID: 10491434).

The CDKN2A A57V mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in fibroblasts demonstrated that it is neutral as measured by no change in protein activity or cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062).

The CDKN2A D68H mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p14/ARF protein (encoded by the CDKN2A locus). This mutation has been identified as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 25370744). In vitro studies in melanoma cells with a p53-proficient/ARF-deficient background expressing the D68H mutant demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating, resulting in increased superoxide levels and decreased cellular senescence compared to wildtype (PMID: 25370744).

The CDKN2A H83N mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 16307646, 21462282). Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by structural modeling and the inability to inhibit CDK4 kinase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 9660926).

The CDKN2A P114S mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation was found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID:19260062). Expression of this mutant in in vitro and in fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062). Structural modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it is strongly predicted to impair protein function (PMID: 8755727).

The CDKN2A P114L mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 7777061). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by the inability to inhibit CDK4/6 kinase activity and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 7777061). Structural analysis of this mutation also demonstrated that it was inactivating (PMID: 8755727).

The CDKN2A L32P mutation is located at the N-terminus of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A E69G mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 19260062). Expression of this mutation in melanoma and fibroblast cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062)

The CDKN2A A60V mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062).

The CDKN2A L16P mutation is located at the N-terminus of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma or pancreatic cancer (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A M53I mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it was likely inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062).

The CDKN2A D84H mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 10498896). Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by structural modeling, decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and the inability to inhibit CDK4 kinase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 9660926, 10498896).

The CDKN2A A60R mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 12950144). Expression of this mutation in melanoma and fibroblast cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062)

The CDKN2A G67S mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in melanoma and fibroblast cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062)

The CDKN2A L63P mutation is located in the ankyrin repeat domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in a melanoma sample with loss of p16 protein expression, but co-occurred in a tumor with promotor methylation and has not otherwise been functionally characterized (PMID: 20703244).

The CDKN2A R87P mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID:10491434). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma and fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and the inability to induce cell cycle arrest leading to increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 10491434, 9607312, 19260062).

The CDKN2A N71K mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma and melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A R99P mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation was found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID:19260062). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in melanoma and fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062).

The CDKN2A P81L mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 10389768).

The CDKN2A E88K mutation is located in the third ankyrin repeat of the CDK binding region. This mutation has been found in melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 compared to wildtype (PMID: 10498896).

The CDKN2A G101W mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation was found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID: 10869234). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma and fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and increased cell proliferation when compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062). Structural modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it is strongly predicted to impair protein function (PMID: 8755727).

The CDKN2A D84G mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, inability to inhibit CDK4/6 kinase activity and inability to induce cell cycle arrest compared to wildtype (PMID: 10491434).

The CDKN2A Q50H mutation is located within the second ankyrin repeat of the protein. This mutation has been identified in ductal carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 32640200). Although not functionally characterized, in vivo studies with yeast expressing CDKN2A Q50P suggest that CDKN2A Q50H is inactivating as measured by CDKN2A Q50P disrupting CDKN2A and CDK4 interaction and ablating cell cycle transition inhibitor function as compared to wildtype (PMID: 14508519).

The CDKN2A P81T mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID:19260062). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma and melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the CDKN2A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136, 19260062,10389768).

The CDKN2A I49S mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma and pancreatic cancer (PMID: 15146471). Expression of this mutation in an RB-negative osteosarcoma cell line and a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6, mislocalization of the p16/INK4A protein and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A D84V mutation is located in the third ankyrin repeat of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma (PMID:28060055). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in an osteosarcoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and the inability to induce cell cycle arrest leading to increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 10491434).

The CDKN2A D84N mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer, esophagial cancer and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (PMID: 10498896). Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by structural modeling, decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and the inability to inhibit CDK4 kinase activity compared to wildtype(PMID: 9660926, 10498896).

The CDKN2A T77P mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in fibroblast cell lines demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19260062).

The CDKN2A R112G mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation was found as a germline variant in families with melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to CDK4 and CDK6 and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20340136).

The CDKN2A G35R mutation is located in the ankyrin repeats of the p16/INK4A protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in osteosarcoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24659262).

This mutation is a truncating mutation in the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain region of the CEBPA protein. Somatic mutations in the bZIP region of CEBPA have been detected in many patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and are associated with a more favorable prognosis (PMID: 34320176, 33951732, 34448807, 38228680). bZIP region truncating mutations occur where the basic region meets the leucine zipper, resulting in DNA binding and dimerization dysfunction (PMID: 11830484). In vitro studies with NI3T3 cells expressing truncating mutations in the CEBPA bZIP region demonstrate that these mutations are inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding and transcriptional activity compared to wild-type (PMID: 11830484).

The CEBPA K313dup mutation is located in the bZIP domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 16453003, 18768433). CEBPA K313dup has also been identified in patients with bi-allelic CEBPA double-mutated acute myeloid leukemia that harbor both an N-terminal truncating mutation and an in-frame bZIP domain mutation (PMID: 19304957, 29025912). There are conflicting data on the biological effect of the CEBPA K313dup. In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing CEBPA K313dup demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced protein stability, which is suggested to contribute to leukemogenesis, compared to wildtype (PMID: 18587575). Conversely, other in vitro studies have demonstrated that CEBPA K313dup results in increased transcriptional activation and overexpression of the N-terminally truncated CEBPA p30 isoform compared to wildtype (PMID: 34226527, 18587575).

Truncating mutations of CEBPA typically occur throughout the protein and can be categorized as classic CEBPA mutations or non-classic CEBPA mutations, depending on the protein region of the mutation. Classic CEBPA mutations include the two main hotspot regions of the protein: the N-terminal region truncating mutations, which lead to the abrogation of the full-length CEBPA p42 isoform, and the C-terminal region truncating mutations in the bZIP region, which impair DNA binding ability and dimerization (PMID: 37621152, 31867767, 11830484, 20884804). Non-classic CEBPA mutations include frameshift or nonsense mutations in the mid-region of the protein, which lead to the loss of CEBPA function (PMID: 24056881, 27034432). Classic CEBPA N-terminal region truncating mutations have been detected in many patients with acute myeloid leukemia and commonly co-occur with bi-allelic C-terminal region mutations (PMID: 31309149, 34320176, 20884804). Classic CEBPA C-terminal region truncating mutations have been detected in many patients with acute myeloid leukemia, and are associated with a more favorable prognosis (PMID: 34320176, 33951732, 34448807, 38228680). Non-classic CEBPA truncating mutations have been less frequently identified in patients with acute myeloid leukemia compared to classic CEBPA mutations, and have been associated with poorer survival (PMID: 29025912).

The CEBPA K302N mutation is located in the bZIP domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing CEBPA K298T demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased protein stability, DNA binding and BCL-2 activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 16254192).

This is an in-frame insertion in the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain region of the CEBPA protein. Somatic mutations in the bZIP region of CEBPA have been detected in many patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and are associated with a more favorable prognosis (PMID: 34320176, 33951732, 34448807, 38228680). bZIP region in-frame deletions or insertions occur where the basic region meets the leucine zipper, resulting in DNA binding and dimerization dysfunction (PMID: 11830484). In vitro studies with NI3T3 cells expressing in-frame insertions in the CEBPA bZIP region demonstrate that these mutations are inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding and transcriptional activity compared to wild-type (PMID: 11830484).

This is an in-frame deletion in the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain region of the CEBPA protein. Somatic mutations in the bZIP region of CEBPA have been detected in many patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and are associated with a more favorable prognosis (PMID: 34320176, 33951732, 34448807, 38228680). bZIP region in-frame deletions or insertions occur where the basic region meets the leucine zipper, resulting in DNA binding and dimerization dysfunction (PMID: 11830484). In vitro studies with NI3T3 cells expressing in-frame deletions in the CEBPA bZIP region demonstrate that these mutations are inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding and transcriptional activity compared to wild-type (PMID: 11830484).

The CEBPA K298T mutation is located in the bZIP domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing CEBPA K298T demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein stability, DNA binding and BCL-2 activation being comparable to wildtype (PMID: 16254192).

The CEBPA Q312dup mutation is located in the bZIP domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 16453003, 20439648). Although not functionally characterized per se, CEBPA Q312dup is suggested to be inactivating as duplication mutations in the bZIP domain lead to disruption in isoform dimerization and DNA binding (PMID: 11242107, 11830484). CEBPA Q312dup has been identified in cases of biallelic CEBPA double-mutated acute myeloid leukemia, patients that harbor both an N-terminal truncating mutation and an in-frame bZIP domain mutation (PMID: 19304957, 29025912). CEBPA Q312dup is suggested to confer sensitivity to standard remission induction chemotherapy as measured by reduced variant allele fraction score in a relapsed patient with cytogenetically normal acute myeloid leukemia harboring CEBPA Q312dup (PMID: 34560908).

This is a truncating mutation in the N-terminal of the CEBPA gene. Truncating mutations in the N-terminal region of CEBPA typically occur in the transcription activation domains (TAD), resulting in a premature stop codon that produces the CEBPA p30 isoform, an N-terminally truncated variant of CEBPA (PMID: 37621152, 31867767). The CEBPA p30 isoform has been detected in many patients with acute myeloid leukemia and commonly co-occur with bi-allelic C-terminal mutations that disrupt CEBPA homodimerization (PMID: 31309149, 34320176, 20884804). In vivo studies with mice expressing both the CEBPA p30 isoform and CEBPA C-terminal frame-shift mutations demonstrate that co-expression is oncogenic as measured by leukemogenesis compared to mice expressing CEBPA p30 alone (PMID: 20884804). The CEBPA p30 isoform is a functional variant identified to bind to gene promoters and repress gene expression independently of the full-length CEBPA p42 isoform (PMID: 17242690). In vitro studies with CD34+ hematopoietic cells and U937 cells expressing the CEBPA p30 isoform demonstrate a switch-of-function as measured by an upregulation of UBC9 expression, which subsequently results in the downregulation of the CEBPA p42 isoform via sumoylation (PMID: 17671234).

The CEBPA R300G mutation is located in the bZIP domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 16871279). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing CEBPA R300G demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of DNA binding and inability to induce BCL-2 acitvation compared to wildtype (PMID: 16254192).

The CEBPA R297G mutation is located in the bZIP domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing CEBPA R297G demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein stability, DNA binding and BCL-2 activation being comparable to wildtype (PMID: 16254192).

The CIC R1515H mutation is located in the repressor domain of the protein (PMID: 27869830). Lung adenocarcinoma cell lines engineered to express this mutation demonstrated an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830). In murine transplantation assays, the CIC R1515H mutation exhibited a modest acceleration of disease progression (PMID: 27869830).  Human embryonic kidney cells and isolated primary oligodendroglioma cells, with coexpression of R132H-mutated IDH1 and the R1515H mutated short isoform of CIC (predicted 1608 amino acids), have reduced clonogenicity (PMID: 25277207, 22072542).

The CIC R181W mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. Lung adenocarcinoma cell lines engineered to express this mutation demonstrated it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830).

The CIC R202Q mutation is located in the HMG box of the protein. This mutation has been identified in oligoastrocytoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 22588899). Biochemical assays of CIC R202Q demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a moderate decrease in DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 31323153).

The CIC-DUX4 fusion retains the majority of the CIC protein and includes the C-terminal region of DUX4, however, it cleaves off both DUX4 homeobox domains (PMIDL 21813156). The chimeric protein resulting from CIC-DUX4 fusion has transforming properties in NIH/3T3 fibroblasts. Compared to wildtype CIC, the fusion mediates transcriptional activation instead of repression of downstream CIC targets, leading to upregulation of the ETS PEA3 subfamily that is normally repressed by CIC; this is likely the cause of its oncogenic activity (PMID: 22072439, 16717057).

The CIC P722L mutation is located in an uncharacterized region of the protein (PMID: 27869830). Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830).

The CIC R1515L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the CIC protein. This mutation has been found in oligodendrogliomas, among other cancers (PMID: 22072542). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 28278156).

The CIC G1098D mutation is located in an uncharacterized region of the protein (PMID: 27869830). Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830).

The CIC G107E mutation is located in the N-terminal of the protein. Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays and a modest acceleration of disease progression in a murine transplantation assay (PMID: 27869830).

CIC deletion is an event that has been identified in prostate cancer (PMID: 36383412). In vivo studies with CIC-deficient Drosophila melanogaster models have demonstrated loss of CIC is inactivating as measured by loss of MAPK regulation, leading to MAPK pathway activation (PMID: 29844126).

The CIC Q247R mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays and a modest acceleration of disease progression in a murine transplantation assay (PMID: 27869830).

The CIC S649F mutation is located in an uncharacterized region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830).

CIC truncating mutations are typically a result of loss or mutation of CIC on chromosome 19q, and are associated with IDH1 and FUBP1 mutations or deletions on chromosome 1p. These mutations have been identified in glioma (PMID: 24117486, 22072542, 21817013, 24086756). CIC mutations were detected with chromosome 1p/19q co-deletion in a study examining patient oligodendrogliomas (PMID: 22588899). Oligodendrogliomas with loss of CIC detected with FUBP1 mutations were found to exclusively co-occur with IDH1 or IDH2 mutations (PMID: 22588899). In vitro studies of truncated CIC in human glioma cell lines have demonstrated that CIC truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by a defect in CIC nuclear targeting to the nucleus (PMID: 26017892).

The CIC R202W mutation is located in the HMG box of the protein. This mutation has been identified in oligodendroglioma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24086756). Biochemical assays of CIC R202W demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a substantial decrease in DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 31323153).

The CIC A281S mutation is located in an uncharacterized region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830).

The CIC R1515C mutation is located in the repressor domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in glioma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24030748). In vitro studies with mouse embryonic stem cells expressing CIC R1515C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to repress ETV4 and ETV5 expression and loss of DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 29844126).

Fusions of CIC typically result from chromosomal translocations and have been infrequently identified in small round cell carcinoma (PMID: 25007147, 22072439, 28188754). Expression of CIC fusions in multiple cancer cell lines has demonstrated that they are likely inactivating as measured by the loss of transcriptional repression and aberrant transcriptional activation (PMID: 24947144, 32788348, 16717057, 30407212).

The CIC R666C mutation is an uncharacterized region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays and a modest acceleration of disease progression in a murine transplantation assay (PMID: 27869830).

The CIC A1185T mutation is located in an uncharacterized region of the protein (PMID: 27869830). Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830).

The CIC R201W mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in oligodendrogliomas, among other cancers (PMID: 25277207, 22072542). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity and colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 28278156).

The CIC Q1516H mutation is located in the repressor domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in lung adenocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by an increased migratory phenotype in invasion assays (PMID: 27869830).

The CREBBP S1680del mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas, among other cancers (PMID: 21390126). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21390126).

The CIC R215W mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in oligodendrogliomas, among other cancers (PMID: 29844126). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 28278156, 29844126).

The CREBBP Y1503S mutation occurs in the histone acetyltransferase domain of the protein and is predicted to disrupt structures involved in substrate binding (PMID: 21390130). When co-expressed as a tandem mutation with Y1503A in transgenic mice and mouse fibroblast cell line, the mutation has a mild effect on expression of CREBBP target genes, is associated with reduction of H3 lysine 18 acetylation, and inhibits cellular proliferation relative to wildtype CREBBP (PMID: 21390130). Cell line acetylation assays have shown that the W1502A/Y1503S mutation abolishes acetylation, likely through defective binding to substrate and acetyl-CoA (PMID: 11691934).

The CREBBP Y1482H mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas, among other cancers (PMID: 21390126). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21390126).

The CREBBP S1436N mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in bladder cancers, among others (PMID: 28970362). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 28970362).

The CREBBP R1446H mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 21390130). Based on the crystal structure, this mutation likely inactivates the protein by interrupting substrate binding. In transgenic mice and mouse fibroblast cell line the mutation reduced expression of CREBBP target genes, resulted in slight reduction of H3 lysine 18 acetylation, and decreased cellular proliferation (PMID: 21390130).

CREBBP deletion is an event that has been identified in acute lymphoblastic leukemia and small cell lung cancer (PMID: 21390130, 30181244). CREBBP deletion mutations that result in the loss of the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain are likely inactivating as they are likely to mirror HAT domain missense mutations that disrupt CREBBP histone acetylation function, target gene transcription and cellular proliferation (PMID: 21390130). Functional assessment of CREBBP deletion mutations that retain the HAT domain and delete other C-terminal domain regions have also been suggested to be likely inactivating as measured by changes in target gene expression and cellular proliferation due to affecting the protein's ability to bind to transcriptional cofactors (PMID: 21390130).

The CREBBP K1320R mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas, among other cancers (PMID: 21390126). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely neutral as measured by HAT activity being comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21390126).

The CREBBP Y1503F mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas, among other cancers (PMID: 21390126). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21390126).

The CREBBP Q1500P mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase domain of the protein and is predicted to disrupt structures involved in substrate binding (PMID: 21390130). In transgenic mice and mouse fibroblast cell line the mutation had no effect on expression of CREBBP target genes, resulted in slight reduction of H3 lysine 18 acetylation, and did not affect cellular proliferation (PMID: 21390130).

CREBBP truncating mutations result in various forms of C-terminally truncated CREBBP proteins. Variants resulting in the loss of the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain (residues 1342-1648) are likely to affect histone acetylation, target gene transcription and cell proliferation as is seen by missense mutations in this domain. Experimental studies on variants retaining the HAT domain but cleaving other C-terminal domains that bind various cofactors indicate effects on target gene expression and cellular proliferation (PMID: 21390130).

The CREBBP Y1503D mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas, among other cancers (PMID: 21390126). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21390126).

The CREBBP R1563S mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase domain of the protein and is predicted to disrupt structures involved in substrate binding (PMID: 21390130). In transgenic mice and mouse fibroblast cell lines, this mutation had no effect on expression of CREBBP target genes and did not affect cellular proliferation (PMID: 21390130).

The CREBBP R1446G mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in bladder cancers, among others (PMID: 28970362). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 28970362).

The CREBBP H1487Y mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas, among other cancers (PMID: 21390126). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21390126).

The CREBBP D1435E mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the CREBBP protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas and bladder cancers (PMID: 21390126, 28970362). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21390126, 28970362).

The CREBBP R1446C mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 21390130). Based on the crystal structure, this mutation likely inactivates the protein by interrupting substrate binding. In a mouse fibroblast cell line, this mutation decreased cellular proliferation (PMID: 21390130). The mutation abolishes normal HAT activity in vitro (PMID: 28970362)

The CREBBP W1502A mutation is located in the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lymphomas, among other cancers, and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 21390130, 26619011). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation, in combination with another CREBBP mutation, might be inactivating as measured by decreased HAT activity, proliferation, and CREBBP-target gene transcription compared to wildtype (PMID: 21390130, 11691934).

The CTNNB1 P44A mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in adrenal and kidney cancer (PMID: 24755523, 27468715, 16909133, 14994125). Expression of this mutation in a hepatoma cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 18282277).

The KAT6A-CREBBP fusion (also MYST3-CREBBP) t(8;16)(p11;p13) is recurrent in a rare subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) that is characterized by monocytic features, erythrophagocytosis and poor prognosis (PMID: 7596149, 18528428, 23102703, 23974201). In the KAT6A-CREBBP rearranged protein, the C-terminal transcriptional activation domain of KAT6A is fused with most of the CREBBP protein, including the chromatin interaction domains (PMID: 23102703, 23974201). CREBBP and KAT6A both have histone deacetylase activity and have been implicated in cell cycle and transcriptional regulation (PMID: 16849538, 23974201). In gene expression studies, patients with the KAT6A-CREBBP fusion have gene expression signatures associated with disruption of hematopoietic differentiation at the myelomonocytic precursor stage (PMID: 16849538, 23974201).

The CTNNB1 D32A mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial, liver and brain cancer (PMID: 21060032, 22832583, 16160475, 12708483). Expression of the D32A mutant in a canine kidney cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cell invasion and three-dimensional growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 15829978).

The CTNNB1 I35S mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial and liver cancer (PMID: 24633194, 28481359, 17187432, 18282277). Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it was activating as measured by increased protein activity compared to wildtype. Endogenous expression of this mutation in liver cancer samples demonstrated increased nuclear and cytoplasmic accumulation of the protein compared to normal liver samples (Abstract: Manring et al. Abstract# 2249, AACR 2012. http://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/72/8_Supplement/2249) (PMID: 10665646, 18282277).

The CTNNB1 S23R is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in liver cancer (PMID: 17187432, 11375957). The DNMT3A L813Q mutation is located between the target recognition domain and the interface between the ADD domain and the catalytic domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A L813Q demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by methyltransferase function and protein stability comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A R803S mutation is located adjacent to the interface between the ADD domain and the catalytic domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A R803S demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A R659H mutation is located in the DNA methylase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 33796225). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A R659H demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A C554Y mutation is located in the ADD domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 23632886). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A C554Y demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A Y660C mutation is located adjacent to the substrate binding motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 27276561). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A Y660C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function and protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A I407T mutation is located adjacent to the PWWP domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 22642896). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A I407T demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function and protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A K455Q mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A K455Q demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A A662D mutation is located in the substrate binding motif of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A A662D demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function and protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A A884V mutation is located in the DNMT3A homodimer interface of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 22490330). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A A884V demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by methyltransferase function and protein stability comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The DNMT3A D768Y mutation is located in the tetramer interface of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing DNMT3A D768Y demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced methyltransferase function compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429321).

The EGFR exon 20 C797Y mutation is located in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. This mutation has been found in malignant peritoneal mesothelioma (PMID: 20942962). Cell line experiments demonstrate that this mutation is activating and sensitive to erlotinib treatment (PMID: 20942962).

The exon 20 EGFR S720P mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 15897572, 22760226, 34526717). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, preclinical models with the S720P mutation show high sensitivity to first-, second-, and third-generation, and Ex20Ins-active EGFR inhibitors (PMID: 34526717). Additionally, one patient with NSCLC harboring this mutation had a partial response to treatment with gefitinib (PMID: 15897572). In a separate study, one patient with NSCLC harboring this mutation in combination with the known oncogenic EGFR G719A mutation had a partial response to treatment with gefitinib (PMID: 22760226).

The EGFR exon 19 E746_T751insIP mutation occurs in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. Experiments with cells expressing mutant EGFR as a result of EGFR exon 19 insertion events demonstrate they are associated with cell transformation, increased proliferation and sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibition (PMID: 22190593). In a clinical study, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring the EGFR E746_T751insIP mutation had a partial response to treatment with gefitinib (PMID: 18325048).

The EGFR V774_C775insPR mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 34526717). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, preclinical models with the V774_C775insPR mutation show resistance to first-, second-, and third-generation EGFR inhibitors, and moderate sensitivity to Ex20ins-active EGFR inhibitors (PMID: 34526717).

The EGFR T847A mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 24002608, 19238633). Although not functionally characterized per se, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR T847A and EGFR G863S was treated with gefitinib and demonstrated progressive disease (PMID: 18000506).

The EGFR exon 21 A864T mutation is located in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain (PMID: 19147750). This mutation has been found in gallbladder and adrenocortical carcinoma (PMID: 23585556, 21761100, 16551849). Cell line experiments demonstrate that this mutation is activating, transforming and partially sensitizing to erlotinib, gefitinib and AEE788 (PMID: 19147750). The EGFR A864T mutation was identified in a single patient with non-small cell lung cancer who exhibited progressive disease following treatment with gefitinib (PMID: 22722798).

The EGFR exon 21 T854S mutation occurs in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. While this mutation has not been functionally validated, EGFR T854A has been demonstrated to confer gain-of-function activity to EGFR. The clinical response data to erlotinib or gefitinib is conflicting. In one report, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring this mutation had progressive disease upon treatment with gefitinib (PMID: 23486275). However, in the MSK-IMPACT clinical series, 2 patients with EGFR T854S mutant NSCLC had concomitant L858R mutations and one of these patients also harbored a T790M mutation had been treated with EGFR TKI, chemotherapy and immunotherapy and had derived clinical benefit as defined as a reduction in tumor size on imaging and documented symptom improvement or stable disease on two consecutive imaging scans ≥30 days apart with symptom improvement (PMID: 28336552).
The EGFR V441I mutation is located in the receptor L-domain of the mutation. In silico analysis suggests that the mutation confers resistance to cetuximab and necitumumab (PMID: 31228284).

The EGFR T354M mutation lies in the extracellular domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in the Ba/F3 cell line demonstrated it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased cell viability compared to wildtype EGFR (PMID: 29533785).

The EGFR V765L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28481359). Although not functionally characterized per se, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR C797S, EGFR L858R and EGFR V765L was treated with afatinib and demonstrated stable disease (PMID: 35574304).

The EGFR exon 20 Y801H mutation occurs in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. This mutation has been found in malignant peritoneal mesothelioma and squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil (PMID: 20942962, 17224267). Cell line experiments demonstrate that this mutation is activating and sensitive to erlotinib treatment (PMID: 20942962).

The EGFR exon 20 G796S mutation is located in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. Cell line experiments demonstrate that this mutation is activating and transforming (PMID: 18193092). In clinical studies, two patients with T790M+ non-small cell lung cancer harboring concurrent G796S mutations had progressive disease after treatment with osimertinib (PMID: 29255376, 28625641).

The EGFR A859_L883delinsV mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR A859_L883delinsV was treated with gefitinib and demonstrated progressive disease (PMID: 18325048).

The EGFR G721S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Hodgkin's lymphoma and non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 25488972, 21057810). In a clinical study, four patients with non-small cell lung cancer harboring mutant PD-L1 or TP53 acquired EGFR G721S as a secondary resistance mutation following treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (Abstract: Raez et al. Abstract# EP16.03-021, Journal of Thoracic Oncology September 2022. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S155608642201423X). In a clinical study, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR G721S and EGFR L858R was treated with gefitinib and demonstrated stable disease with a progression-free survival and overall survival of 3.0 months (PMID: 17192902).

The EGFR G863S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer and pleomorphic carcinoma (PMID: 26317919, 21409490). In vitro drug resistance screening with Ba/F3 cells identified EGFR G863S to confer resistance to lapatinib (PMID: 18588508). In a clinical study, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR G863S and a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR G863S and EGFR T847A were treated with gefitinib and demonstrated stable disease and progressive disease, respectively (PMID: 18000506).

The EGFR S645C mutation occurs in the protein's kinase domain and was identified in a screen that used changes in gene expression after viral transduction as a proxy for oncogene selection. Functional characterization of this mutation demonstrated that EGFR S645C expression is associated with cell transformation in mouse xenograft assays and confers reduced sensitivity to erlotinib, compared to other known EGFR activating mutations (PMID: 27478040).

The EGFR V159E mutation is in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation is likely neutral as colony formation in the presence or absence of EGF when expressed in NIH3T3 cells was similar to wildtype EGFR (PMID: 28979142).

The EGFR A763insLQEA mutation is located in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 34526717). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, preclinical models with the A763insLQEA mutation show high sensitivity to first-, second-, third-generation, and ex20ins-active EGFR inhibitors (PMID: 34526717).

The EGFR exon 19 L747P mutation occurs in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain and is adjacent to the L858R mutation in the EGFR three-dimensional structure (PMID: 22190593). Cell line experiments demonstrate that this mutation is transforming and moderately sensitive to gefitinib and afatinib in vitro (PMID: 22190593). Preclinical models with the L747P mutation show resistance to third-generation EGFR inhibitors, moderate sensitivity to first-generation and Ex20ins-active EGFR inhibitors, and high sensitivity to second-generation EGFR inhibitors (PMID: 34526717). Clinical responses of EGFR L747P-containing non-small cell lung cancers to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors are varied. Several patients with exon 19 insertions that led to the L747P substitution showed clinical response to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, while other patients with L747P substitutions either as a single alteration or as one of two EGFR alterations progressed on these inhibitors (PMID: 22190593, 19536777, 26339441, 26001153, 21531810, 18508816).
