var_description: The EZH2 K665R mutation is located in the SET domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. In silico analysis of EZH2 K665R suggests that the mutation is inactivating (PMID: 28561778).

The EZH2 K515R mutation is located in the CXC domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 29807833). Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is neutral as measured by no change in protein activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 25609585).

The EZH2 A682G mutation is located in the enzymatic SET domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 22323599, 24388756). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in melanoma and breast cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased H3K27 trimethylation, preferential modification of dimethylated H3K27 residues instead of un- or monomethylated residues, and increased tumor growth in a xenograft model compared to wildtype (PMID: 22323599, 25671303).

The EZH2 Y646S mutation is located in the enzymatic SET domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 21796119, 20081860). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in lymphoma cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by preferential modification of dimethylated H3K27 residues instead of un- or monomethylated residues compared to wildtype (PMID: 21078963, 21190999, 25402979).

The EZH2 Y646N mutation is located in the enzymatic SET domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 21796119, 20081860). Expression of this mutation in vitro, in embryonic kidney and lymphoma cell lines, and in transgenic mouse models demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein stability, preferential modification of dimethylated H3K27 residues instead of un- or monomethylated residues, increased levels of H3K27 trimethylation compared to wildtype, and the formation of lymphoma in vivo (PMID: 21078963, 21190999, 25402979, 24469040, 23680150). In addition, a mouse model of B-cell lymphoma expressing this mutation had reduced levels of T-cell infiltrates compared to models expressing wildtype EZH2 (PMID: 30705065).

The FBXW7 R505L mutation occurs in the fourth WD repeat of the protein, which binds to substrates that the SCF complex targets for degradation. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells results in the inability of FBXW7 to bind NOTCH1-IC, and therefore results in the stabilization of NOTCH1. In biochemical assays, FBXW7 R505L can bind MYC, a downstream target of NOTCH1, likely stabilizing MYC protein and activating downstream signaling pathways (PMID: 17646409).

The FBXW7 R689W mutation is located in the WD40 repeat domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrioid carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 29876005). In vitro studies with serous endometrial cancer cell lines expressing FBXW7 R689W demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of protein degradation leading to accumulation of activated RICTOR, AKT, GSK and RPS6KB1 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29963728).

biomark_group: Oncogenic Mutations (excluding Y646S, Y646H, Y646C, Y646F, Y646N, A682G and A692V)
var_description: The EZH2 C576Y mutation is located in the CXC domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in essential thrombocythemia (PMID: 30304655). In vitro studies with patient-derived cells expressing EZH2 C576Y demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by complete loss of methyltransferase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 38072134). Preclinical studies of cells expressing EZH2 C576Y and R690H demonstrate sensitivity to the EZH2 inhibitor EPZ-6438 and EED inhibitor A-395 as measured by lower IC50 values compared to wildtype (PMID: 38072134).

Truncating mutations in FBXW7 can lead to several C-terminally truncated FBXW7 protein forms. Expression of FBXW7 truncated mutant proteins in T-ALL have shown these mutant proteins to behave in a dominant-negative manner by impairing the binding of wildtype encoded FBXW7 to the NOTCH intracellular domain, which is required for the degradation of oncogenic MYC and regulation of other NOTCH target genes (PMID: 17646409). Similarly, experimental studies in cell lines using shRNA knockdown of FBXW7 demonstrated that FBXW7 regulates MYC stability through a MB1 phosphorylation-dependent manner (PMID: 15103331). This is consistent with other studies that suggest that FBXW7 truncating mutations are haploinsufficient (PMID: 18094723).

The FBXW7 W425C mutation is located in the FBXW7 WD40 substrate recognition domain. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it was likely inactivating as measured by decreased binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain (PMID: 30510140). Computational modeling of this mutation predicted that it alters substrate binding (PMID: 30510140).

The FBXW7 G423V mutation is located in the FBXW7 WD40 substrate recognition domain. This mutation was found in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (PMID: 30510140). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it was likely inactivating as measured by decreased binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain (PMID: 30510140). Primary CLL cells from a patient expressing the FBXW7 G423V mutation also demonstrated a change in substrate recognition compared with control CLL cells with wildtype FBXW7 (PMID: 30510140). Computational modeling of this mutation predicted that it alters substrate binding (PMID: 30510140).

The FBXW7 A503V mutation is located in the FBXW7 WD40 substrate recognition domain. This mutation has been found in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 30510140). Computational modeling of this mutation predicted that it alters substrate binding (PMID: 30510140). However, expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it was likely neutral as measured by binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain comparable to wildtype protein (PMID: 30510140).

The FBXW7 R479H mutation occurs in the third WD repeat of the protein, which binds to substrates that the SCF complex targets for degradation. Expression of this mutation in colorectal and osteosarcoma cell lines results in activation of NOTCH1 transcription, likely due to the inability of the SCF complex to effectively target NOTCH1 for degradation (PMID: 17575125).

The FBXW7 R658Q mutation is located in an FBXW7 WD40 repeat domain. This mutation is a cancer hotspot as it is recurrently found in human cancer (PMID: 26619011). However, expression of this mutation in the embryonic kidney cell line HA1E demonstrated that its expression does not correlate with wildtype MYC expression, suggesting that this mutant retains its ability to regulate MYC similarly to wildtype FBXW7 and compared to other dominant negative FBXW7 variants (PMID: 27147599).

FBXW7 deletions have been detected in several types of cancers (PMID: 25314076) and has been functionally demonstrated to be associated with enhanced tumorigenesis (PMID: 21282377). Deletion of FBXW7 in the pancreas of mice accelerates tumorigenesis in KRAS mutated cancer (PMID: 27764699), whilst FBXW7 deletion in the hematopoietic system in mice leads to enhanced cell cycle of stem cells and the formation of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia with p53 loss (PMID: 18367647). Furthermore, experimental studies in cell lines using shRNA knockdown of FBXW7 demonstrated that FBXW7 regulates MYC stability through an MB1 phosphorylation-dependent manner (PMID: 15103331).

The gene S562L mutation is located in the substrate recognition domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in melanomas (PMID: 24838835). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely neutral as measured by similar tumor growth in xenograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 24838835).

The FBXW7 R479P mutation is located in the WD repeat domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in cervical adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 25626421). In vitro studies with Chinese cervical cancer cells expressing FBXW7 R479P demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 31161818).

The FBXW7 R689Q mutation is located in an FBXW7 WD40 repeat domain. This mutation is a cancer hotspot as it is recurrently found in human cancer and therefore, likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011). Expression of this mutation in the embryonic kidney cell line, HA1E, demonstrated that its expression does not correlate with wildtype MYC expression suggesting that this mutant retains its ability to regulate MYC compared to other dominant negative FBXW7 variants (PMID: 27147599).

The FBXW7 G423R mutation occurs in the third WD repeat of the protein, which binds to substrates that the SCF-type ubiquitin ligase complex targets for degradation. This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies in melanocytes expressing FBXW7 G423R demonstrated the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation compared to cells expressing the wildtype protein (PMID: 24838835). In vivo studies with mouse xenograft models expressing both FBXW7 G423R and NRAS G12D also demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by no change in tumor growth compared to control cells (PMID: 24838835).

The FBWX7 I347M mutation is not found in a known FBWX7 domain. Gene expression signatures derived from a pooled screen in kidney cells predict that this mutation corresponds to reduced MYC activity. These data suggest the mutation is neutral because FBXW7 maintains the ability to regulate MYC stability (PMID: 27147599).

The FBXW7 R465L mutation is located in the WD repeat domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic T-cell leukemia and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 19340001). In vitro studies with U2OS cells expressing FBXW7 R465L demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of substrate interaction and degradation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19340001).

The FBXW7 D480N mutation is located in the FBXW7 WD40 substrate recognition domain. This mutation was found in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 30510140). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it was likely neutral as measured by binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain comparable to wildtype FBXW7 (PMID: 30510140).

The FBXW7 T205A mutation occurs in the N-terminal of the FBXW7 protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in decreased ubiquitination and increased stability of FBXW7, due to the inability of the protein to bind PIN1. HCT116 cells expressing this variant formed fewer colonies in growth assays (PMID: 22608923).

The FBXW7 Y545C mutation is located in the FBXW7 WD40 substrate recognition domain. This mutation has been found in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 30510140). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it was likely inactivating as measured by decreased binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain comparable to wildtype FBXW7 (PMID: 30510140).

The FBXW7 S227A mutation occurs in a phosphorylation site of the protein. Expression of this mutation in colorectal cells resulted in decreased phosphorylation of FBXW7 by PI3-kinase. Phosphorylation of FBXW7 was required for the functional activity of FBXW7, including the regulation of downstream gene expression (PMID: 21620836).

The FBXW7 R465H mutation is located in the third WD repeat of the protein, which binds to substrates that the SCF complex targets for degradation. In biochemical assays, FBXW7 R465H was unable to bind and ubiquitinate downstream targets, including the glucocorticoid receptor, PIN1 and DAB2IP (PMID: 22608923, 24912918, 23228967). Expression of this mutation in colorectal cells that lacked wildtype FBXW7 protein resulted in destabilization of FBXW7, leading to increased NOTCH1 stability and gene expression (PMID: 22608923, 17575125). FBXW7 R465H expression in kidney cells does not correlate with MYC activity, suggesting that this mutation disrupts the ability of FBXW7 to effectively regulate MYC activity (PMID: 27147599). Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cell line demonstrated that it had a reduced affinity for its substrate KL5. KL5 stabilization was shown to increased proliferation of the colorectal cancer cell line suggesting that the FBXW7 R465H mutation may be oncogenic (PMID: 28963353).

The FBXW7 R505C mutation is located in the fourth WD repeat of the protein, which binds to substrates that the SCF complex targets for degradation. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (PMID: 30510140). Expression of this mutation in melanocytes results in increased proliferation, in comparison to cells expressing wildtype protein (PMID: 24838835). In cell lines engineered to express the FBXW7 R505C mutation, the SCF complex has a reduced ability to bind and target substrates for degradation including NOTCH1-IC, Cyclin E, Aurora B and MYC (PMID: 17646408, 17575125, 23095493, 30510140). Stabilization of these substrates results in activation of downstream growth pathways (PMID: 24838835, 23095493). Expression of this mutation in colorectal cells that lacked wildtype FBXW7 protein resulted in destabilization of FBXW7, likely leading to increased expression of target proteins (PMID: 22608923, 27147599). This mutation also alters the ubiquitination and degradation of other substrates in a variety of cells types, including the glucocorticoid receptor in T-ALL (PMID: 23228967). Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cell line demonstrated that it had a reduced affinity for its substrate KL5. KL5 stabilization was shown to increased proliferation of the colorectal cancer cell line suggesting that the FBXW7 R505C mutation may be oncogenic (PMID: 28963353).

The FBXW7 R479Q mutation is located in the third WD repeat of the protein, which binds to the substrates that the SCF complex targets for degradation. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells results in the inability of FBXW7 to bind NOTCH1, and therefore leads to the stabilization of NOTCH1 protein. In biochemical assays, FBXW7 R479Q can bind MYC, a downstream target of NOTCH1, likely stabilizing MYC protein and activating downstream signaling pathways (PMID: 17646409, 17646408). In HEK293T cells, FBXW7 R479Q is unable to bind and degrade Cyclin E, leading to increased proliferation and aberrant cell cycle (PMID: 17909001, 17646408). In biochemical studies in rectal cancer cell lines, FBXW7 R479Q was unable to bind MYC, likely resulting in stabilization of MYC protein and enhanced MYC-dependent transcription (PMID: 23676439). Mice engineered to express this mutation in the colon developed a mild intestinal disease, however, mice expressing both the FBXW7 R479Q and APC mutations resulted in an acceleration of intestinal adenoma development (PMID: 23676439). This mutation also alters the ubiquitination and degradation of other substrates in a variety of cell types, including the glucocorticoid receptor in T-ALL (PMID: 23228967).

The FBXW7 R479L mutation occurs in the fourth WD repeat of the protein, which binds to substrates that the SCF-type ubiquitin ligase complex targets for degradation. In vitro studies with wildtype FBXW7-deficient colorectal cells expressing FBXW7 R479L demonstrated the mutation is inactivating as measured by destabilization of FBXW7, likely leading to increased expression of target proteins (PMID: 22608923). Biochemical assays have also demonstrated that FBXW7 R479L is inactivating as measured by the inability to bind downstream substrates, including DAB2IP, to stabilize the protein (PMID: 24912918).

The FBXW7 K11R mutation lies in one of the nuclear localization signals in the FBXW7 protein, which regulates its distribution in the nucleus versus cytoplasm. This mutation impairs the function of the nuclear localization signal, favoring accumulation of FBXW7 in the cytoplasm (PMID: 20815813). This inappropriate protein localization may lead to altered accessibility of FBXW7 to its substrates, although no functional or biological effect of the mutation has been noted in preclinical models.

The FBWX7 S462Y mutation is found within the third WD repeat of the FBWX7 protein . Gene expression signatures derived from a pooled screen in kidney cells predict that this mutation corresponds to reduced MYC activity. These data suggest the mutation is neutral because FBXW7 maintains the ability to regulate MYC stability (PMID: 27147599).

The FBXW7 V154I mutation is located in the N-terminus and affects the alpha-isoform of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it was likely neutral as measured by binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain comparable to wildtype FBXW7 (PMID: 30510140).

The FBXW7 V514F mutation is located in the FBXW7 WD40 substrate recognition domain. This mutation has been found in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it was likely inactivating as measured by decreased binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain comparable to wildtype FBXW7 (PMID: 30510140).

The FBXW7 D520N mutation is located in an FBXW7 WD40 repeat domain. This mutation was found in colorectal tumors and familial adenomatous polyposis carcinomas and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 19420964). This mutation has yet to be functionally characterized but occurs at an evolutionarily conserved site pointing to its perhaps critical role in FBXW7 function (PMID: 11565034).

The FBXW7 T15insVR mutation is located in the N-terminus and affects the alpha-isoform of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 30510140). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by binding to activated NOTCH1 intracellular domain similar to wildtype FBXW7 (PMID: 30510140). However, primary CLL cells from a patient expressing the FBXW7 G423V mutation demonstrated a change in substrate recognition compared with control CLL cells with wildtype FBXW7 (PMID: 30510140).

The FGFR2 D530N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased levels of FGFR2 downstream MAPK pathway activation and decreased kinase activity compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 19147536).

The FBXW7 R465C mutation is located in the third WD repeat of the protein, which binds to the substrates that the SCF-type ubiquitin ligase complex targets for degradation. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 30510140). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 and hematopoietic cells results in the inability of FBXW7 to bind NOTCH1-IC, and therefore results in the stabilization of NOTCH1 protein (PMID: 17646408, 30510140). In biochemical assays, FBXW7 R465C can bind MYC, a downstream target of NOTCH1, likely stabilizing MYC protein and activating downstream signaling pathways (PMID: 17646409). In cell lines, FBXW7 R465C was unable to bind and degrade Cyclin E and Aurora B, leading to increased proliferation and aberrant cell cycle progression (PMID: 17909001, 17646408, 23095493). Impaired degradation of the checkpoint kinase Aurora B may cause its accumulation in the cell, leading to improper cell cycle progression and aneuploidy. Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cell line demonstrated that it had a reduced affinity for its substrate KL5. KL5 stabilization was shown to increased proliferation of the colorectal cancer cell line suggesting that the FBXW7 R465C mutation may be oncogenic (PMID: 28963353).

The FGFR2 Q212K mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in glioma (PMID: 23917401). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 Q212K demonstrated this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 E731K mutation is located in the second tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by enhanced phosphorylation of FGFR2, constitutive activation of the receptor and consequent aberrant downstream activation of the MAPK pathway compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 21928350).

The FGFR2 P582L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 P582L demonstrated this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity and proliferation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2-NRBF2 fusion results from an in-frame rearrangement between N-terminal FGFR2 and C-terminal NRBF2, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. Numerous FGFR2 variants with truncation of exon 18 have been shown in vivo to be activating and oncogenic as measured by rapid induction of mammary tumors in mice (PMID: 35948633). Therefore, while not characterized per se, as a fusion that results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2, this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). In a Phase II clinical trial, a patient with cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-NRBF2 was treated with pemigatinib and demonstrated stable disease with a progression-free survival of 13.1 months (PMID: 33218975).

The FGFR2 P708S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 P708S demonstrated this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 M537I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells suggests that it is activating, as measured by increased FGFR2 phosphorylation and proliferation compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 23908597). In vitro experiments suggest that this variant is resistant to dovitinib but sensitive to ponatinib, as measured by cell proliferation upon drug treatment (PMID: 23908597).

The FGFR2 Q259* mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type III domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 Q259* demonstrated this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 P253R mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation is an autosomal dominant mutation associated with Apert syndrome, a severe craniosynostosis syndrome (PMID: 18552176). Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that the is is likely activating as measured by an increased receptor affinity for fibroblast growth factor ligands (FGFs), leading to enhanced activation of the kinase compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 11121055, 24265351).

The FGFR2 K659N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro kinase assays demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased auto- and effector-phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 17803937, 17525745, 23527311).

The FGFR2 R759Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In silico analysis suggests that the mutation affects protein structure and results in the loss of kinase activity (PMID: 19147536).

The FGFR2-DBP fusion is a fusion of the N-terminus of FGFR2, including the kinase domain, with the C-terminus of DBP. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, other FGFR2 fusions have been shown to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is considered likely oncogenic (PMID: 26048680, 23558953). In a Phase I trial, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-DBP was treated with futibatinib and demonstrated partial response with a progression-free survival of 10.9 months (PMID: 34551969).

The FGFR2-SORBS1 fusion results from an in-frame rearrangement between N-terminal FGFR2 and C-terminal SORBS1, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 35948633). Numerous FGFR2 variants with truncation of exon 18 have been shown in vivo to be activating and oncogenic as measured by rapid induction of mammary tumors in mice (PMID: 35948633). Therefore, while not characterized per se, as a fusion that results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2, this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). In a case report, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-SORBS1 was treated with BGJ398 and TAS-120 and demonstrated a partial response with a progression-free survival of 12.6 months and 15.8 months, respectively (PMID: 31109923).

The FGFR2-ATAD2 fusion results from an in-frame rearrangement between N-terminal FGFR2 and C-terminal ATAD2, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This fusion has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 33218975). Numerous FGFR2 variants with truncation of exon 18 have been shown in vivo to be activating and oncogenic as measured by rapid induction of mammary tumors in mice (PMID: 35948633). Therefore, while not characterized per se, as a fusion that results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2, this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). In a Phase II clinical trial, a patient with cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-ATAD2 was treated with pemigatinib and demonstrated stable disease with a progression-free survival of 8.8 months (PMID: 33218975).

The FGFR2 S267_D273dup mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. Expression of this duplication in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating, as measured by increased tumor growth in mice and colony formation in soft agar compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 26048680). In vitro studies suggest that this duplication is sensitive to small molecule inhibitors of FGFR2, such as BGJ398, as measured by decreased colony formation upon drug treatment (PMID: 26048680).

The FGFR2 M391R mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. This mutation is found in bent bone dysplasia syndrome (PMID: 24908667). Expression of this variant in preosteoblasts demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased activation of downstream signaling effectors and reduced osteoblast differentiation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24908667).

The FGFR2-ERC1 fusion results from an in-frame rearrangement between N-terminal FGFR2 and C-terminal ERC1, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in colon adenocarcinoma (PMID: 35948633). Numerous FGFR2 variants with truncation of exon 18 have been shown in vivo to be activating and oncogenic as measured by rapid induction of mammary tumors in mice (PMID: 35948633). Therefore, while not characterized per se, as a fusion that results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2, this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). In a case report, a patient with lung adenocarcinoma expressing FGFR2-ERC1 was treated with anlotinib and demonstrated stable disease with a progression-free survival of over 8.0 months (PMID: 30745300).

The FGFR2-INA fusion results from an in-frame rearrangement fusing exon 17 of FGFR2 and exon 2 of INA, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 35948633). Numerous FGFR2 variants with truncation of exon 18 have been shown in vivo to be activating and oncogenic as measured by rapid induction of mammary tumors in mice (PMID: 35948633). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing FGFR2-INA demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by increased proliferation and activation of MAPK and PI3K/mTOR pathways compared to vector-controlled cells (PMID: 29767381). Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of NIH3T3 cells expressing FGFR2-INA demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with trametinib plus everolimus as measured by inhibition of cellular growth (PMID: 29767381).

The FGFR2 V564F mutation is located in the kinase domain of the FGFR2 protein. This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 28034880). Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by increased FGFR2 kinase activity compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 25169980, 28034880). This mutation was acquired in patients with FGFR2-fusion-positive cholangiocarcinoma following progression on FGFR kinase inhibitor BGJ398 and pemigatinib (PMID: 28034880, Abstract: Rodon et al. Abstract# CT016. AACR 2023. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/83/8_Supplement/CT016/725419). In addition, this mutation is considered a "gatekeeper" mutation. Structural modeling shows the V564F mutation induces a steric clash with the FGFR2 inhibitor BGJ398. Expression of the V564F mutation in BaF3 and 293T cells also demonstrates resistance to BGJ398 but shows sensitivity to LY2874455 (PMID: 28034880). Preclinical studies of FGFR2 V564F demonstrate sensitivity to RLY-4008 as measured by tumor regression following treatment (PMID: 37270847).

The FGFR2 P253L mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 P253L demonstrated this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467). FGFR2 P253L is suggested to confer resistance to FGFR inhibitor dovitinib as measured by continued cellular proliferation following treatment (PMID: 34272467). FGFR2 P253L is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with FGFR inhibitors pemigatinib, futibatinib, erdafitinib, E7090, infigratinib and AZD4547 as measured by reduced cell viability following treatment (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2-WAC fusion is a fusion of the N-terminus of FGFR2, including the kinase domain, with the C-terminus of WAC. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, other FGFR2 fusions have been shown to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is considered likely oncogenic (PMID: 26048680, 23558953). In a Phase I trial, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-WAC was treated with futibatinib and demonstrated partial response with a progression-free survival of 6.9 months (PMID: 34551969). In a case report, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-WAC and FGFR inhibitor resistance mutations FGFR2 N549K, FGFR2 N549D and FGFR2 V564I was treated with RLY-4008 and demonstrated partial response (PMID: 37270847).

The FGFR2 C278F mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation is found patients with craniosynostosis syndromes (PMID: 16844695). Expression of this mutation in osteoblasts demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased downstream signaling, increased differentiation and increased apoptosis compared to wildtype (PMID: 20004243).

The FGFR2 E636K mutation is located in the second kinase domain of the protein. This mutation is found in melanoma (PMID: 19147536). Mapping of this mutation to the FGFR2 crystal structure suggests that this mutation would impair the kinase activity of the protein, likely leading to loss of function (PMID: 19147536).

The FGFR2-PAWR fusion results from an in-frame rearrangement between N-terminal FGFR2 and C-terminal PAWR, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. Numerous FGFR2 variants with truncation of exon 18 have been shown in vivo to be activating and oncogenic as measured by rapid induction of mammary tumors in mice (PMID: 35948633). Therefore, while not characterized per se, as a fusion that results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2, this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). In a Phase II clinical trial, a patient with cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-PAWR was treated with pemigatinib and demonstrated partial response with a progression-free survival of 6.9 months (PMID: 33218975).

The FGFR2 R6P mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 R6P demonstrated this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity and proliferation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 S782fs*3 mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 35948633). In vivo studies with mice expressing the corresponding mouse isoform FGFR2 S687fs*3 demonstrates that the mutation is activating as measured by increased tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mouse and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633).

The FGFR2 G364E mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 G364E demonstrated this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity and proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 S791T mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 S791T demonstrated this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 P781* mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 35948633). In vivo studies with mice expressing the corresponding mouse isoform FGFR2 P686* demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and of patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633).

The FGFR2 V797* mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 35948633). In vivo studies with mice expressing the corresponding mouse isoform FGFR2 V702* demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and of patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633).

The FGFR2 N82K mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type I domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 N82K demonstrate this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 C62Y mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type I domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 C62Y demonstrate this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 R203H mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 R203H demonstrate this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 V395D mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 V395D demonstrated this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity and proliferation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 E163K mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 E163K demonstrate this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2-PDHX fusion results from an out-of-strand rearrangement between N-terminal FGFR2 and C-terminal PDHX, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in esophageal carcinoma (PMID: 35948633). Numerous FGFR2 variants with truncation of exon 18 have been shown in vivo to be activating and oncogenic as measured by rapid induction of mammary tumors in mice (PMID: 35948633). In vivo studies with murine xenograft models expressing FGFR2-PDHX demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by increased tumor growth (PMID: 29767381). Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of murine xenograft models expressing FGFR2-PDHX demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with ARQ 087 as measured by inhibition of tumor growth (PMID: 29767381).

The FGFR2 S799fs*22 mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and results in the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. This mutation has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 35948633). In vivo studies with mice expressing the corresponding mouse isoform FGFR2 S704fs*22 demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 35948633). Preclinical studies of mice and of patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633).

The FGFR2 A648T mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased levels of downstream MAPK pathway activation and decreased kinase activity compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 19147536).

The FGFR2 L617F mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in HEK 293 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased protein phosphorylation and increased downstream gene expression in low serum compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 23913723). A patient with cholangiocarcinoma developed this mutation upon disease progression after an initial response to Debio1347, and then had a partial response to futibatinib (PMID: 33926920).

The FGFR2 C382Y mutation is located in the helical domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 and MCF10A cells expressing FGFR2 C382Y demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by cell viability and proliferation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 29533785).

The FGFR2 G613S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 G613S demonstrated this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity and proliferation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 M186T mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II of the protein. This mutation has been identified in prostate cancer (PMID: 31874108). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 M186T demonstrate this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 G271E mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased FGF-dependent MAPK pathway activation and mislocalization to intracellular membranes when compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 19147536).

The FGFR2 W290_I291delinsC mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 33926920). Expression of this alteration in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that this alteration is activating, as measured by increased colony formation in soft agar compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 26048680). In vitro studies suggest that this alteration is sensitive to small molecule inhibitors of FGFR2, such as BGJ398, as measured by decreased colony formation upon drug treatment (PMID: 26048680).

The FGFR2-OPTN fusion combines the N-terminus of FGFR2 up to exon 17 with the C-terminus of OPTN starting from exon 10, resulting in a fusion protein containing an intact FGFR2 kinase domain. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, other FGFR2 fusions have been shown to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is considered likely oncogenic (PMID: 26048680, 23558953). This mutation was found in a patient with cholangiocarcinoma who responded to the FGFR inhibitor BGJ398, though with limited durability due to the eventual emergence of acquired FGFR2 resistance mutations (PMID: 28034880).

The FGFR2 E695K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 E695K demonstrated this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 K517R mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased protein phosphorylation in vitro compared to wildtype (PMID: 19147536).

The FGFR2-TNS1 fusion is a fusion of the N-terminus of FGFR2, including the kinase domain, with the C-terminus of TNS1. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, other FGFR2 fusions have been shown to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is considered likely oncogenic (PMID: 26048680, 23558953). In a Phase I trial, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-TNS1 was treated with futibatinib and demonstrated partial response with a progression-free survival of 11.0 months (PMID: 34551969).

The FGFR2 A389T mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 A389T demonstrate this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467). In contrast, other in vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing FGFR2 A389T demonstrate this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 18552176).

The FGFR2 A264T mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type III domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 25148578). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 A264T demonstrated this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 R203C mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein.This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID:15908952). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FGFR2 phosphorylation and activation of the downstream effectors MAPK and STAT3 compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 23527311).

The FGFR2 E160K mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 26343386). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 E160K demonstrate this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 R251Q mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the FGFR2 protein. This mutation has been identified in melanoma and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 25148578, 30115035). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 R251Q demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased ligand binding, loss of FGF-dependent downstream MAPK pathway activation and decreased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19147536). This mutation is one of a spectrum which are characteristically induced by UV exposure (PMID: 19147536). Other in vitro studies with 3T3 cells expressing FGFR2 R251Q demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by cellular proliferation and invasion comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467). Preclinical studies with 3T3 cells expressing FGFR2 R251Q demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with AZD4547, erdafitinib, E7090, futibatinib, pemigatinib and infigratinib as measured by reduced cell viability following treatment (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 K641N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this variant has not been functionally characterized, structural modeling in silico suggests that this mutation is likely activating (PMID: 23908597). FGFR2 K641N was found in an in vitro dovitinib resistance screen, indicating that it is likely resistant to dovitinib (PMID: 23908597).

The FGFR2-FILIP1 fusion is a fusion of the N-terminus of FGFR2, including the kinase domain, with the C-terminus of FILIP1. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, other FGFR2 fusions have been shown to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is considered likely oncogenic (PMID: 26048680, 23558953). In a Phase I trial, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-FILIP1 was treated with futibatinib and demonstrated partial response with a progression-free survival of 4.8 months (PMID: 34551969).

The FGFR2 G542E mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 G542E demonstrated this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2 Q227E mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 Q227E demonstrated this mutation is likely neutral as measured by wildtype comparable transformation activity (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2-BICC1 fusion protein is a fusion of the N-terminus of FGFR2, including the kinase domain, with the C-terminus of BICC1. This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 28034880). Expression of this fusion in NIH3T3 and TERT-HME cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by activation of the MAPK pathway, increased cellular proliferation and anchorage-independent growth of cells in soft agar compared to wildtype protein (PMID: 24122810, 23558953). Additionally, expression of this mutation in cells transplanted into mice resulted in tumorigenesis (PMID: 24122810). This mutation was found in a patient with cholangiocarcinoma who responded to the FGFR inhibitor BGJ398, though with limited durability due to the eventual emergence of acquired FGFR2 resistance mutations (PMID: 28034880). In a Phase I trial, three patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-BICC1 were treated with futibatinib and demonstrated partial response with progression-free survivals of 15.9 months, 4.4 months and 12.7 months, respectively (PMID: 34551969).

The FGFR2 N549H mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 28034880). Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by increased kinase activity of FGFR2, increased cell growth and resistance to FGFR inhibitors such as dovitinib in cell culture (PMID: 23908597). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing FGFR2 N549H also demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation ability and growth advantage compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467). This mutation was acquired in patients with FGFR2-fusion-positive cholangiocarcinoma following progression on FGFR kinase inhibitor BGJ398 and pemigatinib (PMID: 28034880, Abstract: Rodon et al. Abstract# CT016. AACR 2023. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/83/8_Supplement/CT016/725419). In silico, structural modeling of this mutation suggests that it confers resistance to BGJ398 by destabilizing the inactive conformation of the kinase to which BGJ398 binds (PMID: 28034880). Preclinical studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing FGFR2 N549H demonstrate sensitivity to treatment with E7090 and futibatinib as measured by reduced cell viability following treatment (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2-CCDC6 fusion contains the extracellular, transmembrane and kinase domains of FGFR2 fused to the coiled-coil region of CCDC6 (PMID: 23558953). This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 23558953). Expression of this fusion in HEK 293T or TERT-HME cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by factor-independent dimerization and increased proliferation compared to control cells (PMID: 23558953). In a Phase I trial, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-CCDC6 was treated with futibatinib and demonstrated partial response with a progression-free survival of 6.8 months (PMID: 34551969).

The FGFR2 I422V mutation is located in the cytoplasmic domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 I422V demonstrated this mutation is activating as measured by increased transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

In a clinical trial, a patient with cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-ROCK1 was treated with debio1347 and demonstrated stable disease (PMID: 30745300).

The FGFR2 N549D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, this mutation was identified in a screen for BGJ398 resistant FGFR2 mutations in which TEL-FGFR2 expressing cells were exposed to lethal doses of BGJ398 and the resistant clones were analyzed for the presence of mutations (PMID: 28034880).

Preclinical studies of mice and of patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633).

Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). In a Phase I trial, a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2-KIAA1217 was treated with futibatinib and demonstrated partial response with a progression-free survival of 6.8 months (PMID: 34551969).

The FGFR2 L33S mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type I domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 L33S demonstrate this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2-MGEA5 fusion is a fusion of the N-terminal end of the FGFR2 gene with the C-terminal end of the MGEA5 gene. This fusion has been found in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 24550739). A patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma habroring an FGFR2-MGEA5 fusion had a partial response to ponatinib (PMID: 24550739).

The FGFR2 M535I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells suggests that it is activating, as measured by increased FGFR2 phosphorylation and proliferation compared to wildtype FGFR2 (PMID: 23908597). In vitro experiments suggest that this variant is resistant to dovitinib but sensitive to ponatinib, as measured by cell proliferation upon drug treatment (PMID: 23908597).

The FGFR2 H213Y mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation is found in melanoma (PMID: 19147536). Mapping of this mutation to the FGFR2 crystal structure suggests that this mutation would impair the dimerization of the protein, likely leading to loss of function (PMID: 19147536).

The FGFR2 M722I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 M722I demonstrated this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR2-SYNPO2 fusion results from an in-frame rearrangement between N-terminal FGFR2 and C-terminal SYNPO2, causing the truncation of exon 18 of FGFR2. Preclinical studies of mice and patient-derived xenografts expressing truncated FGFR2 exon 18 variants have demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with clinical FGFR2 inhibitors AZD4547, pemigatinib, BGJ398 and debio-1347 as measured by suppressed tumor growth (PMID: 35948633). FGFR2-SYNPO2 was identified as a secondary resistance mutation in a patient with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma following disease progression after treatment with an FGFR inhibitor (Abstract: Cham et al. Abstract# 3472, AACR 2022. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/82/12_Supplement/3472/703515/Abstract-3472-Clinical-outcomes-and-genomic).

The FGFR2 N549K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein (PMID: 23908597). This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 28034880). Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells demonstrates it is activating as measured by increased kinase activity in the absence of ligand, enhanced cell proliferation and resistance to FGFR inhibitors such as dovitinib in cell culture (PMID: 23908597, 18552176, 17525745). This mutation was found in a patient with FGFR2-fusion-positive cholangiocarcinoma following progression on the FGFR kinase inhibitor BGJ398 (PMID: 28034880). Abstract# CT016. AACR 2023. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/83/8_Supplement/CT016/725419).

The FGFR2 R210Q mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 28467829). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR2 R210Q demonstrated this mutation is likely neutral as measured by transformation activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).
