The HRAS T58I mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in Costello's syndrome (PMID: 22488832). The HRAS T58I mutation was found in a patient with a mild manifestation of Costello syndrome. Computational modeling of the mutation demonstrated that it is likely activating, as the mutant protein takes on the active conformation and allows for slow inactivation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26888048).

The HRAS G13D mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer and melanoma (PMID: 25148578, 26561417). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011). One patient with colorectal cancer harboring this mutation demonstrated resistance to the EGFR inhibitor panitumumab (PMID: 26561417).

The HRAS G12delG mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased focus formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 3018526).

The HRAS G13S mutation is located in the GTP/GDP binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in penile squamous cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26216163). In vivo studies with Xenopus oocytes expressing HRAS G13S demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased protein activity and transformation compared to wildtype (PMID: 8430333).

The HRAS G12S mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in bone, breast and cervical cancer (PMID: 24993163, 25695693, 8690291). Expression of this mutation in rat fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased foci formation and soft agar growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 6092966). Structural analysis of the G12 residue demonstrates that it is crucial for HRAS GTP hydrolyzing activity suggesting that any mutation at G12 would render the protein constitutively active (PMID: 9219684).

The HRAS G12_G13insGAG mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in rat adrenal cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and increased cell differentiation compared to wildtype (PMID: 11103938).

The HRAS G12N mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in rat fibroblast cells demonstrated that it was activating as measured by increased focus formation and growth in soft agar compared to wildtype (PMID: 6092966). Structural analysis of the G12 residue demonstrates that it is crucial for HRAS GTP hydrolyzing activity suggesting that any mutation at G12 would render the protein constitutively active (PMID: 9219684).

The HRAS F28L mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in NF-1 deficient murine embryonic fibroblasts demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation and increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 1894650, 25600866).

The HRAS Y64A mutation is located in the switch II region of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Computational modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it impairs dimer formation, possibly altering the recruitment of wildtype HRAS to the plasma membrane (PMID: 24516166).

The HRAS A59G mutation is located in the switch II region of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Structural modeling and in vitro analysis of this mutation demonstrate that it is activating, as measured by maintenance of HRAS in a GTP-bound state which can activate downstream signaling pathways (PMID: 17084704, 20838576).

HRAS amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation has been found in thyroid, head and neck and small cell lung cancers (cBioPortal, MSKCC, April 2017). Overexpression of HRAS in a rat model of breast cancer and a mouse model of skin cancer demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by a correlation between increased expression of HRAS and disease progression (PMID: 1855225, 8221670). Overexpression of HRAS is suggested as a potential alternative mechanism for HRAS-mediated oncogenic transformation (PMID: 3283542, 3283542).

The HRAS G15_K16insGVG mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in rat adrenal cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and increased cell differentiation compared to wildtype (PMID: 11103938).

The IDH1 I99M mutation lies in an uncharacterized region of the IDH1 protein. Unlike the recurrent IDH1 and IDH2 alterations, H133Q does not produce 2-hydroxyglutarate but retains wildtype function when expressed in human kidney cells (PMID: 21996744).

The IDH1 Y139D mutation is located outside exon 4 of the IDH4 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation changes IDH1 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (PMID: 19935646).

The IDH1 G97D mutation is located in the substrate-binding region of the IDH1 protein. This mutation has been found in pediatric glioblastomas and colorectal cancer (PMID: 20479398, 27824159). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation leads to a switch-of-function phenotype, as measured by elevated levels of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) and lack of NADPH production in the presence of isocitrate (PMID: 27824159, 21996744).

The IDH1 H133Q mutation lies next to the recurrently mutated catalytic-site residue R132. However, unlike the recurrent IDH1 and IDH2 alterations, H133Q does not produce 2-hydroxyglutarate but retains wildtype function when expressed in human kidney cells (PMID: 21996744).
The IDH1 V294M mutation is likely neutral, as demonstrated by activity similar to wildtype IDH1 (PMID: 21996744).

The IDH1 Y183C mutation is located in the isopropylmalate dehydrogenase-like domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in meningioma and thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 32716568, 27283500). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing IDH1 Y183C demonstrate that the mutation is neutral as measured by 2-hydroxyglutarate production comparable to wildtype (PMID: 23063752).

The IDH1 R132H mutation is located in the catalytic site of the IDH1 protein. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia and gliomas, among others (PMID: 19935646, 29860938). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation changes IDH1 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the "oncometabolite" D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), and leads to oncogenic activity, as evidenced by aberrant changes in DNA methylation, cytokine independence, dedifferentiation and in vivo increases in early hematopoietic progenitors compared to wildtype IDH1 (PMID: 19935646, 22763442, 23393090). IDH1 mutations at the R132 residue, including R132H, are sensitive to inhibition by AG-120 (Ivosidenib), a small-molecule inhibitor of mutant IDH1, as measured by a decrease in 2-HG level, an increase in the proportion of mature myeloid cells and increased levels of cell surface differentiation markers in treated cells compared to untreated cells (PMID: 29670690). A Phase I clinical trial for ivosidenib involving 268 patients with relapsed or refractory AML harboring IDH1 R132 mutations, including 59 with IDH1 R132H mutation, achieved an overall response rate of 41.6% and a reduction in the percentage of bone marrow blasts in treated patients (PMID: 29860938).

The IDH1 R132Q mutation is located in the IDH1 catalytic site. This mutation is predicted to change IDH1 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the "oncometabolite" D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (PMID: 19935646). The IDH1 R132Q mutation is a rare event in chondrosarcomas, but it has been shown to promote the development of the precursor lesion, enchondroma (PMID: 25730874).

The IDH1 V178I mutation is located in the isopropylmalate dehydrogenase-like domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia and thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 31632056, 20702649). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing IDH1 V178I demonstrate that the mutation is neutral as measured by enzymatic activity and 2-hydroxyglutarate production comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21996744).

The IDH1 V71I mutation is located in the isopropylmalate dehydrogenase-like domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in hepatocellular carcinoma and thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 30977242, 20702649). In vitro studies with 293T cells and BL21(DE3) cells expressing IDH1 V71I demonstrate that the mutation is neutral as measured by enzymatic activity and 2-hydroxyglutarate production comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21996744, 22442146).

The IDH1 R100A mutation is located in the substrate binding region of the IDH1 protein. This mutation has been found in adult glioma (PMID: 21996744). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation leads to a switch-of-function phenotype, as measured by elevated levels of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) and lack of NADPH production in the presence of isocitrate (PMID: 21996744).

The IDH1 R132C mutation is located in the IDH1 catalytic site. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia and glioma, among others (PMID: 19935646,  23954893). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation changes IDH1 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the "oncometabolite" D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), and leads to oncogenic activity in cooperation with HOXA9, as shown by the ability to induce a myeloproliferative disease-like phenotype and increase downstream signaling and cell cycle progression compared to wildtype IDH1 (PMID: 19935646, 23954893). IDH1 mutations at the R132 residue, including R132C, are sensitive to inhibition by AG-120 (Ivosidenib), a small-molecule inhibitor of mutant IDH1, as measured by a decrease in 2-HG level, an increase in the proportion of mature myeloid cells and increased levels of cell surface differentiation markers in treated cells compared to untreated cells (PMID: 29670690). A Phase I clinical trial for ivosidenib involving 268 patients with relapsed or refractory AML harboring IDH1 R132 mutations, including 156 with IDH1 R132C mutation, achieved an overall response rate of 41.6% and a reduction in the percentage of bone marrow blasts in treated patients (PMID: 29860938).

The IDH1 R132L mutation is located in the catalytic site of the IDH1 protein. This mutation has been found in gliomas (PMID: 21326614, 19935646). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation changes IDH1 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), which promotes tumor development by inhibiting a variety of enzymes that require α-KG as a substrate (PMID: 19935646, 23630074). IDH1 mutations at the R132 residue, including R132L, are sensitive to inhibition by AG-120 (Ivosidenib), a small-molecule inhibitor of mutant IDH1, as measured by a decrease in 2-HG levels, an increase in the proportion of mature myeloid cells and increased levels of cell surface differentiation markers in treated cells compared to untreated cells (PMID: 29670690). A Phase I clinical trial for ivosidenib involving 268 patients with relapsed or refractory AML harboring IDH1 R132 mutations, including 9 with IDH1 R132L mutation, achieved an overall response rate of 41.6% and a reduction in the percentage of bone marrow blasts in treated patients (PMID: 29860938).

The IDH1 R49C mutation is a rare alteration that does not produce an increase in D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) levels, but also fails to increase isocitrate-dependent NADPH production. The former suggest that the IDH1 R49C mutation results in a decrease of the enzyme wildtype activity, without an increase in 2-HG oncometabolite generation (PMID: 21996744).

The IDH1 R132S mutation is located in the catalytic site of the IDH1 protein. This mutation has been found in myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms and gliomas (PMID: 22033490, 21912393, 21760534, 25257301). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation changes IDH1 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), which promotes tumor development by inhibiting a variety of enzymes that require aKG as a substrate (PMID: 19935646, 23630074). IDH1 mutations at the R132 residue, including R132S, are sensitive to inhibition by AG-120 (Ivosidenib), a small-molecule inhibitor of mutant IDH1, as measured by a decrease in 2-HG level, an increase in the proportion of mature myeloid cells and increased levels of cell surface differentiation markers in treated cells compared to untreated cells (PMID: 29670690). A Phase I clinical trial for ivosidenib involving 268 patients with relapsed or refractory AML harboring IDH1 R132 mutations, including 13 with IDH1 R132S mutation, achieved an overall response rate of 41.6% and a reduction in the percentage of bone marrow blasts in treated patients (PMID: 29860938).
The IDH1 G123R mutation is inactivating, as measured by decreased NADPH production in an in vitro enzymatic assay compared to wildtype IDH1 (PMID: 20171178).

The IDH1 R100Q mutation is located in the isopropylmalate dehydrogenase-like domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and glioma (PMID: 25344691, 20874727). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing IDH1 R100Q demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased 2-hydroxyglutarate production compared to wildtype (PMID: 24529257, 28330869).
The IDH1 E190K mutation is likely neutral as measured by gene expression profiling of this variant in HA1E cells compared to wildtype IDH1 (PMID: 27147599).

The IDH1 I130M mutation lies close to the recurrently mutated catalytic-site residue R132. However, unlike the recurrent IDH1 and IDH2 alterations, H133Q does not produce 2-hydroxyglutarate but retains wildtype function when expressed in human kidney cells (PMID: 21996744).
The IDH1 P33S mutation was demonstrated to likely be neutral, as gene expression signatures of IDH1 P33S expressing cells were similar to those of wildtype IDH1 expressing cells (PMID: 27147599).

The IDH1 A134D mutation is a rare alterations that does not produce an increase in D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) levels, but also fails to increase isocitrate-dependent NADPH production. The former suggest that the IDH1 A134D mutation results in a decrease of the enzyme wildtype activity, without an increase in 2-HG oncometabolite generation (PMID: 21996744).

The IDH1 G70D mutation is a rare alteration that does not produce an increase in D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) levels, and also fails to increase isocitrate-dependent NADPH production. The former suggest that the IDH1 G70D mutation results in a decrease of the enzyme wildtype activity, without an increase in 2-HG oncometabolite generation (PMID: 21996744).

While the IDH1 S280F mutation has not been functionally characterized, a patient with AML harboring an IDH1 R132C mutation developed resistance to ivosidenib, which was accompanied by the development of a cis S280F mutation (PMID: 29950729).

The IDH1 R123G mutation is located in the catalytic site of the IDH1 protein. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia and gliomas, among others (PMID: 19935646, 29860938). In vitro studies have shown that this mutation leads to a switch in IDH1 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (PMID: 19935646, 23264629). IDH1 mutations at the R132 residue, including R132G, are sensitive to inhibition by AG-120 (Ivosidenib), a small-molecule inhibitor of mutant IDH1, as measured by a decrease in 2-HG level, an increase in the proportion of mature myeloid cells and increased levels of cell surface differentiation markers in treated cells compared to untreated cells (PMID: 29670690). A Phase I clinical trial for ivosidenib involving 268 patients with relapsed or refractory AML harboring IDH1 R132 mutations, including 18 with IDH1 R132G mutation, achieved an overall response rate of 41.6% and a reduction in the percentage of bone marrow blasts in treated patients (PMID: 29860938).

The IDH2 Q316E mutation is located in the drug binding interface of the protein. While the IDH2 Q316E mutation expressed alone in cells does not lead to the production of the oncometabolite 2-Hydroxyglutamate, when expressed in cells in trans with the R140Q mutation, this mutation leads to increased levels of 2-HG. The IDH2 Q316E mutation has been found in patients who have developed resistance to enasidenib, and confers resistance to enasidenib in a mouse model of AML (PMID: 29950729).

The IDH2 R172W mutation is located in the active site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in bile duct adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24550739). In vitro studies with patient-derived cholangiocarcinoma samples expressing IDH2 R172W demonstrate that the mutation changes IDH2 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), as measured by increased levels of 2-HG in mutant cells compared to wildtype (PMID: 22180306).

The IDH2 R140Q mutation is located in the catalytic site of the IDH2 protein. This mutation is found in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), as well as in the germline of patients with D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (PMID: 20567020, 20847235). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation is oncogenic, as shown by the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the "oncometabolite" D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), the accumulation of 2-HG, impaired hepatocyte differentiation, increased cell proliferation, aberrant response to hepatic injury and decreased survival in a leukemia mouse model compared to wildtype (PMID: 20171147, 24440599, 20692206, 25043045, 31932841). In vitro and ex vivo studies have shown that the IDH2 R140Q mutation is sensitive to inhibition by enasidenib, a selective inhibitor of mutant IDH2 enzymes, as measured by reduced intracellular levels of 2-HG level and increased cellular differentiation compared to untreated cells (PMID: 28193778). A Phase 1/2 clinical trial of enasidenib in 107 patients with refractory AML who carry the IDH2 R140Q mutation further demonstrated this mutation's sensitivity to enasidenib as measured by reduced plasma 2-HG level in peripheral blood after one cycle of treatment with 100-mg daily doses of enasidenib (PMID: 28588020).

The IDH2 R172K mutation is located in the catalytic site of the IDH2 protein. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, among others (PMID: 20567020, 33017591). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation changes IDH2 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the "oncometabolite" D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) and leads to oncogenicity, as demonstrated by increased liver 2-HG levels, blocked differentiation, expanded liver progenitor cells and development of premalignant biliary lesions compared to wildtype (PMID: 20171147, 25043045).  In vitro and ex vivo studies have shown that the IDH2 R172K mutation is sensitive to inhibition by enasidenib, a selective inhibitor of mutant IDH2 enzymes, as measured by reduced intracellular levels of 2-HG and increased cellular differentiation compared to untreated cells (PMID: 28193778). A Phase 1/2 clinical trial of enasidenib in 34 patients with refractory AML who carry the IDH2 R172K mutation further demonstrated this mutation's sensitivity to enasidenib as measured by reduced plasma 2-HG levels in peripheral blood after one cycle of treatment with 100-mg daily doses of enasidenib (PMID: 28588020).

The IDH2 I319M mutation is located in the drug binding interface of the protein. While the IDH2 I319M mutation expressed alone in cells does not lead to the production of the oncometabolite 2-Hydroxyglutamate, when expressed in cells in trans with the R140Q mutation, this mutation leads to increased levels of 2-HG. The IDH2 I319M mutation has been found in patients who have developed resistance to enasidenib, and confers resistance to enasidenib in a mouse model of AML (PMID: 29950729).

The IDH2 R172T mutation is located in the active site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28581676). In vitro studies with solid papillary carcinoma with reverse polarity expressing IDH2 R172T demonstrate that the mutation changes IDH2 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), as measured by increased levels of 2-HG in mutant cells compared to wildtype (PMID: 27913435).

The IDH2 R172S mutation is located in the catalytic site of the IDH2 protein. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and osteosarcoma, among others (PMID: 20567020, 24403254). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation changes IDH2 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), as measured by increased levels of 2-HG in mutant cells compared to wildtype (PMID: 20171147, 23264629). In vitro and ex vivo studies have shown that the IDH2 R172 mutations, including R172S, are sensitive to inhibition by enasidenib, a selective inhibitor of mutant IDH2 enzymes, as measured by reduced intracellular levels of 2-HG and increased cellular differentiation compared to untreated cells (PMID: 28193778). A Phase 1/2 clinical trial of enasidenib in 34 patients with refractory AML who carry IDH2 R172 mutations, including R172S, demonstrated sensitivity to enasidenib as measured by reduced plasma 2-HG levels in peripheral blood after one cycle of treatment with 100-mg daily doses of enasidenib (PMID: 28588020).

The IDH2 R172G mutation is located in the IDH2 catalytic site. This mutation is predicted to change IDH2 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the "oncometabolite" D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (PMID: 20171147). Expression of this mutation in rat glioma C6 cells showed that its expression led to decreased IDH2 wildtype enzymatic activity (PMID: 21641335).

The IDH2 R140W mutation is located in the substrate binding region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 20368543). In vitro studies with pediatric acute myeloid leukemia cells expressing IDH2 R140W demonstrate that the mutation changes IDH2 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), as measured by increased levels of 2-HG in mutant cells compared to wildtype (PMID: 21647154).

The IDH2 R172M mutation is located in the IDH2 catalytic site. This mutation is predicted to change IDH2 enzymatic activity, allowing for the conversion of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to the "oncometabolite" D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (PMID: 20171147). Gene expression profiling of HA1E cells expressing this mutation demonstrated that it is likely oncogenic as it had a very similar gene expression signature to cells expressing the known oncogenic IDH2 R172K mutation (PMID: 27147599).

The JAK1 L783F mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May. 2015). Expression of JAK1 L783F caused increased phosphorylation of STAT-5 and ERK and interleukin 3-independent proliferation in immortalized mouse progenitor B cells, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation (PMID: 21393331).

The JAK1 R724H mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May. 2015). JAK R724H transfection led to increased IFN-mediated phosphorylation of the downstream target STAT1 compared to transfection of wildtype JAK1 in JAK1-defective human fibrosarcoma cells. Also, JAK1 R724H expression induced interleukin 3-independent proliferation of mouse progenitor B cells. Collectively, these results suggest an activating and oncogenic role of JAK1 R724H (PMID: 18362173).

The JAK1 S729C mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May. 2015). Transduction of JAK1 S729C increased the levels of phosphorylated JAK1 and STAT-3 and induced interleukin 3-independent proliferation of mouse progenitor B cells, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation (PMID: 23788652).

The JAK1 F958V mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Ba/F3 cells harboring an endogenous JAK1 F958V mutation maintained high levels of phosphorylated JAK1 and STAT5 despite being treated with ATP-competitive JAK1 inhibitors while other isogenic Ba/F3 cells harboring a JAK1 V658I mutation were sensitive to JAK1 inhibition. Additionally, F958V mutant Ba/F3 cells required significantly more JAK1 inhibitor to inhibit proliferation as compared to V658I mutant Ba/F3 cells. Together, this data suggests that the F958V mutation confers resistance to ATP-competitive JAK1 inhibitors (PMID: 21393331)

The JAK1 G1097D mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of JAK1 G1097D in human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased levels of phosphorylated STAT3 and stimulation of soft agar colony formation in STAT-3 deficient MEFs (PMID: 25873174).

The JAK1 K1026E mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the JAK1 protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells resulted in moderate activation of the JAK1 downstream targets STAT1 and STAT5, and led to increased proliferation when expressed in Baf3 cells (PMID: 20868368).

The JAK1 S646F missense mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the JAK1 protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May. 2015). Expression of this mutant induced cytokine-independent proliferation and erythropoietin-independent STAT5 phosphorylation in immortalized mouse progenitor B-cells, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation (PMID: 19470474).

The JAK1 Y652H mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May 2015). Expression of this mutant caused constitutive phosphorylation of STAT-3 and cytokine-independent proliferation in immortalized mouse progenitor B cells, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation (PMID: 21551237).

The JAK1 K648N mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May 2015). Expression of this mutant caused constitutive phosphorylation of STAT-3 and cytokine-independent proliferation in immortalized mouse progenitor B cells, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation (PMID: 21551237).

The JAK1 S703I mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutant activates the JAK-STAT signaling pathway and induces cytokine-independent proliferation of immortalized mouse progenitor B cells, human embryonic kidney cells and human cervical cancer (HeLa) cells (PMID: 23788652, 24825865). JAK1 S703I activates STAT3 and induces an inflammatory response in a human hepatoma cell line (Hep3B) (PMID: 24735922).

The JAK1 F958S mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of JAK1 F958S in HEK293 cells stimulated phosphorylation of pathway effectors including JAK1, STAT1, STAT3 and ERK, and also resulted in increased proliferation as compared to expression of wildtype JAK1 (PMID: 21393331).

The JAK1 V658F mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the JAK1 protein. Expression of the V658F mutation in HEK293 cells induced phosphorylation of the JAK1 downstream targets STAT1, STAT3, STAT5 and ERK suggesting that this mutation is functionally active (PMID: 19139102, 20868368). Expression of this mutant in Baf3 cells also resulted in cytokine independent proliferation suggesting that this mutation is indeed oncogenic (PMID: 20868368). Pathway activation and proliferation mediated by the V658F mutation is sensitive to JAK1 inhibition (PMID: 21393331).

The JAK1 A634D missense mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of the JAK1 protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May 2015). This mutation caused constitutive activation of JAK1 downstream targets, mediated by homodimerization of interleukin receptors 2 and 9 (PMID: 19139102).

The JAK1 A723D mutation is located in the pseudokinase domain of JAK1. Expression of JAK1 A723D results in increased levels of phosphorylated STAT3 and induces inflammatory response in a human hepatoma cell line (Hep3B), suggesting an activating role of the mutation (PMID: 24735922).

The JAK1 R879C mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Transfection of JAK R879C caused increased IFN-mediated phosphorylation of the downstream target STAT1 compared to transfection of wildtype JAK1 in human fibrosarcoma cells defective in JAK1. Also, JAK1 R879C expression increased interleukin 3-induced proliferation of mouse progenitor B cells. Collectively, these results suggest an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation (PMID: 18362173).

The JAK2 C618R mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of JAK2 C618R increases the levels of phosphorylated JAK2 and causes cytokine-independent proliferation in immortalized mouse precursor progenitor (Ba/F3) cells, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation. In the protein expressed by JAK2 C618R, an interaction forms between amino acid residue arginine (R) 618 and glutamic acid (E) 543, which mediates the constitutive activation of JAK2 (PMID: 22960131).

The JAK1 Y1035C mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells resulted in moderate activation of the JAK1 downstream targets STAT1 and STAT5, and led to increased proliferation when expressed in Ba/F3 cells (PMID: 20868368).

The JAK1 F958C mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein (PMID: 21393331). Expression of JAK1 F958C in Ba/F3 cells led to increased STAT5 phosphorylation and interleukin 3-independent proliferation, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role for the mutation (PMID: 21393331).

The JAK1 L910P mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May. 2015). Expression of JAK1 L910P led to increased STAT1, STAT3, STAT5 and ERK phosphorylation in human embryonic kidney cells or hepatocellular carcinoma cells, and caused interleukin 3-independent proliferation of immortalized mouse progenitor B cells, suggesting an activating and oncogenic role of the mutation (PMID: 23788652, 25873174, 20868368).

The TEL-JAK2 fusion protein (also known as the ETV6-JAK2 fusion protein) results from a translocation between the TEL gene, a breakpoint hotspot in leukemias, and the JAK2 gene (PMID: 9360930). TEL-JAK2 fusions are found in hematologic malignancies such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) (PMID: 22733019, 15676212). This fusion protein contains the oligomerization domain of TEL and the kinase domain of JAK2 resulting in a constitutively activated, oligomerized JAK2 protein. Expression of this fusion in Ba/F3 cells results in cytokine-independence, while expression its in zebrafish results in transformation. Additionally, this fusion promotes leukemogenesis when expressed in mice (PMID: 9360930, 22733019, 10845925, 10706877).

Truncating mutations of JAK1 can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated JAK1 proteins. Experimental studies with human gynecologic cancer cell lines harboring JAK1 truncating mutations demonstrated that these cells are defective in IFN-γ-induced antigen processing. Where wildtype JAK1 restored the antigen presenting function of JAK1, it's possible that truncating JAK1 mutations may contribute to immune escape of malignant cells by inhibiting the tumor antigen presentation and JAK1-mediated interferon response of these cells (PMID: 24154688, 12576323, 29121062).

The JAK2 R426K mutation (also cited as JAK2 R277K) is located in the JAK2 FERM domain. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib in cell lines as measured by cell colony formation in the presence of drug (PMID: 26419724). Where ruxolitinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor, the JAK2 R426K mutation had a ~2-fold greater enzymatic activity compared to the ruxolitinib sensitive JAK2 V617F form and consistently required higher concentrations of ruxolitinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50) (PMID: 26419724).

The PCM1-JAK2 fusion protein results from a translocation that fuses the coiled-coil domain of PCM1 to the kinase domain of JAK2 leading to an oligomerized, activated kinase (PMID: 15805263). The coiled-coil domain of PCM1 likely causes oligomerization and activation of the fusion protein similar to other JAK2 fusion genes (e.g. PAX5-JAK2) (PMID: 23372669, 15805263, 21325169). The PCM1-JAK2 fusion has been found in leukemia, lymphoma and myeloproliferative neoplasms and, like other transforming JAK2-fusions, may be the driving oncogenic alteration in these cancers (PMID: 16034466, 16424865, 24913195). Expression of this fusion in Ba/F3 cells induced growth-factor independent proliferation similarly to other activating JAK2 fusions and showed sensitivity to treatment with ruxolitinib (PMID: 22899477).

The JAK2 F1061W mutation occurs in the substrate binding domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-Y931C-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer moderate resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor fedratinib in cell lines as measured by dose-dependent cellular proliferation assay (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 F1061W mutation consistently required higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), and showed weaker kinase activity and strong cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 R683K mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of JAK2 R683K leads to cytokine-independent growth and increased levels of phosphorylated JAK2 and STAT5 in immortalized mouse precursor B (Ba/F3) cells, suggesting an oncogenic and activating role of the mutation (PMID: 18805579). The activating effect of the mutation has been shown to be mediated by disruption of the auto-inhibitory interaction between glutamic acid (E) 627 and arginine (R) 683 (PMID: 23452118). Thus, the mutation impairs the structure of the JAK2 JH2 domain, which causes JAK2 to be partially unfolded, leading to constitutive activation of the protein (PMID: 23748007).

JAK2 exon 12 mutations are found in patients with JAK2 V617F-negative myeloproliferative disorders (PMID: 17267906). Expression of these mutations in Ba/F3 cells led to cytokine-independent proliferation and downstream pathway activation, and transduction of murine bone marrow cells with JAK2 exon 12 mutations led to myeloproliferative disease in vivo when implanted into irradiated mice (PMID: 17267906).

JAK2 fusions, which generally function by replacing the autoinhibitory domain of JAK2 with an oligomerization domain of the fusion partner, are found in several types of hematological malignancies including leukemia, lymphoma and myeloproliferative neoplasms. JAK2 fusions seem to be especially prevalent in BCR-ABL1-like acute lymphoblastic leukemia, where the activated JAK2 kinase phenocopies BCR-ABL causing the disease to be BCR-ABL1-like. (PMID: 25207766, 24913195).

The JAK2 L551P mutation occurs in the pseudokinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib in cell lines as measured by cell colony formation in the presence of drug (PMID: 26419724). Where ruxolitinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor, the JAK2 L551P mutation consistently required higher concentrations of ruxolitinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50) (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 L611V mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was shown to be present in the same subclones of cells as the JAK2 V617F mutation in patients with polycythemia vera. Expression of L611V alone did not affect JAK2 phosphorylation or downstream signaling in immortalized mouse precursor progenitor (Ba/F3) cells. However, simultaneous expression of V617F and L611V caused increased phosphorylation of JAK2, AKT and ERK (but not STAT5) compared to expression of V617F alone, suggesting that the L611V mutation is activating in a JAK2 V617F background (PMID: 20182460).

The JAK2 S1025C mutation occurs in the substrate binding domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-Y931C-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer moderate resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor fedratinib in cell lines as measured by dose-dependent cellular proliferation assay (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 S1025C mutation consistently required higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), and showed weaker kinase activity and strong cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 G571S mutation is located in the JH2 pseudokinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in the germline of a patient with triple-negative essential thrombocythemia (ET).  Expression of this mutation in JAK2-deficient and BaF3 cell lines demonstrated that it is likely neutral as shown by JAK2-STAT5 signaling and cytokine-independent proliferation comparable to wildtype JAK2 (PMID: 26423830).

The JAK2 R683S mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of JAK2 R683S leads to cytokine-independent growth and increased levels of phosphorylated JAK2 and STAT5 in immortalized mouse precursor B (Ba/F3) cells, suggesting an oncogenic and activating role of the mutation (PMID: 18805579). The activating effect of the mutation has been shown to be mediated by disruption of the auto-inhibitory interaction between glutamic acid (E) 627 and arginine (R) 683 (PMID: 23452118). Thus, the mutation impairs the structure of the JAK2 JH2 domain, which causes JAK2 to be partially unfolded, leading to constitutive activation of the protein (PMID: 23748007).

The ATF7IP-JAK2 fusion protein results from a translocation that fuses part of the ATF7IP gene to the kinase domain of JAK2 (Abstract: Roberts et al. Abstract# 786, ASH 2014. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/124/21/786). This JAK2 fusion protein has been found in cases of BCR-ABL1-like pre-B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Abstract: Roberts et al. Abstract# 786, ASH 2014. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/124/21/786). Expression of ATF7IP-JAK2 in Ba/F3 cells leads to cytokine-independent growth and transformation, as well as downstream STAT5 activation (PMID: 25207766 ) (Abstract: Roberts et al. Abstract# 786, ASH 2014. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/124/21/786).

The JAK2 L1026F mutation occurs in the substrate binding domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-Y931C-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer moderate resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor fedratinib in cell lines as measured by dose-dependent cellular proliferation assay (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 L1026F mutation consistently required higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), showed weaker kinase activity and displayed strong cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

JAK2 exon 12 mutations are found in patients with JAK2 V617F-negative myeloproliferative disorders (PMID: 17267906). Expression of these mutations in Ba/F3 cells led to cytokine-independent proliferation and downstream pathway activation, and transduction of murine bone marrow cells with JAK2 exon 12 mutations led to myeloproliferative disease in vivo when implanted into irradiated mice (PMID: 17267906).

JAK2 exon 12 mutations are found in patients with JAK2 V617F-negative myeloproliferative disorders (PMID: 17267906). Expression of these mutations in Ba/F3 cells led to cytokine-independent proliferation and downstream pathway activation, and transduction of murine bone marrow cells with JAK2 exon 12 mutations led to myeloproliferative disease in vivo when implanted into irradiated mice (PMID: 17267906).

The JAK2 G335D mutation is located in the N-terminal FERM domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in the germline of a patient with triple-negative essential thrombocythemia (ET). Expression of this mutation in JAK2-deficient and BaF3 cell lines demonstrated that it is likely neutral as shown by JAK2-STAT5 signaling and cytokine-independent proliferation comparable to wildtype JAK2 (PMID: 26423830).

Chromosome 9p24.1 has been shown to include JAK2 as well as the programmed cell death-1 (PD1) ligand genes, PD-L1 and PD-L2; its amplification is often detected in Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (MLBCL). Amplification of 9p24.1 was associated with increased protein expression and activity as well as increased PD-1 ligand transcription and enhanced sensitivity to JAK2 inhibition (PMID: 20628145).

The JAK2 Y1045* mutation occurs in the substrate binding domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been explicitly functionally validated, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-Y931C-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells suggests that it can confer slight resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor fedratinib in cell lines as measured by dose-dependent cellular proliferation assay (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 Y1045* mutation required only moderately higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), and did not show cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 Y931C mutation occurs in the JAK2 kinase domain. Transformation assays of Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells expressing the JAK2 V617F mutant along with this mutation show increased transformation potential compared to JAK2 V617F alone, similar to that of the fully activated TEL-JAK2 and BCR-ABL (PMID: 26419724). In vitro experiments with ATF7IP-JAK2 Ba/F3 cells expressing JAK2 Y931C demonstrated that the mutation is activating as measured by increased pSTAT5 signaling as compared to wildtype (PMID: 34376782). Expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-mutant Ba/F3 cells also demonstrated that it can confer resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib in cell lines as measured by cell colony formation in the presence of drug (PMID: 26419724). Where ruxolitinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor, the JAK2 Y931C mutation consistently required higher concentrations of ruxolitinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50) (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 L983F mutation occurs in the JAK2 kinase domain. While this mutation has not been explicitly functionally validated, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib in cell lines as measured by cell colony formation in the presence of drug (PMID: 26419724). Where ruxolitinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor, the JAK2 L983F mutation consistently required higher concentrations of ruxolitinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50) (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 L983F mutation also shows resistance in vivo, as mice transplanted with Ba/F3 cells expressing this mutation are resistant to ruxolitinib treatment (PMID: 26419724).

The BCR-JAK2 fusion results from a translocation that fuses the dimerization domain of BCR with the kinase domain of JAK2 (PMID: 16001431). The resulting fusion protein activates STAT5, leads to cytokine-independent growth when expressed in Ba/F3 cells in vitro or in xenograft mouse models and drives myeloproliferative neoplasms when expressed in bone marrow progenitor cells of mice (PMID: 16001431, 22384256, 25664618). The BCR-JAK2 fusion gene has been reported in at least thirteen cases of leukemia or myeloproliferative neoplasms (PMID: 16001431, 18503828, 18537978, 22549126, 23904814, 24913195, 25789185 ).

The JAK2 R683T mutation occurs in the JAK2 kinase domain. Transformation assays of Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells expressing the JAK2 V617F mutant along with this mutation show increased transformation potential compared to JAK2 V617F alone, similar to that of the fully activated TEL-JAK2 and BCR-ABL (PMID: 26419724). In vitro studies with Ba/F3-Epo-R and Ba/F3 cells expressing JAK2 R683 mutations have demonstrated activation as measured by cytokine-independent cell growth, suggesting JAK2 R683T is also activating  (PMID: 19470474). Expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-mutant Ba/F3 cells also demonstrated that it can confer resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib in cell lines as measured by cell colony formation in the presence of drug (PMID: 26419724). Where ruxolitinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor, the JAK2 R683T mutation consistently required higher concentrations of ruxolitinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50) (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 R683T mutation also shows resistance in vivo, as mice transplanted with Ba/F3 cells expressing this mutation are resistant to ruxolitinib treatment (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 H538Q mutation occurs in exon 12 of JAK2. Expression of this mutation caused increased levels of phosphorylated JAK2, STAT5 and ERK, and induced cytokine-independent growth of immortalized mouse progenitor B cells expressing the erythropoietin receptor (BaF3/EpoR cells) (PMID: 17267906).

The JAK2 R683G mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of JAK2 R683G leads to cytokine-independent growth, soft agar colony formation, and increased levels of phosphorylated JAK2 and STAT5 in immortalized mouse precursor B (Ba/F3) cells, suggesting an oncogenic and activating role of the mutation (PMID: 20585391, 18805579). The activating effect of the mutation has been shown to be mediated by disruption of the auto-inhibitory interaction between glutamic acid (E) 627 and arginine (R) 683 (PMID: 23452118). Thus, the mutation impairs the structure of the JAK2 JH2 domain, which causes JAK2 to be partially unfolded, leading to constitutive activation of the protein (PMID: 23748007).

The PAX5-JAK2 fusion has been found in hematological malignancies including acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 25207766). This fusion protein is a nuclear, DNA binding, catalytically active kinase that phosphorylates and activates downstream targets such as STAT proteins in a cytokine-independent manner (PMID: 25515960). Expression of the PAX5-JAK2 fusion in cytokine-dependent mouse precursor-B cells induces cytokine-independent proliferation and increases the activity of the JAK2 downstream target STAT5 (PMID: 25207766).

The JAK2 R1113H mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a monkey cell line (BSC-40) demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by protein phosphorylation compared to wildtype JAK2 (PMID: 15543946).

The JAK2 V1075F mutation occurs in the substrate binding domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-Y931C-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer moderate resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor fedratinib in cell lines as measured by dose-dependent cellular proliferation assay (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 V1075F mutation consistently required higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), and showed weaker kinase activity and strong cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 T875N mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein (cBioPortal, MSKCC; May. 2015). Expression of JAK2 T875N leads to increased phosphorylation of JAK2 downstream targets such as STAT3, STAT5, and ERK in human embryonic kidney (HEK) or immortalized mouse precursor B (Ba/F3) cells and induces cytokine-independent growth of Ba/F3 cells (PMID: 19543316, 20585391). In these cells, JAK2 T875N expression leads to increased kinase activity, proliferation and colony formation compared to other mutations tested (PMID: 21362419). In a mouse transplant model, JAK2 T875N induced a myeloproliferative disease with features of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (PMID: 16804112).

The JAK2 E1024R mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a monkey cell line (BSC-40) demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by protein phosphorylation compared to wildtype JAK2 (PMID: 15543946).

The JAK2 K539L mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation leads to increased kinase activity, cytokine-independent growth and colony formation in methylcellulose, as well increased levels of phosphorylated JAK2 and activation of several downstream targets such as STAT3, STAT5, AKT and ERK when expressed in immortalized mouse precursor B (Ba/F3) cells (PMID: 21362419, 20585391). Injection of bone marrow cells expressing JAK2 K539L in irradiated mice caused a myeloproliferative neoplasm with elevated hematocrit, white blood cell count and platelet count (PMID: 17267906).

The JAK2 F537_K539delinsL mutation occurs in exon 12 of JAK2. Expression of this mutation in immortalized mouse progenitor B cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein and downstream pathway activation and cytokine-independent growth (PMID: 17267906).

The JAK2 D544H mutation occurs in the SH2-pseudokinase linker domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib in cell lines as measured by cell colony formation in the presence of drug (PMID: 26419724). Where ruxolitinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor, the JAK2 D544H mutation consistently required higher concentrations of ruxolitinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50) (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 S1039F mutation required only moderately higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), and did not show cellular resistance measured by the presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 I1018W mutation occurs in the substrate binding domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-Y931C-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer moderate resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor fedratinib in cell lines as measured by dose-dependent cellular proliferation assay (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 I1018W mutation consistently required higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), showed weaker kinase activity and displayed strong cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 Y1045W mutation occurs in the substrate binding domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-Y931C-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer moderate resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor fedratinib in cell lines as measured by dose-dependent cellular proliferation assay (PMID: 26419724). The JAK2 Y1045W mutation consistently required higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), and showed weaker kinase activity and strong cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 V617F mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation is the most prevalent JAK2 mutation and disrupts the protein's autoinhibitory JH2 domain (PMID: 12351625, 21533163). This mutation hyperactivates several JAK2 effectors including STAT5, AKT and the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (PMID: 19543316, 15793561). Expression of JAK2 V617F causes increased proliferation of mouse hematopoietic precursor cells in a cytokine-independent manner (PMID: 15793561). This mutation is found in combination with IDH1/2 mutations in myeloproliferative neoplasms, and in vivo studies have shown that combined JAK2 and IDH1/2 inhibition with ruxolitinib and enasidenib in this context results in greater decrease in tumor burden compared to either drug alone (PMID: 29355841). Preclinical studies with HEL, UKE-1 and SET2 cells expressing JAK2 V617F demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with ruxolitinib, pacritinib, fedratinib and momelotinib as measured by reduced cell viability following treatment (PMID: 37203407).

The JAK2 G417P mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated per se, expression of this mutation in JAK2 V617F-mutant Ba/F3 mouse hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it can confer resistance to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib in cell lines as measured by cell colony formation in the presence of drug (PMID: 26419724). Where ruxolitinib is an ATP-competitive inhibitor, the JAK2 G417P mutation consistently required higher concentrations of ruxolitinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50) (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 W1038C mutation required only moderately higher concentrations of fedratinib for 50% cell proliferation inhibition (measured as IC50), and did not show cellular resistance measured by presence of downstream phospho-STAT5 (PMID: 26419724).

The JAK2 N542_E543del alteration occurs in exon 12 of JAK2. Expression of this alteration in immortalized mouse progenitor B cells expressing the erythropoietin receptor (BaF3/EpoR cells) resulted in increased levels of phosphorylated JAK2, STAT5 and ERK, and induced cytokine-independent growth (PMID: 17267906).

The JAK3 V678M mutation occurs in the pseudokinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased IL3-independent proliferation compared to wildtype JAK3 (PMID: 25193870).

The JAK3 R657W mutation occurs in the pseudokinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased IL3-independent proliferation compared to wildtype JAK3 (PMID: 25193870).

The JAK3 A573V mutation occurs in the pseudokinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased IL3-independent proliferation compared to wildtype JAK3 (PMID: 25193870).

The KDM5C M1_E165DEL mutation results in a N-terminally truncated protein. Expression of this mutation causes reduced KDM5C demethylase activity and protein stability (PMID: 25666439); however further studies are required to ascertain the functional consequences of this mutation.

The JAK3 R657Q mutation occurs in the pseudokinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased IL3-independent proliferation compared to wildtype JAK3 (PMID: 25193870).

The KDM5C P480L mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. In vitro studies with primary patient cells expressing this mutation demonstrated that KDM5C P480L is inactivating as measured by reduction in protein expression and demethylase activity in cells compared to cells that endogenously expressed wildtype KDM5C (PMID: 25666439).

The KDM5C V1075Yfs*2 mutation is located in the PLU-1 domain of the protein. In vitro studies with primary patient cells expressing this mutation demonstrated that KDM5C V1075Yfs*2 is inactivating as measured by reduction in protein expression and demethylase activity in cells compared to cells that endogenously expressed wildtype KDM5C (PMID: 25666439).

In a cohort of 822 prostate tumors, positive nuclear staining for KDM5C was significantly associated with a reduced prostate-specific antigen relapse-free patient survival and was confirmed as an independent prognostic parameter in this context (PMID: 25016185). Knockdown of wildtype KDM5C in prostate cancer cell lines led to decreased cellular proliferation, suggesting KDM5C overexpression is likely activating and likely oncogenic.

The KDM5C D402Y mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. In vitro studies with primary patient cells expressing this mutation demonstrated that KDM5C D204Y is inactivating as measured by reduction in protein expression and demethylase activity in cells compared to cells that endogenously expressed wildtype KDM5C (PMID: 25666439).

Deletions of KDM6A have been identified in patients with Kabuki Syndrome and hematological malignancies. These alterations are characterized by deletion of several exons in the KDM6A gene, resulting in haploinsufficiency of the protein (PMID: 22197486, 27028180) (Abstract: Walker et al. Abstract #1798, ASH, 2009. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/114/22/1798?sso-checked=true). Experimental studies with KDM6A truncating mutations in human bladder cancer cell lines suggest that these mutations lead to enhanced anchorage-independent growth and cell migration (PMID: 25225064, 19330029). Genetically engineered mouse models of pancreatic-specific KDM6A loss with or without KRAS mutation result in the formation of aggressive pancreatic tumors in female mice that display activation of MYC and sensitivity to BET inhibition with the inhibitor JQ1 (PMID: 29533787). Loss of KDM6A may have a role in resistance to chemotherapy in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 31201358).

KDM5C is a tumor suppressor and truncating mutations of this gene are assumed to be associated with protein loss and therefore considered likely oncogenic. Loss of KDM5C exerts an essential role in mammalian DNA replication and KDM5C silencing induces aberrant H3K4me3 levels at active origins, thereby halting DNA replication and ultimately S phase progression (PMID: 25712104). Mutation of the KDM5C gene was first described as causing X-linked intellectual disability (XLID) in 2005 (PMID: 15586325), and has been linked to some forms of cancer (PMID: 21544224, 20181063, 20133580). The prevalence of KDM5C mutations in patients with XLID is estimated to be ~3% (PMID: 23356856), and somatic mutations in this gene have been identified in 4-9% of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) (PMID: 20054297, 24166983, 22138691). Knockdown of KDM5C in von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) -/- ccRCC cells significantly enhanced tumor growth in a xenograft model, suggesting that KDM5C functions as a tumor suppressor in this cancer model (PMID: 21725364, 25111482).

Truncating mutations of KDM6A have been identified in patients with bladder cancer and lead to reduced protein expression (PMID: 24633898). Experimental studies in human bladder cancer cell lines suggest that truncating mutations lead to enhanced anchorage-independent growth and cell migration (PMID: 25225064, 19330029). In addition, urothelial bladder cancers with reduced KDM6A expression were shown to demonstrate increased proliferation in an EZH2-dependent manner. Such tumors were found to be sensitive to EZH2 inhibition and demonstrated delayed tumor onset as well as regression of KDM6A-null bladder tumors in both patient-derived and cell line xenograft models (PMID: 28228601). Loss of KDM6A may have a role in resistance to chemotherapy in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 31201358).

The KIT R135H mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type domain 2 of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 24755471). In vitro studies with immortal mouse melanocytes expressing KIT R135H demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by SCF-induced activation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 23020152).

The KIT W557C mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein and has been found in patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST). This mutation has not yet been functionally validated but a single patient with GIST harboring the W557C and K558_V560del mutations experienced clinical benefit in response to ponatinib treatment after previously progressing on imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib (PMID: 25239608).

The KIT K550_W557del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation was identified in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 25239608). Biological characterization of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating, as evidenced by factor-independent proliferation (PMID: 25239608). In vitro studies suggest that this variant is sensitive to imatinib, suntinib, regorafenib and ponatinib treatment, as evidenced by inhibition of pathway activation and decreased cell viability (PMID: 25239608).

The KIT V825A mutation is located in the activation loop in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in NK/T-cell lymphoma (PMID: 15643509, 16596195). In vitro studies with RUNX1-ETO mutated CD34+ cells expressing KIT V825A demonstrate that the mutation is activating in the context of RUNX1-ETO as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to mock transduced cells (PMID: 24897507). In vitro studies with CD34+ cells expressing KIT V825A alone demonstrated cellular proliferation comparable to mock transduced cells (PMID: 24897507).

The KIT D816N mutation is located in the kinase domain in exon 17 of the protein. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 11369651). Expression of this variant in MO7e leukemia cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein phosphorylation and increased downstream pathway activation (PMID: 11369651).

The KIT V560E mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been identified in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and melanoma (PMID: 22350270, 21690468). KIT V560E has not been functionally validated. Another amino acid substitution at this position (V560D) has been shown to be gain-of-function and oncogenic (PMID: 25239608). In a Phase II trial of imatinib in patients with metastatic melanoma harboring KIT alterations, a patient with a KIT V560E mutation experienced clinical benefit from imatinib treatment (PMID: 21690468). In a case report, a patient with GIST harboring KIT V560E and BRAF V600E was treated with imatinib and achieved maximal response with a decrease in tumor size at twelve months and subsequently underwent a surgical resection (PMID: 34250403). In a second case report, a patient with GIST harboring KIT V560E and reduced copy number of RB1 was treated with imatinib until disease progression and then subsequently treated with sunitinib and demonstrated partial response (PMID: 35982969).

The KIT D816Y mutation is located in the kinase domain in exon 17 of the protein. This mutation has been identified in mast cell disorder (PMID: 16397263, 15790786, 15167915) and leukemia (PMID: 15725473). Biological characterization of this variant in mast cell and Ba/F3 cell lines determined that it is activating and promotes growth, as demonstrated by pathway activation and factor-independent proliferation (PMID: 16397263, 15790786). In vitro studies of cell lines expressing KIT D816Y suggest that this mutation is resistant to treatment with imatinib but sensitive to dasatinib as evidenced by cell viability (PMID: 16397263, 15790786). Though patient responses to imatinib therapy have been mixed, reports indicate that patients with KIT D816Y mutated tumors progress on imatinib treatment (PMID: 15167915, 15725473).

The KIT W557_K558del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 17699867, 14645423, 25239608). Biological characterization of this variant in Ba/F3 and CHO cells demonstrated it is activating and promotes growth, as demonstrated by pathway activation and factor-independent proliferation (PMID: 17699867, 14645423, 25239608). In vitro studies have suggested that this mutation is sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, sorafenib and ponatinib as evidenced by pathway activation and cell viability (PMID: 25239608, 17699867, 14645423). Two patients with GIST whose tumors harbored the KIT E557_K558del mutation had partial responses to treatment with imatinib before acquiring secondary resistance (PMID: 16954519, 15930355).

The KIT T274M mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type domain 3 of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myeloid neoplasms (PMID: 31366621). In vitro studies with immortal mouse melanocytes expressing KIT T274M demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased SCF-induced activation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 23020152).

The KIT N505I mutation is located in the extracellular domain in exon 9 of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 24317392). Expression of this mutation in melan-A cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein activation, cell proliferation and colony formation compared to wildtype KIT (PMID: 24317392). In vitro studies of cells expressing KIT N505I suggest that this mutation is sensitive to sorafenib but not imatinib, as measured by protein activity upon drug treatment (PMID: 24317392).

The KIT V555_V559del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) samples (PMID: 15930355, 18955458). While this variant has not been functionally validated, in a study of 31 GIST patients, one patient with a KIT V555_V559del mutation had a partial response to imatinib (PMID: 15930355). However in a clinical phase II study of gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) patients that were imatinib-resistant, one patient with a KIT V555_V559del mutation was also resistant to sunitinib therapy (PMID: 18955458).

The KIT Y553N mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in thymic cancer (PMID: 21969494, 22357254). While this variant has not been functionally validated, a patient with thymic cancer harboring KIT Y553N had a partial response to imatinib therapy (PMID: 21969494, 22357254). Structural modeling suggests that this mutation stabilizes the active conformation of KIT (PMID: 23588081).

The KIT S476I mutation occurs in the extracellular domain in exon 9 of the protein. This mutation is found in pediatric mastocytosis (PMID: 19865100). Expression of this variant in COS cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein phosphorylation compared to wildtype KIT (PMID: 19865100).

The KIT exon 11 V559F mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, this mutation is found recurrently in gastrointestinal stromal tumor patient samples and comprises a hotspot, suggesting it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

The KIT V560A mutation is located in the exon 11 juxtamembrane domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in gastrointestinal stromal tumors and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 19411681). In vitro studies with COS cells expressing KIT V560A demonstrate the mutation is activating as measured by increased autophosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 16226710).

The KIT Y646D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in melanoma (PMID: 28467829). Although not functionally characterized per se, a patient with mucosal melanoma harboring KIT Y646D was treated with imatinib and demonstrated stable disease with a progression-free survival of roughly four months (PMID: 25695690). The patient was later treated with nilotinib after disease progression and demonstrated a progression-free survival of 0.2 months (PMID: 25695690). Preclinical studies with SK-MEL-28 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate resistance to imatinib as measured by sustained cellular proliferation and inhibition of apoptosis (PMID: 35720122).

The KIT W557_V559delinsC mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 18955458). While this variant has not been functionally validated, in a clinical study in patients with GIST who failed imatinib therapy, a patient with KIT W557_V559delinsC had transient stable disease in response to sunitinib therapy (PMID: 18955458).

The KIT E554_I571del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 16954519). While this variant has not been functionally validated, in a Phase II study of GIST patients treated with imatinib, one patient with KIT E554_I571del had a partial response to imatinib treatment (PMID: 16954519).

The KIT D677N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, preclinical studies with KIT D816V-mutated Ba/F3 cells expressing KIT 677N demonstrate resistance to midostaurin as measured by sustained phosphorylation (PMID: 31270078).

The KIT V559_G565del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 16551858). While this variant has not been functionally validated, in a Phase II study of 147 gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) patients, one patient with this variant became resistant to imatinib treatment without the acquisition of other secondary KIT mutations (PMID: 16551858).

The KIT R888Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in biliary tract adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 29360550). In vitro studies with melanoma cell lines expressing KIT R888Q demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased SCF-induced activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 23020152).

The KIT V530I mutation is located in the transmembrane domain in exon 10 of the protein. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and aggressive fibromatosis (AF) (PMID: 16081693, 20339585). There is conflicting data for this mutation. Expression of KIT V530I in murine myeloid cells resulted in increased KIT basal phosphorylation and increased pathway signaling downstream of KIT compared to wildtype cells. Additionally, cells expressing this mutant exhibited moderate factor independent growth and demonstrated sensitivity to imatinib as evidenced by increased apoptosis and decreased cell replication upon drug administration (PMID: 16081693). A single case study demonstrated that a patient with aggressive fibromatosis (AF) harboring the KIT V530I mutation experienced a dramatic clinical response upon treatment with imatinib (PMID: 20339585). However, population data suggests that this variant is common in the germline and does not predispose to familial cancer syndromes (dbSNP; ClinVar, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/RCV000234206/), this mutation is not commonly found in GIST, and this mutation is not found as the driver mutation in the MSK-IMPACT series (PMID: 28481359).

KIT gene amplifications occur in a subset of melanomas, gliomas and small cell lung carcinomas, among other tumors (cBioPortal, MSKCC, April 2017). KIT gene amplifications are apparently not correlated with KIT protein overexpression in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) and medulloblastomas (PMID: 15869870, 19779861) . In contrast, KIT amplifications correlated with KIT protein overexpression in both ovarian dysgeminomas (PMID: 21523721) and recurrent gliomas (PMID: 17189383), and it occurs more frequently in the latter tumor type. Functionally, KIT amplification has been associated with tumor progression in seminomas (PMID: 16166280) and a case report described a patient with a familial form of GIST displaying an amplification of a KIT mutant allele (PMID: 24868028). Preclinical models of KIT overexpression showed that it enhances proliferation in astrocytes and promotes leukemogenesis in AML1-ETO-positive cells (PMID: 18506689, 15650049) consistent with a oncogenic role of KIT amplification. In a study of 11 patients with melanoma harboring amplified, wildtype KIT, the response rate with imatinib treatment was 0%(PMID: 23775962).

The KIT P551_E554del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutant has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) samples (PMID: 25239608). Biological characterization of this variant in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated it is activating and promotes growth as demonstrated by pathway activation and factor-independent growth (PMID: 25239608). In vitro studies of cells expressing this variant suggest that KIT P551_E554del is moderately resistant to imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib and ponatinib treatment, as evidenced by cell viability (PMID: 25239608). In a phase II study of 147 patients with advanced GIST, one patients with KIT P551_E554del progressed after imatinib therapy (PMID: 16954519).

The KIT D816E mutation is located in the kinase domain in exon 17 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 16551858, 25239608). While this variant has not been functionally validated, another amino acid substitution at this position (D816F) has been shown to be gain-of-function and oncogenic (PMID: 16397263). In vitro studies of patient-derived GIST cell lines expressing KIT D816E in combination with KIT 560_576del were resistant to imatinib treatment, as evidenced by cell viability studies (PMID: 25239608). In a clinical study of 32 patients with GIST, one patient with acquired resistance to imatinib was found to have a secondary KIT D816E mutation at time of relapse (PMID: 16551858).

The KIT P577_D579del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in thymic cancer (PMID: 22357254). While this variant has not been functionally validated, a thymic cancer patient with this alteration had a clinical response to sorafenib therapy (PMID: 22357254).

The KIT P551_W557delinsL mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 25239608). This mutation has not yet been functionally validated but a single patient with GIST harboring the P551_W557delinsL mutation experienced clinical benefit in response to ponatinib treatment after previously progressing on imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib (PMID: 25239608).

The KIT F522C mutation is located in the transmembrane domain in exon 10 of the protein. This mutation has been found in mastocytosis (PMID: 15070706). Expression of this variant in COS-7 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein phosphorylation in the absence of ligand (PMID: 15070706). In vitro studies have shown that the KIT F522C alteration is sensitive to imatinib, as measured by decreased protein activation and decreased cell viability with imatinib treatment (PMID: 15070706). A patient with mastocytosis harboring KIT F522C experienced a clinical response to treatment with imatinib (PMID: 15070706).

The KIT M541L mutation is located in the transmembrane domain in exon 10 of the protein. The KIT M541L mutation has been reported in 7-9% of the population (dbSNP rs3822214) and it is not clear since it occurs frequently in the general population whether or not it is associated with cancer in Caucasians (PMID: 21757432, 25015329, 16307017). This mutation has been identified in aggressive fibromatosis (germline) (PMID: 20664593), Merkel cell carcinoma (PMID: 21498700), mastocytosis, (PMID: 18795925) and chronic eosinophilic leukemia (PMID: 25015329). Biological characterization of KIT M541L in myeloid cells demonstrated that it is activating, as evidenced by cell viability and transformation assays (PMID: 18795925). Four patients with chronic eosinophilic leukemia not otherwise specified with the M541L mutation responded to low dose imatinib therapy (100 mg daily orally) and achieved complete hematological remissions (PMID: 25015329). Further, three patients with aggressive fibromatosis with the germline M541L variant were responsive to imatinib therapy, with one patient achieving a complete response (PMID: 20664593).

The KIT D816A mutation is located in the kinase domain in exon 17 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 18955458). While this variant has not been functionally validated, another amino acid substitution at this position (D816F) has been shown to be gain-of-function and oncogenic (PMID: 16397263). KIT D816A was identified as a secondary KIT mutation in patients with GIST who developed resistance to imatinib and sunitinib therapy (PMID: 18955458).

The KIT K558_V560del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 25239608). This mutation has not yet been functionally validated but a single patient with GIST harboring the W557C and K558_V560del mutations experienced clinical benefit in response to ponatinib treatment after previously progressing on imatinib, sunitinib and regorafenib (PMID: 25239608).

The KIT V852I mutation is located in the kinase domain in exon 18 of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 21642685). While this variant has not been functionally validated, in a Phase II study of 295 melanoma patients treated with imatinib, one patient with KIT V852I progressed on imatinib treatment (PMID: 21642685).

The KIT Y553_Q556del mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 11 of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) (PMID: 15690055). Expression of this variant in human GIST tumor cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased KIT phosphorylation compared to wildtype KIT (PMID: 15690055).
