In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS E62K demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS D33E mutation is located in the Switch I region of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in leukemia and colorectal cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in kidney epithelial cells demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased pathway activation and in vivo tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27147599).

The KRAS K170Q mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 25344691). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS K170Q demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by MAPK signaling activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS D119N mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in leukemia, lymphoma and glioma (PMID: 28958387, 28572459). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in rat medullary and rabbit kidney cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation, decreased binding to negative regulators, increased pathway activation and increased cell outgrowth compared to wildtype (PMID: 10454576, 8552403, 11103938).

The KRAS E76G mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 27149842). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS E76G demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS F156L mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in Cranio-facio-cutaneous syndrome (PMID: 17601930). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in various cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation, decreased binding to negative regulators, and increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20949621, 7877967, 20949621, 17601930).

The KRAS Y64H mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and cervical squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 23456389, 29185262). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS Y64H demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS G13H mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS G13H demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS Q61P mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in acute myeloid leukemia and multiple myeloma (PMID: 22658276, 30201956). This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011). Structure analysis suggests that this mutation could alter the stability, flexibility, and compactness of native KRAS protein structure which could be highly deleterious as assessed by molecular dynamics simulation and trajectories analysis (PMID: 31117243). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS Q61P demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS Q22K mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung cancer and as a germline variant in Noonan syndrome (PMID: 26284123, 20949621). Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast and simian cell lines demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased pathway activation, colony formation and in vivo tumor progression compared to wildtype (PMID: 23059812, 20570890, 11095964, 34117033).

The KRAS T74P mutation is located in the Switch II region of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (Abstract: Waring et al. Abstract# e14536, ASCO 2014. https://ascopubs.org/doi/abs/10.1200/jco.2014.32.15_suppl.e14536). Expression of this mutation in human embryonic kidney and bone marrow cells demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by modestly increased protein activation, increased pathway activation, and increased bone marrow proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19075190).

The KRAS M67R mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in plasma cell myeloma (PMID: 22573403). Biochemical assays and microarray data of KRAS M67R demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased GDP-binding, upregulation of cell-cycle progression genes and downregulation of tumor suppressor genes compared to wildtype (Abstract: Qian et al. Abstract# 2586, AACR 2020. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/80/16_Supplement/2586/642138/Abstract-2586-Identification-of-cancer-associated).

The KRAS K176N mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS K176N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS K117D mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 31938404). While this substitution has not been functionally characterized, it is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011).

The KRAS K178del mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS K178del demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by MAPK signaling activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS R68C mutation is located in the the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Although only characterized in the context of KRAS G12C expression, in vitro studies with KRAS G12C-mutant Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS R68C demonstrate resistance to adagrasib and sotorasib as measured by sustained cell viability (PMID: 34161704). In a case report, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring KRAS G12C acquired KRAS R68C after treatment with adagrasib (PMID: 34161704).

The KRAS Q25H mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with gallbladder cancer. This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized, however, computational analysis predicts that it is inactivating as measured by disruption to protein structure compared to wildtype (PMID: 21375404).

The KRAS G12L mutation is located in the P-loop of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 12460918). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS G12L demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033). Next-generation sequencing of non-small lung cancer patients harboring KRAS G12L demonstrates that the mutation is likely activating as measured by the highest tumor mutation burden compared to other KRAS G12 mutations (PMID: 35280306).

The KRAS L19F mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in leukemia and colorectal, lung and bladder cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein activation, anchorage-independent growth and in vivo tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 17150185, 20147967).

The KRAS E31D mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 31289513). Expression of this mutation in a fibroblast cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by altered morphology, increased cell proliferation, and increased cell migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 31289513).

The KRAS Y71D mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS Y71D demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS K5N mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation was found in the germline of a patient with Noonan syndrome (PMID:17875937). Expression of this mutation in simian and human cell lines demonstrated that it is likely activating, as measured by a modest increase in pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20949621, 25941399).

The KRAS A59G mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in leukemia, lymphoma, and colorectal and lung cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in human embryonic kidney cell lines demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein activation, downstream pathway activation and tumor growth in vivo compared to wildtype (PMID: 26841430, 27147599).

The KRAS G13E mutation is located in the P-loop of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 19521964). While this substitution has not been functionally characterized, it is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011).

The KRAS G12A mutation is located in the P-loop of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 26662311, 23182985). Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is activating as measured by constitutive protein activation due to structural changes compared to wildtype (PMID: 26037647). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to BRAF inhibition in lymphoid cells as measured by decreased pathway activation in the presence of the drug, but is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor cobimetinib (PMID: 30341394). A patient with hairy cell leukemia acquired a KRAS G12D mutation following relapse on the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib but was successfully treated with the cobimetinib for at least twelve months (PMID: 30341394).

The KRAS D153V mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in Noonan syndrome (PMID: 16987887, 16474405). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in various cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation and modestly increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20949621, 17875937, 20949621, 17875937).

The KRAS Y32S mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation and decreased binding to regulatory proteins compared to wildtype (PMID: 26841430, 11333268).

The KRAS T50I mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in melanoma and colorectal cancer (PMID: 25148578, 27149842). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS T50I demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS G60_A66dup mutation is located in the switch-II domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms (PMID: 26854029). Expression of this mutation in primary myeloid progenitor cells and Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by decreased rates of GTPase activity, increased colony growth and increased rates of cell transformation compared to wildtype KRAS (PMID: 26854029).

The KRAS E62_A66dup mutation is located in the switch-2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms (PMID: 26854029). Expression of this mutation in primary myeloid progenitor cells and Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by decreased rates of GTPase activity, increased colony growth and increased rates of cell transformation compared to wildtype KRAS (PMID: 26854029).

The KRAS Y71H mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in Noonan and cardio-facio-cutaneous syndromes (PMID: 21797849). Expression of this mutation in simian cells demonstrated that it may be activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype, despite there being no change in levels of RAS-GTP compared to wildtype (PMID: 23059812).

Wildtype KRAS has no mutations. The absence of mutation in KRAS is clinically relevant as RAS mutation status in stage IV colorectal cancer influences patient responses to the anti-EGFR antibody therapies cetuximab and panitumumab. These drugs are FDA-approved for the treatment of KRAS wildtype colorectal tumors, either alongside chemotherapy or as single agents following progression on standard chemotherapy (Abstract: NCCN Colon 2.2017.https://www.nccn.org/professionals/physician_gls/pdf/colon.pdf).

The KRAS Q61L mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung, colorectal and pancreatic cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in murine cells demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25437878, 26854029).

The KRAS G13V mutation is located in the P-loop of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011). Expression of this mutation in H1299 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32929330).

The KRAS P34L mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation was identified as a germline mutation in Noonan syndrome (PMID: 16474405). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in a simian cell line demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by decreased binding to regulatory proteins and increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20949621).

The KRAS E49* mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 24951259). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS E49* demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS Q61R mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in pancreatic, colorectal, thyroid and lung cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in murine cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation (PMID: 25437878). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS Q61R demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to BRAF inhibition in lymphoid cells as measured by decreased pathway activation in the presence of the drug, but is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor cobimetinib (PMID: 30341394). A patient with hairy cell leukemia acquired a KRAS Q61R mutation following relapse on the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib but was successfully treated with cobimetinib for at least twelve months (PMID: 30341394).

The KRAS K147E mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in a simian cell line demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by constitutive protein activation and increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 23059812).

The KRAS Q61H mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung, pancreatic and colorectal cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in fibroblast and breast cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation, pathway activation and colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 20147967, 25705018, 21993244, 24651010, 34117033).

The KRAS A59T mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011) and has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 31816869). Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cell proliferation and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 31816869). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS A59T demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS N116H mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and colorectal cancer (PMID: 30304655, 30239619). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS N116H demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation contributes to resistance to the KRAS G12C inhibitor ARS853 in a lung cancer cell line harboring this mutation as measured by sustained cell proliferation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 26841430).

The KRAS G60E mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Biochemical assays and microarray data of KRAS G60E demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased GTP-binding, upregulation of cell-cycle progression genes and downregulation of tumor suppressor genes compared to wildtype (Abstract: Qian et al. Abstract# 2586, AACR 2020. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/80/16_Supplement/2586/642138/Abstract-2586-Identification-of-cancer-associated).

The KRAS G12W mutation is located in the P-loop of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 19521964). While this substitution has not been functionally characterized, it is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011).

The KRAS A146V mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal and lung cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in fibroblast and embryonic kidney cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 3043178, 26841430). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS A146V demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to BRAF inhibition in lymphoid cells as measured by decreased pathway activation in the presence of the drug, but is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor cobimetinib (PMID: 30341394). A patient with hairy cell leukemia acquired a KRAS A146V mutation following relapse on the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib but was successfully treated with cobimetinib for at least twelve months (PMID: 30341394).

The KRAS G12S mutation is located in the P-loop of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung, colorectal and breast cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in a lung cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased downstream pathway activation and in vivo tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26184075, 25284075).

The KRAS R68M mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS R68M demonstrate resistance to sotorasib, as measured by sustained cell viability, and sensitivity to adagrasib, as measured by reduced cell viability (PMID: 33971321).

The KRAS D57N mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and plasma cell myeloma (PMID: 22895193, 28234344). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS D57N demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by MAPK signaling activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS Q61A mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in pancreatic cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In silico analysis of the mutation predict that it is likely activating through enhancing the binding flexibility and strength of the protein compared to wildtype (PMID: 35425180).

The KRAS T20M mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 28481359). There is inconclusive functional data about this mutation as in vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS T20M demonstrate the MAPK signaling activity lies between wildtype and the activating control (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS G12F mutation is located in the P-loop of the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung and colorectal cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28572459, 26619011). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS G12F demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033). Two patients with non-small cell lung cancer harboring this mutation, out of a study of 62 patients, responded to combination therapy of the EGFR inhibitor gefitinib and the mTOR inhibitor everolimus (PMID: 20871262).

The KRAS G13S mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and plasma cell myeloma (PMID: 17697521, 2681517). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS G13S demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The KRAS C118S mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a knock-in mouse model exposed to the carcinogen urethane and in an HRAS G13D-expressing xenograft model demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased tumorigenesis compared to wildtype or expression of HRAS G13D alone (PMID: 25394415, 25902334).

The KRAS Y96D mutation is located in the switch-II pocket of the protein. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer. Structural modeling predicts this mutation disrupts the structure of the switch-II binding pocket. While this mutation has not been characterized alone, this mutation confers resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib when expressed with KRAS G12C (PMID: 33824136, 34161704). Two patients with non-small cell lung cancer acquired a KRAS Y96D mutation upon progressing on adagrasib and sotorasib, respectively (PMID: 33824136, 34161704).

The KRAS M67L mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in plasma cell myeloma (PMID: 22573403). Biochemical assays and microarray data of KRAS M67L demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased GDP-binding, upregulation of cell-cycle progression genes and downregulation of tumor suppressor genes compared to wildtype (Abstract: Qian et al. Abstract# 2586, AACR 2020. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/80/16_Supplement/2586/642138/Abstract-2586-Identification-of-cancer-associated).

The KRAS E98* mutation is located in the catalytic G-domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 28978093). In vitro studies using a Novellus FACT assay with Ba/F3 cells expressing KRAS E98* demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced MAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34117033).

The MEK1 G128V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and occurs as a result of a mutation in exon 3 of the MAP2K1 gene. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it was activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E-mutant A375 melanoma cells demonstrated that it can confer resistance to BRAF and MEK inhibition with dabrafenib and trametinib in vitro as measured by sustained cell proliferation upon drug treatment (PMID: 24265153). A patient with relapsed metastatic melanoma presented with the MEK1 G128V mutation after progression on RAF inhibitor therapy (PMID: 24265153).

The MAP2K1 A106T mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast and embryonic kidney cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25164765, 32641410).

The MEK1 E203V mutation is located in the distal kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK1 L101_E102del mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410.

The MEK1 P105_I107del mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, the MEK1 P105_I107delinsS mutation has been shown to be oncogenic and therefore the P105_I107del mutation is considered likely oncogenic. A patient with histiocytic neoplasm harboring the MEK1 P105_I107del mutation had a complete response to treatment with the MEK1/2 inhibitor cobimetinib (PMID: 30867592).

The MEK1 N109_R113del mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and is adjacent to a known oncogenic indel hotspot. This mutation has been found in patients with melanoma whose tumors lack other known driver alterations.  Computational modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it was activating and expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line also demonstrated that it was activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK1 E203Q mutation is located in the distal kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is modestly activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MAP2K1 S327T mutation is located in the distal kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK1 E41_F53del mutation is located in the negative regulatory domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in histiocytosis and melanoma (PMID: 32641410). Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MAP2K1 K97_L98del mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK1 E144K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and occurs as a result of a mutation in exon 3 of the MAP2K1 gene. This mutation has been found in histiocytic neoplasm (PMID: 26566875). There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of the MAP2K1 E144K mutation in 293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream pathway activation associated with mutant MEK1 compared to wildtype MEK1 (PMID: 26566875). However, expression of this mutation in 293T cells in another study demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK1 L50_E51insI mutation is located in the negative regulatory domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in stomach adenocarcinoma (PMID: 32641410). Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK1 P105_I107delinsS mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a cell line model demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased downstream MAP kinase signaling as compared to wildtype (PMID: 28935960).

The MEK1 V154I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the MEK1 protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it was found in a patient with metastatic melanoma who showed resistance to RAF inhibitors (PMID: 24265153).

The MEK1 L98_I103del mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in 293H cells suggests it is activating as measured by increased downstream MAPK pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK1 (PMID: 29483135, 32641410). The activity of this mutant is independent of RAF (PMID: 29483135). This mutant is insensitive to allosteric MEK inhibitors but retains sensitivity to ATP-competitive MEK inhibitors (PMID: 29483135).

The MEK1 P105_A106del mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 32641410).  Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation was resistant to the MEK inhibitor trametinib as measured by sustained pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MAP2K1 I103_K104del mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 32641410). Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 28935960, 29483135, 32641410). The activity of this mutant is RAF-independent (PMID: 29483135). The MED12 G44S mutation occurs in exon 2 of the gene and affects a highly evolutionarily conserved region of the MED12 protein. Affinity purification mass spectrometry analysis performed on wildtype and G44S mutant MED12 proteins revealed that the G44S variant disrupts the MED12-Cyclin C binding interface leading to uncoupling of Cyclin C-CDK8/CDK19 complex from the core Mediator complex, and resulting in loss of Mediator-associated CDK kinase activity (PMID: 24746821).

Truncating mutations of MAP3K1 are seen across the entire length of the gene and are found in various cancer types (PMID: 24386504, 24003131) (cBioPortal, MSKCC, Feb 2017). While some truncating mutations have been shown to be inactivating and oncogenic, because MAP3K1 can act as both a tumor suppressor and an oncogene, others have been shown to be activating and oncogenic (PMID: 24386504, 24003131). Multiple studies point to the link between MAP3K1 kinase activity, normal androgen receptor (AR) function and apoptosis in prostate cancer (PMID:10373563, 11971970). The AR plays a critical role in normal prostate development as well as contributes to prostate carcinogenesis. In one study, overexpression of a truncated, constitutively active MAP3K1 mutant protein led to caspase-dependant apoptosis in AR-positive prostate cancer cells. This effect was not observed in AR-negative cells or with a catalytically inactive form of MAP3K1 (PMID: 10373563). In a separate study, it was shown that AR acetylation was necessary for MAP3K1 induced apoptosis (PMID: 11971970). These results demonstrate the interplay between MAP3K1 and AR pathways and dependence of MAP3K1 induced apoptosis on the intact AR function in prostate cancer cells. (PMID: 24135036, 25899310, 25613373)

In a study of lung cancer, melanoma, and colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines, MED12 knockdown was shown to make the drug-sensitive cell lines H3122, PC9 and H3255, A375, and SW1417 resistant to ALK inhibitors, EGFR inhibitors, and BRAF/MEK inhibitors, respectively. Knockdown of MED12 in these cell lines led to higher levels of phosphorylated MEK and ERK, and that drug resistance was mediated by elevation of TGF-βR2 protein levels, leading in turn to activation of TGF-β signaling. The activation of TGF-β signaling was shown to be both necessary and resistant for drug resistance across all cell lines (PMID: 23178117).

The MAP3K1 T779fs mutation results in truncated catalytically inactive MAP3K1 lacking the kinase domain (residues 1243-1508) (PMID: 25899310). The effect of this mutation in the context of Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LHC) has not been studied, however, given that the most prevalent MAP3K1 alterations in tumors are inactivating it has been speculated that T779fs may confer survival advantage to LHC cells as well, perhaps via abolishing MAP3K1 pro-apoptotic function (PMID: 25899310).

MED12 G44D mutation occurs in exon 2 of the MED12 gene, and affects highly evolutionarily conserved region of the MED12 protein. Affinity purification (AP) mass spectrometry (MS) analysis performed on wildtype and G44D mutant MED12 proteins purifed from Flp-In 293 TRex cells engineered to express these constructs revealed that the G44D variant disrupts the MED12-Cyclin C binding interface, leading to its decreased association with Cyclin C-CDK8/CDK19 complex, and thereby resulting in loss of Mediator-associated CDK kinase activity (PMID: 24746821).

MED12 exon 2 mutations are the most commonly detected of the MED12 mutations and are seen in various tumor types, especially uterine leiomyosarcomas. Among exon 2 mutations, the most common is a hotspot mutation in G44. Several studies have shown that MED12 exon 2 mutations are central to the genesis of tumors such as uterine leiomyoma (UL) and breast fibroadenoma, and suggest that exon 2 mutations rupture the association between MED12 and CDK8/Mediator (PMID: 23913526, 21868628, 23738515, 25038752, 24746821, 29440396).

MED12 truncating mutations occur throughout the protein and cause loss of functional MED12. These mutations have been identified in uterine leiomyomas, breast tumors, chronic lymphocytic leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 28054750). In vitro studies with Flp-In 293 T-REx cells expressing the 5′ end nonsense MED12 mutation MED12 E33* demonstrate that N-terminal truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by MED12 mislocalization and nonsense-mediated mRNA decay avoidance (PMID: 28054750).

The MEN1 S253L mutation is located in exon 3 of the gene. This mutation has been identified in sporadic parathyroid tumors (PMID: 10931084). In vitro studies with COS7, 293T and WI38VA13 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate that MEN1 S253L is inactivating as measured by reduced MEN1 steady-state expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 21819486).

MEN1 truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in loss of protein function. These mutations have been identified in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (PMID: 35287658). In vitro studies in MEN1-deficient human melanocytes demonstrate that MEN1 truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by decreased DNA double-strand break repair and homology-directed repair and increased non-homologous end joining compared to wildtype MEN1 expression (PMID: 23648481).

The MED12 L1224F mutation occurs in the central region of the gene, distinct from the recurrent Glycine (G) 44 mutation observed in uterine leiomyomas. This mutation has been reported as a recurrent hotspot in prostate cancer and may perturb CDK8-dependent modulation of transcriptional programs linked to p53 and androgen signaling (PMID: 12218053, 17612495, 26619011). Cell lines expressing the L1244F mutation did not exhibit impaired interactions between MED12 and Cyclin C or CDK8/19, and did not exhibit reduced kinase activity of CDK8 module. Rather, the MED12 L1224F mutation was associated with reduced interaction with other Mediator components (MED1, MED13, MED13L etc) (PMID: 26383637).

Deletions of MEN1 are associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type1. These heterozygous deletions are typically large in size on chromosome 11q13, encompassing the entire MEN1 gene and correlates with poor prognosis (PMID: 21627674, 9510467, 12746426, 27076911). Conditional knockout of MEN1 in mouse parathyroid glands resulted in parathyroid neoplasia and systemic hypercalcemia (PMID: 14633735). MEN1 deletion specifically in mouse pancreatic beta-cells resulted in hyperplastic islets with increased proliferation and insulinomas. The islet lesions exhibited features of multistage tumor progression, including β-cell dedifferentiation, angiogenesis, and altered expression of both E-cadherin and β-catenin, which mirrors human MEN1 phenotypes (PMID:12941803,16740708).

The MEN1 G331D mutation is located in exon 7 of the gene. This mutation was identified as an acquired resistance mutation in in vivo studies with patient-derived xenograft acute myeloid leukemia mouse models following two months of treatment with menin inhibitor VTP-50469, an analog to revumenib (PMID: 36922589).

The MEN1 M327V mutation is located in exon 7 of the gene. Although not functionally characterized per se, this mutation was identified as an acquired resistance mutation in two patients with KMT2A-rearranged acute myeloid leukemia following treatment with revumenib (PMID: 36922589).

The MEN1 G331R mutation is located in exon 7 of the gene. Although not functionally characterized per se, this mutation was identified as an acquired resistance mutation alongside MEN1 M327I in a patient with cytoplasmic NPM1-mutant acute myeloid leukemia following treatment with revumenib (PMID: 36922589).

The MEN1 M327I mutation is located in exon 7 of the gene. Although not functionally characterized per se, this mutation was identified as an acquired resistance mutation alongside MEN1 G331R in a patient with cytoplasmic NPM1-mutant acute myeloid leukemia following treatment with revumenib (PMID: 36922589).

The MEN1 T349M mutation is located in exon 7 of the gene. Although not functionally characterized per se, this mutation was identified as an acquired resistance mutation in a patient with KMT2A-rearranged acute myeloid leukemia following treatment with revumenib (PMID: 36922589).

MED12 exon 1 mutation-positive tumors, similar to tumors harboring MED12 exon 2 mutations, showed clear overexpression of RAD51B. MED12 exon 1 mutations uncouple Cyclin C-CDK8/19 from core mediator, resulting in the loss of mediator-associated kinase activity, as demonstrated by immunoprecipitation assays. The similarity in loss of mediator-associated CDK activity and RAD51B overexpression in MED12 exon 1- and exon 2-mutated tumors indicates a role of MED12 in the development of uterine leiomyomas harboring either of these mutations (PMID: 24980722).

The MET N1100Y mutation is located proximal to the MET ATP-binding site. Expression of this mutation in breast cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by constitutive protein activation and increased cell mobility and invasion compared to wildtype MET (PMID: 12460923).

The CAPZA2-MET rearrangement results from a fusion between CAPZA2 and MET. While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29102694, 29284707, 27748748, 28512244, 29527595). In a case report, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring the CAPZA2-MET fusion was treated with tepotinib and demonstrated partial response (PMID: 37429463).

var_description: Mutations affecting the splice sites flanking MET exon 14 result in alternative splicing of the MET gene with in-frame loss of the region encoded by exon 14, a region within the juxtamembrane domain of MET (PMID: 16397241, 19096300, 15735036). Loss of MET exon 14 results in the loss of binding to the MET negative regulator CBL, increased MET protein levels, enhanced downstream MET signaling, and promotion of cell growth (PMID: 25971939, 26729443, 25971938, 26215952). A patient with non-small cell lung cancer who progressed on osimertinib after developing a MET exon 14 splice mutation had partial response to and clinical benefit from combination osimertinib plus crizotinib (PMID: 31157314).

The MET E168D mutation is located in the extracellular sema domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung cancer (PMID: 14559814). Expression of this mutation in COS7 cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by modestly increased ligand binding and modestly increased apoptosis with MET inhibition compared to wildtype (PMID: 19723643). However, this mutation is found in 0.6% of the general population (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/variant/7-116699588-G-T?dataset=gnomad_r4) and in the germline context is considered benign (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/variation/VCV000041627.51/?redir=vcv).

The MET T992I mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain in exon 14 of the protein. This mutation has been identified in the germline across multiple cancers (PMID: 25605252, 15735036, 21970370, 21970370). There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. While expression of the MET T992I mutation in Ba/F3 cells and a small cell lung cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased ligand-independent cell proliferation, increased cell invasion and increased production of reactive oxygen species compared to wildtype MET (PMID:14559814, 17322284), other in vitro experiments have documented that there is no difference in protein activation and transforming ability between the MET T992I mutation and wildtype MET when using 293, T17 and MCF-7 cells (PMID: 20670955, 22973954).

The HLA-DRB1-MET fusion is a fusion of exon 5 of HLA-DRB1 to exon 12 of MET. This fusion has been found in a patient with non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 29527595). While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic. A patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring the HLA-DRB1-MET fusion had a near complete response to crizotinib lasting 8+ months (PMID: 29527595).

The MET-DST fusion is a fusion of exon 4 of DST with exon 11 of MET. This fusion has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 36806896). While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29102694, 29284707, 27748748, 28512244, 29527595). The MET-DST fusion is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors as a patient with NSCLC harboring the fusion had marked improvements after one week of treatment with crizotinib (PMID: 36806896).

The MET V1092I mutation is located in the MET ATP-binding site. Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein activation and cell transformation compared to wildtype MET (PMID: 10417759). In vitro studies of cells expressing the MET V1092I mutation show that this mutation is sensitive to the MET inhibitor, EMD1214063, as measured by protein activity following drug treatment (PMID: 24061647). Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET V1092I demonstrate sensitivity to capmatinib, tepotinib, elzovantinib and cabozantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext).

The MET D1002A mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the MET protein. In vitro assays have demonstrated that this mutation is transforming and activating as measured by increased colony formation and decreased ubiquitination as compared to wildtype. Structural modeling predicts that the D1002A mutation would abrogate the salt bridge required for the binding of the Met receptor into the c-Cbl TKB domain binding pocket, which plays a critical role in the downregulation of the receptor and termination of the signaling pathway through receptor ubiquitination (PMID: 15123609).

The MET V1220I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by colony formation in soft agar (PMID: 19783361). In vitro studies have suggested that MET V1220I is sensitive to MET inhibitors SU11274 and EMD1214063, as determined by decreased colony formation upon drug treatment (PMID: 19783361).

The MET Y1230C mutation is located in the kinase domain of MET. When expressed into NIH 3T3 cells the Y1230C mutation displayed increased level of tyrosine phosphorylation in comparison to wild type MET, around 2-to 3-fold higher This mutant was also able to mediate anchorage-independent growth when expressed in NIH 3T3 cells (PMID: 9826708). This mutation also has been observed in solid tumors such as head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) where it induces transformation, tumor proliferation and metastasis by increasing the kinase activity of MET (PMID: 18709663).

The MET Y1235D mutation is located at the site of MET autophosphorylation. Expression of this variant in MPL29 cells demonstrated that this variant is activating, as measured by increased kinase activity and increased invasion through matrigel (PMID: 10734314). This mutation leads to MET activation and confers an invasive phenotype on carcinoma cells transduced with this mutant (PMID: 12460923).

The MET V1188L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by transformed morphology and cell motility (PMID: 24061647). In vitro studies have suggested that MET V1188L is resistant to MET inhibitors SU11274 and EMD1214063, as determined by sustained cell motility upon drug treatment (PMID: 15064724, 24061647).

The CAV1-MET rearrangement results from a fusion of exons 1 and 2 of CAV1 fusing with exons 2 through 21 of MET. While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic. In a case report, a patient with small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR L858R acquired the CAV1-MET fusion after progression on gefitinib and was treated with the combination of crizotinib and osimertinib and demonstrated substantial tumor shrinkage (PMID: 31122565). In another case report, a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring the CAV1-MET fusion was treated with ensartinib and demonstrated progressive disease with a progression-free survival of one month (PMID: 36806896).

var_description: The MET D1010H mutation (referred to as D1028H in an alternate isoform) occurs in exon 14 of the MET gene, which encodes the juxtamembrane domain of the resulting MET protein product. MET D1010 occurs adjacent to a MET exon-14 splice donor site; alterations affecting this splice site lead to exon 14 skipping and subsequently aberrant activation of MET downstream signaling (PMID: 19096300, 25971938). Mutations in this domain have been shown to lead to increased MET stability, enhanced signaling downstream of MET and sensitivity to crizotinib (PMID: 14559814, 15735036, 16227611, 16397241, 19096300, 25971938). There are several clinical reports documenting patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring the MET D1010H mutation who have responded to treatment with crizotinib, including partial responses (PMID: 27343443, 27666659, 26892698) and near complete response (PMID: 25898965).

The MET H1094R mutation is located in the MET tyrosine kinase domain. This mutation was found as a germline mutation in two large families with hereditary papillary renal carcinoma (PMID: 9563489). Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased colony formation and in vivo tumor formation compared to wildtype MET (PMID: 9563489).

The PRKAR2B-MET rearrangement results from a fusion of exon 1 of PRKAR2B fusing with exon 14 of MET. While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29102694, 29284707, 27748748, 28512244, 29527595). In a case report, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring the PRKAR2B-MET fusion and MET A1214dup was treated with crizotinib and demonstrated stable disease (PMID: 36521334, 37429463).

The MET Y1248H mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 28396313). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing MET Y1248H demonstrate resistance to treatment with type I MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors as measured by persistent phosphorylation and cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 28396313).

The MET D1228H mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 36806896). MET D1228H was identified as a secondary resistance mutation in patients with NSCLC harboring MET fusions following MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatments (PMID: 36806896).

var_description: This mutation occurs in the intronic regions flanking exon 14 of MET (PMID: 16397241, 19096300, 15735036). It results in alternative splicing of the gene with in-frame loss of the region encoded by exon 14, a region within the juxtamembrane domain of MET. The splice variant displays loss of binding to the MET negative regulator CBL, increased MET protein levels, enhanced downstream MET signaling, and promotion of cell growth (PMID: 25971939, 26729443, 25971938, 26215952). A patient with non-small cell lung cancer who progressed on osimertinib after developing a MET exon 14 splice mutation had partial response to and clinical benefit from combination osimertinib plus crizotinib (PMID: 31157314).

The MET R1004A mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the MET protein. In vitro assays have demonstrated that this mutation is transforming and activating as measured by increased colony formation and decreased ubiquitination as compared to wildtype. Structural modeling predicts that the R1004A mutation would abrogate the salt bridge required for the binding of the Met receptor into the c-Cbl TKB domain binding pocket, which plays a critical role in the downregulation of the receptor and termination of the signaling pathway through receptor ubiquitination (PMID: 15123609).

The EPHB4-MET fusion is a fusion of exon 9 of EPHB4 to exon 15 of MET. This fusion has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 36806896). In vitro studies with IL-3-depleted Ba/F3 cells expressing EPHB4-MET demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by IL-3–independent cell growth compared to empty vectors (PMID: 36806896). The EPHB4-MET fusion is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors as a patient with NSCLC harboring the fusion had marked improvements after one week of treatment with crizotinib (PMID: 36806896).

The MET H1094Y mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by transformed morphology and cell motility (PMID: 24061647). In vitro studies have suggested that MET H1094Y is sensitive to MET inhibitors SU11274 and EMD1214063, as determined by decreased colony formation and cell motility upon drug treatment (PMID: 15064724, 24061647). Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET H1094Y demonstrate sensitivity to crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib and elzovantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext).

The MET Y1230H mutation occurs within the MET kinase domain. This mutation is typically found in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), specifically in patients who develop resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as crizotinib (PMID: 27666659, 29128427, 28522754, 28396313, 27987579). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased protein phosphorylation, pathway activation and anchorage-independent growth.  Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET Y1230H demonstrate resistance to capmatinib and tepotinib and sensitivity to cabozantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext). A patient with NSCLC harboring the Y1230H mutation had a response to cabozantinib, with in silico modeling demonstrating the ability of cabozantinib to bind to Y1230H-mutant MET (PMID: 9826708, 9326629, 27666659, 29128427, 28522754, 28396313, 27987579, 29128427).

The PTPRZ1-MET fusion occurs between the MET gene and the PTPRZ1 gene, which encodes a member of the receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase family and whose expression is restricted to the central nervous system. This fusion was shown to be present in grade III astrocytomas and secondary glioblastomas (PMID: 25135958, 27748748, 28512244). This fusion results from the fusion of the full-length MET gene with the promoter of the PTPRZ1 gene, resulting in high-level MET expression (PMID: 27748748). Exogenous overexpression of the MET-PTPRZ1 fusion protein in U87MG glioblastoma cell lines resulted in enhanced cell migration and invasion. Expression of this mutation in human astrocyte (HA) and patient-derived IDH wild-type GBM (N33) cell lines and in the U87 MG xenograft model demonstrated that it was activating as shown by increased pathway activation and increased tumor proliferation compared to cells expressing wildtype levels of MET (PMID: 30343896). Patient derived samples of secondary glioma expressing the PTPRZ1-MET fusion demonstrated increased tumor-infiltrating macropahges compared to samples expressing wildtype MET (PMID: 30343896). Expressing of the PTPRZ1-MET fusion in astrocyte cell line models and U87 MG xenograft models demonstrated that this mutation was sensitive to the MET inhbitor PLPB-1001, as shown by inhibition of the increased downstream pathway activation and decreased tumor burden compared to treatment by vehicle or crizotinib (PMID: 30343896). In a Phase II clinical trial for PLPB-1001, 18 recurrent high-grade glioma patients were included, comprised of 9 sGBMs and 9 grade III gliomas carrying the PTPRZ1-MET fusion and/or METex14. Out of six sGBM patients who stayed in the trial, two achieved partial response (PR), two achieved stable disease (SD), and two had progressed disease (PD). Of the nine grade III glioma patients, five achieved SD and four had PD (PMID: 30343896).

The MET P1153L mutation is located in the β4-β5 loop site of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing MET P1153L demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 37577651).

The MET D1246N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 28396313). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing MET D1246N demonstrated resistance to treatment with type I MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors as measured by persistent phosphorylation and cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 28396313). MET D1246N was identified as a secondary resistance mutation in patients with NSCLC harboring MET fusions following MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatments (PMID: 36806896).

The MET V1070E mutation is located in the MET tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased kinase activity and increased anchorage-independent growth compared to wildtype MET (PMID: 25401301).

The MET Y1365F mutation is located C-terminal region of the protein. In vitro studies with MDCK cells expressing MET Y1365F demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced binding of TNS4 to MET compared to wildtype (PMID: 24814316). TNS4 interaction with wildtype MET positively regulates cellular survival, proliferation and migration, and increases MET protein stability in human colon carcinoma and ovarian cells (PMID: 24814316).

The MET M1250T mutation is a rare mutation occurring within the kinase domain of the MET protein. This mutation has been found in cases of papillary renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 10327054). This mutation has been shown to activate MET function in vitro when expressed in NIH3T3 cells and to promote an invasive phenotype in vivo, as demonstrated by increased growth and metastasis in NIH3T3 xenograft models in nude mice (PMID: 9826715, 15557554, 10871851). Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET M1250T demonstrate sensitivity to capmatinib, tepotinib and elzovantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext).

The MET-KDD variant is activating as shown by increased pathway activation when expressed in NIH-3T3 cells. The MET-KDD variant was identified in a patient who had an ALK rearrangement and had acquired resistance to ceritinib. This patient then partially responded to crizotinib treatment. In vitro data of NIH-3T3 cells expressing this variant along with EML4-ALK showed sensitivity to crizotinib but not to ceritinib (PMID: 29284707).

var_description: In-frame deletions affecting the splice sites flanking MET exon 14 result in alternative splicing of the MET gene with in-frame loss of the region encoded by exon 14, a region within the juxtamembrane domain of MET (PMID: 16397241, 19096300, 15735036). Loss of MET exon 14 results in the loss of binding to the MET negative regulator CBL, increased MET protein levels, enhanced downstream MET signaling, and promotion of cell growth (PMID: 25971939, 26729443, 25971938, 26215952).

The MET Y1003C mutation is located in the MET juxtamembrane domain. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, other substitutions at this position (e.g. Y1003F) have been shown to be activating and oncogenic (PMID: 11741535, 15123609, 16227611).

Most MET fusions contain an N-terminally truncated version of MET, including the kinase domain, with a C-terminally truncated version of the fusion partner gene (PMID: 28510278, 27748748). In rare cases such as with the PTPRZ1-MET fusion, the fusion preserves the full-length version of MET and expresses it under the promotor of the fusion partner resulting in MET overexpression (PMID: 27748748). Fusions involving the MET gene occur across numerous tumor types, including non-small cell lung cancer, thyroid cancer, sarcomas and glioblastomas (PMID: 28510278, 27748748, 28512244, 29284707, 29102694, 29284707).  Multiple different MET fusions have been shown to be activating, oncogenic and sensitive to MET inhibitors such as crizotinib both in experimental models as well as in the clinic (PMID: 29102694, 29284707, 27748748, 28512244, 29527595).

The CCDC6-MET fusion is a fusion of exon 1 of CCDC6 with exon 15 of MET. This fusion has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 36806896). While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29102694, 29284707, 27748748, 28512244, 29527595). The CCDC6-MET fusion is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors as a patient with NSCLC harboring the fusion had a partial response to crizotinib with a progression-free survival of 5.0 months (PMID: 36806896).

The MET S1141W mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in papillary renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 24658158). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is likely damaging (PMID: 24658158).

The MET Y1003F mutation occurs at a conserved residue in the protein's juxtamembrane domain. Experiments in vitro and in human kidney cells demonstrated that mutation abrogates the ability of MET to interact with the negative regulator CBL, a ubiquitin ligase promoting degradation of its substrates (PMID: 11741535, 15123609). This likely results in increased signaling through MET and this mutant has oncogenic potential in transformation and growth assays in both a fibroblast and epithelial kidney cell line (PMID: 11741535, 15123609, 16227611).

The MET Y1003 mutation occurs at a conserved residue in the protein's juxtamembrane domain. Experiments in vitro and in human kidney cells demonstrated that the Y1003F mutation abrogates the ability of MET to interact with the negative regulator CBL, a ubiquitin ligase promoting degradation of its substrates (PMID: 11741535, 15123609). This likely results in increased signaling through MET and this mutant has oncogenic potential in transformation and growth assays in both a fibroblast and epithelial kidney cell line (PMID: 11741535, 15123609, 16227611).

The ST7-MET rearrangement results from exon 1 of ST7 fusing with exon 2 of MET. This fusion was identified as an acquired resistance mutation in two patients with ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer following treatment with lorlatinib (PMID: 32086345). While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic. In vitro studies with H3122 cells expressing ST7-MET demonstrate resistance to ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors, except crizotinib, as measured by sustained cell viability following treatment, and sensitivity to MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors, as measured by restored sensitivity to ALK inhibitor lorlatinib (PMID: 32086345). In a case report, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring the ST7-MET fusion was treated with tepotinib and demonstrated progressive disease (PMID: 37429463).

The CD47-MET fusion is a fusion of either exon 5 or exon 7 of CD47 with exon 15 of MET. This fusion has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 36806896). While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29102694, 29284707, 27748748, 28512244, 29527595). The CD47-MET fusion is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors as a patient with NSCLC harboring the fusion had a partial response to treatment with savolitinib with a progression-free survival of 6.5 months (PMID: 36806896).

The MET S290F mutation is located in the extracellular sema domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in congenital melanocytic nevi (PMID: 30359577). In silico analysis suggests that this mutation is a likely neutral passenger mutation (PMID: 30359577).

The MET Y1230N mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is a predicted driver mutation (PMID: 36430388). A patient with MET exon 14 mutated-lung adenocarcinoma was treated with crizotinib and acquired MET Y1230N following disease progression (PMID: 33403024).

The MET R970C mutation (also known as R988C on other transcripts) is located in the protein's juxtamembrane domain. This mutation was identified in the germline of a patient with HER2+ breast cancer as well as in one patient out of 105 patients with triple-negative breast cancer and one patient out of 96 patients with JAK2 V617F-mutated polycythemia vera (PMID: 31004003). There is conflicting data for this mutation (PMID: 25992381). Two studies reported that MET R970C is associated with increased oncogenic function of MET. Experiments in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation leads to constitutive MET phosphorylation and increased cell motility, migration, adhesion and colony formation (PMID: 14559814). Generation of an in vivo transgenic mouse model expressing this mutation demonstrated that it is activating, as all mice harboring the mutation developed autoimmune disease and myeloproliferative syndromes (PMID: 31004003). Treatment of the transgenic mice with the MET inhibitor cabozantinib resulted in an inhibition of the autoimmune and proliferative phenotypes and reduced the number of skin cancers in mice (PMID: 31004003). However, other reports suggest that the R970C mutation is not oncogenic and has no effect on MET phosphorylation (PMID: 22973954, 20670955).

The MET N1100S mutation is located proximal to the MET ATP-binding site. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (Abstract: Pecci et al. Abstract# 9124, ASCO 2022. https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2022.40.16_suppl.9124). Although not functionally characterized, preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET N1100S demonstrate sensitivity to crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib, elzovantinib and cabozantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext).

The MET Y1003N mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 25971938 ). The Y1003 residue is responsible for binding of CBL to MET and the resulting ubiquitin-mediated degradation that follows. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, other substitutions at this position (e.g., Y1003F) have been shown to be activating and oncogenic (PMID: 11741535, 15123609, 16227611, 25971938).

biomark_group: Exon 14 Deletion,Exon 14 in-frame deletions,D1010,Exon 14 splice mutations
var_description: Mutations affecting the splice sites flanking MET exon 14 result in alternative splicing of the MET gene with in-frame loss of the region encoded by exon 14, a region within the juxtamembrane domain of MET (PMID: 16397241, 19096300, 15735036). Loss of MET exon 14 results in the loss of binding to the MET negative regulator CBL, increased MET protein levels, enhanced downstream MET signaling, and promotion of cell growth (PMID: 25971939, 26729443, 25971938, 26215952). A patient with non-small cell lung cancer who progressed on osimertinib after developing a MET exon 14 splice mutation had partial response to and clinical benefit from combination osimertinib plus crizotinib (PMID: 31157314).

var_description: Mutations affecting the splice sites flanking MET exon 14 result in alternative splicing of the MET gene with in-frame loss of the region encoded by exon 14, a region within the juxtamembrane domain of MET (PMID: 16397241, 19096300, 15735036). Loss of MET exon 14 results in the loss of binding to the MET negative regulator CBL, increased MET protein levels, enhanced downstream MET signaling, and promotion of cell growth (PMID: 25971939, 26729443, 25971938, 26215952). A patient with non-small cell lung cancer who progressed on osimertinib after developing a MET exon 14 splice mutation had partial response to and clinical benefit from combination osimertinib plus crizotinib (PMID: 31157314).

The TFG-MET fusion results from the fusion of the 3' end of the TFG gene with the 5' end of the MET gene, including the kinase domain. This mutation has been found in infantile spindle cell sarcoma and pediatric glioblastoma (PMID: 28510278, 27748748). Expression of the TFG-MET fusion in HEK293 cells, Ba/F3 cells, MCF-10A or human cultured astrocytes demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased MET phosphorylation, increased cell transformation, increased cytokine-independent growth, tumor growth in transplanted mice, and sensitivity to the MET inhibitors foretinib and crizotinib compared to wildtype MET (PMID: 27748748, 28512244).

The CLIP2-MET fusion results from the fusion of the 3' end of the CLIP2 gene with the 5' end of the MET gene (PMID: 27748748). This mutation has been found in pediatric glioblastoma (PMID: 27748748). Patient-derived xenografts of cells harboring this mutation were sensitive to MET inhibition with foretinib as measured by decreased tumor growth and decreased MAPK signaling upon drug treatment compared to vehicle (PMID: 27748748)

The MET H1094L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by colony formation in soft agar and tumor growth in mice (PMID: 19783361). In vitro studies have suggested that MET H1094L is sensitive to MET inhibitors SU11274 and EMD1214063, as determined by decreased colony formation, cell motility and tumor growth upon drug treatment (PMID: 19783361, 24061647)

MET amplification results from the gain of the MET gene on chromosome 7q31 and is found in various cancers, including melanoma, lung and renal cancers (PMID: 28481359). Often, this amplification leads to overexpression of the MET protein, which has been demonstrated to contribute to tumorigenesis by increasing downstream pathway activation, proliferation, invasiveness, and angiogenesis (PMID: 16461907, 18077425, 17463250, 19117057, 22869872,17667909). MET amplification has also been shown to contribute to resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including gefitinib and erlotinib and more recently osimertinib, as shown by sustained pathway activation and proliferation in the presence of drug (PMID: 18093943, 17463250, 30073261). In vitro proliferation assays of cell lines with MET amplifications show sensitivity to the MET-specific kinase inhibitor, PHA-665752 (PMID: 17463250, 16461907).
