Loss of MET exon 14 results in the loss of binding to the MET negative regulator CBL, increased MET protein levels, enhanced downstream MET signaling, and promotion of cell growth (PMID: 25971939, 26729443, 25971938, 26215952). A patient with non-small cell lung cancer who progressed on osimertinib after developing a MET exon 14 splice mutation had partial response to and clinical benefit from combination osimertinib plus crizotinib (PMID: 31157314).

The MET D1228Y mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext). Preclinical studies of this mutation demonstrate resistance to cabozantinib and merestinib as measured by increased IC50s compared to wildtype (PMID: 34589997). A patient with EGFR-mutant and MET-amplified lung adenocarcinoma was treated with osimertinib plus savolitinib and acquired MET D1228Y following disease progression (PMID: 33225315).

The MET D1228V mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is deleterious (PMID: 36430388).

The STARD3NL-MET variant is activating as shown by increased pathway activation, colony formation and IL-3-independent growth when expressed in NIH-3T3 and BaF3 cells (PMID: 29284707). The STARD3NL-MET variant was identified in a patient who partially responded to crizotinib. In vitro data of NIH-3T3 cells expressing this variant showed sensitivty to crizotinib (PMID: 29284707).

The MET C526F mutation is located in exon 5 of the gene. Although not functionally characterized, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring MET C526F and a MET exon 14 skipping mutation was treated with crizotinib and the MET C526F mutation disappeared after treatment (PMID: 31055074).

The MET F1200I mutation is located in the MET tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 and human cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein activation and increased cell invasion compared to wildtype MET. In vitro studies of cells expressing the MET F1200I mutation showed that it confers resistance to the MET inhibitors NVP-BVU972 and PF-02341066 as measured by protein activity upon drug treatment (PMID: 21697284, 24173966). Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET F1200I demonstrate sensitivity to capmatinib, tepotinib and elzovantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext).

biomark_group: Exon 14 Deletion,Exon 14 in-frame deletions,D1010,Exon 14 splice mutations
var_description: In-frame deletions affecting the splice sites flanking MET exon 14 result in alternative splicing of the MET gene with in-frame loss of the region encoded by exon 14, a region within the juxtamembrane domain of MET (PMID: 16397241, 19096300, 15735036). Loss of MET exon 14 results in the loss of binding to the MET negative regulator CBL, increased MET protein levels, enhanced downstream MET signaling, and promotion of cell growth (PMID: 25971939, 26729443, 25971938, 26215952).

The MET V1155M mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was identified as an acquired resistance mutation induced by tepotininb in an N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea mutagen screening (PMID: 31279006). Although not functionally characterized per se, preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET exon 14 skipping mutations and MET V1155M demonstrated moderate resistance to crizotinib as measured by an IC50 of 181 nM (PMID: 31279006).

The MET H1106D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. The MET H1106D mutation was shown to be likely activating when expressed in NIH3T3 cells, as measured by modestly increased protein activation compared to wildtype MET (PMID: 10327054). Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET H1106D demonstrate sensitivity to crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib, elzovantinib and cabozantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext).

The MET N375S mutation occurs in the semaphorin domain of the MET protein, which is the ligand binding region for hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). This mutation, which appears to be a common germline polymorphism (PMID:16171945), has been shown to slightly decrease MET binding to HGF (PMID: 19723643), though the biological significance of this change is unknown. In vitro studies using COS-7 cells transfected with the mutant domain suggest that MET N375S mutant cells are less sensitive to the c-MET inhibitor, SU11274 (PMID:19723643).

The MET H1094D mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is a predicted driver mutation (PMID: 36430388).

The MET Y1003* mutation is located in the MET juxtamembrane domain. This mutation was found in a patient with lung adenocarcinoma and was associated with exon 14 skipping, which has been demonstrated to result in protein stabilization and increased cell proliferation (PMID: 16397241, 25079552). This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

The MET V1188I mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is a predicted driver mutation (PMID: 36430388).

The CD74-MET fusion is a fusion of exon 7 of CD74 with either exon 14 or exon 15 of MET. This fusion has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 36806896). While this fusion has not been functionally validated, other fusions of MET are known to be oncogenic and therefore this fusion is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29102694, 29284707, 27748748, 28512244, 29527595). The CD74-MET fusion is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors as a patient with NSCLC harboring the fusion had a partial response to treatment with crizotinib (PMID: 36806896).

The MET exon 19 D1228N mutation occurs in the activation loop of the MET protein. This mutation is typically found in patients with non-small cell lung cancer, specifically in patients who develop resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (PMID: 27343442, 29128427, 28522754, 28396313, 27987579). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that it was activating, as shown by increased pathway activation, proliferation, anchorage-independent growth, and invasion compared to cells expressing wildtype MET (PMID: 29128427, 28522754, 28396313, 27987579). In vitro experiments measuring pathway activation and proliferation demonstrate that this mutation confers resistance to Type I MET inhibitors, including savolitinib, crizotinib, and INC280 but maintains sensitivity to Type II MET inhibitors, including cabozantinib, MGCD265, and merestinib (PMID: 27694386). Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET D1228N demonstrate resistance to crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib and elzovantinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext). A patient-derived organoid study expressing EPHB4-MET fusion and MET D1228N mutation suggests that type III MET inhibitor tivantinib can overcome the acquired resistance of MET D1228N as measured by the low IC50 in a dose-response curve assay (PMID: 36806896).

The KIF5B-MET fusion occurs between the MET gene and the KIF5B gene. The KIF5B-MET variant is activating as shown by increased pathway activation, colony formation and IL-3-independent growth when expressed in NIH-3T3 and BaF3 cells (PMID: 29284707). The KIF5B-MET variant was identified in a patient who responded to crizotinib. In vitro data of NIH-3T3 cells expressing this variant showed sensitivity to crizotinib (PMID: 29284707). In another case study, a patient with a KIF5B-MET fusion was found to respond to MET inhibitor crizotinib (PMID: 29102694).

The MLH1 R487Q mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 25344691). Although not functionally characterized, a patient with ampullary cholangiocarcinoma harboring MLH1 R487Q was treated with tremelimumab in combination with microwave ablation and demonstrated partial response (PMID: 30578687).

The MET L1195V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by protein activation, cell morphology, cell motility and tumor growth in mice (PMID: 15064724, 24061647). In vitro studies have suggested that MET L1195V is resistant to MET inhibitors SU11274 and EMD1214063, as determined by sustained protein activation, cell motility and tumor growth upon drug treatment (PMID: 15064724, 24061647). Preclinical studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing MET L1195V demonstrate sensitivity to capmatinib (Abstract: Nakazawa et al. Abstract# OA19.05, Journal of Thoracic Oncology Vol. 18 No. 11S. https://www.jto.org/article/S1556-0864%2823%2900900-0/fulltext).

The MLH1 R659P mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. In silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation disrupts binding to PMS2 and inhibits formation of the mismatch repair complex (PMID:16724012, 11793442).

The MLH1 V716M mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation is weakly associated with a microsatellite instability (MSI) proband (PMID: 21120944). This mutation is associated with lower MLH1 expression as measured by immunohistochemistry, but studies in silico and in vitro show that MLH1 V716M has no deficiency in mismatch repair (PMID: 21120944). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant neutral (PMID: 24362816).

Truncating mutations in MLH1 result in premature codons and are associated with loss of MLH1 expression, preventing the protein's ability to bind PMS2 (PMID: 15713769, 16216036, 24362816). Loss of this interaction affects the ability of PMS2 to bind to DNA during damage resulting in impairment of endonuclease function during DNA mismatch repair (PMID: 7892206, 11781295, 12697830). Mice deficient in MLH1 spontaneously develop gastrointestinal tumors (GITs) and thymic lymphomas. The types of GITs include well-differentiated and also poorly differentiated and mucinous adenocarcinomas. Furthermore, GIT formation is further promoted by radiation exposure (PMID: 16623753). The intestinal tumors that develop in the MLH1 deficient mice exhibit increased mutation burden consistent with inactivation of mismatch repair (PMID: 10359802). Lymphoid tumors developed in MLH1 deficient mice also exhibit increased mutational burden with IKAROS, a master transcription factor of lymphoid lineage commitment and differentiation, being identified as a key mutational target (PMID: 17086208).

The MLH1 M587V mutation occurs in the C-termimal protein interaction domain of the protein. While this variant has not been functionally characterized, it has been observed in a sporadic case of stomach cancer with microsatellite instability (MSI) in a patient with a family history of gastric carcinoma (PMID: 18206535).

The MLH1 L749P mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. In silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the ability of the protein to dimerize with PMS2 and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutant disrupts mismatch repair (PMID: 20533529). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 K118N mutation is located in the ATPase domain of the protein. In vivo DNA mismatch repair assays with yeast expressing MLH1 K118N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of DNA repair activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 15475387).

The MLH1 P603R mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer syndrome (HNPCC) (PMID: 19117025). Expression of this mutation in yeast and human cells was shown to have no effect on the ability of MLH1 to interact with PMS2, no effect on MH1 stability and no effect on mismatch repair efficiency, suggesting it to be neutral (PMID:21404117, 17510385).

The MLH1 L550P mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this a likely pathogenic variant (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 R725H mutation is located in the C-terminal dimerization domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in ovarian cancer (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing MLH1 R725H demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by reduced protein expression and varied response to DNA damaging agents compared to wildtype (PMID: 28494185).

The MLH1 A681T mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adenocarcinoma and Lynch syndrome (PMID: 27302833, 18033691, 8880570, 16083711, 28449805, 21642682). There is conflicting functional evidence for this mutation. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate MLH1 A681T is inactivating as measured by reduced protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 23403630). In contrast, other in vitro studies with 293T human cells expressing this mutation demonstrate MLH1 A681T is neutral as measured by MLH1 expression level and mismatch repair activity being comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21120944).
The MLH1 N306K mutation is located in the DNA mismatch repair domain of the protein. In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is inactivating (PMID: 30504929).

The MLH1 R755S mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the ability of the protein to dimerize with PMS2 and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant likely pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 E433Q mutation occurs between the DNA mismatch repair domain and the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a yeast-based assay demonstrated that this mutation had no effect on mismatch repair function (PMID: 21136174).

The MLH1 Q689R mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been observed in a urothelial bladder carcinoma (PMID: 25092538). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant neutral (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 K618T mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies of yeast expressing human MLH1 K618T demonstrate rates of mismatch repair similar to wildtype MLH1 (PMID: 19863800). This mutation is considered not pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 P654L mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383).

The MLH1 V384D mutation has been observed in a case of pancreatic cancer which exhibited microsatellite instability (MSI) (PMID: 12037578). A cell line isolated from this tumor harbored the MLH1 V384D mutation as well as an MLH1 C223R mutation. MLH1 V384D is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its frequency in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 R385C mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in melanoma (PMID: 25148578). In vitro studies with mouse embryonic stem cells expressing MLH1 R385C demonstrate that the mutation is neutral as measured by DNA polymerase slippage rate and methylation damage-induced mutagenesis rate comparable to wildtype (PMID: 31784484).

The MLH1 T82A mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in families with Lynch syndrome, including one patient with MSI-high colorectal cancer. In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation inhibits mismatch repair by disrupting hydrogen bonding in the ATPase pocket of the protein (PMID: 22736432). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 L559R mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. In silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein, and in vitro studies demonstrate this mutation disrupts binding to PMS2 and inhibits formation of the mismatch repair complex (PMID: 23435383, 16724012). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant likely pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 G101S mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been observed in a patient with hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer lacking MLH1 expression (PMID: 24278394). In silico, this mutation is predicted to be pathogenic (PMID: 22290698). This variant is considered likely pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 E668K mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer (PMID: 28027327). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is neutral (PMID: 22290698).

The MLH1 A441T mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in glioma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with yeast and HCT116 cells expressing MLH1 A441T demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by DNA mismatch repair activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 17510385).

The MLH1 T117M mutation occurs in the MLH1 ATPase domain. This mutation has been found in families with hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome).\ (PMID: 12919140, 11781295, 8566964). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by diminished mismatch repair compared to wildtype MLH1 (PMID: 12919140, 11781295, 8566964, 20176959). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 N38S mutation occurs in the HATPase domain. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 15713769). Expression of this mutation in yeast results in increased mutation burden (PMID: 15475387).

The MLH1 P648L mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers the effect of this variant pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

Deletion of MLH1 is predicted to promote the loss of MLH1 expression. Reduced expression of MLH1 is associated with defects in the mismatch repair pathway and increased tumor microsatellite instability due to the inability of MLH1 to heterodimerize with one of its molecular partners, thereby preventing effective endonuclease activity necessary for mismatch repair (PMID: 12697830, 11793442, 20533529, 20864418, 18337503, 17135187). Mice deficient in MLH1 spontaneously develop gastrointestinal tumors (GITs) and thymic lymphomas. The types of GITs included well-differentiated and also poorly differentiated and mucinous adenocarcinomas that and GIT formation is further promoted by radiation exposure (PMID: 16623753). The intestinal tumors developed in the MLH1 deficient mice exhibit increased mutation burden consistent with inactivation of mismatch repair with MLH1 loss (PMID: 10359802). Lymphoid tumors developed in MLH1 deficient mice also exhibit increased mutational burden with IKAROS, a master transcription factor of lymphoid lineage commitment and differentiation, being identified as a key mutational target (PMID: 17086208).

The MLH1 L582F mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers the effects of this variant uncertain (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 R725C mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of MLH1. In vitro assays in human cancer cell lines demonstrate that this mutation results in decreased MLH1 protein expression but does not alter mismatch repair (MMR) (PMID: 23403630). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers MLH1 R725C of uncertain effect (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 G67R mutation is located in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in a proband associated with microsatellite instability (MSI) (PMID: 18383312). In silico analysis and in vitro assays demonstrate that MLH1 G67R is inactivating as measured by reduced mismatch repair activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21120944, 18383312).

The MLH1 A111P mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in microsatellite instable high (MSI) tumors lacking MLH1 expression (PMID: 20020535). In an in vitro mismatch repair (MMR) assay, the KDR A11P mutation demonstrated loss of MMR activity (PMID: 20020535). The variant is considered of uncertain effect by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).
The MLH1 R389Q mutation occurs in the HATPase domain. Expression of this mutation in yeast was shown to have no effect on mismatch repair efficiency, suggesting it to be neutral (PMID: 17510385).

The MLH1 P648S mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. In silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation disrupts binding to PMS2 and inhibits formation of the mismatch repair complex (PMID:16724012). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 G454R mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in glioma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with NR-21, NR-22, NR-27, BAT-25 and BAT-26 cells expressing MLH1 G454R demonstrate that the mutation is neutral as measured by protein stability, DNA damage response signaling and DNA repair function being comparable to wildtype (PMID: 36054288).

The MLH1 N551T mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the ability of the protein to dimerize with PMS2 and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers the effect of this variant uncertain (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 K618del mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Lynch syndrome (PMID: 10422993, 12891553, 17569143, 21642682, 21681552.) In vitro studies with Sf9 insect cells expressing this mutation demonstrate MLH1 K618del is inactivating as measured by reduced MLH1 expression and function (PMID: 12891553, 17510385).

The MLH1 Q60P mutation is located in the ATPase domain of the protein. In vivo DNA mismatch repair assays with yeast expressing MLH1 Q60P demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by partial loss of DNA repair activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 15475387).

The MLH1 E172K mutation occurs between the HATPase and DNA mismatch repair domains of the protein. This mutation has been observed in a breast cancer and a colorectal cancer cell line, both of which exhibited microsatellite instability (MSI) (PMID: 20668451, 24755471).

The MLH1 A120S mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colon cancer cell lines exhibiting a hypermutator phenotype and microsatellite instability (PMID: 24755471).

The MLH1 K618A mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. This mutant has been shown to exhibit decreased protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 18205192, 22426235). but exhibited no defects in mismatch repair and was able to interact with PMS2 (PMID: 20533529, 16724012). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant neutral (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 R659L mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383).

The MLH1 G98S mutation is located in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in rectal cancer (PMID: 28481359). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is pathogenic (PMID: 22290698).

The MLH1 V506A mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch Syndrome. In silico studies predict that this mutation disrupts the ability of MLH1 to heterodimerize with PMS2, suggesting it is a loss of function mutation, but this mutation has not been functionally characterized (PMID: 23435383, 18383312). However, The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers the effect of this mutation as uncertain (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 D737V mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the ability of the protein to dimerize with PMS2 and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers the effects of this variant to be uncertain (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 I219V mutation occurs in the DNA mismatch repair domain of the protein. In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is proficient in mismatch repair (PMID: 11781295). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant neutral due to its frequency in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 R265C mutation occurs in the DNA mismatch repair domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a founder mutation in Taiwanese families with Lynch syndrome that exhibit cases of colorectal, gastric, endometrial, ovarian, and other cancers (PMID: 19419416). This mutant has been shown to decrease protein stability, which in turn is speculated to compromise function but does not seem to alter intrinsic protein function (PMID: 18205192, 11781295).

The MLH1 R217C mutation occurs in the DNA mismatch repair domain of the protein.This mutation has no or little effect on MLH1 expression, MMR proficiency, nor PMS2 interaction in assays in colon cancer cell lines and yeast (PMID: 11781295, 17510385, 12810663).

The MLH1 L622H mutation occurs in the C-terminal protein binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a patient with Lynch syndrome. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico studies predict that this mutation compromises the stability of the protein and therefore may reduce the protein's function (PMID: 23435383). The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours considers this variant pathogenic (PMID: 24362816).

The MLH1 G67W mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in conjunction with loss of the wildtype allele in affected individuals in families with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (PMID: 9927034, 16528606). In a yeast-based assay, this mutation showed significantly decreased mismatch repair (MMR) activity and protein expression (PMID: 9927034, 17510385). The variant is considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MPL P106L mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in familiar thrombocythemia (PMID: 23351976). In vitro studies with murine B cells expressing this mutation demonstrate MPL P106L is activating as measured by prolonged survival in the absence of stimulatory factors compared to the wildtype control (PMID: 25538044). Other in vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing this mutation also demonstrate MPL P106L is activating as measured by cytokine-independent growth and constitutive downstream signaling following treatment with thrombopoietin (PMID: 25538044).

The MLH1 R265S mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation demonstrated a mutator phenotype when expressed in yeast and reduced mismatch repair (MMR) in an in vitro MMR assay (PMID: 17210669, 20020535). This variant is considered likely pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MPL W515L mutation occurs in the MPL amphipathic domain that serves as a hinge between the transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains. Expression of this mutation in 32D, UT7, and Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by ligand-independent protein activation, increased pathway activation, increased cell proliferation, growth factor hypersensitivity and in vivo tumor formation compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 16834459).

The MPL R321W mutation is located in the D3 region of the protein. This mutation has been found in the germline of a patient with triple-negative essential thrombocythemia. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in a JAK2-deficient cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 26423830). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells showed that this mutation cannot confer cytokine-independent proliferation nor hypersensitivty to thrombopoietin (PMID: 26423830).

The MPL Y591D mutation is located in the cytoplasmic domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in a patient with triple-negative essential thrombocythemia. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in a JAK2-deficient cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 26423830). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells showed that this mutation cannot confer cytokine-independent proliferation, but has hypersensitivity to thrombopoietin (PMID: 26423830)

The MPL S505N mutation is located in the MPL transmembrane domain. Expression of this mutation in murine B cells demonstrated that it is likely activating, as shown by longer cell survival rates and increased pathway activation compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 8695859, 14764528). This mutation is predicted to promoter ligand-independent dimerization of MPL (PMID: 14764528).

The MPL S204F mutation is located in the D2 region of the protein. This mutation has been found in a patient with triple-negative essential thrombocythemia. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in a JAK2-deficient cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 26423830). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells showed that this mutation cannot confer cytokine-independent proliferation nor hypersensitivty to thrombopoietin (PMID: 26423830).

The MPL T119I mutation is located in the D1 region of the protein. This mutation has been found in a patient with triple-negative essential thrombocythemia. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in a JAK2-deficient cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 26423830). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells showed that this mutation cannot confer cytokine-independent proliferation nor hypersensitivity to thrombopoietin (PMID: 26423830).

The MPL V285E mutation is located in the D2 region of the protein. This mutation has been found in the germline of a patient with triple-negative primary myelofibrosis. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in a JAK2-deficient cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 26423830). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells showed that this mutation cannot confer cytokine-independent proliferation nor hypersensitivity to thrombopoietin (PMID: 26423830).

The MPL E230G mutation is located in the D2 region of the protein. This mutation has been found in a patient with triple-negative essential thrombocythemia. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in a JAK2-deficient cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 26423830). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells showed that this mutation cannot confer cytokine-independent proliferation nor hypersensitivity to thrombopoietin (PMID: 26423830).

The MSH2 G162R mutation is located in the MutS domain II of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Lynch syndrome (PMID: 28874130, 17101317, 18951462). In vitro studies with Sf9 insect cells expressing this mutation demonstrate MSH2 G162R is inactivating as measured by deficient mismatch repair activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 18951462, 17101317).

The MPL W515K mutation is located in the MPL amphipathic domain that serves as a hinge between the transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains. Expression of this mutation in murine B cells and Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling, cytokine-independent proliferation and hypersensitivty to thrombopoietin compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 16868251, 17709604, 26423830). Endogenous expression of this mutation in patient-derived CD34+ cells resulted in spontaneous megakaryocytic growth and stronger proliferative response to growth factors compared to normal CD34+ cells (PMID: 16868251, 17709604).

MSH2 deletion mutations result in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in Lynch syndrome (PMID: 23264089, 17250661, 22781090). In vitro studies with MSH2-deficient mouse embryonic fibroblasts demonstrate that loss of MSH2 is inactivating as measured by increased chromosome aneuploidy, centrosome amplification and defective mitotic spindle organization compared to wildtype (PMID: 16331258).

The MSH2 C697R mutation is located in the MutS domain V of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrioid carcinoma and individuals with Lynch Syndrome, with tumors having MSI-H and loss of MSH2 by immunohistochemistry (PMID: 10471663, 21239990, 14970868, 17973265, 27302833). In vivo studies with yeast and in vitro studies with HCT-116 cells expressing MSH2 C697R demonstrate that this mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of MMR function and decreased protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 17720936, 12377806).

The MSH2 G674R mutation is located in the ATP-binding region of the protein. Studies in E. coli and yeast demonstrate that this mutation binds to other mismatch repair proteins, but has impaired mismatch repair likely due to inability to hydrolyze ATP (PMID:18822302).

The MSH2 A272V mutation occurs in the SH3/SH6 interaction domain of the protein. In silico studies and in vitro mismatch repair assays have demonstrated that this mutation does not affect MSH2 protein expression or mismatch repair efficiency though it is associated with microsatellite instability (PMID: 21120944, 17101317). Additionally, this mutation does not fulfill Amsterdam Criteria for the diagnosis of hereditary non polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) (PMID: 21120944).

The MSH2 S723F mutation occurs in the SH3/SH6 interaction domain of the protein. Studies in cell lines and cell-free assays demonstrate that this mutation does not affect protein levels of MSH2 but disrupts mismatch repair (PMID: 26951660, 22102614). The mutation is considered a variant of uncertain effect according to The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH2 G322D mutation occurs in the SH3/SH6 interaction domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated, it is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH2 A636P mutation occurs in the MutL homologs interaction domain. This mutation is a founder mutation in the Ashkenazi Jewish population (PMID: 12595050). In vitro studies in yeast suggest that this mutation may affect MSH2 protein folding, thus possibly interfering with the protein's normal structure and function (PMID: 10528862).

The MSH2 L390F mutation occurs in the SH3/SH6 interaction domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated, it is considered not pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MPL S204P mutation is located in the D2 region of the protein. This mutation has been found in a patient with triple-negative primary myelofibrosis. There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in a JAK2-deficient cell line demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased JAK2-STAT5 signaling compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 26423830). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells showed that this mutation cannot confer cytokine-independent proliferation nor hypersensitivty to thrombopoietin (PMID: 26423830).

The MSH2 D603N mutation occurs in the MutS domain III of the protein. In silico and in vitro assays have shown that this variant lowers MSH2 protein stability and is defective in mismatch repair (MMR) (PMID: 18951462, 21120944).

The MSH2 G751R mutation occurs in the ATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in families with hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (PMID: 10732761). Studies in yeast-based model systems demonstrate that this mutation destabilizes the ATPase domain, decreases protein levels of MSH2 and disrupts mismatch repair (MMR) (PMID: 17720936). The mutation is considered pathogenic according to The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH2 H639Y mutation is located in the MutS domain V of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MSI-high colorectal cancer and Lynch syndrome (PMID: 9718327, 24362816). In vitro transcriptional assays with lymphoblastoid cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrated MSH2 H639Y is inactivating as measured by aberrant splicing which truncates the exonic enhancer of the protein (PMID: 16395668).

MPL exon 10 mutations have been identified in patients with myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis (a subset of myelodysplastic syndrome), primary myelofibrosis, and essential thrombocythemia (PMID: 27069254, 20428194, 25037629, 21220604, 15837627, 16868251, 16834459, 24986690, 25873496, 29296692). Mutations in Exon 10 of MPL, such as at position W515 or S505, have been shown to promote ligand-independent protein activation, increased pathway activation, increased cell proliferation, increased cell survival, growth factor hypersensitivity and in vivo tumor formation compared to wildtype MPL (PMID: 16834459, 8695859, 14764528).

The MSH2 S860L mutation occurs in the MutL homologues interaction domain of the protein. This mutation has been observed in families with Lynch syndrome (PMID: 22102614, 24362816). In an in vitro mismatch repair assay, this mutation did not affect the mismatch repair efficiency of the protein and is not associated with microsatellite instability (PMID: 22102614). This mutation is considered a likely neutral variant according to The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH2 L310R mutation is located in the MutS domain III of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MSI-high colorectal cancer (PMID: 21590452). In silico analysis predicts that MSH2 L310R is likely inactivating and oncogenic (PMID: 22290698).

Truncating mutations in MSH2 have been identified in individuals with Lynch syndrome and lead to the loss of normal mismatch repair function (PMID: 7726159, 8566964, 8592341, 15528792, 11257106, 24362816). These mutations disrupt the mismatch repair pathway due to partial or whole loss of the MutS domain necessary for the protein's function (PMID: 15528792, 10946232). Mutations causing loss of any domain of MSH2 are likely to disrupt its normal function since the N-terminal domain in required for its binding to mismatched nucleotides in DNA and, additionally, the C-terminal domain is necessary for dimerization, which in its turn is required for normal function (PMID: 23391514).

The MSH2 P349R mutation is located in the MutS domain III of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Lynch syndrome (PMID: 21239990, 24278394, 26300997). In vitro studies with human embryonic stem cells expressing this mutation demonstrated MSH2 P349R is inactivating as measured by reduction in protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 31237724).

The MSH2 L595R mutation is located in the MutS domain III of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Lynch syndrome (PMID: 23990280, 12454801, 26498970). In vitro massive parallel function screening with HEK293 cells and HAP1 MSH2 knockout cells expressing this mutation demonstrated MSH2 L595R is inactivating as measured by the lack of resistance against DNA damaging agent 6-thioguanine compared to wildtype (PMID: 33357406).

The MSH2 A305T mutation is in the MutS II domain of the protein. Studies in E. coli have shown that this mutation has no defects in mismatch binding, ATP release or mismatch repair activity (PMID:18822302).

The MSH2 F694S mutation is located in the MutS domain V of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 21156417). In vitro studies with Sf9 insect cells expressing this mutation demonstrated MSH2 F694S is inactivating as measured by protein instability and deficient mismatch repair activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 27629256).

The MSH6 R1095H mutation occurs in the MutS domain V of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with familial colon cancer (PMID: 12522549) and Lynch Syndrome (PMID: 24040339). Expression of this mutation in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) or a cell-free mismatch repair assay resulted in MSH6 protein levels similar to wildtype cells and did not alter mismatch repair functionality but had been predicted to affect MMR in silico (PMID: 24040339, 23621914, 22581703). This mutation is considered a variant with uncertain effect by the The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH6 R976H mutation occurs in the MutS family domain IV of the protein. This mutation has been found in a case of non-familial colorectal cancer with microsatellite instability (MSI) (PMID: 11807791). In vitro mismatch repair (MMR) studies suggest that this mutation reduces MMR efficiency and affects protein stability and the ability of the protein to bind to DNA (PMID: 11807791, 18790734, 11709755). The mutation is considered a variant with uncertain effect by the The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH6 G39E mutation occurs near the N-terminus of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it is considered not pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH6 R361H mutation occurs between the PWWP domain and the MutS domain I of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated, a patient with urothelial carcinoma harboring a MSH6 R361H mutation had loss of MSH6 expression as measured by immunohistochemistry (PMID: 26674132).

The MSH6 T1219I mutation occurs between the PWWP domain and MutS domain I of the protein. This mutation has been found in a patient with familial colon cancer associated with microsatellite instability (MSI) (PMID: 11709755). In silico studies and in vitro mismatch repair (MMR) assays demonstrate that this mutation is deficient in MMR (PMID: 22102614, 23621914). The mutation is considered a variant with uncertain effect by the The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH6 V509A mutation occurs in the MutS domain I of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it is considered likely not pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH2 D603G mutation occurs in the SH3/SH6 interaction domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated, it is considered likely pathogenic according to criteria established by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (PMID: 24362816).

The MSH6 S144I mutation occurs in the PWWP domain of the protein. In silico studies and in vitro mismatch repair (MMR) assays suggest that this mutation does not disrupt MMR activity (PMID: 21120944).

MSH6 deletion results in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in Lynch syndrome and colorectal cancer (PMID: 12019211, 24090359, 22781090). In vivo studies with MSH6 knockout mice demonstrate that loss of MSH6 is inactivating as measured by defective DNA damage repair response and tumor growth (PMID: 9390556).

The MSH6 R1076C mutation occurs in the MutS domain III of the protein. This mutation has been observed as a germline variant in cases of familial colorectal cancer and in a colorectal cancer patient with negative immunohistochemistry for MSH6 (PMID: 19072991, 21056691).

The exon 5 MSH6 F1088Lfs*5 mutation occurs in MutS domain V of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, insertion of a cytosine at position 3261 (codon 1088 in exon 5 of the MSH6 protein) results in a truncating frameshift mutation and has been associated with late onset endometrial cancer (PMID: 21674763, 15837969).

The MYD88 M232T (also called M219T) mutation is located in the MYD88 toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain. Expression of this mutation in B cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased NF-kappaB signaling, cell proliferation, and enhanced protein oligomerization compared to wildtype MYD88 (PMID: 25359991).

The MYD88 M232T (also called M219T) mutation is located in the MYD88 toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain. Expression of this mutation in B cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased NF-kappaB signaling, cell proliferation, and enhanced protein oligomerization compared to wildtype MYD88 (PMID: 25359991).

Oncogenic activating mutations in MYD88 are seen in 90% of Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) patients, a malignant B-cell lymphoma that is associated with an accumulation of clonal lymphoplasmacytic cells and monoclonal IgM secretion (PMID: 22931316). These gain-of-function mutations trigger NF-κB through interaction with and activation of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) (PMID: 23836557). Ibrutinib is a small molecule, irreversible inhibitor of BTK that covalently binds to C481 within the phosphorylation site of the kinase (PMID: 20615965), and has recently been FDA-approved in the treatment of symptomatic WM (PMID: 27493708). In a multi-center clinical trial of ibrutinib in 63 WM patients, overall response was seen in 90.5% of patients and major responses were seen in 73% of patients, as measured by serum IgM levels, and 2-year progression-free and overall survival rates of 69.1% and 95.2%, respectively (PMID: 25853747). While overall and major response rates were highest among patients with the MYD88-L265P CXCR4-WT genotypes, significant response was also seen in MYD88-L265P CXCR4-WHIM and MYD88-WT CXCR4-WT groups.

The MYD88 S243N (also called S230N) mutation is located in the MYD88 toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain. Expression of this mutation in B cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased NF-kappaB activation and mitogen-independent cell proliferation compared to wildtype MYD88 (PMID: 24534189).

The MYD88 S243N (also called S230N) mutation is located in the MYD88 toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain. Expression of this mutation in B cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased NF-kappaB activation and mitogen-independent cell proliferation compared to wildtype MYD88 (PMID: 24534189).

The MYD88 L265P mutation (also called L252P) is located in the MYD88 toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain. This mutation is found in patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) and is associated with increased severity of disease when found with CXCR4 truncating mutations (PMID: 24553177). This mutation activates downstream signaling including activation of NF-kappaB and STAT3 signaling (PMID: 25723115, 26111727, 24553177). Expression of the MYD88 L265P mutation in activated B cells demonstrated that this mutation is likely oncogenic as shown rapid division in mitogen free media as compred to control cells that rapidly died. The MYD88 L265P mutation often co-occurs with CD79B ITAM mutations in lymphomas. Co-expression of the MYD88 L265P mutation wih the CD79B Y196H mutation failed to recapitulate the phase of B cell proliferation that was seen with expression of MYD88 L265P alone; however, co-expression of the two mutations was shown to drive B cell differentiation, which is necessary for survival, and was also found to break immune tolerance checkpoints, effectively switching the effect of self-antigen recognition from inducing apoptosis to inducing proliferation and plasmablast differentiation (PMID: 28701369). A prospective study of ibrutinib monotherapy with 30 treatment-naive patients with WM that all had the MYD88 L265P mutation showed durable responses, with 100% of the patients having at least a minor response, 83% having a partial response and no patient having a complete response (PMID: 30044692). The estimated 18 month progression free survival for this population was 92% (95%CI: 73%-98%). Within this patient population, a subset of patients had CXCR4 mutations which resulted in a delay in the time to major responses (1.8 vs. 7.3 respectively) (PMID: 30044692).

Truncating mutations of MSH6 have been identified in patients with inherited Lynch syndrome and introduces a premature stop codon which leads to C-terminally truncated forms of the protein, including loss of part or all of the highly conserved MutS domain. Deletion of all or part of this domain causes a loss of ATPase activity, which can lead to impairment of DNA binding and mismatch repair (PMID: 1651234, 9111312, 9822680, 9564049, 24362816). Truncating MSH6 mutations are associated with a defect in mismatch repair (dMMR) and are typically accompanied by microsatellite instability (MSI) and hypermutation in colorectal and endometrial cancers (PMID: 22810696, 24755471).

The MYD88 L265P mutation (also called L252P) is located in the MYD88 toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain. This mutation is found in patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) and is associated with increased severity of disease when found with CXCR4 truncating mutations (PMID: 24553177). This mutation activates downstream signaling including activation of NF-kappaB and STAT3 signaling (PMID: 25723115, 26111727, 24553177). Expression of the MYD88 L265P mutation in activated B cells demonstrated that this mutation is likely oncogenic as shown rapid division in mitogen free media as compred to control cells that rapidly died. The MYD88 L265P mutation often co-occurs with CD79B ITAM mutations in lymphomas. Co-expression of the MYD88 L265P mutation wih the CD79B Y196H mutation failed to recapitulate the phase of B cell proliferation that was seen with expression of MYD88 L265P alone; however, co-expression of the two mutations was shown to drive B cell differentiation, which is necessary for survival, and was also found to break immune tolerance checkpoints, effectively switching the effect of self-antigen recognition from inducing apoptosis to inducing proliferation and plasmablast differentiation (PMID: 28701369). A prospective study of ibrutinib monotherapy with 30 treatment-naive patients with WM that all had the MYD88 L265P mutation showed durable responses, with 100% of the patients having at least a minor response, 83% having a partial response and no patient having a complete response (PMID: 30044692). The estimated 18 month progression free survival for this population was 92% (95%CI: 73%-98%). Within this patient population, a subset of patients had CXCR4 mutations which resulted in a delay in the time to major responses (1.8 vs. 7.3 respectively) (PMID: 30044692).

The gene K1423E mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 1568247). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity, increased GTP-bound RAS, enhanced downstream signaling and ablation of the protein interaction with KRAS compared to wildtype (PMID: 1568247, 16513807, 32697994).

The gene R1204G mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 22807134). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity, increased GTP-bound RAS and reduced interaction with the RAS negative regulator SPRED1 compared to wildtype (PMID: 22807134, 26635368).

The NF1 L90R mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. This germline mutation is absent from population databases (1000G, ESP and ExAC). In silico studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating, as evidenced by its disruptive predicted effect on protein function by different prediction algorithms (PMID: 16199547). Another NF1 mutation affecting the same amino acid residue, NF1 L90P, has been reported in individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1 (PMID: 17426081, 23913538).

The gene G629R mutation is located in the cysteine/serine-rich domain of the protein. The mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 12807981, 18546366, 26962827, 26056819, 24789688). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by aberrant splicing leading to premature protein truncation and loss of protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 23913538, 12807981, 18546366).

The NF1 R1362Q mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in bladder cancer (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with MCF-7 cells expressing NF1 R1362Q demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced GAP activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 32142667).

The NF1 N1430H mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. In vivo studies with yeast expressing NF1 N1430H demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced GAP activity and increased GTP-bound RAS compared to wildtype (PMID: 8628317).

The gene V1398D mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 22807134). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity and increased GTP-bound RAS compared to wildtype (PMID: 22807134).

The gene R1276P mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 9668168). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity and increased GTP-bound RAS as compared to wildtype (PMID: 1568247, 16513807, 32697994). Structural modeling shows that the gene R1276P mutation alters the arginine finger of gene, which is responsible for the hydrolysis of GFP to GDP in RAS (PMID: 9668168, 9219684, 9302992).

The gene L1301R mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 22807134). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity and increased GTP-bound RAS compared to wildtype (PMID: 22807134).

The gene T1324N mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 22807134). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity and increased GTP-bound RAS compared to wildtype (PMID: 22807134).

The gene E1356G mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 22807134, 16138229). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity and increased GTP-bound RAS compared to wildtype (PMID: 22807134).

The gene Y489C mutation is located in the cysteine/serine-rich domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 11258625). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by altered splicing in exon 10b compared to wildtype (PMID: 11258625, 10607834).

The gene R1276Q mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 10712197, 22807134). Structural modeling shows that the gene R1276Q mutation alters the arginine finger of gene which is responsible for the hydrolysis of GFP to GDP in RAS (PMID: 9668168, 9219684, 9302992).

The NF1 L90P mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in the germline of patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (PMID: 17426081, 23913538). In silico studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating, as evidenced by its co-segregation with disease in a family with  neurofibromatosis type 1 and its disruptive predicted effect on protein function by different prediction algorithms (PMID: 17426081, 23913538).

The NF1 R1306Q mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 27149842). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation does not affect protein function (PMID: 23288408).

The gene R1391S mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas (PMID: 9003501). The gene R1204W mutation is located in the GTPase activating protein (GAP)-related domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in neurofibromas and melanomas (PMID: 22807134, 12807981, 26214590). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased GAP activity, increased GTP-bound RAS, and reduced interaction with the RAS negative regulator SPRED1 compared to wildtype (PMID: 22807134, 26635368).

The NF2 L46R mutation decreases the half-life of NF2 in in vitro assays and leads to reduced growth suppression compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 21383154, 20178741). Additionally, this mutation reduces the nuclear translocation of NF2 and its ability to interact with the NF2 binding partner, DCAF1, as well as abrogation of the wildtype's growth suppression. The NF2 L46R mutation confers little change in intrinsic protein function, suggesting that decreased protein stability and/or subcellular localization promotes its oncogenic potential (PMID: 21383154, 20178741). This data is in accordance with reports documenting decreased NF2 protein expression in tumors from meningiomas and schwannomas with mutated NF2 (PMID: 21383154, 20178741).

The NF2 K413E mutation lies in the predicted α-helical domain of NF2 (PMID: 11448944). This mutation decreases the half-life of the NF2 protein compared to wildtype NF2 in in vitro assays. The NF2 K413E mutation confers little change in intrinsic protein function, suggesting a possible oncogenic role by decreasing protein stability (PMID: 21383154). However, expression of this mutation in NF2-null rat schwannoma cell lines conferred a phenotype in growth and motility assays similar to wildtype NF2 (PMID: 11448944).

Deletions in NF2 are commonly detected in patients with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). Alterations usually result in large deletions of the NF2 gene leading to loss of protein function (PMID: 9643284, 15645494). Given the role of NF2 in the membrane-cytoskeleton scaffold, the tumor suppressor function of NF2 is thought to be related to contact-mediated growth inhibition and elevated mTOR and Hippo pathways (PMID: 24726726, 19451229, 22825583)

The NF2 Q324L mutation lies in a predicted α-helical domain of NF2. Expression of this mutation in NF2-null rat schwannoma cell lines conferred a phenotype in growth and motility assays similar to the wildtype protein (PMID: 11448944)

The NF2 E106G mutation lies in the protein's conserved and essential N-terminal FERM domain (PMID: 11448944). Expression of this mutation in NF2-null rat schwannoma cell lines failed to inhibit cell proliferation, cell growth in soft agar or cell spreading compared to the wildtype protein, suggesting that this mutation is inactivating (PMID: 11448944).

The NF2 L535P mutation decreases the half-life of NF2 compared to the wildtype protein in in vitro assays (PMID: 21383154). Expression of this mutant in a rat schwannoma cell line resulted in increased cell growth and motility (PMID: 11448944). The NF2 L535P mutation confers little change in intrinsic protein function, suggesting that decreased protein stability promotes its oncogenic potential (PMID: 21383154). Additional experiments in monkey kidney fibroblasts demonstrated that the L535P mutation alters protein solubility, cell adhesion and protein dimerization (PMID: 10712203). This data is in accordance with reports documenting decreased NF2 protein expression in tumors from meningiomas and schwannomas with mutated NF2 (PMID: 21383154, 20178741).

Truncating mutations of NF2 can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins, and result in loss of NF2 protein function. These alterations are predicted to cause activation of multiple mitogenic signaling pathways, including mTOR and Hippo signaling (PMID: 22825583), which has led to a study of mTOR inhibitors in patients or cell lines with NF2 mutations (PMID: 22825583). Truncating mutations are frequently observed in patients with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) and are associated with poor prognosis (PMID: 8755919, 9643284). Somatic truncating mutations are more commonly frameshift mutations, whereas germline mutations associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 are more commonly nonsense mutations (PMID: 19545378).

The NF2 Q538P mutation is likely inactivating as its expression in NF2-null rat schwannoma cell lines failed to inhibit cell proliferation, cell growth in soft agar or cell spreading compared to expression of the wildtype protein (PMID: 11448944).

The NF2 K79E mutation lies in the protein's conserved and essential N-terminal FERM domain (PMID: 11448944). Expression of this mutation in NF2-null rat schwannoma cell lines failed to inhibit cell proliferation, cell growth in soft agar or cell spreading compared to expression of wildtype NF2, suggesting that this mutation is inactivating (PMID: 11448944). Experiments in monkey kidney fibroblasts demonstrated that the K79E mutation confers a phenotype different from the wildtype, with altered subcellular localization, protein solubility and cell adhesion (PMID: 10712203).

The NF2 T352M mutation lies in the predicted α-helical domain of NF2. Expression of this mutation in NF2-null rat schwannoma cell lines conferred a phenotype in growth and motility assays similar to the wildtype protein (PMID: 11448944). In a separate experiment, expression of the T352M mutant In monkey kidney fibroblasts resulted in decreased cell adhesion, however, no other phenotypic propeties were assessed (PMID: 10712203).

The NF2 A211D mutation decreases the half-life of NF2 compared to the wildtype protein in in vitro assays. The NF2 A211D mutation confers little change in intrinsic protein function, suggesting a possible oncogenic role by decreasing protein stability (PMID: 21383154, 20178741). In a human mesthelioma cell line, expression of A221D exhibits none of the wildtype's growth suppression and decreased binding to putative binding partner DCAF1 (PMID: 20178741). This data is in accordance with reports documenting decreased NF2 protein expression in tumors from meningiomas and schwannomas with mutated NF2 (PMID: 21383154, 20178741).

The NFE2L2 G81D mutation is found at the KEAP1-binding ETGE motif of the protein. Mutations in the ETGE motif inactivate KEAP1-dependent ubiquitination of the NFE2L2 protein (NRF2), and thus stabilize NRF2 (PMID: 18757741, 1875774, 24142871). Stabilization of NRF2 expression has been associated with its increased nuclear accumulation and decreased cellular sensitivity to oxidative stress or chemotherapy (PMID: 18757741).

The NFE2L2 E82V mutation occurs in the protein's conserved ETGE motif which is involved in binding to its repressor, KEAP1. In a yeast two-hybrid screen, this mutation abolished the interaction between NFE2FL2 and KEAP1, suggesting aberrant regulation of NFE2L2 (PMID: 12167159).

The NFE2L2 D29H mutation is located in the KEAP1 binding, DLG motif of the protein. In vitro studies with mouse embryonic fibroblasts expressing NFE2L2 D29H demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased transcriptional activity compared to vector control (PMID: 37062029). Despite being an active mutation, in vitro studies demonstrate that expression of NFE2L2 D29H alone is not sufficient to initiate tumorigenesis, and mutant D29H cooperates with mutant KRAS to promote tumor growth (PMID: 37062029). In silico studies of NFE2L2 D29H predict the mutation stabilizes the NFE2L2 protein and promotes its nuclear accumulation, which has been shown to decrease sensitivity to chemotherapy and oxidative stress (PMID: 1875774,18757741, 24142871).

The NF2 L64P mutation lies in the protein's conserved and essential N-terminal FERM domain (PMID: 11448944) and results in decreased growth suppression compared to the wildtype protein when expressed in cell lines (PMID: 20178741). Expression of this mutation in NF2-null rat schwannoma cell lines failed to inhibit cell proliferation, cell growth in soft agar or cell spreading compared to expression of the wildtype protein, suggesting that this mutation is inactivating (PMID: 11448944). Additionally, expression of this mutant in monkey fibroblasts and a human mesothelioma cell line abrogated NF2 binding to DCAF1, a proposed interacting partner of NF2 (PMID: 20178741).

The NFE2L2 N160S mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. In vivo studies with mice expressing this mutation demonstrate NFE2L2 N160S is activating as measured by robust tumor formation and NFE2L2 overexpression compared to wildtype (PMID: 27147599).

The NFE2L2 G31R mutation is located in the KEAP1 binding, DLG motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in squamous cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vivo studies with mice expressing this mutation demonstrate NFE2L2 G31R is activating as measured by robust tumor formation and NFE2L2 overexpression compared to wildtype (PMID: 27147599).

The NFE2L2 E82D mutation occurs in the protein's conserved ETGE motif, which is involved in binding to its repressor, KEAP1. Protein modeling suggests this mutation will disrupt the association with KEAP1, potentially resulting in constitutive activation of NFE2L2 (PMID: 18757741, 24130096).

The NEF2L2 T80K mutation occurs in the protein's conserved ETGE motif, which is involved in binding to its repressor, KEAP1 (PMID: 18757741, 24130096). Immunoprecipitation assays demonstrated that this mutation has a substantially reduced ability to interact with KEAP1 (PMID: 18757741). Additionally, the NEF2L2 T80K mutation robustly formed tumors in mice, and overexpression of this mutant increased the levels of NFE2L2 protein compared to wildtype (PMID: 27147599).

The NFE2L2 D77H mutation is located in the Kelch domain of the protein. The D77H mutation likely disrupts coordination of an ordered water molecule that stabilizes the interaction of NFE2L2 with its negative regulator, KEAP1, leading to increased protein stabilization and activity (PMID: 16888629). This mutation is a hotspot, suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

NFE2L2 exon 2 in-frame deletions are found across several tumor types. Tumors from the TCGA with NFE2L2 exon 2 in-frame deletions showed high expression of the 27 candidate NRF2 target genes, suggesting that exon 2 in-frame deletion is not inactivating (PMID: 27568559). These mutations were mutually exclusive with other activating NFE2L2 and KEAP1 alterations (PMID: 27568559). Knockdown of NRF2 led to increased apoptosis in cells with exon 2 in-frame deletions versus cells with wildtype NFE2L2 suggesting an increased dependence on the exon 2-deleted form, suggesting that this form is activating (PMID: 27568559). When expressed in 293 cells, NFE2L2 exon 2 in-frame deletion abolished interaction with KEAP1 and led to sustained NRF2 target gene expression (PMID: 27568559).

The NFE2L2 W24C mutation is located in the KEAP1 binding domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. Computational modeling of this protein predicts that it would impair binding to KEAP1, which would result in increased NFE2L2 protein stability and transcriptional activity (PMID: 1875774,18757741, 24142871).

The NFE2L2 Q26L mutation is located in the KEAP1 binding domain of the protein. In addition, this mutation resulted in increased ligand-independent S2 cleavage (PMID: 16738328). In addition, this mutation resulted in increased ligand-independent S2 cleavage (PMID: 16738328). Exogenous expression of the A1701P mutation, in the context of both full-length NOTCH1 as well as an ΔEGF NOTCH1, results in increased NOTCH1 downstream transcriptional signaling when measured by a NOTCH1-responsive reporter (PMID: 16738328). Deletion mutations of NOTCH1 have shown to lead to a frameshift mutation and are associated with poor prognosis and shorter survival in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (PMID: 22077063, 23734977). In patients with T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, deletion mutations cause expression of truncated mRNAs resulting in ligand-independent activation of NOTCH1 due to deletions in the negative regulatory region of the protein. Some of these mutations have shown to be RAG-mediated and display strong gain-of-function effects in experimental studies (PMID: 20852131).

The NOTCH1 A465T mutation is located in the calcium-binding EGF domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in glioma (PMID: 24140581). In vitro studies with CHO cells expressing NOTCH1 A465T demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced LFNG-mediated elongation and downstream signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 36265581).

The NFE2L2 D29Y mutation is located in the KEAP1 binding, DLG motif of the protein. The NOTCH1 C440F mutation is located in the calcium-binding EGF domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in skin basal cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26950094). In silico analysis of NOTCH1 C440F suggests that NOTCH1 is inactivating through disruption of protein folding (PMID: 27228302).

The NOTCH1 V1605del inframe mutation occurs in the Notch1 heterodimerization which is critical for assembly, stabilization and ligand-dependent activation of the NOTCH1 protein (PMID:24651013). Gain-of-function missense and insertion/deletion mutations in this domain are recurrently observed in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) (PMID: 15472075). Therefore, although the functionality of the V1605del mutant has not been specifically investigated, its position in the NOTCH1 HD domain suggests that there is a possibility for this mutation to be activating (PMID: 24651013, 15472075). Other heterodimerization domain mutations result in increased NOTCH1 downstream transcriptional signaling when measured by a NOTCH1-responsive reporter (PMID: 15472075, 16738328). Increased NOTCH1 expression and activity has been shown to upregulate a variety of known oncogenic pathways including PI3K, EGFR, NF-κB; however the mechanism remains unclear and may prove to be cancer-type specific (PMID: 25806268, 22056382, 16618740).

Fusions of NOTCH1 have been detected in patients with breast cancer and hematological malignancies and are likely to lead to NOTCH1 signaling activation. Experimental studies suggest that these alterations can transform cells in cell line experiments using colony forming assays and xenograft animal models, and are likely to be sensitive to NOTCH1 inhibitors (PMID: 22101766, 16688224, 23033986).

The NOTCH1 T349P mutation is located in the calcium-binding EGF domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic T-cell leukemia (PMID: 25595890). The NRAS Q61R mutation is located in the switch II region of the catalytic domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma and lung cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID:23515407, 30552700, 26619011). Knockdown of this endogenously expressed mutation in lung cancer and melanoma cell lines demonstrates that it is activating as measured by decreased cell proliferation, decreased tumor volume in xenograft models and decreased pathway activation compared to control knockdown (PMID: 23515407). Structural analysis of the Q61 residue demonstrates that it is crucial for NRAS GTP hydrolyzing activity suggesting that any mutation at Q61 would render the protein constitutively active (PMID: 10574788, 20194776, 9219684). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation was resistant to the EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, erlotinib, the ALK/MET/RON/ROS1 inhibitor, crizotinib, and the insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor inhibitor, linsitinib, and sensitive to two different MEK inhibitors, selumetinib and trametinib in lung cancer cell line models as measured by decreased cell viability and inhibited pathway activation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 23515407). In a basket trial of refractory solid tumors treated with a single-agent MEK inhibitor, binimetinib, eight patients with codon 61 NRAS-mutated colorectal cancer (n = 1 patient with Q61R) had a significantly longer OS and PFS compared to sixteen patients with colorectal cancer harboring a mutation in codon 12/13 (PMID: 33637626).

A patient with melanoma who was treated with the RAF inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib acquired the NRAS Q61R and T58I mutations and developed drug resistance (PMID: 24265153).
