The RET M980T mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral, as measured by kinase activity comparable to wildtype RET (PMID: 11438491).

The RET R897Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by abolished kinase activity in vitro (PMID: 11438491).

The RET M918V mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely activating, as measured by colony formation and proliferation mildly increased compared to wildtype RET (PMID: 21810974).

While the RET G885R mutation has not been functionally validated, multiple in silico studies have suggested that it is a common single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the population and is likely neutral (PMID: 25733075, 24336963).

The TRIM27-RET fusion protein results from the N-terminus of the tripartite motif of TRIM27 fusing with the truncated C-terminal tyrosine kinase domain of RET. This fusion protein has been found in salivary intraductal carcinoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 31162284, 32326537). Expression of the TRIM27-RET fusion in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that the fusion protein is activating as measured by increased transforming activity and tyrosine phosphorylation as compared to wildtype (PMID: 8753810).

The RET Y791F mutation has been found in the germline of patients with medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) and is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the receptor. There is conflicting evidence of the oncogenic function of the mutation. When found in the germline of patients with MTC, some studies suggest that this mutation is pathogenic (PMID: 12490841, 9506724). Biological experiments have determined that this mutation is constitutively activating and signals through the STAT3 pathway, in contrast to RET wildtype that signals through MAPK pathway (PMID: 15753368, 17209045). In vivo studies with mouse models expressing RET Y791F demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by physiological function comparable to wildtype (PMID: 32275061).

The RET E632_L633del mutation is located adjacent to the cysteine-rich domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in medullary thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 9191060). Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased foci formation compared to wildtype RET (PMID: 9191060).

The RET S649L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in medullary thyroid cancer (PMID: 18322301). Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated it was moderately activating as measured by increased downstream phosphorylation and moderate transforming abilities compared to untransfected NIH3T3 cells (PMID: 18322301).

The RUFY1-RET fusion protein combines the N-terminus of RUFY1 with the C-terminus of RET, preserving the kinase domain of RET. This fusion protien is found in patients with sporadic microsatellite instability-high colorectal cancers (PMID: 30279230). Expression of this fusion protein in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it was activating as shown by increased colony formation and pathway activation compared to expression of RET alone (PMID: 30279230). Cells expressing this mutation in vitro and in an in vivo xenograft model were sensitive to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor regorafenib (PMID: 30279230).

The RET S904F mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells resulted in modestly increased foci formation compared to cells expressing wildtype RET (PMID: 21810974).

The CCDC6-RET fusion results from a translocation fusing the 3'-end of the CCDC6 gene with the 5' end of the RET gene. This fusion has been found in patients with lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 23578175, 30257958, 33161056), pediatric lipofibromatosis-like neural tumors (LPF-NT) (PMID: 31219820), thyroid cancer (PMID: 34237031, 31425920) and breast cancer (PMID: 30446652). This alteration is likely activating and oncogenic as transfection of CCDC6-RET-expressing cells with siRNA targeting RET decreased MAPK pathway signaling and cell proliferation (PMID: 23578175). Multiple patients with non-small cell lung cancer who progressed on EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as afatinib and osimertinib were shown to have the CCDC6-RET fusion at disease progression and then went on to respond to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors in combination with the RET inhibitor BLU-667 (PMID: 30257958, 30073261). In vitro experiments show that expression of the CCDC6-RET fusion in EGFR-mutant cells leads to persistent cell growth in the presence of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors but sensitivity to RET kinase inhibitors such as BLU-667 (PMID: 30257958). A patient with EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer harboring a CCDC6-RET fusion had a response to cabozantinib after developing acquired resistance to osimertinib (Abstract: Chae et al. JCO PO, 2018. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00295). In a Phase I clinical trial of the multikinase RET inhibitor RXDX-105, patients with lung cancer harboring the CCDC6-RET mutation experienced partial responses (3/27) and stable disease (2/27) in response to treatment (PMID: 30487236).  A pediatric patient with papillary thyroid cancer harboring the CCDC6-RET fusion had a tumor response to radioiodine therapy in combination with the RET fusion–targeted inhibitor selpercatinib (PMID: 34237031).

The MYH10-RET fusion results from a translocation including the 5'-end of the MYH10 gene with the 3’-end of the RET gene from exon 12 and including the tyrosine kinase domain of RET. This fusion has been found in malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors and infantile myofibromatosis (PMID: 31219820, 28028925). A patient with infantile myofibroma/hemangiopericytoma harboring the MYH10-RET fusion had a partial response to the RET inhibitor selpercatinib (PMID: 32923911).

Fusions of RET arise from chromosomal translocations that fuse the N-terminal portion of a coiled-coil domain-containing partner protein with the C-terminal kinase-domain-containing portion of RET. These fusion proteins are most commonly found in lung and colorectal cancers and result in constitutive activation of RET kinase activity due to dimerization mediated by the RET fusion partner. RET fusions have been shown to transform cell lines in vitro and promote lung tumorigenesis in mouse models (PMID: 22327623, 25064355). RET fusions have been shown to be sensitive to small molecule inhibitors such as vandetanib and cabozantinib (PMID: 27825636, 27803005) and are FDA-recognized as predictive of response to the inhibitors selpercatinib and pralsetinib (PMID: 32846060, 36122315)(Abstract: Subbiah et al. Abstract# 109, ASCO 2020. https://ascopubs.org/doi/abs/10.1200/JCO.2020.38.15_suppl.109).

The RET A919V mutation is located in the substrate-binding pocket of the RET kinase domain. This mutation has been found in colorectal neuroendocrine carcinoma (PMID: 28730258). In silico structural modeling suggests that this mutation is likely activating, as measured by decreased predicted protein stability of the mutant compared to wildtype (PMID: 19186126).

The RET D631A mutation is located adjacent to the cysteine-rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral, as measured by no increased foci formation or phosphorylation compared to wildtype RET (PMID: 10049754).

The RET E505_G506del mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (PMID: 26765577). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream pathway activation and colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26765577).

The RET Y806C mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this variant has not been functionally validated alone, expression of this variant with RET C634R led to diminished sensitivity to small molecule inhibitors of RET (e.g. ZD6474) (PMID: 19029224). RET Y806C was identified as a secondary resistance mutation in a patient with medullary thyroid cancer harboring RET V804M and RET M918T after treatment with selpercatinib (PMID: 35304457).

The RET F893L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by abolished kinase activity in vitro (PMID: 11438491).

The RET C620R mutation is located in the cysteine-rich domain of RET. Codon 620 mutations are common of FMTC families (about 60%) and were also found in patients expressing the Hirschsprung phenotype (PMID: 9230192). Expression of this mutation into NIH3T3 cells induces transformation and activation of RET as demonstrated by higher levels of phospho-tyrosine. This mutation may be associated with disruption of the transport of RET to the plasma membrane or its maturation (PMID: 9230192).

The RET I852M mutation is located outside the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in individuals with medullary thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 11295841, 21711375). Expression of this mutation in a fibroblast cell line demonstrated that it is weakly activating as measured by a proliferative and invasive phenotype intermediate to other known activating mutations (PMID: 21711375).

The SPECC1L-RET fusion results from a translocation including the 5'-end of the SPECC1L gene with the 3’-end of the RET gene from exon 12 and including the tyrosine kinase domain of RET. This fusion has been found in patients with pediatric infantile fibrosarcoma and uterine cervical sarcoma (PMID: 31219820, 31917708). A patient with infantile fibrosarcoma harboring the SPECC1L-RET fusion had a partial response to the RET inhibitor selpercatinib (PMID: 32923911).

The RET C630Y mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in gastric cancer (PMID: 31620276). In vitro studies with COS7 cells expressing RET C630Y demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased colony formation and migration and increased phosphorylation of RET, AKT and PI3K compared to wildtype (PMID: 34905813). In a case report, a patient with small cell lung cancer harboring RET C630Y was treated with selpercatinib and demonstrated a partial response (PMID: 37922409).

The RET V648I mutation is found in medullary thyroid cancer. Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated it is likely gain-of-function as measured by foci formation comparable to wildtype RET but cell proliferation increased compared to wildtype RET (PMID: 21810974).

The RET S891A mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the RET protein. Germline S891A mutations have been found in familial medullary thyroid carcinoma (FMTC) and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A) (PMID: 20554711). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased level of downstream STAT3 activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 24561444, 15753368).

The RET C618R mutation is located in the cysteine-rich domain of RET. Codon 618 mutations are common of FMTC families (about 60%) and were also found in patients expressing the Hirschsprung phenotype (PMID: 9230192). Expression of this mutation into NIH3T3 cells induces transformation and activation of RET as demonstrated by higher levels of phospho-tyrosine. This mutation may be associated with disruption of the transport of RET to the plasma membrane or its maturation (PMID: 9230192).

The RET V804M mutation is at a classical gatekeeper residue, regulating access to the ATP binding site within the RET kinase domain (PMID: 17047083). This mutation is biologically active and is able to transform cells in culture. Furthermore, this mutation confers resistance to kinase inhibitors, such as vandetanib and PP1 which inhibit RET by binding to this region (PMID: 17047083). A patient with hereditary RET V804M-mutated multiple endocrine neoplasia 2A and medullary thyroid cancer had a complete response to treatment with LOXO-292 (Abstract: Wirth et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.19.00189).

The RET T338I mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in the germline of some patients with medullary thyroid cancer (PMID: 15531548, 21810974). There is conflicting experimental data for this mutation. Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by foci formation comparable to wildtype RET and a neutral score in Align-GVGD analysis in silico (PMID: 21810974). Conversely, in the same study, cell proliferation of NIH-3T3 cells expressing the RET T338I mutation was significantly increased compared to wildtype RET (PMID: 21810974).

The RET C634Y mutation is located in the cysteine-rich domain of RET. Expression of this mutation into NIH3T3 cells induces transformation and activation of RET as demonstrated by higher levels of phospho-tyrosine. Expression of the C634Y mutant induced the highest transforming activity in comparison with other cysteine mutations at codons 609, 611, 618, 620 and 630. This mutation is being thought to disrupt the transport of RET to the plasma membrane or is maturation (PMID: 9230192). RET C634 mutations are correlated with the development of MEN2A, as they are the most frequent mutations in MEN2A (about 80%).

The RET G810S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, this mutation was identified as a secondary resistance mutation in a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring the KIF5B-RET fusion after treatment with selpercatinib (PMID: 35304457). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation results in steric hindrance to RET inhibitors due to the bulky residue substitution (PMID: 29650534).

The KIF5B-RET fusion is activating as it causes aberrant activation of RET kinase and induces anchorage-independent growth activity when expressed in NIH3T3 cells (PMID: 22327624). This fusion is present in about 1-2% of lung adenocarcinomas from people from United States and Japan (PMID: 22327624) and has been found in lung metasteses to the brain (Abstract: Facchinetti et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.19.00073). In a Phase I clinical trial of the multikinase RET inhibitor RXDX-105, patients with the KIF5B-RET mutation had no objective response (PMID: 30487236). Among patients with KIF5B-RET expressing lung tumors, eight of nineteen had stable disease and eleven of nineteen had progression of disease (PMID: 30487236). Expression of this fusion protein in Ba/F3 cells similarly demonstrated that this fusion protein had a higher IC50 (190nmol/L) than non-KIF5B-RET containing Ba/F3 cells lines (103 nmol/L for CCDC6-RET and 87nmol/L for NCOA4-RET) (PMID: 30487236).

The RET R873Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by abolished kinase activity in vitro (PMID: 11438491).

The RET D631G mutation is located adjacent to the cysteine-rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral, as measured by no increased foci formation or phosphorylation compared to wildtype RET (PMID: 10049754).

The RET-SEPTIN9 fusion contains the extracellular and kinase domains of RET fused to the oligomerizing SEPTIN9 guanine nucleotide-binding domain. This fusion has been found in pheochromocytoma (Abstract: Mweempwa et al. JCO PO, 2021. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.21.00127?bid=93111472&cid=DM8163). While this fusion has not been functionally characterized per se, RET fusions that are in-frame and contain the RET kinase domain are generally considered likely activating and likely oncogenic (PMID: PMID: 22327623, 25064355). A patient with pheochromocytoma harboring the RET-SEPTIN9 fusion had a partial response to treatment with selpercatinib (Abstract: Mweempwa et al. JCO PO, 2021. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.21.00127?bid=93111472&cid=DM8163).

The RET C634S mutation is located in the cysteine-rich domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in medullary thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 15277225). Expression of this mutation in PC Cl 3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased kinase activity, downstream pathway activation, and colony formation compared to wildtype RET (PMID: 15277225).

The RET E921K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by abolished kinase activity in vitro (PMID: 11438491).

The RET V804L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Conflicting studies suggest that this variant is likely activating, though not as strongly as other mutations (PMID: 9242375, 15184865). Expression of this variant in RAT1 cells led to cell proliferation, but did not lead to transformation (PMID: 15184865, 9242375). A patient with KIF5B-RET fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer who responded to and then progressed on vandetanib was shown to harbor a V804L mutation at progression that subsequently responded to LOXO-292 (Abstract: Wirth et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.19.00189).

The RET C609Y mutation is located in one of the six cysteine residues closest to the cell membrane. This mutation has been found in patients with familial medullary thyroid carcinoma (FMTC) and Hirschsprung disease (PMID: 9230192). Expression of RET C609Y in NIH3T3 cells induced transformation and activation of RET as demonstrated by increased levels of phospho-tyrosine, suggesting that this mutation is activating (PMID: 9230192). The RET C609Y mutation disrupts the transport of RET to the plasma membrane or its maturation, thus indicating that this mutation may have a role in Hirschsprung's disease (PMID: 9230192).

The RET A883F mutation is located in the protein's kinase domain and promotes transition to the active form of the protein, resulting in increased kinase activity and enhanced signaling (PMID: 24561444). RET A883F mutations are an uncommon cause of the MEN2B syndrome, characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, multiple mucosal neuromas, intestinal ganglioneuromas and marfanoid habitus (PMID: 24561444).

Truncating mutations in SETD2 occur in the C-terminal portion of the protein leading to loss of the SRI domain, reduced H3K36 trimethyltransferase activity and is considered an oncogenic event (PMID: 23417712, 24509477). SETD2 mutations are often associated with MLL rearranged leukemias and is associated with enhanced leukemia development in mice (PMID: 24509477). In patients with gliomas, SETD2-truncating mutations are specifically detected in high-grade tumors (PMID: 23417712). Furthermore, truncating mutations in renal cell carcinomas are associated with replication stress and impaired DNA repair (PMID: 25728682).

SETD2 deletions are associated with loss of SETD2 mRNA expression. In patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), these alterations are associated with loss of TP53, genomic complexity and poor-prognosis (PMID: 27282254). SETD2 deletions have also been identified in patients with T cell lymphomas leading to loss of H3K36 methylation. Experimental studies of SETD2 depletion in mouse and human T cells showed enhanced cell proliferation in malignant cells (Abstract: McKinney et al. Abstract #1052, ASH 2016. https://ash.confex.com/ash/2016/webprogram/Paper96954.html). Treatment with the ATR inhibitor RP-3500 is predicted to be synergistic with SETD2 loss as measured by a genome-wide CRISPR screening that identified loss of SETD2 as a target alteration for sensitivity to this inhibitor (PMID: 34911817, 30532030).

The SETD2 R2510H mutation is located in the SRI (Set2-Rpb1-interacting) domain of the SETD2 protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as it abolished tubulin binding and methylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 34157286).

The RNF43 G659fs*41 mutation is located in the cytoplasmic domain of the protein and results in the loss of the C-terminal region. This mutation has been identified in colon cancer, stomach cancer, endometrial cancer and high microsatellite unstable (MSI-H) BRAF V600E-mutant tumors (PMID: 31811196). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RNF43 G659fs*41 demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by Wnt signaling inhibition, protein expression and localization comparable to wildtype (PMID: 31811196). Preclinical studies of MSI-H colon cancer cell lines expressing RNF43 G659fs*41 and BRAF V600E demonstrate sensitivity to GSK3 inhibitor CHIR99021 as measured by inhibition of cellular growth (PMID: 31811196).

Truncating mutations in RNF43 occur throughout the gene body and result in loss of function of the protein (PMID: 23096461)(Spit et al. EMBO 2020. https://www.embopress.org/doi/full/10.15252/embj.2019103932). In colorectal and endometrial cancers, RNF43 truncating mutations occur predominantly in microsatellite-unstable tumors and are mutually exclusive with inactivating APC mutations (PMID: 25344691). In pancreatic cancer cell lines, RNF43 truncating mutations cause Wnt-signaling dependency via increased levels of membrane Frizzled and are sensitive to Wnt inhibition (PMID: 23847203).

The SF3B1 R625G mutation occurs in the protein's HEAT domain, which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 33031100). Expression of this alteration in melanoma cell lines results in dysregulated gene expression and altered splicing at 3' exon/intron splice sites (PMID: 25788694). SF3B1 mutations located within the heat domain have been associated with aberrant splicing, resulting in degradation of the targeted transcripts and downregulation of the associated protein (PMID: 26565915).

The R1625C mutation in SETD2 resides in the catalytic domain of the enzyme. Expression of this mutation resulted in the complete loss of H3K36me3 and diminished binding to the histone H3 tail, leading to protein instability. Expression of the R1625C mutation causes diminished enzymatic activity (PMID: 27528607); however additional studies are required to ascertain the functional consequences of this mutation.

The SF3B1 E622D mutation occurs in the HEAT domain, which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation results in abnormal recruitment of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA, thus leading to aberrant splicing of target transcripts (PMID: 25428262, 21909114). Gene expression and splicing profiling of CD34+ cells from patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) harboring this mutation demonstrated that mutant SF3B1 predominantly affects genes involved in myelodysplastic syndrome pathogenesis, iron homeostasis, mitochondrial metabolism and RNA splicing/processing (PMID: 25428262).

The SF3B1 R625C mutation occurs in the protein’s HEAT domain, which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in uveal melanoma (UVM) (PMID: 33031100). Mutations within this domain alter SF3B1-mediated splicing, resulting in the degradation of SF3B1-targeted transcripts and aberrant protein expression in the cell (PMID: 26565915). In patient-derived UVM and myelodysplastic syndrome samples, the R625C mutation has been found to alter the splicing and gene expression signatures (PMID: 23861464, 24434863).

The SF3B1 H662D mutation occurs in the HEAT domain of SF3B1 which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 33031100). While this variant has not been functionally characterized, primary samples from patients with uveal melanoma and myelodysplastic syndromes with the H662Q/R variants exhibit aberrant gene expression and splicing signatures (PMID: 25428262).

The SF3B1 K700R mutation occurs in the HEAT domain of SF3B1 which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. Cell lines expressing this mutation have splicing comparable to wildtype cells (PMID: 26565915) but cell lines expressing the variant K700E have altered splicing (PMID: 24434863, 25428262). However, this mutation is a hotspot, suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

The SF3B1 K741Q mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SF3B1 K741Q demonstrate that the mutation has a switch-of-function as measured by a moderate increase in aberrant splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 33777335).

The SF3B1 K700E mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in myelodysplastic syndromes and other heme malignancies, as well as breast cancer (PMID: 30846499, 33031100). The K700E mutation disrupts the binding of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA, resulting in abnormal splicing of key gene transcripts (PMID: 23160465, 23335386, 21909114, 25428262, 25424858, 24434863, 25428262). Exogenous expression of the K700E mutation in HEK293 cells resulted in the use of an alternate branch point sequence resulting in aberrant 3' splice site selection and nonsense-mediated decay, resulting in protein downregulation (PMID: 26565915). In mouse models, the expression of K700E results in anemia, erythroid dysplasia and an expansion of the hematopoietic stem cell pool (PMID: 27622333). Expression of this mutation in myeloid cell lines demonstrated that it enhances IL6 production and NFkB activity, and may affect innate immunity (PMID: 30846499). In mammary epithelial and breast cancer cells, the K700E mutation enhances cell migration and invasion, promotes tumorigenesis in combination with mutant PIK3CA, induces aberrant splicing leading to activation of AKT and NF-κB, and sensitizes breast cancer cells to AKT inhibitors MK2206 and GDC0068 (PMID 33031100).

The SF3B1 K666T mutation occurs in the HEAT domain of SF3B1 which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in uveal melanoma (UVM) and breast cancer (PMID: 33031100). This alteration likely disrupts the binding of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA resulting in abnormal splicing of key gene transcripts (PMID: 24434863). Endogenous expression of the SF3B1 K666T mutation in HEK293 cells resulted in deregulation of a subset (~0.5%) of splice junctions, mostly caused by the use of an alternative 3' splice site upstream of the canonical 3' splice site (PMID: 26842708). The oncogenic potential of this mutation has yet to be experimentally characterized; however, the splicing signature of a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and a patient with UVM harboring this mutation clustered with other oncogenic SF3B1 signatures (PMID: 24434863).

The SF3B1 R625H mutation occurs in the HEAT domain which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in uveal melanoma (UVM) (PMID: 33031100). SF3B1 mutations located within the heat domain have been associated with aberrant splicing, resulting in degradation of the targeted transcripts and downregulation of the associated protein (PMID: 26565915). In samples from patients with UVM and myelodysplastic syndrome, this mutation has been found to alter gene expression and the splicing signature (PMID: 23861464, 24434863).

The SF3B1 R625L mutation occurs in the HEAT domain which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 33031100). SF3B1 mutations located within the heat domain have been associated with aberrant splicing, resulting in degradation of the targeted transcripts and downregulation of the associated protein (PMID: 26565915). In samples from patients with uveal melanoma and myelodysplastic syndrome patients, this mutation has been found to alter gene expression and the splicing signature (PMID: 23861464, 24434863).

The SF3B1 K666M mutation occurs in the HEAT domain of SF3B1 which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation likely disrupts the binding of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA resulting in abnormal splicing of key gene transcripts (PMID: 24434863). The splicing signature of a patient with uveal melanoma harboring this mutation clustered with other oncogenic SF3B1 signatures (PMID: 24434863).

The SF3B1 E622Q mutation occurs in the HEAT domain which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 33031100). SF3B1 mutations located within the heat domain have been associated with aberrant splicing, resulting in degradation of the targeted transcripts and downregulation of the associated protein (PMID: 26565915). While this mutation has not been functionally validated, the E622D variant results in dysregulated gene expression and a disrupted splicing signature in uveal melanoma patient samples (PMID: 25428262, 21909114).

The SF3B1 G742D mutation occurs in the HEAT domain of SF3B1 which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (PMID: 33031100). This alteration results in abnormal recruitment of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA leading to aberrant splicing of target gene transcripts (PMID: 25428262, 21909114, 27818134). Analysis of RNA expression in patients with CLL with this mutation showed altered gene expression, clustering with other patients harboring SF3B1 mutations (PMID: 24434863, 27818134).

The SF3B1 R625D mutation occurs in the HEAT domain which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. In samples from patients with myelodysplastic syndrome, this mutation has been found to alter gene expression and splicing signature (PMID: 24434863).

The SF3B1 I665F mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SF3B1 I665F demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by aberrant splice burden and structural conformation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 33777335).

The SF3B1 D781E mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SF3B1 D781E demonstrate that the mutation has a switch-of-function as measured by increase in aberrant splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 33777335).

The exon 14 SF3B1 Y623C mutation is located in the fourth HEAT domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, myelodysplastic syndromes and uveal melanoma (PMID: 26565915, 22096241, 23793026). In vitro analysis of patient cells harboring this mutation suggests that it is comparable to wildtype, though this could be explained by the low allele frequency of the mutation in the patient sample (PMID: 26565915).

The SF3B1 H662R mutation occurs in the HEAT domain which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in uveal melanoma (UVM) (PMID: 33031100). This mutation results in abnormal recruitment of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA, leading to aberrant splicing of target gene transcripts (PMID: 25428262, 21909114). Global analyses of primary samples from UVM indicated that patients harboring this SF3B1 mutation have aberrant gene expression and splicing signatures (PMID: 25428262).

The SF3B1 K741N mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SF3B1 K741N demonstrate that the mutation has a switch-of-function as measured by increase in aberrant splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 33777335).

The SF3B1 L833F mutation is located in the HEAT repeats 9-12 region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 29617667). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the yeast equivalent Hsh155 V502F demonstrate that the mutation has a switch-of-function as measured by aberrant splicing activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 32320410).

The SF3B1 G740E mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 23086750). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SF3B1 G740E demonstrate that the mutation has a switch-of-function as measured by increase in aberrant splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 33777335).

The SF3B1 H662Q mutation occurs in the HEAT domain which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This alteration results in abnormal recruitment of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA, leading to aberrant splicing of target gene transcripts (PMID: 25428262, 21909114). Global analyses of CD34+ myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) patient samples and primary samples from uveal melanoma patients harboring this SF3B1 mutation have aberrant gene expression and splicing signatures (PMID: 25428262, 25428262).

The SF3B1 K666R mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the SF3B1 protein. This mutation has been found in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) (PMID: 25428262). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation has a switch-of-function effect as evidenced by the abnormal recruitment of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA, leading to aberrant splicing of target gene transcripts in mutant SF3B1 cells compared to wildtype (PMID: 25428262, 21909114). Furthermore, global profiling of CD34+ cells from patients with MDS harboring this mutation demonstrated that mutant SF3B1 leads to dysregulated gene expression and aberrant splicing (PMID: 25428262).

The SF3B1 R957Q mutation occurs in the HEAT domain of SF3B1 which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. R957Q has not been functionally tested. However, this alteration likely results in abnormal recruitment of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA, leading to aberrant splicing of target gene transcripts (PMID: 23160465).

The SF3B1 K666N mutation occurs in the HEAT domain of SF3B1 which functions as a scaffolding region for protein interactions. This mutation has been found in breast cancer and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 33031100). This alteration likely disrupts the binding of splicing machinery to pre-mRNA resulting in abnormal splicing of key gene transcripts (PMID: 24434863). An endometrial cell line expressing the K666N mutation was dependent on the wild-type copy of SF3B1 for proliferation and not the mutant form, suggesting that one copy of the wild-type allele is required for proliferation (PMID: 25788694).

The SF3B1 K741E mutation is located in the HEAT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in clear cell renal cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SF3B1 K741E demonstrate that the mutation has a switch-of-function as measured by increase in aberrant splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 33777335).

The SMAD2 S467A mutation is located in the MH2 domain. In vitro assays demonstrate that this mutation is inactivating as measured by abolished receptor-mediated phosphorylation and decreased SMAD2 transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 9346908).

The SMAD2 K375A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation disrupts SMAD2 homotrimer formation, however, the impact of SMAD2 homotrimers on transcription has yet to be determined (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD2 K420A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation disrupts SMAD2 homotrimer formation (PMID: 11779503) and prevents phosphorylation of SMAD2, thus disrupting the ability of SMAD2 to interact with transcription factors (PMID: 14729957).

The SMAD2 V319D mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation reduces the binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4. Consequently, the SMAD2-SMAD4 complex cannot translocate to the nucleus resulting in abberrant TGFß-regulated transcription (PMID: 11274206).

The SMAD2 D450E mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells led to decreased binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4, likely resulting in reduced translocation of the complex to the nucleus and altered anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 23139211).

The SMAD2 P305L mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells led to decreased binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4, likely resulting in reduced translocation of the complex to the nucleus and altered anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 23139211).

The SMAD2 D300N mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells led to decreased binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4, likely resulting in reduced translocation of the complex to the nucleus and altered anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 23139211).

The SMAD2 N387P mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation does not impact binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4 (PMID: 11779503). Additional functional studies are required to determine the full biological consequence of this mutation.

SMAD2 deletions have been associated with induction of the epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) and increased angiogenesis in preclinical studies of squamous cell carcinoma. Similar observations have been made in metastatic breast cancer and mouse hepatocytes mouse models and cell line studies (PMID: 22204491, 18618014, 20852387, 20010874, 16382155, 15133179, 19276350). Notably, studies in mice have shown that loss of SMAD2 does not alter tumor burden, but increases tumor invasiveness and susceptibility after chemically induced carcinogenesis (PMID: 12384562, 18618014). This suggests that loss of SMAD2 can promote a metastatic tumor phenotype, possibly through derepression of the EMT-promoting factor SNAIL or other SMAD2 transcriptional targets, but is itself not sufficient to trigger tumor formation (PMID: 18618014).

The SMAD2 S276L mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells led to decreased binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4, likely resulting in reduced translocation of the complex to the nucleus and altered anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 23139211).

The SMAD2 Y406H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation does not impact binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4, therefore, additional functional studies are required to determine if this alteration is oncogenic (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD2 R310H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation reduces the binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4. Consequently, the SMAD2-SMAD4 complex cannot translocate to the nucleus resulting in abberrant TGFß-regulated transcription (PMID: 11274206).

The SMAD2 S465A mutation is located in the MH2 domain. In vitro assays demonstrate that this mutation is inactivating as measured by abolished receptor-mediated phosphorylation and decreased SMAD2 transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 9346908).

The SMAD2 T413N mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells led to decreased binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4, likely resulting in reduced translocation of the complex to the nucleus and altered anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 23139211).

The SMAD2 D450H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation reduces the binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4. Consequently, the SMAD2-SMAD4 complex cannot translocate to the nucleus altering anti-proliferative TGFß-regulated transcription (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD2 Y426A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation disrupted SMAD2 homotrimer formation (PMID: 11779503). Expression of SMAD2 Y426A abolished binding of SMAD2 to the TGF‐β receptor complex, resulting in defective TGF‐β induced phosphorylation and defective association with SMAD4 (PMID: 9463378).

The SMAD2 R321Q mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cancer cell was associated with TGFß-mediated growth inhibition, suggesting that this mutant may disrupt normal TGFß function, and promote an oncogenic effect (PMID: 16828225). This residue is a critical target for SMAD ubiquitination regulatory factor (Smurf) proteins (PMID: 20937913, 16828225).

While truncating mutations in SMAD2 have been detected throughout the entire gene, they most often occur in the M2 protein domain and are predicted to be associated with reduced protein expression and consequently abrogated TGFß signaling (PMID: 23139211). SMAD2 mutations that result in a protein lacking an intact MH2 domain, truncated at residue 425, or phosphorylation sites at residues S465 and S467, disrupt the ability of SMAD2 to form active SMAD complexes (PMID: 15711891, 12894231, 11779503).

The SMAD2 S467P mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells led to decreased binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4, likely resulting in reduced translocation of the complex to the nucleus and altered anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 23139211).

The SMAD2 R428A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation disrupts SMAD2 homotrimer formation, however, the impact of SMAD2 homotrimers on transcription has yet to be determined (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD2 D300H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation disrupts SMAD2 homotrimer formation, however, the impact of SMAD2 homotrimers on transcription has yet to be determined (PMID: 11779503). Biochemical assays have also demonstrated that this mutation reduces the binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4. Consequently, the SMAD2-SMAD4 complex cannot translocate to the nucleus resulting in aberrant TGFß-regulated transcription (PMID: 11274206).

The SMAD2 F346V mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical experiments, this protein can form a complex with SMAD4, suggesting this mutation does not alter binding to SMAD partners (PMID: 11274206). Additional functional studies are required to determine the full biological consequence of this mutation.

The SMAD2 W368H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD2 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation does not impact binding of SMAD2 to SMAD4. Additional functional studies are required to determine the full biological consequence of this mutation (PMID: 11779503, 11274206).

The SMAD4 V465M mutation is located in the C-terminus MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In HEK293T cells, expression of this mutation resulted in a modest decrease in BMP signaling, however, the difference was not statistically significant compared to wildtype SMAD4 (PMID: 22316667). Additional studies are necessary to determine the full functional consequence of this mutation.

The SMAD4 P102L mutation is located in the MH1 domain, which is important for DNA binding. Expression of this mutation in mammary cell lines was associated with decreased TGFß signaling, as evidenced by luciferase assays and complete loss of SMAD4 DNA binding (PMID: 14647410).

The SMAD4 R441P mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical studies, this mutation showed no defects in its ability to homodimerize or heterodimerize with SMAD2 (PMID: 11779503, 11274206, 10822381 ). Additionally, the SMAD4 R441P mutation did not exhibit defects in TGFß-induced transcriptional activation, and did not display dominant-negative inhibition of wildtype SMAD4, as measured by a luciferase-reporter assay (PMID: 10822381).

The SMAD4 E33* mutation is located in the MH1 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 23139211). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 E33* demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 Y513A mutation is located in the C-terminal MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this variant did not impact the formation of SMAD2 and SMAD4 heterodimers (PMID: 11779503). Therefore, additional studies are necessary to determine the full functional consequence of this mutation.

The SMAD4 V370D mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical studies, this mutation affects the ability of SMAD4 to oligomerize leading to reduced formation of SMAD2-SMAD4 heterodimers, likely impacting the transcription of TGFß target genes (PMID: 9214508, 11779503, 11274206, 10092624). In cell lines, expression of this mutation resulted in FHL1-SMAD4 interaction, a complex important in cell proliferation and differentiation (PMID: 19139564).

The SMAD4 F408fs mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 30636020). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 F408fs demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 G491fs mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 30636020). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 G491fs demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 D537H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation decreased the ability of SMAD4 to interact with SMAD2, which likely effects downstream anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD4 R378A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation was shown to have a reduced interaction with phosphorylated SMAD2, likely resulting in decreased anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 15350224).

The SMAD4 P130S mutation is located in the MH1 domain, which is important for DNA binding. Expression of this mutation in mammary cell lines was associated with decreased TGFß signaling, as evidenced by luciferase assays and a modest reduction in the ability of SMAD4 to bind DNA (PMID: 14647410).

The SMAD4 D351H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners (PMID: 23139211). A colorectal cell line that endogenously harbors the D537Y mutant exhibits reduced interaction between SMAD4 and SMAD2, resulting in loss of SMAD complex formation and reduced SMAD-mediated TGFß signaling. Expression of this mutation in colorectal cell lines was associated with reduced anti-proliferative TGFß-mediated transcription, thus resulting in loss of functional SMAD4 activity (PMID: 14715079).

The SMAD4 R515I mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrioid carcinoma (PMID: 29876005). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 R515I demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 L109fs mutation is located in the MH1 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 30636020). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 L109fs demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 L43V mutation is located in the MH1 domain, which is important for DNA binding. Expression of this mutation in mammary cell lines was associated with decreased TGFß signaling, as evidenced by luciferase assays and complete loss of DNA binding (PMID: 14647410).

The SMAD4 E330G mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In HEK293T cells, expression of this mutation resulted in a modest decrease in BMP signaling, however, the difference was not statistically significant compared to wildtype SMAD4 (PMID: 22316667). Additional studies are necessary to determine the full functional consequence of this mutation.

The SMAD4 R361G mutation is located at a highly conserved residue in the C-terminal MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners (PMID: 25523272). This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot. In HEK293T cells, expression of this mutation resulted in a modest decrease in BMP signaling, though not statistically significant compared to wildtype SMAD4 (PMID: 22316667). A patient with juvenile polyposis and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, which are both syndromes of aberrant TGF-ß signaling, harbored a germline SMAD4 R361G mutation that was absent in unaffected family members (PMID: 15031030).

The SMAD4 R515A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation decreased the ability of SMAD4 to interact with SMAD2, which likely effects downstream anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD4 R100T mutation is located in the MH1 domain, which is important for DNA binding. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in the inability of SMAD3 R268C to oligomerize with SMAD4, leading to decreased TGFß-mediated transcription (PMID: 10092624). In addition, this mutation demonstrated complete loss of DNA binding (PMID: 14647410).

The SMAD4 K507A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation decreased the ability of SMAD4 to interact with SMAD2, likely with implications for anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD4 R361C mutation occurs in the MH2 domain, which serves as an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding proteins. In biochemical studies, this mutation affects the ability of SMAD4 to oligomerize, which could have implications for the formation of SMAD2-SMAD4 dimers (PMID: 9214508). Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in the inability of SMAD4 R361C to oligomerize with SMAD3, resulting in reduced anti-proliferative TGFß-mediated transcription (PMID: 10092624, 26488212, 14647410).

The SMAD4 R515G mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in mammary cell lines resulted in decreased TGFß signaling, as evidenced by luciferase activity (PMID: 14647410).

The SMAD4 Y413_R416del mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 30636020). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 Y413_R416del demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 K428A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation decreased the ability of SMAD4 to interact with SMAD2, which likely effects downstream anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 11779503).

The SMAD4 R496H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HT-29 cell lines resulted in decreased SMAD-mediated transcription, likely leading to altered TGFß -mediated growth control (PMID: 26488212).

The SMAD4 D537E mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. (PMID: 23139211). Biochemical studies demonstrated that the D537E mutant disrupts oligomerization of SMAD4 (PMID: 9214508). Expression of this mutation in colorectal cell lines led to reduced anti-proliferative TGFß-mediated transcription, thus resulting in loss of functional SMAD4 activity (PMID: 14715079).

The SMAD4 R420H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical studies, this mutation did not alter the ability of SMAD4 to bind with SMAD2. Additional functional studies are required to confirm this alteration is neutral. (PMID: 11779503, 11274206).

The SMAD4 R497H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in mammary cell lines was associated with decreased TGFß signaling, as evidenced by luciferase assays and a modest reduction in the ability of SMAD4 to bind DNA (PMID: 14647410).

The SMAD4 C324Y mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in thyroid cancer cell lines resulted in reduced anti proliferative growth regulated by TGFß. Cell lines expressing the SMAD4 C324Y mutation could grow in anchorage-independent conditions and their morphology became more fibroblast-like. These changes corresponded to reduction in the levels of E-Cadherin, consistent with an epithelial to mesenchymal transformation (PMID: 22109972).

The SMAD4 D493A mutation is located in the MH1 domain, which is important for DNA binding. In biochemical assays, this mutation had a decreased ability to heterodimerize with SMAD3 or SMAD2, likely resulting in decreased anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 15350224).

Truncating mutations in SMAD4 typically occur in the M2 domain are associated with loss of protein function (PMID: 23139211). Truncating variants disrupting or lacking the MH2 domain can abrogate the ability of SMAD4 to form multimeric SMAD complexes and active DNA-binding complexes (PMID: 11553622, 10340381, 9094310) and these alterations have shown to abrogate growth-inhibiting TGFß signaling (PMID: 15711891).

The SMAD4 D537V mutation is located at the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and ovarian cancer, and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28120820, 28481359). In silico analysis suggests that SMAD4 D537V is inactivating as measured by SMAD4 D537 hotspot mutations disrupting the interaction between SMAD4 and SMAD3, leading to transcriptional dysregulation (PMID: 34963661, 10022869).

The SMAD4 D493N mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in gallbladder carcinoma, colorectal cancer and ductal carcinoma, and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24997986, 24951259, 26804919). Although the SMAD4 D493N allele has not been functionally characterized, in vitro studies with COS-1 cells expressing mutant SMAD4 D493A demonstrated is likely inactivating as measured by reduced association with R-SMAD in coimmunoprecipitation analysis as compared to wildtype (PMID: 15350224).

The SMAD4 E526Q mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in gallbladder cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 29360550). In silico analysis of SMAD4 E526Q suggests that the mutation is inactivating and deleterious (PMID: 32151199).

The SMAD4 K507Q mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in mammary cell lines was associated with decreased TGFß signaling, as evidenced by luciferase assays (PMID: 14647410).

The SMAD4 G508S mutation occurs in the MH2 domain, which facilitates interactions with SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical studies, this mutation affects the ability of SMAD4 to oligomerize, which could have implications for the formation of SMAD2-SMAD4 dimers (PMID: 9214508). Expression of SMAD4 G508S mutation significantly reduced (but did not abolish) ligand-dependant reporter activation compared to the wildtype protein. This suggests that the SMAD4 G508S mutation may not completely abolish SMAD4 transcriptional activity, but rather diminish it below critical levels (PMID: 9153220).

The SMAD4 W302* mutation is located in the SAD region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 30636020). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 W302* demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 D493H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical studies, this mutation was associated with reduced formation of SMAD2-SMAD4 heterodimers, likely impacting anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 11274206). In cell lines experiments, expression of this mutation resulted in FHL1-SMAD4 interaction, a complex important in cell proliferation and differentiation (PMID: 19139564).

The SMAD4 D493G mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adenomatous hyperplasia and lung adenocarcinoma, and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 30121391, 28481359). Although the SMAD4 D493G allele has not been functionally characterized, in vitro studies with COS-1 cells expressing mutant SMAD4 D493A demonstrated is likely inactivating as measured by reduced association with R-SMAD in coimmunoprecipitation analysis as compared to wildtype (PMID: 15350224).

The SMAD4 W398V mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation did not impact the formation of SMAD2-SMAD4 heterodimers (PMID: 11274206). Additional studies are required to determine the full functional consequence of this mutation.

The SMAD4 Y353L mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Immunohistochemical staining of a pancreatic tumor with a SMAD4 Y353L mutation demonstrated strong nuclear staining, which is inconsistent with other SMAD4 loss-of-function mutations. Further functional studies are required to determine if this mutation is indeed loss-of-function. this mutation is a hotspot, suggesting that it is potentially oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

The SMAD4 G386D mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HT-29 cell lines resulted in decreased SMAD-mediated transcription, likely leading to altered TGFß -mediated growth control (PMID: 26488212).

The SMAD4 A532H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation disrupted the formation of SMAD2-SMAD4 heterodimers, which likely impacts downstream anti-proliferative TGFß signaling (PMID: 11274206).

The SMAD4 R361H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical assays, this mutation decreased the ability of SMAD4 to interact with SMAD2, resulting in decreased anti-proliferative TGFß-mediated transcription (PMID: 11779503, 11274206, 17132729).

The SMAD4 D351N mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 27612425). In silico analysis of SMAD4 D351N suggests that the mutation is inactivating and deleterious (PMID: 32151199).

The SMAD4 G86V mutation is located in the MH1 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 29937994). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 G86V demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The SMAD4 H132Y mutation is located in the MH1 domain, which is important for DNA binding. Cell lines expressing this mutation did not respond to TGF-beta stimulation, suggesting that this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 25275298).

The SMAD4 Y353S mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in a yeast-2-hybrid assay demonstrated it was likely inactivating as measured by a decrease in SMAD3 binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 25502805).

The SMAD4 W509R mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In HEK293T cells, expression of this mutation resulted in a modest decrease in BMP signaling, however, the difference was not statistically significant compared to wildtype SMAD4 (PMID: 22316667). Additional studies are necessary to determine the full functional consequence of this mutation.

The SMAD4 G419V mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HT-29 cell lines was associated with decreased SMAD-mediated transcription, likely leading to altered TGFß-mediated growth control (PMID: 26488212).

The SMAD4 E330K mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in HT-29 cell lines resulted in decreased SMAD-mediated transcription, likely leading to altered TGFß -mediated growth control (PMID: 26488212).

SMAD4 deletions gives rise to pleiotropic and and tissue-dependent effects in tumorigenesis as demonstrated in different model systems (PMID: 22321641, 22321641, 17114584, 9482899, 10773876, 9506519, 10626800). For example SMAD4 deletions promote metastasis in pancreatic cancer but is not sufficient to initiate tumor formation; in contrast, these alterations are sufficient to promote tumor progression and initiation in head and neck cancer. Additionally, in transgenic mouse models of head and neck cancer and lung cancer, deletion of SMAD4 results in increased genomic instability and tumor development (PMID: 19841536, 25893305). In colon cancer cell lines, depletion of SMAD4 results in abrogation of TGFß-mediated growth inhibition (PMID: 9482899).

The SMAD4 D537G mutation is located at the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 27612425). In silico analysis suggests that SMAD4 D537G is inactivating as measured by SMAD4 D537 hotspot mutations disrupting the interaction between SMAD4 and SMAD3, leading to transcriptional dysregulation (PMID: 34963661, 10022869).

The SMAD4 D537A mutation is located at the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and cholangiocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 33262464, 29712892). In silico analysis suggests that SMAD4 D537A is inactivating as measured by SMAD4 D537 hotspot mutations disrupting the interaction between SMAD4 and SMAD3, leading to transcriptional dysregulation (PMID: 34963661, 10022869).

The SMAD4 G352E mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26416732). In silico analysis of SMAD4 G352E suggests that the mutation is inactivating and deleterious (PMID: 32151199).

The SMAD4 E330A mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells resulted in decreased formation of SMAD3-SMAD4 heterodimers, resulting in decreased anti-proliferative TGFß-mediated transcription (PMID: 17994767).

The SMAD4 D351H mutation is located in the MH2 domain, which is an interaction surface for SMAD4 binding partners. In biochemical studies, this mutation affects the ability of SMAD4 to oligomerize, which has implications for the formation of SMAD2-SMAD4 dimers (PMID: 9214508). In biochemical assays in HeLa cells, expression of this mutation resulted in decreased binding to SMAD2, resulting in decreased anti-proliferative TGFß transcriptional activity (PMID: 11274206, 14715079,14647410, 11779503, 14715079).

The SMARCA4 K785R mutation is located in the ATP binding pocket of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma (PMID: 23143597). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing SMARCA4 K785R demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to rescue SMARCA2 loss compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCA4 G1232D mutation occurs downstream of the protein's helicase domain. In vitro studies suggest this mutation results in reduction of SMARCA4's ATPase activity, leading to abnormal cell cycle and mitotic defects, and ultimately causing an increase in chromosome instability (PMID: 23698369).

The SMAD4 G510R mutation is located in the MH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28243320). Immunohistochemistry analysis of patient-derived colorectal cancer samples expressing SMAD4 G510R demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of SMAD4 immunohistochemistry staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 30636020).

The R978* mutation introduces a stop codon within SMARCA4's ATPase domain. This mutation leads to loss of SMARCA4 protein (a tumor suppressor) expression, thereby conferring oncogenic potential (PMID: 24658002, 24658004).

The SMARCA4 E821K mutation is located in the SNF2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in astrocytoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 29263181). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing SMARCA4 E821K demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a deficiency in chromatin opening and inducing gene expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCA4 A1186T mutation is located in the helicase C-terminal domain of the protein. In vitro studies with 293T and SMARCA2-knockdown NCI-H1944 cells expressing SMARCA4 A1186T demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by cell growth rescue following SMARCA2 knockdown comparable to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

SMARCA4 deletions cause reduced protein expression and have been detected in patients with lung cancer, ovarian carcinoma and colorectal cancer (PMID: 23139211, 18381774, 26942101, 11481457). Experimental studies show that SMARCA4 microdeletions encode proteins that can still interact with members of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, but result in abrogation of RB1 cell cycle arrest (PMID: 21520050). Additionally, heterozygous loss of SMARCA4 in mice can lead to the spontaneous development of epithelial tumors (PMID: 11163203). A mouse model of SMARCA4 inactivation in lung cancer suggests that loss of SMARCA4 results in a distinct phenotype with increased dependency on the oxidative phosphorylation pathway (PMID: 29892061).

The R1093* mutation results in a premature stop codon after arginine 1093 within SMARCA4's ATPase domain. This mutation leads to loss of SMARCA4 protein (a tumor suppressor) expression, thereby conferring oncogenic potential (PMID: 24658004, 24658001).

The SMARCA4 R1192C mutation is located in the ATP binding pocket of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 31558468). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing SMARCA4 R1192C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by deficiency in chromatin opening and inducing gene expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCA4 T910M mutation occurs within the protein's ATP-binding domain. In vitro studies suggest that this mutation results in loss of SMARCA4's ATPase activity, leading to abnormal cell cycle and mitotic defects, and ultimately causing an increase in chromosome instability (PMID: 23698369, 26842758).

The SMARCA4 R1135W mutation is located in the DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in gastric adenoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 27175599). In vitro studies with 293T and SMARCA2-knockdown NCI-H1944 cells expressing SMARCA4 R1135W demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by inability to rescue SMARCA2 loss and deficiency in opening chromatin compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCA4 G1162C mutation is located in the helicase C-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29681454). In vitro studies with 293T and SMARCA2-knockdown NCI-H1944 cells expressing SMARCA4 G1162C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to rescue SMARCA2 loss compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCA4 E1083G mutation was identified in a mutagenesis screen (PMID:16287714). This substitution is predicted to disrupt a structurally conserved α-helix within the lobe that participates in DNA translocation, but does not contain the ATPase catalytic site (PMID: 24172864). In vitro studies showed that the E1083G variant was stable, assembled into SWI/SNF-related complexes, and retained full ATPase activity. However, its nucleosome remodeling function was diminished by approximately 50% (PMID:16287714, 24172864). DNase I hypersensitivity assays demonstrated that the mutant Brg1 protein complexes, while being recruited to the β-globin locus control region (LCR), failed to effectively open up the chromatin configuration, thus perturbing transcription from the LCR. In addition, histone acetylation and DNA methylation patterns at the LCR were also altered. Consequently, mouse embryos bearing only one E1083G mutant Brg1 allele (Brg1null/ENU1) developed normally until mid-gestation, after which they exhibited a block in erythroid lineage development, leading to anemia and death (PMID:16287714). However, mice bearing both mutant alleles (Brg1ENU1/ENU1) are demonstrated to survive embryogenesis, but then exhibit a postnatal developmental phenotype associated with runting and incompletely penetrant lethality (PMID: 24172864).

The SMARCA4 R1243W mutation is located in the helicase C-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in biliary tract adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 29712892). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing SMARCA4 R1243W demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a deficiency in chromatin opening and inducing gene expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCA4 R1189* mutation causes a premature stop codon premature to functional domains in the protein. The variant has been observed in a family where a carrier developed rhabdoid tumors with loss of the SMARCA4 wildtype, which was associated with loss of immunoreactivity (PMID: 20137775). The variant also resulted in the expression of a truncated protein in cell lines, indicating that it is likely subject to nonsense-mediated decay (PMID: 20137775).

The SMARCA4 E882K mutation is located in the SNF2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma (PMID: 23143597). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing SMARCA4 E882K demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to rescue SMARCA2 loss compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCA4 G1232S mutation is located in the helicase C-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma (PMID: 22885699). In vitro studies with 293T and SMARCA2-knockdown NCI-H1944 cells expressing SMARCA4 G1232S demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to rescue SMARCA2 loss compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The majority of SMARCA4 mutations are nonsense, frameshift or splice-site mutations, leading to truncation or total loss of the SMARCA4 protein (PMID: 24658002, 24658004, 24658001, 25060813). The ATPase domain and bromodomain of SMARCA4 are located in the C-terminal part of the protein, which are particularly affected by truncating mutations, rendering SMARCA4 enzymatically-dead and non-functional (PMID: 18301784). The bromodomain is thought to be critical for SMARCA4 binding to acetylated histones and guiding the SWI/SNF complex to the chromatin (PMID: 18301784).

The SMARCA4 R1189Q mutation is located in the ATP binding pocket of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 27149842). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing SMARCA4 R1189Q demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a deficiency in chromatin opening and inducing gene expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 33144586).

The SMARCB1 R366C mutation is located in the C-terminal coiled-coil domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 26416732). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SMARCB1 R366C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced nucleosome eviction at the BAF complex site and decreased DNA accessibility compared to wildtype (PMID: 31759698).

The SMARCB1 K363N mutation is located in the C-terminal coiled-coil domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29681454). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SMARCB1 K363N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced nucleosome eviction at the BAF complex site and decreased DNA accessibility compared to wildtype (PMID: 31759698).

Truncating mutations in SMARCB1 are often found in malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs), lead to loss exons 4 and 5 of the gene and subsequent loss of protein function (PMID: 9671307). Loss of SMARCB1 in MRTs can lead to activation of the Hedgehog pathway via aberrant activation of GLI1, a direct protein interactor of SMARCB1 (PMID:21076395). SMARCB1 loss was also shown to activate the downstream Wnt/Beta-catenin pathway and is important in hepatocyte differentiation. (PMID:23435428,). SMARCB1-mutant MRT xenografts in mice have also been shown to be sensitive to EZH2 inhibition, suggesting that these tumors may be dependent on EZH2 enzymatic activity (PMID:23620515). Reintroduction of SMARCB1 protein in SMARCB1-deleted MRT cell lines resulted in growth arrest through histone-deacetylase(HDAC)-dependent down-regulation of cyclin-D1, demonstrating another mechanism by which this tumor suppressor functions (PMID:12138206, 30755442).

SMARCB1 deletions are associated with loss of the protein and are found primarily in malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) (PMID:22797305,23074045). While homozygous deletions in mice are embryonic lethal, heterozygous SMARCB1 deletions can lead to numerous different types of cancers including rhabdoid tumors, and soft tissue sarcomas, often with biallelic loss of SMARCB1 (PMID:11263494,11313485,11095756,12450796). In humans, germline deletions and mutations in SMARCB1 are the basis for familial cancer syndromes (PMID:10521299,9892189).

The SMARCB1 R377C mutation is located in the SNF5 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with HCT116 CRC cells expressing SMARCB1 R377C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 30108113).

The SMARCB1 R377H mutation is located in the SNF5 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in meningioma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 11161377). In vitro studies with TTC1240 cells expressing SMARCB1 R377C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased interaction of the SMARCB1 coiled-coil C-terminal domain compared to wildtype (PMID: 31759698).

The W535 residue is located in the transmembrane helix 7 of SMO near the pivot residues involved in activating class A G-protein coupled receptors (PMID: 25759020, 23636324). In vitro, this mutation confers constitutive ligand-independent activation of the SMO receptor resulting in high downstream activity of the Hedgehog signaling pathway, suggesting that SMO W535L may have oncogenic activity (PMID: 9422511).

The SMO Q477E mutation is located in the ligand binding pocket of the protein. In vitro studies with ASZ001 BCC cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO Q477E interferes with the binding of SMO inhibitor vismodegib and confers drug resistance as measured by cellular growth following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 25759020).

The SMARCB1 K364del mutation is located in the C-terminal coiled-coil domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in glioma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing SMARCB1 K364del demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced nucleosome eviction at the BAF complex site and decreased DNA accessibility compared to wildtype (PMID: 31759698).

The SMO V414A mutation is located in the pivot region of transmembrane helix 5 of the protein. This mutation has been reported in basal cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 25801792). Expression of SMO V414A in SMO-null MEF cells demonstrated that this mutation is likely neutral as measured by Hedgehog signaling and activity in both basal and stimulated conditions as determined by mRNA levels of Gil1 comparable to those in wildtype cells (PMID: 25801792).

The SMO D473Y mutation occurs in the vismodegib drug binding site. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, in silico analysis suggests that SMO D473Y disrupts the hydrogen binding network in the drug binding site (PMID: 25306392). A patient with basal cell carcinoma harboring the SMO D473Y exhibited resistance to vismodegib (PMID: 25306392).

This SMO mutation is located in the protein's activating domain and is thought to play a key role in enabling conformational changes from the active to the inactive states (PMID: 2575902).
