In vitro, this mutation confers constitutive ligand-independent activated SMO leadingt to high downstream Hedgehog signalling activity. SMO C469Y mutations have been identified in tumors with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759020, 25759019, 25199678).

The SMO L412F is located in the activating domain of the protein. In vitro studies with ASZ001 BCC cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO L412F is activating as measured by constitutive ligand-independent activated SMO, leading to high downstream Hedgehog signaling activity (PMID: 25759020). SMO L412F mutations have been identified in tumors with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759020, 25759019, 25199678).

The SMO E518K mutation is located in the Frizzled domain of the protein. In vitro studies with CH310T1/2 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO E518K is likely neutral as measured by signaling activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21123452). SMO E518K is suggested to be resistant to SMO inhibitor vismodegib as measured by increased signaling activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21123452).

The SMO L221R mutation is located in the ligand-binding pocket of the protein. In vitro studies with C3H10T1/2 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO L221R interferes with the binding of SMO inhibitor LDE-225 and confers drug resistance as measured by cellular growth following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 20881279).

The A459V SMO mutation was identified in basal cell carcinomas with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759019). This mutations maps distal to the ligand binding pocket of SMO. In vitro, A459V mutant SMO displays increased basal activity leading to increased Hedghog signalling and shows reduced vismodegib sensitivity when expressed in C3H10T1/2 cells (PMID: 25759019).

In vitro, the SMO D473G mutation confers resistance to vismodegib (GDC-0449) by inhibiting drug binding without affecting the ability of SMO to transduce Hedgehog signaling (PMID: 19726788). This mutation was first identified by sequencing the tumor of a patient with medulloblastoma with acquired resistance to vismodegib (GDC-0449).

The SMO D384N mutation is located in the ligand binding pocket of the protein. In vitro studies with C3H10T1/2 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO D384N interferes with the binding of SMO inhibitor vismodegib and confers drug resistance as measured by cellular growth following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 25759019).

This SMO mutation is located in the protein's activating domain and is thought to play a key role in enabling conformational changes from the active to the inactive states (PMID: 2575902). In vitro, this mutation confers constitutive ligand-independent activated SMO leadingt to high downstream Hedgehog signalling activity. SMO I408V mutations have been identified in tumors with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759020, 25759019, 25199678).

The SMO T241M mutation is located distal to the ligand binding pocket of SMO. This mutation was identified in basal cell carcinomas with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759019). In vitro studies with C3H10T1/2 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO T241M is activating as measured by constitutive ligand-independent activated SMO, leading to high downstream Hedgehog signaling activity (PMID: 25759019).

The S387N SMO mutation was identified in basal cell carcinomas with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759019). This mutations maps distal to the ligand binding pocket of SMO. In vitro, S387N mutant SMO displays increased basal activity leading to increased Hedghog signalling and shows reduced vismodegib sensitivity when expressed in C3H10T1/2 cells (PMID: 25759019).

This SMO mutation is located in the protein's activating domain and is thought to play a key role in enabling conformational changes from the active to the inactive states (PMID: 2575902). In vitro, this mutation confers constitutive ligand-independent activated SMO leadingt to high downstream Hedgehog signalling activity. SMO F460L mutations have been identified in tumors with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759020, 25759019, 25199678).

SMO amplification is a rare event detected at low frequencies in melanomas, gliomas and breast cancer (Abstract: Zehir A et al. Nature Medicine, 2017. http://doi:10.1038/nm.4333). In a lung cancer cell line, SMO amplification was detected as a mechanism for resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibition (PMID: 26124204). Although the Hedgehog signaling pathway has been implicated in tumorigenesis and SMO overexpression in fibroblast cell lines confirm this, no direct role for the amplification of SMO has been characterized (PMID: 20215540, 24202394).

The SMO E518A mutation is located in helix seven of the protein. SMO 518A is suggested to confer resistance to SMO inhibitor vismodegib treatment as measured by significant signaling activity in vitro when treated with vismodegib (PMID: 21123452).

The SMO N219D mutation is located in the protein's extracellular ligand binding pocket. In vitro studies with C3H10T1/2 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO N219D interferes with the binding of SMO inhibitors vimodegib and LDE-225 and confers drug resistance as measured by cellular growth following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 25759019).

The SMO V321M mutation is located in the activating domain of the protein. In vitro studies with ASZ001 BCC cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO V321M is activating as measured by constitutive ligand-independent activated SMO, leading to high downstream Hedgehog signaling activity (PMID: 25759020). SMO V321M mutations have been identified in tumors with acquired resistance to vismodegib therapy (PMID: 25759020, 25759019, 25199678).

The SMO W281C mutation is located in the protein's ligand-binding pocket. In vitro, this mutation interferes with the binding of SMO inhibitors, including vismodegib and LDE-225, conferring drug resistance (PMID: 25759020, 25759019, 25199678). In vitro studies with ASZ001 BCC cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO W281C is activating as measured by constitutive ligand-independent activated SMO, leading to high downstream Hedgehog signaling activity (PMID: 25759020).

The SMO H231R mutation is located in the protein's ligand binding pocket. In vitro, this mutation interferes with the binding of SMO inhibitors, including vimodegib and LDE-225, thus conferring drug resistance (PMID: 25759020, 25759019).

The SMO K575M mutation occurs in the protein's carboxy terminal cytoplasmic tail (PMID:16339184), an important domain for interacting with G proteins and facilitating signal transduction in the Hedgehog signaling pathway (PMID:12499255). Although rare, this mutation has been observed in a human hepatocellular cancer (HCC) cell line (cBioPortal, MSKCC, 2014) as well as in one tumor from a 67-year-old female patient with HCC (PMID:16339184). In this tumor, SMO expression was significantly higher compared to the patient-matched normal, non-neoplastic liver tissue. In addition, this tumor displayed a significant increase in the expression of two SMO transcriptional targets, Gli1 and Ptc, thus suggesting that the K575M mutation is activating (PMID:16339184).
The SOCS1 F79L mutation is located in the SH2 domain of the SOCS1 protein. In silico analysis predicts that mutation is damaging (PMID: 36813059).

The SMO Q635E mutation is located in the ligand binding pocket of the protein. This mutation was identified in a patient with basal cell carcinoma who acquired resistance to vismodegib (PMID: 25759020). In vitro studies with ASZ001 BCC cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrate SMO Q635E interferes with the binding of SMO inhibitor vismodegib and confers drug resistance as measured by cellular growth following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 25759020).

The SPOP W131A occurs in the protein's conserved Meprin and Traf Homology (MATH) domain, which recruits substrate proteins (PMID: 18218622, 19818708). Crystallographic studies indicate that this residue coordinates hydrophobic side chains of SPOP substrates and this mutation perturbs interactions with such proteins in transfected Drosophila cells (PMID: 19818708). The potential oncogenic effect of this is unclear but the other mutations in this domain disrupt degradation of SPOP target genes.

Truncating mutations in SOCS1 can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its activity (PMID: 23296022, 29625055). SOCS1 encodes a protein named Suppressor of Cytokine Signaling 1, a member of the STAT-induced STAT inhibitors (SSI) that plays a key role in the negative feedback regulation of the JAK/STAT3 pathway after cytokine-mediated activation (PMID: 29674694). SOCS1 truncating mutations have been identified in patients with Hodgkin and diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (DLBCL), where they have been shown to convey a poor prognosis (PMID: 28302137, 26336985, 23296022). These inactivating mutations in SOCS1 are thought to result from aberrant B-cell somatic hypermutation in these lymphoid malignancies (PMID: 19734449). Truncating mutations in SOCS1 have been identified in patients with DLBCL and Hodgkin lymphoma (PMID: 28302137, 26336985, 29625055).

The SPOP M117I mutation occurs in the protein's conserved Meprin and Traf Homology (MATH) domain, which recruits substrate proteins (PMID: 18218622, 19818708). This mutation has been shown to impede SPOP-mediated ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of estrogen receptor α (ESR1) in a transfected kidney cancer cell line (PMID: 25766326). This could possibly have an oncogenic effect through perturbed estrogen-receptor signaling in endocrine-regulated tissue.

The SPOP S80R mutation occurs in the protein's conserved Meprin and Traf Homology (MATH) domain, which recruits substrate proteins (PMID: 18218622, 19818708). This mutation has been shown to impede SPOP-mediated ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of estrogen receptor α (ESR1) in a transfected kidney cancer cell line (PMID: 25766326). This could possibly have an oncogenic effect through perturbed estrogen-receptor signaling in endocrine-regulated tissue.

The SPOP E50K mutation occurs in the protein's conserved Meprin and Traf Homology (MATH) domain, which recruits substrate proteins (PMID: 18218622, 19818708). This mutation has been shown to impede SPOP-mediated ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of estrogen receptor α (ESR1) in a transfected kidney cancer cell line (PMID: 25766326). This could possibly have an oncogenic effect through perturbed estrogen-receptor signaling in endocrine-regulated tissue.

The SPOP K134N mutation occurs in the protein's conserved Meprin and Traf Homology (MATH) domain, which recruits substrate proteins (PMID: 18218622, 19818708). Transfection of this mutation into kidney cancer cells demonstrated that SPOP K134N is inactivating as measured by abrogated ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of SPOP target, DDIT3 (PMID: 24990631).

Truncating mutations in SPOP can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its function (PMID: 29625055). SPOP encodes a product named Speckle-type POZ protein which functions as a substrate adaptor for the cullin3-RING ubiquitin ligase. Through this mechanism, SPOP is involved in the ubiquitination of a wide array of proteins, effectively regulating many cellular processes. SPOP alterations have been implicated in the pathogenesis of prostate, endometrial and kidney cancer (PMID: 31495053). SPOP has been shown to lead to genomic instability and tumorigenesis via upregulation of transcription factors that lead to a coordinated activation of the PI3K and androgen receptor signaling pathways in mice (PMID: 28292441, 26374986). SPOP tumor-suppressive activities have also been attributed to its role in the negative regulation of cyclin E1 and c-MYC through ubiquitination (PMID: 30237511, 28414305). Oncogenic mutations involving the SPOP substrate-binding domain have been identified in patients with prostate cancer, where they appear to grant increased sensitivity to abiraterone treatment (PMID: 22610119, 30068710, 29625055). Truncating mutations in SPOP have been identified in patients with endometrial as well as other types of carcinomas (PMID: 29625055).

SRC3 impinges on androgen-receptor (AR) signaling, and the perturbation of this pathway is a proposed mechanism for the oncogenic effect of this mutation (PMID: 23559371, 24508459). In addition, conditional expression of the F133V SPOP mutation in the prostate in mouse models has been shown to promote tumorigenesis in the setting of PTEN loss. Neither the SPOP mutation nor PTEN loss alone is able to promote proliferation or tumorigenesis. However, mice expressing the F133V mutation in the context of heterozygous PTEN loss developed high grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia at six months, and in the context of homozygous PTEN loss developed highly invasive carcinoma (PMID: 28292441, 29202479). Expression of this mutation in HeLa cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as shown by decreased colocalization with binding partner and substrate, DAXX (PMID: 30244836).

Truncating mutations in STAG2 occur across the gene body and lead to loss of protein expression, likely due to non-sense mediated mRNA decay (PMID: 25010205). Depletion of STAG2 in wild-type urothelial carcinoma and bladder cancer cell lines resulted in significant chromosomal abnormalities but no changes in cell proliferation, indicating it's importance in maintaining chromosomal stability (PMID: 24121789). Correction of STAG2 aberrations in glioblastoma cell lines restored sister chromatid cohesion and resulted in reduced chromosomal instability (PMID: 21852505). Interestingly, STAG2 truncating mutations in AML patients does not result in chromosomal aberrations, and patients have a normal karyotype (PMID: 22417201).

The STK11 S216F mutation lies in the kinase domain of STK11. Structural modeling suggests it plays a role in complex formation with substrates. In an assay assessing STK11 function by measuring activity of downstream target AMPK, S216F was found to suppress the activity of the protein compared to the wildtype (PMID: 19892943). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing STK11 S193Y demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of kinase activity and decreased TP53-mediated transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34849607).

The STK11 R304W mutation is located in the protein's kinase domain. In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutant exhibits a loss of autophosphorylation activity and an inability to phosphorylate the p53 tumor suppressor protein, a known target of STK11. Together, these data suggest a loss of normal kinase function (PMID: 9837816). Additionally, experimental studies demonstrated that this mutant is associated with a reduced ability to suppress cell growth and significant changes in subcellular localization compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 12552571).

In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing STK11 K78I demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of kinase activity and decreased TP53-mediated transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34849607).

STK11 frameshift, nonsense, or splice site mutations result in a truncated and inactive protein product and occur most commonly located within the kinase domain (PMID: 24652667). Truncating mutations of STK11 tend to be somatic and biallelic resulting in truncated protein products (PMID: 21516316). These mutations are common in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 25079552), and to a lesser frequency in cervical cancer (PMID: 19340305). Studies show truncating mutations affect the ability of STK11 to bind to cofactor magnesium ions resulting in kinase inactivity (PMID: 19892943), and may also affect targeted drug sensitivities.

Deletion mutations of STK11 are extremely common in patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, leading to loss of protein expression (PMID: 21532627, 16582077). Studies show that deletion mutations affect the ability of STK11 to bind to cofactor magnesium ions resulting in kinase inactivity (PMID: 19892943), and may also predict drug sensitivities. Histopathological analysis of clinical samples of breast cancer tissues revealed that expression level of LKB1 (protein product of STK11) demonstrated an unfavorable disease prognosis, showing negative correlation with breast cancer TNM stage, and positive correlation with ER/PR status and E-cadherin expression (PMID: 25178656). Cell culture experiments also revealed that loss/reduction in LKB1 expression resulted in enhanced migration, invasion, deregulation of cell polarity, and acquisition of the mesenchymal phenotype (PMID: 25178656).

The TET2 I1873T mutation is located in the DSBH domain of the protein. When expressed in HEK293 cells, this protein showed proper cellular localization but showed decreased catalytic activity, as cells expressing this variant lacked 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (PMID: 24697267).

Truncating mutations of TET2 disrupt the C-terminal catalytic domain of the protein, predicted to cause gene inactivation and are considered oncogenic events (PMID: 21057493, 24315485). Consequently, these alterations abrogate TET2 enzymatic function to generate 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) (PMID: 21057493).

The TET2 S1898F mutation occurs at a highly conserved residue involved in substrate coordination. In enzymatic assays, this alteration decreased TET2 activity compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 24315485).

In in vitro experiments the composite K1299E/S1303N mutation decreases enzymatic activity, compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 24315485) but the effect of this mutation alone is unknown.

The TET2 R1896S mutation is located in the DSBH domain of the protein. When expressed in HEK293 cells, this protein showed proper cellular localization but showed decreased catalytic activity, as cells expressing this variant lacked 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (PMID: 24697267).

The TET2 R1262A mutation is located at a residue involved in the hydrogen binding of methylated cytosine (m6C) in substrate DNA. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate TET2 R1262A is likely neutral as measured by minimal effect on enzymatic activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 24315485).

The TET2 C1193W mutation is located in the conserved cysteine-rich domain of the protein. When expressed in HEK293 cells, this protein showed proper cellular localization but showed decreased catalytic activity, as cells expressing this variant lacked 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (PMID: 24697267).
The S1290A mutation of TET2 had a minor effect on enzymatic activity as a composite S1290A/Y1295A variant in a in vitro assay and is likely a neutral variant (PMID: 24315485).

The TET2 R1214W mutation is located in the conserved TET2 functional domain. An in vitro ChIP-qPCR experiment demonstrated that this mutation is not properly recruited to methylated histones compared to wildtype TET2 (PMID: 28130413).

The TET2 M1293A mutation occurs at a residue involved in binding to DNA by insertion into the minor groove of the substrate. In in vitro experiments the M1293A/Y1294A double mutation slightly lowers DNA affinity and decreases enzymatic activity, compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 24315485) but the effect of this mutation alone is unknown

The TET2 W1291R mutation occurs at a residue involved in binding to DNA by insertion into the minor groove of the substrate. In in vitro experiments the W1291R mutation decreases enzymatic activity, compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 24315485)

The TET2 H1904R mutation occurs at a residue involved in the hydrogen binding of methylated cytosine (m6C) in substrate DNA. In in vitro experiments the H1904R mutation does not alter DNA binding but does, however, decrease enzymatic activity, compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 24315485). No tumorigenic effect for this variant has been demonstrated.

The TET2 R1261G mutation is located in the conserved cysteine-rich domain of the protein. When expressed in HEK293 cells, this protein showed proper cellular localization but showed decreased catalytic activity, as cells expressing this variant lacked 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (PMID: 24697267).

TET2 deletions are detected only as heterozygous mutations leading to haploinsufficiency, recurrent in patients with myeloid malignancies and considered oncogenic events (PMID: 22017486, 21625234). TET2 loss in mice enhances engraftment capacity over wild type expressing cells and and sensitivity to hypomethylating agents (PMID: 25224413). In addition, conditional deletion of TET2 in mice cause enhanced stem cell renewal capacity and the spontaneous development of myeloproliferation in vivo (PMID: 21723200). TET2 loss may contribute to evasion of immune surveilance and resistance to immnotherapy in some cancers (PMID: 31310587).

The TET2 Y1294A mutation occurs at a residue involved in binding to DNA by insertion into the minor groove of the substrate. In in vitro experiments the M1293A/Y1294A double mutation slightly lowers DNA affinity and decreases enzymatic activity, compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 24315485) but the effect of this mutation alone is unknown.

Selective deletion of TNFAIP3 (also called A20) in mature T cells in mice presented no detectable pathology. However, adoptively transferred TNFAIP3-null CD8 T cells showed elevated NF-kB activity; higher production of IFNγ and TNFα; reduced expression of the inhibitory programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) receptor; and demonstrated improved ability to eliminate melanoma tumor cells in mice (PMID: 25024217). Cell culture and in vivo studies in TNFAIP3-deficient CD4 T cells indicate that TNFAIP3 binds to the MTOR complex, inhibits its activity, and promotes autophagy; providing insight into the manner in which MTOR and autophagy regulate survival in CD4 T cells (PMID: 26043155).

The TET2 N1387A mutation is located at a residue involved in the hydrogen binding of methylated cytosine (m6C) in substrate DNA. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate TET2 N1387A is likely inactivating as measured by decreased enzymatic activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 24315485). This mutation was found to not affect DNA binding (PMID: 24315485).

The TET2 Y1902A mutation is located at a residue involved in the recognition of methylated cytosine (m6C) in substrate DNA. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate TET2 Y1902A is likely inactivating as measured by decreased enzymatic activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 24315485). This mutation was found to not affect DNA binding (PMID: 24315485).

Truncating mutations of TP53 occur throughout the gene and lead to the production of several C-terminally truncated protein forms. These alterations are predicted to be inactivating and are associated with poor prognosis (PMID: 11900253, 11753428, 16007150, 21467160, 19336573). Experimental studies have revealed that truncating mutations promote cancer cell proliferation, survival and metastasis, since ectopic expression of these mutations in melanoma cells increased cell motility and tumor formation in vivo. This was due in part to aberrant localization of truncated proteins to the mitochondria, regulating genes involved in cell survival, including CypD (PMID: 27759562).

Truncating mutations in TNFAIP3 can occur throughout the entire gene and have been shown to lead to impairment of its inhibitory activity on the NF-κB pathway (PMID: 27479826). TNFAIP3 encodes a Zn-finger protein and ubiquitin-editing enzyme that has been shown to be involved in immune response regulation (PMID: 29515565, 31030956). TNFAIP3 has been shown to negatively regulate several cytokine-mediated signaling cascades by terminating NF-kappa B activity (PMID: 28469620, 26642243). Germline truncating mutations in TNFAIP3 have been shown to lead haploinsufficiency manifested by early-onset autoimmune disease phenotype in the affected families (PMID: 26642243). Truncating mutations in TNFAIP3, leading to loss of this protein, have been identified in patients with diffuse large B-cell and marginal zone lymphomas, as well as several carcinomas (PMID: 19258598, 29625055).

In vitro studies with various human cancer cell lines expressing TP53 H168P also demonstrated the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced growth suppressive activity as compared to wildtype (PMID: 29979965, 30224644).

The TP53 S240R mutation occurs in the DNA binding domain of the protein. The tetramerization domain of TP53 is critical for the proper oligomerization and function of the p53 tumor suppressor protein. Mutations of the tetramerization domain, specifically those around G334 that affect the hinge region between the alpha helix and the beta strand, have been shown to result in structural changes that preclude proper oligomerization of the protein and therefor disrupt proper functioning (PMID: 16007150, 16460008).

The TP53 P278L mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. In vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating, as evidenced by failure to transactivate p53 target genes in the mutant compared to wildtype (PMID: 16861262).

TP53 P153H also had altered transcriptional activity of target genes in a luciferase assay compared to wildytype TP53 (PMID: 15781620).

The DNA-binding domain (DBD) of TP53 allows for contact with target DNA sequences to transactivate downstream genes. Mutations in the DBD result in conformational changes of the protein, altering contact of TP53 with its target DNA sequences and thereby altering transcriptional function (PMID: 8023157, 11900253). Given that TP53 directs the transcription of proteins that enable apoptosis, the inactivation of TP53 results in cells harboring damaged DNA and overall genomic instability (PMID: 11900253, 11900253).

Given that TP53 directs the transcription of proteins that enable apoptosis, the inactivation of TP53 results in cells harboring damaged DNA and overall genomic instability (PMID: 11900253, 11900253).

In vivo studies with yeast expressing TP53 F113C demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the loss of transactivational activity as compared to wildtype (PMID: 27328919, 12826609). In vitro studies with various human cancer cell lines expressing TP53 F113C also demonstrated the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced growth suppression activity as compared to wildtype (PMID: 29979965, 30224644).

The TP53 N239S mutation is located in the protein's DNA binding domain. This mutant has lost the wild type p53 tumor suppresive function because this mutant is unable to bind to DNA and p53 target promoters. Moreover, it fails to regulate the transcription of p21. Additionally, xenografts studies have shown that this mutant promotes tumorigenesis in p53 null MEFs (PMID: 22553460).

The TP53 H179R mutation is located in the protein's DNA binding domain. Expression of this mutant failed to induce expression of genes involved in apoptosis or cell cycle arrest (PMID: 17361096). The TP53 Y163C mutation is located in the protein's DNA-binding domain. Cells expressing TP53 Y220S displayed angiogenetic properties, andibroblasts expressing this mutation exhibited resistance to doxorubicin hydrochloride (DX) (PMID: 15977174).

The TP53 G245D mutation is located in the protein's DNA binding domain. The ZBP-89/mutant TP53 interaction abrogated induction of the cell cycle gene p21 and other apoptotic proteins, leading to reduced apoptosis (PMID: 22214764). Additionally, expression of this mutation in head and neck cancer cell lines was associated with the inability of TP53 to suppress colony growth, as compared to wildtype TP53 and is associated with reduced expression of p21 suggesting that the G245D mutation inactivates the function of p53 (PMID: 25119136).

In vivo studies with yeast expressing TP53 C277G demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the loss of transactivational activity as compared to wildtype (PMID: 27328919, 12826609). In vitro studies with various human cancer cell lines expressing TP53 C277G also demonstrated the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced growth suppressive activity as compared to wildtype (PMID: 29979965, 30224644).

The TP53 L348S mutation is located in the protein's oligomerization domain. Structural studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating, as evidenced by the mutant's decreased ability to form TP53 tetramers compared to wildtype TP53, which likely impacts TP53 DNA binding activity (PMID: 20978130).

In vivo studies with yeast expressing TP53 V272A demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the partial loss of transactivational activity as compared to wildtype (PMID: 27328919, 12826609).

The TP53 C124R mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a yeast functional assay demonstrated that it is likely inactivating (PMID: 9115587.)

The TP53 G356A mutation occurs in the protein's tetramerization domain. In biochemical assays, this TP53 mutation enhanced the formation of TP53 tetramers (PMID: 20978130). Further functional data is required to determine if this mutation is indeed gain-of-function.

The tetramerization domain of TP53 is critical for the proper oligomerization and function of the p53 tumor suppressor protein. Mutations of the tetramerization domain, specifically those around G334 that affect the hinge region between the alpha helix and the beta strand, have been shown to result in structural changes that preclude proper oligomerization of the protein and therefor disrupt proper functioning (PMID: 16007150, 16460008).

The TP53 H297N mutation occurs in the protein's DNA binding domain. In biochemical assays, this mutation did not alter the DNA binding ability of TP53 (PMID: 19462533). Further functional assays need to be completed to determine if this alteration is oncogenic.

However, other in vitro studies with various human cancer cell lines expressing TP53 T125K demonstrated that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by growth suppression activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 29979965, 30224644).

The TP53 I255F mutation occurs in the protein's DNA binding domain. Expression of this mutation in TP53-null cells resulted in an increased interaction with PBF, an oncogene implicated in the regulation of TP53 target genes, such as p21 (PMID: 25408419).

The TSC1 G305W mutation was identified in a patient with symptoms of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), an autosomal dominant disorder that results in the development of hamartomas in various organs. Cells engineered to overexpress the TSC1 G305W mutation showed no effect on S6K phosphorylation compared to TSC1 wildtype-expressing cells (PMID: 18830229).

The TSC1 K82T mutation is suggested to be non-pathogenic based on functional studies (PMID: 21309039) and structural analysis of the TSC1 protein (PMID: 23857276). Expression of this mutant in a cell lines did not alter the ratio of T389-phosphorylated S6K to total S6K compared to wildtype TSC1 (PMID: 21309039).

The TSC1 R246K mutation was identified in a patient with symptoms of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), an autosomal dominant disorder that results in the development of hamartomas in various organs. Cells engineered to overexpress the TSC1 R246K mutation showed no effect on S6K phosphorylation compared to TSC1 wildtype-expressing cells (PMID: 18830229).

The TSC1 V128del mutation is a rare alteration in cancer but was also identified in a family with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) disorder. Cells transfected with TSC1 V128del mutant showed decreased levels of TSC1 protein levels compared to wildtype. As a consequence, TSC1 V128del was less efficient inhibiting mTOR pathway (as measured by an increase in S6K phosphorylation), which in turn activates protein synthesis and other proliferation-related cellular processes (PMID: 18830229).

A study evaluated the effect of TSC1 missense mutations in urothelial cell lines without endogenous TSC1 expression. Cells transfected with TSC1 F158C mutation showed a decreased expression of TSC1 due to a decreased stability of the mutant protein compared to wildtype (PMID: 18397877).

Cells transfected with TSC1 M224R mutant showed decreased levels of TSC1 protein levels compared to wildtype. As a consequence, TSC1 M224R was less efficient inhibiting mTOR pathway (as measured by an increase in S6K phosphorylation), which in turn activates protein synthesis and other proliferation-related cellular processes (PMID: 18830229).

TSC1 deletions are associated with impaired binding of TSC1 to interacting proteins (PMID: 11741833, 10353610) and are considered oncogenic events. TSC1 deletions are predicted to prevent the ability of TSC1 to inhibit the mTOR pathway (PMID: 23485365), leading to constitutive mTOR pathway activation and an oncogenic phenotype (PMID: 24529379). Deletion of TSC1 in mouse prostate epithelium is inactvating and oncogenic as measured by generation of prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PMID: 30733194).

The TSC1 T417I mutation was found in the germline DNA of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) patients from Japanese cohorts (PMID: 10570911, 10607950). However, subsequent functional characterization of cells expressing TSC1 T417I mutant failed to show any effects on TSC1 protein expression or cellular localization, suggesting this might be a rare polymorphism present in Japanese population (PMID: 18397877).

As a consequence, TSC1 L117P was less efficient inhibiting mTOR pathway (as measured by an increase in S6K phosphorylation), which in turn activates protein synthesis and other proliferation-related cellular processes (PMID: 18830229).

The TSC1 N198_F199delinsI mutation is located in the Rho-activating domain of the TSC1 protein. This mutation has been found in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) syndrome (PMID: 17304050, 11781698). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating, as measured by decreased levels of TSC1 protein and increased S6K phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 18830229).

The TSC1 R1097H mutation lies outside of a known functional domain of the TSC1 protein. The TSC1 R1097H mutation was identified in a patient with symptoms of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), an autosomal dominant disorder that results in the development of hamartomas in various organs (PMID: 18830229). Cells engineered to overexpress the TSC1 R1097H mutation showed no effect on S6K phosphorylation compared to TSC1 wildtype-expressing cells (PMID: 18830229).

The TSC1 V220F mutation has not been functionally characterized. However, this mutation was identified in a patient with bladder cancer who had a durable non-RECIST response to everolimus (PMID: 22923433).

The TSC1 H68R mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the TSC1 protein. This mutation has been found in bladder cancer (PMID: 18397877). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating, as measured by decreased stability of the mutant protein compared to wildtype (PMID: 18397877).

The TSC1 S35Q mutation was identified in a screening of bladder tumors. TSC1-null bladder cell lines engineered to express S35Q mutant displayed protein expression levels similar to the wildtype. However, TSC1 S35Q mutation was shown to create a cryptic splicing donor site which, when translated, would produced a prematurely truncated TSC1 protein, likely preventing its tumor-suppressive function (PMID: 18397877).

A study evaluated the effect of TSC1 missense mutations in urothelial cell lines without endogenous TSC1 expression. Cells transfected with TSC1 H105R mutation displayed aberrant RNA splicing due to the use of a cryptic splice aceptor, leading to a prematurely truncated TSC1 protein (PMID: 18397877).

There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation has a diffuse cytoplasmic mislocalization pattern compared to wildtype, yet retains the ability to bind TSC2 and suppress mTOR signaling (PMID: 18397877).

The TSC1 G1035S mutation was identified in a patient with symptoms of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), an autosomal dominant disorder that results in the development of hamartomas in various organs. Cells engineered to overexpress the TSC1 G1035S mutation showed no effect on S6K phosphorylation compared to TSC1 wildtype-expressing cells (PMID: 18830229).

Truncating mutations of TSC1 lead to loss of protein function. These alterations affect the ability of TSC1 to act as a molecular scaffold for TSC2 and TBC1D7 in the formation of the TSC complex. This disrupts the function and/or subcellular localization of the complex and prevents it from inhibiting the mTOR pathway via interactions with RHEB (PMID: 23485365, 20301399), leading to constitutive mTOR pathway activation and an oncogenic phenotype (PMID: 24529379).

The U2AF1 Q157P mutation is located in the second zinc finger of the U2AF1 protein. This mutation has been found in myelodysplastic syndrome, among others (PMID: 33122737, 25267526). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by differential splicing of exons and minigene constructs as well as increased isoform switching compared to wildtype (PMID: 25267526, 25311244). Preclinical drug studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the ATR inhibitors, VE-821, VE-822, and AZ 20, as measured by increased DNA damage compared to untreated cells and cells expressing wildtype U2AF1 (PMID: 30054334).

The U2AF1 I24V mutation is located in a zinc finger domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The U2AF1 S34Y mutation is located in the zinc finger domain 1 of the protein. Upon expression of the U2AF1 S34Y in a human erythroleukemic cell line, differential splicing was observed in an order of magnitude of hundreds of exons with isoform switching occurring for a few genes (PMID: 25267526). In assays in a human embryonic kidney cell line this mutant causes alternative splicing of minigene constructs, notably to a lesser extent than the S34F mutation (PMID: 25311244). The observed phenotypes are likely due to altered RNA binding, considering that the mutation substitutes the smaller amino acid serine for a bulkier residue in phenylalanine, possibly with differential effects dependent on a pre-mRNAs sequence (PMID: 22158538). Expression of this mutation in HeLa demonstrated that this mutation was sensitive to the ATR inhibitors, VE-821, VE-822, and AZ 20, as shown by increased DNA damage compared to untreated cells and cells expressing wildtype U2AF1 (PMID: 30054334).

The U2AF1 R156H mutation is located in a zinc finger domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The U2AF1 E159_M160insYE mutation is located in a zinc finger domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The U2AF1 R156Q mutation is located in a zinc finger domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it was likely neutral as measured by no change in splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The U2AF1 I24T mutation occurs in a Zinc-finger domain of the protein. The residue is conserved between the human and yeast isoforms. In an in vitro assay using the yeast isoform, the I24T mutation was found to decrease RNA binding three-fold compared to the wildtype (PMID: 26215567). Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it was inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The U2AF1 S34F mutation is located in the protein's highly conserved first zinc finger domain which is likely important for RNA binding. This mutation has been found in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 30054334, 30846499). Cell line experiments in kidney and hematopoietic cells demonstrated that the U2AF1 S34F mutation was associated with increased RNA splicing and exon skipping (PMID: 22158538, 25311244, 31961934). Upon expression of the mutant in a human erythroleukemic cell line differential splicing was observed in an order of magnitude of hundreds of exons with isoform switching occurring for a few genes (PMID: 25267526). A study utilizing inducible expression of S34F mutant U2AF1 in transgenic mice demonstrated that the mutant protein alters RNA splicing in hematopoietic cells, thus affecting normal hematopoiesis and contributing to disease progression (PMID: 25965570). The observed phenotypes are likely due to altered RNA binding, considering that the mutation substitutes the smaller amino acid serine for a bulkier residue in phenylalanine, possibly with differential effects dependent on a pre-mRNAs sequence (PMID: 22158538). Expression of this mutation in HeLa cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as shown by increased splicing perturbation and R loop accumulation (RNA:DNA hybrid and ssDNA transcription intermediate) compared to cells expressing WT U2AF1 (PMID: 30054334). Expression of U2AF1 S34F was also found to elicit an ATR response. Treatment of HeLa and CD34+ cells expressing this mutation with the ATR inhibitors, VE-821, VE-822, and AZ 20 demonstrated sensitivity to ATR inhibition as shown by increased DNA damage and cell death (PMID: 30054334). Expression of this mutation in myeloid cell lines demonstrated that it induces IL-6 production and NFkB activity, and may affect innate immunity (PMID: 30846499).

The VHL L63P mutation occurs in the acidic domain of the VHL protein. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells results in the inability of VHL L63P to degrade HIF-1α and HIF-2a, leading to increased stability of HIF-1α and HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression likely leads to activation of HIF target genes (PMID: 15611064).

The VHL N78S mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. In renal cell cancer cell lines, the mutant VHL N78S protein is unstable and targeted for proteasomal degradation. The reduced ability of VHL to degrade HIF-2α results in increased expression of HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression leads to activation of HIF target genes, including p27, Cyclin-D and GLUT-1 (PMID: 19602254).

The VHL R82P mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. In biochemical experiments, expression of this mutation results in the inability of a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex to form. Therefore, HIF1α is not effectively ubiquitinated, HIF1α-mediated transcription is enhanced (PMID: 10823831).

The VHL S65L mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells results in the inability of VHL S65L to degrade HIF-1α and HIF-2a, leading to increased stability of HIF-1α and HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression likely leads to activation of HIF target genes (PMID: 15611064).

Therefore, HIF1α is not effectively ubiquitinated, HIF1α-mediated transcription is enhanced (PMID: 10823831, 10535940).

The VHL H115Q mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. The VHL H115Q mutation has been observed in von Hippel-Lindau disease (PMID: 12202531). In silico analysis predicts this mutation is inactivating as it interferes with the HIFα binding site of VHL (PMID: 24969085).

The VHL L128F mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with renal cell carcinoma cells expressing this mutation demonstrate VHL L128F is likely neutral as measured by HIF1a binding and expression of HIF1a-regulated genes comparable to wildtype (PMID: 11865071).

The VHL S65P mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in clear cell renal cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 11505222). In vitro studies with 786-O cells expressing VHL S65P demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced protein stability and binding to HIF2a, and increased cell migration and invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 35505422).

The VHL L118R mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Biochemical studies demonstrated that VHL L118R has a decreased binding affinity for protein chaperones, leading to misfolding of VHL (PMID: 14636579). VHL L118R is unable to form a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex, likely resulting in decreased stability of VHL and increased HIFα activity (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL R69C mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells results in the inability of VHL R69C to degrade HIF-1α and HIF-2α, leading to increased stability of HIF-1α and HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression likely leads to activation of HIF target genes (PMID: 15611064).

VHL deletions are frequently detected in patients with Von Hippel-Lindau and are predicted to result in reduced protein function (PMID: 23632291, 25093046). Large-scale deletions of VHL affecting adjacent genes likely correlate with specific disease phenotypes (PMID:19764026). Loss of VHL leads to inappropriate activation of HIF downstream target genes, thus promoting tumorigenesis in normoxic conditions (PMID: 21386872).

The VHL G114R mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Biochemical studies demonstrated that VHL G114R has a decreased binding affinity for protein chaperones, leading to misfolding of VHL (PMID: 14636579, 27179072). VHL G114R is unable to form a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex, likely resulting in decreased stability of VHL and increased HIFα activity (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL L158P mutation occurs in a highly conserved residue critical for VHL's binding to the transcription elongation factors, Elongin B and C; this interaction helps to stabilize the VHL protein. In in vitro studies, the L158P mutant led to decreased binding of VHL to Elongin B and C, and reduced ubiquitination of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF1), which regulates the transcription of genes in response to hypoxic conditions (PMID: 10535940, 10973499, 19602254). Future studies are necessary to determine the exact functional consequence of this mutation.

The VHL A149P mutation occurs in the protein's α-domain that coordinates binding to Elongin B/C, proteins that maintain the stability of VHL. Biochemical studies demonstrated that VHL A149P has a decreased binding affinity for protein chaperones, leading to misfolding of VHL (PMID: 14636579). VHL A149P is unable to form a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex, likely resulting in decreased stability of VHL and increased HIFα activity (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL V155A mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells and 786-O stable cells expressing this mutation demonstrated VHL V155A is inactivating as measured by increased protein instability compared to wildtype (PMID: 26503325).

The VHL S111C mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Expression of this mutation in renal cancer cell lines resulted in increased HIF1α expression due to reduced binding of HIF1α to VHL. Increased HIF1α protein leads to enhanced HIF-mediated transcription and reduction of p53-mediated apoptosis (PMID: 22071692).

The VHL S65W mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate VHL S65W is inactivating as measured by the inability to degrade HIF1a and HIF2a, leading to subsequent activation of HIF target genes, compared to wildtype (PMID: 15611064).

The VHL L158Q mutation is located in a highly conserved residue critical for elongin C binding and in a hotspot region for VHL mutations. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrated VHL L158Q is inactivating as measured by destabilization of the protein (PMID: 2706960).

The VHL H191D mutation occurs in the protein's α-domain, a protein binding domain. Expression of this mutation in fibroblast or renal cell carcinoma cell lines resulted in decreased binding to SOCS1 and CUL2, proteins that make up an E3 ligase complex that targets phosphorylated JAK2 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation. Therefore, cells expressing the VHL H191D mutation were found to have increased JAK2 signaling. (PMID: 21685897).

The VHL F119S mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Biochemical studies demonstrated that VHL F119S has a decreased binding affinity for protein chaperones, leading to misfolding of VHL (PMID: 14636579). VHL F119S is unable to form a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex, likely resulting in decreased stability of VHL and increased HIFα activity (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL Q96P mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. In biochemical experiments, expression of this mutation resulted in the inability of a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex to form. Therefore, HIF1α is not effectively ubiquitinated, and HIF1α-mediated transcription is enhanced (PMID: 10823831).

The VHL L89H mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in clear cell renal cell carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 21715564). In vitro studies with NCI-H28 malignant pleural mesothelioma cells expressing VHL L89H demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased HIF1a expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 32234874). VHL L89H is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with HIF1a inhibitor YC-1 as measured by dose-and-time-dependent manner induction of apoptosis in cells following treatment (PMID: 32234874).

The VHL I151S mutation occurs in the protein's α-domain that coordinates binding to Elongin B/C, proteins that maintain the protein stability of VHL. Biochemical studies demonstrated that VHL I151S has a decreased binding affinity for protein chaperones, leading to misfolding of VHL (PMID: 14636579, 27179072). VHL I151S is unable to form a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex, likely resulting in increased HIFα activity (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL N90I mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. In biochemical experiments, expression of this mutation resulted in the inability of a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex to form. Therefore, HIF1α is not effectively ubiquitinated, HIF1α-mediated transcription is enhanced (PMID: 10823831).

The VHL R64P mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells results in the inability of VHL R64P to degrade HIF-1α and HIF-2a, leading to increased stability of HIF-1α and HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression likely leads to activation of HIF target genes (PMID: 15611064, 10823831).

The VHL L188Q mutation occurs in the protein's α-domain that coordinates binding to Elongin C, a protein that coordinates the stability of VHL. Expression of this mutation in renal cancer cell lines results in the reduced ability of VHL to degrade HIF-2α, leading to increased stability of HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression leads to activation of HIF target genes, including p27, Cyclin-D and GLUT-1 (PMID: 19602254).

The VHL Q145H mutation occurs in the acidic domain of the VHL protein. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells results in the inability of VHL Q145H to degrade HIF-2α, leading to increased stability of HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression likely leads to activation of HIF target genes (PMID: 15611064).

Truncating mutations of VHL lead to the formation of several C-terminally truncated protein forms and have been detected in patients with sporadic renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 22825683). These alterations have been demonstrated to disrupt the interaction between VHL and HIF (PMID: 12050673, 12004076). Loss of VHL leads to inappropriate activation of HIF downstream target genes, thus promoting tumorigenesis in normoxic conditions (PMID: 21386872).

The VHL C162F mutation occurs in the protein's α-domain, a protein binding domain. Expression of this mutation in fibroblast or renal cell carcinoma cell lines resulted in decreased binding to SOCS1 and CUL2, proteins that make up an E3 ligase complex that targets phosphorylated JAK2 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation. Therefore, cells expressing the VHL C162F mutation were found to have increased pro-oncogenic JAK2 signaling (PMID: 21685897).

The VHL W117L mutation is located within the CCT complex-binding region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in conventional renal cell carcinoma and serous cystadenomas and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 22158988, 16488999). Although not functionally characterized, in vivo studies with HEK cells expressing VHL W117C suggest that VHL W117L is inactivating as measured by VHL W117C impairing VHL folding through disrupting binding with eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC as compared to wildtype (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL R167W mutation occurs in the α-domain of the protein and is one of the most common mutation found in patients both Type I and Type II disease (PMID: 25563310, 12202531). Expression of this mutant in HEK293T cells leads to a reduced ability of VHL to stabilize Jade-1 protein, a renal cell precursor protein (PMID: 14973063). Jade-1 is a critical tumor suppressor in renal cells, and reduced expression of Jade-1 is expected to be oncogenic (PMID: 23824745). Future studies are necessary to determine the exact functional consequence of this mutation.

The VHL E70K mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells results in the inability of VHL E70K to degrade HIF-1α and HIF-2α, leading to increased stability of HIF-1α and HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression likely leads to activation of HIF target genes (PMID: 15611064).

The VHL Y112D mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α); this interaction regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. While expression of this mutation in renal cell carcinoma cells results in decreased E2F1 transcriptional activity, similar to wildtype VHL (PMID: 23744542), this mutation is a hotspot that is recurrently found in patients with cancer, suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

Th VHL V130L mutation is located in the beta domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease and Chuvash polycythemia (PMID: 9829912, 12202531, 12393546, 24581539). While this mutation is considered likely pathogenic in the germline setting, its role in the somatic setting is unknown.

The VHL S111R mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Expression of this mutation in renal cancer cell lines resulted in increased HIF1α expression due to reduced binding of HIF1α to VHL. Increased HIF1α protein leads to enhanced HIF-mediated transcription and reduction of p53-mediated apoptosis (PMID: 22071692).

The VHL D121G mutation is located in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. While expression of D121G in renal cell carcinoma cell lines did not alter binding to HIF or the expression of HIF-regulated genes (PMID: 11865071), this mutation is a hotspot that is found recurrently in patients with cancer suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

The VHL W117C mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrated VHL W117C is inactivating as measured by protein instability due to disruption in chaperone-mediated folding compared to wildtype (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL R167Q mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. The VHL R167Q mutant disrupts binding of VHL to the transcription elongation factor, elongin C (PMID: 24755468, 10535940, 19030229), destabilizes the VHL protein and limits its ability to degrade the hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF2α (PMID: 10535940).

The VHL P81L mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in paraganglioma and renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 17102082, 22241717, 24446253). Although VHL P81L has not been functionally characterized, in vitro studies with VHL-deficient mouse embryonic stem cells expressing the VHL P81S allele demonstrated this mutation is inactivating as measured by the loss of TCEB1 binding and HIF1a degradation, suggesting VHL P81L could also be inactivating (PMID: 23990666).

The VHL V84L mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (PMID: 25078357; 8592333; 16502427). In vitro studies with renal carcinoma cells overexpressing this mutation demonstrate VHL V84L is likely inactivating as measured by ineffective extracellular matrix formation (PMID: 10823831). However, normal expression levels of this mutation in the cell did not affect VHL or HIF1a function (PMID: 10823831). In contrast, in vivo studies with mice expressing this mutation demonstrate VHL V84L is likely neutral as measured by tumor growth suppression that is comparable to wildtype (PMID: 11331612).

The Q164R mutation is located in the alpha domain of VHL which interacts with Elongin C. This mutation leads to an increased proteosomal degradation of VHL leading to a decreased protein half-life resulting in reduced levels of VHL in the cell. This mutant can therefore be regarded as an inactivating, potentially oncogenic mutation of VHL (PMID: 26503325)

The VHL L188V mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrated VHL L188V is inactivating as measured by the inability to form the VHL elongin BC complex compared to wildtype (PMID: 19228690).

The VHL F76del mutation occurs in a region of the protein that interacts with other proteins. It has been observed in the germline of families with von Hippel-Lindau disease (PMID: 20567917, 12624160). In an in vitro assay, the mutation abrogated binding to HIF1α, HIF2α and fibronectin, as well as failed to regulate HIF1α under normoxia like the wildtype protein (PMID: 11331613). The mutation thus likely reduces the tumor-suppressive ability of VHL in a manner typical to other loss-of-function mutations, namely HIF dysregulation.

The VHL N150K mutation occurs in the protein's α-domain that coordinates binding to Elongin B/C, proteins that maintain the stability of VHL. Biochemical studies demonstrated that VHL N150K has a decreased binding affinity for protein chaperones, leading to misfolding of VHL (PMID: 14636579). VHL N150K is unable to form a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex, likely resulting in decreased stability of VHL and increased HIFα activity (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL R200W mutation is located in the protein's α-domain, a protein binding domain. Expression of this mutation in fibroblast or renal cell carcinoma cell lines resulted in decreased binding to SOCS1 and CUL2, proteins that make up an E3 ligase complex that targets phosphorylated JAK2 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation. Therefore, cells expressing the VHL R200W mutation were found to have increased JAK2 signaling. Expression of this mutation in mice results in a hematopoietic disorder that is dependent on enhanced JAK2 signaling activity (PMID: 21685897).

The VHL R161Q mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (PMID: 16314641, 17102088, 20960261, 21362373, 23404858, 23842656). In vitro studies with VHL-defective renal cancer cells expressing this mutation demonstrate VHL R161Q is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to HIF1a and reduced protein activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 25371412).

The VHL Y98H mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α; this interaction regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. In biochemical experiments, VHL Y98H does not ubiquitinate and degrade HIF1α, leading to increased HIF1α-mediated gene expression (PMID: 10823831).

The VHL Y98N mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α; this interaction regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. In biochemical experiments, expression of this mutation results inhibits the formation of a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex. Therefore, downstream targets such as HIF1α are not targeted for degradation, leading to increased HIF1α-mediated gene expression (PMID: 10535940, 10823831).

The VHL L158V mutation is located in a highly conserved residue critical for elongin C binding and in a hotspot region for VHL mutations. In vitro studies with VHL-negative renal carcinoma cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrated VHL L158V is inactivating as measured by destabilization of the protein (PMID: 19602254).

The VHL S65A mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. While expression of this mutation in 293T cells did not affect the ability of VHL to degrade HIF-1α and HIF-2α (PMID: 15611064), this mutation is a hotspot found recurrently in patients with cancer, suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

The VHL L118P mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF1α), which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Biochemical studies demonstrated that VHL L118P has a decreased binding affinity for protein chaperones, leading to misfolding of VHL (PMID: 14636579). VHL L118P is unable to form a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex, likely resulting in decreased stability of VHL and increased HIFα activity (PMID: 14636579).

The VHL Y112C mutation is located in coding exon 1 of the gene. This mutation has been identified in pheochromocytoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 30185211). While this variant has not been functionally characterized, in vitro studies with RCC4 cells expressing mutant VHL Y112H demonstrated that the mutation was inactivating as measured by reduced interaction with HIF-α through co-precipitation as compared to wildtype, suggesting that VHL Y112C may also be inactivating (PMID: 10823831). Overexpression of VHL Y112C demonstrated selective resistance against BET degrader treatment in RKO VHL-/- cells compared to wildtype VHL overexpression (PMID: 36329119).

The VHL S68W mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α, which regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. Expression of this mutation in 293T cells results in the inability of VHL S68W to degrade HIF-1α and HIF-2α, leading to increased stability of HIF-1α and HIF-2α. Elevation of HIF protein expression likely leads to activation of HIF target genes (PMID: 15611064). Expression of VHL S68W in renal cancer cell lines results in resistance to apoptosis (PMID: 18544564).

The WT1 S341A (in citation S273A) mutation is located outside of the DNA-binding, zinc-finger domain of the protein. In an in vitro assay, WT1 S341A (in citation S273A) synergistically activated the Mis promoter with SOX9 or SF1 comparable to wildtype WT1 (PMID: 12855602)

The WT1 D464N (in citation D396N) mutation is located in the DNA-binding, zinc-finger domain of the protein. This mutation was found in a patient with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Mutation of WT1, in general, is a negative prognostic indicator in AML as patients with WT1 mutations have an inferior response to chemotherapy (PMID: 18591546, 18559874). In an in vitro assay, WT1 D464N (in citation D396N) failed to synergistically activate the Mis promoter with SOX9 or SF1 compared to wildtype WT1 (PMID: 12855602)

The VHL H115R mutation is located in the VHL beta domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. The VHL H115R mutation has been observed in von Hippel-Lindau disease (PMID: 12202531). In silico analysis predicts this mutation is inactivating as it interferes with the HIF1a binding site of VHL (PMID: 24969085).

Truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated WT1 proteins. Mutation of WT1, in general, is a negative prognostic indicator in AML as patients with WT1 mutations have an inferior response to chemotherapy (PMID: 18591546, 18559874, 25110071). WT1 truncating mutations may act as dominant negatives and may affect the nuclear localization of the protein (PMID: 12796362, 8618823).

The WT1 R462W (in citation R394W) mutation is located in the DNA-binding, zinc-finger domain of the protein. Mutation of WT1, in general, is a negative prognostic indicator in AML as patients with WT1 mutations have an inferior response to chemotherapy (PMID: 18591546, 18559874). In an in vitro assay, WT1 R462W (in citation R394W) failed to synergistically activate the Mis promoter with SOX9 or SF1 compared to wildtype WT1 (PMID: 12855602)

The EWSR1-WT1 fusion is a t(11;22)(p13;q12) chromosomal translocation where the EWSR1 exon 7 fuses to the WT1 exon 8. Two isoforms are derived from the splicing between zinc fingers 3 and 4, inserting or removing the 3 amino acids lysine, threonine and serine (-KTS or +KTS) (PMID: 9591781, 11237525). While EWSR1-WT1/-KTS has been shown to have oncogenic properties in some studies, others have shown that EWSR1-WT1/+KTS must synergize with p53 loss in order to be oncogenic (PMID: 24321497). In vitro studies with patient-derived desmoplastic small round cell tumor cell lines expressing this fusion protein demonstrate the EWSR1-WT1 fusion protein is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and dysregulation of various signaling pathways compared to wildtype (PMID: 34885181). EWSR1-WT1 fusion is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with small-molecule inhibitor UNC2025 as measured by reduced cellular proliferation following treatment (PMID: 34885181).

The WT1 H445Y (in citation H377Y) mutation is located in the DNA-binding, zinc-finger domain of the protein. Mutation of WT1, in general, is a negative prognostic indicator in AML as patients with WT1 mutations have an inferior response to chemotherapy (PMID: 18591546, 18559874). In an in vitro assay, WT1 H445Y (in citation H377Y) failed to synergistically activate the Mis promoter with SOX9 or SF1 compared to wildtype WT1 (PMID: 12855602)

The WT1 F222S (in citation F154S) mutation is located outside of the DNA-binding, zinc-finger domain of the protein. In an in vitro assay, WT1 F222S (in citation F154S) synergistically activated the Mis promoter with SOX9 or SF1 comparable to wildtype WT1 (PMID: 12855602)

AKT2 fusions generally arise from chromosomal translocation of the N-terminus of a partner protein fused with the C-terminal AKT2 kinase domain of AKT2, such that fusion protein excludes the regulatory pleckstrin homology domain. In vitro studies with OVCAR8 and HEK-293T cell lines expressing the BCAM-AKT2 fusion have demonstrated AKT2 fusions to be activating as measured by constitutive activation of AKT2 compared to wildtype (PMID: 25733895).

The AKT2 E17K is located in the pleckstrin homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in thyroid and breast cancer and in hypoinsulinemic hypoglycemia (PMID: 29615459, 28481359, 22722201, 27135926, 21979934, 24285683). Expression of this mutation in a cervical cancer cell line and in adipocytes demonstrated that it was activating as measured by increased plasma membrane recruitment and pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 21979934).

The AKT2 G161V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 25551293). There is conflicting functional data for this mutaion. Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by the absence of pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25551293). However, expression of this mutation in melanocytes demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased evasion of apoptosis compared to wildtype (PMID: 25551293).

The AKT2 I289M mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 28481359). Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25551293).

The AKT2 K181M mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cancer cell line demonstrated that it changes the function of the protein as measured by loss of canonical kinase activity and pathway activation with an alternate phosphoinositide binding profile compared to wildtype. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation may be resistant to the AKT inhibitor, MK2206 when expressed in a lung cancer cell line as measured by decreased cell death compared to wildtype upon drug treatment (PMID: 25551293).

The AKT2 R368C mutation is located at a highly conserved amino acid residue in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 22307544, 19738612). Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25551293).

The BCAM-AKT2 fusion involves the N-terminus of BCAM fused to the C-terminus of AKT2, containing the AKT2 kinase domain but lacking the regulatory pleckstrin homology domain. This mutation has been found in ovarian cancer. Expression of the BCAM-AKT2 fusion in ovarian cancer and embryonic kidney cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by constitutive protein activation and increased foci formation compared to vector control (PMID: 25733895).

The AKT2 D324N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it is paralogous to AKT1 D323N, which is likely oncogenic and a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011).

AKT2 amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation had been found in breast, pancreatic, ovarian and lung cancer (PMID: 28572459). Overexpression of AKT2 in pancreatic cancer cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased tumor formation in a xenograft model compared to wildtype expression levels (PMID: 8622988).

The AKT2 R170W is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial and stomach cancer (PMID: 24071849). Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25551293).

The AKT2 H355Y mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25551293).

The VHL Y112H mutation occurs in the protein's β-domain that coordinates binding to hypoxia-inducible transcription factor, HIF1α; this interaction regulates oxygen homeostasis in the cell. In biochemical experiments, expression of this mutation inhibits the formation of a functional VHL-Elongin B/C complex. Therefore, HIF1α is not effectively ubiquitinated and HIF1α-mediated transcription is enhanced. This mutation is partial loss of function (PMID: 10823831).

ARID2 truncation mutations result in various C-terminally truncated protein forms leading to protein inactivation (PMID: 21822264, 23047306). Functional studies have demonstrated that siRNA knockdown of ARID2 reduces protein levels of other subunits of the PBAF complex, suggesting that ARID2 is necessary for PBAF complex stability. In addition, loss of ARID2 expression abolishes transcription of the interferon (IFN)-induced transmembrane protein 1 (IFITM1), which is needed for IFN-induced anti-proliferative activity in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (PMID:15985610, 16847454). Though further evidence is needed, these observations suggest that ARID2 functions as a tumor suppressor.

The VHL P40fs* mutation is located in the N-terminal (GXEEX)8 repeat motif of the protein. This mutation has been found in follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (Abstract: Robbrecht et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00244). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, a tumor from a patient with metastatic sarcoma that progressed on chemotherapy and was subsequently treated with the anti-VEGF kinase inhibitor pazopanib for 22 months harbored this mutation and showed positive staining for HIF-1alpha and GLUT1, both of which are indicative of functional loss of VHL (Abstract: Robbrecht et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00244).

Truncating mutations in ATR result in various forms of C-terminal deleted protein products. Heterozygous loss of ATR in a mismatch repair deficient background is associated with high levels of genetic instability (PMID: 15282542) and heterozygous loss of ATR in mice is associated with increased tumor formation (PMID: 10691732)

The B2M M1K mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein and alters the initiation codon. This mutation has been found in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 22137796). Endogenous expression of this mutation in a lymphoma cell line and computational modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by loss of protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 22137796).

B2M deletions result in loss of the protein. These mutations have been found in melanoma and lymphoma (PMID: 29070816, 28507804). Loss of B2M in lymphoma cell lines resulted in cancer cell evasion of immune surveillance (PMID: 1898655, 22137796, 25294904).

The B2M M1I mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein and alters the initiation codon. Endogenous expression of this mutation in a lymphoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by loss of protein expression (PMID: 11894933).

B2M truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. Expression of B2M mutations in lymphoma cell lines resulted in decreased protein stability and increased cancer cell evasion of immune surveillance compared to wildtype (PMID: 1898655, 22137796, 25294904).

The B2M M1R mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein and alters the initiation codon. This mutation has been found in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 22137796). Computational modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by loss of protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 22137796).

The B2M M1T mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein and alters the initiation codon. This mutation has been found in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 22137796). Computational modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by loss of protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 22137796).

The B2M M1V mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein and alters the initiation codon. Endogenous expression of this mutation in a lymphoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by loss of protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 24947018).

The BARD1 C83R mutation is located in the RING domain of the protein (PMID: 29367421). This BARD1 mutation has been found in patients with familial breast cancer. Biochemical assays demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by reduced ubiquitination of histone H2A and altered mononucleosomal binding patterns (PMID: 29367421). In addition, this alteration increased the expression of estrogen metabolism genes in breast cancer cell lines (PMID: 29367421).

The BARD1 (BRCA1-associated RING domain protein 1) encodes the BRCA1-associated RING domain protein 1 which forms a stable core complex with BRCA-1 (PMID: 8944023), a tumor suppressor that functions to maintain genome integrity by repairing DNA double-stranded breaks through homologous recombination and cell-cycle checkpoint activation (PMID: 20029420).Truncating mutations of BARD1 are assumed to be associated with loss of protein and therefore considered oncogenic.

The BARD1 L44R mutation is located in the RING domain of the protein (PMID: 27239795). Expression of this mutation in HeLa cell lines demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by the inability to form a heterodimer complex with BRCA1 and the resulting inability to function as an E3 ubiquitin ligase (PMID: 27239795).
