The BARD1 R99E mutation is located in the RING domain of the protein (PMID: 27239795). Expression of this mutation in HeLa cell lines demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by decreased ubiquitin ligase activity, though it retains the ability to dimerize with BRCA1 comparable to wildtype (PMID: 27239795).

Deletions of BARD1 are found in patients with breast cancer and are thought to serve as an alternative breast cancer susceptibility gene to BRCA1 (PMID: 20842729). In vitro studies using Bard1-null mouse mammary carcinoma cell lines show that BARD1 is required for maintenance of chromosomal stability and homologous recombination of DNA double-strand breaks (PMID: 17848578). BARD1 null mice develop breast cancer (PMID: 20029420).

The translocation of BCL6 is frequent in lymphatic malignancies. Often these translocations fuse BCL6 to an immunoglobulin (Ig) gene locus, or less commonly, to the locus of a non-Ig gene (PMID: 17625604,12389616). BCL6 is a transcriptional regulator in germinal centers, from which human lymphomas often derive. Likely, the translocations cause deregulation of BCL6 expression and expression of its target genes, but no precise mechanism has been defined (PMID: 15024721).

The BARD1 C78S mutation is located in the RING domain of the protein (PMID: 29367421). This BARD1 mutation has been found in patients with familial breast cancer. Biochemical assays demonstrated that this mutation is likely neutral as measured by ubiquitination of histone H2A or mononucleosomal binding patterns comparable to wildtype (PMID: 29367421). In addition, this alteration did not impact the expression of estrogen metabolism genes in breast cancer cell lines (PMID: 29367421).

Translocations involving IGH and BCL6 are recurrent in patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and high-grade B cell lymphomas (PMID: 26980727). The resultant IGH-BCL6 fusion protein pairs enhancer regions of IGH upstream of the coding sequence of BCL6, resulting in upregulation of BCL6 (PMID: 8557040, 30323893). IGH-BCL6 fusion proteins have been implicated in "double-hit" and "triple-hit" lymphomas, which typically express multiple rearrangements (MYC, BCL2, BCL6 rearrangements) and have a poor prognosis (PMID: 27821509, 26980727, 29903764). Lymphoma cell lines engineered to express the IGH-BCL6 protein and model "double hit" lymphomas are highly proliferative and give rise to tumors in transplantation assays (PMID: 30323893).

The amplification of BCL6 has been observed across a range of tumor types. Specifically, in follicular lymphoma BCL6 amplification was observed in a cohort of tumors lacking otherwise typical IGH/BCL2 rearrangements (PMID: 18500267, 24887414). BCL6 is a transcriptional regulator in germinal centers, from which human lymphomas often derive. In model systems, overexpression of BCL6 results in an anti-apoptotic and chemotherapy resistant phenotype (PMID: 15577913, 16142238).

Amplification of BRD4 occurs when multiple copies of the genome harboring the BRD4 gene are produced in the cell, resulting in multiple copies of the encoded protein. BRD4 overexpression in HeLa and NIH3T3 cells leads to dysregulated cell cycle as appropriate levels are required for cell cycle maintenance and progression (PMID: 19596781, 12192049, 15456879). Overexpression of BRD4 in HeLa cells leads to increased Pol II (Polymerase II) phosphorylation which can enhance transcriptional output and lead to aberrant gene expression (PMID: 22509028).

Fusions of BRD4 arise from chromosomal translocations of BRD4 and a variety of partner proteins (PMID: 25564152, 12543779, cbioportal, MSKCC, 2017). Experimental studies suggest expression of these fusions result in dysregulated BRD4 cellular localization and aberrant cell signaling (PMID: 12543779, 23128391). However additional studies are required to fully understand the functional consequences of these alterations.

The BRIP1 E511G mutation is located between helicase domains II and III of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in patients with breast cancer (PMID: 31822495). Expression of this protein in a cervical cancer cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents compared to wildtype, although there was no change in protein stability or cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 31822495).

BRIP1 deletions have been identified in patients with breast and ovarian cancer (PMID: 21964575). Experimental studies demonstrate that these alterations can affect BRIP1 protein stability and its interaction with BRCA1 (PMID: 18628483). Additionally, loss of BRIP1 in human cell lines led to abnormal cell adhesion, cell proliferation with dysregulated sugnaling pathways including Myc, Wnt, PTEN and DNA damage response (PMID: 24040146).

The BRIP1 A349P mutation has been observed in individuals with Fanconi anemia (PMID: 16116424). The mutation is located next to a highly conserved cysteine residue which is part of a putative functional iron-sulfur domain. In vitro experiments showed that the mutated protein contained less iron atoms than the wildtype protein and abolishes DNA helicase activity without disrupting DNA-binding and ATPase ability (PMID: 20639400). No oncogenic ability for this variant has been demonstrated.

This increase in ATPase activity was accompanied by a modest increase in helicase activity, although the interpretation of this is complicated by differential effects on the unwinding of short and long substrates (PMID: 14983014, 17145708).

Additionally, loss of BRIP1 in human cell lines led to abnormal cell adhesion, cell proliferation with dysregulated signaling pathways including Myc, Wnt, PTEN and DNA damage response (PMID: 24040146).

The BRIP1 K52R mutation, which occurs at a residue that is conserved in many ATPases and helicases, has been shown to abolish such proteins' ability to hydrolyze ATP (PMID: 2846277, 8196650). In vitro biochemical studies demonstrated that K52R-mutated BRIP1 protein exhibits no ATPase or helicase activity (PMID: 14983014). In a separate study, U2OS cells over-expressing the K52R BRIP1 mutant failed to repair DNA damage at the same rate as wild-type cells, suggesting that this mutation leads to defects in double-strand break repair (DSBR); this mutation was shown to function in a dominant-negative manner (PMID: 11301010). Furthermore, when a second mutation was introduced eliminating the BRCA1 binding domain of BRIP1, no changes in DSBR were observed, indicating that the effect of this mutation is dependent on BRIP1's interaction with BRCA1.

The BRIP1 P47A mutation is located in helicase domain I of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in patients with breast and ovarian cancer (PMID: 31822495). Expression of this protein in vitro and in a cervical cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased protein activity, decreased protein stability, and increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents compared to wildtype (PMID: 14983014, 31822495).

The BRIP1 R251C mutation is located in the DEAD domain of the protein. This variant has been identified in 0.001% of Non-Finnish European chromosomes by the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC: http://exac.broadinstitute.org). It has been reported in a patient with Fanconi anemia in trans with a second BRIP1 variant, although the pathogenicity of the second variant has not been established (PMID: 23613520). This variant is located within helicase motif (PMID: 11301010). In in vitro studies, this variant abolished the protein's DNA binding ability and helicase activity, and failed to rescue function in a complementation assay (PMID: 24573678).

The BTK C481G mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (PMID: 27282255, 31243043). While in vitro studies of this mutation suggest that it may be weakly activating as measured by phosphorylation of downstream effectors that was slightly elevated from wildtype but much less than the BTK C481S or C481T mutations, the strength of the data suggests this variant is inconclusive (PMID: 31243043).

The BTK V416L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 35196427). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing BTK V416L demonstrate that the mutation is a kinase dead mutant as measured by significant reduction in BTK Y223 and PLCG2 phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 35196427) (Abstract: Montoya et al. Abstract# 641-CLL, Blood 2022 Vol 140. https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/140/Supplement%201/1811/492374/Kinase-Dead-BTK-Mutations-Confer-Resistance-to). Despite loss of enzymatic activity, the BTK V416L mutation functions effectively in AKT and ERK pathway signaling activation (PMID: 35196427). In vitro studies with BTK-dependent human B cell lymphoma cells expressing BTK V416L demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased BCR signaling independent of PLCG2 Y1217 phosphorylation compared to wildtype (Abstract: Montoya et al. Abstract# 641-CLL, Blood 2022 Vol 140. https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/140/Supplement%201/1811/492374/Kinase-Dead-BTK-Mutations-Confer-Resistance-to). Preclinical studies of this mutation demonstrate resistance to ARQ-531, acalabrutinib, pirtobrutinib, ibrutinib, zanubrutinib and vecabrutinib as measured by increased IC50 values and loss of binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 35196427). Preclinical studies of this mutation demonstrate resistance to pirtobrutinib, fenebrutinib and vecabrutinib, as measured by increased IC50 values compared to wildtype, and sensitivity to ibrutinib and ARQ-531, as measured by IC50 values comparable to wildtype (PMID: 35196427). In a case report, a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia was treated with pirtobrutinib and acquired BTK V416L following disease progression (PMID: 35196427).

The BTK R28L mutation is located in the pleckstrin homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in families with X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA), but otherwise has not been functionally validated (PMID: 12204007).

The BTK C481F mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (PMID: 28418267, 26182309, 27282255). Expression of this mutation in fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased kinase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 27282255). However, this mutation has been found in at least three CLL patients who progressed on ibrutinib and is at the C481 residue that is crucial for irreversible drug binding, suggesting it may be an ibrutinib resistance mutation (PMID: 28418267, 26182309).

However, this mutation has been found in at least eight CLL patients who progressed on ibrutinib and is at the C481 residue that is crucial for irreversible drug binding, suggesting it may be an ibrutinib resistance mutation (PMID: 28418267, 31243043, 29381098, 28049639, 26182309).

The BTK T474I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (PMID: 26182309)(Abstract: Woyach et al, Abstract# 642-CLL, ASH 2019. https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/134/Supplement_1/504/426369/Resistance-to-Acalabrutinib-in-CLL-Is-Mediated). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing BTK T474I demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased BTK Y223 autophosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 35196427). Structural studies have demonstrated that this mutation attenuates binding of the drug ibrutinib to the BTK protein (PMID: 27626698). This mutation is analogous to the T315I gatekeeper mutation in the BCR-ABL1 Fusion protein (PMID: 17684099, 27571029). Preclinical studies of this mutation demonstrate resistance to ARQ-531, acalabrutinib, pirtobrutinib, zanubrutinib and vecabrutinib as measured by increased IC50 values compared to wildtype (PMID: 35196427). In a case report, two patients with CLL were treated with pirtobrutinib and acquired BTK T474I following disease progression (PMID: 35196427).

The BTK R544S mutation occurs at a conserved arginine residue in the protein's activation loop where it interacts with residue Y551 upon its phosphorylation (PMID: 20826165, 20052711). In in vitro kinase assays, this mutation mediates a two-fold increase in activity compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 20826165).

The BTK Y551F mutation occurs within the protein's activation loop at a conserved tyrosine that is phosphorylated upon BTK kinase activation (PMID: 20826165, 20052711). The BTK C481S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 28049639, 28418267, 27282255, 24869598, 27199251, 27626698, 29296715, 31243043, 31180577, 26182309). Expression of this mutation in fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased kinase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 27282255). This mutation has been found in at least two CLL patients who progressed on ibrutinib, suggesting it may be an ibrutinib resistance mutation (PMID: 27626698, 29296715).

In a clinical trial, a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia harboring BTK L528W was treated with NX-2127 and demonstrated sensitivity as measured by BTK degradation in CD19+ B cells (Abstract: Montoya et al. Abstract# 641-CLL, Blood 2022 Vol 140. https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/140/Supplement%201/1811/492374/Kinase-Dead-BTK-Mutations-Confer-Resistance-to).

Truncating and frameshift mutations of CALR are found in the majority of patients with myeloproliferative neoplasms lacking MPL or JAK 2 mutations and lead to cytokine-independent growth when expressed in Ba/F3 cells (PMID: 24325356, 24325359). Many frameshift mutations, especially indels in exon 9, shift the protein to reading frame 1 which results in novel, positively-charged, C-terminal amino acids (PMID: 24325356). CALR truncating mutations are associated with increased risk for myelofibrotic transformation among patients with myeloproliferative neoplams (PMID: 30304655).

The BTK R28S mutation is located in the pleckstrin homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and families with X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA), but otherwise has not been functionally validated (PMID: 15024743, 31180577).

While frameshift mutations in exon 9 of CALR are generally considered oncogenic, in-frame insertions or deletions in exon 9 of CALR are seen at high levels in germline populations of healthy individuals and are generally considered to be benign polymorphisms (PMID: 27466382, 28028029, 27384487).

While frameshift mutations in exon 9 of CALR are generally considered oncogenic, in-frame insertions or deletions in exon 9 of CALR are seen at high levels in germline populations of healthy individuals and are generally considered to be benign polymorphisms (PMID: 27466382, 28028029, 27384487).

CASP8 promoter hypermethylation corresponds with decreased CASP8 expression and resistance to apoptosis by the TRAIL pathway in a variety of tumors including Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma, glioblastoma multiforme, medulloblastoma and rhabdomyosarcoma (PMID: 11593392, 10969767). Loss of CASP8 has been shown to increase the metastatic potential of neuroblastoma tumor cell lines in vivo (PMID: 16397500).

The CASP8 G384A mutation (also cited as CASP8 G325A) is located in the C-terminal region of the CASP8 second death effector domain. Expression of this protein in the head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cell line T3M-1 Cl-10 demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased NF-κB activity compared to wildtype CASP8. In addition, expression of this mutation in HEK293 and T3M-1 Cl-10 cells demonstrated that it reduced CASP8 caspase and antiproliferative activity compared to wildtype CASP8 (PMID: 23659359).

CASP8 truncating mutations have been identified in a variety of carcinomas, most commonly in gastrointestinal cancers (PMID: 15531912, 12949717, 15705878). Experimental studies have shown that truncating mutations lead to significantly reduced apoptosis, since encoded caspase 8 protein is unable to mediate death-receptor induced apoptosis, as well as impaired PARP cleavage compared to CASP8 wildtype cells (PMID:15531912, 12949717, 15705878). Additionally, cell line studies using head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cell lines suggest truncating mutations of CASP8 are associated with chemoresistance to cisplatin, but not etoposide (PMID: 19852930).

CASP8 deletions are associated with gene inactivation and commonly results in the premature termination of translation. Experimental studies of CASP8 deletions demonstrate that these alterations lead to significantly reduced apoptosis, since CASP8 is unable to mediate death-receptor induced apoptosis, and impaired PARP cleavage compared to CASP8 wildtype cells (PMID: 12055196, 15531912, 15705878).

The CASP8 R307W mutation (also cited as CASP8 R248W) leads to a caspase-8 deficiency state, formerly known as autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome type 2B (PMID: 12353035). Caspase-8 deficiency state is characterized by splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and autoimmunity.

CBFB truncating mutations typically result in the loss of the protein. Loss of CBFB has been identified in breast cancer (PMID: 22722202). Truncation mutations of CBFB are likely inactivating as measured by loss of RUNX1 expression, resulting in breast cancer tumorigenesis (PMID: 22722202, 22024923).

The CBFB-MYH11 fusion combines most of the CBFB gene with the 3' tail of the MYH11 gene (PMID: 8929537, 15156186 ). Mouse modeling of the CBFB-MYH11 fusion gene demonstrated that it inhibits the differentiation of hematopoietic cells (PMID: 8929537). Expression of CBFB-MYH11 alone was not sufficient for leukemogenesis, however, a combination of CBFB-MYH11 and additional mutations acquired through random mutagenesis led to the development of myeloid leukemia in mice compared to random mutagenesis alone (PMID: 8929537, 15044690). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as demonstrated by the ability of the protein product of this gene to transform NIH 3T3 cells (PMID: 9844935).

The CCND1 T286A mutation is located directly at a nuclear export phosphorylation site of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 29969496). Expression of this mutation in a murine fibroblast cell line demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased nuclear localization and stability, colony formation and in vivo tumor growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 16732330, 11124803).

The CCND1 Y44D mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) (PMID: 24145436). Expression of this mutation in MCL cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein stability and nuclear localization compared to the wildtype (PMID: 27713153).

The CCND1 T286I mutation is located directly as a nuclear export phosphorylation site of the protein. This mutation has been found in uterine and esophageal cancers (PMID: 16732330, 29969496). Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein stabilization and colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 23733133).

CCND1 truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated CCND1 proteins. These mutations have been found in uterine, bladder, pancreatic and head and neck cancer (cBioPortal, MSKCC, May 2015). While the specific deletions may vary slightly, all truncated proteins result in loss of threonine 286 in the CCND1 protein, a critical phosphorylation site that modulates the nuclear localization and stability of the protein (PMID: 9832503, 16732330). There is conflicting functional information for these mutations. Endogenous expression of a CCND1 truncation mutation in a lymphoma cell line demonstrated that it may be activating as measured by increased mRNA transcript stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 17299095). However, expression of multiple CCND1 truncation variants in rat embryonal fibroblasts demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by reduced colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 9926916).

The CCND1 L283_D294del mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 29969496). CCND1 D289 is a necessary residue for the phosphorylation of CCND1 T286 by GSK-3B to degrade CCND1 (PMID: 16732330). The CCND1 L283_D294del alteration is activating as measured by the aberrant accumulation of CCND1 in the nucleus and promotion of cellular transformation (PMID: 16732330, 9832503).

The CCND1 P287A mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 28481359). Expression of this mutation in a murine fibroblast cell line demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased protein nuclear localization, stability and colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 16732330).

The CCND1 D289A mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased colony formation on soft agar compared to wildtype (PMID: 16732330).

CCND1 amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation is one of the most common copy-number alterations in human tumors (PMID: 20164920). Overexpression of this CCND1 in vitro and in a mouse model demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activity and cell proliferation (PMID: 8114739, 9407965).

The CCND1 D289_D292del mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 12955092, 29969496). Expression of this mutation in murine fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased nuclear localization, protein stability and colony formation in soft agar compared to wildtype (PMID: 16732330).

The CCND1 P287S mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 12955092). While this mutation is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011), this mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

The CCDN1 V293A mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been suggested to decrease CCDN1 binding to CRM1 (PMID: 18946086). Further functional studies are required for the characterization of this mutation.

The CCND1 P287T is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma, uterine, endometrial and cervical cancer (PMID: 12955092). While this mutation is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011), this mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

The CCND1 D289del mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 12955092, 29969496). CCND1 D289 is a necessary residue for the phosphorylation of CCND1 T286 by GSK-3B to degrade CCND1 (PMID: 16732330). The CCND1 D289del alteration is activating as measured by the aberrant accumulation of CCND1 in the nucleus and promotion of cellular transformation (PMID: 16732330, 9832503).

The IGH-CCND1 fusion involves the N-terminus of IGH fused to the C-terminus of CCND1. This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 16402392, 25596256, 14514791, 16690963). Expression of this mutation in clinical samples of lymphoma demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation (PMID: 16402392, 25596256, 14514791, 16690963).

Amplification of CCND2 typically leads to the overexpression of the protein. CCND2 amplification has been identified in B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia, gastric cancer, colon cancer and glioblastoma (PMID: 7742549, 10666388, 16012517, 31568682). In vivo studies with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cell lines overexpressing CCND2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular invasion compared to vector-alone transfected controls (PMID: 12112307). In a Phase II trial, three patients with previously treated stage IV squamous cell lung cancer harboring CCND2 amplification were treated with palbociclib and one patient demonstrated stable disease (PMID: 31302234).

The CCND1 C47S mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) (PMID: 24145436). Expression of this mutation in MCL cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein stability and nuclear localization compared to wildtype (PMID: 27713153).

The CCND3 P284L mutation is located in the PEST domain of the protein (PMID: 24913233). This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 31774495, 21796119). Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 22885699).

CCND3 amplification is detected in a variety of human tumors, albeit at low frequencies (<10%) (cBioPortal, MSKCC, June 2015). Of the three functionally-related cyclin D genes (CCND1, CCND2, and CCND3) only the role of CCND1 in oncogenesis has been studied extensively. By analogy to CCND1, amplification of CCND3 is expected to promote aberrant entry into the cell cycle (PMID: 8114739), suppression of senescence and inhibition of apoptosis. Evaluation of all samples in the TCGA PanCanAtlas analysis identified recurrent, focal amplification of CCND3 (PMID: 29625050).

The IGH-CCND3 fusion involves the N-terminus of IGH fused to the C-terminus of CCND3. This mutation has been found in multiple B-cell malignancies (PMID: 11418483, 11675358, 15543617). Analysis of mRNA expression in primary tumor samples demonstrated an association of IGH-CCND3 fusion with CCND3 overexpression (PMID: 11418483).

The CCND3 T285A mutation (also cited as CCND3 T286A) is located in the PEST domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro and in murine fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein stability and nuclear localization compared to wildtype (PMID: 9832503).

The CCND3 T283A mutation is located in the PEST domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 31558468, 21796119). Expression of this mutation in embryonic kidney, B-cell and lymphoma cell lines demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased protein stability and cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24913233, 22885699).

The CCND3 Q276* mutation is located in the PEST domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 21796119, 24388756). Expression of this mutation in embryonic kidney and B-cell cell lines demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased protein stability as compared to wildtype (PMID: 22885699, 24913233).

The CCND3 I290R mutation is located in the PEST domain of the protein (PMID: 24913233). This mutation has been found in lymphoma (PMID: 21796119, 24388756). Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is activating, as measured by increased protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 22885699).

The CCND3 D286_L292trunc mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated CCND1 proteins. Mutations in CCND3 that result in a truncated cyclin D3 protein lacking the C-terminal-most 30 amino acids eliminate a critical phosphorylation site (threonine 283) that confers proteolytic destruction of cyclin D3 (PMID: 9832503). Mutant tumors, therefore, are expected to possess aberrantly stabilized cyclin D3, which can, in turn, lead to increased activity of CDK4/6 and increased proliferation.

CCNE1 amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation has been found in a variety of cancers including bladder, ovarian and breast cancer (PMID: 12845634). Overexpression of CCNE1 in fibroblast cell lines and in a transgenic mouse model demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cell cycle progression, genomic instability, and the development of hepatocellular carcinomas in vivo (PMID: 8384376, 12419181, 30878468).

CCNE1 overexpression has been found in a variety of cancers including bladder, ovarian and breast cancer (PMID: 12845634). Overexpression of CCNE1 in fibroblast cell lines and in a transgenic mouse model demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cell cycle progression, genomic instability, and the development of hepatocellular carcinomas in vivo (PMID: 8384376, 12419181, 30878468).

Amplification of CD274 (more commonly PD-L1) has been detected across several tumor types including Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL), mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (MLBCL), small cell lung cancer, among others (PMID: 20628145, 29902298, 29377256, 27069084, 27620277). In preclinical assays, cells overexpressing PD-L1 exhibit increased features of immune evasion, due to binding of the PD-1 cell surface receptor expressed on immune cells (PMID: 28302645). In addition, the tyrosine kinase JAK2 is included in the 9p24.1 amplification region of PD-L1, which can also activate transcription of PD-L1 (PMID: 20628145). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that HL cells with PD-L1 amplification are sensitive to JAK2 inhibition (PMID: 24610827, 29467301). Patients with PD-L1 amplification have been found to have objective responses to PD-1/PD-L1-targeted immune therapies (PMID: 29902298, 28356247).

The CD79B Y197F mutation (also cited as CD79B Y196F) is located in the first ITAM motif of the protein, the domain that initiates B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling (PMID: 20054396, 21796119, 29641966). This variant is predominantly found in patients with activated-B cell (ABC) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (PMID: 20054396). DLBCL cell lines engineered to express the CD79B Y197F mutation demonstrated increased IgM surface presentation, as demonstrated by flow cytometry, suggesting a defect in receptor internalization and activation of chronic BCR signaling (PMID: 20054396).

The CD79B Y197H mutation (also cited as CD79B Y196H) is located in the first ITAM motif of the protein, the domain that initiates B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling (PMID: 20054396, 21796119, 29641966). This variant is predominantly found in patients with activated-B cell (ABC) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (PMID: 20054396). DLBCL cell lines and B cells engineered to express the CD79B Y197H mutation demonstrated increased IgM surface presentation, as demonstrated by flow cytometry, suggesting a defect in receptor internalization (PMID: 20054396, 28701369). In addition, cell lines expressing CD79B Y197H had reduced LYN expression, a kinase that negatively regulates BCR signaling, consistent with chronic activation of BCR signaling (PMID: 20054396).

The CD79B Y197N mutation is located in the ITAM motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24253023). Although not functionally characterized, a patient-derived xenograft of activated B-cell-like diffuse large B-cell lymphoma harboring CD79B Y197N and MYD88 L265P demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with kinase inhibitor ibrutinib (Abstract: Wu et al. Abstract# 625, ASH 2015. https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/126/23/2759/135214/Biomarker-Predictive-Ibrutinib-Response-Using).

The CD79B Y197C mutation (also cited as CD79B Y196C) is located in the first ITAM motif of the protein, the domain that initiates B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling (PMID: 20054396, 21796119, 29641966). This variant is predominantly found in patients with activated-B cell (ABC) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (PMID: 20054396). DLBCL cell lines engineered to express the CD79B Y197C mutation demonstrated increased IgM surface presentation, as demonstrated by flow cytometry, suggesting a defect in receptor internalization and activation of chronic BCR signaling (PMID: 20054396).

The CD79B Y197S mutation is located in the ITAM motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 21796119). Although not functionally characterized, a patient with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma harboring CD79B Y197S and MYD88 L273P demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with kinase inhibitor ibrutinib as measured by complete response for ten months (Abstract: Bloehdorn et al. Abstract# 627, ASH 2018. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006497119403376).

The CD79B E198G mutation (also cited as CD79B E197G) is located in the first ITAM motif of the protein, the domain that initiates B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling (PMID: 20054396, 21796119, 29641966). This variant is predominantly found in patients with activated-B cell (ABC) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (PMID: 20054396). DLBCL cell lines engineered to express the CD79B E198G mutation demonstrated increased IgM surface presentation, as demonstrated by flow cytometry, suggesting a defect in receptor internalization activation of chronic BCR signaling (PMID: 20054396).

The CDK12 K764R mutation (also cited as CDK12 K765R) occurs in the kinase domain and reduces the catalytic activity of CDK12 (PMID: 24554720). Ovarian cancer cell lines expressing this mutation exhibit defects in homologous recombination in vitro (PMID: 25712099).

The CDK12 K975E mutation has been found in patient ovarian cancer samples (PMID: 21720365, 24554720). This mutation does not decrease CDK12 kinase activity or disrupt the CDK12-Cyclin K interaction (PMID: 24554720, 25712099). However, ovarian carcinoma samples harboring the K975R alteration have aberrant expression of genes in DNA repair pathways (PMID: 25712099).

CDK12 amplification significantly co-occurs with ERBB2 amplification in breast and gastric cancer (PMID: 20932292, 21097718, 26658019). CDK12 may be an oncogene in the context of breast cancer as it has been linked to transcriptional addiction, tumor invasion and PARP-inhibitor resistance, though the data is still inconclusive (PMID: 28187285, 27880910, 28334900).

The CDK12 L996F mutation occurs in the kinase domain and reduces the catalytic activity of CDK12 (PMID: 21720365, 24554720). This mutation has been shown to disrupt the interaction between CDK12 and Cyclin K which may lead to disruption of DNA repair genes such as BRCA1 (PMID: 25712099). Ovarian cancer patient samples with the L996F alteration have decreased expression of genes in homologous recombination pathways (PMID: 25712099).

CDK12 deletions result in loss of protein function, resulting in defects in DNA repair pathways and consequent genomic instability (PMID: 25712099). Knockdown of CDK12 by siRNA expression in ovarian cancer cell lines markedly reduced BRCA1 expression and disrupted homologous recombination repair (PMID: 24554720). Experimental studies suggest that CDK12 deficiency confers sensitivity to PARP1/2 inhibitors (PMID: 24240700).

CDK12 truncating mutations result in loss of protein function, resulting in defects in DNA repair pathways and consequent genomic instability (PMID: 25712099). Knockdown of CDK12 by siRNA expression in ovarian cancer cell lines markedly reduced BRCA1 expression and disrupted homologous recombination repair (PMID: 24554720). Additionally, CDK12 truncating mutations were shown to disrupt the interaction between CDK12 and cyclin K as compared to wildtype, leading to downregulation of genes involved in the homologous repair pathway (PMID: 25712099, 21720365). In patients with ovarian cancer, CDK12 inactivation was associated with increased genome instability and the presence of numerous tandem duplications (PMID: 26787825).

The CDK12 R882L mutation occurs in the kinase domain and reduces the catalytic activity of CDK12 (PMID: 21720365, 24554720). This mutation decreases homologous recombination and BRCA1 expression in ovarian cancer cell lines (PMID: 24554720, 25712099). Ovarian cancer patient samples with the CDK12 R882L alteration have been shown to have decreased expression of genes in homologous recombination pathways (PMID: 25712099).
The CDK12 D877N mutation, which occurs in the protein's kinase domain, reduces the catalytic activity of CDK12 (PMID: 24554720) and is thought to be a loss-of-function alteration.

The CDK12 W719* mutation is a frameshift alteration that results in the truncation of CDK12 in the kinase domain (PMID: 24554720). This mutation has been shown to disrupt the interaction between CDK12 and Cyclin K which may lead to dysregulation of DNA repair genes such as BRCA1 (PMID: 25712099). Ovarian cancer patient samples with the W719* alteration have decreased expression of genes in homologous recombination pathways (PMID: 25712099).

The CDK12 G909R mutation occurs in the kinase domain and reduces the catalytic activity of CDK12 (PMID: 24554720). Ovarian cancer cell lines expressing this mutation have defective homologous recombination in vitro (PMID: 25712099).

The CDK12 Y901C mutation occurs in the protein's kinase domain and reduces the catalytic activity of CDK12 (PMID: 21720365, 24554720). This mutation has been shown to disrupt the interaction between CDK12 and Cyclin K which may lead to dysregulation of DNA repair genes such as BRCA1 (PMID: 25712099). Ovarian cancer patient samples with the Y901C alteration have been shown to have decreased expression of genes in homologous recombination pathways (PMID: 25712099).

The CDK12 E928_L929insYTKI in-frame insertion mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein (PMID: 25712099). This alteration has been identified in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (PMID: 25712099). In vitro studies in HEK 293 cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrated the alteration is inactivating as measured by the protein's inability to interact with cyclin K, ablating kinase activity (PMID: 25712099).

The CDK4 R24C mutation is located within the CDK4 regulatory domain. Expression of this mutation in mouse embryo fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein activity, cell proliferation, ability to escape senescence and decreased contact-mediated growth inhibition. Homozygous CDK4 R24C mice developed tumors in various tissues and are highly susceptible to carcinogen-induced melanoma (PMID:11756559, 11606789).

The CDK4 K22A mutation is located directly on a CDK4 regulatory site. In vitro expression of this mutation demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by decreased binding of a negative regulator (p16INK4a) which would render CDK4 constitutively active. The CDK4 K22A mutation was also found to have reduced binding to CCND1 (PMID: 9228064, 9426066, 9712735).

CDK4 amplification results from the gain of the CDK4 gene on chromosome 12q13-14. Often, this leads to the overexpression of CDK4 protein, which has been demonstrated to induce hyperplasia and malignant transformation of human fibroblasts and astrocytes (PMID: 8101826, 10970848, 20534551). CDK4 overexpression is mutually exclusive with other genetic events in the same pathway, such as truncating mutations in RB1 or CDKN2A, and leads to the constitutive activation of the cell cycle. Mechanistically, increased availability of CDK4 results in the formation of CDK4/6-cyclin D complexes that are able to overcome p16-mediated inhibition and lead to cell cycle progression (PMID: 28303264). CDK4-amplified tumors are sensitive to inhibition with CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib and abemaciclib (PMID: 25028469, 23569312).

The CDK6 A197T mutation was found in ten microcephalic children of a consanguineous eight-generation family diagnosed with autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (MCPH). Expression of this mutation demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by reduced cell proliferation and centrosome malfunction (PMID: 23918663).

CDK6 overexpression is the biological consequence of diverse genomic alternations, including CDK6 gene amplification (PMID: 17989712, 22476749), translocation events involving CDK6 locus (PMID: 11940479, 19145199, 23127611, 12900351) and aberrant transcriptional activation driven by other oncogenic fusion events (e.g. MLL rearrangements, PMID: 24736461, 24764564). CDK6 expression promotes proliferation, transformation, and tumorigenicity of p16INK4a/Arf-null astrocytes, suggesting an oncogenic role played by CDK6 in glioblastoma development (PMID: 20534551). CDK6 knockdown experiments demonstrated that CDK6 is the major regulator of cellular proliferation in MLL-rearranged acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cell line, hence suggesting that up-regulation of CDK6 expression may be a tumor-promoting event in leukemia (PMID: 24736461, 24764564). Mechanistically, it is believed that the increased availability of CDK6 results in the formation of CDK4/6-cyclin D complexes that are able to overcome p16-mediated inhibition and lead to cell cycle progression.

CDKN1B deletions result in the loss of the protein. This mutation is found in hematologic malignancies (PMID: 18073348, 21422114) and are associated with loss of protein expression (PMID; 24185511, 23555276). Deletion of CDKN1B in a transgenic mouse model resulted in the development of spontaneous pituitary adenomas and increased susceptibility to carcinogen-induced cancer (PMID: 8646779, 23460367).

The CDKN1B V109G mutation is located in between the inhibitory region and the nuclear localization signal of the protein. This mutation has been found in thyroid and prostate cancer (PMID: 21177330, 18645269). This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

CDKN1B truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations have been found in endocrine cancers (PMID: 8646779, 17519308). Expression of a truncating mutation in cervical cancer and pituitary tumor cell lines demonstrated it was inactivating as measured by mislocalization of the protein compared to wildtype (PMID: 25416039). Deletion of CDKN1B in a transgenic mouse model resulted in the development of spontaneous pituitary adenomas and increased susceptibility to carcinogen-induced cancer (PMID: 8646779, 23460367).

The CDKN1B P133T mutation is located in between the inhibitory region and the nuclear localization signal of the protein. This mutation has been found in parathyroid adenoma (PMID: 21289244). Expression of this mutation in a pituitary cell line demonstrated that it is neutral as measured by no change in protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 21289244).

CDKN2C truncating mutations typically result in the loss of the protein. Loss of CDKN2C has been identified in myeloma, lymphoma, glioblastoma, meningioma, melanoma, thyroid cancer and parathyroid cancer (PMID: 25576899, 16960149, 23616356, 22133722,18829482, 18381405, 11485924). In vitro studies in multiple cancer cell lines expressing CDKN2C truncating mutations have demonstrated that loss of CDKN2C is inactivating as measured by promotion of cell cycle progression and cellular proliferation from the loss of negative regulatory activity (PMID: 22997239, 19411068, 17409423).

The CDKN1B G9R mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in parathyroid adenoma (PMID: 21289244). Expression of this mutation in a pituitary tumor cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 21289244).

Deletion of the CDKN2C locus is associated with reduced expression of CDKN2C (PMID:18829482). By FISH, CDKN2C was found to be deleted in 55 of 369 (15%) of multiple myeloma cases. Patients with hemizygous or homozygous CDKN2C deletions had a worse overall survival. Furthermore, cases with homozygous deletions of CDKN2C were the most proliferative myelomas (PMID: 18829482). Another study showed a similar lower overall survival in patients with CDKN2C deletions, but only in patients who had received autologous stem cell transplant, versus less intense treatments (PMID:21994415). Mice lacking Ink4c develop spontaneous tumors not observed in the parental strain (PMID: 14500377).

The CHEK2 S372F mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased kinase activity (less than 15%) compared to wildtype (PMID: 28743916).

The CHEK2 R117G mutation is located in the CHEK2 forkhead-associated domain. Expression of this mutation in cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by reduced protein activation and impaired DNA damage response compared to wildtype CHEK2 (PMID: 16982735, 16835864).

CHEK2 is a tumor suppressor gene and truncating mutations are therefore considered to be likely oncogenic. Truncating mutations in CHEK2 have been associated with increased risk of breast, prostate and colorectal cancer in various populations (PMID: 19401704, 27464310, 28779002).

The CHEK2 E64K mutation is located in the SQ/TQ domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with familial breast cancer (PMID: 22419737). Expression of this mutation in yeast demonstrated that it is inactivating as demonstrated by decreased DNA damage repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 22419737).

The CHEK2 I157T mutation is located within the protein's FHA domain which is responsible for the substrate specificity of CHEK2 (PMID: 16816021). This mutation is associated with an increased risk of developing certain cancers, including colorectal (PMID: 16816021), breast (PMID: 15239132) and prostate (PMID: 14612911, 15492928). Data from functional studies evaluating this mutant are inconclusive. Some studies show the I157T mutant exhibits decreased substrate binding, while others report no difference compared to wildtype (PMID: 11053450, 11298456, 12049740, 11571648). This variant is present in population databases (rs17879961) at frequencies up to 2.6% in the Finnish population (ExAc). Large meta-analyses of several thousand cases and controls show that this variant confers an increased risk of breast cancer (OR=1.48-1.58) (PMID: 22799331, 23713947) and colorectal cancer (OR=1.48-1.67) (PMID: 22901170, 23713947). A stronger association between this variant and lobular breast cancer has been reported (OR= 4.17) (PMID: 22799331 ). Additionally, the CHEK2 p.Ile157Thr variant has also been associated with an increased risk of other cancer types (PMID: 15492928, 15087378, 25798211). In summary, while this variant shows incomplete penetrance, it has been associated with an increased risk of certain cancer types, as is classified as pathogenic.

The CHEK2 E321K mutation is located in the CHEK2 kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in a colorectal cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by an impaired DNA damage response after treatment with ionizing radiation compared to wildtype CHEK2 (PMID: 16835864).

The CHEK2 H371Y mutation is located within the activation loop of the CHEK2 protein kinase domain. There is conflicting functional evidence for this mutation. In vitro functional studies show that CHEK2 proteins harboring this mutation have a significantly decreased kinase activity compared to wildtype CHEK2 protein. Further, this mutation decreased the protein's capacity for phosphorylation, which also contributed to dampened activity levels (PMID: 21618645, 25884806). Functional studies have shown that CHEK2 H371Y causes a decreased level of phosphorylation and enzymatic activity as compared to wild-type CHEK2 protein, but not a complete loss of activity (PMID: 21618645). Other in vitro studies with mouse embryonic stem cells and in vivo studies with yeast expressing CHEK2 H371Y have demonstrated that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein function and stability comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34903604, 30851065). This variant is present in population databases (rs531398630, 0.38% in the East Asian population, Broad Exac database). It has been reported in patients affected with familial breast cancer and with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in the Chinese population (PMID: 21618645, 18484200, 23960188, 25884806). One large study found CHEK2 H371Y in 4.24% of familial breast cancer patients, as compared to 1.76% of unselected breast cancer cases, and 0.73% of controls. For familial breast cancer cases, odds ratio of developing breast cancer was 5.99 compared to controls (CI- 1.9818.19, p=0.002) (PMID: 21618645).

The CHEK2 P85L mutation is located in the CHEK2 kinase domain. This mutation is considered a founder allele in the Ashkenazi Jewish population but is not associated with increased cancer risk (PMID: 16998506). Expression of this mutation in yeast demonstrated that it is neutral, as shown by its ability to rescue CHEK2-deleted cell phenotypes (PMID: 15649950).

The CHEK2 E161del mutation is located in the FHA protein interaction domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in familial breast cancer (PMID: 16982735). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by a reduced DNA damage response compared to wildtype controls (PMID: 16982735).

The CHEK2 I189V mutation is located in the FHA protein interaction domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in familial breast cancer (PMID: 22419737). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as evidenced by reduced DNA damage response and protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 22419737).

The CHEK2 R180H mutation is located in the FHA domain of the protein. There is inconclusive evidence describing this mutation. Expression of this mutation in U2OS cells demonstrated that while expression and stability of this mutation are decreased compared to wildtype, the function of this protein may be similar to wildtype (PMID: 16982735).

The CHEK2 S428F mutation is located in the CHEK2 kinase domain. This mutation is considered a founder allele in the Ashkenazi Jewish population and is associated with an approximately two-fold increase in breast cancer risk (PMID: 16998506). Expression of this mutation in yeast demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by its inability to rescue CHEK2-deleted cell phenotypes (PMID: 15649950).

The CHEK2 R145W mutation is located in the FHA protein interaction domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in familial breast cancer (PMID: 11719428, 15535844, 22419737). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as evidenced by reduced DNA damage response and protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 11719428, 16982735, 11390408, 11298456, 12049740, 11571648).

The CHEK2 R181C mutation is located in the FHA domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with familial breast cancer (PMID: 22419737, 31050813). While prediction algorithms such as AlignGVGD, SIFT and PolyPhen2 suggest this mutation is likely neutral, this mutation has otherwise not been functionally characterized (PMID: 22419737, 31050813).

The CHEK2 R346H mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. There is conflicting evidence about the biological and oncogenic effects of the mutation. In vitro studies with CHEK2-knockout mouse embryonic stem cells expressing CHEK2 R346H demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 34903604). However, other in vitro studies with CHEK2-knockout hTERT-RPE1 cells expressing CHEK2 R346H demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by phosphorylation levels comparable to wildtype (PMID: 31050813).

The CHEK2 K373E mutation is located in the kinase domain of the CHEK2 protein. This mutation has been found in familial breast cancer, among others (PMID: 27716909). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased kinase activity, autophosphorylation and sensitivity to DNA damage compared to wildtype (PMID: 27716909).

CRLF2 fusion proteins are generally thought to result in increased CRLF2 protein expression. CRLF2 alterations characterize a subgroup of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) patients that lack the BCR-ABL1 fusion (known as Ph-like/BCR-ABL1-like ALL) but demonstrate a gene expression profile similar to that of BCR-ABL1-positive ALL (PMID: 25207766, 28033648, 27870571). CRLF2 alterations are associated with mutations in JAK as well as deletions in IKZF1, CDKN2A/2B, PAX5, and BTG1. Comprehensive data from several studies suggest that CRLF2 over-expression is associated with poor prognosis in high risk (HR) but not in standard risk (SR) pediatric and adult patients with ALL (PMID: 20139093, 21106984, 22150304, 20018760). (Abstract: Chen, I et. al. http://ascopubs.org/doi/abs/10.1200/jco.2011.29.15_suppl.9505).

The CRLF2 F232C mutation is located near the extracellular and transmembrane domains of the CRLF2 protein. This mutation has been found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 20018760, 19965641). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling, protein dimerization, and cytokine independent growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 16732321, 16414957, 20018760).

The P2RY8-CRLF2 fusion occurs due to an interstitial deletion within the pseudoautosomal region of chromosomes XP22.3/Y11.3, resulting in the fusion of CRLF2 with the G-protein-coupled purinergic receptor P2RY8. The fusion protein has been identified in Philadelphia chromosome-like acute lymphoblastic leukemia and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 29997224). The P2RY8-CRLF2 fusion protein is likely activating as measured by overexpression of CRLF2 mRNA and protein (PMID: 19641190, 20139093, 22150304).

Amplification of CRLF2 can occur through chromosomal translocation of CRLF2 with IGH and fusion of CRLF2 with the G-protein-coupled purinergic receptor P2RY8 (PMID: 28033648). CRLF2 overexpression has been identified in Down syndrome-associated acute lymphoblastic leukemia and pediatric and adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 22150304, 20139093, 21106984, 22150304, 20018760; Abstract: Chen et al. Abstract# 9505, ASCO 2011. http://ascopubs.org/doi/abs/10.1200/jco.2011.29.15_suppl.9505). Overexpression of CRLF2 has been strongly associated with JAK, IKZF1, CDKN2A/2B, PAX5 and IL-7Ra mutations (PMID: 19838194, 20139093, 28033648, 21536738). Acute lymphoblastic leukemia tumors expressing amplified CRLF2 have identified a BCR-ABL1-like kinase signature, even in the absence of BCR-ABL1 translocation (PMID: 19838194, 20139093). In vitro studies of cells expressing CRLF2 kinase, JAK2 kinase and pseudokinase domain mutations demonstrated induced constitutive activation of JAK2/STAT5 and PI3-kinase signaling pathways, and factor-independent growth that could be pharmacologically inhibited upon treatment with a JAK inhibitor (PMID: 19641190,19965641, 19838194, 20018760).

The CSF1R Y561_I564del mutation is located in the kinase domain of the CSF1R protein. The mutation has been found in familial and sporadic histiocytic neoplasms (PMID: 31768065). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased cytokine independent growth and activated downstream signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 31768065). Structural modeling predicts that the Y561_I564del mutation alters the inactive CSF1R conformation, and drug efficacy studies in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation might be sensitive to the CSF-1R inhibitors pexidartinib and BLX945 (PMID: 23478061, 31768065, 26235028).

The CSF1R I794T mutation is located in the protein kinase domain. This mutation is found in patients with hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids. Expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as shown by the inability to sustain growth in the presence of CSF1 as compared to cells expressing WT CSF1R (PMID: 24145216).

The CSF1R Y546_K551del mutation is located in the kinase domain of the CSF1R protein. The mutation has been found in familial and sporadic histiocytic neoplasms (PMID: 31768065). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased cytokine independent growth and activated downstream signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 31768065). Structural modeling predicts that the Y546_K551del mutation alters the inactive CSF1R conformation, and drug efficacy studies in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation might be sensitive to the CSF1R inhibitors pexidartinib and BLX945 (PMID: 23478061, 31768065, 26235028).

The CSF1R P386L mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the CSF1R protein. The mutation has been found in familial and sporadic histiocytic neoplasms (PMID: 31768065). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased cytokine independent growth and activated downstream signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 31768065). Structural modeling predicts that the P386L mutation alters CSF1R dimerization, and drug efficacy studies in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation might be sensitive to the CSF1R inhibitors pexidartinib and BLX945 (PMID: 23478061, 31768065, 26235028).

The CSF1R M875T mutation is located in the protein kinase domain. This mutation is found in patients with hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids. Expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as shown by the inability to sustain growth in the presence of CSF1 as compared to cells expressing WT CSF1R (PMID: 24145216).

CSF1R fusions generally arise from chromosomal translocation of the N-terminus of a partner protein fused with the C-terminus of CSF1R. These mutations have been identified in leukemia (PMID: 33197935, 17360941, 27870571). In vitro studies with BaF3 cells expressing RBM6-CSF1R fusion demonstrated that the fusion protein is activating as measured by IL-3-independent cell growth (PMID: 17360941). CSF1R fusions are suggested to be sensitive to treatment with ABL inhibitors imatinib and dasatinib as measured by induction of apoptosis in MKPL-1 cells and bone marrow-derived cells expressing CSF1R fusions (PMID: 17360941, 24186003, 27870571).

The CSF1R E633K mutation is located in the protein kinase domain. This mutation is found in patients with hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids. Expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as shown by the inability to sustain growth in the presence of CSF1 as compared to cells expressing WT CSF1R (PMID: 24145216).

The RBM6-CSF1R Fusion results from a translocation that fuses the N-terminal 36 amino acids of RBM6 with the C-terminal 399 amino acids of CSF1R (PMID: 17360941). This mutation has been found in leukemia (PMID: 17360941). Expression of this fusion in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by growth factor-independent transformation and formation of a myeloproliferative disease when transplanted into mice (PMID: 17360941).

The CSF1R W450_E456del mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the CSF1R protein. The mutation has been found in familial and sporadic histiocytic neoplasms (PMID: 31768065). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased cytokine independent growth and activated downstream signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 31768065). Structural modeling predicts that the W450_E456del mutation alters CSF1R dimerization, and drug efficacy studies in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation might be sensitive to the CSF-1R inhibitors pexidartinib and BLX945 (PMID: 23478061, 31768065, 26235028).

The IGH-CRLF2 fusion protein is a result of reciprocal chromosomal translocation of CRLF2 with IGH. This fusion protein has been identified in Philadelphia chromosome-like acute lymphoblastic leukemia and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 29997224). The IGH-CRLF2 fusion is likely activating as measured by the overexpression of CRLF2 mRNA and protein (PMID: 19641190, 20139093, 22150304).

The CSF3R T618I mutation is located in the Fibronectin-type III domain of the protein. This mutation is highly prevalent in patients with chronic neutrophilic leukemia (PMID: 28028025, 25239264, 23604229). Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells transplanted in murine bone marrow demonstrated that this mutation is activating because all the transplanted mice developed a myeloproliferative disorder. The resultant myeloproliferative disorder was sensitive to the JAX1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib (PMID: 24081659).

The CSF1R G585_K619delinsA mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with pediatric-onset leukoencephalopathy (PMID: 30982608). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it has been classified as pathogenic based on American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMGG) guidelines: it is absent from population databases, predicted to change the length of the protein, and is located in a functional domain where pathogenic mutations have previously been reported (PMID: 30982608).

Truncating mutations in the C-terminal domain of CSF3R affect the cytoplasmic tail of the CSF3R transmembrane receptor. These mutations have been found in chronic neutrophilic leukemia, atypical chronic myeloid leukemia, B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and other hematological malignancies (PMID: 23656643, 32577374). Truncating mutations at amino acid positions 738–792 and 793–823 impair membrane internalization of the CSF3R protein and disrupt receptor degradation, respectively, both resulting in sustained activation of STAT5A, an oncogenic transcription factor, and dysregulation of SRC family–TNK2 kinases (PMID: 28439110, 23656643). C-terminal truncating mutations have been shown to be activating in vitro as demonstrated by increased colony formation in CSF3R truncated cells versus CSF3R wild-type cells (PMID: 28439110). Cells with C-terminally truncated CSF3R may be sensitive to dasatinib and ruxolitinib (PMID: 23656643, 28439110).

CTCF truncating mutations often result in nonsense-mediated decay and commonly occur in the N-terminal portion of the gene. Hotspot frameshift alterations at CTCF codons 202 and 204 result in truncated CTCF proteins lacking zinc finger domains (PMID: 24130125, 25079317). Truncating CTCF mutations have been identified in non-small cell lung cancer, uterine cancer and breast cancer (PMID: 31340001, 30086769). CTCF truncating mutations have been detected in different protein domains and have been suggested to be inactivating as measured by altered binding specificities (PMID: 23636398).

CTCF deletions typically lead to nonsense-mediated decay and is associated with tumors with defective mismatch repair and microsatellite instability (PMID: 24130125, 26330387). Experimental studies demonstrate that CTCF deletion leads to DNA methylation and loss of MYC transcriptional activity (PMID: 19568526). While complete loss of CTCF is embryonic lethal, CTCF haploinsufficiency has been demonstrated to alter global methylation patterns, predispose mice to a range of cancers and is associated with shortened overall lifespan (PMID: 24794443).

The CTCF Y226C mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 30649385). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing CTCF Y226C demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by DNA binding and transcription regulation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 34657170).

The CTCF H284P mutation is located in the CTCF zinc finger 1 (ZF1) region. This mutation is a cancer hotspot as it is recurrently found in human cancer and is therefore likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011). While this mutation has not been functionally validated, mutations in the ZF1 region may selectively impair CTCF DNA occupancy and activity (PMID: 11782357, 24794443).

The CTCF H284Y mutation is located in the CTCF zinc finger 1 (ZF1) region. This mutation is a cancer hotspot as it is recurrently found in human cancer and is therefore likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011). While this mutation has not been functionally validated, mutations in the ZF1 region may selectively impair CTCF DNA occupancy and activity (PMID: 11782357, 24794443).

The CTCF P378L mutation is located in the third zinc-finger domain of the CTCF protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 28319062). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by clonogenic growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 28319062).

The CTCF R377H mutation is located in the third zinc-finger domain of the CTCF protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer (PMID: 28319062). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by clonogenic growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 28319062).

CXCR4 amplification has been identified in multiple myeloma, breast cancer and lung cancer, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 16344916, 21623238, 26190113).  In vitro studies with bone marrow-derived extra-medullary disease cell lines overexpressing CXCR4 demonstrated that the alteration is activating as measured by increased invasion and higher bone metastasis (PMID: 26190113). In contrast, silencing of CXCR4 in the cell line led to inhibited tumor growth and reduced cell survival (PMID: 26190113).

The CXCR4 S338* mutation is located in the C-terminal of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (PMID: 24553177). In vitro studies with BCWM.1 cells transduced with somatic CXCR4 C-terminal domain mutations demonstrate that CXCR4 S338* is likely activating as measured by other CXCR4 C-terminal truncation mutations having significant upregulation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation, increased cellular migration and decreased CXCR4 internalization as compared to wildtype (Abstract: Cao et al. Abstract# 2715, ASH 2012. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/120/21/2715). CXCR4 S338* has been identified to confer resistance against Bruton's tyrosine kinase, mTOR inhibitor rapamycin and PI3K inhibitors in WM cells expressing the mutation (PMID: 24711662).

The CXCR4 V320Efs*23 mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the CXCR4 protein. This mutation has been identified in patients with WHIM syndrome (PMID: 36089616). In vitro studies with K562 cells expressing this mutation have demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased ERK and ATK phosphorylation, increased cellular migration and decreased CXCR4 internalization compared to wildtype (PMID: 36089616).

Frameshift mutations in the C-terminus of CXCR4 have been found in patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) (PMID: 24553177, 24366360). Co-occurrence of these mutations with MYD88 L265P mutation in patients with WM is associated with increased severity of disease, including intermediate bone marrow involvement (PMID: 24553177, 24366360). Though these mutations leave the functional domains of the protein intact, they likely interrupt serine residues in the C-terminal tail of the protein that are needed for regulation of the protein, leading to increased downstream signaling (PMID: 10521508, 20929726)

Truncating mutations in the C-terminus of CXCR4 have been found in patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) and in the germline of patients with warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections and myelokathexis (WHIM) syndrome (PMID: 24553177, 24366360). Co-occurrence of these mutations with MYD88 L265P mutation in patients with WM is associated with increased severity of disease, including increased bone marrow involvement (PMID: 24553177, 24366360). Though these mutations leave the functional domains of the protein intact, they delete serine residues in the C-terminal tail of the protein that are needed for regulation of the protein, leading to increased downstream signaling (PMID: 10521508, 20929726).

The CXCR4 R334* mutation is located at the C-terminus of the protein and truncates the distal portion of the C-terminus. This mutation has been identified in patients with WHIM syndrome (PMID: 32784523, 21070597). In vitro studies with CD34+ and K562 cell lines expressing CXCR4 R334* demonstrated that the mutation is activating as measured by enhanced calcium flux and cellular migration as compared to wildtype (PMID: 15781337).

The DDR2 T654M mutation is located in the kinase domain of the DDR2 protein. This mutation has been found in squamous lung cancer (PMID: 24296828). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is a resistance mutation to the kinase inhibitor dasatinib, functioning analogously to the T790M gatekeeper mutation in EGFR (PMID: 24296828).

The DDR2 L63V mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the DDR2 protein. This mutation has been found in squamous lung cancer (PMID: 22328973, 23822953). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased cytokine independent growth, kinase activity, and clonogenic growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 23822953, 22328973).

The DDR2 G505S mutation is located in the DDR2 juxtamembrane region. Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype DDR2 but failed to show increased colony formation. However, expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells led to increased IL3-independent growth compared to wildtype DDR2 (PMID: 23822953, 22328973).

The CTCF R339W mutation is located in the third zinc finger domain of the CTCF protein. This mutation has been found in colon, stomach, and Wilms’ tumors, among others (PMID: 11782357, 1317258). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of context-specific CTCF binding at regulatory regions involved in cell proliferation and angiogenesis, but no change in CTCF binding at other regulatory sites across the genome compared to wildtype (PMID: 11782357, 21896759).

The CTCF H284N mutation is located in the CTCF zinc finger 1 (ZF1) region. This mutation is a cancer hotspot as it is recurrently found in human cancer and is therefore likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011). While this mutation has not been functionally validated, mutations in the ZF1 region may selectively impair CTCF DNA occupancy and activity (PMID: 11782357, 24794443).

The DDR2 G253C mutation is located in the discoidin-like domain of the DDR2 protein. This mutation has been found in squamous lung cancer (PMID: 22328973). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by cytokine independent growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 22328973).

DDR2 amplification has been identified in colorectal cancer, breast cancer, urothelial carcinoma, liposarcoma and non-small cell lung cancer, and is associated with poor prognosis (PMID: 28476831, 28147276, 27793038, 28099935, 26390252). In vitro studies in Hep3B cells expressing amplified DDR2 expression demonstrate that overexpression of DDR2 is activating as measured by increased epithelial-to-mesenchymal activity, cellular invasion and migration compared to normal expression (PMID: 26362312).

The DDR2 T654I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the DDR2 protein. This mutation has been found in squamous lung cancer (PMID: 24296828). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is a resistance mutation to the kinase inhibitor dasatinib, functioning analogously to the T790M gatekeeper mutation in EGFR (PMID: 24296828).

The DDR2 I638F mutation is located in the DDR2 kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in multiple cell lines has resulted in conflicting data, with one study indicating that this mutation may lead to modest increases in colony formation and cell proliferation (PMID: 22328973) while another study indicates that this mutation has no effect on pathway activation and colony formation (PMID: 23822953).

The DDR2 G774V mutation is located in the DDR2 kinase domain. While expression of G774V DDR2 in NIH-3T3 cells failed to increase the number of colonies formed in soft agar compared to wildtype DDR2, it was sufficient to support IL-3-independent growth of Ba/F3 cells compared to wildtype DDR2 or vector (PMID: 22328973).

The DDR2 S768R mutation is located in the kinase domain. This mutation is found in patients with lung cancer (PMID: 25173530, 22328973). While this mutation has not yet been functionally validated, in silico modeling suggests that it may affect kinase activity (PMID: 22328973).

The DDR2 L239R mutation is located in the discoidin-like domain of the DDR2 protein. This mutation has been found in squamous lung cancer (PMID: 22328973). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by cytokine independent growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 22328973).

The ERBB3 R475W mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrioid carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 33016334). Although not functionally characterized, in vitro studies with HEC-1 and HEC-1-B cells expressing ERBB3 R475W and ERBB2 V842I + T798I demonstrate sensitivity to treatment with kinase inhibitor neratinib as measured by decreased cell viability (PMID: 33473169).

The ERBB3 K329E mutation is located in the Furin-like region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 30181556). Although not functionally characterized, a bladder urothelial carcinoma patient harboring ERBB3 K329E demonstrated moderate sensitivity to treatment with trastuzumab and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (PMID: 29413684).

The ERBB3 V714M mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung cancer (PMID: 23680147). Expression of this mutation in breast epithelial, breast cancer and colonic epithelial cell lines demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by very minimal change in pathway activation and no change in cell proliferation or colony formation alone or when coexpressed with ERBB2 compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147).

The ERBB3 G284R mutation is located in the extracellular ligand-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma and breast and colon cancer (PMID: 23680147, 22895193, 27284958, 28481359, 29360550). Expression of this mutation in breast cancer, colonic epithelial, and murine B-cell cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation, colony formation and tumor growth in xenografts compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147).

The ERBB3 P262H mutation is located in the extracellular ligand-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colon and ovarian cancer (PMID: 23680147). Expression of this mutation in breast cancer, colonic epithelial, and murine B-cell cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation, colony formation and tumor growth in xenograft compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147).

The ERBB3 V104L mutation is located in the extracellular ligand-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in bladder, breast and colon cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28572459, 26619011). This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

The ERBB3 M91I mutation is located in the receptor L domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in bladder cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 25096233). Although not functionally characterized, preclinical studies with KRAS-mutated bladder cancer cell lines expressing ERBB3 M91I demonstrated resistance to treatment with afatinib and dacomitinib (PMID: 29430509).

The ERBB3 A232T mutation is located in the extracellular ligand binding region within the domain I/II interface of the protein. This mutation has been identified in biliary tract adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 29360550). In vitro studies with colonic cells expressing ERBB3 A232T demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased colony formation and ERK1/2 activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147).

The ERBB3 R103G mutation is located in the enzymatically inactive kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in bladder cancer. While this mutation has not yet been functionally characterized, one patient with bladder cancer harboring both this mutation and ERBB2 amplification had a clinical response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor afatinib (PMID: 27044931).

The ERBB3 V104M mutation is located in the extracellular ligand-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma, breast and endometrial cancer (PMID: 28481359, 24997986, 29349598). Expression of this mutation in breast cancer and colonic epithelial cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation, colony formation and tumor growth in xenograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147)(Abstract: Cabel et al. JCO PO, 2018, https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.17.00243).

The ERBB3 A232V mutation is located in the extracellular ligand-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in cholangiocarcinoma and colon and breast cancer (PMID: 28481359, 29420467). Expression of this mutation in colonic epithelial cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and colony formation when coexpressed with ERBB2 compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147).

The ERBB3 R669C mutation is located in the enzymatically inactive kinase domain of the ERBB3 protein. This mutation has not been functionally characterized; however, computational modeling of this mutation demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by disruption of protein stability (PMID: 23741632).

The ERBB3 T389K mutation is located in the extracellular ligand-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast and colon cancer (PMID: 20668451, 25344691). Expression of this mutation in breast cancer and colonic epithelial cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and colony formation when coexpressed with ERBB2 compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147).

ERBB3 amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast, gastric and ovarian cancer and frequently co-occurs with amplification of other members of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, including EGFR or ERBB2 (PMID: 24886126). Expression of ERBB3 is associated with worse survival across multiple cancer types including breast, colorectal, gastric, melanoma, ovarian, head and neck, pancreatic, and cervical cancer (PMID: 23221996).

The ERBB3 Q809R mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in gastric cancer (PMID: 23680147). Expression of this mutation in breast cancer, colonic epithelial, and murine B-cell cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation and colony formation when coexpressed with ERBB2 compared to wildtype (PMID: 23680147).
