The FGFR4 R203C mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in mesothelioma (PMID: 26928227). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR4 R203C demonstrated this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR4 V550L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in rhabdomyosarcoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 21412928). In vitro studies with human RMS559 cells expressing FGFR4 V550L demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by constitutive activation of the FGF receptor compared to wildtype (PMID: 29487419). Preclinical studies of FGFR4 V550L suggest the mutation is sensitive to FGFR4-specific inhibitor FGF401 and HSP90 inhibitor NVP-AUY922 as measured by reduced signaling and cell proliferation upon drug treatment (PMID: 36097178). FGFR4 V550L has demonstrated resistance to FGFR4-specific inhibitors BLU-9931 and H3B6527 and pan-FGFR inhibitor LY2874455 as measured by lack of growth inhibition in preclinical studies (PMID: 36097178).

The FGFR4 E128K mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR4 E128K demonstrated this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR4 R154H mutation is located in the Ig-like C2-type II domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR4 R154H demonstrated this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

The FGFR4 Y367C mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 28572459). Expression of this mutation in a breast cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 19946327).

FLCN truncation mutations typically result in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in fibrofolliculoma, lung cysts and renal cancer (PMID: 28656962). In vivo studies with FLCN-deficient xenograft tumors in nude mice demonstrated that loss of FLCN is inactivating as measured by decreased ribosomal protein S6 activation as compared to wildtype (PMID: 19843504). Ectopic expression of FLCN in FLCN-deficient human tumors in a mouse xenograft model suppressed activated EGFR signaling in a Rab7A-dependent manner (PMID: 28656962). Truncating FLCN mutations are suggested to be sensitive to treatment with EGFR inhibitor afatinib as measured by suppressed tumor growth in a FLCN-deficient xenograft model (PMID: 28656962).

The FGFR4 R493Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adenocarcinoma (PMID: 24755471). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR4 R493Q demonstrated this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased proliferation and transformation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34272467).

Translocations involving MYB1 and GATA1 are found in patients with acute basophilic leukemia (ABL) (PMID: 21474671, 9233581). ABL is a leukemia that results in the expansion of basophils and is more prevalent in infants (PMID: 21474671, 9233581). The resultant MYB-GATA1 protein fuses the N-terminal DNA binding and TAD domains of MYB and the C-terminal zinc finger of GATA1. The MYB1-GATA1 protein truncates the negative regulatory domain of MYB1, resulting in the activation of the MYB1 promoter (PMID: 21474671). Expression of the MYB-GATA1 fusion in murine cells resulted in blocked differentiation and proliferation of granulocytic precursor cells, as evidenced in hematopoietic assays (PMID: 21474671).

Truncating mutations for GATA2 are typically found in the ZF1 and ZF2 domains of the protein and can result in the loss of protein expression. GATA2 truncating mutations have been identified in myelodysplastic syndromes, and are associated with poor prognosis (PMID: 28637621, 36455197). In vivo studies with biallelic GATA2 knockout-mouse models of acute promyelocytic leukemia demonstrate that loss of GATA2 is inactivating as measured by increased PML-RARA-driven aberrant self-renewal and leukemogenesis compared to GATA2 expressing-mice (PMID: 34125173).

FUBP1 truncation mutations occur throughout the gene and are associated with decreased FUBP1 protein expression (PMID: 24117486). Loss of FUBP1 on chromosome 1p is associated with IDH1 and CIC mutations on chromosome 19q in gliomas (PMID: 24117486, 22072542, 21817013). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing central DNA-binding domain truncated FUBP1 demonstrate that FUBP1 truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by reduced transcriptional activity compared to full-length FUBP1 (PMID: 30500954).

The GATA2 L321F mutation lies in the zinc finger 1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated it is likely inactivating, as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wild type GATA2 (PMID: 22649106).

The GATA2 A318T mutation lies in the zinc finger 1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated it is likely inactivating, as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype GATA2 (PMID: 22649106).

The GATA2 R308P mutation lies in the zinc finger 1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated it is likely neutral, as measured by no differences in DNA-binding and transcriptional activity compared to wildtype GATA2 (PMID: 24371770).

The gene G35V mutation is located close to a residue that in yeast is a target for methylation and has effects on gene regulation (PMID: 21685365). In glioblastoma tumor samples, this mutation was associated with a distinct transcriptional profile and alternate lengthening of telomeres (PMID: 22286061). In a separate set of glioblastoma samples, mutation at G35 was associated with genome-wide hypomethylation and never co-occured with IDH1 mutations (PMID: 23079654). This alteration is a known cancer hotspot (PMID: 26619011).

The gene G35R mutation is located close to a residue that in yeast is a target for methylation and thus influences gene regulation (PMID: 21685365). In glioblastoma tumor samples, this mutation was associated with a distinct transcriptional profile and alternate lengthening of telomeres (PMID: 22286061). In a separate set of glioblastoma samples, mutation at G35 was associated with genome-wide hypomethylation and never co-occured with IDH1 mutations (PMID: 23079654). This alteration is a known cancer hotspot (PMID: 26619011).

The gene K28M mutation is located close to a residue that is a target for methylation and has effects on gene regulation in yeast (PMID: 21685365). In samples from patients with pediatric glioblastoma, this mutation is associated with a distinct transcriptional profile and alternate lengthening of telomeres (PMID: 22286061). This alteration is a known cancer hotspot (PMID: 26619011).

The GATA2 G320D mutation lies in the zinc finger 1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated it is likely activating, as measured by increased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype GATA2 (PMID: 22649106).

Translocations involving IgH and IRF4 are found in patients with germinal center-derived B-cell lymphomas (PMID: 10557056, 21487109). The IgH enhancer region fuses with IRF4, resulting in the upregulation of IRF4 expression (PMID: 10557056, 21487109). Patients with IRF4-IgH fusions have activation of the oncogene BCL6 and disrupted plasma cell differentiation, suggesting that the IRF4 fusion is functioning as an oncoprotein (PMID: 21487109).

IKZF1 deletions occur in pediatric and adult patients with B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Several studies reported an association of IKZF1 deletion with unfavorable prognosis, especially for patients negative for BCR-ABL1 translocation. Gene expression profiling of patients with IKZF1-deleted ALL who had a poor outcome suggested that IKZF1 impairment is associated with an increased expression of hematopoietic stem-cell genes and a reduced expression of B-cell-lineage associated genes (PMID: 19129520, 26202931, 27067989, 27815723).

Translocations involving IRF4 are found in patients with multiple myeloma, anaplastic large cell lymphomas, and B-cell lymphomas (PMID: 27626696, 30093402, 21487109, 10557056). Common IRF4 fusion partners include DUSP22 and IgH and are predicted to increase the activity of IRF4 (PMID: 21487109, 10557056). IRF4 fusion proteins in patients with anaplastic large cell lymphomas are indicative of a favorable prognosis (PMID: 30093402).

Translocations involving DUSP22 and IRF4 are frequent in ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphomas and other lymphoproliferative disorders (PMID: 30093402, 21030553). The DUSP22-IRF4 fusion protein disrupts the DUSP22 phosphatase domain and likely activates IRF4 activity (PMID: 21030553, 27626696). Patients with DUSP22-IRF4 fusions have reduced JAK-STAT pathway activity and are predicted to have a more favorable outcome, similar to ALK-positive patients (PMID: 30093402).

Amplification of KDM5A is observed across many cancers, including breast cancer, and results in overexpression of the KDM5A protein (PMID: 22937203). Knockdown of KDM5A in cell lines with KDM5A amplification reduced cell proliferation and growth in soft agar compared to cells without KDM5A amplification, suggesting it is oncogenic (PMID: 2293720). KDM5A amplification has also been correlated to resistance to EGFR inhibitors in breast cancer (PMID: 2293720).

In human liposarcomas (both well-differentiated and dedifferentiated), a proportion of tumors contain amplification of the MDM2 or CDK4 loci. However, dedifferentiated liposarcomas are always associated with amplification of either 6q23 or 1p32. Amplification of c-JUN at 1p32 results in its increased expression. In dedifferentiated human liposarcomas, differentiation of tumour cells into adipocytes was blocked by JUN expression by interference with CEBPb function (PMID: 17418412). Amplification of JUN is associated with amplification of MDM2, one of the earliest oncogenic events in liposarcoma development, suggesting that amplification of JUN is essential during early tumorigenesis (PMID: 19449367).

The KDR T771R mutation is located in the transmembrane domain in exon 16 of KDR. This mutation has been repeatedly identified in patients with angiosarcoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26422291, 19723655). Patient samples bearing KDR T771R demonstrated the mutation is likely activating as measured by strong and diffuse KDR protein expression (PMID: 19723655).

The KDR S1100F mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. This mutation has been found in squamous cell carcinomas (PMID: 25589618). Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation is oncogenic as shown by increased tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308).

The KDR G800D mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation was oncogenic as shown by increased tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308).

The KDR S925F mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation is oncogenic as shown by tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308).

The KDR Q472H mutation is a germline mutation that has been identified in several cancers, including lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer and rhabdomyosarcoma (PMID: 24599305, 24793135, 21712447) (Abstract: Mockus et al. Abstract# 73, AACR 2015. http://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/75/15_Supplement/73). Experiments in cells lines demonstrated that this variant increases phosphorylation of the KDR protein following stimulation with its ligand, VEGF-A; this was associated with increased microvessel density in non-small cell lung tumor samples (PMID: 21712447).

The KDR D1052N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in basal cell carcinoma and breast cancer (PMID: 25759019, 28153863). In vitro studies with CHO cells expressing KDR D1052N demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased phosphorylation and enzymatic activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 33035615).

The KDR L840F mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Endogenous expression of this mutation in patient-derived tumor cells demonstrated that it is resistant to multiple anti-VEGF and VEGFR2 inhibitors compared to cells expressing wildtype KDR (PMID: 29588308). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by reduced protein phophorylation due to loss of ATP binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 29588308). The conformation of this mutation that prevents ATP binding also results in decreased inhibitor binding, and kinase activity assays revealed the L840F mutation to be resistant to the VEGFR2 inhibitors axitinib, cabozantinib, dovitinib, and lenvatinib compared to wildtype (PMID: 29588308). Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation was oncogenic as shown by tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308).

Amplification of KDR corresponds to copy number changes in the gene that lead to higher protein expression. Increased expression of KDR promotes angiogenesis and tumor growth (PMID: 11114740). In preclinical studies in non small cell lung cancer cell lines, amplification of KDR was associated with VEGF-induced activation of mTOR, p38, and tumor cell invasiveness (PMID: 26578684).

The KDR G800R mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation is oncogenic as shown by increased tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308).

The KDR R1032Q mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Kinase activity assays demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating with reduced kinase activity (PMID: 29588308). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that it was sensitive to the strong VEGFR2 inhibitor cabozantinib as shown by reduced cell proliferation and reduced pathway activation upon treatment (PMID: 29588308).

The KDR G843D mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation was oncogenic as shown by tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308).

The KDR A1065T mutation is located in the protein's intracellular kinase domain. In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutant results in constitutive autophosphorylation of the KDR protein and is sensitive to treatment with the kinase inhibitors, sorafenib and sunitinib (PMID: 19723655).

The KDR R1051Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro and in vivo studies with CHO and Sk-Mel-31 cells expressing KDR R1051Q demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased phosphorylation of PI3K/Akt, anchorage-independent and -dependent growth, tumor growth and metastasis compared to wildtype (PMID: 33035615). Other in vitro studies with melanoma cells expressing KDR R1051Q also demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased ATP production and glutamine uptake compared to wildtype (PMID: 33744390). Preclinical studies with xenograft mouse models expressing KDR R1051Q demonstrate sensitivity to treatment with linifanib as measured by tumor growth inhibition following treatment (PMID: 33035615).

The KEAP1 G333C mutation is located in the Kelch domain of the protein.  Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by abolished binding to NRF2 resulting in failure to suppress NRF2-mediated transcription (PMID: 24322982). This mutation was not able to catalyze IKKbeta ubiquitination, consistent with a decrease of E3 ligase activity on NRF2 (PMID: 19818716).

The KDR D717V mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation was oncogenic as shown by tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutant results in constitutive autophosphorylation of the KDR protein and is sensitive to treatment with the kinase inhibitors sorafenib and sunitinib (PMID: 19723655).

The KEAP1 C249Y mutation occurs in the IVR (intervening region) domain of the protein and was identified in cholangiocellular carcinoma. Expression of KEAP1 C249Y in HEK 293 cells showed that this is a loss of function mutation. Unlike the wildtype KEAP1 protein, which suppressed the transcriptional activity of NRF2, KEAP1 C249Y failed to repress NRF2 activity as measured by luciferase assay. Further, NRF2 ubiquitination was observed to be substantially reduced in cells expressing the KEAP1 249Y mutant, despite the fact that the binding interaction of KEAP1 with either NRF2 or the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cullin-3 was not compromised by the C249Y substitution (PMID: 18692501).

The KEAP1 T142M mutation is located in the BTB domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 T142M demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 R470H mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 26503331). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 R470H demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 R470C mutation is located in the KEAP1 KELCH domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by increased binding affinity for NRF2 that ultimately results in reduced KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 and increased NRF2 stability and activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

The KEAP1 C23Y mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Q293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by reduced ability to ubiquitinate target NRF2 compared to wildtype KEAP1, allowing NRF2 to transcriptionally activate its targets (PMID:17822677).

The KDR R1022Q mutation is located in the KDR tyrosine kinase domain. Expression of this mutation in Colo-320 cells that were injected into mice demonstrated that this mutation is oncogenic as shown by increased tumor formation compared to cells expressing a dominant negative version of the protein (PMID: 29588308).

The KEAP1 D479G mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 D479G demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KDR C482R mutation occurs in the immunoglobulin-like domain V of the extracellular region of the protein, located outside of the VEGF-binding region (PMID: 25411163, 18931684). Cell-based studies of this mutation show conflicting results. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 and 293-EBNA cells demonstrated KDR C482R is likely neutral as measured by no change in protein expression or pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 21712447, 18931684). Expression of this mutation in hemangioma endothelial cells, however, demonstrated that KDR C482R is activating as measured by increased interaction with cofactors and reduced expression of the VEGFR2 pathway inhibitor, VEGFR1, compared to wildtype (PMID: 18931684).

The KEAP1 G186R mutation is located in the KEAP1 intervening region domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by increased binding affinity for NRF2 that ultimately results in reduced KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 and increased NRF2 stability and activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

The KEAP1 S102L mutation is located in the BTB domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung cancer (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 S102L demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 R272C mutation is located in the KEAP1 intervening region domain. Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by impaired degradation of NRF2 resulting in increased NRF2 transcriptional activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 18316592).

The KEAP1 P278S mutation is located in the BACK domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 P278S demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 S243C mutation is located in the KEAP1 intervening region domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by increased binding affinity for NRF2 that ultimately results in reduced KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 and increased NRF2 stability and activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

The KEAP1 S338L mutation occurs in the DGR (double glycine repeat or Kelch repeat) domain of KEAP1 protein and it was identified in gallbladder adenocarcinoma. Expression of KEAP1 S338L in HEK 293 cells showed that this is a loss of function mutation. Unlike the wildtype KEAP1 protein, which suppressed the transcriptional activity of NRF2, KEAP1 S338L failed to repress NRF2 activity as measured by luciferase assay. Further, the S338L substitution was shown to cause significant abrogation in the association of NRF2 with the mutant KEAP1 protein, consequently leading to substantial reduction in NRF2 ubiquitination and degradation, thereby resulting in NRF2 activation (PMID: 18692501).

The KEAP1 G417R mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 G417R demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of NRF2 transcriptional regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 E117K mutation is located in the BTB domain of the protein. In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 E117K demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 G423V mutation is located in the KEAP1 KELCH domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by increased binding affinity for NRF2 that ultimately results in reduced KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 and increased NRF2 stability and activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

The KEAP1 G430C mutation is located in the KEAP1 KELCH domain. Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by impaired binding to and degradation of NRF2 resulting in increased NRF2 transcriptional activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 18316592).

The KEAP1 D422N mutation is located in the KEAP1 KELCH domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by increased binding affinity for NRF2 that ultimately results in reduced KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 and increased NRF2 activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

The KEAP1 G379D mutation occurs in the DGR (double glycine repeat or Kelch repeat) domain of the KEAP1 protein and was identified in gallbladder adenocarcinoma. Expression of the KEAP1 G379D mutant in HEK 293 cells showed that this is a loss of function mutation. Unlike the wildtype KEAP1 protein, which suppressed the transcriptional activity of NRF2, KEAP1 G379D failed to repress NRF2 activity as measured by luciferase assay. Further, G379D was shown to cause significant abrogation in the association of NRF2 with the mutant KEAP1 protein, consequently leading to substantial reduction in NRF2 ubiquitination and degradation, thereby resulting in NRF2 activation (PMID: 18692501).

The KEAP1 E611D mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 22980975). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 E611D demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by wildtype comparable NRF2 regulation (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 R204P mutation is located in the BACK domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 R204P demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 D389Y mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 22980975). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 D389Y demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 S144F mutation is located in the BTB domain of the protein. In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 S144F demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by NRF2 regulation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 G480W mutation is located in the KEAP1 KELCH domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating, as shown by decreased protein expression and decreased binding affinity for various KEAP1 targets, including mildly decreased binding affinity for NRF2 compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

The KEAP1 R415G mutation is located in the KEAP1 KELCH domain. Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by impaired binding to and degradation of NRF2 resulting in increased NRF2 transcriptional activity (PMID: 18316592).

KEAP1 deletions have been identified in patients with lung cancer and lead to loss of KEAP1 protein expression. Although functional studies have primarily been performed to characterize KEAP1 missense mutations, KEAP1 deletions are predicted to reduce the ability of KEAP1 to suppress NRF2 leading to upregulation of NRF2 target pathways. KEAP1 regulated NRF2 target pathways include those associated with antioxidants, oxidative stress and drug efflux pumps in cancer cells that have been associated with chemotherapy resistance (PMID: 17020408, 24142871). In addition, the biliary tract cancer (BTC) cell line TGBC24TKB that harbors homozygous deletion of the KEAP1 gene is observed to be resistant to the chemotherapeutic agent 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and this resistance is associated with NRF2 activation (PMID: 18692501).

The KEAP1 L268P mutation is located in the BACK domain of the protein. In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 L268P demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

KEAP1 truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated KEAP1 proteins resulting in loss of protein expression. Although functional studies have only been performed for KEAP1 missense mutations, truncating mutations are predicted to reduce the ability of KEAP1 to suppress NRF2 leading to upregulation of NRF2 target pathways. KEAP1 regulated NRF2 target pathways include those associated with antioxidants, oxidative stress and drug efflux pumps in cancer cells that have been associated with chemotherapy resistance (PMID: 24142871, 17020408, 24322982).

The KEAP1 V155F mutation is located in the KEAP1 intervening region domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by increased binding affinity for NRF2 that ultimately results in reduced KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 and increased NRF2 stability and activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

The KEAP1 G603W mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 27923066). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 G603W demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of NRF2 transcriptional regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 R601W mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 22980975). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 R601W demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of NRF2 transcriptional regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 G524C mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 20668451). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 G524C demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of NRF2 transcriptional regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 R470S mutation is located in the Kelch motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 25151357). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing KEAP1 R470S demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by partial loss of NRF2 regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27478040).

The KEAP1 G333S mutation is located in the Kelch domain of KEAP1. In vitro studies with H838 cells expressing KEAP1 G333S demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by inhibition of KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 (PMID: 17020408).

Truncating mutations of KMT2A are typically heterozygous and can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated KMT2A proteins which typically lack methyltransferase activity. Mice heterozygous for KMT2A do not form tumors spontaneously, suggesting that these mutations are not sufficient to induce tumor transformation alone, however may lead to dysregulation of genes involved in tumorigenesis including Myc (PMID: 25998713).

As opposed to expression of KMT2A fusion genes, overexpression of human KMT2A in drosophila flies did not induce cell cycle progression and lethality, indicating that KMT2A amplification has weaker oncogenic potential compared to rearrangements (PMID: 15378024). It has been suggested that impaired degradation of KMT2A contributes more to malignant transformation than high expression (PMID: 17908926).

The KEAP1 R320Q mutation is located between the KEAP1 intervening region and KELCH domains. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as shown by increased binding affinity for NRF2 that ultimately results in reduced KEAP1-mediated degradation of NRF2 and increased NRF2 stability and activity compared to wildtype KEAP1 (PMID: 24322982).

KMT2A-MLLT1 (or MLL-MLLT1) rearrangements typically partner the 5' portion of KMT2A upstream of the MLLT1 fusion partner (PMID: 20153263). Translocations involving KMT2A (MLL) and MLLT1 are found in patients with hematologic malignancies, including acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 17855633, 23628958). The KMT2A-MLLT1 oncoprotein is aberrantly targeted to KMT2A-regulated genes, resulting in constitutive activation of gene programs capable of transforming hematopoietic cells (PMID: 20153263). Human and murine hematopoietic cells engineered to express the KMT2A-MLLT1 fusion exhibit altered hematopoietic lineage identity, enhanced proliferation of hematopoietic progenitor cells and disrupted chromatin states (PMID: 28572162, 28572162, 17957188, 28068328).

The majority of KMT2A rearrangements are balanced translocations, leading to the expression of in-frame, gain-of-function fusion proteins. Around 80 different KMT2A fusion partners have been described, of which the most frequently occurring are members of the ENL-associated protein (EAP) complex. EAP complex components interact with several important transcriptional cofactors, and the KMT2A fusion proteins are suggested to mediate high expression of leukemic signature genes (PMID: 25998713, 23628958). Expression of the fusion protein KMT2A-AF9 in the bone marrow of mice was sufficient to induce leukemia, suggesting a strong oncogenic potential of KMT2A fusion proteins (PMID: 18455126). Mice with endogenous expression of KMT2A fusion proteins do not develop any other malignancies, underlining a hematopoietic stem cell-specific oncogenic capacity of KMT2A translocations (PMID: 8681380, 11265751).

The KMT2A-MLLT3 protein results from the fusion of the N-terminal of KMT2A with the C-terminal SET and transactivation domains of MLLT3 (PMID: 21123966, 20395514). Translocations involving KMT2A and MLLT3 (also MLL-AF9) are found in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and are associated with poor prognosis and frequent relapse (PMID: 21123966, 20395514). Expression of KMT2A-MLLT3 results in the expansion of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, enhanced colony formation, increased migration, and activation of self-renewal gene signatures, as evidenced in hematopoietic assays (PMID: 16862118, 27344946). In well-established murine models, expression of KMT2A-MLLT3 results in overt leukemia and requires the activity of AF9 (PMID: 20395514, 11265751). KMT2A-MLLT3 associates with the DOT1L histone methyltransferase complex, modifies histone H3 on lysine K79 and activates transcriptional elongation (PMID: 19956800, 21741597). In preclinical studies, KMT2A-MLLT3 expressing hematopoietic cells and murine models are sensitive to DOT1L or bromodomain inhibitors (PMID: 21741597, 21964340).

KMT2A-ELL (or MLL-ELL) rearrangements result from the chromosomal translocation t(11;19)(q23;p13.1). This fusion protein has been identified in various hematological malignancies (PMID: 10995463, 26185637, 26949571, 33608309). In vivo studies with mice expressing KMT2A-ELL demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by the development of acute myeloid leukemia compared to vector control mice (PMID: 10995463).

Truncating mutations of KMT2C can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins leading to reduced mRNA expression (PMID: 23259788). These mutations are commonly located upstream of the SET domain, which is crucial for its methyltransferase activity, suggesting that lost KMT2C methyltransferase activity is a contributor to oncogenesis in these tumors (PMID: 25537518). An in-frame deletion of the SET domain leads to the development of ureter epithelial tumors in mice, underlining the importance of this domain for tumor suppression function of KMT2C (PMID: 19433796). KMT2C is frequently mutated in diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinomas (DGA) and low KMT2C expression correlated with advanced tumor stage (PMID: 30108106). Knockdown of KMT2C in HFE-145 gastric epithelial cells demonstrated that KMT2C loss is oncogenic as shown by a moderate increase in proliferation, increased colony formation, increased migration and expression of proteins associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (PMID: 30108106). Reexpression of KMT2C in DGA cell lines and xenograft models slowed migration and invasion, reduced spheroid formation and reversed resistance to chemotherapy (PMID: 30108106).

The KMT2C A1685S mutation occurs in the high-mobility-group (HMG) binding motif of the KMT2C protein (PMID: 25151357, 25998713). This region is involved in the binding of transcription factors and cofactors, and leads to a concentration of KMT2C near distal enhancers (PMID: 25998713). Mutation at A1685 may disrupt tumor suppression by preventing enhancer function and disabling transcription associated with cellular identity and differentiation (PMID: 25998713).

The MEK2 L46F mutation is found in patients with melanoma resistan to RAF inhibition. Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E mutated melanoma cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating, as shown by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 21383288). In vitro studies of cells expressing MEK2 V35M suggest that this mutation is resistant to the RAF/MEK inhibitors dabrafenib and trametinib but sensitive to the ERK inhibitor VRT11E as measured by protein activity and cell proliferation following drug treatment (PMID: 24265153).

KMT2A partial tandem duplications duplicate exons 2 to 10 or duplicate exons 2 to 8  This alteration has been found in acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 8656671, 29567781, 9136917 ) and is associated with poor prognosis (PMID: 29351983, 12149299, 11840285) and short duration of remission (PMID: 12149299, 9426057).  Expression of this alteration in a mouse knock-in model demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased histone H3/H4 acetylation and histone H3K4 methylation within the homeobox gene promoters, leading to overexpression of the homeobox genes, as well as increased granulocyte-macrophage colony-forming progenitor cells and pluripotent hemopoietic progenitor cells (PMID: 16981007, 18617636).

The KMT2C S3660L mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation occurs frequently as a germline variant in the common population, suggesting that it is likely neutral and not sufficient to cause oncogenic transformation (PMID: 24965397).

KMT2C deletions are frequently detected in patients with leukemia and lead to haploinsufficiency of KMT2C (PMID: 24794707, 11891048, 9834205). KMT2C knockdown in leukemia mouse models has been shown to regulate animal survival in specific genetic subgroups (PMID: 24794707), suggesting that KMT2C deletion cooperates with other genetic events to induce oncogenesis. Since KMT2C functions to methylate histones at enhancer regions, loss of KMT2C would likely lead to dysregulated expression of target genes (PMID: 24081332, 23166019).

The MEK2 S222D mutation is located in the MEK2 kinase domain. Expression of this mutation with either the MEK2 S218D or the MEK2 S226D mutations in embryonic kidney cells resulted in increased pathway activation compared to widltype MEK2; however, the S222D mutation was not tested alone (PMID: 16439621).

The MEK2 C125S mutation is an analog of an activating MEK1 mutation that is known to cause resistance to RAF/MEK inhibitors (PMID: 21383288). Expression of the MEK2 C125S mutation in A375 cells (endogenously expressing the BRAF V600E mutation) and HEK293 cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating, as shown by increased kinase activity, pathway activation, and cell proliferation that is resistant to the RAF/MEK inhibitors dabrafenib and trametinib compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 24265153, 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 K101M mutation is located in the MEK2 kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as it did not increase pathway activation (PMID: 16439621). However, one study showed that expression of MEK2 K101M in zebrafish embryos led to an elongation phenotype similar to other activating mutations of MEK2, suggesting that K101M MEK2 may be able to activate the MAPK pathway through other protein interactions in vivo (PMID: 19376813).

The MEK2 P128L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 H123Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 F57C mutation is located in helix A of the N-terminal region upstream of the MEK2 kinase domain. This mutation has been found in patients with cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 16439621).

The MAP2K2 M150L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 S226D mutation is located in the MEK2 kinase domain. Expression of this mutation with the MEK2 S222D mutation in embryonic kidney cells resulted in increased pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK2; however, the S226D mutation was not tested alone (PMID: 16439621).

The MEK2 Q60P mutation is located in the MEK2 N-terminal regulatory domain. Expression of this mutation in A375 cells (endogenously expressing the BRAF V600E mutation) and HEK293 cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating, as shown by increased kinase activity and pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 24265153, 24055054, 24265154, 32641410). The Q56P mutation in MEK1, the homologous mutation to the Q60P mutation of MEK2, increases the kinase activity and causes resistance to selumetinib (AZD6244), an allosteric MEK inhibitor, as well as to BRAF inhibitors PLX4720 and vemurafenib (PMID:19915144, 23569304). Q60P mutation in MAP2K2 has a similar effect, leading to increased kinase activity, elevated levels of phosphorylated ERK1/2 and resistance to the MEK inhibitor trametinib and BRAF inhibitors dabrafenib and vemurafenib (PMID: 24055054, 24265154).

The MEK2 V64D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 I107N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 Y134C mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MAP2K2 A110V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 K61T mutation is located in the negative regulatory domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 V35M mutation is found in patients with melanoma resistant to RAF inhibition (PMID: 21383288). Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E mutant melanoma cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK2. In vitro studies of cells expressing MEK2 V35M suggest that this mutation is resistant to the RAF/MEK inhibitors dabrafenib and trametinib but sensitive to the ERK inhibitor VRT11E as measured by protein activity and cell proliferation following drug treatment (PMID: 24265153).

The MEK2 D71N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 E207K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation is an analog of an activating MEK1 mutation. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410). A patient-derived melanoma cell line endogenously expressing MAP2K2 E207K along with activating BRAF mutations was more resistant to the MEK inhibitor AZD6244 compared to cells with BRAF mutations alone (PMID: 22197931).

The MEK2 L46_E55del mutation is located in the negative regulatory domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in a RASopathy syndrome (PMID: 32641410). Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 F57V mutation is located in the negative regulatory domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with the neuro-cardio-facio-cutaneous family of syndromes (PMID: 16439621, 18456719, 18042262). Expression of this mutation in embryonic kidney cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased levels of pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 16439621, 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation is sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib when expressed in an embryonic kidney cell line as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 Y134H mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in histiocytic neoplasms (PMID: 30867592). Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased downstream ERK signaling, cytokine-independent growth, and MEK1/2-inhibitor sensitivity in vitro compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 30867592). A patient with histiocytic disease harboring the MEK2 Y134H mutation had a complete response to treatment with the MEK1/2 inhibitor cobimetinib (PMID: 30867592).

The MEK2 G132D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 F57L mutation has been found in patients with the neuro-cardio-facio-cutaneous family of syndromes (PMID: 16439621, 18456719, 18042262). Expression of this mutation in embryonic kidney cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased levels of pathway activation compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 16439621).

The MAP2K2 P268R mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 L181M mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410). In vitro studies demonstrate that this mutation was sensitive to the MEK inhibitor trametinib as measured by decreased pathway activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 32641410).
The MEK2 S154F mutation is located in the MEK2 kinase domain. In vitro kinase assays demonstrate that this mutation has similar kinase activity to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 27301426).

The MAP2K2 R231H mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in an embryonic kidney cell line demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 32641410).

The MEK2 N126D mutation is found in a familial case of cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome (PMID: 25487361). Expression of this mutation in A375 cells (endogenously expressing the BRAF V600E mutation) demonstrated that this mutation is activating, as shown by increased kinase activity, pathway activation and cell proliferation that is resistant to the RAF/MEK inhibitors dabrafenib and trametinib compared to wildtype MEK2 (PMID: 24265153).

The MAP2K4 S251N mutation is located within the kinase domain. Expression of the mutation in NIH3T3 cells resulted in diminished phosphorylation of MAP2K4 downstream targets such as JNK and MBP suggesting that the S251N mutant MAP2K4 protein may function as a dominant negative. Expression of this mutation also resulted in increased anchorage independent growth of NIH3T3 cells suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic (PMID: 20668451). This result is consistent with the behavior of embryonic stem cells stably transfected with the S257A/T261A catalytically inactive MAP2K4 mutant, which exhibited a transformed phenotype (PMID: 15122334).

The MAP2K4 A279T mutation is located within the kinase domain. Expression of the mutation in NIH3T3 cells resulted in diminished phosphorylation of MAP2K4 downstream targets such as JNK and MBP suggesting that the A279T mutant MAP2K4 protein may function as a dominant negative. Expression of this mutation also resulted in increased anchorage independent growth of NIH3T3 cells suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic (PMID: 20668451). This result is consistent with the behavior of embryonic stem cells stably transfected with the S257A/T261A catalytically inactive MAP2K4 mutant, which exhibited a transformed phenotype (PMID: 15122334). However, another study showed that overexpression of A279T in HEK293T cells did not actually significantly reduce JNK phophosphorylation as compared to overexpression of wildtype MAP2K4 suggesting that the complete functional consequences of this mutation may be context-dependent (PMID: 21896780).

The MAP2K4 R134Q mutation is located within the MAP2K4 kinase domain. This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells did not significantly change the phosphorylation of the MAP2K4 downstream target, JNK, and did not significantly change the invasive potential of cells (PMID: 21896780).

The MAP2K4 R134W mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 22722193). In silico analysis of MAP2K4 R134W suggests that the mutation is likely inactivating by stabilizing the inactive autoinhibited dimer state of the protein (PMID: 33101607).

The MAP2K4 R154W mutation is located within the kinase domain. Expression of the mutation in NIH3T3 cells resulted in diminished phosphorylation of MAP2K4 downstream targets such as JNK and MBP suggesting that the R154W mutant MAP2K4 protein may function as a dominant negative. Expression of this mutation also resulted in increased anchorage independent growth of NIH3T3 cells suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic (PMID: 20668451). This result is consistent with the behavior of embryonic stem cells stably transfected with the S257A/T261A catalytically inactive MAP2K4 mutant, which exhibited a transformed phenotype (PMID: 15122334).

The MAP2K4 N234I mutation is located within the kinase domain. Expression of the mutation in NIH3T3 cells resulted in diminished phosphorylation of MAP2K4 downstream targets such as JNK and MBP suggesting that the N234I mutant MAP2K4 protein may function as a dominant negative. Expression of this mutation also resulted in increased anchorage independent growth of NIH3T3 cells suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic (PMID: 20668451). This result is consistent with the behavior of embryonic stem cells stably transfected with the S257A/T261A catalytically inactive MAP2K4 mutant, which exhibited a transformed phenotype (PMID: 15122334).

The MAP2K4 R228K mutation is located within the kinase domain. Expression of the mutation in NIH3T3 cells resulted in diminished phosphorylation of MAP2K4 downstream targets such as JNK and MBP suggesting that the R228K mutant MAP2K4 protein may function as a dominant negative. Expression of this mutation also resulted in increased anchorage independent growth of NIH3T3 cells suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic (PMID: 20668451). This result is consistent with the behavior of embryonic stem cells stably transfected with the S257A/T261A catalytically inactive MAP2K4 mutant, which exhibited a transformed phenotype (PMID: 15122334).

Truncating mutations in MAP2K4 result in loss of the C-terminus and subsequent loss of protein stability. Characterization of three truncating mutations (I295fs*23, W310*, R304*) demonstrated the loss of phosphorylation of downstream MAP2K4 substrate JNK1 and complete loss of MAP2K4 encoded protein MKK4 activity (PMID: 21896780). In the same study, mouse lung cancer models, inactivation of MAP2K4 in conjunction with a KRAS G12D mutation resulted in an increased frequency and accelerated growth of lung neoplasias, and increased tumor cell migration and invasion (PMID: 21896780).

The MAP2K4 R304* mutation is located within the MAP2K4 kinase domain. The MITF E318K mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer, colon cancer, melanoma and ovarian cancer (PMID: 34289891). In vitro studies with renal carcinoma cell lines and melanoma cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrate that MITF E318K is activating as measured by increased cellular invasion, cellular migration and differential expression of MITF target genes compared to wildtype (PMID: 22012259, 22080950).

Amplification of MITF has been associated with increased survival and differentiation in cancer cells (PMID: 12086670,15607961, 15623583, 15716956). MITF is amplified in >15% of metastatic melanoma (PMID: 12789286). In BRAF V600E mutant melanoma, expression of MITF activates downstream of MAP kinase and confers resistance to RAF and MEK inhibition (PMID: 24185007). Functional studies of overexpressed MITF in BRAF V600E mutant melanoma cell lines rendered the cells resistant to RAF, MEK, and ERK inhibition (PMID: 24265153).

MDM4 maps to a region which is frequently amplified in breast cancers (PMID: 7585611, 9523192). FISH analysis on primary tumors followed by in-situ hybridization analysis on mRNA levels revealed that MDM4 gene copy numbers were elevated with a concomitant increase in MDM4 mRNA expression (19% of breast, 19% of colon and 18% of lung cancers) (PMID: 15199139). Western blotting confirmed that protein levels were elevated (PMID: 15199139).

Loss of MITF is suggested to support resistance to BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib treatment through the constitutive activation of EGFR (PMID: 25789707).

Cell line studies suggest that mTOR E2014K is sensitive to allosteric inhibitors of mTOR, such as rapamycin (PMID:24625776).

The MTOR I2500M mutation occurs near the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells results in increased phosphorylation of downstream mTORC1 and mTORC2 targets S6K, 4EBP1 and AKT compared to wildtype mTOR, including in conditions of nutrient deprivation (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR C1483Y mutation occurs in the FRAP-ATM-TRAP (FAT) domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased phosphorylation of downstream mTORC1 substrate 4EBP1 and cell proliferation compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838, 26255626). A leukemia cell line harboring this mutation was shown to be hypersensitive to rapamycin (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR A1428T mutation is located in the FAT domain of the protein. This mutation is found in kidney cancer (PMID: 26255626, 24631838). Expression of this mutation in HEK-293T cells demonstrated that this mutation is mildly activating as measured by slightly increased downstream pathway activation compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR W1456R mutation occurs proximal to the FAT domain. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblasts results in increased phosphorylation of mTORC1 and mTORC2 targets S6K1 and AKT compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 22460905, 23322780).

The MTOR Y1450D mutation is located in the FAT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adenocarcinoma, papillary carcinoma and focal cortical dysplasia type II (PMID: 27149842, 29615459, 25799227). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate MTOR Y1450D is activating as measured by phosphorylated S6 immunoblotting and mTOR kinase assay results indicating increased mTOR activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 25799227, 26779999).

The MTOR F1888V mutation is located in the FAT domain of the protein. In one experiment, expression of this mutation in human epithelial cells was described to result in phosphorylation of the downstream mTOR target S6K similar to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838), while in a separate study, expression of the mutation in human epithelial cells resulted in increased phosphorylation of downstream pathway effectors, such as 4EBP1, compared to wildtype MTOR (PMID: 27482884).

The MTOR L2209V mutation is found in kidney cancer (PMID: 24631838). Expression of this mutation in HEK-293T cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased downstream pathway activation compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR A1459P mutation occurs in the FAT domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblasts results in increased phosphorylation of the downstream mTORC1 pathway target S6K compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR A2226S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation is found in kidney cancer (PMID: 24631838). Expression of this mutation in HEK-293T cells demonstrated that this mutation is mildly activating as measured by slightly increased downstream pathway activation compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR K1452N mutation occurs in the FAT domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblasts results in increased proliferation and phosphorylation of the downstream mTORC1 pathway targets S6K and 4EBP1 compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838, 26255626).

The MTOR L2230V missense mutation occurs in the kinase domain of mTOR protein. Expression of MTOR L2230V in human fibroblast cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased phospho-S6K levels and cell growth compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 27482884). Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cells resulted in increased growth and sensitivity to rapamycin in an allograft model compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 27482884).

The MTOR S2215F mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells or in mouse allografts results in increased phosphorylation of the downstream mTORC1 targets S6K compared to wildtype mTOR, including in conditions of serum deprivation, as well as increased tumor growth in vivo (PMID: 24631838, 27482884).

The MTOR S2215Y mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells results in increased phosphorylation of downstream mTORC1 targets S6K and 4EBP1 compared to wildtype mTOR, including in conditions of serum deprivation (PMID: 24631838, 20190810, 24336570). MTOR S2215Y failed to form colonies alone in a single colony formation assay, but was able to transform cells in combination with a KRAS activating mutation (PMID: 20190810).

The MTOR E2288K mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblasts results in increased focus formation, anchorage-independent growth, tumor formation and phosphorylation of mTORC1 and mTORC2 targets S6K1 and AKT compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 23322780).

The MTOR L2216P mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation is found in kidney cancer (PMID: 24631838). Expression of this mutation in HEK-293T cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased phosphorylation of downstream S6K1 compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR A8S mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human epithelial cells results in phosphorylation of downstream mTOR targets 4EBP1, S6K and AKT similar to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 20190810).

The MTOR R2505Q mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human epithelial cells results in phosphorylation of the downstream mTOR target S6K similar to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR C1483F mutation occurs in the FRAP-ATM-TRAP (FAT) domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells resulted in increased mTORC1 pathway activation as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of downstream substrates S6K1 and 4EBP1 as well as increased mTORC2 activation compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838, 26255626, 27482884).

The MTOR T1977I mutation occurs between the FAT and FRB domains of the protein. Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cells results in increased proliferation, cell survival and mTOR downstream signaling compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 26432419).

The MTOR T1977S mutation is located adjacent to the FAT domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human epithelial cells results in phosphorylation of the downstream mTOR target S6K similar to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR C1483R mutation occurs in the FRAP-ATM-TRAP (FAT) domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells resulted in increased phosphorylation of downstream mTORC1 substrate S6K1 compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838)

The MTOR E2419K mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells results in increased phosphorylation of the downstream mTORC1 target S6K compared to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24625776). A patient with urothelial carcinoma harboring the MTOR E2419K mutation in combination with the MTOR E2014K mutation had an extraordinary response to the combination of treatment with everolimus and pazopanib (PMID: 24625776).

The MTOR I2500F mutation occurs near the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells results in increased phosphorylation of downstream mTORC1 and mTORC2 targets S6K, 4EBP1 and AKT compared to wildtype mTOR, including in conditions of nutrient deprivation (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR F1888I mutation occurs in the FRAP-ATM-TRAP (FAT) domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells results in increased mTORC1 pathway activation as evidenced by phosphorylation of downstream substrate S6K1 (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR L2220F mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK-293T cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased phosphorylation of downstream effectors, such as S6K1, compared to wildtype MTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MTOR A41P mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human epithelial cells results in phosphorylation of the downstream mTOR target S6K similar to wildtype mTOR (PMID: 24631838).

The MUTYH G382D mutation (also cited as MUTYH G396D) is located in the NUDIX domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis (PMID: 19506731). In vitro studies with MutY-deficient E. coli expressing this mutation demonstrated MUTYH G382D is inactivating as measured by enzymatic inactivity in the in vitro glycosylase assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 25820570).

The MUTYH R168C mutation (also cited as MUTYH R182C) is located in the HhH-GPD domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis and colorectal cancer (PMID: 19506731, 15236166). In vitro studies with MutY-deficient E. coli expressing this mutation demonstrated MUTYH R168C is inactivating as measured by enzymatic inactivity in an in vitro glycosylase assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 25820570).

The MUTYH R231C mutation (also cited as MUTYH R245C) is located in the HhH-GPD domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis and colorectal cancer (PMID: 19506731, 15890374). In vitro studies with lymphoblastoid cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrate MUTYH R231C is inactivating as measured by impaired DNA glycosylase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 23108399). In addition, in vitro studies with MutY-deficient E. coli expressing this mutation also demonstrated MUTYH R231C is inactivating as measured by enzymatic inactivity in an in vitro glycosylase assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 25820570).

The MUTYH E466del mutation (also cited as MUTYH E480del) is located in the NUDIX domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis (PMID: 25638157). In vitro studies with MutY-deficient E. coli expressing this mutation demonstrated MUTYH E466del is inactivating as measured by enzymatic inactivity in an in vitro glycosylase assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 25820570).

Truncating mutations in MUTYH occur throughout the entire gene and lead to loss of the MUTYH protein. These mutations have been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis (PMID: 21962078). In vitro studies with lymphoblastoid cell lines expressing these mutations demonstrate MUTYH truncation is inactivating as measured by increased spontaneous mutagenesis compared to wildtype MUTYH expression (PMID: 23108399).

The MUTYH R260Q mutation (also cited as MUTYH R274Q) is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PMID: 19245865, 19443904). In vitro studies with MutY-deficient E. coli expressing this mutation demonstrate MUTYH R260Q is inactivating as measured by enzymatic inactivity in an in vitro glycosylase assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 25820570).

The MUTYH P391L mutation (also cited as MUTYH P405L) is located in the NUDIX domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis (PMID: 19506731). In vitro studies with MutY-deficient E. coli expressing this mutation demonstrated MUTYH P391L is inactivating as measured by enzymatic inactivity in an in vitro glycosylase assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 25820570).

The MUTYH R95W mutation (also cited as MUTYH R109W) is located in exon 3 of the gene. This mutation has been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis, Lynch syndrome and colorectal cancer (PMID: 19732775, 25980754). In vitro studies with H1299 cells expressing this mutation demonstrated MUTYH R95W is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA glycosylase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 24799981).

The MUTYH Y165C mutation (also cited as MUTYH Y179C) is located in HhH-GPD domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in MUTYH-associated polyposis (PMID: 24444654). In vitro studies with MutY-deficient E. coli expressing this mutation demonstrated MUTYH Y165C is inactivating as measured by enzymatic inactivity in an in vitro glycosylase assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 25820570).
The MYC P72S mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the MYC protein. \nIn silico analysis predicts that mutation is damaging (PMID: 35045798).

Amplification of MYC is correlated with an increase in the expression of the MYC gene (PMID: 22464321,15083194), which leads to the transcriptional activation of MYC target genes. MYC target genes regulate various cellular processes involved in oncogenesis including proliferation, inhibiting exit from the cell cycle, stimulating vascularization and enhancing genomic instability (PMID: 22464321,10378696,16934487,19029958). Genomic amplification of MYC is observed in a large number of tumor types. A study of genomic amplification across many cancer types identified focal amplifications of MYC in 14% of all cancers, with additional enrichment for large scale arm-level copy number alterations encompassing the MYC gene locus (PMID: 20164920).

The IGK-MYC fusion results from the t(2;8)(p12;q24) translocation fusing a region 3' of the MYC gene to a region 5' of the IGK locus. This fusion leads to deregulated overexpression of MYC in blood cells (PMID: 24957271, 21887927, 19351371, 19246886). MYC overexpression results in activation of MYC target genes genes that regulate various cellular processes involved in oncogenesis including proliferation, inhibiting exit from the cell cycle, stimulating vascularization and enhancing genomic instability (PMID: 22464321,10378696,16934487,19029958). In vitro expression of the MYC gene fused to elements of the IGK locus resulted in increased MYC expression, and transformation of a lymphoblastoid cell line into cells that behaved similar to Burkitt's Lymphoma cell lines (PMID: 8502472, 7731690, 8816814) suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic. This translocation has been found in blood cancers, most commonly Burkitt's lymphoma (PMID: 22333947).

The MYC T73A mutation has been strongly associated with increased MYC protein stability and decreased ubiquitination in a study looking specifically at leukemia cell lines (PMID: 10706881). Phosphorylation of the highly conserved T73 residue leads to ubiquitin-mediated MYC protein degradation and therefore, mutation of this residue is thought to stabilize the MYC protein (PMID: 20399964). MYC target genes regulate various cellular processes involved in oncogenesis including proliferation, inhibiting exit from the cell cycle, stimulating vascularization and enhancing genomic instability (PMID: 22464321,10378696,16934487,19029958). In vitro and in vivo expression of the T73A mutant protein resulted in increased chromosomal instability and human mammary epithelial cells expressing the T73A mutant acquire phenotypic changes including increased aggregation, anchorage-independence, and growth in suspension (PMID: 21266350, 18642118). In addition, mammary specific in vivo expression of the T73A mutant resulted in the development of mammary adenocarcinomas, altogether suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic (PMID: 21266350). The T73 residue of MYC corresponds to the T58 residue in an alternative isoform.

The MYC T73N mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma (PMID: 31558468). In vitro studies with mouse hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and in vivo studies with mice expressing MYC T73N demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by lower median survival and alterations in transcriptional signatures compared to wildtype (Abstract: Arthur et al. Abstract# 1267 ASH 2022. https://ash.confex.com/ash/2022/webprogram/Paper166712.html).

The MYC S161L mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the MYC protein and is also referred to as S146L in the literature. This mutation has been found in B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 31527074). In vitro studies in MCG10A cells with this mutation have demonstrated that it is activating as demonstrated by an increased affinity for TRAPP, a cofactor of MYC, upregulation of MYC target genes and increased cellular proliferation in low attachment conditions compared to wildtype (PMID: 36018850). Transwell migration of S161L cells was reduced compared to wildtype, however, MYC overexpression has been shown to downregulate migration (PMID: 36018850).

The MYC P74Q mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 27276561). In vitro studies with mouse hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and in vivo studies with mice expressing MYC P74Q demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by lower median survival and alterations in transcriptional signatures compared to wildtype (Abstract: Arthur et al. Abstract# 1267 ASH 2022. https://ash.confex.com/ash/2022/webprogram/Paper166712.html).

The IGH-MYC fusion results from the t(8;14)(q24;q32) translocation, which places MYC expression under the control of enhancer elements within an immunoglobulin gene intron. This fusion leads to deregulated overexpression of MYC in blood cells (PMID: 16934487, 22333947). MYC overexpression results in activation of genes and signaling pathways that induce proliferation, cell cycle progression and vascularization (PMID: 22464321,10378696,16934487,19029958). This translocation has been found in blood cancers, most commonly Burkitt's lymphoma (PMID: 22333947).

The IGL-MYC fusion results from the t(2;8)(p12;q24) translocation fusing a region 3' of the MYC gene to a region 5' of the IGL locus. In vitro expression of the MYC gene fused to elements of the IGL locus resulted in increased MYC expression (PMID: 7731690). MYC overexpression results in activation of MYC target genes genes that regulate various cellular processes involved in oncogenesis including proliferation, inhibiting exit from the cell cycle, stimulating vascularization and enhancing genomic instability (PMID: 22464321,10378696,16934487,19029958). Expression of the fusion gene in vitro also transformed a lymphoblastoid cell line into cells that behaved similar to Burkitt's Lymphoma cells and expression of the fusion gene in vivo led to the development of lymphoma (PMID: 8502472, 8816814, 11034608) suggesting that this mutation is oncogenic. This translocation has been found in blood cancers, most commonly Burkitt's lymphoma (PMID: 22333947).

The PVT1-MYC fusion protein joins the 5' end of the noncoding PVT1 gene, containing microRNA binding sites, fused to MYC. This fusion protein occurs in a subtype of medulloblastoma known as "group 3," which are frequently MYC amplified (PMID: 22134537). The most prevalent forms of this fusion protein skip MYC exon 1. Endogenous expression of this fusion in medulloblastoma samples suggested that its mechanism of action may be to drive overexpression of MYC. In vitro studies of cells endogenously expressing the fusion protein showed that knockdown of either MYC or miR-1204 (one of the microRNAs that target PVT1) inhibited cell proliferation (PMID: 24298051).

The MYC T73I mutation is is a cancer hotspot mutation (PMID: 26619011). Expression of this mutation in various cell lines demonstrated that it is likely activating, as shown by reduced inhibitory protein phosphorylation compared to wildtype MYC (PMID: 10825194). However, expression of this mutation in rat embryo fibroblasts dramatically reduced cell oncogenic activity compared to wildtype MYC (PMID: 20713710).

MYC translocations are known to occur in a wide range of hematological malignancies and place MYC expression under the control of enhancer elements of immunoglobulin genes, including the heavy chain (14q32), kappa light chain (2p12) or the lambda light chain (22q11) (PMID: 16934487, 22333947). Translocation of the MYC gene enables increased expression of MYC mRNA and protein, which can lead to activation of MYC target genes and aberrant activation of oncogenic signaling.

The RLF-MYCL fusion results from a translocation fusing the RLF gene and the MYCL gene. This fusion has been identified in 9% of primary small cell lung cancer samples and cell lines (PMID: 23716474, PMID: 22941189). In vivo studies have demonstrated that the RLF-MYCL fusion is activating as measured by increased cell viability, increased tumor burden and increased metastases in a CRISPR/Cas9-based mouse model of small cell lung cancer induced by the RLF-MYCL fusion (PMID: 34344693).

Amplification of gene is found in several cancer types, including small cell lung cancer (PMID: 29596783, 27298335). gene amplification tends to be mutually exclusive with amplification of other MYC family members (including MYC and MYCN) and these aberrations have distinct cellular phenotypes  (PMID: 31164374). Small cell lung cancer mouse models have shown increased expression of gene, and models engineered to knockout gene expression have reduced lung cancer progression (PMID: 29596783).

MYC-nick is a transcriptionally inactive, cytoplasmically cleaved form of MYC. It is cleaved by a family of calcium-dependent cysteine proteases known as calpains, and is known to promote the acetylation of tubulins. Increased-levels of MYC-nick have been observed to promote cellular differentiation, which opposes the classical role of MYC as a promoter of proliferation (PMID: 20691906). While MYC-nick is likely to be expressed in a multitude of cell types, it has been confirmed to be expressed by immunoblotting in B-cells, thymic tumors, prostate cancer xenografts, neuroblastoma, medulloablastomas and colon cancer cells (PMID: 24696454).

The MYCN P44L mutation is located in the N-terminal transactivation domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in neuroblastoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 23334666). Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification copy number analysis of Wilms tumor patient samples with this mutation demonstrated MYCN P44L is likely activating as measured by overexpression of MYCN (PMID: 25749049).

Amplification of MYCN increases expression of the MYCN gene (PMID: 15013217,12612655). A MYCN gene signature derived from shRNA-mediated silencing of MYCN in neuroblastoma cells indicates that MYCN activates genes in pathways related to the cell cycle and DNA repair, and represses genes associated with neuronal differentiation (PMID: 23091029). In a study using transgenic mice, overexpression of MYCN in neuroectodermal cells led to the development of neuroblastoma and induced genomic copy number alterations syntenic (on the same chromosome) with those generally observed in human neuroblastomas (PMID: 9214616).
