While the majority of research focuses on MYCN in neuroblastoma, MYCN amplification or overexpression has been shown to contribute to tumorigenesis in various other cancer types (PMID: 22139329, 22035742, 21533284, 16116477).

The NKX2-1 A369V mutation (also cited as NKX2-1 A339V) is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in multinodular and papillary thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 19176457). Expression of this mutation in PCCL3 normal rat thyroid cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased pathway activation and cell proliferation compared to wildtype NKX2-1 (PMID: 19176457).

The TRB-NKX2-1 fusion results from the fusion of the TRB gene, a T cell receptor, with the NKX2-1 gene. This fusion has been found in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 21481790). Patient samples harboring this fusion were shown to have high NKX2-1 expression as measured by western blot compared to samples not harboring this fusion (PMID: 21481790). High expression of NKX2-1 in NIH3T3 and BJ-EHT cells in combination with RAS or MYC significantly increased the number of colonies in a soft agar assay compared to expression of each gene alone, suggesting that the TRB-NKX2-1 fusion is likely activating (PMID: 21481790).

The IGH-NKX2-1 fusion results from the fusion of the IGH gene, the immunoglobulin heavy locus, with the NKX2-1 gene. This fusion has been found in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 21481790). Patient samples harboring this fusion were shown to have high NKX2-1 expression as measured by western blot compared to samples not harboring this fusion (PMID: 21481790). High expression of NKX2-1 in NIH3T3 and BJ-EHT cells in combination with RAS or MYC significantly increased the number of colonies in a soft agar assay compared to expression of each gene alone, suggesting that the IGH-NKX2-1 fusion is likely activating (PMID: 21481790).

Fusions of NKX2-1 have been identified in patients with T cell lymphoblastic leukemia, in which NKX2-1 has shown to be fused to a variety of partner genes. These alterations lead to increased NKX2-1 expression (PMID: 21481790). High expression of NKX2-1 in NIH3T3 and BJ-EHT cells in combination with RAS or MYC significantly increased the number of colonies in a soft agar assay compared to expression of each gene alone, suggesting that these fusions are likely activating (PMID: 21481790).

The TRA-NKX2-1 fusion results from the fusion of the TRA gene, a T cell receptor, with the NKX2-1 gene. This fusion has been found in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 21481790). Patient samples harboring this fusion were shown to have high NKX2-1 expression as measured by western blot compared to samples not harboring this fusion (PMID: 21481790). High expression of NKX2-1 in NIH3T3 and BJ-EHT cells in combination with RAS or MYC significantly increased the number of colonies in a soft agar assay compared to expression of each gene alone, suggesting that the TRA-NKX2-1 fusion is likely activating (PMID: 21481790).

gene amplification has been detected at low frequency in a few tumor types, including breast cancer, nerve sheath tumors and ovarian cancer (Zehir A et al. Nature Medicine, 2017. http://doi:10.1038/nm.4333). The amplification is associated with increased expression levels in cancer cell lines and its depletion correlated with decreased cellular proliferation (PMID: 24874471, 18757432, 21664949). Assuming the amplification is associated with increased protein levels this suggest a putative oncogenic role for gene amplification, although this has not been directly described.

NKX2-1 is located at 14q13.3, a focally amplified region in lung cancer that includes also NKX2-8, PAX9 and MBIP. Gene amplification of NKX2-1 is associated with overexpression of the encoded protein and induces increased proliferation and survival. There is functional cooperation between the coamplified 14q13.3 genes. (PMID: 17925434, 18212743). NKX2-1 directly transactivates the receptor tyrosine kinase ROR1, which in turn sustains a favorable balance between prosurvival PI3K-AKT and proapoptotic p38 signaling (PMID: 22439932).

The NSD2 E1099K mutation is located in the AWS domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 24076604). Expression of NSD2 E1099K in ALL cells is activating as measured by global changes in H3K36 methylation, increased malignant transformation and increased cellular growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 24076604, 23823660).

The IGH-NSD2 fusion occurs within the context of the t(4;14) translocation and involves the Eμ enhancer of IGH fused to the NSD2 gene, thus resulting in the NSD2 gene being under control of IgH super enhancer elements (PMID: 9787135). The t(4;14) translocation is recurrently found in multiple myeloma and monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (PMID: 23980095, 10945609, 11861292). In vitro experiments in t(4;14)-positive multiple myeloma cell lines with NSD2 overexpression (KMS-11) demonstrated that the translocation (and resulting fusion) are likely activating as knockdown of NSD2 results in cell-cycle arrest and reduced cell adhesions. Additionally, NSD2 knockdown or knockout in KMS-11 cells reduced myeloma tumor formation in xenograft models (PMID: 17942756) suggesting that overexpression of NSD2 contributes to tumorigenicity of multiple myeloma cells harboring t(4;14).

The BCAN-NTRK1 fusion protein results from a fusion between BCAN and NTRK1. This fusion protein has been identified in glioma (PMID: 28695888). In vivo studies with mice harboring BCAN-NTRK1 demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by tumor formation compared to control mice (PMID: 28695888). Preclinical studies of the fusion demonstrate sensitivity to entrectinib as measured by decreased cellular viability following treatment (PMID: 28695888). In a case report, a patient with a glioneuronal tumor harboring BCAN-NTRK1 was treated with entrectinib and demonstrated a 60% lesion reduction (PMID: 29872694).

Amplification of NTRK1 has been found in malignant melanoma and is associated with worse clinical outcome (PMID: 26496938). Titrated expression of exogenous NTRK1 in cells lacking NTRK1 led to checkpoint inhibition resulting from oncogene-induced growth arrest, suggesting that this alteration is activating (PMID: 26496938).

The NTRK1 G667S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, two patients with G669S mutations alone or in combination with an NTRK1 G595R mutation had resistance to larotrectinib, and two patients with G669S mutations alone or in combination with NTRK1 G667C had resistance to selitrectinib (PMID: 30624546, 33004339, 29466156). In vitro studies have shown that this mutation is resistant to larotrectinib but sensitive to entrectinib and Type II inhibitors (PMID: 33328556)(Abstract: Wei et al. Abstract# 2136, AACR 2016. https://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/76/14_Supplement/2136.short).

The NTRK1 V710A mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation is found in lung cancer (PMID: 27272783). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by a significant reduction in auto-phosphorylation of NTRK1 and lower levels of downstream pathway activation than wildtype (PMID: 27272783).

The TPR-NTRK1 fusion joins the carboxy terminus of NTRK1 with different amino-terminal portions of the TPR (translocated promoter region) gene on chromosome 1 (PMID: 7851906, 9172002). This fusion has been found in thyroid cancer and dendritic cell neoplasms (PMID: 10074915, 16483615, 29920189). Expression of this fusion in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by increased focus formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 1532241).

The NTRK1 A608D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, one patient with pancreatic cancer harboring the NTRK1 A608D mutation had resistance to larotrectinib (PMID: 29466156)

The NTRK1 R761W mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, a patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR L747_P753delinsS and T790M acquired NTRK R761W following treatment with osimertinib (PMID: 29571987).

The NFASC-NTRK1 fusion joins the amino terminus of the neurofascin gene to the carboxyl terminal portion of the NTRK1 gene, inlcuding the kinase and transmembrane domains of NTRK1. This fusion has been found in glioblastoma (PMID: 23917401). Expression of this fusion in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased proliferation, soft agar colony growth and tumorigenicity in mice compared to wildtype NTRK1 (PMID: 24647444, 23917401).

The MPRIP-NTRK1 (also known as RIP-TRKA) fusion is the result of a chromosomal rearrangement in which the N-terminus of the myosin phosphatase-Rho-interacting protein (MPRIP) protein, including its coiled-coil domains, is fused with NTRK1, resulting in its constitutive dimerization and kinase activation. This fusion has been found in lung cancer (PMID: 24162815). Expression of MPRIP-NTRK1 in Ba/F3 or NIH-3T3 cells demosntrated that it is activating as measured by cytokine-independent proliferation and increased anchorage-independent growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 24162815).

The LMNA-NTRK1 fusion joins the amino terminus of lamin A/C with the carboxyl terminus of NTRK1. This fusion has been found in melanoma, histiocytic neoplasm, metastatic breast cancer and sporadic microsatellite instability-high colorectal cancers (PMID: 24445538, 29920189, 30279230) (Abstract: Rosen et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO.19.00009). Expression of this fusion in NIH3T3 and melan-a cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by constitutive activation of the kinase, increased activation of downstream signaling pathways, increased colony formation and increased growth of cells in xenograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 24445538, 30279230). Additionally, expression of this protein in c-Kit+ mouse bone marrow cells and Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased colony formation and IL-3 independent proliferation compared to cells expressing empty vector (PMID: 29920189). A patient with metastatic breast cancer harboring this fusion had a complete intracranial response to larotrectinib (Abstract: Rosen et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO.19.00009).

The ARHGEF2-NTRK1 fusion protein results from a fusion between ARHGEF2 and NTRK1. While this fusion has not been functionally characterized, biological characterization of other NTRK1 fusions demonstrates that they are activating as measured by increased downstream pathway activation, suggesting that this fusion is also likely activating (PMID: 24162815, 26565381, 26216294). In a case report, a patient with a glioneuronal tumor harboring ARHGEF2-NTRK1 was treated with entrectinib and demonstrated dramatic response (PMID: 35821677).

Fusions of NTRK1 arise from chromosomal translocations that generally fuse the N-terminal portion of a partner protein with the C-terminal portion of NTRK1, which includes the NTRK1 kinase domain. These fusion proteins are most commonly found in a subset of patients with lung adenocarcinoma. Biological characterization of NTRK1 fusions demonstrates that they increase downstream pathway activation and are variably sensitive to pan-TRK inhibitors, including ARRY-470, CEP-701, entrectinib and larotrectinib (PMID: 24162815, 26565381, 26216294).

The CD74-NTRK1 fusion is the result of a chromosomal rearrangement that fuses the major histocompatibility complex class II CD74 with NTRK1. This fusion has been found in lung cancer (PMID: 24162815 ). Expression of CD74-NTRK1 in Ba/F3 or NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by cytokine-independent proliferation and increased anchorage-independent growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 24162815).

TRKAIII is an NTRK1 splice variant characterized by the loss of amino acids 192-284 from the extracellular domain. This mutation is found in neuroblastoma (PMID: 15488758). Expression of this mutation in non-transformed cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased kinase activity, downstream pathway activation and tumorigenicity when implanted in mice compared to wildtype NTRK1 (PMID: 15488758).

The EPS15-NTRK1 fusion joins the N-terminus of EPS15 with the C-terminus of NTRK1, including the NTRK1 kinase domain. This mutation has been found in lung cancer  (Abstract: Rosen et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO.19.00009). While this fusion has not been functionally characterized, biological characterization of other NTRK1 fusions demonstrates that they are activating as measured by increased downstream pathway activation (PMID: 24162815, 26565381, 26216294), suggesting that this fusion is also likely activating. A patient with metastatic lung cancer to the brain harboring the EPS15-NTRK1 fusion had a complete intracranial response to larotrectinib (Abstract: Rosen et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO.19.00009).

The NTRK1 G667C mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized alone, it has been identified in patients as a resistance mutation to kinase inhibitors like entrectinib (PMID: 26546295, 29466156, 33004339). Structural modeling shows that the G667C mutation induces steric clashes with larotrectinib. While initial reports suggested that this mutation showed sensitivity to selitrectinib (PMID: 28578312), three patients with G667C mutations progressed on selitrectinib, and in vitro studies have demonstrated decreased sensitivity of this mutation to selitrectinib (PMID: 33004339).

The NTRK1 F589L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, three patients with this mutation either alone (one patient) or in combination with NTRK1 G595R mutation (two patients) had resistance to larotrectinib (PMID: 31406350, 29466156). Structural studies have demonstrated that this mutation is a gatekeeper mutation, and in vitro studies have demonstrated that it is resistant to larotrectinib but may be sensitive to Type II inhibitors (PMID: 33328556)(Abstract: Wei et al. Abstract# 2136, AACR 2016. https://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/76/14_Supplement/2136.short)

Delta-NTRK1 (Delta-TRKA) is an in-frame deletion within NTRK1 that results in the loss of 75 amino acids from its extracellular domain (PMID: 11073967). This mutant has been found in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 11073967). Expression of this mutant in 32D cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by cytokine-independent proliferation and kinase activation of downstream effector pathways compared to wildtype (PMID: 11073967).

The NTRK1 G595R mutation is located in the kinase domain of the NTRK1 protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancers, among others (PMID: 26546295, 29466156). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased ATP affinity and kinase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 28578312). The NTRK1 G595R mutation has also been identified in patients as a resistance mutation to kinase inhibitors like entrectinib and larotrectinib (PMID: 26546295, 29466156). Structural modeling shows that the G595R mutation induces steric clashes with larotrectinib. However, the TRK inhibitor LOXO-195 is able to accommodate bulky side chains without steric clashes, and shows inhibitory activity against the NTRK1 G595R mutation (PMID: 28578312).

The TFG-NTRK1 fusion joins the amino terminal portion of the TFG gene on chromosome 3 with the carboxy terminus of NTRK1, including the kinase domain. This fusion has been found in thyroid cancer and histiocytic neoplasms (PMID: 16256137, 29920189). Expression of this fusion in mouse fibroblast cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by constitutive activation and cell transformation (PMID: 7565764, 9488046).

The NTRK1 G667A mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, a patient with colorectal cancer harboring this mutation in cis with a G595R mutation progressed on selitrectinib (PMID: 33004339). In vitro studies have shown that this mutation is resistant to selitrectinib and repotrectinib (PMID: 33004339)

The NTRK2 R734C mutation lies in the kinase activation loop. However, it does not induce constitutive activation nor is there a correlation with transformation or migration of cells in culture (PMID: 21242122). This mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by lower autophosphorylation levels than wildtype NTRK2 when expressed in cells in vitro (PMID: 21242122).

The ETV6-NTRK2 fusion protein is found in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Expression of this protein in c-Kit+ mouse bone marrow cells and Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased colony formation and IL-3 independent proliferation compared to cells expressing empty vector (PMID: 29920189). A patient-derived xenograft from a patient with refractory secondary AML expressing this fusion protein was found to be senstive to the TRK inhibitor larotrectinib and the same patient was subsequently found to experience a partial remission on larotrectinib with ETV6-NTRK2 transcript levels having reduced expression (PMID: 29920189).

The NTRK2 R715G mutation lies in the kinase activation loop. However, it does not induce constitutive activation nor is there a correlation with transformation or migration of cells in culture (PMID: 21242122). This mutation is neutral as demonstrated by similar autophosphorylation levels as wildtype NTRK2 when expressed in cells in vitro, but without pronounced activation of the downstream proliferation pathway (PMID: 21242122).

Fusions of NTRK2 arise from chromosomal translocations that generally fuse the N-terminal portion of a partner protein with the C-terminal portion of NTRK2, which includes the NTRK2 kinase domain. Biological characterization of NTRK2 fusion proteins suggests that the fusion partner often facilitates ligand-independent dimerization, resulting in constitutive kinase activity (PMID: 27843590, 24647444, 24445538, 24162815). NTRK2 fusion proteins have demonstrated sensitivity to targeted pan-NTRK inhibitors, including larotrectinib and entrectinib (PMID: 26603524, 26884591, 26797418, 26457764).

The NTRK3 G623E mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized, a patient with pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma harboring ETV6-NTRK3 was treated with entrectinib and acquired NTRK3 G623E following disease progression (PMID: 36703785). Preclinical studies with ETV6-NTRK3-mutant Ba/F3 expressing NTRK3 G623E demonstrate resistance to taletrectinib, selitrectinib, ensartinib, entrectinib, larotrectinib, repotrectinib, altiratinib and cabozantinib as measured by increased IC50 values compared to wildtype (PMID: 34429303).

The NTRK2 M713I mutation lies in the kinase activation loop; however, it does not induce constitutive activation nor is there a correlation with transformation or migration of cells in culture (PMID: 21242122). This mutation is associated with lower autophosphorylation levels than wildtype NTRK2 when expressed in cells in vitro (PMID: 21242122).

The NTRK3 G696A mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While the NTRK3 G696A mutation has not been functionally characterized alone, it is homologous to the NTRK1 G667C mutation that has been identified in patients as a resistance mutation to kinase inhibitors like entrectinib and larotrectinib (PMID: 26546295). One patient with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor demonstrated acquired NTRK3 G696A and NTRK3 G623R mutations upon progression on larotrectinib (PMID: 29466156). Structural modeling shows that the G696A mutation induces steric clashes with larotrectinib, and in vitro experiments demonstrate that this mutation has reduced sensitivity to first-generation TRK inhibitors (PMID: 30333516, 26546295, 28578312). However, the TRK inhibitor LOXO-195 (Selitrectinib) is able to accommodate bulky side chains without steric clashes and shows inhibitory activity against the NTRK3 G696A mutation (PMID: 28578312).

The BTBD1-NTRK3 oncogenic fusion is a chimeric protein containing the oligomerization domain (BTB/POZ) and the Kelch protein-protein interaction domain of the Topoisomerase I-interacting protein BTBD1 and the tyrosine kinase domain of NTRK3 (PMID:24705251). Expression of BTBD1-NTRK3 in Tp53-null primary astrocytes induced the appearance of high grade astrocytomas when intracranially injected in mice, suggesting it is an activating mutation (PMID:24705251).

The UBE2R2-NTRK3 fusion protein is found in patients with multiple myelomas (PMID: 29920189). Expression of this protein in c-Kit+ mouse bone marrow cells and Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased colony formation and IL-3 independent proliferation compared to cells expressing empty vector (PMID: 29920189).

The NTRK3 G623R mutation is located in the ATP binding pocket of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally validated alone, expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells in a construct containing an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion led to resistance to entrectinib, as measured by cell proliferation in vitro (PMID: 26884591). A patient with mammary analogue secretory carcinoma harboring a ETV6-NTRK3 fusion responded to entrectinib until acquisition of a secondary NTRK3 G623R mutation and associated progression on entrectinib (PMID: 26884591). Two patients with this mutation progressed on larotrectinib, and in vitro studies demonstrate decreased sensitivity to larotrectinib (PMID: 29466156, 33328556). The G623R mutation does show sensitivity to the next-generation NTRK inhibitor LOXO-195 (Selitrectinib) in kinase and cell proliferation assays (PMID: 28578312).

The EML4-NTRK3 fusion protein combines the N-terminus of EML4 with the C-terminus of NTRK3, preserving the kinase domain of NTRK3. This fusion protien is found in patients with sporadic microsatellite instability-high colorectal cancers (PMID: 30279230, 30643016). Expression of this fusion protein in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it was activating as shown by increased colony formation and pathway activation compared to expression of NTRK3 alone (PMID: 30279230). Cells expressing this mutation were sensitive to the TRK tyrosine kinase inhibitor entrectinib (PMID: 30279230).

The HNRNPA2B1- NTRK3 Fusion protein is found in patients with multiple myelomas (PMID: 29920189). Expression of this protein in c-Kit+ mouse bone marrow cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased colony formation compared to cells expressing empty vector (PMID: 29920189). This mutation, however, did not result in IL-3 independent proliferation when expressed in Ba/F3 cells.

The NTRK3 I695V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 12738854). In vitro studies with RKO cells expressing NTRK3 I695V demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by colony growth inhibition comparable to wildtype (PMID: 23874207).

The ETV6-NTRK3 oncogenic fusion is the product of genome rearrangement between chromosomes 12 and 15 resulting in a chimeric protein containing the oligomerization domain of the transcription factor ETV6 and the tyrosine kinase domain of NTRK3. This fusion is commonly found in congenital fibrosarcoma (PMID: 9462753, 11801301, 10895816), secretory breast carcinoma (PMID: 12450792) and congenital mesoblastic nephroma (PMID: 9823307), and less commonly found in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 25207766, 21401966, 29920189), thyroid cancer (PMID: 24327398, 24135138) and gliomas (PMID: 23583981, 24705251). The ETV6-NTRK3 fusion has constitutively active kinase activity that has been shown to transform non-tumor cells in vitro and to be tumorigenic in mice (PMID: 10702799, 12450792). Expression of this fusion protein in hematopoietic cells results in cytokine-independent growth (PMID: 21804605), dependent on insulin signaling. Mammary breast cancer cells expressing this fusion undergo transformation, as evidenced by 3D matrigel assays (PMID: 21148487). Mice engineered to express this fusion protein in mammary tissues developed a fully penetrant, invasive breast cancer. Expression of ETV6-NTRK3 resulted in an upregulation of the c-Jun/Fosl1 AP1 complex, and transformation required c-Jun activity (PMID: 18068631). Expression of this mutation in a genetically engineered mouse model demonstrated that it is activating as shown by the development of an aggressive lymphoid leukemia with complete penetrance (PMID: 29880614). Treatment of bone marrow cells harvested from the mice or Ba/F3 cells expressing the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion were sensitive to the TRK-specific inhibitor, larotrectinib, and the TRK, CSF1R, AURK-specific inhibitor, PLX7486 as compared to cells expressing a spectrum of Philadelphia chromosome-like ALL alterations (PMID: 29880614). In a case report, a patient with metastatic lung atypical carcinoid harboring the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion was treated with repotrectinib and demonstrated a partial response lasting over ten months (PMID: 38113652). In a second case report, a patient with pancreatic carcinoma and congenital long QT syndrome harboring the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion was treated with larotrectinib and subsequently repotrectinib and demonstrated partial responses followed by disease progression (PMID: 38271657).

Fusions of NTRK3 arise from chromosomal translocations that generally fuse the N-terminal portion of a partner protein with the C-terminal portion of NTRK3, which includes the NTRK3 kinase domain. Biological characterization of NTRK3 fusion proteins demonstrates that they are oncogenic as shown by anchorage-independent colony formation and increased tumor growth in xenograft models (PMID: 27148571). NTRK3 fusion proteins have demonstrated sensitivity to targeted pan-NTRK inhibitors, including larotrectinib and entrectinib (PMID: 26603524, 26884591, 26797418, 26457764).

The KANK1-NTRK3 fusion protein combines the N-terminus of KANK1 with the C-terminus of NTRK3, preserving the kinase domain of NTRK3. This fusion protien is found in patients with sporadic microsatellite instability-high colorectal cancers (PMID: 30279230). Expression of this fusion protein in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it was activating as shown by increased colony formation and pathway activation compared to expression of NTRK3 alone (PMID: 30279230). Cells expressing this mutation were sensitive to the TRK tyrosine kinase inhibitor entrectinib (PMID: 30279230).

The NTRK3 G608S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colon cancer (PMID: 23874207). Expression of NTRK3 G608S in colon cancer cell lines resulted in caspase cleavage and colony formation similar to wildtype NTRK3, suggesting this mutation is likely neutral (PMID: 23874207).

The NTRK3 F617L mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it has been found as an acquired mutation in a patient with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor who progressed on larotrectinib (PMID: 30624546). This mutation is analogous to the L1196M gatekeeper mutation in ALK and is predicted to confer resistance to first-generation TRK inhibitors such as larotrectinib and entrectinib (PMID: 31738426).

The PALB2 K18R mutation lies on the N-terminal coiled-coil motif of the PALB2 protein responsible for BRCA1 binding. Ectopic expression of the K18R mutation in 293T cells did not affect endogenous BRCA1 interactions, and only modestly reduced homologous recombination efficiency when overexpressed in PALB2-depleted cells. In addition, expression of the K18R mutation in PALB2-deficient cells had no effect on ionizing radiation-induced foci formation compared to wild type PALB2 (PMID: 28319063).

The PALB2 N241D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 21932393). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, prediction algorithms such as SIFT, PolyPHEN and Align GVGD suggest that this mutation is likely neutral (PMID: 21932393).

The PALB2 L1143P mutation is in the WD40 domain of the PALB2 protein, which mediates protein-protein interactions between various homologous recombination (HR) proteins such as BRCA2 and RAD51 (PMID: 19737859, 17200672, 19584259). In vitro interaction assays of purified recombinant PALB2 L1143P showed a decrease in BRCA2, RAD51C and XRCC3 binding. In addition, overexpression of the L1143P mutation in PALB2-deficient cells demonstrated a modest decrease in double-stranded break-initiated HR, and a slight increase in sensitivity to ionizing radiation (PMID: 24141787).

PALB2 truncating mutations can form several forms of C-terminally truncated PALB2 protein and are found in breast cancers. As such, PALB2 is considered a rare breast cancer susceptibility gene. In patient studies, PALB2 truncation mutations were shown to significantly increase the risk of breast cancer, with similar risks for estrogen receptor-positive and -negative breast cancer. PALB2 truncation mutations have also been found in cases of hereditary male breast cancer (PMID: 28858227, 18053174, 25529982, 29484706, 28279176, 28779002).

The PALB2 T1030I mutation is in the WD40 domain of the PALB2 protein, which mediates protein-protein interactions between various homologous recombination (HR) proteins such as BRCA2 and RAD51 (PMID: 19737859, 17200672, 19584259). In vitro interaction assays of purified recombinant PALB2 T1030I showed a decrease in RAD51 and RAD51C binding. In addition, overexpression of the T1030I mutation in PALB2-deficient cells demonstrated a decrease in protein stability compared to wild type PALB2, as well as other PALB2 mutations (PMID: 24141787).

The PALB2 R37H mutation lies on the N-terminal coiled-coil motif of the PALB2 protein responsible for BRCA1 binding. Ectopic expression of the R37H mutation in 293T cells did not affect endogenous BRCA1 interactions, and only modestly reduced homologous recombination efficiency when overexpressed in PALB2-depleted cells. In addition, expression of the R37H mutation in PALB2-deficient cells had no effect on ionizing radiation-induced foci formation compared to wild type PALB2 (PMID: 28319063).

The PALB2 Y28C mutation lies on the N-terminal coiled-coil motif of the PALB2 protein responsible for BRCA1 binding. Ectopic expression of the Y28C mutation in 293T cells reduced endogenous BRCA1 interactions, and reduced homologous recombination (HR) efficiency when overexpressed in PALB2-depleted cells. In addition, expression of the Y28C mutation in PALB2-deficient cells resulted in decreased ionizing radiation-induced foci formation compared to wild type PALB2. Although the Y28C mutation showed impaired foci formation, it remained resistant to DNA-damaging agents, suggesting residual HR activity is sufficient to confer resistance (PMID: 28319063).

The PALB2 K30N mutation lies on the N-terminal coiled-coil motif of the PALB2 protein responsible for BRCA1 binding. Expression of the K30N mutation in PALB2-depleted cells did not affect homologous recombination efficiency (PMID: 28319063).

The PALB2 L35P mutation lies on the N-terminal coiled-coil motif of the PALB2 protein responsible for BRCA1 binding. Ectopic expression of the L35P mutation in 293T cells reduced endogenous BRCA1 interactions, and significantly reduced homologous recombination efficiency when overexpressed in PALB2-depleted cells. In addition, expression of the L35P mutation in PALB2-deficient cells resulted in decreased ionizing radiation-induced foci formation compared to wild type PALB2, as well as increased sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents (PMID: 28319063).

The PALB2 L939W mutation is located in the WD40 domain of the PALB2 protein, which mediates protein-protein interactions between various homologous recombination (HR) proteins such as BRCA2 and RAD51 (PMID: 19737859, 17200672, 19584259). There is conflicting functional data for this mutation. In vitro interaction assays of purified recombinant PALB2 L939W showed a decrease in BRCA2 and XRCC3 binding. In addition, overexpression of the L939W mutation in PALB2-depleted cells demonstrated a modest decrease in double-stranded break-initiated HR, and a slight increase in sensitivity to ionizing radiation (PMID: 24141787). Other in vitro studies have shown that the PALB2 L939W mutation has no HDR functional impact and no effect on BRCA1, BRCA2 and RAD51 complex formation (PMID: 31636395, 31586400). In a multicenter case-control study of PALB2 L939W mutation in breast cancer, the alteration was identified in 10/1741 (0.57%) patients with breast cancer and in 8/1534 (0.52%) control patients (PMID: 27595995).

Amplification of PDCD1LG2 has been detected across several tumor types including Hodgkin's lymphoma and mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 27069084, 29377256, 26850007, 26317899). In biochemical assays, cells overexpressing PDCD1LG2 demonstrate increased features of immune evasion from binding of the PD-1 cell surface receptor expressed on immune cells (PMID: 29167175). In addition, the tyrosine kinase JAK2 and PDCD1LG1 are included in the 9p24.1 amplification region of PDCD1LG2 (PMID: 20628145). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that cHL and MLBCL cell lines with PDCD1LG2 amplification are sensitive to JAK2 inhibition as measured by decreased tumor growth and prolonged survival (PMID: 24610827, 29467301). Patients with PDCD1LG2 amplification have been found to have an objective response to PD-1/PD-L1-targeted immune therapies (PMID: 29902298, 28356247).

The PDGFRB C843G mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was identified in a patient with Philadelphia-chromosome-like acute lymphoid leukemia who initially responded to imatinib, became resistant and was resistant to dasatinib and nilotinib (PMID: 29434033). Expression of this mutation in the AGGF1-PDGFRB fusion in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating (PMID: 29434033). Expression of this mutant fusion protein also conferred resistance to imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib and ponatinib compared to the wildtype fusion protein as shown by proliferation and downstream signaling (PMID: 29434033). This mutant fusion protein was sensitive to CHZ868, a broad-spectrum kinase inhibitor.

The ETV6-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of ETV6 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in chronic myeloproliferative malignancies (PMID: 22271894, 24687085). Expression of this mutation in CD34+ hematopoietic cells and in a genetically engineered mouse model demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein stability, pathway activation, and cytokine-independent colony formation compared to vector control and the development of myeloproliferative disease in mouse models (PMID: 22271894, 19100521, 19644140, 19100521). Eighteen patients with myeloid malignancies harboring this mutation demonstrated a 10-year survival rate of 90% when treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 24687085).

The GIT2-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of GIT2 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in chronic myeloproliferative disorders. While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, one patient with chronic myeloproliferative disorder harboring this mutation demonstrated a complete hematologic remission to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 17296564).

The ATF7IP-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of ALF7IP fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in B‐progenitor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 24628626, 29133777). Expression of this mutation in a murine B cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cytokine-independent growth and glucocorticoid resistance compared to vector control (PMID: 29133777, 26703895). One patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia harboring this mutation demonstrated a complete remission when treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor, dasatinib (PMID: 29133777).

The SPTBN1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of SPTBN1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative disease. While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, one patient with atypical myeloproliferative disorder harboring this mutation demonstrated a complete molecular remission to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 18262053).

The BIN2-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of BIN2 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms. While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, one patient with a myeloproliferative neoplasm harboring this mutation demonstrated a strong clinical response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 20085582).

The GPIAP1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of GPIAP1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in chronic myeloproliferative disorders (PMID: 17296564). While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, one patient with chronic myeloproliferative disorder harboring this mutation demonstrated a complete hematologic remission to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 17296564).

Amplification of PDGFRB has been observed in a range of tumor types and is associated with elevated expression of PDGFRB protein in choroid plexus carcinomas and sarcomatoid non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 21729646, 18157090). There is no direct evidence that increased PDGFRB levels are oncogenic. Data are conflicting as to whether or not PDGFRB protein expression correlates with the response of solid tumors to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) that inhibit PDGFRB (e.g. imatinib) (PMID: 16630177, 18515258, 18612157, 18670317).

The KANK1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of KANK1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms. Expression of this mutation in human and murine B cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and increased cell proliferation compared to vector control. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the kinase inhibitor imatinib in murine B cells as measured by decreased pathways activation and cell proliferation in the presence of the drug. (PMID: 21685469).

The PDGFRB E472D mutation is located in the immunoglobulin-like Domain 5 region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in undifferentiated intimal sarcoma (PMID: 29113426). Immunohistochemistry staining of patient-derived tumor tissue samples harboring PDGFRB E472D demonstrates that the mutation is activating as measured by increased phosphorylation compared to control samples (PMID: 29113426).

The PDGFRB N666H mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in a syndrome that has features similar to infantile myofibromatosis, Kosaki overgrowth syndrome, and Penttinen syndrome (PMID: 28726812). Endogenous expression of this mutation in patient-derived fibroblast cells demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by constitute protein activation and activation of downstream pathway effectors. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib in patient-derived fibroblast cells as measured by decreased pathway activation and cell proliferation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 28726812).

The WDR48-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of WDR48 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms (PMID: 20085582). While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, one patient with a myeloproliferative neoplasm harboring this mutation demonstrated complete cytogenetic remission to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 20085582).

The PDGFRB P596L mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in melanoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing PDGFRB P596L demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced phosphorylation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 34494111).

The HIP1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of HIP1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia. Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased PDGFRB phosphorylation and cytokine-independent cellular proliferation compared to vector control (PMID: 9616134).

The TP53BP1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of TP53BP1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative disorders. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the kinase inhibitor imatinib in patient-derived granulocytes and macrophages as measured by decreased colony formation in the presence of the drug. One patient with an eosinophilic myeloproliferative disorder harboring this mutation demonstrated a clinically significant response before relapse to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 15492236).

The PDGFRB P584R mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in a brain overgrowth phenotype (PMID: 25454926). Expression of this mutation in breast cancer cells, murine B cells and fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation, growth factor-independent growth, colony formation and in vivo tumor growth compared to wildtype and the PDGFRB R561C mutation (PMID: 26455322). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the tyrosine kinase inhibitors imatinib, nilotinib and ponatinib in murine B cells as measured by decreased pathway activation and cell proliferation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 26455322).

The PDGFRB V665A mutation occurs in the juxtamembrane domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in Penttinen syndrome (PMID: 26279204). Expression of this mutation in cervical cancer cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by reduced protein expression and activation and decreased pathway activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26279204).

The NIN-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of NIN fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative disorders (PMID: 15087377). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, one patient with chronic myeloid leukemia harboring this mutation demonstrated hematological and cytogenetic remission with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 15087377).

The PDGFRB L658P mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified as a recurrent germline mutation in patients with Primary Familial Brain Calcification (PFBC) (PMID: 23255827, 26599395). Cells engineered to express this mutation have reduced protein expression, altered cellular localization, altered downstream PLC-gamma signaling and complete loss of autophosphorylation activity (PMID: 26599395). This alteration is hypothesized to alter signaling and proliferation in mesenchymal cells (PMID: 23255827).

The PDGFRB P660T mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was identified as a heterozygous germline mutation in a family with members diagnosed with familial infantile myofibromatosis (IM) (PMID: 23731542). Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 and NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by kinase activation and transformation potential in cell culture-based assays comparable to wildtype PDGFRB (PMID: 26455322).

The PDGFRB N666K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in infantile myofibromatosis (PMID: 23731537). Expression of this mutation in murine B cells and fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein and pathway activation and increased in vivo tumor growth (PMID: 26455322). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the tyrosine kinase inhibitors imatinib, nilotinib, and ponatinib as measured by decreased pathway activation and cell proliferation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 26455322).

The AGGF1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of AGGF1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL). Expression of this mutation in murine B cells and bone marrow cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and cytokine-independent cell proliferation as compared to vector control. One patient with B-cell ALL harboring this mutation demonstrated a rapid response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib but later relapsed and was subsequently resistant to imatinib, dasatinib and nilotinib (PMID: 29434033).

The PDGFRB R561C mutation is located in the juxtamembrane domain of the protein. This mutation was identified as a recurrent heterozygous germline mutation found in several families with members diagnosed with familial infantile myofibromatosis (IM) (PMID: 23731542, 23731537). Expression of PDGFRB R561C mutation in Ba/F3 and NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that this variant results in constitutive activation of PDGFRB protein and its downstream effectors, confers growth factor independence and demonstrates transformation potential (PMID: 26455322). In addition, Ba/F3 cells expressing PDGFRB R561C were tumorigenic in vivo when introduced into immunodeficient BALB/c rag2-/- mice (PMID: 26455322). The PDGFRB R561C variant renders cells sensitive to inhibition by treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors imatinib, nilotinib and ponatinib (PMID: 26455322).

The GOLGA4-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of GOLGA4 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the kinase inhibitor imatinib in patient-derived granulocytes and macrophages as measured by decreased colony formation in the presence of the drug. Two patients with myeloproliferative neoplasms harboring this mutation demonstrated either sustained cytogenetic and molecular remission or complete hematological response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 20085582).

The KIAA1509-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of KIAA1509 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms (PMID: 15496975). While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, one patient with a myeloproliferative neoplasm harboring this mutation demonstrated a sustained complete remission to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 15496975).

The RABEP1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of RABEP1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (PMID: 24951465). Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cytokine-independent proliferation compared to vector control and the development of hematopoietic malignancies in in vivo mouse models (PMID: 11588050).

The CEP85L-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of CEP85L fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative neoplasms. While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, one patient with a myeloproliferative neoplasm with eosinophilia harboring this mutation demonstrated a hematologic, cytogenetic and long-term molecular remission with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 15496975).

The PDGFRB E1071W mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Cells engineered to express this mutation have reduced protein expression and altered downstream signaling, namely reduced PLC-gamma signaling (PMID: 26599395). This alteration is hypothesized to alter signaling and proliferation in mesenchymal cells (PMID: 23255827, 26599395).

The EBF1-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of EBF1 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 26872634, 24186319). Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cytokine-independent cellular proliferation compared to vector control (PMID: 22897847). Two case reports of patients with refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia harboring this mutation demonstrated a complete response after treatment with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib combined with chemotherapy (PMID: 23835704, 24186319).

The PRKG2-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of PRKG2 fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative disease (PMID: 18262053, 17296564). While this fusion protein has not yet been functionally tested, two patients with atypical myeloproliferative disorder and chronic myeloproliferative disorder harboring this mutation demonstrated complete molecular and hematologic remissions to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 18262053, 17296564).

The PDE4DIP-PDGFRB fusion involves the N-terminus of PDE4DIP fused to the C-terminus of PDGFRB, containing the PDGFRB transmembrane domain and kinase domain. This mutation has been found in myeloproliferative disorders. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the kinase inhibitor imatinib in patient bone marrow cells as measured by decreased pathway activation in the presence of the drug. One patient with a myeloproliferative disorder with eosinophilia harboring this mutation demonstrated complete clinical and hematologic remission to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib (PMID: 12907457).

The PDGFRB R987W mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified as a recurrent germline mutation in patients with Primary Familial Brain Calcification (PFBC) (PMID: 23255827, 26599395). Cells engineered to express this mutation have reduced protein expression, altered cellular localization and altered downstream PLC-gamma signaling (PMID: 26599395). This alteration is hypothesized to alter signaling and proliferation in mesenchymal cells (PMID: 23255827).

The PHF6 R274Q mutation is located in the PHD2 domain of the protein. This mutation was identified in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 27479181). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, another amino acid substitution at this position (R274E) has been shown to be likely loss-of-function and likely oncogenic (PMID: 24554700).

PHF6 truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations are found in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia and are predominantly found in male patients (PMID: 12676923). In a study of myeloid neoplasms, 39 out of 62 patients (63%) with PHF6 mutations had mutations that led to a truncated protein (nonsense, frameshift or splice site) (PMID: 27479181). Loss of PHF6 in mouse models results in impaired migration of neurons in the cortex (PMID: 23791194).

The PIM1 H68Y mutation lies in the N terminus of the protein, in what is likely a β sheet that interacts with the catalytic domain. In vitro assays of kinase activity showed that this variant increased PIM1 activity above the level of the wildtype. This effect is hypothesized to be due to H68Y promoting the kinase active state of the protein (PMID: 15808862).

The PIM1 E142D mutation is located in the protein kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 32187361). In silico analysis suggests that this mutation is inactivating as measured by assessing the spectroscopic and thermodynamic properties of soluble recombinant PIM1 mutant proteins, suggesting decreased stability of the mutant protein (PMID: 23755147).

The PIM1 L2V mutation occurs in the N terminus of the protein, prior to a kinase domain. In a lymphoma cell line, expression of L2V did not alter cell proliferation or viability compared to the wildtype. In a colony formation assay, however, the mutated protein altered morphology and increased the number of colonies. Additionally, the L2V mutation increased protein stability and decreased sensitivity to inhibitor compound ibrutinib. Expression of the mutant also modulated expression of modulators and effectors in the NFκB pathway (PMID: 27904766).

The PIM1 E124Q mutation is located in the protein kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 34478526). In silico analysis suggests that this mutation is inactivating as measured by assessing the spectroscopic and thermodynamic properties of soluble recombinant PIM1 mutant proteins, suggesting decreased stability of the mutant protein (PMID: 23755147).

The PIM1 P123M residue lies in a hinge domain of the PIM1 protein. The mutation of proline to a methionine did not alter the configuration of crystal structures of PIM1 and in in vitro assays displayed kinase activity similar to the wildtype protein (PMID: 15808862).

The PIM1 N82K mutation is located in a hairpin connecting a β sheet with an α sheet containing the protein's catalytic domain. In in vitro assays, this mutation significantly reduced the enzymatic activity of PIM1, likely due to the importance of the asparagine residue in intramolecular bonds (PMID: 15808862).

The PIM1 Y53H mutation is located in the protein kinase domain of the protein. In silico analysis suggest that this mutation is inactivating as measured by assessing the spectroscopic and thermodynamic properties of soluble recombinant PIM1 mutant proteins, suggesting decreased stability of the mutant protein (PMID: 23755147).

The PIM1 P81S mutation is located in a hairpin connecting a β sheet with an α sheet containing the protein's catalytic domain. In in vitro assays, this mutation significantly reduced the enzymatic activity of PIM1, likely due to the importance of the proline in the tertiary structure (PMID: 15808862).

The PIM1 L193F mutation is located in the activation loop of the PIM1 protein. In in vitro assays, this mutation significantly reduced the enzymatic activity of PIM1, likely due to differences in the packing of the bulkier phenylalanine residue (PMID: 15808862).

The PIM1 S97N mutation occurs in the N-terminal kinase domain of the protein. In a lymphoma cell line, expression of L2V did not alter cell proliferation or viability compared to the wildtype. In a colony formation assay, however, the mutated protein altered morphology and increased the number of colonies. Additionally, the L2V mutation increased protein stability and decreased sensitivity to inhibitor compound ibrutinib. Expression of the mutant also modulated expression of modulators and effectors in the NFκB pathway (PMID: 27904766).

The PIM1 L182F mutation is located in the protein kinase domain of the PIM1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by reduced PIM1 activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27556513).

The PIM1 E135K mutation is located in the protein kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was identified in patients with diffuse large cell lymphoma and acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 19734423). In silico analysis suggests that this mutation is inactivating as measured by assessing the spectroscopic and thermodynamic properties of soluble recombinant PIM1 mutant proteins, suggesting decreased stability of the mutant protein (PMID: 23755147). In vitro biochemical assays demonstrated PIM1 E135K was likely neutral with no significant difference in PIM1 kinase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 15808862).

The PHF6 K235E mutation is located in the PHD2 domain of the protein. This mutation was identified in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 27479181). In an in vitro DNA binding assay, the DNA binding ability of PHF6 K235E was abolished in comparison to wildtype PHF6 (PMID: 24554700) suggesting the mutation is loss-of-function.

The PRKAR1A R335L mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain B of the PRKAR1A protein. This mutation has been found in acrodysostosis (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036).

The PRKAR1A A213D mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain A of the PRKAR1A protein. This mutation has been found in Carney complex (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036). In silico analysis suggests that this mutation impacts cAMP binding (PMID: 26405036).

Fusions of PDGFRB arise from chromosomal translocations that generally fuse the N-terminal portion of a partner protein with the C-terminal portion of PDGFRB, which includes the PDGFRB kinase domain. These fusion proteins are typically found in myeloproliferative neoplasms (PMID: 24687085). Fusions of PDGFRB result in constitutive PDGFRB kinase activity as demonstrated by increased pathway activation and factor-independent growth when expressed in hematopoietic cells (PMID: 18483217, 20581310, 22897847, 22271894). Myeloproliferative diseases harboring PDGFRB fusions have been shown to be sensitive to treatment with imatinib (PMID: 24687085).

The PRKAR1A Y175C mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain A of the protein. This mutation has been found in acrodysostosis (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036).

The PRKAR1A G289W mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain B of the PRKAR1A protein. This mutation has been found in Carney complex (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036). In silico analysis suggests that this mutation impacts cAMP binding (PMID: 26405036).

The PRKAR1A A213T mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain A of the PRKAR1A protein. This mutation has been found in acrodysostosis (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036).

PRKAR1A deletion results in loss of protein function. PRKAR1A deletion has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma and adrenocortical tumors (PMID: 27995993, 14500362). In vivo studies have demonstrated that knockdown of PRKAR1A increased lung lesions in mice compared to wildtype (PMID: 27995993). In vitro studies have demonstrated that knockdown of PRKAR1A in A549 cells results in increased growth, increased migration of cells, decreased E-cadherin expression, and increased Snail1 expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 27995993).

The PRKAR1A Q285R mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain B of the PRKAR1A protein. This mutation has been found in acrodysostosis (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036).

The PHF6 R274E mutation is located in the PHD2 domain of the protein. This mutation was identified in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 27479181). In an in vitro DNA binding assay, the DNA binding ability of PHF6 R274E was abolished in comparison to wildtype PHF6 (PMID: 24554700) suggesting the mutation is loss-of-function.

The PRKAR1A A328V mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain B of the PRKAR1A protein. This mutation has been found in acrodysostosis (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036).

The PRKAR1A G289E mutation is located in the cAMP-binding domain B of the PRKAR1A protein. This mutation has been found in acrodysostosis (PMID: 26405036). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by impaired dissociation of PRKAR1A from the catalytic PKA subunits upon cAMP binding and reduced PKA activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26405036).

Truncating mutations of RAD21 have been identified in patients with myeloid malignancies and is associated with significantly reduced RAD21 expression (PMID: 25006131). Assessment of the clonal evolution of RAD21 truncating mutations demonstrated that they most commonly occur as a late event in leukemia development. Since RAD21 is a subunit in the cohesion complex, loss of RAD21 is associated with reduction in the expression of other cohesion proteins including SMC1A and leads to defective chromosomal separation and cell bridging (PMID: 28116354).

Deletion mutations of RAD21 have been identified in patients with myeloid malignancies and cause significantly reduced RAD21 expression (PMID: 25006131). Assessment of the clonal evolution of these mutations demonstrated that they most commonly occur as a late event in leukemia development. Since RAD21 is a subunit in the cohesion complex, loss of RAD21 causes reductions in the expression of other cohesion proteins including SMC1A and leads to defective chromosomal separation and cell bridging (PMID: 28116354).

The RAF1 S259F mutation of RAF1 lies in the conserved region (CR2) of the protein. Expression of RAF1 S259F leads to reduced 14-3-3 binding and loss of phosphorylation, likely facilitating binding to RAS-GTP (PMID: 20679480). In contrast to the somatic mutation, germline expression of the RAF1 S257L mutation does not generally cause cancer, but instead leads to one of the closely related developmental disorders Noonan or LEOPARD syndrome (PMID: 17603483).

The RAF1 D486N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Noonan syndrome, a RASopathy with germline activation of the MAPK pathway (PMID: 22826437). While the D486N mutation is kinase-inactivating, cells harboring this mutation have increased phospho-MEK and phospho-ERK compared to control cells through increased heterodimerization with and activation of BRAF (PMID: 22826437).

The RAF1 S257W mutation occurs in a highly conserved region of the protein. This mutation is suggested to impair the binding of protein 14-3-3 to conserved region 2 of CRAF, leading to more potent activation of CRAF in response to RAS signaling (PMID: 7867061, 12077328). In contrast to the somatic mutation, germline expression of the RAF1 S257W mutation does not generally cause cancer, but instead leads to one of the closely related developmental disorders Noonan or LEOPARD syndrome (PMID: 17603483).

The RAF1 D447N mutation is located in the CR3 domain, outside the activation loop of the protein. Expression of this mutation in A375 melanoma cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by RAF1 kinase activity, downstream pathway activation and dimerization comparable to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487). In an in vitro mutagenesis screen, this mutation conferred mild resistance to RAF inhibitors through a mechanism involving heterodimerization with B-RAF (PMID: 23737487).

The RAF1 S259A mutation of RAF1 lies in the conserved region (CR2) of the protein (PMID: 20679480). Expression of RAF1 S259A in NIH-3T3 cells leads to increased phosphorylation of downstream effectors and colony growth in soft agar compared to wildtype RAF (PMID: 24569458).

The RAF1 S427G missense mutation leads to a substitution of serine (S) by glycine (G) at position 427, which is located in the highly conserved kinase region of the CRAF protein. Expression of RAF1 S427G in mouse fibroblasts increases levels of phosphorylated MEK and ERK. Also, the S427G mutation induces moderate levels of soft agar colony formation and protects the fibroblasts from staurosporine-induced cell death. Taken together, this data suggests an activating and oncogenic role of RAF1 S427G (PMID: 16585161). RAF1 S427G has only been found as a germline mutation; a secondary genetic event, such as loss of the tumor suppressor gene RAF kinase inhibitor protein (RKIP), has been suggested to be necessary for oncogenic transformation (PMID: 19357705).

The RAF1 K106N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in histiocytic neoplasms (PMID: 30867592). Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased downstream ERK signaling, cytokine-independent growth, and MEK1/2-inhibitor sensitivity in vitro compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 30867592). A patient with histiocytic disease harboring the RAF1 K106N mutation had a complete response to treatment with the MEK1/2 inhibitor cobimetinib (PMID: 30867592).

The RAF1 R554K mutation is located in the CR3 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in 293T and A375 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by downstream RAF signaling comparable to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487). In vitro studies have suggested that this mutation may confer resistance to vemurafenib and dabrafenib as measured by moderately increased RAF1 activation in the presence of the drug compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487).

RAF1 amplification is a rare event in cancer, occurs at a low frequency in bladder tumors and is assumed to be an oncogenic event (Abstract: Zehir A et al. Nature Medicine 2017. http://doi:10.1038/nm.4333). RAF1 amplification significantly correlates with advanced stage, tumor progression and shorter survival in urinary bladder cancers, although a direct effect on RAF1 protein overexpression was not demonstrated (PMID: 11389083). Another study showed a trend toward the association between RAF1 protein overexpression and high grade bladder tumors (PMID: 16517112). Preclinical studies in breast cancer cells showed that EZH2-mediated amplification of the RAF1 gene causes increased signaling in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway and increased levels of unphosphorylated (active) beta-catenin, which stimulate cell proliferation, self renewal and survival (PMID: 21215703).

The RAF1 P261T mutation is located in the CR2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in A375 melanoma cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased RAF1 kinase activity, downstream pathway activation and dimerization compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487). In vitro, this mutation conferred resistance to RAF inhibitors through a mechanism involving heterodimerization with B-RAF (PMID: 23737487).

The GOLGA4-RAF1 fusion protein combines the N-terminus of GOLGA4 with the C-terminus of RAF1 (exons 8-17), preserving the RAF1 kinase domain and lacking the regulatory RBD and C1 domains. This fusion protein has been found in melanoma (PMID: 30835257). A patient with metastatic melanoma who progressed on combination ipilimumab and nivolumab had a partial response to serial treatment with the MEK inhibitors trametinib and cobimetinib (PMID: 30835257). While this fusion has not been functionally characterized, immunohistochemistry analysis of tumor biopsies suggests this fusion is activating as measured by activated MAPK signaling in the tumor (PMID: 30835257).

The RAF1 P261L mutation is located in the CR2 regulatory region of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with Noonan or LEOPARD syndromes. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is likely activating, as shown by increased protein activation compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 20679480).

Fusions of RAF1 arise from chromosomal translocations between RAF1 and other partner genes. These alterations cause increased RAF1 activity and activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (PMID: 20526349, 27810072, 19363522). Knockdown of the gene fusion reduces proliferation and invasion of pancreatic carcinoma cells, supporting the notion that RAF1 fusion genes may be driving oncogenesis (PMID: 23637631). There have been several case reports of patients with RAF1 fusion-positive cancers who have responded to treatment with MEK1/2 inhibitors (Abstract: Kim et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.17.00138)(Abstract: Touat et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00298)(PMID: 30835257). However, these responses may be context dependent, as a patient with GATM-RAF1 fusion-positive pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma progressed on treatment with trametinib (Abstract: McEvoy et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.19.00159).

The RAF1 T491I mutation is located in the activation segment of the RAF1 protein. This mutation has been observed in a patient with Noonan syndrome (PMID: 30732632, 17603483). Expression of this mutant in COS-1 cells demonstrates that it is kinase-impaired (results in impaired MEK activation) but still leads to increased ERK activation (PMID: 17603483).

The RAF1 L613V mutation is located C-terminal to the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been observed in patients with Noonan syndrome, a RASopathy with germline activation of the MAPK pathway (PMID: 21339642). Mouse models harboring this mutation are associated with elevated phospho-MEK and phospho-ERK activity as well as increased heterodimerization with BRAF, and this is linked to features of primary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (PMID: 22826437, 21339642, 28548091). Multiple in vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to MEK inhibition (PMID: 22826437, 21339642, 28548091).

The RAF1 S257L mutation occurs in a highly conserved region of the protein. Ectopic expression of RAF1 S257L in human lung epithelial cells or mouse fibroblasts increased downstream MAPK pathway signaling and stimulated soft agar colony formation, underlining its potential role as a driving oncogenic mutation (PMID: 24569458). This is suggested to impair the binding of protein 14-3-3 to conserved region 2 of CRAF, leading to more potent activation of CRAF in response to RAS signaling (PMID: 7867061, 12077328). In contrast to the somatic mutation, germline expression of the RAF1 S257L mutation does not generally cause cancer, but instead leads to one of the closely related developmental disorders Noonan or LEOPARD syndrome (PMID: 17603483).

The RAF1 G356E mutation is located in the CR3 domain, inside the ATP-binding P-loop of the protein. Expression of this mutation in A375 melanoma cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by RAF1 kinase activity, downstream pathway activation and dimerization comparable to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487). In an in vitro mutagenesis screen, this mutation conferred mild resistance to RAF inhibitors through a mechanism involving heterodimerization with B-RAF (PMID: 23737487).

The RAF1 R391W mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 27273450). Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased kinase activity, cell proliferation and growth in soft agar compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 27273450).

The RAF1 I448V missense mutation leads to a substitution of isoleucine (I) by valine (V) at position 448, which is located in the highly conserved kinase region of the CRAF protein. Although a high level of phosphorylated ERK has been found in RAF1 I448V-mutated leukemia cells, transgenic expression of the mutation does not increase MEK and ERK phosphorylation. However, expression of RAF1 I448V protected cells from staurosporine-induced cell death, suggesting that the mutation contributes to oncogenesis (PMID: 19357705). The RAF1 I448V mutation has only been detected as a germline mutation, and it has been suggested that different secondary genetic events are necessary for the induction of malignancy (PMID: 19357705).

ESRP1-RAF1 fuses exon 13 of ESRP1 to exon 6 of RAF1, resulting in a protein product comprised of the majority of ESRP1, including its three RNA recognition motifs, and the C-terminal kinase domain of RAF1. Expression of the ESRP1-RAF1 fusion gene in RWP1 prostate cancer cells resulted in increased phosphorylation of MEK and ERK, both of which are downstream components of the RAF1 signaling pathway. Additionally, expression of this fusion resulted in increased proliferation of the RWP1 cells. The ESRP1-RAF1-mediated proliferative gain was sensitive to the tyrosine protein kinase inhibitor, sorafenib, and the MEK inhibitor, U0126 (PMID: 20526349).

The RAF1 S257P mutation is located in the CR2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in A375 melanoma cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased RAF1 kinase activity, downstream pathway activation and dimerization compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487). In vitro, this mutation conferred resistance to RAF inhibitors through a mechanism involving heterodimerization with B-RAF (PMID: 23737487).

The RAF1 G361A mutation is located in the CR3 domain, inside the ATP-binding P-loop of the protein. Expression of this mutation in A375 melanoma cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased RAF1 kinase activity, downstream pathway activation and dimerization compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487). In vitro, this mutation conferred resistance to RAF and MEK inhibitors through a mechanism independent of heterodimerization with BRAF (PMID: 23737487).

The QKI-RAF1 fusion results from a translocation joining the homodimerization domain and RNA-binding domain of QKI to the kinase domain of RAF1, replacing the auto-inhibitory domain of the kinase (PMID: 28806393). This fusion has been found in rare pediatric low-grade (pLGGs) gliomas and spindle cell sarcoma (PMID: 28912153, 23583981, 30517658, 33948563, 35050712). In vitro studies have demonstrated that the QKI-RAF1 fusion protein leads to constitutive activation of CRAF kinase as measured by cell viability assay and kinase activity (PMID: 28806393). A novel RAF dimer inhibitor, LY3009120, can affect dimerization of the fusion and shows inhibitory activity against QKI-RAF1 homodimerization and downstream signaling (PMID: 28806393). In vivo studies have demonstrated that QKI-RAF1 fusion signaling is sensitive to the downstream MEK1/2 inhibitor trametinib and combined MAPK and PI3K/mTOR pathway inhibition using trametinib and everolimus (PMID: 28806393). A patient with spindle cell sarcoma harboring the QKI-RAF1 fusion had a sustained response to the MEK1/2 inhibitor trametinib (PMID: 35050712).

The RAF1 S259P mutation of RAF1 lies in the conserved region (CR2) of the protein and has been detected in patients with colon cancer. This mutation is likely to lead to reduced 14-3-3 binding and loss of phosphorylation and facilitates binding to RAS-GTP (PMID: 20679480). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RAF1 S259P demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased phosphorylation of ERK1/2 compared to wildtype and positive control RAF1 S257 (PMID: 38127827). In a case report, a patient with advanced myxofibrosarcoma harboring RAF1 S259P was treated with combination trametinib and palbociclib and demonstrated a complete response (PMID: 38127827).

The SRGAP3-RAF1 fusion gene retains complete in-frame coding of the RAF1 kinase domain along with the SRGAP3 Fes/CIP4 homology domain, which may play a role in subcellular localization. Expression of the SRGAP3-RAF1 fusion in NIH3T3 cells resulted in elevated levels of phopshoryated MEK, a downstream target of the RAF1 signaling pathway. In addition, cells expressing this fusion demonstrated a transformed phenotype as evidenced by their anchorage-independent growth, suggesting this fusion gene is oncogenic (PMID: 19363522).

The RAF1 S427T mutation is located in the CR3 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in A375 melanoma cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by RAF1 kinase activity, downstream pathway activation and dimerization comparable to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487).

The ATG7-RAF1 fusion gene retains the RAF1 serine/threonine kinase domain but removes an N-terminal autoinhibitory Ras Binding Domain (RBD). Knockdown of the ATG7-RAF1 fusion in PL5 pancreatic cancer cells, which endogenously express this fusion, significantly decreased cell proliferation and invasiveness, suggesting the ATG7-RAF1 fusion is oncogenic (PMID: 23637631). This mutation was found in a patient with pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (Abstract: Touat et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00298). The patient did not respond to sorafenib but responded to the MEK inhibtor cobimetinib with regression of symptoms and a complete cytologic response (Abstract: Touat et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00298).

The RAF1 E478K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colorectal cancer (PMID: 16266992).
