Expression of this mutation in COS cells and in vitro assays demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased kinase activity through constitutive heterodimerization compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 16266992, 20130576).

The RAF1 S259C mutation is located in the conserved region (CR2) of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26286987). In vitro studies with Ba/F3 and MCF10A cells expressing RAF1 S259C demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by cell viability and proliferation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 29533785).

The RAF1 M469I mutation is located in the CR3 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in 293T and A375 cells demonstrated that it is modestly activating as measured by slightly increased downstream RAF signaling compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 23737487). In vitro studies have suggested that this mutation may confer resistance to vemurafenib and dabrafenib as measured by increased downstream MAPK pathway signaling and upregulated RAF1 activation in the presence of the drug  (PMID: 23737487).

The RAF1 P261S mutation is located in the CR2 regulatory region of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with Noonan or LEOPARD syndromes. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is likely activating, as shown by increased protein activation compared to wildtype RAF1 (PMID: 17603483, 20679480).

The PML-RARA fusion protein combines the N-terminus of PML with the C-terminus of RARA and retains domains within the RARA protein that allow dimerization and DNA binding. This fusion protein is found in patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia (PMID: 1652369, 1652369). Expression of the PML-RARA fusion protein in human hematopoietic stem cells demonstrated that it was oncogenic as shown by failure of the cells to fully differentiate and ability of the cells to survive independent of growth factors compared to wildtype hematopoietic stem cells (PMID: 10942402). In vitro and clinical studies show that the PML-RARA fusion protein is sensitive to treatment with trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide (PMID: 15160934).

The BCOR-RARA fusion protein is a result of a t(X;17)(p11;q12) translocation between the BCOR gene and RARA gene. This fusion protein is found in acute promyelocytic leukemia (PMID: 20807888). The BCOR-RARA fusion protein is activating as it shares common features with other characterized RARA fusion proteins such as a dominant negative manner on RARA transcriptional activation and leads to aberrant subcellular relocalization (PMID: 20807888).

RARA R276W mutation has been identified in patients with single acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). Patients harboring this mutation typically display other genetic alterations at the RARA locus (either translocations or truncating events) and show acquired resistance to all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) treatment. COS7 cells expressing R276W-mutant chimeric PML-RARA protein demonstrated a decreased binding efficiency for retinoic acid compared to cells expressing the wildtype protein (PMID: 27148563, 19865110, 11438209, 23670176).

The GTF2I-RARA fusion protein is composed of the N-terminal of GTF2I and the RARA protein, excluding exons 1 and 2. The GTF2I-fusion protein was identified in a patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia and has been shown to self associate and be a dominant negative regulator in RARA/RXR pathways. In luciferase assays, the GTF2I-RARA fusion negatively regulates the retinoic acid response unit, similar to other RARA fusion proteins that are resistant to ATRA therapy (PMID: 25284716). Additionally cell lines expressing the fusion protein were found to overexpress RING finger protein 8 (RNF8). Complexed with RARA, RNF8 blocks promyelocytic cell differentiation (PMID: 30992691).

RARA fusion proteins retain domains of the RARA protein that allow dimerization and allow binding to DNA. These fusion proteins are found in patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (PMID: 1652369, 1652369). RARA fusion proteins are thought to have a dominant-negative effect on wildtype RARA transcriptional activity and may function to regulate a novel set of transcriptional targets that are not regulated by wildtype RARA. Patients with APL expression RARA fusion proteins are treated with trans retinoic acid (ATRA) or arsenic trioxide but a high rate of patients relapse due to resistance (PMID: 24720386).

The ROS1 L1947R mutation occurs in the protein's kinase domain and is often identified in the context of a ROS1 fusion protein. FIG-ROS1 Ba/F3 cells expressing the L1947R mutation demonstrated increased resistance to crizotinib compared to control FIG-ROS1 Ba/F3 cells, as measured by sustained cell growth and protein activation upon drug treatment (PMID: 24218589).

KDELR2-ROS1, a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of the 5' end of KDELR2 with the 3' end of with ROS1 (PMID: 22980976). The oncogenic potential of this fusion has not been functionally tested.

The ROS1 F2004C mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung cancer (Abstract: Doebele et al. Abstract# LBA-28, ESMO 2019. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923753419603777). Expression of this mutation in the context of a ROS1 fusion in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated decreased sensitivity to ROS1 inhibition (PMID: 26372962). Structural studies based on homology to ALK predict that ROS1 F2004C would confer resistance to ceritinib (PMID: 27401242). At least one patient with ROS1-fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer acquired the ROS1 F2004C mutation upon disease progression on treatment with entrectinib (Abstract: Doebele et al. Abstract# LBA-28, ESMO 2019. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923753419603777).

LRIG3-ROS1, a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of exon 16 of EZR with exon 35 of ROS1, results in a constitutively active protein containing the ROS1 kinase domain. This fusion demonstrated transforming capabilities when tested in foci forming assays in vitro, and also demonstrated the ability to form subcutaneous tumors in nude mice (PMID: 22327623).

SLC34A2-ROS1 is a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of SLC34A2 (exon 4) and ROS1 (exon 32 and 34), creating a short and long transcript, respectively. This in-frame mutation generates a protein with constitutively active kinase activity (PMID: 22215748, 22919003). This fusion demonstrated transforming capabilities when tested in foci forming assays in vitro, and also demonstrated the ability to form subcutaneous tumors in nude mice (PMID: 22327623).

The ROS1 V2098I mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein at a site implicated in inhibitor binding. In a murine B-cell line a V2098I -mutated FIG-ROS1 construct conferred increased resistance to crizotinib, as compared to the unmutated construct in cell-growth assays. The mutated construct showed slightly reduced sensitivity to the inhibitor foretinib (PMID: 24218589).
YWHAE-ROS1 is a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of YWHAE (exon 4) to ROS1 (exon 36) (PMID: 24875859). The oncogenic potential of this fusion has not been functionally tested.

The ROS1 S1986Y mutation lies in tyrosine kinase domain the of the ROS1 protein. It has been detected in a patient with ROS1-fusion positive lung cancer in concert with mutation S1986F. The two alterations at the same residue were associated with resistance to crizotinib but subsequent sensitivity to lorlatinib. In a murine B-cell line expression of individual S1986F- and S1986Y-mutated ROS1-fusion constructs were resistant to crizotinib and ceritinib but not lorlatinib, as assessed by cell viability and pathway activation assays (PMID: 27401242).
TFG-ROS1 is a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of TFG (exon 4) to ROS1 (exon 36) (PMID: 24875859). The oncogenic potential of this fusion has not been functionally tested.

CD74-ROS1 is a rearrangement mutation characterized by the fusion of CD74 (exon 6) and ROS1 (exon 34). This fusion generates a protein with constitutive kinase activity (PMID: 22215748, 22919003, 22327623, 18083107). CD74-ROS1 demonstrated transforming capabilities when tested in foci forming assays in vitro, and also demonstrated the ability to form subcutaneous tumors in nude mice (PMID: 22327623). A patient with non-small cell lung cancer harboring a CD74-ROS1 fusion responded to treatment with brigatinib and ceritinib after progressing on crizotinib (Abstract: Hegde et al. JCO PO, 2018. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00267).

MSN-ROS1 is a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of MSN (exon 9) to ROS1 (exon 34). This novel fusion has been identified in a tumor sample from a patient with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with crizotinib (PMID: 25264305).

LIMA1-ROS1 is a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of LIMA1 (exon 10) to ROS1 (exon 36). This novel fusion has been identified in a tumor sample from a patient with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with crizotinib (PMID: 25264305).

Fusions of ROS1 arise from chromosomal translocations that fuse the N-terminal portion of a partner protein with the C-terminal kinase-domain-containing portion of ROS1. These fusion proteins are found in a variety of cancer types and result in constitutive activation of ROS1 kinase activity. Biological characterization of specific ROS1 fusion proteins demonstrates that they are activating as shown by enhanced proliferation and colony formation and that they are sensitive to treatment with the tyrosine kinase inhibitors crizotinib and entrectinib (PMID: 23719267, 22919003, 22215748, 28465216). Preliminary clinical data suggests that lorlatinib may also be efficacious in patients with ROS1 fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer, including those with central nervous system disease (PMID: 31669155).

The ROS1 G2101A mutation lies in the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein. In a murine B-cell line a G2101A-mutated CD74-ROS1 construct conferred increased resistance to crizotinib, as compared to the unmutated construct in cell-growth assays. The mutated construct showed slightly reduced sensitivity to the inhibitor foretinib. The variants is analogous to the previously described ALK G1269A resistance mutation (PMID: 25688157, 24675041, 22235099).

The ROS1 C2060G mutation lies in the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein. In a murine B-cell line a C2060G-mutated FIG-ROS1 construct conferred increased resistance to crizotinib, as compared to the unmutated construct in cell-growth assays. The mutated construct showed slightly reduced sensitivity to the inhibitor foretinib (PMID: 24218589).

The ROS1 G2032R mutation is located in the protein's kinase domain and is associated with acquired resistance to crizotinib in ROS1-rearranged non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 25688157, 24047073, 23724914). In vitro studies with A549 cells expressing ROS1 G2032R demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased cellular invasion and migration, increased expression of MMP-9 and TWIST1 and induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition compared to wildtype (PMID: 29477381). Preclinical studies and structural analysis of ROS1 G2023R demonstrate that the mutation confers resistance by interfering with crizotinib binding (PMID: 25351743, 23724914, 25033171). This mutation corresponds to the G1202R ALK kinase domain mutant (PMID: 23724914, 27401242). Preclinical studies of ROS1 G2023R demonstrate sensitivity to combination treatment of TWIST1 siRNA and crizotinib as measured by reduced cellular viability and invasion (PMID: 29477381).

EZR-ROS1 is a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of exon 10 of EZR with exon 34 of ROS1, results in a constitutively active protein containing the ROS1 kinase domain (PMID: 22327623). This fusion demonstrated transforming capabilities when tested in foci forming assays in vitro, and also demonstrated the ability to form subcutaneous tumors in nude mice (PMID: 22327623).

The ROS1 S1986F mutation lies in the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein. It has been detected in a patient with ROS1-fusion-positive lung cancer in concert with the S1986Y mutation. The two alterations at the same residue were associated with resistance to crizotinib but subsequent sensitivity to lorlatinib. In a murine B-cell line expression of individual S1986F- and S1986Y-mutated ROS1-fusion constructs were resistant to crizotinib and ceritinib but not lorlatinib, as assessed by cell viability and pathway activation assays (PMID: 27401242).

The ROS1 F2004V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was found as a secondary mutation in a patient with lung adenocarcinoma who had progressive disease in the brain and bones after treatment with crizotinib, entrectinib and brigatinib but who had a dramatic response to treatment with lorlatinib (Abstract: Dimou et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.19.00013). This mutation may confer resistance to entrectinib and brigatinib but remains sensitive to lorlatinib. Structural studies based on homology to ALK predict that ROS1 F2004V would confer resistance to ceritinib (PMID: 27401242).

The FIG-ROS1 fusion is characterized by the fusion of the 3' region of ROS1 (exon 35) to the 5' region of FIG (exon 7); this fusion results from an intra-chromosomal deletion in chromosome 6 (PMID: 12661006). The FIG-ROS1 fusion results in a constitutively active ROS1 kinase (PMID: 2827175, 12661006).

The ROS1 E1935G mutation occurs in an uncharacterized region ten amino acid residues prior to the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein. In a murine B-cell line a E1935G-mutated FIG-ROS1 construct conferred increased resistance to crizotinib, as compared to the unmutated construct in cell-growth assays. The mutated construct showed slightly reduced sensitivity to the inhibitor foretinib (PMID: 24218589).

CCDC6-ROS1 is a fusion rearrangement mutation resulting in the fusion of the 3' region of ROS1 (exon 34) to the 5' region of CCDC6 (exon 6). This fusion retains the coiled-coil domain of CCDC6 and the kinase domain of ROS1 (PMID: 22975805, 25870798). The oncogenic potential of this fusion has not been functionally tested.

The ROS1 L1951R mutation lies in the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein. In vitro studies in a CD74-ROS1-transformed cell line demonstrated that L1951R confers resistance to crizotinib and ceritinib as measured by cell viability and pathway activation assays. This effect is likely due to steric hindrance (PMID: 25351743).

The CEP85L-ROS1 fusion protein combines the N terminal of CEP85L until exon 8 with the C-terminal of ROS1 starting at exon 36 and is found in CNS tumors, angiosarcoma and glioblastoma (PMID: 23637631, 25204415, 30171048). The breakpoint preserves the coiled-coil domain of CEP85L and the tyrosine kinase domain of ROS1, and is predicted to possess transforming abilities (PMID: 23637631, 25204415, 30171048). Expression of this fusion protein in BaF3, NIH3T3, and immortalized human astrocyte cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by IL3 independent growth, pathway activation and increased colony formation compared to ectopic expression of wildtype ROS1. Expression of this fusion in BaF3 cells also demonstrated that it is sensitive to multiple TKIs including crizotinib, foretinib, cabozantinib, ceritinib, brigatinib, AZD3463, lorlatinib, and entrectinib proliferation, pathway activation and colony formation (PMID: 30171048).

Amplification of ROS1 has been shown to result in an increase in ROS1 transcript and ROS1 protein levels in cancer cell lines that is sensitive to ROS1 inhibition demonstrating that ROS1 amplification is likely activating (PMID: 25978031). Studies in cancer cell lines have demonstrated that ROS1 amplification can lead to resistance to EGFR inhibitors in cells that are otherwise sensitive to EGFR inhibition (PMID: (PMID: 25978031).

The GOPC-ROS1 fusion protein combines the N terminus of GOPC until exon 7 with the C-terminus of ROS1 starting at exon 35 and is found in CNS tumors (PMID: 30171048). This is the most frequent ROS1 fusion found in glioblastomas (GBMs). Expression of this fusion protein in BaF3 and immortalized human astrocyte cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by IL3 independent growth and increased colony formation compared to ectopic expression of wildtype ROS1 (PMID: 30171048). Expression of this fusion in BaF3 cells also demonstrated that it is sensitive to multiple TKIs including crizotinib, foretinib, cabozantinib, ceritinib, brigatinib, AZD3463, lorlatinib, and entrectinib as measured by proliferation, pathway activation and colony formation with lorlatinib having the highest potency (PMID: 30171048). In a case report, a patient with ER-positive HER2-negative breast cancer harboring GOPC-ROS1 demonstrated an exceptionally response to crizotinib therapy and a subsequent modest response to cabozantinib after development of crizotinib resistance (PMID: 37487149).

The ROS1 G1971E mutation lies in the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein. In a murine B-cell line a G1971E-mutated FIG-ROS1 construct conferred increased resistance to crizotinib, as compared to the unmutated construct in cell-growth assays. The mutated construct showed slightly reduced sensitivity to the inhibitor foretinib (PMID: 24218589).

SDC4-ROS1, a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of exon 2 of SDC4 with exon 33 or 34 of ROS1, results in a constitutively active protein containing the ROS1 kinase domain (PMID: 22327623). This fusion demonstrated transforming capabilities when tested in foci forming assays in vitro, and also demonstrated the ability to form subcutaneous tumors in nude mice (PMID: 22327623).

TPM3-ROS1, a rearrangement mutation that results in the fusion of exon 8 of TPM3 with exon 35 of ROS1, results in a constitutively active protein containing the ROS1 kinase domain (PMID: 22327623). This fusion demonstrated transforming capabilities when tested in foci forming assays in vitro, and also demonstrated the ability to form subcutaneous tumors in nude mice (PMID: 22327623).

The RUNX1 P200S mutation occurs in the DNA binding domain of RUNX1. Recombinant assays demonstrated that the mutant protein cannot bind DNA and has decreased transactivation activity (PMID: 18192504). These defects likely lead to dysregulation of gene expression due to the ineffective recruitment of transcriptional complexes.

The ROS1 D2033N mutation lies in the tyrosine kinase domain of the ROS1 protein. It has been detected in a patient with CD74-ROS1-fusion positive lung cancer with acquired resistance to crizotinib. In a murine B-cell line a D2033N-mutated CD74-ROS1 construct conferred reduced sensitivity to crizotinib while cabozantinib was equally effective as against the unmutated CD74-ROS, as measured in growth and downstream signaling assays. Experiments also supported the notion that D2033N confers resistance to ceritinib, brigatinib and lorlatinib. The analogous mutation in ALK (D1203N) confers crizotinib resistance in vitro and molecular studies indicate that mutations at these residues are important due to their being located at binding surface for ATP (PMID: 26673800).

The R201Q mutation in RUNX1 resides in the highly conserved DNA binding domain. Whilst protein stability is unaffected, expression of this mutant causes reduced DNA-binding ability similar to RUNX1 knockdown suggesting a dominant-negative function (PMID: 17290219, 25490895, 10508512). Experimental studies using iPS cells suggest that the R201Q mutation predisposes cells to leukemic transformation partly through genomic instability (PMID: 25490895) and enhanced proliferative potential of immature hematopoietic progenitor cells (PMID: 21725049).
The RUNX1 D198G mutation is located in the DNA-binding domain. Expression of this mutation causes reduced DNA-binding potential at target gene promoter regions (PMID: 22318203).

Fusions of RUNX1 are commonly detected in patients with hematopoietic malignancies. Chromosomal rearrangements with RUNX1 have been identified with uncommon partners, and approximately 21 translocations have been identified at the molecular level. Most translocations contain the RUNX1 RHD domain and act as a dominant negative or diminish the ability of RUNX1 to recruit activating complexes (PMID: 21174539).

The RUNX1 R166Q mutation (called R139 in other isoforms) is a loss-of-function mutation that occurs in the DNA binding domain of RUNX1. This alteration is hypothesized to affect the ability of RUNX1 to recruit the appropriate transcriptional complexes to DNA (PMID: 10508512).

The RUNX1 K110N mutation resides in the DNA interacting region of RUNX1. Expression of this mutation leads to impaired RUNX1 DNA binding in a dominant negative fashion and likely results in defective recruitment of transcriptional machinery and disruption of gene expression (PMID: 15156185, 11830488).

The RUNX1 W279* mutation (known as W252 in other isoforms) resides in the DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation was found in a patient with congenital thrombocytopenia that evolved into a high-grade myelodysplastic syndrome. This mutation results in a frameshift alteration causing truncation of RUNX1. It is hypothesized to inhibit DNA binding and reduce the recruitment of transcriptional machinery to target genes (PMID: 25893166).

The RUNX1 G69R mutation occurs upstream of the DNA binding domain of RUNX1 and has been identified in patients with leukemia as well as healthy individuals (PMID: 12874780, PMID: 12393679). Recombinant assays demonstrated that the mutant protein can still bind DNA and heterodimerize with CBFβ (core binding factor β) (PMID: 18192504).

The RUNX1 R204Q mutation resides in the DNA binding domain of RUNX1. Recombinant assays demonstrated that the mutant protein cannot bind DNA and has decreased transactivation activity (PMID: 18192504, 11830488). These defects likely lead to dysregulation of gene expression due to the ineffective recruitment of transcriptional complexes.

The RUNX1 S318fsX300 mutation results in the premature truncation of RUNX1 and likely disrupts DNA binding interactions. Expression of this mutation in murine bone marrow transplantation models results in a myelodysplastic disease that can progress to leukemia with co-expression of the oncogene Evi1 (PMID: 18192504).

The RUNX1 R204* mutation occurs in the DNA-binding domain. The mutation produces a frameshift alteration that ablates RUNX1 DNA binding activity leading resulting in the inability of RUNX1 to recruit the appropriate transcriptional machinery (PMID: 10068652, 15156185, 11830488).

Truncating mutations in RUNX1 are most commonly caused by chromosomal translocations that result in a truncation and fusion of RUNX1 to heterologous proteins, inhibiting its function, and predisposing to certain types of leukemia, lymphomas, and myelodysplastic syndromes (PMID: 15386419,17394134,15864279).

The RUNX1 K110E mutation resides in the DNA interacting region of RUNX1. This mutation has been found in a family with familial platelet disorder predisposed to acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 15156185). Expression of this mutation leads to impaired RUNX1 DNA binding in a dominant negative fashion and likely results in defective recruitment of transcriptional machinery and disruption of gene expression (PMID: 15156185, 11830488).

Translocations involving ETV6 (also TEL) and RUNX1 (also AML1) are recurrent in patients with B-acute lymphoblastic leukemias and are associated with good prognosis (PMID: 7780150, 8609706). The resultant ETV6-RUNX1 fusion protein pairs the entire coding region of RUNX1 with the promoter and central repression domain of ETV6 (PMID: 15156184). The ETV6-RUNX1 fusion can still bind target genes, yet ETV6 recruits histone deacetylase (HDAC) repressive complexes instead of p300-CBP (core binding protein) activating complexes to these regions (PMID: 11001911, 28299659). Genes that are typically activated by RUNX1 are repressed by the ETV6-RUNX1 fusion (PMID: 15156184). Expression of ETV6-RUNX1 results in enhanced self-renewal and survival in murine models and leukemic patient samples (PMID: 18202291, 16044150). Hematopoietic cells expressing ETV6-RUNX1 are sensitive to HDAC inhibition (PMID: 10490596).

The RUNX1 R166G mutation resides in the runt homology domain of the protein. Experimental studies demonstrate that the R166G mutation suppresses the transactivation ability of wildtype RUNX1 and reduces DNA-binding capacity (PMID: 22318203).

The RUNX1 A149* mutation results in premature truncation of the C-terminal of RUNX1. Recombinant assays demonstrated that the mutant protein cannot dimerize with CBFβ (core binding factor β) or bind DNA (PMID: 18192504). These defects likely lead to dysregulation of gene expression.

The RUNX1 D198N mutation occurs in the runt homology domain of RUNX1 and likely disrupts DNA binding and transcription factor complex recruitment. Recombinant assays have shown that this mutation can no longer bind DNA (PMID: 12393679). Furthermore, expression of this mutation in murine bone marrow transplantation models results in a myelodysplastic disease that can progress to leukemia with co-expression of the oncogene Evi1 (ecotropic viral integration site 1) (PMID: 18192504).

RUNX1 plays important roles in the recruitment of transcriptional activation machinery. Increased RUNX1 expression likely leads to enhanced recruitment of transcriptional complexes to chromatin (PMID: 25592647).

The RUNX1-RUNX1T1 fusion results in the fusion of the RUNX1 RHD (Runx homology domain) with almost the entirety of the ETO coding region (PMID: 4125056, 21174539). The RUNX1-RUNX1T1 fusion product lacks the transactivation domain and therefore cannot bind the transcriptional coactivator p300-CBP. Instead, RUNX1-RUNX1T1 interacts mainly as a transcriptional repressor by recruiting co-repressor complexes such as NCoR (nuclear corepressors), mSin3A, SMRT (Silencing mediator of retinoid acid and thyroid hormone receptor) and HDACs (histone deacetylases) to repress hematopoietic genes normally activated by RUNX1 (PMID: 9819404, 19414342).

The RUNX1-ZNF423 fusion results from the chromosomal rearrangement t(16:21)(q12, q22). This mutation has been identified in NUP98-rearranged acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 37714925). In vitro studies with murine bone marrow and Ba/F3 cells expressing RUNX1-ZNF423 demonstrate that the fusion is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, colony formation and transforming activity compared to control vector (PMID: 37714925). In vivo studies with patient-derived xenograft mouse models demonstrate that the RUNX1-ZNF423 fusion cooperates with the NUP98-NSD1 fusion to promote leukemia relapse and chemoresistance through accelerating energy metabolism pathways (PMID: 37714925).

The RUNX1-EVI1 fusion results in the fusion of the RUNX1 RHD (Runx homology domain) with the EVI1 coding region (PMID: 19016745, 15156182). The RUNX1-EVI1 fusion product lacks the transactivation domain and therefore cannot bind the transcriptional coactivator p300-CBP. The RUNX1-EVI1 fusion protein outcompetes wildtype RUNX1 for binding to DNA allowing for the recruitment of histone deacetylase (HDAC) complexes instead of activating complexes. Genes that are typically activated by RUNX1 are repressed by the RUNX1-EVI1 fusion (PMID: 19016745, 15156182).

The RUNX1 R201* mutation is a frameshift mutation that truncates the C-terminal of RUNX1. The mutant protein is thought to outcompete wildtype RUNX1 for binding to DNA, allowing for recruitment of histone deacetylase (HDAC) complexes instead of activating complexes (PMID: 20549580). The R201* alteration results in defective megokaryopoiesis in hematopoietic stem cells (PMID: 26021490).

The RUNX1 R107C mutation maps to the DNA interacting region of RUNX1. This alteration likely disrupts the contact of RUNX1 with DNA resulting in defective recruitment of transcriptional machinery and disruption of gene expression (PMID: 15156185).

The RUNX1 H105Q mutation resides in the runt homology domain of the protein. Experimental studies demonstrate that the H105Q mutation suppresses the transactivation ability of wildtype RUNX1 and reduces DNA-binding capacity. Expression of this mutation in myeloid cells led to a block in myeloid differentiation and enhanced clonogenic capability (PMID: 22318203).

The SDHB R242H mutation is located in the 4Fe-4S ferredoxin-type domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in paragangliomas, pheochromocytomas, SDHB deficient renal cell carcinoma and GIST (PMID: 12000816, 12213855, 17102084, 22270996, 24276837, 25025441, 21173220). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SDHB R242H is inactivating as measured by reduced SDH enzymatic activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 25972245).

The RUNX1 Y140* mutation results in premature truncation of the C-terminal of RUNX1. Recombinant assays demonstrated that the mutant protein cannot dimerize with CBFβ (core binding factor β) or bind DNA (PMID: 18192504). These defects likely lead to dysregulation of gene expression.

SDHA truncating mutations can form C-terminally truncated SDHA proteins. These mutations are found in patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors and adrenal tumors (PMID: 22974104, 21752896). Protein structural analysis of SDHA S384* and R31* demonstrated truncating SDHA mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of protein function (PMID: 21505157).

SDHB truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein. These mutations have been identified in phaeochromocytomas (PMID: 14500403). In vivo studies with SDHB-deficient yeast demonstrate loss of SDHB is inactivating as measured by increased ROS production and HIF1 stabilization (PMID: 17884808).

SDHB deletion mutations result in the loss of the SDHB protein. These mutations have been identified in hereditary paraganglioma (PMID: 19389109). In vivo studies with SDHB-deficient yeast demonstrate loss of SDHB is inactivating as measured by increased ROS production and HIF1 stabilization (PMID: 17884808).

The SDHB S100F mutation is located in the 2Fe-2S ferredoxin-type domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PMID: 17639058, 33031286). Structural analysis predicts that this mutation is likely inactivating as the amino acid residue is highly conserved and the substitution between a nonpolar side chain for an uncharged polar could lead to impaired protein function (PMID: 17639058).

The SDHB R46Q mutation is located in the 2Fe-2S ferredoxin-type domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in pheochromocytoma, paraganglioma, renal cell carcinoma and GIST (PMID: 12618761, 14500403, 18362451, 23083876, 23282968). In vitro studies with HeLa cells and UOK269 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SDHB R46Q is inactivating as measured by reduced protein half-life compared to wildtype (PMID: 22835832, 26719882).

The SDHB C196Y mutation is located in the 4Fe-4S ferredoxin-type domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in sporadic and familial pheochromocytoma and paragangliomas (PMID: 12000816, 25494863, 23666964, 25683602, 24781345, 21172883, 17652212). In vitro studies with HeLa cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SDHB C196Y is inactivating as measured by reduction in the mutant protein half-life (PMID: 22835832). SDHB C196Y is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with histone deacetylase inhibitors as measured by the increased half-life of the SDHB protein (PMID: 22835832).

The SDHB I127S mutation is located in the 2Fe-2S ferredoxin-type domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in paragangliomas, pheochromocytomas and SDH-deficient GIST (PMID: 15987702, 16912137, 17200167, 19001511, 19215943, 23282968, 25683602). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SDHB I127S is likely neutral as measured by SDH enzymatic activity and mitochondrial localization comparable to wildtype (PMID: 25972245).

The SDHC G75D mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified as a germline alteration in head and neck paraganglioma, SDH-deficient GIST and Carney triad (PMID: 19351833, 23282968, 24886695, 26173966). This mutation has not been functionally characterized.

The SDHB W200C mutation is located in the 4Fe-4S ferredoxin-type domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in paraganglioma, pheochromocytoma, renal cell carcinoma and GIST (PMID: 17143317, 20119652, 19184535, 21173220). In vitro studies with HeLa cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SDHB W200C is inactivating as measured by decreased half-life compared to the wildtype SDHB protein (PMID: 22835832).

SDHC truncation mutations can form several forms of C-terminally truncated SDHC proteins. SDHC is a known susceptibility gene for paraganglioma (PGL) syndrome and SDHC mutations are found in head and neck PGLs. Head and neck PGLs associated with SDHC mutations are virtually exclusively benign and seldom multifocal. SDHC mutations were also found in select cases of adrenocortical carcinoma; however, given the rarity of adrenocortical carcinomas and SDHC mutations, the role of SDHC loss in adrenocortical carcinoma pathogenesis remains unclear (PMID: 28819017, 27700540, 16249420).

Truncating mutations in SDHD can occur anywhere throughout the gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its protein product. SDHD encodes a subunit of the Succinate Dehydrogenase (SDH) complex, an enzyme that is part of the Krebs cycle and complex II of the respiratory chain (PMID: 20226277). Loss of SDH complex has been shown to lead to succinate accumulation, which behaves as an oncometabolite to induce tumor formation through multiple mechanisms (PMID: 31039394). Reduced expression of SDHD has been reported in colorectal and gastric cancer (PMID: 12883710). Germline mutations in SDHD, including truncating variants, have been associated with the development of paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas (PMID: 28099933, 12111639, 29545045).

The SDHC R133* mutation is located in the transmembrane subunit domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in both benign head and neck paraganglioma and malignant hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma with metastasis (PMID: 24423348). Tissue analysis of a patient with malignant hereditary paraganglioma harboring SDHC R133* suggested that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of heterozygosity and loss of SDHB protein expression (PMID: 24423348).

Truncation mutations in SPEN lead to loss of function or loss of protein expression and is considered an oncogenic event. In hormone dependent breast cancers, SPEN binds to and acts as a repressor of ER transcriptional activity, and loss of SPEN increases cell proliferation, tumor growth, and survival of breast cancer cell lines. Furthermore, SPEN protein and RNA expression levels in patient samples predicted better responses to tamoxifen therapy (PMID:26297734).

The SRC Q531 mutation results in a truncated SRC protein after codon 531. Importantly, codon 530 harbors the principal regulatory phospho-tyrosine, and this truncation results in a constitutively active C-SRC kinase protein (PMID: 9988270).

The SRSF2 H99L mutation is located between the RNA recognition motif and the serine-arginine rich domains of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is neutral as measured by no change in splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

Loss of SDHD accompanied by other genetic alterations or a "multi-hit" process is implicated in tumor formation. Deletion of SDHD in SDHD-ESR conditional knockout mouse tissues as well as newly derived cell lines showed only partial and inconsistent activation of HIF-1α pathway and pseudo-hypoxic response. Subsequent microarray analysis of adrenal medulla and kidney tissues revealed consistent up-regulation of p21WAF1/Cip1, a protein implicated in cell cycle, senescence, and cancer (PMID:24465590).

SRC amplification is a rare event occurring in a few tumor types, most notably bladder and colorectal cancer and melanoma at low frequency (Abstract: Zehir A et al. Nature Medicine, 2017. http://doi:10.1038/nm.4333). In mouse models, SRC has a role in tissue regeneration and is in an APC-null setting required for tumorigenesis (PMID: 24788409). Cell line experiments and mouse models also indicate that SRC has a role in development of other cancers, such as pancreatic cancer, through regulation of tissue-specific signaling pathways (PMID: 22589274, 11114744). Although no distinct function has been ascribed to the gene amplification it is likely to mirror that of hyperactivation by other means and thus have potential to transform (PMID: 11114744, 15060621).

The SRSF2 P107H mutation is located between the RNA recognition motif and the serine-arginine rich domains of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by no change in splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The SRSF2 P95H mutation is located in the RNA binding domain of the protein, between the canonical RRM and the SR domains. The P95H mutation in SRSF2 is commonly detected in patients with myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 30846499). Mouse models with this mutation produce a myelodysplasia phenotype leading to acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 25965569, 27135740). The P95H mutation led to global splicing alterations and abnormal RNA binding of SRFS2 (PMID: 25965569, 26261309, 31961934), which affected cells enriched in cancer and apoptosis signaling (PMID: 26124281). Experimental studies have shown that P95H expressing cells are sensitive to treatment with the splicing inhibitor E7107 (PMID: 27135740). Expression of this mutation in HeLa demonstrated that this mutation was sensitive to the ATR inhibitors, VE-821, VE-822, and AZ 20, as shown by increased DNA damage compared to untreated cells and cells expressing WT U2AF1 (PMID: 30054334). Expression of this mutation in myeloid cell lines demonstrated that it induces IL-6 production and NFkB activity, and may affect innate immunity (PMID: 30846499).

The SRSF2 P95R mutation is located in the RNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 31366621). In vitro studies with HeLa and K562 cells expressing SRSF2 P95R demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by dysregulation in splicing pattern recognition leading to aberrant splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 31040863).

The SRSF2 R86_G93dup mutation is located in the RNA recognition motif of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The SRSF2 S54F mutation is located in the RNA recognition motif of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The SRSF2 P95L mutation is located in the RNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic myeloid leukemia and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 31366621). In vitro studies with HeLa and K562 cells expressing SRSF2 P95L demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by dysregulation in splicing pattern recognition leading to aberrant splicing compared to wildtype (PMID: 31040863).

The SRSF2 R94_P95insR mutation is located between the RNA recognition motif and the serine-arginine rich domains of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The SRSF2 R102del mutation is located between the RNA recognition motif and the serine-arginine rich domains of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The SRSF2 P95_R102del mutation is located between the RNA recognition motif and the serine-arginine rich domains of the protein. Expression of this mutation along with the likely neutral SRSF2 P107H mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The SRSF2 S54A mutation is located in the RNA recognition motif of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by increased splice defects compared to wildtype (PMID: 31961934).

The STAT3 F384V mutation occurs in the protein's DNA-binding domain and has been described in patients with a primary immunodeficiency condition known as the hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) (PMID: 22751495, 18602572, 17881745 ). HIES-related mutations in the DNA-binding domain of STAT3 have been shown to confer dominant negative characteristics to the protein, resulting in its diminished DNA-binding ability, though specific functional assessment of the STAT3 F384V mutation has yet to be done (PMID: 17676033). This mutation is recurrent in human cancer and comprises a hotspot, suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

The STAT3 K658N mutation lies in the SH2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a monkey fibroblast-like cell line demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased phosphorylated STAT3 protein compared to wildtype STAT3 (PMID: 27345172).

The STAT3 F384Y mutation occurs in the protein's DNA-binding domain and has been described in patients with a primary immunodeficiency condition known as the hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) (PMID: 22751495, 18602572, 17881745 ). HIES-related mutations in the DNA-binding domain of STAT3 have been shown to confer dominant negative characteristics to the protein, resulting in its diminished DNA-binding ability, though specific functional assessment of the STAT3 F384Y mutation has yet to be done (PMID: 17676033). Moreover, this mutation is recurrent in human cancer and comprises a hotspot, suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

STAT3 Y640F missense mutation occurs in the Src homology 2 (SH2) domain- the domain that mediates the dimerization and activation of STAT3 protein. Y640F is a recurrent mutational hotspot in T cell-large granular lymphocytic leukemia (T-LGLL) (PMID: 25586472). NK cell lines YT and NKYS, or STAT3-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) stably expressing the mutant, as well as bone marrow biopsy samples harboring the STAT3 Y640F mutation revealed increased phospho-STAT3 levels in the nucleus both by western blotting and by immunohistochemical staining (PMID: 25586472, 25873174, 22591296). In addition, NK cell line KAI3 expressing the STAT3 Y640F variant demonstrated significant positive progressive selection under limiting concentration of the cytokine interleukin-2 (IL-2) when compared to cells transduced with wildtype STAT3. Conversely, silencing STAT3 expression with short hairpin RNA (shRNA) showed growth inhibition in mutant NK lines YT and NKYS (PMID: 25586472). In addition, in vitro studies expressing the STAT3 Y640F variant in HEK 293 cells demonstrated significant induction of the luciferase reporter gene under the control of STAT3-responsive cis-inducible element under basal and interleukin-6 (IL-6)-stimulated conditions (PMID: 22591296). STAT3-null MEFs expressing Y640F variant produced a large number of colonies in soft agar colony formation assay, and was shown to be highly tumorigenic in vivo (PMID: 25873174).

The STAT3 E616K mutation lies in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype STAT3 (PMID: 30054295).

The STAT3 F384L mutation occurs in the protein's DNA-binding domain and has been described in patients with a primary immunodeficiency condition known as the hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) (PMID: 22751495, 18602572, 17881745 ). HIES-related mutations in the DNA-binding domain of STAT3 have been shown to confer dominant negative characteristics to the protein, resulting in its diminished DNA-binding ability, though specific functional assessment of the STAT3 F384L mutation has yet to be done (PMID: 17676033). Moreover, this mutation is recurrent in human cancer and comprises a hotspot, suggesting that it is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011).

The STAT3 G618R mutation lies in the SH2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype STAT3 (PMID: 28356514).

The STAT3 D427H mutation lies in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cell lines demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype STAT3 (PMID: 30054295).

STAT3 D661V missense mutation occurs in the Src homology 2 (SH2) domain- the domain that mediates the dimerization and activation of STAT3 protein, and is frequently found in large granular lymphocytic leukemia (LGLL). Analysis of bone marrow biopsy samples harboring the STAT3 D661V mutation obtained from patients with LGLL revealed increased phospho-STAT3 levels in the nucleus both by western blotting and by immunohistochemical staining when compared to samples obtained from a healthy control. Similarly, RNA expression analysis showed up-regulation of STAT3 target genes in STAT3 D661V mutant sample. In addition, in vitro studies expressing the STAT3 D661V variant in HEK 293 cells demonstrated significant induction of the luciferase reporter gene under the control of STAT3-responsive cis-inducible element under basal and interleukin-6 (IL-6)-stimulated conditions, indicating, therefore, that D661V mutation causes activation of STAT3 transcriptional activity (PMID: 22591296).

STAT3 S614R missense mutation occurs in the Src homology 2 (SH2) domain- the domain that mediates the dimerization and activation of STAT3 protein. This variant of STAT3 has been identified in lymphomas arising from Natural Killer (NK) or gamma-delta-T cells (NKTCLs) as well as in gamma-delta T cell lines (PMID: 25586472). Transduction of NK cell line KAI3 with STAT3 S614R variant demonstrated significant positive progressive selection of cells bearing the mutant STAT3 under limiting concentration of the cytokine IL-2 when compared to cells transduced with wildtype STAT3 (PMID: 25586472). One case study described the emergence of dominant clones of NK cells harboring the STAT3 S614R variant as the disease progressed from T cell-large granular lymphocyte (T-LGL) leukemia to NK-LGL leukemia. Analysis of the mutant samples by Western blotting demonstrated an increase in the levels of phospho-STAT3 as well as in the expression of its target gene MCL-1, suggesting that STAT3 S614R mutation results in enhanced transcriptional activity (PMID: 25709890).

The STAT3 C426R mutation is located in the DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing STAT3 C426R demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased reporter activity in non-stimulated conditions compared to wildtype (PMID: 29378236).

The missense mutation H410R occurs in the DNA-binding domain of the STAT3 protein, unlike most other mutations that occur in the src homology- 2 (SH2) domain, and has been reported to increase the transcriptional activity of STAT3. In vitro studies expressing STAT3 H410R variant in HEK293 cells was shown to increase the levels of phospho-STAT3, as well as the activity of cis-inducible response elements in luciferase reporter assay. In addition, quantitative PCR experiment showed that expression levels of six known STAT3 target genes were up-regulated by the H410R variant (PMID: 26419508).

The STAT3 N647I mutation lies in the SH2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a monkey fibroblast-like cell line demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased phosphorylated STAT3 protein compared to wildtype STAT3 (PMID: 27345172).

The STAT3 E616del mutation is located in the SH2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 23872306). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing STAT3 E616del demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased reporter activity in non-stimulated conditions compared to wildtype (PMID: 29378236).

G64V missense mutation occurs in the N-terminal region of SUFU protein that is involved in mediating binding to MCL-1 and to GLI transcription factor. This variant retained its ability to bind to MCL-1 and BCL-2, repressed GLI-mediated transcription, and is sensitive to inhibition by BH3-mimetic drugs in cell cultures and in vivo (PMID: 28945232).

N328K missense mutation occurs in the internally disorganized region (IDR) in SUFU protein, which includes the BH3 sequence; GSK3β and PKA phosphorylation sites; and functions as a switch for toggling SUFU conformation and activity. This substitution abolishes binding of MCL-1 to SUFU, resulting in SUFU protein stability and suppression of GLI-transcriptional activity. This variant is not responsive to treatment with BH3-mimetic drugs in cell cultures or in vivo (PMID: 28945232).

The SUFU I57N missense mutation occurs in the N-terminal region that is involved in mediating binding to MCL-1 and to GLI transcription factor. This variant retained its ability to bind to MCL-1 and BCL-2, repressed GLI-mediated transcription, and was observed to be sensitive to inhibition by BH3-mimetic drugs in cell culture experiments (PMID: 28945232).

R339W missense mutation occurs in the internally disorganized region (IDR) in SUFU protein, which includes the BH3 sequence; GSK3β and PKA phosphorylation sites; and functions as a switch for toggling SUFU conformation and activity. This substitution, while retaining GLI-binding interaction, abolished binding of MCL-1 to SUFU, resulting in suppression of GLI-transcriptional activity. This variant is sensitive to treatment withBH3-mimetic drugs in cell culture experiments (PMID: 28945232).

G334D missense mutation occurs in the internally disorganized region (IDR) in SUFU protein, which includes the BH3 sequence; GSK3β and PKA phosphorylation sites; and functions as a switch for toggling SUFU conformation and activity. This substitution does not appear to affect its interactions with either MCL-1 or GLI, and is sensitive to inhibition by BH3-mimetic drugs in cell culture experiments (PMID: 28945232).

The TGFBR2 P525L mutation occurs in the protein's subdomain XI, which is a conserved domain across type I and II TGFß receptors. Cell line experiments in lung epithelial and monkey fibroblast cell lines demonstrated that this mutation suppresses antiproliferative TGFß signaling in a dominant-negative manner. Notably, it does not prevent ligand binding or autophosphorylation, but inhibits transphosphorylation of TGFBR1, which is the likely mechanism for its phenotypic effect (PMID: 7862150).

S351G missense mutation occurs in the internally disorganized region (IDR) in SUFU protein, which includes the BH3 sequence; GSK3β and PKA phosphorylation sites; and functions as a switch for toggling SUFU conformation and activity. This substitution, while retaining GLI-binding interaction, abolished binding of MCL-1 to SUFU, resulting in SUFU protein stability and suppression of GLI-transcriptional activity. This variant is not responsive to treatment with BH3-mimetic drugs in cell culture experiments (PMID: 28945232).

Truncating mutations in SUFU can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its function (PMID: 29625055). SUFU encodes a negative regulator of the hedgehog signaling pathway and, through its effects on the Gli transcription factors, it has been shown to be involved in human development and the regulation of cell proliferation (PMID: 10559945, 10806483, 10564661). Germline SUFU mutations have been implicated in the development of childhood medulloblastoma, as well as familial multiple meningiomas (PMID: 12068298, 22958902). Truncating mutations leading to loss of SUFU have been identified in patients with several types of carcinomas as well as medulloblastomas (PMID: 29625055, 12068298, 17102621)

The TGFBR2 D379G mutation occurs in the TGFBR2 serine/threonine kinase domain. Experiments in cell lines isolated from T-cell lymphoma demonstrated that this variant is dominant negative, causing loss of TGFBR2 at the membrane and disrupting signaling through the TGFß pathway. This ultimately leads to loss of TGFß-mediated inhibition of growth (PMID: 8668164).

STAT3 D661Y missense mutation occurs in the Src homology 2 (SH2) domain- the domain that mediates the dimerization and activation of STAT3 protein. This variant has been described in T cell-large granular lymphocytic leukemia (T-LGLL); and in lymphomas arising from Natural Killer (NK) cells [NK/T cell lymphomas (NKTCLs)] and gamma-delta-T cells [gamma-delta-T-cell-derived lymphomas (gamma-delta-PTCLs)], as well as in NK and gamma-delta-T- cell lines (PMID: 25586472). Higher levels of phospho-STAT3 was detected in NK cell line SNK6 harboring the STAT3 D661Y variant. NK cell line KAI3 expressing the STAT3 D661Y variant demonstrated significant positive progressive selection under limiting concentration of the cytokine IL-2 when compared to cells transduced with wildtype STAT3, suggesting that this is an activating mutation (PMID: 25586472).

The TGFBR2 R537P mutation is located in the protein's serine/threonine kinase domain. This alteration is associated with high TGFBR2 kinase activity in an immortalized cell line of buccal origin which is homozygous for the mutation. TGFß, but not activin, treatment fails to phosphorylate SMAD proteins 2 and 3 but not 1 and 5. Also, the phosphorylation of SMAD1/5 in this cell line is TGFß independent and diphosphorylation decreased, signaling that this mutation has diverging effect on different downstream pathways (PMID: 18339844).

Frameshift insertions and deletions that result in a truncated TGFBR2 protein are found in cancers with microsatellite instability (MSI) (PMID: 7585632), leading to reduced protein expression (PMID: 17456004). Truncating mutations in TGBR2 most commonly occur within the big adenine tract in the receptor type II (BAT-RII) region, resulting in loss of the cytoplasmic domain, which is necessary for catalytic activity (PMID: 9927040). Experiments in cell lines have shown that mutations in the BAT-RII region abrogate TGFß-mediated growth inhibition, and proposed to increase chemotherapy susceptibility (PMID: 16310402, 9927040, 11309634, 17985359).

The TGFBR1 V419L mutation occurs in the kinase domain and has been found in a patient with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (PMID: 28679693). In vitro assays demonstrate this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased SMAD2 phosphorylation and downstream transcriptional output (PMID: 28679693).

TGFBR2 deletions have been detected in patients with colorectal and gastric cancer, and are associated with loss of protein expression. These alterations have been shown to abrogate TGFß-mediated growth inhibition, and proposed to increase chemotherapy susceptibility (PMID: 25521327, 25736321). Additionally, deletion of TGFBR2 in mice with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma accelerated tumorigenesis in vivo due to defective TGFß-signaling (PMID: 27558455).

The TMPRSS2 T112M mutation (also cited as TMPRSS2 T75M) is located in the intracellular domain of the protein. This variant is considered a polymorphism and has been identified in sporadic prostate cancer (PMID: 11745466, 25040002). Although not functionally characterized, TMPRSS2 T112M mutations are predicted to be likely neutral as the residue is not conserved between species (PMID: 11745466).

The TGFBR2 E526Q mutation is located in the protein's serine/threonine kinase domain. Experiments in human esophageal carcinoma cell lines demonstrated that this mutation was dominant negative, resulting in lack of nuclear translocation of SMAD proteins, the normal downstream effectors of TGFß signaling (PMID: 10789724). Additionally, a buccal carcinoma cell line homozygous for the variant shows no response to TGFß ligand, as measured by phosphorylation by TGFBR1, TGFBR2 and receptor-associated SMAD proteins (PMID: 18339844).

Truncating mutations in TNFRSF14 can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its activity (PMID: 27257180, 29625055). TNFRSF14 encodes a Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) receptor superfamily member that has been shown to be involved in signal transduction pathways that regulate inflammatory and T-cell immune responses (PMID: 27982078, 21402741, 11742858). This gene has also been known for its role in mediating herpes virus entry into cells (PMID: 22017438, 24307582). TNFRSF14 aberrations have been associated with worse prognosis in follicular lymphoma, and they also seem to increase the susceptibility to allogeneic T-cells received during bone marrow transplantation (PMID:20884631, 27103745). Reduced expression of this protein has been reported in follicular (PMID: 27257180), marginal zone (PMID: 27297871) and Hodgkin (PMID: 26650888) lymphomas, and this gene has also been shown to act as a tumor suppressor in bladder carcinomas by promoting apoptosis (PMID: 30066919). Additionally, truncating mutations in TNFRSF14 have been identified in exome-sequencing studies in other malignancies (PMID: 29625055)

The STAT3 E616G mutation lies in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype STAT3 (PMID: 30054295).

The TSC2 S1774T mutation is located outside of a known functional domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by TSC1 signal, TSC2 signal, T389/S6K ratio and computational modeling by SIFT comparable to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 A447V mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by TSC1 signal, TSC2 signal, T389/S6K ratio and computational modeling by SIFT comparable to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 Y598C mutation is located in the tuberin domain of the TSC2 protein. This mutation has been found in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) syndrome (PMID: 22903760).  In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by reduced TSC1 protein expression, which suggests a reduction in TSC1-TSC2 complex formation, as well as increased levels of S6K phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 V1500M mutation is located outside of a known functional domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by TSC1 signal, TSC2 signal, T389/S6K ratio and computational modeling by SIFT comparable to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 H1620R variant was identified in a screening of individuals suspected to have tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) syndrome. Subsequent functional assessment was performed by co-transfecting 293T cells with TSC1, S6K and TSC2 H1620R expression constructs, and then performing immunoblots with TSC1, TSC2 and phospho S6K antibodies and comparing the results with a wildtype construct and a bona fide TSC2 pathogenic variant (R611Q). Cells transfected with TSC2 H1620R variant showed reduced TSC2 and TSC1 protein expression, suggesting an effect on TSC2 stability and on the formation of TSC1-TSC2 complexes, respectively, as well as an increased phosphorylation of S6K. Altogether, TSC2 H1620R variant promotes downstream mTOR pathway activation (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 S918C mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by TSC1 signal, TSC2 signal, T389/S6K ratio and computational modeling by SIFT comparable to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

Subsequent functional assessment was performed by co-transfecting 293T cells with TSC1, S6K and TSC2 L830R expression constructs, and then performing immunoblots with TSC1, TSC2 and phospho S6K antibodies and comparing the results with a wildtype construct and a bona fide TSC2 pathogenic variant (R611Q). Altogether, TSC2 L830R variant promotes downstream mTOR pathway activation (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 E254K mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by TSC1 signal, TSC2 signal, T389/S6K ratio and computational modeling by SIFT comparable to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 L1750Afs25 mutation is located in the GAP domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by significantly reduced TSC1 signal as well as a significantly increased T389/S6K ratio compared to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 P1381L mutation is located outside of a known functional domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by TSC1 signal, TSC2 signal, T389/S6K ratio and computational modeling by SIFT comparable to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

Truncating mutations in TSC2 invariably result in the loss of its C-terminal GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain. In the absence of GAP activity, TSC2 is likely unable to inhibit RHEB, even if the other two members (TSC1 and TBC1D7) of the TSC complex are intact, which can causes constitutive activation of the mTOR pathway (PMID: 14729330, 24529379) consistent with the oncogenic role of these mutations. Cells depleted of TSC2 display constitutive activation of the mTOR pathway and are sensitive to the mTOR inhibitor, rapamycin (PMID: 14561707, 25724664).

The TSC2 T1623I variant was identified in a screening of individuals suspected to have tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) syndrome. Subsequent functional assessment was performed by co-transfecting 293T cells with TSC1, S6K and TSC2 T1623I expression constructs, and then performing immunoblots with TSC1, TSC2 and phospho S6K antibodies and comparing the results with a wildtype construct and a bona fide TSC2 pathogenic variant (R611Q). Cells transfected with TSC2 T1623I variant showed reduced TSC2 and TSC1 protein expression, suggesting an effect on TSC2 stability and on the formation of TSC1-TSC2 complexes, respectively, as well as an increased phosphorylation of S6K. Altogether, TSC2 T1623I variant promotes downstream mTOR pathway activation (PMID: 22903760).
