In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by increased levels of S6K phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 S1036P mutation is located between the tuberin and GAP domains of the TSC2 protein. This mutation has been found in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) syndrome (PMID: 21332470). This mutation is likely inactivating as measured by increased levels of downstream S6K phosphorylation compared to wildtype, suggesting that TSC2 S1036P cannot negatively regulate the mTORC1 complex (PMID: 21332470).

The TSC2 S433C mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by TSC1 signal, TSC2 signal, T389/S6K ratio and computational modeling by SIFT comparable to wildtype TSC2 (PMID: 22903760).

The TSC2 A614D mutation is found in families diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Cells transfected with TSC2 A614D mutant constructs showed a disrupted hamartin-tuberin interaction, leading to an increased S6K and S6 phosphorylation and a decrease in RHEB GTPase activity, leading to mTOR pathway activation (PMID: 11741832, 15483652).

The XPO1 E571K mutation resides in the highly conserved heat repeat domain H12A of the protein, which is critical for XPO1 cargo function (PMID: 27312795, 21642962 ). This mutation is frequently detected in patients with B-cell lymphoma, classical Hodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphoblastic leukemia, where the mutation has been detected in approximately 25% of patients (PMID: 27312795, 27479820, 21741593). This mutation is a hotspot (PMID: 26619011). Mouse models of XPO1 E571K have demonstrated that this mutation is oncogenic as shown by increased B-cell proliferation in vitro and in vivo compared to XPO1 wildtype mice (Abstract: Taylor et al. Abstract# 879, ASH 2017. https://ash.confex.com/ash/2017/webprogram/Paper103909.html).

The MAGI3-AKT3 fusion involves the N-terminus of MAGI3 fused to the C-terminus of AKT3, containing the pleckstrin homology and kinase domains of AKT3. This mutation has been found in breast cancer. Expression of this mutation in a breast cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by constitutive protein activation and increased foci formation compared to vector control. In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is modestly sensitive to the AKT ATP-competitive inhibitor, GSK-690693, but resistant to the AKT allosteric inhibitor, MK2206, when expressed in a breast cancer cell line as measured by pathway activation (PMID: 22722202).

The AKT3 E17K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 24265153, 22622578, 28481359). Expression of this mutation in a melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased protein activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 18813315).

The XPO1 R749Q mutation is located in the C-terminal CRE1 domain of the protein. This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26619011). Expression of this mutation in isogenic colorectal cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased nuclear transport and resistance to DNA-damaging agents compared to wildtype (Abstract: Totinger et al. Abstract# 853, AACR 2022. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/82/12_Supplement/853/700509).

AKT3 fusions typically involve the N-terminus of a partner protein fused to the C-terminus of AKT3, containing the AKT3 kinase domain. These mutations have been found in breast cancer. Expression of an AKT fusion protein in a breast cancer cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by constitutive protein activation and increased foci formation compared to vector control (PMID: 22722202).

AKT3 amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation has been found in glioblastoma, ovarian, endometrial, melanoma and breast cancer (PMID: 25737557, 15466193, 18451171, 20647317, 17178867, 24138071). Overexpression of AKT3 in a glioma cell line and in a BRAF V600E-expressing melanoma cell line demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased DNA repair mechanisms and enhanced cell survival following radiation, increased pathway activation in cooperation with BRAF V600E and resistance to targeted RAF inhibitors (PMID: 25737557, 15466193, 18451171, 20647317).

The ARAF G322S mutation is located in the highly conserved kinase domain of the protein (PMID: 24569458). This mutation has been found in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 25608663). Expression of this mutation in cholangiocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased pathway activation. However, the mutation did not affect the viability of these cells compared to wildtype (PMID: 25608663).

The XPO1 C528S mutation is located in the cargo-binding groove of the XPO1 protein. This mutation has not been implicated in any oncogenic process, but has however been shown to inhibit interactions with cargo molecules as well as small-molecular inhibitors of XPO1 function (PMID: 23034282, 27680702).

The ARAF S214T mutation is located in the conserved region-2 domain of the protein and occurs specifically at a phosphorylation site that negatively regulates ARAF activation. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinomas. Expression of this mutation in lung epithelial cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24569458).

The ARAF G387D mutation is located within the hinge loop region of the kinase domain of the protein.  This mutation has been found in patients with melanoma and nephroblastoma (PMID: 33953400). Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E and NRAS Q61L melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is activating in the presence of the RAF dimer (type II) inhibitor belvarafenib as measured by increased kinase activity, phosphorylation of downstream targets, as well as enhanced growth in cellular assays and mouse models of cancer in the presence of belvarafenib compared to controls (PMID: 33953400). In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to other RAF dimer (type II) inhibitors such as AZ-628 and LXH-254 but retains sensitivity to downstream MAPK inhibitors such as cobimetinib (MEK) and GDC-0994 (ERK) (PMID: 33953400).

The ARAF P462L mutation is located within the kinase domain of the protein.  This mutation has been found in patients with melanoma (PMID: 33953400). Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E and NRAS Q61L melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is activating in the presence of the RAF dimer (type II) inhibitor belvarafenib as measured by increased kinase activity, phosphorylation of downstream targets, as well as enhanced growth in cellular assays and mouse models of cancer in the presence of belvarafenib compared to controls (PMID: 33953400). In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to other RAF dimer (type II) inhibitors such as AZ-628 and LXH-254 but retains sensitivity to downstream MAPK inhibitors such as cobimetinib (MEK) and GDC-0994 (ERK) (PMID: 33953400).

The ARAF S214A mutation is located in the conserved region-2 domain of the protein and occurs specifically at a phosphorylation site that negatively regulates ARAF activation (PMID: 24569458). This mutation has been found in Erdheim-Chester disease (PMID: 26566875). A patient with Erdheim-Chester disease harboring this mutation demonstrated clinical regression with over 50% reduction in mutant cell-free DNA in response to the RAF kinase inhibitor sorafenib (PMID: 26566875).

The ARAF G387R mutation is located within the hinge loop region of the kinase domain of the protein.  This mutation has been found in patients with melanoma and nephroblastoma (PMID: 33953400). Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E and NRAS Q61L melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is activating in the presence of the RAF dimer (type II) inhibitor belvarafenib as measured by increased kinase activity, phosphorylation of downstream targets, as well as enhanced growth in cellular assays and mouse models of cancer in the presence of belvarafenib compared to controls (PMID: 33953400). In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to other RAF dimer (type II) inhibitors such as AZ-628 and LXH-254 but retains sensitivity to downstream MAPK inhibitors such as cobimetinib (MEK) and GDC-0994 (ERK) (PMID: 33953400).

The ARAF G377R mutation is located within the kinase domain of the protein.  This mutation has been found in patients with melanoma (PMID: 33953400). Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E and NRAS Q61L melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is activating in the presence of the RAF dimer (type II) inhibitor belvarafenib as measured by increased kinase activity, phosphorylation of downstream targets, as well as enhanced growth in cellular assays and mouse models of cancer in the presence of belvarafenib compared to controls (PMID: 33953400). In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to other RAF dimer (type II) inhibitors such as AZ-628 and LXH-254 but retains sensitivity to downstream MAPK inhibitors such as cobimetinib (MEK) and GDC-0994 (ERK) (PMID: 33953400).

The ARAF Q349_F351delinsL mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PMID: 34459688). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing ARAF Q349_F351delinsL demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and MEK1/2 compared to wildtype (PMID: 37572153).

The ARAF Q347_A348del mutation is located in the highly conserved kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in Langerhans cell histiocytosis and was co-expressed with the ARAF F351L mutation. Expression of this mutation in human cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype. Expression of this mutation along with ARAF F315L in human cells was also activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to either mutation alone and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24652991).

The ARAF S214F mutation is located in the conserved region-2 domain of the protein and occurs specifically at a phosphorylation site that negatively regulates ARAF activation. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinomas. Expression of this mutation in lung epithelial cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24569458).

The ARAF P216A mutation is located in the conserved region-2 domain of the protein and is a hotspot residue (PMID: 29247016). This mutation has been found in histiocytic neoplasms. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, a patient with histiocytosis harboring this mutation in conjunction with a hotspot KRAS mutation had a complete response to the MEK1/2 inhibitor cobimetinib (PMID: 30867592).

The ARAF F351L mutation is located in the highly conserved kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in Langerhans cell histiocytosis and was co-expressed with the ARAF Q347_A348del mutation. Expression of this mutation in human cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype. Expression of this mutation along with ARAF Q347_A348del in human cells was also activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to either mutation alone and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24652991).

The ARAF S214C mutation is located in the conserved region-2 domain of the protein and occurs specifically at a phosphorylation site that negatively regulates ARAF activation. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinomas. Expression of this mutation in lung epithelial cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 24569458).

The ARAF G387N mutation is located within the hinge loop region of the kinase domain of the protein.  This mutation has been found in patients with melanoma and nephroblastoma (PMID: 33953400). Expression of this mutation in BRAF V600E and NRAS Q61L melanoma cell lines demonstrated that it is activating in the presence of the RAF dimer (type II) inhibitor belvarafenib as measured by increased kinase activity, phosphorylation of downstream targets, as well as enhanced growth in cellular assays and mouse models of cancer in the presence of belvarafenib compared to controls (PMID: 33953400). In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that this mutation confers resistance to other RAF dimer (type II) inhibitors such as AZ-628 and LXH-254 but retains sensitivity to downstream MAPK inhibitors such as cobimetinib (MEK) and GDC-0994 (ERK) (PMID: 33953400).

The ARAF N217I mutation is located in the conserved region-2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 25608663). Expression of this mutation in cholangiocarcinoma cell lines demonstrates that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and increased cell viability compared to wildtype (PMID: 25608663).

The AURKA F31I mutation is located in the aurora box of the protein (PMID: 12208850). The AURKA F31I variant is a germline variant associated with increased cancer risk (PMID: 15867347, 12881723). Expression of this mutation in Rat1 cells demonstratd that it is likely activating as measured by increased transformation compared to wildtype (PMID: 12881723).

ARID1B deletion results in the loss of the ARID1B protein. This mutation has been found in neuroblastoma (PMID: 23202128). Endogenous ARID1B deletion results in increased colony formation compared to re-expression of wildtype and loss of ARID1B in neuroblastoma and pancreatic cell lines results in increased cell viability and growth-factor independent proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 22233809, 23660946, 26340334).

ARID1B truncation mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations have been found in neuroblastoma (PMID: 28521285). Endogenous ARID1B deletion results in increased colony formation compared to re-expression of wildtype and loss of ARID1B in neuroblastoma and pancreatic cell lines results in increased cell viability and growth-factor independent proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 22233809, 23660946, 26340334).

AURKA is located in chromosomal region 20q13.2, which is an amplification hotspot in multiple tumor types including breast, bladder, ovarian, pancreatic and colon cancers (PMID: 10914715, 9606188). Amplification of AURKA leads to overexpression of AURKA protein, which has been demonstrated to induce cellular transformation in rodent fibroblasts and to generate tumors in xenograft models (PMID: 9606188). Mechanistically, AURKA overexpression is involved in the induction of centrosome duplication-distribution abnormalities and aneuploidy in both mouse fibroblasts (leading to transformation) and human breast epithelial cells (PMID: 9771714).

The AXL A273V mutation is located in the immunoglobulin V-set domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 32321774). Although not functionally characterized, in vitro studies with HCC827 and PC-9 cells expressing AXL A273V demonstrate that the mutation is resistant to erlotinib and MGCD265 as measured by persistent cell proliferation (Abstract: Wang. Abstract# 4903, AACR 2018. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/78/13_Supplement/4903/629404/Abstract-4903-AXL-inhibition-overcomes-erlotinib). AXL A273V demonstrated sensitivity in preclinical studies to combination treatment with erlotinib and MGCD265 as measured by decreased cell cycle progression in S phase, enhanced apoptosis and repressed cell migration compared to single-agent treatment (Abstract: Wang. Abstract# 4903, AACR 2018. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/78/13_Supplement/4903/629404/Abstract-4903-AXL-inhibition-overcomes-erlotinib).

The overexpression of AURKB is rare and the AURKB gene locus does not seem to be amplified in a majority of tumors, although in some cases low-level copy number changes have been observed in non-small cell lung cancer tumors (PMID: 16222316). In a mouse model, AURKB overexpression contributes to oncogenesis through induction of aneuploidy as well as inhibition of the cell cycle inhibitory protein p21cip1 (PMID: 26240282).

AXL amplification is an infrequent event occurring in higher frequency in a few tumor types such as anal cancer, uterine sarcomas and cervical cancer (PMID: 27764792). In vitro cell line and in vivo mouse model studies have demonstrated AXL amplification is activating as measured by the inhibition of overexpressed AXL decreasing cellular proliferation (PMID: 23264849, 25966280). AXL overexpression has been associated with resistance to tyrosine-kinase inhibitors in lung cancer cell lines and HER2 inhibitor trastuzumab in breast cancer (PMID: 22751098, 35594351). The oncogenic mechanism of AXL overexpression is likely related to AXL's role in MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT ligand-independent signaling (PMID: 25337673).

The BCL10 R58Q mutation is located in the CARD domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lymphoid neoplasms, specifically activated B cell–like diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (ABC-DLBCLs)(PMID: 35658124). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by significantly higher NF-κB activity in an NF-kB reporter assay, greater MALT1 activity in a MALT1 enzymatic reporter assay, and significantly increased p65 nuclear staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 35658124). In vivo studies suggest that the BCL10 R58Q mutant confers resistance to BTK inhibitors such as ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, or zanubrutinib as measured by sustained proliferation of tumors in a xenograft model upon drug treatment (PMID: 35658124).

Truncating mutations of BCL10 occur either within or C-terminal to the CARD domain of the protein. Experimental studies have shown that mutations within the CARD domain cannot induce cell death or activate NF-kB signaling. In contrast, mutations after the CARD domain, while retaining NF-kB signaling, failed to induce apoptosis (PMID: 9989495, 10319863).

Translocations involving BCL10 and IGH are found in patients with mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) B-cell lymphoma, localized to the lung or stomach (PMID: 9989495, 14760068, 15356642, 17122510). The resultant IGH-BCL10 rearrangement pairs the IGH enhancer upstream of the entirety of the BCL10 gene, resulting in overexpression of the BCL10 protein (PMID: 11830492, 9989495, 15682443). Activated BCL10 initiates NF-ĸB and JNK signaling pathways, leading to enhanced B-cell proliferation (PMID: 15878976, 26668357). Overexpression of BCL10 results in reduced B-cell receptor (BCR)-mediated apoptosis and enhanced B cell survival, demonstrating that the fusion is oncogenic (PMID: 15878976). Patients with an IGH-BCL10 fusion are typically not responsive to Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy (PMID: 20520640, 17167822, 14760068).

The BCORL1-ELF4 fusion protein includes exons 1-11 of BCORL1 and exon 8 of ELF4 (PMID: 21499249). This fusion protein has been identified in patients with hepataceullar carcinoma. Expression of BCORL1-ELF4 in a luciferase transcriptional reporter assay demonstrated that BCORL1-ELF4 had reduced transcriptional activity compared to controls (PMID: 21499249).

The BCL10 E140* truncating mutation is located in the C-terminal region of BCL10. This mutation has been found in lymphoid neoplasms, specifically activated B cell–like diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (ABC-DLBCLs). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by significantly higher NF-κB activity in an NF-kB reporter assay, greater MALT1 activity in a MALT1 enzymatic reporter assay, and significantly increased p65 nuclear staining compared to wildtype (PMID: 35658124). In vivo studies suggest that the BCL10 E140* mutant confers resistance to BTK inhibitors such as ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, or zanubrutinib as measured by sustained proliferation of tumors in a xenograft model upon drug treatment (PMID: 35658124).

BCL10 deletions are detected in patients with lymphoma and commonly result in the expression of truncated protein forms (PMID: 10845924). Experimental studies have shown that these mutations lose the ability to induce cell death and often demonstrate defective NF-kB signaling when compared to wildtype BCL10 cells, suggesting they are loss-of-function (PMID: 9989495, 10319863).

The BCORL1 Q1076H mutation is not located in a characterized functional domain of the protein. Expression of BCORL1 Q1076H in melanoma cells resulted in vemurafenib resistance as evidenced in proliferation and signaling assays in collaboration with BRAF V600E (PMID: 29605720).

Truncating mutations in BCORL1 occur throughout the entire gene, producing peptides lacking the nuclear receptor recruitment motif (LXXLL) and the C-terminus (PMID: 21989985). BCORL1 is a transcriptional co-repressor that binds to class II histone deacetylases to interact with CTBP1 and affect the repression of E-cadherin (PMID:22210327). Truncating mutations in BCORL1 have been identified in a subset of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) leading to its proposal as a tumor suppressor (PMID: 21989985).

The BIRC3 G297D mutation lies in the BIR3 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

Deletion of a region of 11q that encodes BIRC3 is found in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and is associated with increased disease progression (PMID: 30487125). CLL cell lines engineered to have BIRC3 deletions show that the absence of BIRC3 is associated with activation of the NFkB pathway, increased expression of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members and increased sensitivity to NF-kB inhibition compared to cells expressing wildtype BIRC3 (PMID: 30487125).

The BIRC3 C319Y mutation lies in the BIR3 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

Truncating BIRC3 mutations have been identified in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 26837699, 22308293). Expression of truncated BIRC3 lacking the RING finger domain in mouse cell lines demonstrated that BIRC3 loss is likely activating, as measured by increased foci formation, tumorigenicity and downstream signaling (PMID: 26094954, 22308293). Chronic lymphocytic leukemia cell lines engineered to have BIRC3 deletions show that absent BIRC3 expression is associated with activation of the NFkB pathway, increased expression of antiapoptotic BCL-2 family members and sensitivity to NF-kB inhibition compared to cells expressing wildtype BIRC3 (PMID: 30487125).

The BIRC3 H574A mutation is located in the RING finger domain of the BIRC3 protein. In vitro experiments have demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by focus formation and increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype controls (PMID: 26094954).

The BIRC3 S278R mutation lies in the BIR3 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

The BIRC3 R172I mutation lies in the BIR2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

The BIRC3 G472R mutation lies in the CARD domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

The BIRC3 T536R mutation lies on the C-terminal end of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wildtype BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

The BIRC3 S7I mutation lies at the N-terminal end of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

The BIRC3 S248C mutation lies between the BIR2 and BIR3 domains of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a mouse fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

The BIRC3 T488M mutation lies in the CARD domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

BTG1 truncation mutations can form several forms of C-terminally truncation BTG1 proteins. BTG1 deletions were found in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and are speculated to be a driver event in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 22359517).

Deletions in BTG1 have been identified in patients with B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 22343534, 29407587, 27151989). Loss of BTG1 enhances the stem cell renewal capacity of hematopoietic progenitor cells and mediates the upregulation of BCL6 in murine models (PMID: 29408281).

The BTG1 Q36H mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the BTG1 protein. This mutation has been identified in patients with diffuse large B cell lymphomas (PMID: 36656933). In vitro and vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by loss of MYC association and increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype germinal center B-cells (PMID: 36656933).

CDK8 amplification refers to the presence of multiple copies of the CDK8 gene due to copy number gain that leads to the overexpression of the encoded protein. Knockdown of CDK8 in multiple cell line models with high CDK8 expression inhibited cell proliferation. CDK8 kinase activity was necessary for β-catenin-driven signaling and transformation and CDK8 was found to drive expression of the oncogene, MYC, in a β-catenin-dependent manner. In addition, overexpression of wildtype CDK8 in immortal murine fibroblast (NIH 3T3) cells induced focus formation, anchorage-independent colony growth, and tumor formation in immuno deficient animals, whereas expression of a kinase-dead CDK8 variant did not. These observations confirm that CDK8 overexpression is oncogenic (PMID: 18794900).

The CDKN2B E35* mutation is located in the nuclear export signal of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 25873077). Expression of this mutation in a renal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased protein activity and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25873077).

The BLM C1055S mutation is located in the ATPase domain of the BLM protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in Bloom Syndrome (PMID: 17407155). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased ATPase and helicase activity compared to wildtype controls (PMID: 10069810, 11399766).

The CDKN2B A23E mutation is located in the cell cycle inhibitory region of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 25873077). Expression of this mutation in a renal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased protein activity and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25873077).

The CDKN2B D86N mutation is located in the cell cycle inhibitory region of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 25873077). Expression of this mutation in a renal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased protein activity and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25873077, 23715670).

CDKN2B deletions result in the loss of the protein. This mutation has been found in pancreatic cancer and lymphoma (PMID: 28892048, 20118908). Decreased expression of CDKN2B in melanocytes resulted in increased cell proliferation, and deletion of CDKN2B in a transgenic mouse model resulted in the development of pancreatic cancer (PMID: 26183406, 28892048).

CDKN2B hypermethylation results in decreased expression of the protein. This alteration has been found in acute lymphoid and myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and multiple myeloma (PMID: 17489980, 19064397). Decreased expression of CDKN2B in melanocytes resulted in increased cell proliferation and deletion of CDKN2B in a transgenic mouse model resulted in the development of pancreatic cancer (PMID: 26183406, 28892048).

CDKN2B truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations have been found in meningioma and renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 11485924, 25873077). Decreased expression of CDKN2B in melanocytes resulted in increased cell proliferation, and deletion of CDKN2B in a transgenic mouse model resulted in the development of pancreatic cancer (PMID: 26183406, 28892048).

The BIRC3 R448Q mutation lies in the CARD domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by a lack of foci formation and downstream signaling comparable to wild type BIRC3 (PMID: 26094954).

CYLD truncation mutations occur throughout the entire gene and result in reduced expression of the protein (PMID: 23426135). Truncating CYLD mutations have been identified in multiple myeloma, as well as in several skin tumors such as cylindromas, trichoepitheliomas and spiradenomas (PMID:23426135, 27775078). In vitro studies with CYLD-deficient HeLa and SiHa cells demonstrate that loss of CYLD is inactivating as measured by loss of the regulatory mechanisms for signaling pathways causing aberrant activation of NF-kB (PMID: 18977328).

The DOT1L E186A mutation is located in the catalytic DOT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with NCI-H460 cells expressing DOT1L E186A demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased levels of H3K79me2 on the RAF1 promoter compared to wildtype (PMID: 37256945).

Truncating mutations in BLM have been found in patients with Bloom syndrome who progress to early-onset colorectal cancer (PMID: 26358404). Deleterious mutations in BLM lead to increased genetic instability in gastric cancer, even in cancers with concurrent microsatellite instability (PMID: 11532193).

Truncating mutations in CHEK1 have been found in the C-terminus and kinase domains, and result in shortened, non-functional peptides (PMID: 18716058, 14681223, 23508805). Originally identified as a mediator of DNA damage response, CHEK1 is a tumor suppressor that induces cell cycle arrest at the G2/M phase by phosphorylating CDK1, among other mechanisms (PMID: 23508805). Heterozygous loss of this gene, but not full loss, has been shown to induce tumor formation in WNT1 oncogenic mice (PMID:10859164). Truncating mutations in CHEK1 have been identified in patients with stomach, endometrial and colorectal cancers (PMID: 12124347, 10757443, 11691784).

The CDKN2B P40T mutation is located in the nuclear export signal of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 25873077). Expression of this mutation in a renal cancer cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased protein activity and increased colony formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25873077).

The DOT1L S225L mutation is located in the catalytic DOT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29937994, 28481359). In vitro studies with NCI-H460 cells expressing DOT1L S225L demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased levels of H3K79me2 on the RAF1 promoter and increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 37256945).

The DOT1L I232N mutation is located in the catalytic DOT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with NCI-H460 cells expressing DOT1L I232N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced levels of H3K79me2 on the RAF1 promoter and reduced cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 37256945).

The DOT1L R231Q mutation is located in the catalytic DOT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in small cell lung carcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro and in vivo studies with NCI-H460 cells and cell-derived xenograft mouse models expressing DOT1L R231Q demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased levels of H3K79me2 on the RAF1 promoter, increased cellular proliferation and tumor growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 37256945). Preclinical studies with cell-derived xenograft mouse models expressing DOT1L R231Q demonstrated resistance to treatment with cisplatin, vinorelbine and SGC0946, as measured by reduced tumor inhibitory activity, and sensitivity to combination treatment SGC0946 plus binimetinib, as measured by reduced tumor growth (PMID: 37256945).

EED deletion mutations result in the loss of the protein and likely result in the loss of function of the PRC2 complex. These mutations have been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 22396593). In vivo studies with PRC2-deficient xenograft mouse studies demonstrate loss of EED is inactivating as measured by PRC2 loss driving tumor growth and cell proliferation (PMID: 25119042).

EED truncation mutations typically result in the loss of the protein and likely result in the loss of function of the PRC2 complex. These mutations have been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 22396593). In vivo studies with PRC2-deficient xenograft mouse studies demonstrate loss of EED is inactivating as measured by PRC2 loss driving tumor growth and cell proliferation (PMID: 25119042).

EPHA3 deletion mutations result in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 22829656). In vivo studies with mouse xenograft models with low expression of EPHA3 demonstrated that EPHA3 re-expression lowers tumor volume and decreases cell proliferation compared to EPHA3-deficient cells (PMID: 22829656).

The EPHB1 R84H mutation is located in the ephrin binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in colorectal cells resulted in compartmentalization of tumor cells in co-culture experiments with ephrin B ligand-presenting cells comparably to wildtype EPHB1 (PMID: 28108514).

Truncating mutations in EPHA3 occur throughout the entire gene and result in reduced expression of this protein (PMID: 28169277). These mutations have been identified in colorectal tumors (PMID: 28169277). In vivo studies with mouse xenograft models with low expression of EPHA3 demonstrated that EPHA3 re-expression lowers tumor volume and decreases cell proliferation compared to EPHA3-deficient cells (PMID: 22829656).

The EPHB1 G628W mutation occurs in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in colorectal cells resulted in disruption of epithelial integrity and the inability to compartmentalize tumor cells in co-culture experiments with ephrin B ligand presenting cells (PMID: 28108514). These data suggest that EPHB1 G628W expressing cells have an increased propensity to metastasize due to aberrant cell contact-dependent ephrin signaling (PMID: 28108514).

The EPHB1 R351W mutation occurs in the fibronectin domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in colorectal cells resulted in disruption of epithelial integrity and the inability to compartmentalize tumor cells in co-culture experiments with ephrin B ligand presenting cells (PMID: 28108514). These data suggest that EPHB1 R351W expressing cells have an increased propensity to metastasize due to aberrant cell contact-dependent ephrin signaling (PMID: 28108514).

The ERCC4 R689S mutation is located in the nuclease domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a fibroblast cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased protein stability and the inability to repair DNA crosslinks compared to wildtype (PMID: 23623386, 24027083).

The ERCC4 E875G mutation is located in the ruvA-like domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial breast cancer and has been identified in a large percentage of the population (PMID: 24465539). Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by reduced binding to DNA compared to wildtype (PMID: 24004570).
ERCC4 deletions result in the loss of the protein. Loss of ERCC4 in fibroblasts and in a transgenic mouse model results in defective DNA repair and growth retardation (PMID: 9580660, 14729965).

The ERCC4 S786F mutation is located in the nuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in familial breast cancer (PMID: 24027083). Expression of this mutation in ERCC4-knockout mouse embryo fibroblasts demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by the decreased ability to repair DNA crosslinks compared to wildtype (PMID: 24027083).

The DOT1L A1003S mutation is located outside of the DOT domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in small cell lung carcinoma (PMID: 26168399). In vitro studies with NCI-H460 cells expressing DOT1L A1003S demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 37256945).

The ERCC4 L230P mutation is located in the helicase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in Fanconi anemia (PMID: 23623386). Expression of this mutation in fibroblasts demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased protein stability and impaired nuclear localization compared to wildtype (PMID: 23623386).

ERCC4 truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations have been found in Xeroderma Pigmentosum Type F (PMID: 8887684). Endogenous expression of ERCC4 truncating mutations in fibroblasts demonstrated they are inactivating as measured by decreased protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 9580660).

ETV1 amplification is an event that has been identified in melanoma (PMID: 20160028, 23908683).  In vitro studies with human melanocytes overexpressing ETV1 in combination with activating NRAS or BRAF mutations demonstrated that amplification of ETV1 is activating as measured by induced anchorage-independent growth compared to singular NRAS and BRAF mutations (PMID: 20160028).

The TMPRSS2-ETV1 fusion replaces the 5' end of ETV1 with the 5' UTR of TMPRSS2 (PMID: 18563191). ETV1 is a member of the ETS family of transcription factors and the fusion causes overexpression of ETV1 due to the androgen-responsive TMPRSS2 promoter region. Studies in prostate cancer cell lines and knock-in mice show that this fusion contributes to tumorigenesis by altering metabolic processes (PMID: 23512661).

ETV1 overexpression in prostate cancer may occur due to translocations that fuse the 5' untranslated region of a highly expressed gene (such as TMPRSS2) to an early exon of ETV1 (usually involving exons 1-6). Gene fusions of ETV1 are highly heterogeneous and involve several different gene partners (PMID: 23814484, 23625457). The MIPOL1 gene locus next to the active FOXA1 gene implicated in prostate cancer pathogenesis is a common site of ETV1 full-length translocation, occurring in patient tumors as well as two prostate cancer cell lines. While there is some evidence that the truncated ETV1 may have differential activity compared to full-length ETV1, genetic evidence suggests both the truncated and full-length protein can be oncogenic (PMID:18794142, 21298110,17671502).

The EWSR1 (Ewing sarcoma breakpoint region 1) gene encodes the EWS protein. The EWSR1-ETV1 fusion encodes a chimeric protein with the N-terminal RNA-binding domain of EWSR1 and the C-terminal DNA-binding domain of ETV1 (PMID: 7700648). EWSR1-ETV1 is the third most common ETS fusion in Ewing sarcoma to EWSR1-FLI1 and EWSR1-ERG. EWSR1-ETV1 has been poorly studied as compared to the more prevalent and highly homologous EWSR1-FLI1 fusion. EWSR1-FLI1 expression is associated with malignant transformation of mesenchymal stem cells (PMID: 16357154) and causes transcriptional dysregulation. It binds to and opens GGAA repetitive elements in the chromatin to activate transcription. Conversely, it binds to canonical ETS binding GGAA sites and suppresses transcription (PMID: 25453903). The EWSR1-ETV1 fusion t(7;22)(p22;q12) has been shown to activate transcription of fibroblast growth factor 10 (FGF10), which is involved in mesenchymal cell growth (PMID: 25109552).

Truncating mutations in FAS occur throughout the entire gene and generally lead to loss of protein expression (PMID: 11454987). FAS is a cell membrane protein that, when bound to its ligand on T-cytotoxic lymphocytes (FasL) induces activation of the caspase cascade, resulting in apoptosis (PMID: 28424702). Inactivation of FAS through mutation or silencing has been shown to facilitate immune escape in tumors (PMID: 12204534, 28521443). Loss of FAS has been reported in colorectal carcinomas, adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and mucose-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)-lymphomas (PMID: 28521443, 11454987, 10190897).

FGF3 amplification is an event identified in breast cancer and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 9205106, 31123723). In vitro studies with MCF-7 cells overexpressing FGF3 demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by the increased cellular proliferation compared to FGF4-expressing cells and control cells (PMID: 10845805).

The EPHB1 R90C mutation occurs in the ephrin binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in colorectal cells resulted in compartmentalization of tumor cells in co-culture experiments with ephrin B ligand-presenting cells comparably to wildtype EPHB1 (PMID: 28108514).

FGF19 amplifications are detected across multiple tumor types, with higher frequency in breast and head and neck cancers (PMID: 28481359, 23550210). The gene is located close to other oncogenes, particularly CCND1, making it hard to discern which is the targeted gene for amplification (PMID: 24265351). Overexpression of FGF19 is tumorigenic in cell lines and mouse models of liver cancer and its overexpression has also been described in clinical specimens of hepatocellular cancer (PMID: 21397858, 22309595). Assuming the amplification is associated with increased FGF19 protein levels, this suggests an oncogenic role for the alteration.

FGF4 amplification is an event identified in breast cancer and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 25950492, 31123723). In vitro studies with EF43 cells overexpressing FGF4 demonstrated that amplification of FGF4 is activating as measured by increased angiogenesis and tumor growth compared to FGF4-null EF43 cells (PMID: 9407972, 7591288).

The FH K477dup mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in fumarate hydratase deficiency and leiomyoma (PMID: 9635293, 23612258, 25985877). This mutation has not yet been characterized.

The FH Y465C mutation (sometimes called Y422C) is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (PMID: 12772087, 21398687). Endogenous expression of this mutation in lymphoblastoid cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by reduced protein activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 16597677).
The FH S186N mutation is located in the lyase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in cutaneous leiomyoma (PMID: 28481359). This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

FH truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations have been found as germline mutations in leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (PMID: 11865300, 15937070, 12772087, 12761039). Endogenous expression of these mutations in cutaneous leiomyomata samples demonstrated that they are inactivating as measured by reduced protein activity compared to normal skin samples (PMID: 11865300).

The FH M195T mutation (sometimes called M152T) is located in the lyase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (PMID: 12772087, 22764886). This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.

The FH T330P mutation (sometimes called T287P) is located in the lyase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in uterine and cutaneous leiomyoma (PMID: 16309500). This mutation has not yet been functionally characterized.
FLT1 amplification has been observed in some cases of colorectal and head and neck cancer (PMID: 28481359). No oncogenic effect has been ascribed to the amplification of FLT1.

FH deletions result in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been found as germline mutations in leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (PMID: 11865300, 15937070, 12772087, 12761039). Endogenous FH deletion in cutaneous leiomyomatosis samples resulted in reduced protein activity compared to normal skin samples (PMID: 11865300).

The CMSS1-FLT1 rearrangement results from the N-terminal region of CMSS1 fusing with the intact tyrosine kinase domain of FLT1. This fusion has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 37792599). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing CMSS1-FLT1 demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and constitutive activation compared to vector control (PMID: 37792599). Preclinical studies of this fusion demonstrate sensitivity to axitinib as measured by decreased cell viability following treatment (PMID: 37792599).

The FH G397R mutation (sometimes called G354A) is located in the lyase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (PMID: 19183174, 20618355. 19967458, 12761039, 25790038, 26900816). Endogenous expression of this mutation in peripheral blood lymphocytes demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by reduced protein activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 21398687).

The FOXO1 S22P mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24388756). In vitro studies with FOXO1-depleted SUDHL4 cells expressing FOXO1 S22P demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by co-hyperactivation of PI3K/AKT and SAPK signaling and loss of phosphorylation (PMID: 34380064).

The FOXO1 L217A mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 L217A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The PAX7-FOXO1 fusion protein combines the N terminus of PAX7, including the PAX7 DNA binding domain, with the C-terminus of FOXO1. This fusion protein is found in patients with rhabdomyosarcoma. The presence of the PAX7-FOXO1 fusion gene suggests a poorer prognosis, though to a lesser extent than the PAX3-FOXO fusion gene (PMID: 29367756, 26008753, 22089931, 22454413)

The FOXO1 N216A mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 N216A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The FOXO1 H215A mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 H215A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The FOXO1 S205N mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26647218). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 S205N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The FOXO1 I186T mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 I186T demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding and transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The FOXO1 L219A mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 L219A demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by transcriptional activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The gene T24A mutation is located in an N-terminal phosphorylation site of the gene protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional repression, reduced downstream signaling, and altered insulin-mediated transcription compared to wildtype (PMID: 16670091, 17646672).

The FOXO1 L183P mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 L183P demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding and transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The FOXO1 M1L mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. In vitro studies with FOXO1-depleted SUDHL4 cells and in vivo studies with mice expressing M1L demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased mature B cell expression and co-hyperactivation of PI3K/AKT and SAPK signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 34380064).

The FOXO1 A166V mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 32187361). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 A166V demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The FOXO1 R214A mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 R214A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The FOXO1 L168V mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 L168V demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

FOXO1 truncation mutations occur throughout the gene and likely lead to loss of the protein. In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing C-terminal and N-terminal truncated FOXO1 transcripts demonstrate that FOXO1 truncation mutations are likely inactivating as measured by N-terminal fragment transcripts having reduced binding to PLK1 compared to full-length FOXO1 (PMID: 24407358).

The FOXO1 I213A mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 I213A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The gene R514C mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in neurodevelopmental disorders (PMID: 26647308). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity and abnormal cellular localization compared to wildtype (PMID: 26647308).

Truncating mutations of FOXP1 are found across the length of the gene and likely lead to loss of functional protein. In vitro studies of FOXP1 knockdown in prostate cancer and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma cell lines demonstrated that loss of functional FOXP1 protein is inactivating and likely oncogenic, as measured by accelerated androgen-dependent cell proliferation and enhanced cell migration compared to control (PMID: 25329375, 38279090).

Amplification of FOXP1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. FOXP1 amplification has been identified in MALT and follicular lymphomas (PMID: 15703784, 16200457). In vitro studies with breast cancer cell lines overexpressing FOXP1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased chemokine and cytokine expression and lymphocyte migration compared to low expression FOXP1 (PMID: 30579865). In contrast, in vitro studies with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma cell lines overexpressing FOXP1 inhibited cellular proliferation, migration and invasion, suggesting a tissue-specific effect (PMID: 38279090).

The IGH-FOXP1 Fusion places the FOXP1 gene under the control of the IGH locus and leads to overexpression of full-length FOXP1 protein (PMID: 24416450). This mutation is found in marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of MALT type and may be diagnostic of the disease (PMID: 17122510, 15703784). In vitro studies with U-2932, SU-DHL-4, SU-DHL-6 and SU-DHL-7 cells overexpressing FOXP1 demonstrate that the IGH-FOXP1 fusion is likely activating as measured by increased tumor suppression following FOXP1 knockdown (PMID: 21460242).

The gene P1132L mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in melanomas (PMID: 27659111).  In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by increased proliferation and invasion, especially in glutamate depleted conditions, compared to wildtype (PMID: 27659111).

The gene P1133S mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in melanomas (PMID: 27659111).  In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by increased proliferation and invasion, especially in glutamate depleted conditions, compared to wildtype (PMID: 27659111).

The gene G762E mutation is located in the glutamate binding domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in melanomas (PMID: 27659111, 24455489). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is likely oncogenic as measured by increased proliferation and invasion, especially in glutamate depleted conditions, compared to wildtype (PMID: 27659111).

The gene G889E mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in melanomas (PMID: 24739903, 27659111). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by defective NMDA receptor assembly and reduced ion channel function compared to wildtype (PMID: 27659111). Inactivation of GRIN2A led to increased proliferation and invasion, especially in glutamate depleted conditions (PMID: 27659111).

Somatic mutations in GRIN2A were identified in ~25% of malignant melanoma samples following whole exome sequence analysis, and functional characterization of truncating or nonsense GRIN2A mutants [W372*, Q891*, W1271*, R920K] revealed reduced binding and loss of NMDA receptor complex formation between GRIN1 and mutant GRIN2A. GRIN2A mutants demonstrated increased anchorage-independent growth in soft agar and increased migration. Knockdown of GRIN2A expression in melanoma cells resulted in increased proliferation of cells bearing wildtype, but not mutant, GRIN2A. These GRIN2A somatic loss-of-function mutations exerted a dominant negative effect and inhibited the tumor suppressive phenotype of wildtype GRIN2A in melanoma (PMID: 24739903).

The FOXO1 T24I mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 31558468). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 T24I demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of AKT phosphorylation and DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

ID3 truncation mutations typically target the C-terminus and result in non-functional proteins. These mutations have been identified in Burkitt lymphoma (Abstract: Love et al. Abstract# 3906, ASH 2015. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/126/23/3906). In vitro studies with C2C12 cells expressing ID3 truncated in the C-terminal and N-terminal regions demonstrated that ID3 truncating mutations in the C-terminus are inactivating as measured by loss of inhibition of the MCK-CAT reporter gene as compared to wildtype (PMID: 9016574).

The ID3 L64F mutation lies in the helix-loop-helix domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Burkitt lymphoma cell lines demonstrated it is inactivating, as measured by decreased association with the transcription factor TCF3 and increased survival compared to wildtype ID3 (PMID: 22885699).

The ID3 P56S mutation lies in the helix-loop-helix domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Burkitt lymphoma cell lines demonstrated it is inactivating, as measured by increased survival compared to wildtype ID3 (PMID: 22885699).

The IGF1R M1255I mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in R-cells demonstrated that it is likely activating, as shown by increased downstream pathway activation compared to wildtype IGF1R. However, intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the protein was not affected by the mutation (PMID: 22778948).

The FOXO1 N216K mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 24388756). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXO1 N216K demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding and transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 35079069).

The IGF1R A1347V mutation is located in the C-terminal end of the protein. Expression of this mutation in R-cells demonstrated that it is likely activating, as shown by increased downstream pathway activation compared to wildtype IGF1R. However, intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the protein was not affected by the mutation (PMID: 22778948).

The IGF1R R10L mutation is found at the N-terminus of the protein. Endogenous expression of this mutation in fibroblasts derived from a patient with severe growth retardation demonstrated that it was inactivating, as shown by impaired IGF1R autophosphorylation as compared to control fibroblasts with wildtype IGF1R (PMID: 23045302).

IKBKE amplification is a rare event occurring across a few tumor types with higher frequencies observed in adrenocortical carcinoma, nerve sheath tumors, breast cancer and uterine sarcoma (cBioPortal, Zehir, A et al. Nature Medicine, 2017). IKBKE amplification has been observed in breast tumors and human cell line models for the disease and is associated with IKBKE overexpression, augmented cellular proliferation and increased oncogenicity (PMID: 25365225, 17574021). This suggests an oncogenic role for the amplification of IKBKE, likely attributable to its role in the regulation of NFκB signaling.

The IL7R S185C mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation is found in patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemias. Expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that it is activating when expressed with dimerization partner CRLF2, as shown by increased downstream pathway activation and increased growth factor-independent cell proliferation compared to wildtype cells or expression of IL7R S185C or CRLF2 alone (PMID: 21536738).

Deletions of INPP4B are often the result of copy number deletions at 4q31.1-3 leading to loss of the INPP4B genomic locus. Knockdown of INPP4B in cell lines is associated with increased phosphorylated AKT (PMID: 19647222, 21127264) and SGK3 (PMID: 25428846), both of which are downstream mediators of the PI3K pathway. Additionally, INPP4B knockdown was associated with anchorage independent growth and invasiveness (PMID: 19647222). Mouse xenografts of INPP4 knockdown cell lines demonstrated increased tumor volume relative to INPP4 wildtype cells (PMID: 21127264). Additionally, mice with loss of INPP4B in the context of PTEN loss developed thyroid tumors (PMID: 25883023). Profiling of TCGA data revealed a tendency for alterations in INPP4B and PTEN as well as in INPP4B and PIK3CA to co-occur (PMID: 25883023).

The IL-7R T244_I245insCPT mutation occurs within the IL-7R transmembrane domain. Expression of this mutant receptor led to constitutive, ligand-independent signaling as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of downstream targets such as STAT5, AKT and BAD. In addition, the IL-7R T244_I245insCPT mutant protein could form homodimers and signal constitutively independent of and γc JAK3; however, this mutant remained dependent on the presence of JAK1. Expression of this mutant receptor in cell lines and xenograft models led to increased proliferation and increased tumor volume indicating that this mutation is oncogenic. Cells expressing the T244_I245insCPT mutant were found to be sensitive to JAK-STAT pathway inhibitors including pyridone-6, CP-690550, and INCB018424 (PMID: 21892159).

Truncating mutations of the INPP4B gene result in loss of protein expression. Functional studies of INPP4B truncating mutations have yet to be done; however, models of INPBB4 knockdown or deletion result in increased pathway activation and increased transformation (PMID: 19647222, 21127264, 25428846).

KLF4 encodes a Kruppel family transcription factor that is known to be required for normal skin development (PMID: 17130451). KLF4 regulates the cell cycle through a p53-mediated mechanism (PMID: 31515251) and inhibits epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in gastrointestinal (GI) malignancies (PMID: 24168184). Somatic mutations in KLF4 have been previously reported in non-NF2 meningiomas (PMID: 31123420, 23348505). KLF4 is considered to be a tumor suppressor, and its loss has been implicated in the disease progression of several GI carcinomas, in which it is associated with a worse prognosis (PMID: 24168184, 29062163, 20699379).

Amplification of IRS2 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. Overexpression of IRS2 has been identified in breast cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 17043687, 16127164, 30250623). In vivo studies with mouse models of hepatocarcinogenesis overexpressing IRS2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by decreased apoptosis compared to wildtype (PMID: 16127164). In vitro studies with SNU1079 cells overexpressing IRS2 demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased migratory and invasive capacities compared to the silencing of IRS2 (PMID: 26684807). Preclinical studies with patient-derived xenograft models of small-cell lung cancer harboring IRS2 amplification demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with ceritinib as measured by inhibition of cell growth and impaired tumor sphere formation (PMID: 32099898).

The IGH-MALT1 fusion protein is a result of the T(14;18)(q32;q21) chromosomal translocation, fusing the N-terminus of IGH with the C-terminus of MALT1. This fusion protein has been reported in MALT lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma (PMID: 12406890, 19965626, 30089750). While this fusion has not been functionally characterized, other MALT1 fusion proteins including the C-terminus of MALT1 have been shown to be activating as measured by the aberrant activation of NF-kb signaling (PMID: 22689981).

The KLF4 K409Q mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in secretory meningiomas and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 23404370). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing KLF4 K409Q demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by upregulation of the HIF-1a pathway compared to wildtype (PMID: 32245394).

The BIRC3-MALT1 fusion, also known as the API2-MALT1 fusion, is associated with mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)-type lymphomas (PMID: 12651604). Expression of this fusion protein in a human B cell lymphoma cell line demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased downstream NFκB signaling and increased proliferation compared to wildtype MALT1 protein (PMID: 15598810, 11262391). The fusion protein has been shown to be transforming as measured by colony formation in NIH3T3 cells (PMID: 15184680).

The MEF2B T70R mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the MEF2B protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by decreased binding of HDAC4, which results in increased MEF2B activity (PMID: 15567413).

Amplification of MCL1 is found commonly across a large spectrum of tumor types. In vitro and in vivo studies have shown that MCL1 amplification can cooperate with MYC overexpression to promote lung tumorigenesis by facilitating evasion of MYC-induced apoptosis in pulmonary alveolar cells (PMID: 21406400). Additional studies of transgenic mice have shown that MCL1 expression in hematolymphoid tissues enhanced cell viability in vitro and in vivo (PMID: 9787159).

The MEF2B D83V mutation resides in the MADS-box domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (PMID: 29477338). Expression of this mutation in different cell lines has been shown to both enhance and reduce MEF2B transcriptional activity (PMID: 30205047, 23974956). Expression of the D83V alteration leads to defective DNA binding of the MEF2B co-repressor CABIN1 (PMID: 26245647, 23974956). In vivo studies with mice expressing MEF2B D83V demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by the inability of CABIN1 to negatively regulate MEF2B, leading to germinal center enlargement and lymphoma development (PMID: 30205047).

The MEF2B K4E mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26245647). In vitro studies with HEK293A cells expressing this mutation demonstrate the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by reduced MEF2B transcriptional activity and inability to activate transcription of downstream targets due to ineffective DNA binding (PMID: 26245647, 23974956).

MEF2B amplification results in MEF2B protein overexpression. Overexpression of MEF2B has been identified in ovarian cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma, esophageal cancer and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 23550210, 21796119). In vitro studies with HEK293A cells overexpressing MEF2B demonstrate that MEF2B amplification is activating as measured by increased epithelial-mesenchymal transition and increased cell migration (PMID: 26245647).

The MEF2B N81Y mutation is located in the MADS-box domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (PMID: 23974956). Expression of the N81Y alteration in B cells leads to defective DNA binding of the MEF2B co-repressor CABIN1 with no effect on transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 23974956). In silico analysis predicts that MEF2B N81Y is likely activating by increasing the stability of the MEF2B dimer (PMID: 23974956).

The MRE11 K464R mutation is located adjacent to the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (PMID: 37759323). In vitro studies with SKOV3 cells expressing MRE11 K464R demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased binding to RAD50/RPS3 and enhanced non-homologous end joining repair efficiency compared to wildtype (PMID: 37759323). Preclinical studies with this mutation demonstrate resistance to olaparib as measured by sustained cell viability following treatment (PMID: 37759323). Knockdown of RAD50/RP3S3 was demonstrated to restore sensitivity to olaparib in SKOV3 cells expressing MRE11 K464R (PMID: 37759323).

The MEF2B Y69H mutation is located in the MADS-box domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (PMID: 23974956). Expression of the Y69H alteration in B cells leads to defective DNA binding of the MEF2B co-repressor CABIN1 (PMID: 23974956). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate that MEF2B Y69H is likely activating as measured by increased transcriptional activity of BCL6 (PMID: 23974956).

The MRE11 N117S mutation is located in the metallophos domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in ataxia telangiectasia-like disorder (PMID: 10612394, 12966088). In vitro studies with ATLD cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrated MRE11 N117S is inactivating as measured by impaired interaction with NBS1 compared to wildtype (PMID: 12966088, 23080121).

The MEF2B E77K mutation is located in the MADS-box domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (PMID: 23974956). Expression of the E77K alteration in B cells leads to defective DNA binding of the MEF2B co-repressor CABIN1 (PMID: 23974956). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate that MEF2B E77K is likely activating as measured by increased transcriptional activity of BCL6 (PMID: 23974956).

The MSH3 K383Rfs*32 mutation is located in the 8-deoxyadenosine (A8) repeat region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in melanoma and colorectal cancer (PMID: 24755471, 24265153). Endogenous expression of this mutation in HCT116 cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by loss of MSH3 protein expression (PMID: 23724141, 18922920). Reexpression of wildtype MSH3 in HCT116 cells was shown to stabilize the elevated microsatellite instability phenotype in these cells (PMID: 23724141, 18922920).

MRE11 truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and lead to loss of the protein (PMID: 23912341). These mutations have been identified in bladder cancer and ataxia telangiectasia-like disorder (PMID: 33558481, 28436950). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing C-terminally truncated MRE11 demonstrate MRE11 truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by reduced DNA binding and subsequent decrease in DNA repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 33558481). Loss of MRE11 has been shown to lead to PARP inhibitor sensitivity in endometrial carcinoma cell lines (PMID: 24927325).

MSH3 deletion results in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in MLH1-deficient colorectal cancer (PMID: 14871813). In vivo studies with MSH3-deficient mice demonstrate loss of MSH3 is inactivating as measured by defective mismatch repair activity and tumor development (PMID: 10706084).

NCOR1 is a tumor suppressor and truncating mutations in this gene are assumed to be oncogenic. In breast cancer, NCOR1 acts as a co-repressor and recruitment to DNA is necessary for ligand-dependent transcriptional repression by estrogen receptor (ER) (PMID:21102521). A similar feature is seen with thyroid-hormone receptors and retinoic acid receptors, although the ability of NCOR1 to repress transcription in this setting is ligand-independent (PMID:7566114).

The NFKBIA E14* mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in ectodermal dysplasia with immune deficiency (PMID: 18412279). Endogenous expression of this mutation in patient samples demonstrated NFKBIA E14* is activating as measured by strong negative inhibition on NF-kB signaling compared to control samples (PMID: 18412279).

The NFKBIA L34P mutation is located outside of a known functional domain. This mutation has been found in a patient with autoinflammatory disease (PMID: 32750042). Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by sustained NF-κB signaling inhibition (PMID: 32750042). In vivo data in a genetically engineered mouse model and in myeloid cells harboring the mutation show decreased expression of NF-κB-induced genes and decreased NF-κB nuclear translocation (PMID: 32750042).

NBN truncating mutations are predicted to result in a mutant NBN protein that lacks the forkhead-associated and BCRT domains and can therefore no longer bind to and repair DNA double-stranded breaks. These mutations are found in the germline of patients with Nijmegen breakage syndrome which is characterized by microcephaly, growth retardation, immunodeficiency, and cancer predisposition (PMID: 9590180).

Truncating mutations in NFKBIA occur throughout the entire gene, lead to loss of the NFKBIA protein and result in alteration of the NF-κB pathway (PMID: 27647909). NFKBIA is has been shown to inhibit NF-KB activity, which is involved in inflammatory responses in humans (PMID: 18412279). Certain alterations in NFKBIA have been associated with gastric cancer and glioblastoma multiforme (PMID: 28670959, 25215581). Truncating mutations in NFKBIA have been identified in nasopharyngeal carcinomas (PMID: 27647909).

The NSD1 Y1971C mutation is located in the SET domain of the NSD1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by abolished methyltransferase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 37150325).

The NSD1 T2029 mutation is located in the SET domain of the NSD1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as demonstrated by increased methyltransferase activity resulting in H3K36 trimethylation compared to wildtype, which is only capable of HEK36 dimethylation (PMID: 37150325).

The NFKBIA S32I mutation was found in a patient with severe anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with T-cell immunodeficiency. Endogenous expression of this mutation in patient fibroblast samples and expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is activating, as it stabilizes the NFKBIA protein and inhibits the NF-kB signaling pathway compared to wildtype NFKBIA (PMID: 14523047).

The NSD1 R2017L mutation is located in the SET domain of the NSD1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by abolished methyltransferase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 37150325).

Damaging, truncating mutations are enriched in certain subtypes of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, specifically laryngeal tumors (PMID: 29176703). Restoration of NSD1 function in glioma and neuroblastoma cells lacking NSD1 leads to a reduction in colony formation and cell proliferation (PMID: 20018718).

The NFKBIA S36Y mutation was found in a patient with mild anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency. Endogenous expression of this mutation in patient fibroblast samples demonstrated that it is likely activating, as it stabilizes the NFKBIA protein and inhibits the NF-kB signaling pathway compared to control samples (PMID: 23864385).

The NT5C2 D407A mutation lies in the tip region of the arm segment of the protein.  This mutation has been found in patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) following treatment with 6-mercaptopurine (PMID: 30910786). The mutation is likely activating as demonstrated by increased 5'-nucleotidase activity of recombinant protein expressing the mutation compared to wildtype NT5C2 (PMID: 23377281, 29990496, 30910786). In vitro studies suggest that the NT5C2 D407A mutation shows increased resistance to mercaptopurine and thioguanine therapy compared to wildtype NT5C2, but shows sensitivity to nelarabine and mizoribine as measured by cell viability (PMID: 23377281, 29342136). Crystallization, structural modeling and biochemical characterization of this mutant protein demonstrate that it is activating as it disrupts a regulatory switch responsible for NT5C2 self-inactivation (PMID: 30910786).

Truncating mutations of MSH3 can result in loss of MSH3 protein expression due to loss of heterozygosity of the wildtype allele (PMID: 27476653). Loss of MSH3 has been found in the germline of patients with colorectal adenomatous polyposis as well as in patients who have developed early-onset cancers (PMID: 27476653, 28528517). While truncating mutations in MSH3 have not been implicated in Lynch syndrome per se, they have been shown to exacerbate the MSH6-null phenotype in patients with concurrent MSH6 mutations and can cooperate with MSH6 loss for tumorigenesis (PMID: 28528517, 10706084).

The NT5C2 D407E mutation is located in the arm region of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) following treatment with 6-mercaptopurine (PMID: 30910786). Crystallization, structural modeling and biochemical characterization of this mutant protein demonstrate that it is activating as it disrupts a regulatory switch responsible for NT5C2 self-inactivation (PMID: 30910786). This mutation shows increased nucleotidase activity under basal conditions but still responds to allosteric activation (PMID: 30910786).

The NFKBIA M37K mutation was found in a patient with ectodermal dysplasia with immune deficiency. Endogenous expression of this mutation in patient samples demonstrated that it is likely activating, as it stabilizes the NFKBIA protein and inhibits the NF-kB signaling pathway compared to control samples (PMID: 23708964).

Crystallization, structural modeling and biochemical characterization of this mutant protein demonstrate that it is activating as it disrupts a regulatory switch responsible for NT5C2 self-inactivation (PMID: 30910786).

Crystallization, structural modeling and biochemical characterization of this mutant protein demonstrate that it activating as it responds to allosteric activators much more strongly than wildtype NT5C2 (PMID: 30910786).

The NT5C2 K359Q mutation lies in the regulatory helix A domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) following treatment with 6-mercaptopurine (PMID: 30910786). The mutation is likely activating as demonstrated by increased 5'-nucleotidase activity of recombinant protein expressing the mutation compared to wildtype NT5C2 (PMID: 23377281, 29990496). Crystallization, structural modeling and biochemical characterization of this mutant protein demonstrate that it is activating as it forces the protein into an  active configuration, resulting in high levels of nucleotidase activity in the absence of allosteric activators (PMID: 30910786).
