The PIK3CB A593V mutation is located in the C2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a kidney epithelial cell line demonstrated that it was likely neutral as measured by no in vivo xenograft tumor formation (PMID: 27147599).

The PIK3CB E552K mutation is located in the helical domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast and intestinal cancer (PMID: 28481359, 28481359). Expression of this mutation in human mammary epithelial cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by modestly increased pathway activation and soft agar growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 16339315).

The PIK3CB D1067A mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in glioblastoma. Expression of this mutation in embryonic kidney and breast cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation compared to wildtype. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is resistant to high concentrations (>1uM) of the pan-PI3K inhibitor GDC-0941 in breast cancer cell lines as measured by sustained cell proliferation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 26759240).

The NT5C2 D407Y mutation is located in the arm region of the protein. This mutation has been found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) following treatment with 6-mercaptopurine (PMID: 30910786). Crystallization, structural modeling and biochemical characterization of this mutant protein demonstrate that it is activating as it disrupts a regulatory switch responsible for NT5C2 self-inactivation (PMID: 30910786). This mutation shows increased nucleotidase activity under basal conditions but still responds to allosteric activation (PMID: 30910786).

The PIK3CB D1067Y mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancer. Expression of this mutation in embryonic kidney, breast cancer and rat embryonic cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and soft agar growth compared to wildtype. The oncogenic activity of this mutation was potentiated by PTEN knockdown. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is resistant to high concentrations (>1uM) of the pan-PI3K inhibitor GDC-0941 in breast cancer cell lines as measured by sustained cell proliferation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 26759240).

PIK3CB amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung, breast and ovarian cancers, among others (reviewed in PMID: 25533673). Overexpression of PIK3CB in chicken embryo fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and colony formation (PMID: 16432180). Amplification of PIK3CB predicts inferior prognosis in DLBCL as measured in a cohort of 60 patients (PMID: 24418330).

The PIK3CB D1067V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in renal cell carcinoma, glioblastoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, thyroid carcinoma and endometrial carcinoma as well as in an EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer tumor biopsy with acquired erlotinib resistance. Expression of this mutation in fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation, cell proliferation and in vivo tumor formation compared to wildtype. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the PI3K inhibitor TGX-211 in patient-derived renal-cell carcinoma cells as well as fibroblast and lung cancer cell lines as measured by decreased cell viability and pathway activation in the presence of the drug but is resistant to the EGFR inhibitor erlotinib in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma cells as measured by sustained pathway activation and proliferation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 25982275).

The PIK3CB E470K mutation is located in the C2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in intestinal cancer (PMID: 28481359, 25344691). Expression of this mutation in hematopoietic and breast cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased growth factor-independent proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 29533785).

The PIK3CB E497D mutation is located in the C2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 24390350). Expression of this mutation in a kidney epithelial cell line demonstrated that it was activating as measured by modestly increased in vivo xenograft tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27147599).

The PIK3CB E633K mutation is located in the helical domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 20668451). Expression of this mutation in embryonic kidney and fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 23734178).

The ACPP-PIK3CB fusion results in the fusion of ACPP exons 1-2 with PIK3CB exons 2-22, including the PIK3CB catalytic kinase domain. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 26000489). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer tumor samples demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased PIK3CB protein expression, which has been shown to be activating in chicken embryo fibroblasts by increased pathway activation and colony formation (PMID: 16432180).

The PIK3CB E1051K mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in castration-resistant prostate cancer (PMID: 28843286). Expression of this mutation in rat embryo cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation, cell proliferation and growth in soft agar compared to wildtype (PMID: 29279775). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to the PI3K inhibitor, TGX-211, in colon cancer and glioma cell models as measured by decreased cell viability and pathway activation in the presence of the drug (PMID: 29279775).

The PMS2 G857A mutation occurs between the mismatch repair domain and the C-terminal dimerization domain of the protein. This mutation results in mismatch repair (MMR) activity comparable to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009). This mutation is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its prevalence in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

The PIK3CB A1048V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in intestinal cancer (PMID: 28481359). Expression of this mutation in a kidney epithelial cell line demonstrated that it was activating as measured by increased in vivo xenograft tumor formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27147599).

The PMS2 R107W mutation is located in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation results in decreased mismatch repair (MMR) proficiency in an in vitro assay compared to wildtype PMS2 (PMID: 27435373).

The PMS2 E41A mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation results in decreased ATP hydrolysis and mismatch repair (MMR) activity compared to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009, 20864418).

The PMS2 K541E mutation is located between the mismatch repair domain and the C-terminal dimerization domain of the protein. This mutation results in mismatch repair (MMR) activity comparable to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009). When found in the germline, this mutation is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its prevalence in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

PIK3CB fusions typically involve the N-terminus of another protein fused to the C-terminus of PIK3CB. The most common fusion partner ACPP (PMID: 26000489). These mutations have been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 26000489). PIK3CB fusions likely lead to elevated PIK3CB expression (PMID:16432180). Overexpression of PIK3CB in chicken embryo fibroblasts demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased pathway activation and colony formation (PMID: 16432180).

The PMS2 S46N mutation occurs in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colon cancer associated with constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome (PMID: 24027009). This mutation results in decreased mismatch repair (MMR) activity compared to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009).

The PMS2 E5K occurs in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its prevalence in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

The PMS2 G207E mutation occurs near the DNA mismatch repair domain. This mutation has been found in Lynch syndrome and microsatellite instability (MSI) colon polyps (PMID: 19479271). This mutation results in decreased mismatch repair (MMR) proficiency in an in vitro assay compared to wildtype PMS2 (PMID: 24027009).

The PMS2 S815L mutation is located in the C-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Lynch syndrome (PMID: 20186688, 16472587, 23837913, 28365877, 27435373). In vitro studies with mismatch repair assays and HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate PMS2 S815L is inactivating as measured by decreased protein stability and impaired mismatch repair activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 28365877, 27435373).

The PMS2 T485K mutation occurs between the mismatch repair domain and the C-terminal dimerization domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline variant in bladder cancer (PMID: 15256438). This mutation results in mismatch repair (MMR) activity comparable to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009). This mutation is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its prevalence in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

The PMS2 R20Q mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung cancer (PMID: 23981578). Expression of this mutation in drosophila leads to tumor formation upon UV irradiation, and expression in human cells results in increased focus formation and decreased mismatch repair compared to wildtype PMS2 (PMID: 23981578, 24027009).

The PMS2 P470S occurs between the mismatch repair domain and the C-terminal dimerization domain. This mutation is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its prevalence in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

The PMS2 I668V mutation occurs proximal to the C-terminal dimerization domain. This mutation is found as a germline variant in the Inuit population and leads to a new splice site that results in a truncated protein (PMID: 25691505). Patients with this variant are predisposed to cancer in a bimodal distribution that depends on the zygosity of the mutation, such that individuals with two copies of the mutation develop cancer earlier than those with one copy (PMID: 25691505).

Truncating mutations in PMS2 can produce several C-terminally truncated protein forms, affecting all or part the nuclease domain, thus eliminating the ability of PMS2 to incise the DNA flanking a mismatch. In addition, the loss of the MLH1 binding domain, which is found near the C-terminud of PMS2, causes PMS2 protein instability and inhibits the ability of PMS2 to heterodimerize, bind to damaged DNA and perform its endonuclease function (PMID: 7892206, 12697830). Truncating mutations are frequently detected in individuals with inherited Lynch syndrome, but also in constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome (PMID: 21376568, 20487569, 9488480, 16144131, 23582141, 24362816). Mouse modeling of PMS2 deletion results in the development of various cancers, including spontaneous thymic lymphoma and sarcoma. PMS2-deficient mice were also found to have increased sensitivity to chemical carcinogens (PMID:10439048). Tumors from PMS2-deficient mice have high microsatellite instability and have increased mutation accumulation (PMID: 7628019, 10874005, 9500552). Together, this data suggest that loss of PMS2 may contribute to tumor formation.
The PMS2 I66T mutation is located in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation results in mismatch repair (MMR) activity comparable to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 27435373).

The PMS2 S46I mutation is located in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in colon, endometrial and gastric cancers associated with Lynch syndrome and Turcot syndrome (PMID: 2257789, 18602922, 17557300, 16144131). This mutation results in decreased mismatch repair (MMR) activity compared to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays and is bioinformatically predicted to be pathogenic (PMID: 23709753, 24027009, 27435373).

The PMS2 I18V mutation occurs in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation results in mismatch repair (MMR) activity comparable to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009). This mutation is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its prevalence in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

The PMS2 H479Q mutation occurs between the mismatch repair domain and the C-terminal dimerization domain of the protein. This mutation results in mismatch repair (MMR) activity comparable to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009).

The PMS2 L585I mutation occurs between the mismatch repair domain and the C-terminal dimerization domain of the protein. This mutation results in mismatch repair (MMR) activity comparable to wildtype PMS2 in in vitro MMR assays (PMID: 24027009). This mutation is not considered pathogenic by The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours due to its prevalence in the general population (PMID: 24362816).

Large deletions in PMS2 leading to loss of PMS2 protein expression have been detected in families with Lynch syndrome (PMID: 18602922, 23837913). Deletion mutations in PMS2 are predicted to cause defective repair mismatches and produce insertion/deletion loops, which are most frequently associated with microsatellite repeat sequences (PMID: 16472587). Mouse modeling of PMS2 deletion results the development of various cancers, including spontaneous thymic lymphoma and sarcoma. PMS2-deficient mice were also found to have increased sensitivity to chemical carcinogens (PMID:10439048). Tumors from PMS2-deficient mice have high microsatellite instability and have increased mutation accumulation (PMID: 7628019, 10874005, 9500552). Together, this data suggest that loss of PMS2 may contribute to tumor formation.

The POLD1 E245K mutation is located adjacent to the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLD1 E245K suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLD1 E245K-mutant colon adenocarcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLD1 L606M mutation is located in motif A of the polymerase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in brain cancer and various hypermutated cancers (PMID: 25642631, 29056344). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the yeast-equivalent POLD1 L612M mutation demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced replication fidelity, increased ribonucleotide incorporation by seven-fold and increased spontaneous mutation rate compared to wildtype (PMID: 23245697, 19540301, 17121822).

The POLD1 L632M mutation is located in the polymerase domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLD1 L632M suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLD1 L632M-mutant brain glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLD1 R1016H mutation is located in the zinc-finger polymerase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 27149842). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLD1 R1016H suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLD1 R1016H-mutant solid tumors (PMID: 29056344).

The POLD1 E318K mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLD1 E318K suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLD1 E318K-mutant primitive neuroectodermal tumors and non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 29056344).

The POLD1 L474P mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vitro studies with fibroblast and intestinal cells expressing POLD1 L474P demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased somatic single-base substitution mutation burden and proofreading deficiency compared to wildtype (PMID: 38658779, 34594041).

The POLD1 R689W mutation is located in the polymerase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 27149842). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLD1 R689W suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLD1 R689W-mutant brain glioblastoma and colon adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLD1 S478N mutation is within the DNA polymerase family B exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been found with high penetrance in patients with familial colorectal cancer (PMID: 23263490). Expression of the POLD1 S478N mutation in yeast showed a mutation rate 12-fold higher than yeast expressing wildtype POLD1, suggesting this mutation is inactivating (PMID: 23263490).

The POLD1 D402N mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in prostate cancer (PMID: 23265383). In vitro studies with HEC1A cells overexpressing POLD1 D402N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by deficiency in proofreading compared to wildtype (PMID: 38067377).

The POLE V464A mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. Mutational analysis of a patient-derived colorectal cancer sample harboring POLE V464A demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a mismatch repair deficiency single base substitution (MMRd SBS) signature of over 30% (PMID: 35398880). In a clinical trial, a patient with colorectal cancer harboring POLE V464A was treated with nivolumab and achieved complete response (PMID: 35398880).

The POLE F367V mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in ultramutated endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 31829442). Analysis of tumors with this mutation suggested that it is likely inactivating as measured by POLE-score, a metric that takes into account tumor mutation burden as well as mutation signature compared to wildtype POLE and known POLE inactivating mutations (PMID: 31829442).

The POLE G6R mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in plasma cell myeloma (PMID: 30545397). Mutational analysis of a patient-derived colorectal cancer sample harboring POLE G6R demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a mismatch repair deficiency single base substitution (MMRd SBS) signature of over 30% (PMID: 35398880). In a clinical trial, a patient with colorectal cancer harboring POLE G6R was treated with nivolumab and demonstrated progressive disease (PMID: 35398880).

The POLE S461T mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE S461T suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in a patient with POLE S461T-mutant glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE R446Q mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 28776572). Mutational analysis of a patient-derived colorectal cancer sample harboring POLE R446Q demonstrates that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by an attenuated POLE single base substitution (SBS) signature of under 15%, indicating proficient proofreading mechanisms (PMID: 35398880). In a clinical trial, a patient with colorectal cancer harboring POLE R446Q was treated with nivolumab and demonstrated progressive disease (PMID: 35398880).

The POLE F367S mutation has been found in a colorectal carcinoma with an ultrahypermutator phenotype (PMID: 25228659). The residue is located in the protein's exonuclease domain and in vitro assays show that this variant reduces POLE's proofreading activity (PMID: 25228659). The variant is also found in mismatch-repair deficient colorectal cancer cell lines (PMID: 21157497). Whole genome sequencing data analysis from colorectal cancer samples harboring POLE F367S demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by sample mutational patterns, such as high mutation density and mutational strand asymmetry, that indicate proofreading deficiency (PMID: 32012149).

The POLE P436R mutation is located near the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation is recurrent in ultramutated endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 31829442). Analysis of tumors with this mutation suggested that it is likely inactivating as measured by POLE-score, a metric that takes into account tumor mutation burden as well as mutation signature compared to wildtype POLE and known POLE inactivating mutations (PMID: 31829442).

The POLE D275V mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 23528559). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE D275V suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE D275V-mutant lung adenocarcinoma and brain glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE A463D mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE A463D suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE A463D-mutant glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE S459del mutation is located in the exonuclease of the protein. While this variant has not been biologically characterized, missense mutations at this position (e.g., S459F) have been shown to be likely oncogenic and to ablate the proofreading activity of the protein, suggesting that this mutation is likely oncogenic (PMID: 25228659).

The POLE V411L mutation is located in a conserved residue in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation is recurrent in colorectal and endometrial carcinoma and is associated with hypermutation (PMID: 23636398). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrates that it is likey inactivating as measured by increased numbers of point mutations in DNA proofreading experiments in vitro (PMID: 25228659). Whole genome sequencing data analysis from colorectal cancer samples harboring POLE V411L demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by sample mutational patterns, such as high mutation density and mutational strand asymmetry,  that indicate proofreading deficiency (PMID: 32012149). A patient with colorectal cancer harboring the POLE V411L mutation had a durable complete response to treatment with pembrolizumab (Abstract: Silberman et al. JCO PO, 2019. https://ascopubs.org/doi/full/10.1200/PO.18.00214).

The P286S mutation of POLE is recurrent in colorectal and endometrial carcinoma and is located in a conserved residue in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This alteration likely perturbs its native proofreading function, leading to large numbers of point mutations throughout the genome (PMID: 25228659).

The POLE L424I mutation has been found in a colorectal carcinoma with an ultrahypermutator phenotype (PMID: 25228659). The residue is located in the protein's exonuclease domain and in vitro assays show that this variant reduces POLE's proofreading activity (PMID: 25228659).

The POLE S297F mutation is located in exon 9 of the protein. Mutations of amino acid S297 have been observed in ultra-mutated cases of colorectal and endometrial cancer (S297F, S297Y), and they exhibit the characteristic mutation spectrum of other exonuclease domain mutations (PMID: 25228659). S297F mutations were more frequent than P286 and V411 mutations in a Chinese cohort of endometrioid carcinoma (PMID: 24472300). Whole genome sequencing data analysis from colorectal cancer samples harboring POLE S297F demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by sample mutational patterns, such as high mutation density and mutational strand asymmetry, that indicate proofreading deficiency (PMID: 32012149).

The POLE S461P mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE S461P suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE S461P-mutant glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE S459Y mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in ultramutated endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 31829442). Analysis of tumors with this mutation suggested that it is likely inactivating as measured by POLE-score, a metric that takes into account tumor mutation burden as well as mutation signature compared to wildtype POLE and known POLE inactivating mutations (PMID: 31829442).

The POLE Y458C mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE Y458C suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE Y458C-mutant colon adenocarcinomas (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE S297Y mutation is located in exon 9 of the protein. Mutations of amino acid S297 have been observed in ultra-mutated cases of colorectal and endometrial cancer (S297F, S297Y), and they exhibit the characteristic mutation spectrum of other exonuclease domain mutations (PMID: 25228659). S297F mutations were more frequent than P286 and V411 mutations in a Chinese cohort of endometrioid carcinoma (PMID: 24472300).

The POLE D368Y mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation is recurrent in ultramutated endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 31829442). Analysis of tumors with this mutation suggested that it is likely inactivating as measured by POLE-score, a metric that takes into account tumor mutation burden as well as mutation signature compared to wildtype POLE and known POLE inactivating mutations (PMID: 31829442).

The POLE L424V mutation is in a highly conserved residue in the active site of the protein's exonuclease domain (PMID: 23263490). L424V has been found as a germline variant in families with colorectal cancer, where it was associated with a severe disease phenotype and loss of the wildtype in some but not all affected carriers (PMID: 23263490). Mutations in the equivalent residue in the yeast ortholog and in vitro assay using human constructs show that this variant reduces POLE's proofreading activity (PMID: 23263490, 25228659).

The POLE A463V mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 28776572). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE A463V suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE A463V-mutant lung squamous cell carcinoma and uterine endometrial adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE E978K mutation is located in the DNA pol B domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE E978K suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in a patient with POLE E978K-mutant unknown primary squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE A288V mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE A288V suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE A288V-mutant glioblastoma and stomach neuroendocrine carcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE M444K mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation is recurrent in ultramutated endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 31829442). Analysis of tumors with this mutation suggested that it is likely inactivating as measured by POLE-score, a metric that takes into account tumor mutation burden as well as mutation signature compared to wildtype POLE and known POLE inactivating mutations (PMID: 31829442).

The POLE F367L mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in serous carcinoma (PMID: 26763250). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE F367L suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE F367L-mutant glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE R47W mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic T-cell leukemia (PMID: 31697823). Mutational analysis of a patient-derived pancreatic cancer sample harboring POLE R47W demonstrates that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by an attenuated POLE single base substitution (SBS) signature of under 15%, indicating proficient proofreading mechanisms (PMID: 35398880). In a clinical trial, a patient with pancreatic cancer harboring POLE R47W was treated with nivolumab and demonstrated progressive disease (PMID: 35398880).

The POLE S461L mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 25124163). In vivo studies with yeast expressing POLE S461L demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased mutation rate compared to wildtype (PMID: 38219146).

The POLE P286H mutation is recurrent in colorectal and endometrial carcinoma and is located in a conserved residue in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This alteration likely perturbs its native proofreading function, as shown in in vitro experiments, leading to large numbers of point mutations throughout the genome (PMID: 25228659). Whole genome sequencing data analysis from colorectal cancer samples harboring POLE P286H demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by sample mutational patterns, such as high mutation density and mutational strand asymmetry, that indicate proofreading deficiency (PMID: 32012149).

The P286R mutation of POLE is recurrent in colorectal and endometrial carcinoma, associated with hypermutation and is located in a conserved residue in the exonuclease domain of the protein (PMID: 23636398). This alteration likely perturbs its native proofreading function, as shown in in vitro experiments, leading to large numbers of point mutations throughout the genome (PMID: 25228659). Whole genome sequencing data analysis from colorectal cancer samples harboring POLE P286R demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by sample mutational patterns, such as high mutation density and mutational strand asymmetry, that indicate proofreading deficiency (PMID: 32012149).

The POLE A456P mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in various tumors, including colon and endometrial cancers, with ultrahigh substitution mutation frequencies (PMID: 25228659, 23636398, 31829442, Abstract: Zhang et al., Abstract# e15531, ASCO Annual Meeting 2021. https://ascopubs.org/doi/abs/10.1200/JCO.2021.39.15_suppl.e15531). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, alignment studies comparing POLE to T4 DNA polymerase have suggested that this mutation is likely inactivating (PMID: 26763250, 31624068, 23528559, 29056344). A pediatric patient with ultra-hypermutated medulloblastoma harboring a mutation signature of germline POLE deficiency had a germline POLE A456P mutation (PMID: 31624068).

The POLE E978G mutation is located in the DNA pol B domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE E978G suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE E978G-mutant glioblastoma and uterine carcinosarcoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE D275G mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in caecal carcinoma (PMID: 28481359). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE D275G suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in a patient with POLE D275G-mutant pancreas ductal adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE P286L mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrial carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28776572). In vivo studies with yeast expressing POLE P286L demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 32424176).

The POLE P436H mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in glioma (PMID: 28805995). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE P436H suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE P436H-mutant glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE D368N mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 25124163). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE D368N suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in a patient with POLE D368N-mutant appendiceal adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE D275A mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE D275A suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in a patient with POLE D275A-mutant glioblastoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE P436S mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrioid carcinoma (PMID: 28776572). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE P436S suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE P436S-mutant colorectal carcinoma, glioblastoma and osteochondroma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE A463T mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE A463T suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in a patient with POLE A463T-mutant oligodendroglioma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE G330R mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized, a patient with biliary tract cancer harboring POLE G330R was treated with nivolumab and achieved stable disease (PMID: 35398880).

The POLE D435G mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized, a patient with colorectal cancer harboring POLE D435G was treated with nivolumab and achieved partial response (PMID: 35398880).

The POLE K425R mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. Mutational analysis of a patient-derived pancreatic cancer sample harboring POLE K425R demonstrates that the mutation is inactivating as measured by a mismatch repair deficiency single base substitution (MMRd SBS) signature of over 30% (PMID: 35398880). In a clinical trial, a patient with pancreatic cancer harboring POLE K425R was treated with nivolumab and demonstrated progressive disease (PMID: 35398880).

The POLE V411M mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation is found in colorectal and endometrial cancers (PMID: 25124163, 30917185). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it is a statistically significant hotspot and is therefore likely oncogenic (PMID: 26619011)

The POLE Y458H mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrium carcinoma (PMID: 25233892). In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE Y458H suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE Y458H-mutant colorectal carcinoma and brain primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE C810G mutation is located in the DNA pol B domain of the protein. In vivo human mutagenesis screening of POLE C810G suggests that the mutation is inactivating as measured by hypermutation status in patients with POLE C810G-mutant glioblastoma and rectal adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29056344).

The POLE M295R mutation is located in the exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation is recurrent in ultramutated endometrial carcinoma (PMID: 31829442). Analysis of tumors with this mutation suggested that it is likely inactivating as measured by POLE-score, a metric that takes into account tumor mutation burden as well as mutation signature compared to wildtype POLE and known POLE inactivating mutations (PMID: 31829442).

The POLE S459F mutation has been found in colorectal carcinomas with an ultrahypermutator phenotype (PMID: 25228659). The residue is located in the protein's exonuclease domain and in vitro assays show that this variant ablates POLE's proofreading activity (PMID: 25228659).

The POT1 R117C mutation lies in the OB1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HeLa and patient-derived lymphoblastoid cell lines demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased telomere binding, decreased TPP1 binding, and increased telomere length. Analysis of patient samples also showed that the mutation is associated with increased telomere length (PMID: 26403419).

The POT1 Y89C mutation lies in the OB1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in recombinant protein assays demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding, and analysis of patient samples showed that the mutation is associated with increased telomere length (PMID: 24686849).

The POT1 Q94E mutation lies in the OB1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in recombinant protein assays demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding, and analysis of patient samples showed that the mutation is associated with increased telomere length (PMID: 24686849).

POT1 truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein. These mutations have been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, Hodgkin's lymphoma, angiosarcoma and melanoma (PMID: 33934394). In vitro studies with POT1-knockdown in ovarian cancer cell lines demonstrate loss of POT1 is inactivating as measured by increased proliferation, tumorigenesis and HDAC inhibition compared to control cells (PMID: 29546066). Conditional deletion of POT1 in mice leads to DNA damage response at telomeres, resulting in senescence and chromosome instability (PMID: 16839876).

The POT1 Y223C mutation lies in the OB2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibrosarcoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased telomere binding, increased telomere length, and increased chromosomal aberrations (PMID: 23502782).

The POT1 Y36N mutation lies in the OB1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibrosarcoma cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased telomere binding, increased telomere length, and increased chromosomal aberrations (PMID: 23502782).

The POT1 I78T mutation is located in the POT1 OB1 domain. This mutation has been identified as a germline mutation among families with familial melanoma. In vitro experimental data demonstrated that this mutation is likely loss-of-function as shown by the reduced ability to bind to telomeric sequences. Expression of this mutation in HT1080 cells showed elongated telomeres compared with cell expressing wildtype POT1 (PMID: 30586141).

The PAX8-PPARG fusion protein is a result of t(2;3) (q13;p25) translocation between the PAX8 gene (2q13) and the PPARG gene (3p25). This fusion protein has been identified in follicular thyroid carcinoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 10958784). In vitro studies with Nthy-ori 3-1 cells expressing this fusion demonstrate the PAX8-PPARG fusion protein is activating as measured by increased cell growth and decreased G0/G1 resting state cells compared to control empty vector cells (PMID: 15077183).

The POT1 R273L mutation lies in the OB2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in recombinant protein assays demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding, and analysis of patient samples showed that the mutation is associated with increased telomere length (PMID: 24686849).

The POT1 S322L mutation lies in an unknown functional domain of the protein. Patient-derived fibroblasts and human fibrosarcoma cell lines expressing this mutation demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by increased telomere dysfunction and increased telomere length (PMID: 27013236).

RAC1 gene amplification has been detected in patients with breast cancer (PMID: 31895772). Experimental studies using RNAi have shown that RAC1 may be responsible for resistance to HER2-targeted therapies since the knockdown of RAC1 leads to sensitivity in previously lapatinib-resistant tumors (PMID: 23474757, 24072884). In vitro studies with lung cancer cells overexpressing RAC1 demonstrate amplification of RAC1 is activating as measured by decreased cellular proliferation and migration following RAC1 silencing (PMID: 22549160).

The RAC1 C18Y mutation occurs in the guanine nucleotide binding pocket domain of the protein. When expressed in HEK293T cells, the RAC1 C18Y mutation was associated with increased levels of activated RAC1 compared to wildtype RAC1, as quantified by PAK1 pulldown (PMID: 28115009) consistent with the mutation conferring an oncogenic phenotype to RAC1.

The RAC1 P29L is located in the highly conserved Switch 1 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in 3T3 cells and in nude mice demonstrated that RAC1 P29L is activating as measured by cellular transformation in colony-forming assays and enhanced tumor growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 23382236).

The G12V mutation in RAC1 is located in a highly conserved residue residing in the GTPase domain and is responsible for interacting with phosphatases (PMID: 23284172). As a result, this mutation exhibits constitutive activation through increased GDP cycling, leading to maintenance of RAC1 in its GTP-bound state. Expression of this mutation in 3T3 cells leads to cellular transformation in colony forming assays and tumor growth in nude mice in vivo (PMID: 23382236).

The RAC1 C176Y mutation (also cited as RAC1 C157Y) is located in the guanidine loop of GTP, suggesting that GDP or GTP affinity is affected with this mutation. Consistent with this, affinity experiments with GDP/GTP demonstrate that C176Y causes elevated cycling and GDP dissociation, maintaining RAC1 in a GTP-bound state that is constitutively active. Expression of this mutation in 3T3 cells leads to cellular transformation in colony-forming assays and enhanced tumor growth in nude mice in vivo (PMID: 23382236).

The RAC1 P34R mutation occurs at a conserved residue in the RAS domain of RAC1. Upon transient expression in an epithelial cell line, the mutation caused increased phosphorylation of downstream targets PAK1 and MEK, as compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 27646943).

The RAC1 P29S mutation, which is located in the highly conserved Switch 1 domain, increases RAC1 activation and binding to downstream effector proteins such as PAK1 (PMID: 23284172, 22842228). This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 31257073). In vitro studies using RAC1 knockdown demonstrated that the P29S mutation enhances melanoma cell proliferation, migration and mesenchymal phenotype (PMID: 22842228, 2546593, 31257073). In addition, this mutation leads to elevated MAPK signaling resulting in resistance to RAF and MEK inhibitors, demonstrated in both in vitro and in vivo modeling (PMID: 25056119). Furthermore, GTP and GDP affinity experiments demonstrated that the P29S mutation enhances GDP dissociation leading to maintenance of RAC1 in a GTP-bound, constitutively active state (PMID: 23284172). The P29S mutation in RAC1 is the third most common mutation leading to melanoma (in sun-exposure cases) and is seen in 4-7% of all patients (PMID: 25465943; 22842228).

The RAC1 Q61R mutation is located in a highly conserved amino acid of the Ras superfamily. This mutation has been identified in seminomas (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RAC1 Q61R is activating as measured by increased RAC1 activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 26619011).

RAD50 deletions have been identified in patients with myeloid malignancies (cBioPortal, MSKCC, January 2017), and are associated with reduced RAD50 protein expression (PMID: 14684699). Consistent with this, RAD50 haploinsufficiency in mice corresponded to hematopoietic failure and a predisposition to cancer (PMID: 12208847). Based on RAD50 function, deletion mutations are likely to cause defective repair of damage via either the homologous recombination (HR) or nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) pathways (PMID: 2659437, 15309560).

The RAD50 D69N mutation is located in the Walker A domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vivo studies with yeast expressing RAD50 D69N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by inactivation of TEL1/ATM and reduced ATP binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 32187176).

The RAD50 L1237F mutation is located in the putative exonuclease domain of the protein. This mutation was recorded after whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of tumor tissue from a 51 year-old female with invasive small cell cancer of the ureter (PMID: 24934408). Recreation of the mutation in yeast, mouse embryonic fibroblasts as well as breast and endometrial carcinomas revealed that the MRX complex was intact but signaling via the ATM checkpoint pathway was impaired, thereby preventing the stoppage of DNA replication upon identification of DNA damage, and instead allowing damaged DNA to be propagated into daughter cells (PMID: 24934408). The patient, whose RAD50 mutation was hemizygous, displayed an outlier curative response during an open-label Phase I trial to treatment with irinotecan and the CHK1 inhibitor, AZD7762; this result indicates that synthetic lethality was a result of inhibiting both the ATM and ATR checkpoint pathways as well as the clonal hemizygous nature of the mutation (PMID: 24934408).

The RAD50 D69Y mutation is located in the Walker A domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24030381). In vivo studies with yeast expressing RAD50 D69Y demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by inactivation of TEL1/ATM and reduced ATP binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 32187176).

Truncating mutations of RAD50 lead to several forms of C-terminally truncated protein forms and this is associated with either complete protein degradation or reduced protein expression (PMID: 16288216). Truncating mutations of RAD50 have been observed in families with a high predisposition to breast and ovarian cancer (PMID: 14684699). Consistent with this, RAD50 haploinsufficiency in mice leads to hematopoietic failure and a predisposition to cancer (PMID: 12208847). In preclinical experiments, a series of RAD50 truncating mutations made in S. cerevisiae were associated with severely impaired in meiotic double strand break formation, telomere length maintenance and non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) (PMID:21892167).

The L234fs mutation of RAD50, also known as 687delT, is a low-penetrance risk allele commonly found in Finnish populations, which leads to a frameshift with a premature translation stop at codon 234 (PMIDs: 14684699, 16474176). The nuclear localization of RAD50 protein is normal in mutant cells (PMID: 16385572). However, an examination of peripheral blood T-lymphocytes from patients bearing this mutation revealed chromosomal aberrations (PMID: 16385572). Both simple and complex chromosomal rearrangements were found more frequently in carriers than in healthy controls (PMID: 16385572). Western blot analysis on protein levels showed decreased RAD50 protein expression indicating that a stable protein product was not produced (PMID: 16385572). Thus the RAD50 L234fs mutation may promote genomic instability and a pre-disposition to cancer via haploinsufficiency (PMID: 16385572).

Truncating mutations in RAD51 occur across the gene and are predicted to lead to loss of this protein. RAD51 is involved in homologous recombination and double-strand DNA damage repair (PMID: 28575658). Truncating mutations in RAD51 can lead to development of a phenotype resembling Fanconi Anemia in Zebrafish (PMID:28512217). Loss-of-heterozygosity in this locus has been reported in breast carcinomas (PMID: 18632222). Loss of RAD51 has been identified in small cell lung carcinomas and is associated with worse prognosis in the absence of chemo- or radiotherapy (PMID: 28236982). Truncating mutations in RAD51 have been identified in thyroid carcinomas (PMID: 28481359).

Deletion of RAD51B is found in several tumor types and has been shown in vitro to be haploinsufficient, leading to centrosome fragmentation, aneuploidy, impaired homologous recombination and reduced homologous recombination DNA repair (PMID: 16778173, 25260587, 10938124). Loss of RAD51B sensitizes cells to DNA damaging agents such as cisplatin (PMID: 10938124).

The RAD51B R47* mutation is located in the N-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in families with cutaneous melanoma and breast cancer (PMID: 25600502, 26845104). In silico and in vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating, as evidenced by its predicted effect of causing a truncated or absent protein due to a premature stop codon, as well as its inability to rescue homologous recombination when transfected into RAD51B-deficient cells compared to wildtype vector (PMID: 34635660).

The HMGA2-RAD51B fusion and other fusions involving HMGA2 juxtapose the two or three first exons of the protein to its fusion partner, thus separating the N-terminal DNA-binding domain of the HMGA2 from its regulatory domain (PMID: 11450849). This fusion may result in deregulation of downstream targets and deregulation of a uterine-specific splice variant of RAD51B (PMID: 9892177). The HMGA2-RAD51B fusion has exclusively been detected in uterine leiomyomas (PMID: 26787895, 9892177). Its presence is associated with increased levels of HMGA2 transcript and a distinct transcriptome profile (PMID: 26787895).

Truncating mutations of RAD51B have been found in the germlines of patients with melanoma, breast and ovarian cancers (PMID: 25600502, 24139550, 26261251). \nIn vitro studies have demonstrated that reduction or loss of RAD51B expression, a likely consequence of RAD51B truncating mutations, results in loss of DNA repair functions, as measured by impaired RAD51 foci formation, increased sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents and reduced homologous repair efficiency in the mutant compared to wildtype (PMID: 25368520, 16778173). Furthermore, reduction of RAD51B levels also leads to genome instability, as evidenced by increased levels of chromosomal aberrations, increased aneuploidy and centrosome fragmentation in the mutant compared to wildtype (PMID: 16778173).

The RBM10 V419E mutation (also cited as RBM10 V354E) is located in the RNA recognition motif 2 domain (RRM2). The V419E mutant was found in the human lung adenocarcinoma epithelial cell line, A549. RBM10 mutations may contribute to lung adenocarcinoma progression by causing deregulation of the alternative splicing of NUMB, a natural inhibitor of the NOTCH pathway (PMID: 24332178, 20007775).

The RHOA L69R mutation is located in the switch II region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 31558468). Rhotekin binding assays of RHOA L69R demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased citron kinase binding compared to both GTP-bound and GDP-bound wildtype (Abstract: Qian et al. Abstract# 2586, AACR 2020. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/80/16_Supplement/2586/642138/Abstract-2586-Identification-of-cancer-associated).

RBM10 deletions have been identified as the cause of TARP syndrome is associated with defects in exon splicing due to loss of RBM10 nuclear function and is considered an oncogenic event (PMID: 24000153). Similarly, RBM10 mutations in lung cancer is associated with defects in splicing of the NOTCH regulator, NUMB, leading to the promotion of cell proliferation (PMID: 24332178). Consistent with this, knockdown of RBM10 in human cancer cell lines enhanced tumor growth in mouse xenograft experiments (PMID: 26853560). Additionally, experimental studies have shown that depletion of RBM10 in HeLa cells enhanced cell colony formation; in contrast, overexpression of wildtype RBM10 reduced the clonogenic capacity of A549 human lung adenocarcinoma epithelial cells (PMID: 24332178).

Truncating mutations of RBM10 have been identified as the cause of TARP syndrome (PMID: 24000153). Recently, RBM10 truncating alterations were shown to frequently occur in lung adenocarcinomas (PMID: 21910224, 22980975), particularly in male patients (PMID: 25079552), leading to loss of protein function. Experimental studies have shown that depletion of RBM10 in HeLa cells enhanced cell colony formation and over expression of wild-type RBM10 reduced the clonogenic capacity of A549 human lung adenocarcinoma epithelial cells (PMID: 24332178). Since RBM10 has been reported to regulate the splicing of several known cancer genes, mutations in RBM10 may contribute to tumor growth by affecting the wildtype activity of its target genes (PMID: 24000153). Integrative analysis of RBM10 mutation and RNA expression data identified nonsense (E177*) and frameshift (F227fs*39) mutations in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) patients lacking canonical oncogenes (PMID: 28091594). These protein truncating variants were associated with significantly reduced RBM10 expression, which, in turn, correlated with poor overall survival. Biochemical assays suggested that these truncating or frameshift mutations exhibited distinct loss of splicing function (PMID: 28091594).

The RHOA G14V mutation is located in the GTP binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 26437031). In vitro studies with Swiss3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA G14V is inactivating as measured by cell cycle arrest and inhibition of downstream signaling, cellular proliferation and invasion (PMID: 19515453). Similarly, RHOA G14V expression inhibits invasion capacity in immortalized human T lymphocytes (PMID: 24584070).

The RHOA E40T mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with NIH 3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA E40T is activating as measured by increased stress fiber and foci formation and increased transcriptional activity (PMID: 9482732).

The RHOA L57V mutation is located in the RAS domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse adenocarcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26251521). Expression of RHOA L57V in human embryonic kidney cells demonstrated the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased RHOA activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 24816253). RHOA L57V is suggested to be resistant to treatment with ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 as measured by cell survival compared to wildtype (PMID: 24816253).

The RHOA A161P mutation is located in the GTP-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 26574607). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in 293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased binding to GTP and nucleotide cycling in radioisotope kinetic assays as well as increased downstream transcription in luciferase assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 26574607).

The RHOA T37A mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in follicular lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vivo studies in yeast expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA T37A is inactivating as measured by inhibiting binding to downstream effectors mDIA, PKN, ROCK1 and ROCK2 compared to wildtype (PMID: 15993039). Overexpression of RHOA T37A immortalized human mammary epithelial cells to a greater extent than cells expressing wildtype RHOA (PMID: 19147561).

The RHOA E40K mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 32187361). In vitro studies with AGS and MKN-45 cells expressing RHOA E40K demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased proliferation and migration compared to wildtype and empty vector cells (Abstract: Jeon et al. Abstract# 5112, AACR 2020. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/80/16_Supplement/5112/643704/Abstract-5112-Interaction-between-RHOA-mutated).

The RHOA G17A mutation is located in the GTP binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in ductal carcinoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with LLC-PK1 cells and NIH 3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA G17A is inactivating as measured by reduced RHOA activity due to inhibiting GTP and GDP binding (PMID: 22491204, 16472675).

The RHOA A161E mutation is located in the GTP-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 24413737, 26574607). Expression of this mutation in vitro, in NIH 3T3 and in 293T cells demonstrated that it is a dominant negative as measured by decreased binding to GTP in pulldown experiments and in radioisotope kinetic assays compared to wildtype, leading to attenuated stress fiber formation (PMID: 24413737, 26574607).

The RHOA R5W mutation is located in the N terminus of the protein. Biochemical experiments have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by its effect on β-catenin, and may act as a dominant-negative to promote tumor growth (PMID: 28522256, 29796182) (Abstract: Schaefer et al, Abstract# A29, AACR 2018. https://mcr.aacrjournals.org/content/18/5_Supplement/A29).

The RHOA G17V mutation is located in the GTP binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 24413734). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA G17V is inactivating as measured by reduced RHOA activity due to inhibited GTP and GDP binding (PMID: 24413737). RHOA G17V expression causes increased proliferation and invasion capacity compared to expression of wildtype RHOA in human immortalized T cells or T lymphocyte lymphoma cells (PMID: 24413737, 24584070).

The RHOA R5Q mutation is located in the N-terminus of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 25044415, 28481359). In silico analysis of RHOA R5Q predicts that the mutation is inactivating by inhibiting the binding of RHOA to GEF (PMID: 25044415).

The RHOA Y34F mutation is located in the GTP binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 32187361). In vitro studies with human lung microvascular endothelial cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA Y34F is inactivating as measured by reduced RHOA activity due to inhibited GTP and GDP binding (PMID: 24398689).

The RHOA Y42F mutation is located in the highly conserved core effector domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 25044415). In vitro studies with RAW264.7 cells expressing RHOA Y42F demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by suppressed tumorigenesis and no effect in cell proliferation and NF-kB activation in the presence of hydrogen peroxide compared to wildtype (PMID: 28712859).

The RHOA G17E mutation is located within the region of the RHOA protein that binds GTP/GDP suggesting that this mutation may affect RHOA GTP/GDP binding. RHOA G17E expression causes increased proliferation compared to wildtype RHOA expression in breast cancer cells (PMID: 24816255).

The RHOA E40N mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with NIH 3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate that RHOA E40N is likely inactivating as measured by reduced formation of stress fibers and reduced foci compared to wildtype (PMID: 9482732).

The RHOA C16R mutation is located in the GTP-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 26574607). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in 293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased binding to GTP and nucleotide cycling in radioisotope kinetic assays as well as increased downstream transcription in luciferase assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 26574607).

The RHOA E40W mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with NIH 3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate that RHOA E40LW is likely inactivating as measured by the inability to bind downstream effector ROCK1, reduced formation of stress fibers, reduced foci and decreased transactivation of targets in a reporter assay compared to wildtype (PMID: 9482732).

The RHOA L69P mutation is located in the switch II region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in ampullary cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26804919). Rhotekin binding assays of RHOA L69P demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased citron kinase binding compared to both GTP-bound and GDP-bound wildtype (Abstract: Qian et al. Abstract# 2586, AACR 2020. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/80/16_Supplement/2586/642138/Abstract-2586-Identification-of-cancer-associated).

The RHOA Y42S mutation is located in the highly conserved core effector domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 32187361). In vitro studies with MKN74 cells and in vivo studies with orthotopic xenograft models expressing RHOA Y42S demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased migration activity and upregulation of cell metabolism- and cell cycle-related pathways compared to wildtype (PMID: 31485674).

The RHOA A161V mutation is located in the GTP-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 26574607). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in 293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream transcription in luciferase assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 26574607).

The RHOA E47K mutation is located in the effector domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in mesothelioma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 26928227). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing RHOA E47K demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduction in protein phosphorylation and cell spreading compared to wildtype (PMID: 31570889).

The RHOA T37Y mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This mutation is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with NIH 3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA T37Y is inactivating as measured by the inability to bind downstream effectors ROCK1 and PKN (PMID: 9482732).

The RHOA Y42C mutation is located in the highly conserved core effector domain of the RHOA protein. This domain is an important binding site for other proteins mediating activation or inactivation of RHOA (PMID: 24816255). This mutation has been found in diffuse gastric cancer (PMID: 31771969). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in a transgenic mouse model demonstrated that it is activating as measured by decreased GTP hydrolysis and increased pathway activation compared to wildtype and the in vivo development of diffuse gastric cancer with concurrent CDH1 deletion (PMID: 31771969). Knockdown of the endogenous expression of this mutation in a gastric cancer cell line resulted in decreased proliferation (PMID: 24816255). However, expression of this mutation in human embryonic kidney cells led to decreased RHOA signaling as measured by reduced RHOA-GTP levels (PMID: 24816253).

The RHOA K118E mutation is located in the GTP-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 26574607). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in 293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream transcription in luciferase assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 26574607).

The RHOA E40L mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with NIH 3T3 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate that RHOA E40L is likely inactivating as measured by the inability to bind downstream effector ROCK1, reduced formation of stress fibers, reduced foci and decreased transactivation of targets in a reporter assay compared to wildtype (PMID: 9482732).

The RHOA Y34C mutation is located in the GTP binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 32187361). In vitro studies with Sf9 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA Y34C is inactivating as measured by reduced RHOA activity in the presence of downstream target phospholipase D compared to wildtype (PMID: 9565577).

The RHOA C16F mutation is located in the GTP-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 26574607). Expression of this mutation in vitro and in 293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream transcription in luciferase assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 26574607).

Overexpression of RHOA in rat hepatocellular carcinoma cells caused activation of RHOA downstream signaling and stimulated invasion in vitro and in vivo (PMID: 10213513). Also, RHOA overexpression increased the proliferation and migration in human cervical cancer (HeLa) cells (PMID: 25104222). Inhibition of RHOA expression by siRNA or expression of a dominant-negative form of RHOA reduced the proliferation and tumorigenicity, and enhanced chemosensitivity in human gastric cancer cells. This suggests a potentially oncogenic role of RHOA overexpression (PMID: 15448013).

The RHOA G62E mutation is located in the switch II region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Burkitt lymphoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 31558468). Rhotekin binding assays of RHOA G62E demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased citron kinase binding compared to both GTP-bound and GDP-bound wildtype (Abstract: Qian et al. Abstract# 2586, AACR 2020. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/80/16_Supplement/2586/642138/Abstract-2586-Identification-of-cancer-associated).

The RHOA T19N mutation is located in the GTP binding site of the protein. There is conflicting evidence about the biological and functional effects of the mutation. In vitro studies with immortalized human T lymphocytes expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA T19N is inactivating as measured by reduced RHOA activity due to inhibited GTP and GDP binding and increased cellular proliferation and invasion (PMID: 24584070). In contrast, in vitro studies with human mammary epithelial cells overexpressing the mutation demonstrate RHOA T19N is likely neutral as measured by cell senescence after 20 population doublings compared to wildtype and constitutively active RHOA G14V, which had no signs of senescence (PMID: 19147561).
The SETBP1 T864 allele is associated with disease progression in CMML and JMML and is listed in the NCCN Guide for Myelodysplastic Syndrome (v 2.2018) as a prognostic marker (PMID: 34155503).
The SETBP1 I865 allele is associated with disease progression in CMML and JMML and is listed in the NCCN Guide for Myelodysplastic Syndrome (v 2.2018) as a prognostic marker (PMID: 34155503).

The RHOA E40Q mutation is located in the effector region motif of the protein. This is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with Sf9 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate RHOA E40Q is likely neutral as measured by wildtype comparable RHOA activity in the presence of downstream target phospholipase D (PMID: 9565577).

As a member of the mTORC2 complex, RICTOR functions in regulating diverse cellular processes including proliferation, survival and apoptosis. In the context of cancer, RICTOR and the mTORC2 complex have been shown to influence cancer cell metastasis (PMID: 20978191), proliferation and apoptosis (PMID: 19934294, 19185849). Studies in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that RICTOR overexpression exhibits transforming capabilities, as evidenced by IL3-independent growth (PMID: 26370156). Conversely, knock-down of RICTOR in cell lines and mouse models resulted in anti-tumor effects, thus supporting an oncogenic role for RICTOR amplification/overexpression (PMID: 26370156).

The SETBP1 S869R mutation is located within the SKI homology region of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and Schinzel-Giedion syndrome (PMID: 28346496, 20436468, 28447248). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation leads to moderately increased protein stability due to proteasomal evasion (PMID: 28346496).

The SETBP1 D868N mutation is located within the SKI homology region of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and Schinzel-Giedion syndrome (PMID: 28346496, 20436468, 23222956). Computational modeling of this mutant protein suggested that it likely alters protein structure and function (PMID: 23222956). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation leads to increased protein stability due to proteasomal evasion, as well as increased proliferation and colony formation (PMID: 28346496, 23832012). Individuals with this mutation have a higher likelihood of progressing to malignancy that those with other SETBP1 mutations (PMID: 23222956).

The SETBP1 E858K mutation is located within the SKI homology region of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and Schinzel-Giedion syndrome (PMID: 29225884, 20436468, 23222956). Computational modeling of this mutant protein suggested that it likely alters protein structure and function (PMID: 23222956).

The SETBP1 I871S mutation is located within the SKI homology region of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (PMID: 23443343). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, another amino acid substitution at this position (I871T) was shown to be likely gain-of-function and likely oncogenic (PMID: 28346496)

The SETBP1 D868Y mutation is located within the SKI homology region of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (PMID: 23558523). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, another amino acid substitution at this position (D868N) has been shown to be likely gain of function and likely oncogenic (PMID: 28346496, 23222956).

The SETBP1 G870S mutation is located within the SKI homology region of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and Schinzel-Giedion syndrome (PMID: 28346496, 20436468). Expression of this mutation in human cells demonstrated that it is activating, as shown by increased protein stability, increased downstream pathway activation and increased cell proliferation compared to expression of wildtype SETBP1 (PMID: 28346496, 23222956).

The SOX9 P70R mutation occurs in the dimerization domain of the SOX9 protein and has been identified in patients with campomelic dysplasia. In biochemical assays, the SOX9 P70R mutation causes a reduction in sequence-specific DNA binding compared to wildtype SOX9, likely resulting in loss of SOX9-dependent target gene activation (PMID: 10446171). The ability of SOX9 P70R to transform cells has not yet been functionally tested (PMID: 10446171).

The SETBP1 I871T mutation is located within the SKI homology region of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and Schinzel-Giedion syndrome but is found more commonly in Schinzel-Giedion syndrome (PMID: 28346496, 20436468, 23222956). Expression of this mutation in cell lines demonstrated that this mutation leads to moderately increased protein stability due to proteasomal evasion, as well as increased proliferation and colony formation (PMID: 28346496, 23832012).

Overexpression of RHOA in rat hepatocellular carcinoma cells caused activation of RHOA downstream signaling and stimulated invasion in vitro and in vivo (PMID: 10213513). Also, RHOA overexpression increased the proliferation and migration in human cervical cancer (HeLa) cells (PMID: 25104222). Inhibition of RHOA expression by siRNA or expression of a dominant-negative form of RHOA reduced the proliferation and tumorigenicity, and enhanced chemosensitivity in human gastric cancer cells. This suggests a potentially oncogenic role of RHOA overexpression (PMID: 15448013).

The SOX9 L142P mutation occurs in the HMG DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of the SOX9 L142P mutation in colorectal cancer cell lines results in decreased beta-catenin/WNT transcriptional activity due to disruption in SOX9 DNA binding capacity. Colorectal cancer cell lines expressing the SOX9 L142P alteration formed colonies in vitro and tumors in murine xenograft models. Reintroduction of SOX9 protein resulted in decreased colony and primary/metastatic tumor growth in mice, suggesting that this mutation is indeed loss of function (PMID: 27429045).

SOX9 deletions have been identified in patients with campomelic dysplasia and are predicted to result in protein instability (PMID: 9002675). Based on the role of SOX9 as a transcription factor, these alterations are predicted to result in the inability of SOX9 to bind to target genes and activate effector transcription (PMID: 10446171, 12783851) and are considered oncogenic events. Loss of SOX9 in the mouse intestine leads to colonic hyperplasia (PMID: 18794798). Experiments in genetic mouse model of basal cell carcinoma (BCC) showed that SOX9 is expressed from the earliest step of tumor formation in a WNT/β-catenin-dependent manner. SOX9 was demonstrated to directly control a gene regulation network promoting stemness, extracellular matrix deposition, and cytoskeleton remodeling while repressing epidermal differentiation. SOX9 deletion in the context of constitutive activation of Hedgehog signaling prevented BCC formation and led to a progressive loss of oncogene-expressing cells (PMID: 26095047).

Truncating mutations of SOX9 are commonly detected in patients with Campomelic Dysplasia (CD) and is considered an oncogenic effect. Experimental studies have demonstrated that loss of the C-terminal domain results in the inability of SOX9 to activate effector transcription (PMID: 10446171). In contrast however, immunohistochemistry (IHC) studies of colorectal cancers with SOX9 truncating mutations showed increased levels of SOX9 protein expression, suggesting that the truncated protein may have oncogenic properties separate from the loss of its ability to activate transcription of effector genes (PMID: 27248473).

The SOX9 K398A mutation occurs at a putative site of SUMO conjugation. In a murine mesenchymal cell line, the K398A mutant protein demonstrated increased stability and transactivation, likely by blocking SUMOylation and subsequent ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (PMID: 15694126)

The STAT5B Q706L mutation lies in the transactivation domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human cell line demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by downstream signaling comparable to wildtype STAT5B (PMID: 27697773).

The SUZ12 E610V mutation lies in the VEFS domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a lymphoblast cell line demonstrated it is likely inactivating, as measured by decreased H3K27me3 levels (PMID: 28229514).

The STAT5B T628S mutation lies in the SH2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human cell line demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling and increased proliferation compared to wildtype STAT5B (PMID: 24825865).

The STAT5B N642H mutation is located in Src homology 2 (SH2) domain of the protein. This mutation is a gain-of-function mutation that has been found in numerous cases of leukemia and lymphoma (PMID: 23596048, 24947020, 24972766, 25749351, 30573779). In a transgenic mouse model, human STAT5B N642H expression leads to leukemia or lymphoma development when compared to STAT5B wildtype expression, and it presents as a transplantable CD8+ T cell disease (PMID: 29200404). The STAT5B N642H mutation showed enhanced and prolonged tyrosine phosphorylation in vitro when compared to wildtype STAT5B, and also demonstrated a distinct change in the DNA methylome and gene expression profiles of CD8+ T-cells in vivo (PMID: 29200404). These mutant cells were also sensitive to JAK and Aurora kinase inhibitors, as measured by neoplastic T-cell expansion and organ infiltration in vivo (PMID: 29200404).
The SUZ12 E610G mutation lies in the VEFS domain of the protein. In vitro assays demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating, as measured by decreased H3K27me3 levels (PMID: 22053108).

The SUZ12 D605V mutation lies in the VEFS domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a lymphoblast cell line demonstrated it is likely inactivating, as measured by decreased H3K27me3 levels (PMID: 22053108).

Truncation and deletion of SUZ12 has been found in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) (PMID: 31492675). In vivo CRISPR studies of SUZ12 loss demonstrated that SUZ12 loss can cooperate with JAK3 mutation to drive T-ALL and leads to increased signaling through PI3K, VEGF and WNT pathways (PMID: 31492675).

The SUZ12 F603L mutation lies in the VEFS domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a lymphoblast cell line demonstrated it is likely inactivating, as measured by decreased H3K27me3 levels (PMID: 22053108).

Translocations involving TCF3 and PBX1 are recurrently identified in patients with B-acute lymphoblastic leukemias (B-ALL) and are associated with good outcome (PMID: 23181981, 8608207, 24781017). The TCF3-PBX1 resultant fusion protein combines the N-terminal transactivation domain of TCF3 with the C-terminal DNA binding domain of PBX1 (PMID: 23181981, 27088431).
