The gene expression landscape of BLL expressing TCF3-PBX1 is thought to be characteristically different than other BLL subtypes due to the fact that both fusion partners are transcription factors (PMID: 30631148). Downstream targets of TCF3-PBX1 include EBF3, as well as WNT family members RORB and WNT16B (PMID: 30631148). Expression of TCF3-PBX1 in hematopoietic cells results in the activation of non-canonical WNT signaling (PMID: 30631148, 10500199). RORB inhibition was found to decrease viability of TCF3-PBX1-positive patient-derived cells and cell lines, especially in combination with the chemotherapeutic agent vincristine (Abstract: Teppo et al. Abstract #128:4077, American Society of Hematology 2016. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/128/22/4077).

TBX3 truncating mutations can form several forms of C-terminally truncated TBX3 proteins. Germline TBX3 truncation mutations are found in patients with ulnar-mammary syndrome. TBX3 truncation mutations are also found in patients with breast cancer and tend to be clustered around the TBX3 DNA-binding T-domain. Expression of select TBX3 truncation mutations in vitro as well as in COS-3 cells revealed that TBX3 truncation mutations may decrease TBX3 DNA-binding and transcriptional activity (PMID: 26579496, 11689487).

Truncating mutations in TCF3 can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its activity (PMID: 29625055). TCF3 encodes a member of the E protein family of helix-loop-helix transcription factors, and it has been shown to be involved in lymphocyte, skin and neural development by regulating the Wnt signaling pathway (PMID: 25990863,17018284, 24832538). Chromosomal translocations involving TCF3 have been shown to be associated with the development of several lymphoid malignancies (PMID: 25729575, 27461063, 31575852). Germline truncating mutations in TCF3 have been shown to lead to severe hypogammaglobulinemia and predispose to B-ALL (PMID: 30063982, 28532655). Additionally, somatic truncating mutations in TCF3 have been identified in patients with several types of carcinomas (PMID: 29625055)

The TCF3-HLF fusion protein combines the N-terminus of TCF3 with exon 4 of HLF and is found in patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemias (PMID: 23181981). RNA- and DNA- sequencing experiments on patient samples revealed that leukemias with TCF3-HLF tended to have deletions in PAX5, BTG1 or VPREB1, mutations in RAS pathway genes and tended to express a gene expression signature enriched for stem cell and myeloid features. Patient-derived xenograft models revealed that TCF3-HLF leukemias were sensitive to glucocorticoids, anthracyclines and antimitotic agents in clinical development, including the BCL2-specific inhibitor venetoclax (ABT-199) (PMID: 26214592).

The TCF3 D561E mutation lies in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is inactivating, as measured by decreased association with ID3 compared to wildtype TCF3 (PMID: 22885699).

The TCF3 V557E mutation lies in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a human fibroblast cell line demonstrated it is inactivating, as measured by decreased association with ID3 compared to wildtype TCF3 (PMID: 22885699).

The TCF3 N551K mutation resides in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Although experimental studies have demonstrated that the N551K mutation binds to many of the same target genes as the wildtype TCF3 protein, the N551K mutation alters the binding motif of TCF3 leading to differential gene expression patterns. One such downstream target is AKT1, an important component of PI3K signaling, which usually repressed by TCF3, is activated by expression of the N551K mutation (PMID: 22885699, 24492847).
The TERT P923L mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the TERT protein. In silico analysis suggests that this mutation is deleterious (PMID: 29976374).

The TERT R1084* mutation is located in the CTE region of the protein and results in a truncated protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and in the germline of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (PMID: 17460043, 32923861). This mutation has not been functionally characterized.

TERT promoter mutations are able to reactivate TERT transcription by creating de novo consensus binding sites for the ETS family of transcription factors (PMID: 23348506, 23348503, 23530248, 23887589, 24657534).TERT promoter mutations have been widely associated with advanced forms of cancer and metastatic disease (PMID: 23348506, 23530248, 25048572). The former points to TERT promoter mutations as a potential biomarker of disease severity, and constitutes the first example of a prevalent pan-cancer, somatic mutation lying in a gene regulatory region.

The TERT P704S mutation is located in the reverse transcriptase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in aplastic anemia and dyskeratosis congenita (PMID: 18931339). In vitro studies with WI-38 VA-13 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate TERT P704S is inactivating as measured by decreased telomerase activity and significantly shorter telomeres (PMID: 18042801).

Amplification of TERT is found in multiple cancer types. In vitro studies suggest that TERT amplification confers a growth advantage to cells, as cells transformed with multiple copies of TERT clonally outgrow cells with fewer copies of TERT (PMID: 18482052). Clinically, increased TERT mRNA levels are associated with shorter overall survival and poor outcome in merkel cell carcinoma and acral lentiginous melanoma, respectively (PMID: 25301727, 25219713).

The TERT H412Y mutation is located in the RNA-interacting domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in dyskeratosis congenita and plasma cell myeloma (PMID: 18931339, 30545397). In vitro studies with WI-38 VA-13 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate TERT H412Y is inactivating as measured by decreased telomerase activity and significantly shorter telomeres (PMID: 18042801).

The TERT P308Hfs*43 mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein and results in a truncated protein. This mutation has been identified in pancreatic cancer and has been found as a germline variant (PMID: 32923861). This mutation has not been functionally characterized.

The TERT L392Vfs*146 mutation is located in the RNA-interacting domain of the protein and results in a truncated protein. This mutation has been identified in prostate cancer and lymphoma (PMID: 32923861). Although not functionally characterized, clinical analysis of a patient expressing this germline mutation demonstrated TERT L392Vfs*146 is likely inactivating as measured by significantly shorter telomeres compared to control patients (PMID: 32923861).

The TERT H876Q mutation is located in the reverse transcriptase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in dyskeratosis congenita (PMID: 18931339). In vitro studies with WI-38 VA-13 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate TERT H876Q is inactivating as measured by decreased telomerase activity and significantly shorter telomeres (PMID: 18042801).

The TERT Y846C mutation is located in the reverse transcriptase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in aplastic anemia and dyskeratosis congenita (PMID: 18931339). In vitro studies with WI-38 VA-13 cells expressing this mutation demonstrate TERT Y846C is inactivating as measured by decreased telomerase activity and significantly shorter telomeres (PMID: 18042801).

The MLL-TET1 fusion results from the t(10;11) (q22,q23) translocation, which creates a fusion protein between MLL and TET1. This fusion is found in acute myeloid leukemias (PMID: 12646957). The MLL-TET1 fusion protein can act as a transcriptional activator by targeting key oncogenes such as MEIS1 and HOXA9 (PMID: 23818607). This fusion has also been observed in rare cases of other hematologic malignancies such as in B-cell and T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (PMID: 19144982, 24323992).

TET1 deletions lead to reduced protein expression, are frequently observed in patients with myeloid malignancies and are considered oncogenic events (PMID: 19420352, 21625234). Consequently, these alterations abrogate TET1 enzymatic function to generate 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC). Deletion of TET1 in mice leads to the development of B-cell lymphoma. In these studies, loss of 5-hmC caused reduced hypermethylation of DNA and defects in chromosome maintenance and DNA repair (PMID: 25867473). In colorectal cancer cells, loss of TET1 led to activation of the WNT pathway and cell proliferation (PMID: 25362856).

Truncating mutations of TET1 disrupt the C-terminal catalytic domain of the protein, predicted to cause gene inactivation (PMID:22156206). Consequently, these alterations abrogate TET1 enzymatic function to generate 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) (PMID: 19372391, 21057493).

The TOP1 G737S mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 11844605). Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 G737S was identified as an acquired resistance mutation in a patient with non-small cell lung cancer following treatment with irinotecan and cisplatin (PMID: 11844605).

The TOP1 R364H mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 R364H has been identified preclinically in RC0.1 and RC1 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by persistent TOP1 activity following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 11280753).

The TOP1 A653P mutation is located in the linker domain of the protein. Biochemical assays of TOP1 A653P demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased DNA cleavage-religation activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 12904303). This mutation has been identified preclinically in yeast to confer resistance to treatment to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by prolonged cell viability compared to wildtype (PMID: 12904303).

Amplification of TOP1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in breast cancer, ovarian cancer and liver cancer (PMID: 33144457, 26207989, 30132517). In vivo studies with yeast overexpressing TOP1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents and ribosomal DNA instability compared to normal expression levels (PMID: 11353773, 28961461). Preclinical studies with patient-derived liver cancer xenograft models harboring TOP1/2 amplification demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with nitidine chloride as measured by reduced protein and mRNA expression (PMID: 30132517). Other preclinical studies with camptothecin-resistant ovarian cancer cells harboring TOP1 amplification demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with evodiamine as measured through increased apoptosis (PMID: 26207989). TOP1 amplification is suggested to not be a marker for camptothecin sensitivity in breast cancer as preclinical studies with patient-derived breast cancer cells did not find a correlation between TOP1 expression levels and camptothecin treatment response (PMID: 31783818, 26959889). One hundred and six patients with metastatic colorectal cancer harboring TOP1 copy number alterations were treated with irinotecan and patients with increasing TOP1 copy number alterations were associated with increased objective response to treatment (PMID: 28077117).

The TOP1 T729E mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. In vivo studies with yeast expressing TOP1 T729E demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to bind and cleave DNA compared to wildtype (PMID: 35291312). This mutation has been identified preclinically in yeast to confer resistance to treatment to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by prolonged cell viability compared to wildtype (PMID: 18772225).

The TOP1 T729A mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. In vitro studies with PC-7/CPT cells expressing TOP1 T729A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased TOP1 activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 1332703). This mutation has been identified preclinically in PC-7/CPT cells to confer resistance to treatment to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by prolonged cell viability compared to wildtype (PMID: 1332703).

The TOP1 G365S mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with DLDSNR6 cells expressing TOP1 G365S demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced protein expression and activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 23836376). This mutation has been identified preclinically in DLDSNR6 cells to confer resistance to treatment to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin, camptothecin derivative SN-38 and indolocarbazole derivative J-107088 as measured by reduced cell growth inhibition compared to wildtype (PMID: 23836376).

The TOP1 D583G mutation is located in the catalytic core domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 D583G has been identified preclinically in CPT-K5 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by persistent TOP1 activity following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 1849260).

The TOP1 F361S mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 F361S has been identified preclinically in U-937 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by persistent TOP1 activity following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 8300570).

The TOP1 Y723F is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. In vivo studies with yeast expressing TOP1 Y723F demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased G4-associated genome instability compared to wildtype (PMID: 35291312). In silico analysis suggests that this mutation confers resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin through decreased binding affinity (PMID: 9488644).

The TOP1 G717R mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. In vitro studies with DLDSNR6 cells expressing TOP1 G717R demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced protein expression and activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 23836376). This mutation has been identified preclinically in DLDSNR6 cells to confer resistance to treatment to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin, camptothecin derivative SN-38 and indolocarbazole derivative J-107088 as measured by reduced cell growth inhibition compared to wildtype (PMID: 23836376).

The TOP1 D533G mutation is located in the catalytic core domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 D533G has been identified preclinically in CPT-K5 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by persistent TOP1 activity following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 1849260).

The TOP1 L617I mutation is located in the core subdomain III of the protein. In vitro studies with HCT116 cells expressing TOP1 L617I demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein expression and activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21619602). This mutation has been identified preclinically in HCT116 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by decreased TOP1-DNA cleavage complexes, double-stranded break formations and cell cycle perturbations following treatment with camptothecin derivative SN-38 compared to SN-38 sensitive HCT116 cells (PMID: 21619602).

The TOP1 E710G mutation is located in the linker domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HCT116 cells expressing TOP1 E710G demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein expression and activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21619602). This mutation has been identified preclinically in HCT116 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by decreased TOP1-DNA cleavage complexes, double-stranded break formations and cell cycle perturbations following treatment with camptothecin derivative SN-38 compared to SN-38 sensitive HCT116 cells (PMID: 21619602).

The TOP1 T729K mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, in vivo studies with yeast expressing TOP1 T729K demonstrated resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by prolonged cell viability compared to wildtype (PMID: 18772225).

The TOP1 R621H mutation is located in the core subdomain III of the protein. This mutation has been identified in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 22397650). In vitro studies with HCT116 cells expressing TOP1 R621H demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein expression and activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 21619602). This mutation has been identified preclinically in HCT116 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by decreased TOP1-DNA cleavage complexes, double-stranded break formations and cell cycle perturbations following treatment with camptothecin derivative SN-38 compared to SN-38 sensitive HCT116 cells (PMID: 21619602).

The TOP1 W736* mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 11844605). In vivo studies with yeast expressing TOP1 W736* demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased G4-associated genome instability compared to wildtype (PMID: 35291312). TOP1 W736* was identified as an acquired resistance mutation in a patient with non-small cell lung cancer following treatment with irinotecan and cisplatin (PMID: 11844605).

The TOP1 N722S mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 N722S has been identified preclinically in CEM/C2 cells to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by persistent TOP1 activity following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 7882333).

The TOP1 E418K mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 E418K has been identified preclinically in yeast to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by persistent TOP1 activity following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 12097280).

The TP63 R379C mutation does not occur in a functionally defined domain of the protein. In yeast reporter assays, expressing R379C in two different isoforms of TP63 did not significantly alter transcriptional activity compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 28849221).

The TOP1 G363C mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Although not functionally characterized per se, TOP1 G363C has been identified preclinically in yeast to confer resistance to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin as measured by loss of camptothecin-stimulated DNA cleavage following treatment compared to wildtype (PMID: 8395982).

The TOP1 Q421R mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with DLDSNR6 cells expressing TOP1 Q421R demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced protein expression and activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 23836376). This mutation has been identified preclinically in DLDSNR6 cells to confer resistance to treatment to TOP1 inhibitor camptothecin, camptothecin derivative SN-38 and indolocarbazole derivative J-107088 as measured by reduced cell growth inhibition compared to wildtype (PMID: 23836376).

Translocations involving TP63 are found in patients with ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphomas (ALCLs), primary cutaneous ALCL, peripheral T-cell lymphomas, and B-cell lymphomas (PMID: 26104084, 24894770, 22496164). TP63-rearrangements are associated with poor prognosis and tend to be refractory to multiple treatment regimens (PMID: 26104084, 24894770). Rearrangements involving TP63 result in a truncated protein that resembles a dominant negative form of TP63 (ΔNp63) which functions as an oncogene in some contexts (PMID: 26104084, 22855598). The most frequent TP63 fusion partner is TBL1XR1, a protein that functions as a nuclear corepressor (PMID: 22855598).

Truncating mutations in TP63 can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to a truncated protein (PMID: 29885760). Alternative splicing of TP63 has been shown to result in multiple isoforms that vary in their functions; they have been shown to be involved in skin development and maintenance, stem cell regulation, heart development and aging (PMID: 26374530, 30283353, 29481901, 23686138, 22158419). Germline mutations, including truncating variants, involving the N-terminal transactivation domain of TP63 have been shown to lead to an aberrant isoform and leads to a hereditary condition characterized by varying combinations of ectodermal dysplasia (PMID: 18364388, 20556892). Loss of TP63 has been shown to lead to tumor progression in bladder cancer cell lines through a mechanism that involves aberrant epithelial differentiation (PMID: 12368193). TP63 has also been shown to act as a tumor suppressor in skin cancer mouse models through a mechanism that involves Wnt/ β-catenin signaling (PMID: 29885760). Truncating mutations in TP63 have been identified in patients with uterine carcinomas and cutaneous melanomas (PMID: 29625055).

ZRSR2 truncating mutations result in several forms of C-terminally truncated protein. These mutations are found in myelodysplastic syndrome and are predominantly found in male patients given the location of ZRSR2 on the X chromosome (PMID: ). Knockdown of ZRSR2 in HEK293T cells showed aberrant splicing and global intron retention, showing the importance of ZRSR2 in the splicing of U12-type introns. Knockdown of ZRSR2 in human hematopoietic stem cells showed reduced proliferation and colony formation but also showed defects in differentiation. Together this suggests that loss of ZRSR2 may contribute to defective differentiation due to splicing defects (PMID: 25586593).

The ACVR1 R206H mutation is located in the glycine-serine-rich domain of the ACVR1 protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) and in diffuse pontine gliomas (DIPG) (PMID: 24705252, 24705254). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling and transcription compared to wildtype (PMID: 20463014, 24769718, 24705254, 22977237, 20463014).

The ACVR1 G328E mutation is located in the kinase domain of the ACVR1 protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) and in diffuse pontine gliomas (DIPG) (PMID: 24705252, 24705254). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling and transcription compared to wildtype (PMID: 24705254, 20463014, 24769718).

The ACVR1 G328V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the ACVR1 protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) and in diffuse pontine gliomas (DIPG) (PMID: 24705252, 24705254). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling and transcription compared to wildtype (PMID: 24705254, 20463014, 24769718, 24705250). Expression of this mutation in vivo resulted in altered oligodendrocyte differentiation and signaling when co-expressed with other oncogenic mutations (PMID: 32142668).

The ACVR1 G356D mutation is located in the kinase domain of the ACVR1 protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) and in diffuse pontine gliomas (DIPG) (PMID: 24705252, 24705254). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling and transcription compared to wildtype (PMID: 18952055, 20463014, 24769718).

Amplification of ALOX12B typically results in the overexpression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in gastric cancer and leiomyosarcoma (PMID: 34790376, 26541895). In vitro studies with C33A cells overexpressing ALOX12B demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation via upregulation of the PI3K/ERK1 signaling pathway (PMID: 32724378).

The ACVR1 Q207E mutation is located in the glycine-serine-rich (GS) domain of the protein, next to the most common ACVR1 mutation in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), R206H. This mutation has been identified in glioma (PMID: 31683698). This mutation has been observed in a patient with FOP and causes skeletal phenotypes similar to R206H when overexpressed in the limbs of chickens (PMID: 24852373). In vitro studies with NIH/3T3 cells expressing ACVR Q207E demonstrated the mutation is activating as measured by constitutive BMP signaling through a luciferase reporter assay as compared to wildtype (PMID: 24852373).

Truncating mutations in the tumor suppressor AXIN2 lead to loss of its encoded protein function and subsequent loss of repression of the oncogenic Wnt/beta-catenin pathway. Truncating AXIN mutations have been documented in multiple tumor types including colorectal cancers (CRCs) where exon 7 mutations lead to early stop codons that eliminate the DIX (dishevelled and AXIN) carboxy-terminal domain of the protein, necessary for AXIN's oligomerization and inhibitory function in the Wnt-pathway (PMID: 15802015). Additionally, insertions in AXIN DNA exon 5 leading to carboxy-terminal truncation of AXIN protein has been observed in a medulloblastoma patient sample, which corresponded with increased nuclear beta-catenin staining indicating aberrant activation of the Wnt-pathway in that sample (PMID: 17373666).

Truncating mutations in BCL11B occur throughout the entire gene and result in decreased expression or loss of this protein. BCL11B is a transcription factor that binds DNA through zinc-finger domains and has been implicated in the development of the immune and nervous systems in humans (PMID: 29985992). BCL11B is a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor and mutations leading to its inactivation have been implicated in the pathogenesis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) (PMID: 21878675)(Abstract: De Keersmaecker et al. Abstract# 471, ASH 2015. http://www.bloodjournal.org/content/116/21/471?sso-checked=true). Truncating mutations of BCL11B have been identified in patients with multiple subtypes of T-ALL (PMID: 21878675).

Heterozygous deletion of BCL11B occurs in about 10% of T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) (PMID: 26219558). Reduced BCL11B is associated with abnormal immune-related transcription and poor prognosis in T-ALL (PMID: 25023966). Loss of BCL11B in murine models results in a lack of pre-T cell receptor (TCR) presentation on the cell surface (PMID: 12717433).

BCL2L1 amplification is an event associated with the gain of chromosomal arm 20q, resulting in increased BCL2L1 protein expression. Overexpression of BCL2L1 is associated with colorectal adenoma-to-carcinoma progression (PMID: 22009326). BCL2L1 amplification in gastric cancer cell lines has demonstrated sensitivity to BCL2L1 inhibitor ABT-737 (PMID: 26401016).

The BCL11B N441K mutation occurs in the DNA binding domain of BCL11B. This mutation was identified in a patient with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Expression of the BCL11B N441K mutation in Jurkat cells resulted in reduced DNA binding and heterodimerization, functioning as a dominant negative. Zebrafish expressing this alteration demonstrated T-cell lineage defects and disruption of hematopoietic stem-cell migration (PMID: 27959755).

The CDKN1A S31R mutation is located between the cyclin and CDK domains of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in breast, colorectal, and lung cancers (PMID: 7655464, 18046503, 20127253, 17293864, 20363991). While this mutation has been found as a germline mutation in many cancer types, it has not been functionally characterized and population studies have been inconclusive (PMID: 7655464, 18046503, 20127253, 17293864).

BMPR1A truncating mutations typically result in the loss of BMPR1A function. Loss of BMPR1A has been identified in prostate cancer and juvenile polyposis syndrome (PMID: 10850425, 20843829). In vitro studies with 786-O, 293T, 4T1 and MDA-MB-231 renal cancer cells demonstrated that loss of BMPR1A is inactivating as measured by promotion of lung-specific metastasis from loss of BMP signaling (PMID: 35842443).

CDKN1A truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins and are mostly located in the N-terminus of the protein. These mutations have been found in bladder cancer (PMID: 24777035). Loss of CDKN1A in fibroblasts, colorectal cancer cells and in a transgenic prostate cancer mouse model results in decreased cell quiescence, increased mitotic defects and increased prostate neoplasia (PMID: 23624841, 19106607, 24317508).

The CIITA C715Y mutation occurs in an undescribed domain of the protein. Expression of the variant in DEV, a nodular-lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NLPHL)-derived cell line, resulted in decreased surface HLA expression as evidenced by flow cytometric experiments (PMID: 26549456).

CDKN1A deletions result in the loss of the protein and are infrequently identified in cancer. Loss of CDKN1A in fibroblasts, colorectal cancer cells and in a transgenic prostate cancer mouse model demonstrated the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased cell quiescence, increased mitotic defects and increased prostate neoplasia compared to wildtype (PMID: 23624841, 19106607, 24317508). Loss of CDKN1A in HCT116 cells demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with Polo-like kinase 1 inhibitor Poloxin as measured by increased anti-apoptosis, DNA repair and cell survival (PMID: 25483104).

CIITA fusion proteins were identified in 38% of primary mediastinal B-cell lymphomas and 15% of classical Hodgkin lymphomas. These fusion products were found to downregulate surface HLA class II expression and lead to overexpression of ligands of the receptor molecule programmed cell death 1 (PCD1) (PMID: 21368758).

The NUBP1-CIITA fusion protein is composed of the first nine exons of NUBP1 and all but the first exon of CIITA. Expression of the variant in DEV, a nodular-lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NLPHL)-derived cell line, resulted in decreased surface HLA expression as evidenced by flow cytometric experiments. This mutation is predicted to function as a dominant negative (PMID: 26549456).

The CIITA D71N mutation occurs in the N-terminal activation domain of the protein. Expression of the variant in DEV, a nodular-lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NLPHL)-derived cell line, resulted in no change in HLA expression as evidenced by flow cytometric experiments (PMID: 26549456).

Deletions of the CIITA gene have been identified in a range of lymphomas. Loss of CIITA is associated with downregulation of MHC class II expression and overexpression of ligands for PD-1, a receptor that mediates immune suppression (PMID: 28479318, 26599546, 26549456).

The CIITA T636M mutation occurs in the N-terminal activation domain of the protein. Expression of the variant in DEV, a nodular-lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NLPHL)-derived cell line, resulted in decreased surface HLA expression as evidenced by flow cytometric experiments. This mutation is predicted to function as a dominant negative (PMID: 26549456).

The CIITA-PIERCE2 fusion, also known as CIITA-BX648577, is composed of exons 1-4 of CIITA and exon 2 of PIERCE2, and this variant was identified in a Hodgkin's lymphoma cell line. Downregulation of the fusion using RNA interference resulted in increased surface HLA expression while overexpression of the variant decreased HLA expression, suggesting that the CIITA-PIERCE2 fusion protein disrupts MHC cell surface expression (PMID: 21368758).

The CIITA S11P mutation occurs in the N-terminal activation domain of the protein. Expression of the variant in DEV, a nodular-lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NLPHL)-derived cell line, resulted in no change in HLA expression as evidenced by flow cytometric experiments (PMID: 26549456).

CIITA truncating mutations typically result in loss of protein. These mutations have been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PMID: 19229048). Loss of CIITA is demonstrated to be inactivating as measured by downregulation of MHC class II expression and overexpression of ligands for PD-1 compared to wildtype (PMID: 28479318, 26599546, 26549456).

Truncating mutations in CUX1 occur throughout the entire gene and result in reduced protein expression (PMID: 24316979). CUX1 is a transcription factor that has been shown to serve as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor (PMID: 23212519). Loss of CUX1 leads to activation of the PI3K signaling pathway and tumor growth (PMID: 24316979). Truncating mutations in CUX1 have been found in acute myeloid leukemia and have been associated with poor prognosis (PMID: 24316979).

CUL3 deletion mutations typically results in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with conditional or floxed CUL3 MEF cells demonstrate that loss of CUL3 is inactivating as measured by loss of cyclin E regulation and decreased cell viability compared to control cells (PMID: 17339333).

The DDX3X R351W mutation is located in the helicase domain of the DDX3X protein. This mutation has been found in medulloblastomas (PMID: 27180681). In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by increased stress granule formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27180681).

In vitro studies with the pNIC28 vector expressing full transcript DDX3X, C-terminal truncated transcript DDX3X and N-terminal truncated transcript DDX3X demonstrated that loss of the C-terminal domain of DDX3X is inactivating as measured by the loss of binding to blunt-ended double-helix compared to full transcript DDX3X (PMID: 34056415).

In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by increased stress granule formation, and impaired protein translation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27180681).

The DICER1 E1705A mutation occurs in the protein's RNaseIIIb binding domain. In enzymatic assays, DICER1 E1705A has reduced ability to cleave double stranded RNA substrates (PMID: 17920623). Therefore, this mutation likely leads to ineffective miRNA processing.

The DICER1 E1813A mutation is located in the RNaseIIIb binding domain of DICER1. Enzymatic assays of DICER1 E1813A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced ability to cleave double-stranded RNA substrates compared to wildtype (PMID: 17920623).

The DDX3X Y38A mutation is located in the EIF4E binding region of the DDX3X protein. In vitro studies demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased interaction with EIF4E, reduced protein translation, and increased clonogenic growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 17667941).

The DICER1 E1813G mutation is located in the RNase IIIb domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in Wilms tumor and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 23620094). In vitro studies with DICER1-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts expressing DICER1 E1813G demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced miRNA-5p processing and activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 31417090).

Deletions of DICER1 reduce protein expression, leading to haploinsufficiency (PMID: 19903759, 26513514). Loss of DICER1 has been identified in myelodysplasia and secondary leukemia (PMID: 20305640). In vitro studies with DICER1-deficient mouse myeloid progenitor cells demonstrated that loss of DICER1 is inactivating as measured by blocked monocyte differentiation, depleted macrophages and induced myeloid dysplasia compared to wildtype (PMID: 22353998). In contrast, an in vitro study demonstrated DICER1 deletion in tumor-associated macrophages was associated with anti-tumoral effects and allowed for tumor eradication with anti-PD1 therapeutics or CD40 blockade (PMID: 27295554).

The DICER1 D1709E mutation occurs occurs in the protein's RNaseIIIb binding domain. In enzymatic assays, DICER1 D1709E has reduced RNaseIIIb activity, resulting in decreased formation of mature miRNA duplexes (PMID: 22187960). Therefore, this mutation likely leads to ineffective miRNA processing.

Expression of this mutation in murine cell lines a reduction in miRNA expression and increased cell growth, as evidenced by proliferation assays (PMID: 26033159). Therefore, this mutation likely leads to ineffective miRNA processing.

DICER1 germline truncating mutations result in various forms of C-terminally truncated DICER1 protein and the loss of DICER1 protein function. These mutations have been identified in pleuropulmonary blastoma (PMID: 21266384, 21501861). In vitro studies with DICER1-deficient mouse myeloid progenitor cells demonstrated that loss of DICER1 is inactivating as measured by blocked monocyte differentiation, depleted macrophages and induced myeloid dysplasia compared to wildtype (PMID: 22353998, 20305640).

The gene G1809R mutation is located in the RNaseIIIB binding domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in endometrial cancers, among others (PMID: 26033159, 29315962). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced mature miRNA duplex formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26033159).

DIS3 truncations mutations are infrequent and typically result in the loss of protein function (PMID: 33951891). Germline truncating DIS3 mutations have been identified in multiple myeloma (PMID: 30967618). Truncating mutations of DIS3 are suggested to be inactivating due to the loss of the exonucleolytic active RNB and S1 domains (PMID: 30967618).

The DIS3 R780K mutation is located in the RNB domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in multiple myeloma (PMID: 24150935). In vitro studies with HEK293-derived cells expressing DIS3 R780K demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by inhibition of exoribonucleolytic activity and reduced proliferative capacity and metabolic activity (PMID: 24150935, 26193331).

Gene expression studies of samples from patient with pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas with EPAS1 mutations showed overexpression of hypoxia-associated genes (PMID: 23418310).

In vitro assays showed that this mutation significantly reduced hydroxylation compared to the wildtype, as well as its ability to bind VHL. Additionally, the mutated EPAS1 protein displayed increased protein stability and transcriptional activity similar to the wildtype (PMID: 22931260). Gene expression studies of samples from patient with pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas with EPAS1 mutations showed overexpression of hypoxia-associated genes (PMID: 23418310).

In vitro studies with ectopically expressed wildtype EPHA7 in PCa cells demonstrate that loss of EPHA7 is inactivating as measured by reduced cell proliferation and cell migration compared to functionally inactivated EPHA7 (PMID: 29022918).

ERRFi1-/- mice develop spontaneous tumors in various organs and are highly susceptible to chemically induced formation of skin tumors (PMID: 16648858).

Expression of this mutation in a fibroblast cell line demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by the inability to repair UV- and cisplatin-mediated DNA damage compared to wildtype (PMID: 29980530).

ERRFI1 truncation mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein. Loss of ERRFI1 has been identified in lung cancer, melanoma and cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 22701735, 16819504, 24550739). In vitro studies with U251 cells expressing full-length and truncated ERRFI1 transcripts demonstrate that truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by the truncated ERRFI1 transcripts being unable to interact with AKT to negatively regulate signaling compared to full-length ERRFI1 (PMID: 29335246).

The TMPRSS2-ETV4 fusion replaces the 5' end of ETV4 with the 5' UTR of TMPRSS2. ETV4 is a member of the ETS family of transcription factors and the fusion causes overexpression  ETV4 due to the androgen-responsive TMPRSS2 promoter region (PMID: 16585160). Overexpression of ETV4 has been shown to lead to the co-activation of the PI3K and RAS signaling pathways in both human and mouse prostate cancer cells. In vivo studies have shown that overexpression of ETV4 but not other ETS genes promotes metastasis through the induction of the PI3K and RAS signaling pathways (PMID: 23918374). Additionally, ETV4 was shown to be required for anchorage-independent growth and enhanced proliferation of the prostate cancer cell line PC3 (PMID: 21373373).

The TMPRSS2-ETV5 fusion replaces the 5' end of ETV5 with the 5' UTR of TMPRSS2. ETV5 is a member of the ETS family of transcription factors and the fusion causes overexpression of ETV5 due to the androgen-responsive TMPRSS2 promoter region. Overexpression of ETV5 itself increases invasive behavior in prostate cancer cell lines (PMID: 18172298, 22425584). Overexpression of ETS family members ETV 1, 4, and 5 have been shown to increase prostate cell migration and activate the PI3K and RAS signaling pathways (PMID: 22012618, 19657377).

The EWSR1-ETV4 fusion (t(17;22)(q12;q12)) is also known as EWSR1-E1AF. Wildtype ETV4 serves as a transcription factor and activates matrix metalloproteinase genes among many others. The fusion with EWSR1 has been hypothesized to lead to tumor progression (PMID: 8605035) although further studies are needed to determine the mechanism of oncogenicity. While this fusion has not been functionally validated, small case studies have confirmed the presence of EWSR1-ETV4 fusions in Ewing's Sarcoma patients by Southern blot, RT-PCR, and FISH (PMID: 8834175, 8605035, 22429598), and other EWSR1 fusions are known to be oncogenic drivers in Ewing's Sarcoma (PMID:11715049, 25453903, 12432241, 17250957).

EWSR1 fusions generally arise from chromosomal translocations of the N-terminus of EWSR1 (usually involving exons 7-10) to the C terminus of another protein. These fusions have been detected in patients with Ewing sarcoma, and involve EWSR1 translocation with several different gene partners including EIA-F, SMARCA5 and the POU family of transcription factors (PMID: 21113140, 8605035, 8834175, 23329308, 28505004). Experimental studies with the EWSR1-SMARCA5 fusion in NIH3T3 cells led to anchorage-independent growth and colony formation in soft agar (PMID: 21113140). EWSR1 fusions are diagnostic in patients with Ewing sarcoma, however, detailed research is required to characterize their functional role in cancer (Abstract: NCCN Bone Cancer. Volume# v.2017. https://www.nccn.org/professionals/physician_gls/pdf/bone.pdf).

FANCD2 is part of the Fanconi anemia complementation group (FANC). Fanconi anemia consists of a spectrum of hereditary disorders characterized by chromosomal instability and defective DNA repair which leads to cancer predisposition (PMID: 31537806). Truncating mutations in FANCD2 can occur throughout the entire gene (PMID: 31586946). FANCD2 is a tumor suppressor involved in homologous recombination DNA repair that maintains fork stability during DNA replication and recruits Polθ to sites of double-strand breaks and alternate end-junction repair (PMID: 27264184). Truncating mutations and loss of FANCD2 have been identified in hereditary prostate cancer (PMID: 29659569) and sporadic and hereditary breast cancer, where they are associated with worse prognosis (PMID: 17333336, 28386063).

The FANCD2 L153S mutation is located in a region of the protein not associated with a specific domain. The FANCD2 L153S mutation was found in a T-ALL patient with chemotherapy toxicity. In a cell line derived from this individual tumor, the mutation resulted in reduced protein expression, decreased protein stability, and increased sensitivity to ionizing radiation (PMID: 17096012).

The gene T4511I mutation is located in the cytoplasmic domain of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in gliomas (PMID: 23354438). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by reduced gene affinity for binding β-catenin leading to increased cellular proliferation, colony formation, and xenograft formation compared to wildtype (PMID: 23354438).

Truncating mutations of FANCG can occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein function. FANCG truncating mutations have been identified in Fanconi anemia (PMID: 11093276). In vitro studies with COS cells expressing C-terminal truncated variants of FANCG demonstrate that truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by the inability to bind to FANCC and the lack of mitomycin C sensitivity compared to full-length FANCG (PMID: 10961856).

The FAT1 A4419S mutation occurs in the cytoplasmic domain of the protein. Ectopic expression of the mutant in a human glioma cell line abrogates tumor-suppressive phenotypes of the wildtype protein, in particular cell growth, colony formation and xenograft formation (PMID: 23354438). The A4419S mutation also decreased FAT1's affinity for β-catenin, suggesting dysregulation of the WNT pathway as a mechanism for its oncogenic potential (PMID: 23354438).

The FAT1 P4309A mutation occurs in the cytoplasmic domain of the protein. Ectopic expression of the mutant in a human glioma cell line abrogates tumor-suppressive phenotypes of the wildtype protein, in particular cell growth, colony formation and xenograft formation (PMID: 23354438). The P4309A mutation also decreased FAT1's affinity for β-catenin, suggesting dysregulation of the WNT pathway as a mechanism for its oncogenic potential (PMID: 23354438).

Truncating mutations of FAT1 account for approximately half of FAT1 mutations found in human cancers, particularly in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas, lung squamous cell and uterine corpus endometrioid carcinomas (cBioPortal, MSKCC, May 2015, PMID: 24718888). Inactivation of FAT1 has been shown to promote oncogenic WNT signaling and tumorigenesis (PMID: 23354438). Experimental studies in both cell lines and mouse models demonstrated the ability of FAT1 to suppress cancer cell growth by binding β-catenin and antagonizing its nuclear localization. Additionally, expression of truncating mutations of FAT1 in glomerulotubuar disease led to loss of FAT1 protein expression, impaired cell-to-cell adhesion, and reduced cellular migration, the latter which could be rescued by a RAC activator (PMID: 26905694). FAT1 mutations have also been found at a low incidence in breast cancer and have been shown to be associated with resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition. Among 1,501 cases of ER+/HER2- breast cancer, FAT1 alterations were found in 2% of primary and 6% of metastatic cases. Patients with a deleterious FAT1 mutation who received CDK4/6-inhibitor therapy had a progression-free survival (PFS) of 2.4 months compared to 10.1 months for patients with wildtype FAT1 or FAT1 missense mutations. FAT1 knockdown and knockout in MCF7 cells demonstrated resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition, as shown by sustained cell proliferation in the presence of CDK4/6 inhibitor, abemaciclib, as compared to WT MCF7 cells. In addition, FAT1 loss in MCF7 and CAMA-1 cells resulted in increased CDK6 protein expression through induction of the HIPPO pathway effectors, YAP and TAZ (PMID: 30537512).

Truncating mutations in FBXO11 have been identified in the CASH domain of the protein (PMID: 22113614). FBXO11 is an F-box protein, one of the subunits of the SCF ubiquitin protein ligase complexes involved in proteasomal degradation (PMID: 27156687). FBXO11 is involved in the ubiquitination of BCL6, a proto-oncogene involved in the pathogenesis of some lymphomas (PMID: 27166359), as well as the Snail family of transcription factors (PMID: 25827072). Loss of FBXO11 by epigenetic mechanisms like miR-21 inactivation has been shown to induce tumorigenesis (PMID: 25589783). Truncating mutations in FBXO11 have been reported in diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (DLBCL) (PMID: 22113614)

The FOXA1 Y259C mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243370). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models and cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FOXA1 transcriptional activity, increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor, and the formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

Homo- and heterozygous deletion of the FAT1 locus on chromosome 4q35 leads to the loss of FAT1 expression and has been described in several tumors. Loss of FAT1 has been mechanistically associated with increased growth and invasion via beta-catenin mislocalization in both oral carcinomas and gliomas and has been shown to promote oncogenic WNT signaling and tumorigenesis (PMID: 21617878, 23354438). FAT1 deletions have also been found at a low incidence in breast cancer and have been shown to be associated with resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition. Among 1,501 cases of ER+/HER2- breast cancer, FAT1 alterations were found in 2% of primary and 6% of metastatic cases. Patients with a deleterious FAT1 alteration, including deletions, who received CDK4/6-inhibitor therapy had a progression-free survival (PFS) of 2.4 months compared to 10.1 months for patients with wildtype (WT) FAT1 or FAT1 missense mutations. FAT1 knockdown and knockout in MCF7 breast cells demonstrated resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition, as shown by sustained cell proliferation in the presence of CDK4/6 inhibitor, abemaciclib, as compared to WT MCF7 cells. In addition, FAT1 loss in MCF7 and CAMA-1 cells resulted in increased CDK6 protein expression through induction of the HIPPO pathway effectors, YAP and TAZ (PMID: 30537512).

The FOXA1 R261G mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243372). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased androgen receptor transcriptional activity and increased cell proliferation in androgen-depleted media and in the presence of the anti-androgen enzalutamide compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243372).

The FOXA1 R265_Q271del mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243372). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as shown by increased androgen receptor transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243372).

Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models and cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FOXA1 transcriptional activity, increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor, and the formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 F254_E255del mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243370). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models also resulted in a shift in the chromatin landscape resulting in more open chromatin peaks compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 L455M mutation is located in the protein's C-terminal transactivating domain and has been identified in castrate-resistant prostate cancer samples. Stable overexpression of FOXA1 L455M in LNCaP prostate cancer cells esulted in increased proliferation and repression of the androgen receptor (AR) transcriptional program in the presence of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) (PMID: 22722839).

The FOXA1 S250F mutation is located in the Wing2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 30531871). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing FOXA1 S250F demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased transcriptional activity and protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 32888433).

The FOXA1 R261C mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243370). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models and cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FOXA1 transcriptional activity, increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor, and the formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 P358fs mutation is located in the C-terminal regulatory region of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243372). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer cell lines demonstrated that it is likely activating as shown by stronger binding to canonical FOXA1 DNA binding sites compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243372).

The FOXA1 F400I mutation is located in the protein's C-terminal transactivating domain and has been identified in castrate-resistant prostate cancer samples. Stable overexpression of the FOXA1 F400I mutant in LNCaP prostate cancer cells was associated with increased proliferation in the presence of tamoxifen. However, no significant differences in cell proliferation was observed when comparing frank FOXA1 overexpression versus wildtype FOXA1 (PMID: 22722839). In a separate experiment, stable expression of FOXA1 F400I in DU145 prostate cancer cells demonstrated that the mutant is unable to suppress SLUG as well as wildtype FOXA1. This derepression of SLUG conferred greater cell motility in DU145 cells expressing mutant FOXA1, likely by activating the epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) (PMID: 23539448).

The FOXA1 R219C mutation is located in the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243370). There is functional data for this mutation suggesting it is neomorphic. Expression of this mutation in human embryonic kidney cells and prostate cancer organoid models demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by decreased FOXA1 transcriptional activity and decreased formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370). However, expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models also resulted in a shift in the chromatin landscape resulting in more open chromatin peaks compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 F266L mutation is located in the Wing2 region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in prostate cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vivo xenograft studies with mice expressing FOXA1 F266L demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased tumor growth and transcription of estrogen response genes compared to wildtype (PMID: 32888433).  Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models and cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FOXA1 transcriptional activity, increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor and the formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 L388M mutation is located in the protein's C-terminal transactivating domain and has been identified in castrate-resistant prostate cancer samples. Stable overexpression of FOXA1 L388M in LNCaP prostate cancer cells resulted in increased proliferation and repression of the androgen receptor (AR) transcriptional program in the presence of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) (PMID: 22722839).

The FOXA1 I176M mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243372). The FOXA1 I360* mutation is located in the C-terminal regulatory region of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243372). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer cell lines and zebrafish embryos demonstrated that it activating as shown by stronger binding to canonical FOXA1 DNA binding sites, an expanded cistrome compared to wildtype and a higher rate and extent of metastases compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243372). Cells expressing this mutation were sensitive to AR knockdown and treatment with the WNT inhibitor, XAV939 as demonstrated by decreased cell viability (PMID: 31243372).

Amplification of FOXA1 occurs when the FOXA1 genomic locus is specifically replicated or "amplified" to increase the number of DNA segments containing the FOXA1 gene relative to wildtype cells. FOXA1 amplification is typically associated with higher FOXA1 expression, and has been identified in breast cancer (PMID: 19372580), lung adenocarcinomas (PMID: 25079552, 2298097), squamous cell carcinomas (PMID: 22960745), esophageal adenocarcinomas (PMID: 12234996), anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 19470727) and prostate cancer (PMID: 23622249, 21147910, 22722839). Several studies in human prostate cancer cell lines, including LNCaP and PC-3M model systems, have demonstrated that over-expression of FOXA1 results in increased proliferation (PMID: 22722839, 23539448). Consistent with this, knockdown of FOXA1 in LNCaP and PC-3 cell lines resulted in decreased cell motility, as well as decreased proliferation compared to controls, likely mediated through cyclin D1 levels and G1 arrest (PMID: 22138582).

The FOXA1 M253K mutation is located in the protein's DNA-binding forkhead (FKHD) domain. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243370). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models and cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FOXA1 transcriptional activity, increased cell proliferation in the absense of epidermal growth factor and the formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370). Stable expression of FOXA1 M253K in DU145 prostate cancer cells demonstrated that this mutant is unable to suppress SLUG expression relative to the wildtype protein, which conferred greater motility as measured by in-vitro invasion assays, likely by activating the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (PMID: 23539448).

The FOXA1 H247Q mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243370). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models and cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FOXA1 transcriptional activity, increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor, and the formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 F266S mutation is located in the Wing2 region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in prostate cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 31324884). In vitro studies with FOXA1-null LNCaP cells expressing FOXA1 F266S demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to rescue FOXA1-mediated gene expression (PMID: 31324884).

The FOXA1 S453fs* mutation is located in the protein's N-terminal forkhead FKHD domain and has been identified in castrate-resistant prostate cancer samples. Stable overexpression of FOXA1 G87R in LNCaP prostate cancer cells resulted in increased proliferation and repression of the androgen receptor (AR) transcriptional program in the presence of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) PMID: 22722839). Additionally, expression of this mutation in LNCaP cells led to enhanced tumor growth in a mouse xenograft model compared to cells expressing wildtype FOXA1 (PMID: 22722839).

FOXA1 deletions are associated with loss of FOXA1 protein expression and likely to confer FOXA1 loss-of-function. Deletion of FOXA1 in the prostate of mice leads to hyperplasia, enhanced cellular proliferation and abnormal morphology (PMID: 24840332). Luminal-specific deletion of FOXA1 in the mouse prostate results in high rates of epithelial cell proliferation and increased expression of basal cell markers (PMID: 24840332), indicating that FOXA1 may play a role in promoting and maintaining epithelial cell differentiation.

The FOXA1 M253_N256del mutation is located in the wing-2 region of the forkhead DNA-binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243370). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models and cell lines demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased FOXA1 transcriptional activity, increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor, and the formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 P359fs mutation is located in the C-terminal regulatory region of the protein. This mutation has been found in prostate cancer (PMID: 31243372). Expression of this mutation in prostate cancer cell lines and zebrafish embryos demonstrated that it is activating as measured by stronger binding to canonical FOXA1 DNA binding sites, an expanded cistrome compared to wildtype, increased signaling through the WNT/beta-catenin pathway and a higher rate and extent of metastases compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243372). Cells expressing this mutation were sensitive to AR knockdown and treatment with the WNT inhibitor, XAV939 as demonstrated by decreased cell viability (PMID: 31243372).

Expression of this mutation in human embryonic kidney cells and prostate cancer organoid models demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by decreased FOXA1 transcriptional activity and decreased formation of colonies with exaggerated lumens compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370). However, expression of this mutation in prostate cancer organoid models demonstrated that it activating as measured by increased cell proliferation in the absence of epidermal growth factor compared to wildtype (PMID: 31243370).

The FOXA1 G87R mutation is located in the protein's N-terminal forkhead FKHD domain and has been identified in castrate-resistant prostate cancer samples. Luminal-specific deletion of FOXA1 in the mouse prostate results in high rates of epithelial cell proliferation and increased expression of basal cell markers (PMID: 24840332), indicating that FOXA1 may play a role in promoting and maintaining epithelial cell differentiation. C-terminal truncating mutations of FOXA1 that preserve the forkhead domains may not alter the binding of FOXA1 with DNA but rather alter the interaction of FOXA1 with other cofactors (PMID: 26544944).

Amplification at GLI1 locus leads to GLI1 gene overexpression. In a study in mouse cell lines, overexpression of GLI1 increased colony formation, and injection into nude mice showed tumorigenecity comparable to Ras oncogene (PMID: 3563490, 1825351).
