The LZTR1 W105R mutation occurs in the first Kelch motif of the protein (PMID: 30442762). This variant has been identified in patients with glioblastoma (PMID: 30442762). Hematopoietic cell lines engineered to express the LZTR1 W105R mutation exhibited increased MAPK pathway activation, consistent with reduced CUL3-mediated ubiquitination of RAS (PMID: 30442762). In vitro studies suggest that LZTR1 W105R is resistant to imatinib, as evidenced by cellular proliferation assays (PMID: 30442762).

The LZTR1 R198G mutation occurs in the third Kelch motif of the protein (PMID: 30442762). This variant has been identified in patients with glioblastoma (PMID: 30442762). Hematopoietic cell lines engineered to express the LZTR1 R198G mutation exhibited increased MAPK pathway activation, consistent with reduced CUL3-mediated ubiquitination of RAS (PMID: 30442762). Biochemical studies demonstrated that LZTR1 R198G had reduced CUL3-ubiquitination activity against KRAS (PMID: 30442762). In vitro studies suggest that LZTR1 R198G is resistant to imatinib, as evidenced by cellular proliferation assays (PMID: 30442762).

The LZTR1 R284C mutation occurs in the fourth Kelch motif of the protein (PMID: 30442762). This variant has been identified in patients with Noonan Syndrome (PMID: 30442762). Hematopoietic cell lines engineered to express the LZTR1 R284C mutation exhibited increased MAPK pathway activation, consistent with reduced CUL3-mediated ubiquitination of RAS (PMID: 30442762). In vitro studies suggest that LZTR1 R284C is resistant to imatinib, as evidenced by cellular proliferation assays (PMID: 30442762).

The LZTR1 Y119C mutation occurs in the second Kelch motif of the protein (PMID: 30442762). This variant has been identified in patients with Noonan Syndrome (PMID: 30442762). Hematopoietic cell lines engineered to express the LZTR1 Y119C mutation exhibited increased MAPK pathway activation, consistent with reduced CUL3-mediated ubiquitination of RAS (PMID: 30442762). In vitro studies suggest that LZTR1 Y119C is resistant to imatinib, as evidenced by cellular proliferation assays (PMID: 30442762).

The LZTR1 H287Y mutation occurs in the fifth Kelch motif of the protein (PMID: 30442762). This variant has been identified in patients with Noonan Syndrome (PMID: 30442762). Hematopoietic cell lines engineered to express the LZTR1 H287Y mutation exhibited increased MAPK pathway activation, consistent with reduced CUL3-mediated ubiquitination of RAS (PMID: 30442762). In vitro studies suggest that LZTR1 H278Y is resistant to imatinib, as evidenced by cellular proliferation assays (PMID: 30442762).

The LZTR1 G404R mutation occurs in the sixth Kelch motif of the protein (PMID: 30442762, 24362817). This variant has been identified in patients with Schwannomatosis (PMID: 30442762). Hematopoietic cell lines engineered to express the LZTR1 G404R mutation exhibited increased MAPK pathway activation, consistent with reduced CUL3-mediated ubiquitination of RAS (PMID: 30442762). In vitro studies suggest that LZTR1 G404R is resistant to imatinib, as evidenced by cellular proliferation assays (PMID: 30442762).

The LZTR1 P520L mutation occurs in the first BTB domain of the protein (PMID: 30442762, 24362817). This variant has been identified in patients with Schwannomatosis (PMID: 30442762). Hematopoietic cell lines engineered to express the LZTR1 P520L mutation exhibited increased MAPK pathway activation, consistent with reduced CUL3-mediated ubiquitination of RAS (PMID: 30442762). In vitro studies suggest that LZTR1 P520L is resistant to imatinib, as evidenced by cellular proliferation assays (PMID: 30442762).

Translocations involving IGH and MAFB are found in patients with multiple myeloma (MM) and IGH rearrangements are predicted to be the primary initiating event in this disease (PMID: 28726797, 28584253). IGH-MAFB rearrangements (t(14;16)) typically partner 3' IGH enhancer regions upstream of the MAFB gene, resulting in upregulation of MAFB expression (PMID: 24638926, 28726797). IGH fusion proteins are the product of altered class switch recombination during plasma cell differentiation or abnormal VDJ rearrangement (PMID: 26282654). In murine models, overexpression of MAFB results in plasma cell neoplasms and the activation of B-cell like transcriptional programs in hematopoietic cell populations (PMID: 22903061). Expression of MAF fusion proteins delineates a subgroup of MM patients that have a poor prognosis (PMID: 11877296, 20410185, 15257707, 28584253).

Translocations involving MECOM are recurrent in myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemias (AML) (PMID: 28538183). The resultant fusion proteins typically contain most of the MECOM protein recombined with regulatory units of other transcription factors, leading to increased or altered transcriptional activity of MECOM (PMID: 28538183, 30526151). Common MECOM fusion partners include ETV6 and RUNX1, among others (PMID: 28538183, 30526151). In biochemical assays, expression of MECOM fusions results in transformation and the development of hematopoietic malignancies in murine models (PMID: 28538183, 18337762, 10677531). MECOM rearrangements may require additional genetic events to cooperatively drive AML (PMID: 11781838, 17227832).

Translocations involving GATA2 and MECOM are recurrent in acute myeloid leukemia and are predictive of poor prognosis (PMID: 22887804, 24703711, 24703906). GATA2-MECOM rearrangements position a distal GATA2 enhancer upstream of MECOM, resulting in activation of MECOM expression and GATA2 haploinsufficiency (PMID: 24703711, 28630119, 24703906). Deletion of the GATA2 enhancer results in silencing of MECOM expression, as well as inhibition of growth and differentiation of AML cell lines and patient samples (PMID: 24703711, 24703906). Murine models engineered to express the GATA2-MECOM allele develop an overt leukemia, dependent on GATA2 enhancer activity (PMID: 24703906). GATA2-MECOM expressing cells are sensitive to BET bromodomain inhibitors, due to depletion of superenhancer activity (PMID: 24703711).

MGA deletion events are infrequent; however, loss of MGA is predicted to increase MYC activity and MGA inactivating mutations have been observed in multiple cancer types, including lung, leukemia, and lymphoma and are generally mutually exclusive with other MYC alterations. Therefore, MGA deletion events are assumed to be oncogenic (PMID: 10601024).

MGA truncating mutations may lead to the expression of varying C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations typically result in deletion of the basic motif and helix-loop-helix DNA-binding domain required for suppressing MYC-dependent transformation and are therefore assumed to result in increased MYC activity. MGA truncation mutations are found to be mutually exclusive with MYC alterations (PMID: 23039309).

The KMT2A-MLLT10 fusion is a result of the N-terminal DNA binding domain of KMT2A and the C-terminal of MLLT10, containing the leucine zipper domain (PMID: 29563185). Translocations involving KMT2A and MLLT10 are recurrent in a variety of hematopoietic malignancies including adult and pediatric T-ALL and acute myeloid leukemia, among others (PMID: 23673860, 22846743). Biochemical assays demonstrated that KMT2A-MLLT10 can bind chromatin and the histone methyltransferase DOT1L (PMID: 15851025). Expression of KMT2A-MLLT10 in hematopoietic cell lines results in the activation of leukemogenic gene expression programs and enhanced H3K79 methylation (PMID: 23673860, 29563185).

Translocations involving MLLT10 are recurrent in a variety of hematopoietic malignancies including adult and pediatric T-ALL and acute myeloid leukemia, among others (PMID: 23673860). In MLLT10 fusion proteins, the N-terminal part of the protein, including the chromatin binding PHD domain, is lost but the fusion protein retains the leucine zipper motif (PMID: 11756182). Often the MLLT10 protein fuses with other leukemogenic related proteins such as MLL, NAP1L1, HNRNPH1, DDX3X and PICALM, and the resultant fusion proteins function as chromatin modifying proteins (PMID: 23673860). T-ALL patient samples containing MLLT10 fusions demonstrate activation of leukemogenic gene expression programs, including activation of HOXA (PMID: 23673860).

Translocations involving PICALM and MLLT10 are recurrent in a variety of hematopoietic malignancies including adult and pediatric T-ALL and acute myeloid leukemia, among others (PMID: 23831922, 23670296, 16826225, 23673860). PICALM-MLLT10 rearranged oncoproteins typically contain most of the PICALM reading frame and the C-terminal of MLLT10, containing the leucine zipper domain (PMID: 22064352). In the resultant PICALM-MLLT10 protein, the C-terminal of MLLT10 functions as chromatin modifying protein that binds histone modifying enzymes like DOT1L (PMID: 23673860. The nuclear export signal, which comprises part of the clathrin-binding domain, in the PICALM protein is also required for the activity of the PICALM-MLLT10 fusion (PMID: 24397609, 23487024). Biochemical assays in hematopoietic cells that express the PICALM-MLLT10 fusion revealed increases in HOXA gene expression, altered H3K79 methylation, and enhanced transformation capacity (PMID: 15843827, 24397609, 22064352). PICALM-MLLT10 fusions are associated with an immature phenotype and poor prognosis in T-ALL (PMID: 12676784, 9616163).

Amplification of MN1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. MN1 amplification has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 28440611, 28892045, 33974912). In vivo studies with mice overexpressing MN1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by induction of lethal acute myeloid leukemia compared to control (PMID: 17494859). Preclinical studies suggest that MN1 overexpression may confer resistance to all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) treatment and chemotherapy in the context of acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 17494859, 22905229).

MLLT3 fusions generally arise from chromosomal translocations that fuse the N-terminal end of a partner gene with the C-terminal end of MLLT3, such that the fusion proteins exclude the MLLT3 YEATS domain. MLLT3 fusions have been found in acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 26762252, 25843568). Expression of MLLT3 fusion KMT2A-MLLT3 in the THP1 cell line demonstrated that it is activating due to aberrant transcription leading to significant cell proliferation and monoblastic differentiation (PMID: 26762252). In vitro studies with the bone-marrow-derived LSK cells expressing the KMT2A-MLLT3 fusion demonstrated sensitivity to inhibition of DOT1L co-factor AF10 as measured by impaired colony formation (PMID: 25464900).

Truncating mutations of MST1 can occur throughout the gene and typically result in loss of protein function. In vitro studies with COS-7 cells expressing N-terminal and C-terminal truncated variants of MST1 demonstrate that C-terminal truncation of MST1 is inactivating as measured by decreased interaction with AR compared to wildtype and N-terminal truncated MST1 (PMID: 21512132).

MTAP deletions are associated with homozygous deletions in the 9p21 chromosomal region that also includes the tumor suppressors CDKN2A, p16-INK4A, and p19-ARF (PMID: 27068473, 26912360). MTAP-deleted cancer cell lines have increased expression of polyamine synthesis byproducts, including 2-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) due to reduced MTAP-dependent cleavage activity (PMID: 27068473, 26912360). These metabolic byproducts inhibit PRMT5, an arginine methyltransferase, and sensitize MTAP-deleted cancer cell lines and murine models to purine inhibitors (PMID: 27068473, 26912360, 31257072).

MTAP truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. MTAP-deleted cancer cell lines have increased expression of polyamine synthesis byproducts, including 2-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) due to reduced MTAP-dependent cleavage activity (PMID: 27068473, 26912360). These metabolic byproducts inhibit PRMT5, an arginine methyltransferase, and sensitize MTAP-deleted cancer cell lines and murine models to purine inhibitors (PMID: 27068473, 26912360, 31257072).

Truncating mutations of MYH11 can occur throughout the gene and typically result in loss of protein function. These mutations have been identified in colorectal cancer and prostate cancer (PMID: 29517504). In vitro studies with MSI colorectal cancer cell lines expressing MYH11 frameshift mutations demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of ATPase regulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 18796164, 29517504).

The MYH11 K1256del mutation is located in the four lysine stretch of the myosin tail domain of the protein. This mutation has been found as a germline mutation in families with familial thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections (FTAAD) (PMID: 35614093). Expression of this mutation in a mouse model demonstrated it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased contractility, decreased cell adhesion, and predisposition to aortic aneurisms compared to wildtype (PMID: 35614093).

The MYH11 R669H mutation is located in the globular head domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in individuals with congenital cardiac malformation (PMID: 17956658). Structural studies suggest that this mutation may interfere with actin binding based on its location in the protein (PMID: 17956658).

The MYH11 R669C mutation is located in the globular head domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in individuals with congenital cardiac malformation (PMID: 17956658). Structural studies suggest that this mutation may interfere with actin binding based on its location in the protein (PMID: 17956658).

NKX3-1 truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in prostate cancer (PMID: 11085535). In vitro studies with PTEN-null prostatic epithelium cells demonstrated loss of NKX3-1 is inactivating as measured by decreased cell proliferation, increased cell death and prevention of tumor initiation following NKX3-1 re-expression (PMID: 16697957).

The EWSR1-NR4A3 t(9;22)(q22;q12) chromosomal rearrangement fuses the amino acid terminal of EWSR1 to the complete amino acid sequence of NR4A3. This fusion replaces the RNA recognition domain of EWS with the DNA binding domain of NR4A3 (PMID: 10359536). Novel activity of the oncogenic fusion protein has been shown in human bone marrow cell studies to increase expression of neuromedin B and negative regulators of the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, among other genes important in the promotion of proliferation and inhibition of differentiation (PMID: 22592656, 11673470). Further, in vitro cellular assays in COS cells and human chondrocytes have shown a dramatic increase in activation of NR4A3 transcriptional targets from the fusion protein compared to wild-type NR4A3, confirming its oncogenicity (PMID: 10359536).

NOTCH4 is a transmembrane receptor that is part of the Notch signaling pathway, a family of proteins implicated in embryonic development (PMID:21948802). NOTCH4  inhibits endothelial sprouting and angiogenesis, and truncating mutations involving the ankyrin repeats domain have been shown to inactivate this function and lead to VEGF-mediated angiogenesis (PMID: 15187023). Truncating mutations in NOTCH4 have been reported in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas (PMID:22006338) as well as in head and neck adenoid cystic carcinomas (PMID: 31483290).

Truncating mutations in NTHL1 occur throughout the gene and lead to loss of the NTHL1 protein (PMID: 30753826). NTHL1 is involved in DNA base-excision repair and acts as a tumor suppressor (PMID: 30753826). Germline truncating mutations in NTHL1 lead to adenomatous polyposis, colorectal cancer, as well as other malignancies such as breast carcinomas (PMID: 25938944, 30753826).

The NUP98-NSD1 fusion occurs frequently, especially in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The resulting protein encodes the amino-terminal portion of NUP98 including the FG repeat domain, which can bind to CBP/p300 histone acetyltransferase, fused to the C-terminal portion of NSD1, which contains multiple PHD domains, a PWWP domain, and a Set2-family HMT domain reported to target H3K36 (PMID:17589499). The NSD1-NUP98 fusion may promote leukemogenesis by blocking EZH2 repression of the Hox-A locus through colocalizing H3K36 methylation and histone acetylation at regulatory DNA elements and subsequently blocking normal differentiation (PMID: 17589499, 27889185). Retroviral transduction of NUP98-NSD1 into myeloid progenitor cells stunted differentiation and kept cells proliferating as undifferentiated progenitors. Transduced cells showed upregulation of multiple HoxA genes and Meis1, similar to other transforming fusions like MLL-AF9 (PMID: 17589499). This fusion was identified in six of 124 pediatric patients with AML (4.8%) and was strongly associated with a poor prognosis (PMID:23630019, 11895789).

The BRD4-NUTM1 fusion is formed by an in-frame fusion of 15q14 to the N-terminus of BRD4 resulting in the retention of the BRD4 bromodomains. This fusion protein has been identified in NUT midline carcinoma (PMID: 32371576, 17934517). Overexpression of BRD4-NUTM1 in cell lines and in murine xenograft models demonstrate the fusion protein is activating as measured by MYC-dependent differentiation block and dysregulation of histone acetylation and transcription (PMID: 17934517, 21447744). In addition, knockdown of BRD4-NUTM1 fusion-expressing cells also demonstrated the fusion protein is activating as measured by restoration of differentiation (PMID: 20676058). BRD4-NUT fusion proteins are suggested to be sensitive to bromodomain inhibitor treatment as they target the bromodomain of BRD4 to dissociate the fusion protein from the MYC promoter (PMID: 25688404). In a clinical trial, four patients with NUT carcinoma harboring BRD4-NUTM1 were treated with BMS-986158 and one patient achieved partial response with 60% disease regression, one patient achieved an initial 36.6% disease regression followed by disease progression after 11.3 weeks, and two patients did not experience clinical benefit (PMID: 37384867).

The NUP98-HOXA9 fusion results from the chromosomal translocation t(7;11)(p15;p15) and results in the DNA binding domain of HOXA9 fusing with the N-terminus of NUP98, including the FG repeat domain. This fusion has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia, chronic myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 26418229). In vitro studies and in vivo studies with myeloid cells and mice expressing NUP98-HOXA9 demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, increased transcriptional gene activity and induction of acute myeloid leukemia compared to vector controls (PMID: 11157742, 16818636, 14561764).

The PAK5 S364L mutation is located adjacent to a proline-rich motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 28467829). In vitro studies with hMELT cells expressing PAK5 S364L demonstrate that the mutation is likely activating as measured by increased melanocyte proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 29875996).

Expression of PAK1 results in activation of the MAPK pathway and inhibition of MERLIN (NF2) and promotes anchor-independent growth (PMID: 22105362). SiRNA-mediated knockdown of PAK1 in cell lines harboring PAK1 gene amplification results in inhibition of growth and induction of apoptosis (PMID: 21482786).

The PAK5 S312C mutation is located in the linker region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in adenocarcinoma (PMID: 18948947). Expression of the PAK5 S312C mutation in human cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype PAK5 (PMID: 23836671).

The PAK5 D421N mutation is located adjacent to a proline-rich motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 22622578). In vitro studies with hMELT cells expressing PAK5 D421N demonstrate that the mutation is likely activating as measured by increased melanocyte proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 29875996).

The PAK5 E294K mutation is located adjacent to a proline-rich motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 26343386). In vitro studies with hMELT cells expressing PAK5 E294K demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by kinase activity and melanocyte proliferation comparable to wildtype (PMID: 29875996).

The PAK5 E144K mutation is located in the auto-inhibitory domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with hMELT cells expressing PAK5 E144K demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by statistically insignificant melanocyte proliferation and kinase activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 29875996).

The PAK5 T538N mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cells lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype PAK5 (PMID: 23836671).

The PAK5 S573N mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with 293 cells expressing PAK5 S573N demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased kinase activity and constitutive activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 11756552).

The PAK5 V463L mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cells lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype PAK5 (PMID: 23836671).

The PAK5 V593I mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cells lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling compared to wildtype PAK5 (PMID: 23836671).

The PAK5 M173I mutation is located in the linker region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with hMELT cells expressing PAK5 M173I demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by statistically insignificant melanocyte proliferation and kinase activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 29875996).

The PAX3-FOXO1 fusion, also previously known as PAX3-FKHR, results from the chromosomal translocation t(2;13) (q35;q14). This fusion has been identified in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (PMID: 12039929, 22454413). In vitro studies with A673 cells expressing PAX3-FOXO1 demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by increased transcriptional activity of PAX3 target genes compared to wildtype (PMID: 7862145). Preclinical studies of PAX3-FOXO1 demonstrate sensitivity to KDM3B inhibitors PFI-63 and PFI-90 as measured by repression of PAX3 target genes and increased apoptosis (Abstract: Kim et al. Abstract# 47, AACR 2021. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/81/13_Supplement/47/669252/Abstract-47-Identification-of-first-in-class-KDM3B).

The PIK3CD E525K mutation is located in the helical domain of the kinase and is activating. This mutation is homologous to the oncogenic PIK3CA E545K mutant. Expression of p110delta E525K in unstimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells increased phospho-AKT levels as compared to wildtype (PMID: 24165795). Patient's with germline p110delta E525K mutation had increased p110d-AKT-mTOR signaling and enhanced glucose uptake in T cells which lead to senescence (PMID: 24165795). T cell PI3K-AKT pathway activation was reduced when treated with p110delta-selective inhibitors in vitro (PMID: 24136356, 24165795).

The PIK3CD C416R mutation is located in the kinase C2 domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic T-cell leukemia and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28671688). In vitro studies with patient-derived B cells expressing PIK3CD C416R demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by hyperphosphorylation of AKT compared to wildtype (PMID: 24610295).

The PIK3CD E1021K mutation is located in the C loop of the kinase domain and is activating. This mutation aligns two nucleotides away from, and is thought to have a similar gain of function effect as, the PIK3CA H1047R mutation. Expression of p110delta E1021K versus wildtype showed increased membrane association, lipid kinase activity (increased production of PIP3) and AKT phosphorylation in in vitro biochemical assays, human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and p110delta knockout mice (PMID: 24136356). Patient's with germline p110delta E1021K mutation had higher PIP3 levels in leukocytes and increased p110d-AKT-mTOR signaling and enhanced glucose uptake and gycolysis in T cells which lead to senescence (PMID: 24136356, 24165795). A patient with a germline p110delta E1021K mutation and severe lymphoproliferation was treated with rapamycin and experienced a restoration of naive T cells to normal levels and function, and reduced hepatospenomegaly and lymphadenopathy (PMID: 24165795).

The PIK3CD G971R mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 and MCF10A cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased factor-independent proliferation compared to wildtype PIK3CD (PMID: 29533785).

Truncating mutations in PIK3R3 result in PIK3R3 C-terminal truncated proteins (PMID: 27766312). In a single study with lymphatic endothelial cells harboring PIK3R3 mutations, mutant cells were demonstrated to exhibit increased phosphorylated AKT and were associated with increased sensitivity to PI3K inhibitors wortmannin and LY294 as well as mTOR inhibitor rapamycin when compared to normal endothelial cells (PMID: 25424831).

The PLCG1 S520F mutation is located in the PLCXc catalytic domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human and mouse cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling activity and increased foci formation compared to wildtype PLCG1 (PMID: 24497536). In vitro studies suggest that the PLCG1 S520F mutation is sensitive to PLCG1 downstream inhibitors, including tacrolimus and U73122, as measured by decreased downstream signaling activity (PMID: 24497536).

The PIK3CD G124D mutation is located between the p85 binding domain and the RAS binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 and MCF10A cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased factor-independent proliferation compared to wildtype PIK3CD (PMID: 29533785).

The PIK3CD N334K mutation is located in the C2 domain of the protein and is activating. This mutation is homologous to the oncogenic PIK3CA N345K mutant, which has increased membrane binding, a disrupted interaction with the iSH2 domain of the regulatory subunit p85 and increased PI3K signaling. Expression of p110delta N334K in unstimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells increased phospho-AKT levels as compared to wildtype (PMID: 24165795). Patient's with germline p110delta N334K mutation had increased p110d-AKT-mTOR signaling and enhanced glucose uptake in T cells which forces the differentiation of naive CD8+ T cells into short-lived effector cells at the expense of long-term memory T and B cells (PMID: 24165795).

The PAX7-FOXO1 fusion, also previously known as PAX7-FKHR, results from the chromosomal translocation t(1;13)(p36;q14). This fusion has been identified in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (PMID: 36722003). In vivo studies with Drosophila models expressing PAX7-FOXO1 demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by increased cellular invasion compared to vector control (PMID: 16938866). In vitro studies with CW9019 cells expressing PAX7-FOXO1 also demonstrate the fusion is activating as measured by upregulation of NFkB signaling and disruption of myogenic differentiation compared to wildtype (PMID: 22374423).

The PLCG1 S345F mutation is located in the PLCXc catalytic domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human and mouse cell lines demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling activity and increased foci formation compared to wildtype PLCG1 (PMID: 24497536). In vitro studies suggest that the PLCG1 S345F mutation is sensitive to PLCG1 downstream inhibitors, including tacrolimus and U73122, as measured by decreased downstream signaling activity (PMID: 24497536).

The PLCG1 R707Q mutation is located in the SH2 domain of the protein. Expression of the mutation in human cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream signaling activation, apoptosis resistance, migration and invasion (PMID: 25252913).

The PLCG1 R48W mutation is located in the PH1 domain of the PLCG1 protein. There is conflicting biological data for this mutation. In vitro studies have demonstrated that in the human embryonic kidney cell line HEK293T this mutation is neutral as demonstrated by similar NFAT transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 27369867). However, in vitro studies have demonstrated that in the T-cell line J.gamma1, this mutation is activating as demonstrated by increased NFAT, AP-1 and NFΚB transcriptional activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 31376383). In silico analysis predicts that mutation is damaging (PMID: 31376383).

Amplification of PDK1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. PDK1 amplification has been identified in breast cancer, prostate cancer and ovarian cancer (PMID: 21542898, 23401739, 33403023). In vitro studies with ovarian cancer and non-small cell lung cancer cell lines overexpressing PDK1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, adhesion and invasion compared to vector control (PMID: 32071289, 27878287). In vivo studies with nude mice overexpressing PDK1 also demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased tumor growth compared to PDK1-knockdown mice (PMID: 32071289).

The COL1A1-PDGFB fusion is a result of fusing COL1A1 in-frame with most of the PDGFB protein, deleting exon 1 of PDGFB (PMID: 17431412, 8988177). Translocations of COL1A1 and PDGFB are frequent in patients with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, a soft tissue sarcoma that develops in the skin (PMID: 17431412, 12131162). In addition, COL1A1-PDGFB fusions are found in patients with giant cell fibroblastomas and adult superficial fibrosarcomas (PMID: 17431412, 8988177). Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans tumors with COL1A1-PDGFB rearrangements have increased expression of PDGFB, suggesting the fusion activates PDGFB (PMID: 17431412). The fusion protein is processed into a mature PDGFB ligand that activates PDGFB signaling, leading to increased cellular proliferation (PMID: 10446987). Expression of COL1A1-PDGFB in cell lines and murine models results in transformation and sensitivity to PDGF receptor small molecule inhibition (PMID: 10446987, 11420709).

Truncating mutations of PML typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with SAOS‑2 cells expressing truncated variants of PML demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by inhibition of TP53 transcription and apoptosis compared to wildtype (PMID: 17172828).

Truncating mutations in PMAIP1 that affect the BH3 or mitochondrial targeting domains lead to loss of protein function. Loss of PMAIP1, through truncation or other mechanisms, has been identified in mantle cell lymphoma (PMID: 24457957). In vitro studies with HeLa cells expressing PMAIP1 truncating mutations in the BH3 and mitochondrial targeting domains demonstrate these mutations are inactivating as measured by the inability to release cytochrome C from the mitochondria, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction (PMID: 14500711).

Deletion of PML typically results in the loss of protein expression. In vivo studies with PML-knockout mice demonstrate that deletion is inactivating as measured by increased incidence of leukemia compared to control mice (PMID: 11181703).

The PMS1 Q233* mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in a hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer patient (PMID: 8072530). Sequence analysis has demonstrated that PMS1 Q233* is inactivating as the mutation introduces a premature stop codon that leads to inactivation of the protein (PMID: 8072530).

PMS1 truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and typically lead to loss of protein function. These mutations have been identified in hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer and inherited mesothelioma (PMID: 8072530, 28687356). In vivo studies with yeast expressing PMS1 truncating mutations in the linker arm region demonstrate these mutations are inactivating as measured by defects in DNA mismatch repair and DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 22659005).

In vitro studies have shown that PTPN2 knockdown in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia cells leads to increased proliferation and cytokine sensitivity (PMID: 20473312). PTPN2 knockdown also leads to transformation and increased proliferation of Ba/F3 cells in combination with wildtype and mutant JAK1 expression (PMID: 21551237). Overexpression in PTPN2 null cells leads to decreased JAK1 activity (PMID: 21791476).

The PTPRD V1565I mutation is located in the protein's first phosphatase domain, which is considered the catalytic domain (PMID 16557282). In a primary melanoma cell culture, this mutation caused decreased growth inhibition and apoptosis (PMID: 19074898).

Truncating mutations in PRPRD can produce serveral C-terminally truncated protein forms, which are likely inactivating. Ectopic expression of tumor-derived PTPRD mutations in cancer cell lines attenuate the tumor suppressive functions of the wildtype protein, resulting in increased cell growth and migration (PMID: 19478061, 25113440).

The PTPRD R1088C mutation occurs in one out of eight fibronectin type III (FN3) domains in the protein. When expressed in a colon cancer cell line this mutation caused a decrease in growth suppression compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 19478061).

The PTPRD G446E mutation is located in the protein's second fibronectin type III domain which is an extracellular region that can promote cell-cell adhesion (PMID: 8393854). In a primary melanoma cell culture, this mutation caused decreased growth inhibition and apoptosis (PMID: 19074898). In a human embryonic kidney cell line this mutation causes increased levels of phosphorylated desmoplakin, likely due to loss of normal PTPRD function (PMID: 25113440).

PTPRS truncation mutations typically result in loss of the protein. These mutations have been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 19000305). In vitro studies with specific PTPRS-knockdown HCT116, SW620 and KM12L4A colorectal cancer cell lines demonstrated that loss of PTPRS is inactivating as measured by loss of ERK and AKT negative regulation as compared to wildtype (PMID: 29915291).

Deletion mutations in PTPRD lead to protein inactivation. Experimental studies using glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and melanoma cell lines containing deletions of PTPRD demonstrate that these alterations are associated with cell growth suppression and apoptosis (PMID: 19074898). Consistently, mimicking PTPRD loss, PTPRD knockdown in immortalized human astrocytes was associated with increased cell growth in vitro and enhanced tumor growth in vivo (PMID: 19478061). Additionally, loss of PTPRD in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma was shown to result in hyper-phosphorylation of the oncoprotein STAT3, leading to its activation (PMID: 19478061, 26267899).

Truncating mutations of QKI typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with QKI-knockdown A549 cells demonstrate that loss of QKI is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion (PMID: 35600368).

The RAB35 A151T mutation occurs in a residue that is conserved in Ras-like GTPases, and is paralogous to a well-documented KRAS missense mutation A146T. Stable expression of RAB35 A151T variant in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated growth factor-independent elevation in AKT phosphorylation and caused inhibition of serum starvation-induced apoptosis, as assessed by cleaved Poly Adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-Ribose Polymerase (PARP) and cleaved caspase-3 levels. The A151T variant also induced significantly higher number of NIH-3T3 colonies in focus formation assay, compared to wildtype RAB35, indicating oncogenic potential. This in vitro transformation of NIH-3T3 cells due to RAB35 A151T variant was shown to occur in a phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)-dependent manner (PMID: 26338797).

The PTPRD P1311T occurs in one out of eight fibronectin type III (FN3) domains in the protein. When expressed in a colon and head-and-neck cancer cell line, this mutation caused a decrease in growth suppression and increased phosphorylation of STAT3 compared to the wildtype protein (PMID: 19478061, 26267899).

The RAB35 F161L mutation occurs in a residue that is conserved in Ras-like GTPases, and is paralogous to a well-documented KRAS missense mutation F156L. Stable expression of RAB35 F161L variant into NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated growth factor-independent elevation in AKT phosphorylation and caused inhibition of serum starvation-induced apoptosis, as assessed by cleaved Poly Adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-Ribose Polymerase (PARP) and cleaved caspase-3 levels. The F161L variant also induced significantly higher number of NIH-3T3 colonies in focus formation assay, compared to wildtype RAB35, indicating oncogenic potential. This in vitro transformation of NIH-3T3 cells due to RAB35 F161L variant was shown to occur in a phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)-dependent manner (PMID: 26338797).

Deletion mutations of QKI typically result in the loss of protein expression. Loss of QKI has been identified in colorectal cancer, prostate cancer and oral cancer (PMID: 19686745, 24153116, 24918581). In vitro studies with QKI-knockdown A549 cells demonstrate that loss of QKI is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion (PMID: 35600368).

Truncating mutations of RASA1 occur across the entire gene, the majority of them (~95%) being located upstream or within the C-terminal GAP domain (cBioPortal, MSKCC, April 2015). In a study of patients with capillary ‘malformation-arteriovenous’ malformation syndrome (CM-AVM), heterozygous RASA1 mutations (mostly truncations and other loss-of-function alterations) caused loss of RASA1 protein expression (PMID: 24038909). Loss of RASA1 causes abnormal RAS/MAP regulation upon PDGF stimulation (PMID: 9121432) and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling (PMID: 9034330, 1689011, 2173144).

Translocations involving RBM15 and MRTFA (also known as MKL1) are found in patients with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (PMID: 11344311, 15849773, 11431691). The resultant RBM15-MRTFA fusion protein maintains the functional domains of both proteins, include the SAP domain of MRTFA and the SPOC motifs of RBM15, which mediate chromatin localization and RNA binding, respectively (PMID: 11344311). The oncogenic activity of this fusion protein is predicted to result from a culmination of RBM15 and MRTFA activation (PMID: 18667423). The RBM15-MRTFA fusion protein results in altered RBM15-dependent myeloid differentiation and MRTFA-dependent binding to serum responsive genes (PMID: 17283045). In biochemical assays, RBM15-MKL1 increasingly activate serum responsive reporter genes and other aberrant transcriptional programs (PMID: 12944485). RBM15-MRTFA also promotes transformation, cellular proliferation and altered binding to chromatin remodeling proteins in functional experiments (PMID: 18667423, 22927943). In addition, expression of the RBM15-MKL1 in murine models results in the development of AMKL (PMID: 19287095)

The Y35C mutation of RHEB occurs at a tyrosine residue conserved across the superfamily of small GTPases. This residue maintains the active state of RHEB by inhibiting its intrinsic GTP hydrolysis but sensitizing the protein to TSC2-mediated GTP hydrolysis (PMID: 22819219). The expression of this mutant increases phosphorylation of mTOR target S6K in a human embryonic kidney cell line (PMID: 24631838). This suggests that the mutation leads to a survival advantage for the cell, by blocking inhibitory signals.

The RASA1 Y472H mutation increases anchorage-independent growth of human melanoma cell lines and tumor growth in mouse xenograft models. In the same model system, the Y472H mutant protein abrogates the wildtype protein's negative effect on RAS activity, suggesting an oncogenic effect by depression of downstream RAS signaling (PMID: 26993606).

Truncating mutations in RECQL can occur anywhere throughout the protein and are predicted to disrupt its activity (PMID: 25945795). RECQL encodes a member of the RecQ DNA helicase family and has been shown to be involved in several types of DNA damage repair (PMID: 26125302, 15899892). Germline truncating mutations in RECQL are associated with increased risk of breast cancer (PMID: 25915596, 25945795, 29351780). Truncating mutations in RECQL have been identified in breast and colorectal carcinomas as well as other malignancies (PMID: 28481359).

The Y35H mutation of RHEB occurs at a tyrosine residue conserved across the superfamily of small GTPases. This residue maintains the active state of RHEB by inhibiting its intrinsic GTP hydrolysis but sensitizing the protein to TSC2-mediated GTP hydrolysis (PMID: 22819219). The expression of this mutant increases phosphorylation of mTOR target S6K in a human embryonic kidney cell line (PMID: 24631838). This suggests that the mutation leads to a survival advantage for the cell, by blocking inhibitory signals.

The L481F mutation of RASA1 abrogates the wildtype's suppressive effect on anchorage-independent growth in experiments in human melanoma cell lines. In the same model system, the mutant protein also abrogates the wildtype's negative effect on RRAS activity, suggesting a oncogenic effect by depression of downstream Ras signaling (PMID: 26993606).

Amplification of RHEB has been found in breast cancer and head and neck squamous cell cancer (PMID: 20388784). In vivo studies with mice overexpressing RHEB demonstrate RHEB amplification is activating as measured by constitutive mTOR signaling activation and tumor development compared to wildtype mice (PMID: 20388784).

The Y35N mutation of RHEB occurs at a tyrosine residue conserved across the superfamily of small GTPases. This residue maintains the active state of RHEB by inhibiting its intrinsic GTP hydrolysis but sensitizing the protein to TSC2-mediated GTP hydrolysis (PMID: 22819219). When expressed in a human embryonic kidney cell line this mutation increases the intrinsic hydrolytic activity of RHEB while impeding the effect of TSC2 and results in higher levels of phosphorylated S6K after rapamycin treatment (PMID: 26255626, 24631838). This suggests that the mutation leads to a survival advantage for the cell, by blocking inhibitory signals. Notably, Y35N also increases MAPK activation via binding to and inhibition of AMPK in fibroblast and embryonic kidney cell lines, as well as increases xenograft tumor formation (PMID: 27399332).

The RHEB P37L mutation is located in the RAS domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in megalencephaly (PMID: 29051493). In vivo studies with mice overexpressing this mutation demonstrate RHEB P37L is activating as measured by increased S6 phosphorylation levels compared to empty vector conditions (PMID: 34038402).

The RHEB G63A mutation is located in the RAS domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HeLa cells overexpressing this mutation demonstrate RHEB G63A is activating as measured by increased S6 phosphorylation levels compared to wildtype (PMID: 24648513).

The RHEB E40V mutation is located in the RAS domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in hemimegalencephaly, focal cortical dysplasia and acute lymphoblastic T-cell leukemia (PMID: 33434304, 28671688). Immunostaining of patient brain sections for phosphorylated S6 demonstrated RHEB E40V is activating as measured by strong immunoreactivity indicating increased mTOR activity compared to non‐mTOR‐related focal cortical dysplasia and postmortem control specimens (PMID: 33434304).

The RIT1 T76insTLDT mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of the RIT1 T76insTLDT mutant in mouse fibroblast cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by activation of MEK and PI3K signaling pathways and increased colony formation compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 24469055).

The RIT1 F82L mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast and HEK293 cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased proliferative response to growth factors, increased protein stability and activation of downstream MAPK and PI3K signaling pathways leading to increased colony formation compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 24469055, 30872527).

Deletion mutations of RASA1 are associated with reduced protein and activity. Loss of RASA1 causes abnormal RAS/MAP regulation upon PDGF stimulation (PMID: 9121432) and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling (PMID: 9034330, 1689011, 2173144). Homozygous RASA1 knockout mice are embryonic lethal and have defects in vascular and nervous systems. Cells derived from these mice display abnormal RAS/MAP regulation upon PDGF stimulation (PMID: 9121432). A patient with BRAF V600E-mutant Langerhans Cell Sarcoma progressed on BRAF inhibitors and was found to have deletion of RASA1 upon disease progression, which later responded to combined BRAF and MEK inhibition (PMID: 30977771).

The RIT1 A57G mutation is located in the switch II region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by an increased proliferative response to growth factors and increased protein stability compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 30872527).

The RIT1 E81G mutation is located in the switch II region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by an increased proliferative response to growth factors and increased protein stability compared to wildtype protein (PMID: 30872527).

The RIT1 T83P mutation is located in the switch II region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by an increased proliferative response to growth factors and increased protein stability compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 30872527).

The RIT1 A77T mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased Elk1 expression, a downstream transcription factor of ERK, in a luciferase assay compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 26714497).

The RIT1 T83del mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of the RIT T83del mutant in mouse fibroblast cells was associated with activation of MEK and PI3K signaling pathways leading to increased colony formation in cell line experiments (PMID: 24469055).

The RIT1 Y89H mutation is located in the switch II region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by an increased proliferative response to growth factors and increased protein stability compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 30872527).

The RIT1 A77S mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by activation of MEK and PI3K signaling pathways, leading to increased colony formation, enhanced tumor growth in mouse xenograft experiments and increased sensitivity to MEK and PI3K inhibitors compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 24469055).

The RIT1 Q40L mutation is located proximal to the GTP binding domain of the protein. Overexpression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cells demonstrated it is likely neutral as measured by MAPK and PI3K signaling levels, colony formation and tumor formation in xenograft models comparable to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 24469055).

The RIT1 R122L mutation is located otuside of the switch II region of the protein. Expression of this mutation in mouse fibroblast cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by activation of MEK and PI3K signaling pathways and increased colony formation in cell line experiments compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 24469055).

The RIT1 Q79L mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of the RIT1 Q79L mutation in mouse fibroblast cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by activation of MEK and PI3K signaling pathways, increased colony formation, enhanced tumor growth in mouse xenograft experiments and increased sensitivity to MEK and PI3K inhibitors compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 24469055).

The RRAGC T90N mutation is located in the Gtr1/RagA domain of the RRAGC protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is activating as demonstrated by increased mTOR activation and cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 37749558).

The RIT1 A77P mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in HEK293 and mouse fibroblast cells demonstrated that it is activating as shown by an increased proliferative response to growth factors, increased protein stability, increased downstream PI3K and MAPK signaling and increased colony formation compared to wildtype protein (PMID: 24469055, 30872527).

The RRAS G38V mutation is located in the GTP/GDP binding domain of the protein. This mutation is analogous to the HRAS G12V mutation (PMID: 8002932). In vitro studies with Sf9 and 32D cells expressing RRAS G38V demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by constitutive activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 8002932, 15772154).

The RRAS Q87L mutation is located in the GTP/GDP binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung cancer, leukemia and pancreatic cancer (PMID: 24705357, 28167572, 29146900). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that this mutation suppresses cell death and induces transforming capacity and tumorigenesis as measured by cell viability assay and xenograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 9349502, 8084601). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is sensitive to treatment with wortmannin, LY294002 (PI3K inhibitor) or PD98059 (MEK1/2 inhibitor) (PMID: 9349502, 8084601). Structural studies suggest that this mutation is directly involved in GTP hydrolysis (PMID: 2199064).

The RRAS Q72H mutation is located in the GTP/GDP binding domain of the protein and is a statistically significant hotspot. In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells expressing RRAS Q72H demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased transforming activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 36476833).

The RTEL1 M492I mutation has been identified in 8/8570 of Ashkenazi Jewish chromosomes by the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD : http://gnomad.broadinstitute.org), and has been reported in the literature in a compound heterozygous state in individuals with severe dyskeratosis congenita (DC) also known as Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (HHS) (PMID: 23453664, 27418648). In addition, an individual heterozygous for this variant had pulmonary fibrosis (PMID: 23959892). Experimental studies demonstrated that this variant caused telomere shortening in blood leukocytes derived from patients as well as in unaffected heterozygous carrier parents (PMID: 23959892, 19461895).

Truncating mutations in RTEL1 can occur anywhere throughout the gene and are predicted to lead to loss of protein (PMID: 29625055, 28507545). RTEL1 encodes a DNA helicase involved in telomeric-length regulation (PMID: 21097466) and maintenance of genomic stability (PMID: 18957201).  Germline truncating mutations in RTEL1 have been associated with the development of Hoyeraal Hreidarsson syndrome, a genetic disease characterized by a severe form of congenital dyskeratosis and increased risk of hematologic malignancies (PMID: 23329068, 20507306, 28507545). Certain germline polymorphisms in RTEL1 have also been associated with increased prostate cancer risk (PMID: 31762827). Truncating mutations in RTEL1 have been identified in multiple malignancies including breast and colon carcinomas, as well as melanomas (PMID: 29625055).

RYBP is a tumor suppressor and truncating mutations in this gene are assumed to be oncogenic. RYBP directly interacts with MDM2 and decreases p53 ubiquitination, leading to stabilization of p53 and an increase in p53 activity. RYBP induces cell-cycle arrest and is involved in the p53 response to DNA damage, and its loss of expression may thus be important in cancer disease progression (PMID:19098711).

The RIT1 M90I mutation is located in the switch II domain of the protein. Expression of the M90I mutation in NIH3T3, HEK293 and MEF cells demonstrated it is activating as measured by increased colony formation in vitro, increased proliferative response to growth factors, and increased tumor growth in mouse xenografts compared to wildtype RIT1 (PMID: 24469055, 30872527). This is due to activation of MEK and PI3K signaling pathways, where MEK and PI3K inhibitors, AZD-6244 and GDC-0941 respectively, caused reduction in colony forming ability (PMID: 24469055). Expression of this mutation in the germline of mice resulted in a phenotype resembling human Noonan syndrome (PMID: 30872527).

Truncating mutations in SESN can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its protein product (PMID: 29625055). SESN encodes a member of the sestrin family, proteins that are induced by TP53 and play a role in the cellular adaptation to oxidative stress and DNA damage (PMID: 18692468, 30318520). Sestrins have also been implicated in aging attenuation and deficiencies have been shown to lead to accelerated aging in mice (PMID: 24055102). These aging features are among other things characterized by obesity and muscle degeneration, in line with the role of SESN1 in myoblast differentiation (PMID: 29511169). SESN1 has also been shown to negatively regulate MTOR signaling through the GATOR complex (PMID: 18692468, 25263562). Truncating mutations in SESN1 have been identified in multiple malignancies including melanomas and several carcinomas (PMID: 29625055).

Truncating mutations in SESN2 can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its protein product (PMID: 29625055). SESN encodes a member of the sestrin family, proteins that are induced by TP53 and play a role in the cellular adaptation to oxidative stress and DNA damage (PMID: 18692468, 27463837). SESN2 has been shown to negatively regulate MTOR signaling through the GATOR complex to regulate metabolic homeostasis (PMID: 18692468, 25457612). Sestrins have also been implicated in aging attenuation, and deficiencies have been shown to lead to accelerated aging in mice characterized by obesity and muscle degeneration (PMID: 24055102). Truncating mutations in SESN have been identified in multiple solid malignancies including uterine and colorectal carcinomas (PMID: 29625055).

The SET-NUP214 fusion is a result of the chromosomal translocation t(9;9)(q34;q34) or the recurrent deletion del(9)(q34.11q34.13) (PMID: 19166587). This fusion has been found in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and B lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (PMID: 19166587). Expression of the SET-NUP214 fusion in the T-ALL cell line LOUCY and the AML cell line MEGAL demonstrated that it is activating as measured by downstream HOX gene expression that could be repressed upon downregulation of the fusion protein (PMID: 19166587). Expression of this fusion in HeLa and HEK293T cells demonstrated altered nuclear-cytoplasmic transport through interaction with XPO1, reducing the nuclear export of mRNAs and nuclear export signal proteins and resulting in inhibition of transcriptional regulation by NF-kB (PMID: 27714368).

Truncating mutations in SESN3 can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its protein product (PMID: 29625055). SESN3 encodes a member of the sestrin family, proteins that are induced by TP53 and play a role in the cellular adaptation to oxidative stress and DNA damage (PMID: 18692468, 27463837). SESN3 has been shown to negatively regulate MTOR signaling through the GATOR complex to regulate metabolic homeostasis (PMID: 18692468, 25457612, 22958918). Sestrins have also been implicated in aging attenuation, and deficiencies have been shown to lead to accelerated aging in mice characterized by obesity and muscle degeneration (PMID: 24055102). Truncating mutations in SESN3 have been identified in multiple solid malignancies including uterine, colorectal and several other carcinomas (PMID: 29625055).

The SH2D1A Y7C missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein, and it was identified in XLP patients. This substitution led to a remarkable reduction in the protein half-life, and this variant failed to block recruitment of SHP-2 phosphatase. Loss of protein stability and its biochemical consequences were likely reasons for disease onset (PMID: 11477068).

The SH2D1A S28R missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein, and it was identified in XLP patients. This substitution led to a remarkable reduction in the protein half-life and failed to block recruitment of SHP-2 phosphatase. Loss of protein stability and its biochemical consequences were likely reasons for disease onset (PMID: 11477068).

The SH2D1A T53I missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein and was identified in XLP patients. This substitution severely impaired non-phosphotyrosine interactions while preserving the binding of SH2D1A to phosphorylated CD150, and was also able to recruit SHP-2 phosphatase. This variant, however, failed to bind three other SH2D1A-interacting receptors- CD244, CD229 and CD84 (PMID: 11477068).

Truncating mutations in SH2D1A can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its protein product (PMID: 29625055). SH2D1A encodes a protein with a SH2 domain involved in the stimulation of T and B lymphocytes. It has been shown to act as an inhibitor of the signaling lymphocyte-activation molecule by blocking the recruitment of the SHP-2 phosphatase to its docking site (PMID: 12458214). Mutations in SH2D1A have been shown to lead to Duncan disease (aka. X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome type 1), an immunodeficiency characterized by extreme susceptibility to infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and a high risk of malignant B-cell lymphoma development (PMID: 11493483, 29649976). This phenotype has been shown to result from inadequate B-lymphocyte proliferation control (PMID: 9774102).  Additionally, SH2D1A has been implicated in the development of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, characterized by hyperproliferation of macrophages and T-cells (PMID: 28196537). Truncating mutations in SH2D1A have been identified in multiple malignancies including uterine, breast and several other carcinomas in addition to EBV-associated lymphomas (PMID: 29625055, 29649976).

The SH2D1A P101L missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein, and it was identified in XLP patients. This substitution led to a remarkable reduction in the protein half-life, and, although this variant could bind to CD150 peptide in vitro, it failed to block recruitment of SHP-2 phosphatase. Loss of protein stability and its biochemical consequences were likely reasons for disease onset (PMID: 11477068).

The SH2D1A V102G missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein and it was identified in XLP patients. This substitution led to a remarkable reduction in the protein half-life, and this variant failed to block recruitment of SHP-2 phosphatase. Loss of protein stability and its biochemical consequences were likely reasons for disease onset (PMID: 11477068).

The SH2D1A R32Q missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein and was identified in XLP patients. This substitution not only substantially decreased the protein half-life, but also abolished SH2D1A binding to both phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated forms of CD150 family of receptors, and also completely failed to block recruitment of SHP-2 phosphatase, thus leading to disease manifestation (PMID: 11477068).

The SH2D1A T68I missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein, and was identified in XLP patients. Although this variant retained its ability to bind phosphorylated CD150, it showed complete loss of binding interaction with its non-phosphorylated form. Its ability to block SHP-2 recruitment, however, was severely impaired, thus leading to disease manifestation (PMID: 11477068).

The SH2D1A Q99P missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein, and it was identified in XLP patients. This substitution led to a remarkable reduction in the protein half-life, and failed to block recruitment of SHP-2 phosphatase. Loss of protein stability and its biochemical consequences were likely reasons for disease onset (PMID: 11477068).

The SH2D1A C42W missense mutation occurs in the SH2 domain of SH2D1A protein and was identified in XLP patients. This substitution interferes with SH2D1A phospho-tyrosine binding pocket; and abolished SH2D1A binding to both phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated forms of CD150 family of receptors, thus leading to disease manifestation (PMID: 11477068).

The SHOC2 S2G mutation is located in exon 1 of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with Noonon-like syndromes (PMID: 19684605, 23918763). Expression of this mutation in COS1 cells demonstrated that it is likely activating, as measured by moderately increased pathway activation compared to wildtype SHOC2 (PMID: 19684605).

The SHOC2 M173I mutation is located in exon 2 of the protein. This mutation was found in patients with Rasopathy. Expression of this mutation in COS1 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased pathway activation compared to wildtype SHOC2 (PMID: 25137548).

Deletions of SHQ1 are seen in prostate cancer patient samples, and are associated with TMPRSS2-ERG fusion tumors (PMID: 20579941). Although the mechanism of action is unknown, it is known that SHQ1 plays an integral role in ribosomal RNA and telomerase RNA processing and metabolism, and loss of function of this protein can lead to a decrease in small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) levels and to defects in ribosomal RNA processing (PMID: 19019820,19383767).

SHQ1 (SHQ1, H/ACA ribonucleoprotein assembly factor) is located on chromosome 3p13, a locus that is frequently deleted in prostate cancers or where somatic mutations has been observed and are associated with TMPRSS2-ERG fusions (PMID: 20579941). While the exact mechanism of action of SHQ1 is currently unknown, SHQ1 is suggested to function in rRNA processing, has been shown to be involved in the formation of a protein-RNA complex (snoRNP [small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein] known as the H/ACA box (PMID: 19383767, 12228251) and is considered a tumor suppressor. SHQ1 truncating mutations occur very rarely in various tumor types, however since the function of SHQ1 is predicted to be a tumor suppressor, truncating mutations of the gene which are thought to be associated with loss of protein are considered likely oncogenic.

Truncating mutations in SLX4 can occur throughout the entire gene and are predicted to lead to loss of its function (PMID: 21240275). SLX4 encodes a protein that serves as an assembly factor of multiple endonuclease complexes involved in the cellular response to DNA damage, including replication fork failure (PMID: 19596236, 19595721, 19596235). SLX4 germline variants have also been implicated in the development of BRCA-negative breast and ovarian cancer (PMID: 23840564, 23211700). Truncating mutations in SLX4 have been identified in patients with Fanconi anemia (PMID: 21240275) as well as in melanomas and carcinomas arising in the endometrium, breast or stomach (PMID: 29625055).

The SOS1 P478L mutation is located in the pleckstrin homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream pathway activation, increased colony formation in soft agar and increased tumor growth in allograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOS1 I327T mutation is located in the Dbl homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by downstream pathway activation and colony formation in soft agar comparable to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOS1 N233Y mutation is located in the Dbl homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in cell lines and NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased RasGTP, increased downstream pathway activation, increased colony formation in soft agar and increased tumor growth in allograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 27304678, 30635434).

The SOS1 R552S mutation is located adjacent to the PH domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing this mutation demonstrate SOS1 R552S is likely activating as measured by increased ERK activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27304678).

The SOS1 D309Y mutation is located in the Dbl homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma and Noonan syndrome (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by increased colony formation in soft agar and increased tumor growth in allograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOS1 D265N mutation is located in the Dbl homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by downstream pathway activation and colony formation in soft agar comparable to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOS1 L938F mutation is located in the CDC25-homologous catalytic domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by downstream pathway activation and colony formation in soft agar comparable to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOS1 R552G mutation is located adjacent to the PH domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in Noonan syndrome (PMID: 17586837). In vitro studies with COS-1 cells expressing SOS1 R552G demonstrate the mutation is activating as measured by an increase in active RAS-GTP and downstream ERK signaling activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 17143282).

The SOS1 G604V mutation is located in the Ras exchange motif of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased downstream pathway activation, increased colony formation in soft agar and increased tumor growth in allograft models compared to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOS1 N535S mutation is located in the pleckstrin homology domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by downstream pathway activation and colony formation in soft agar comparable to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOS1 G434R mutation has been identified in melanoma. Cell line experiments demonstrate that this mutation is likely activating and likely oncogenic as measured by a modest increase in ERK activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27304678).

The SOS1 M269R mutation occurs in the RhoGEF domain. Cell line experiments demonstrate that this mutation is likely activating and likely oncogenic as measured by increased ERK activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27304678, 24297905, 25712082, 17143285).

The SOS1 R1051G mutation is located in the PxxP domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by downstream pathway activation and colony formation in soft agar comparable to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SOX17 A96G mutation is located in the HMG box of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrioid carcinosarcoma and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with AN3CA, HEC1A and Ishikawa cells expressing SOX17 A96G demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by wildtype comparable β-catenin mediated transcription and further reduced proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 28978154).

SOX17 deletion mutations result in the loss of the SOX17 protein. These mutations have been identified in colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer and esophageal cancer (PMID: 18413743, 17875931, 22846201, 21514720, 24407731). In vitro studies with SOX17 knockdown in normal human cholangiocytes demonstrated loss of SOX17 is inactivating as measured by increased tumorigenic capacity and cellular proliferation compared to normal SOX17 expression (PMID: 28237397).

The SOX17 S403I mutation is located in the central domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in endometrioid cancer and is a statistically significant hotspot (PMID: 28481359). In vitro studies with AN3CA, HEC1A and Ishikawa cells expressing SOX17 S403I demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by β-catenin mediated transcription comparable to wildtype and further reduced proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 28978154).

The SOS1 E846K mutation is the causal genetic alteration of a subset of Noonan syndrome (NS) patients. In vitro studies and mouse models show that SOS1 E846K mutation leads to an increase in the active RAS-GTP and downstream ERK signaling activation (PMID: 17143285, 21041952).

Truncating mutations in SPRED1 can occur throughout the entire gene, seem to be enriched in the WH1 domain, and are predicted to lead to loss of its function (PMID: 29625055). SPRED1 encodes a protein that has been shown to act as an inhibitor the MAPK signaling cascade and regulate hematopoiesis in bone marrow cells (PMID:15465815). Furthermore, SPRED1 has been shown to directly affect KRAS anchorage to the cell membrane (PMID: 15465815). Its loss has been shown to lead to tumorigenesis in zebrafish mucosal melanoma models by the same MAPK-mediated mechanism (PMID: 30385465). Germline truncating mutations in SPRED1 have been implicated in the development of Legius (aka. NF1-like) syndrome, a hereditary disease characterized by neurodevelopmental and skin pigmentation abnormalities, as well as an increased risk for developing pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (PMID: 24469042, 27081556, 24334617). Truncating mutations in SPRED1 have been identified in patients with AML, melanoma and carcinomas arising from the endometrium and stomach (PMID: 27081556, 29625055).

The SOS1 I733V mutation is located in the Ras exchange motif of the protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma and Noonan syndrome (PMID: 30635434). Expression of this mutation in NIH-3T3 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by downstream pathway activation and colony formation in soft agar comparable to wildtype (PMID: 30635434).

The SS18-SSX1 fusion protein combines the N-terminus of SS18 and C-terminus of SSX1, retaining protein-protein interaction motifs in both fusion partners. This fusion protein is found in over 90% of patients with synovial sarcoma (PMID: 26905812). Primary synovial sarcoma cells expressing the SS18-SSX1 fusion protein as well as exogenous expression of the fusion protein in a mesenchymal stem cell line demonstrated that this fusion protein interacts with WNT pathway transcription factors and activates the expression of certain WNT target genes even in the absence of WNT ligand stimulation (PMID: 26905812).

SOX17 is a tumor suppressor and encodes a member of the SRY-related HMG-box (SOX) family of transcription factors, acting as an important antagonist of the canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway by promoting the degradation of β-catenin/TCF via a GSK3β-independent mechanism (PMID: 17875931, 27738313, 28237397). Relative to SOX17 deletion, SOX17 truncating mutations are observed rarely and occur in tumor types with high mutation burden including melanoma, colorectal cancer and endometrial cancers (PMID: 22588877, 23550210). Truncating mutations are assumed to be associated with loss of SOX17 protein and are therefore considered likely oncogenic.

Translocations involving TAL1 are frequent in T-lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) (PMID: 2467296, 16826225, 2400810). Expression of TAL1 in murine models, especially in collaboration with other T-ALL oncogenes, results in the expansion of immature thymocytes, inhibition of hematopoietic differentiation, and leukemic transformation (PMID: 20516195). Fusion oncoproteins typically place most of the TAL1 gene under control of an atypical promoter, leading to T-ALL upregulation (PMID: 16826225, 28652130). TAL1 commonly fuses with SIL, resulting in activation of TAL1 and may be associated with poor prognosis (PMID: 25304610, 29279377).

The t(X:18)(p11.2;q11.2) translocation is characteristically found in all synovial sarcomas and fuses chromosome 18 to the X chromosome. The SS18-SSX2 fusion is one of two common fusions resulting from the translocation (PMID: 7951320, 8760306). SS18 is a ubiquitously expressed protein with a QPGY domain, whereas the SSX proteins, such as SSX2, carry KRAB-like domains and are expressed almost exclusively in the testis The SS18-SSX2 protein, which contains both the SS18 transcriptional activator and the SSX transcriptional repressor, has been shown to bind to native SWI/SNF complexes in human cells. While studies were not performed with SSX2, pulldown assays also confirmed that SSX1, and specifically the C-terminus of SSX1 which is conserved in the fusion, was capable of binding to core histones (PMID: 11734557). The fusion protein is thought to evict BAF47, another intrinsic BAF complex protein, due to the addition of the SSX protein, which leads to retargeting of the complex and broad changes in gene expression (PMID: 29861296). Knockdown of the SS18-SSX fusion was shown to lead to proliferation arrest in synovial sarcoma cell lines suggesting the dependency of the cells on the fusion protein and its downstream effects.

Recurrent translocations involving TAL1 and SIL are found in patients with T-acute lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) (PMID: 25304610). The promoter region of SIL fuse with the majority of the C-terminal TAL1 protein, placing TAL1 under atypical control of the SIL promoter (PMID: 25304610) and leading to TAL1 overexpression. SIL-TAL1 fusions are found in patients with CD3+TCRαβ+ T-ALL and to CD3− T-ALL with TCRD deletions (PMID: 8459224, 1387813, 11960364). SIL-TAL1 fusions have been associated with poor prognosis in some T-ALL studies (PMID: 25304610).

TCL1A amplification results in the overexpression of the protein. Overexpression of TCL1A has been identified in T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 36129940). In vitro studies with B-cell lymphoma lines overexpressing TCL1A demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by accelerated cell cycle transition and impaired apoptotic damage (PMID: 36179280).

Translocations involving the regulatory units of TRA and TCL1A are found in patients with T-cell acute lymphocytic leukemias and T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) (PMID: 9407948, 24825865, 10077617). TRA-TCL1A fusions result in the recombination of N-terminal TRA promoter and enhancer regions in frame with the open reading frame of TCL1A (PMID: 9407948), leading to activation of TCL1A. In preclinical studies, overexpression of TCL1A results in the activation of AKT, a downstream effector of T-cell receptor signaling (PMID: 17890451). TRA-TCL1A likely hyperactivates TCR signaling, leading to oncogenic AKT signaling (PMID: 17890451).

The ASPSCR1-TFE3 fusion is a result of chromosomal translocation der(17)t(X:17)(p11:q25). This fusion is pathognomonic to alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS) (PMID: 17543078). Expression of the ASPSCR1-TFE3 fusion in mouse embryonic mesenchymal cells and their subcutaneous implantation in nude mice resulted in the formation of vascularized tumors with histology resembling ASPS (PMID: 27979841). In a Phase II clinical trial of the VEGFR-inhibitor axitinib plus the anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab in patients with sarcoma, the three-month progression-free survival was 72.7% (95% CI: 37.1%-90.3%) among the twelve patients with ASPS harboring this fusion (PMID: 31078463).

The YAP1-TFE3 fusion has been identified in epitheloid haemangioendotheliomas, including those that are negative for the WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion as well as soft tissue sarcomas (PMID:23737213). The resulting protein contains the N-terminus of YAP1 fused to the C-terminus of TFE3, which removes the ability of YAP1 to be regulated by the canonical Hippo pathway. Expression of this fusion in NIH 3T3 and human sarcoma cell lines resulted in aberrant constitutive nuclear localization of the fusion protein, promotion of anchorage-independent growth, and increased proliferation. Additionally, xenografts of YAP1-TFE3-expressing cells into NSG mice promoted tumorigenesis and metastasis (Abstract: Merritt, N. et al. Abstract #3359, AACR 2018. http://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/78/13_Supplement/3359).

Fusions that place the TFE3 gene downstream of strong promoters are found in aggressive subtypes of renal cell carcinomas and alveolar soft part sarcomas (PMID: 22705279, 8872474, 30849994) and are pathognomonic to a subset of these diseases (PMID: 25048860). These fusions, such as PRCC-TRE3 (PMID: 33019842), YAP1-TFE3 (PMID: 23737213), SFPQ-TFE3 (PMID: 30061365) and ASPSCR1-TFE3 (PMID: 27979841) have been shown in vitro to increase TFE3 function as measured by increased nuclear localization, increased occupancy at consensus E-box motifs, activation of the PI3K pathway, and result in increased cell proliferation (PMID: 33019842, 23737213, 30061365, 27979841).

The SFPQ-TFE3 fusion results from the Xp11 translocation event that places the TFE3 gene downstream of the SFPQ gene promotor. This fusion is found in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) (PMID: 28315422, 26274027, 30061365). Characterization of this fusion in an RCC patient derived xenograft model demonstrated that this fusion is likely activating as measured by increased TFE3 nuclear staining, increased genomic occupancy of TFE3 at consensus E-box motifs as measured by ChIP-seq, upregulation of PI3K-pathway genes, and increased activation of the PI3K pathway as measured by western blot compared to control (PMID: 30061365). Knockdown of TFE3 in this model attenuated PI3K pathway signaling (PMID: 30061365).
