The TGFBR1 C41Y mutation is located in the protein's ligand binding domain. Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells resulted in reduced phosphorylation of TGFBR1 effector genes, including the SMAD proteins, suggesting that this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 21358634).

The PRCC-TFE3 fusion results from the chromosomal translocation (X;1)(p11;q21), placing the TFE3 gene downstream of the PRCC gene promotor. This fusion protein has been identified in renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 11313942). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells overexpressing the PRCC-TFE3 fusion protein demonstrated that the fusion protein is activating as measured by constitutively activated upregulation of E3 ubiquitin ligase PRKN increasing cell survival and proliferation as compared to wildtype TFE3 (PMID: 33019842). PRCC-TFE3 fusion is suggested to confer resistance to mitochondrial ROS inducer PEITC treatment as measured by in vitro studies with UOK120 cells expressing PRCC-TFE3 experiencing significantly less cell death in response to treatment as compared to UOK109 cells expressing the NONO-TFE3 fusion protein (PMID: 33019842).

The TGFBR1 G52R mutation is located in the ligand binding domain and has been found in families with multiple self-healing squamous epithelioma (MSSE). Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells demonstrated reduced phosphorylation of downstream effectors of TGFBR1, including the SMAD proteins, in a reporter assay compared to the wildtype (PMID: 21358634, 23358096).

TGFBR1 deletions have been detected in patients with pancreatic cancer, biliary duct cancer and lymphoma (PMID: 9850059, 10515889). These alterations have been shown to abrogate TGFß-mediated growth inhibition (PMID: 9850059). Additionally, deletion of TGFBR1 in mice resulted in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma accelerated tumorigenesis in vivo due to defective TGFß-signaling (PMID: 27558455).

TGFBR1 truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein function. These mutations have been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 10656986, 11212236). In vitro studies with tumor-derived cell lines expressing these cytoplasmic domain truncating mutations demonstrate truncating TGFBR1 mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of cell surface receptors and TGFBR1 signaling (PMID: 11212236).

The TGFBR1 R487Q mutation occurs in the kinase domain of the protein and has been observed in families with Loeys-Dietz syndrome. This mutation is predicted to be deleterious in modeling experiments (PMID: 16928994, 16791849). Dysregulation of TGFβ pathway members has been observed in aortic tissue from a carrier of the TGFBR1 R487Q mutation (PMID: 25116393).

Translocations involving TLX1 are recurrently found in patients with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) (PMID: 28671688). Rearrangements typically position TLX1 under the control of a strong T-cell enhancer, leading to activation of TLX1 transcriptional activity (PMID: 27451956). TLX1-positive rearrangements lead to the activation of TLX1 expression, as evidenced by gene expression studies (PMID: 27451956). Overexpression of TLX1 in murine models results in aneuploidy and the development of T-ALL, suggesting that TLX1 rearrangements function as oncoproteins (PMID: 20972433, 21326611).

The TGFBR1 S387Y mutation is located in a linker region between the protein's VII and IX domains, which are likely involved in substrate recognition. Expression of this mutation in a lung epithelial cell line resulted in reduced receptor activity as demonstrated in a transactivation assays (PMID: 9809982).

The exon 1 TGFBR1*6A deletion alteration is a deletion of three alanine residues in the N-terminal domain of the protein. The variant is a putative risk allele (rs11466445) for colorectal cancer and additional data imply that it might be associated with an increased risk of other cancers, such as breast and ovarian, in certain populations (PMID: 17848956, 20429896, 19882361, 22905183). Experiments in cell lines found this variant decreases TGFß-mediated growth inhibition compared to wildtype possibly resulting in a growth advantage (PMID: 10582683, 16204663). Somatic acquisition of this variant has been observed in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (PMID: 16204663).

Amplification of TNFRSF17 typically results in overexpression of the protein. TNFRSF17 amplification has been identified in multiple myeloma (PMID: 22804669, 27127303, 26960399). In vitro studies with MM1R cells overexpressing TNFRSF17 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and survival compared to vector control (PMID: 27127303).

Translocations involving TLX3 are recurrently found in patients with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) (PMID: 27451956, 28671688, 11587205, 12399963). TLX3 has several fusion partners; however, rearrangements most commonly position TLX3 under the control of the regulatory units of BCL11B, leading to activation of TLX3 transcriptional activity (PMID: 27451956, 15334547). TLX3-positive rearrangements lead to the activation of TLX3 expression, as evidenced by gene expression studies (PMID: 27451956). Overexpression of TLX3 in biochemical assays results in transformation, suggesting that TLX3 rearrangements function as oncoproteins (PMID: 16804919, 29296717).

Deletions of TP53BP1 are found in glioblastomas, particularly of the proneural subtype. In glioma cell lines, low levels of TP53BP1 sensitized glioma cells to ionizing radiation (IR), both in vitro and in vivo. The cells failed to fully repair the damaged DNA upon IR exposure, with a prolonged cell-cycle arrest and increased apoptosis, suggesting its importance in the NHEJ DNA repair pathway (PMID:22915756). In a lymphoma mouse model, TP53BP1 homozygous deletion in a p53-null background led to significant acceleration of lymphomagenesis (PMID:16260621). Cancerous cells exhibited high rates of structural aberrations, chromosomal missegregation, and accumulation of aneuploid cells, suggesting a role of TP53BP1 in maintaining chromosome structure and number.

The TGFBR1 P83L mutation is located in the ligand binding domain and has been found in families with multiple self-healing squamous epithelioma (MSSE). Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells demonstrated reduced phosphorylation of downstream effectors of TGFBR1, including the SMAD proteins, in a reporter assay compared to the wildtype (PMID: 21358634).

TP53BP1 truncation mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein. These mutations have been identified in stomach adenocarcinoma, prostate adenocarcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 33359708). In vitro studies with 293T cells expressing various TP53BP1 truncating mutations demonstrate these mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of DNA repair function and nuclear localization (PMID: 33359708). Loss of TP53BP1 in BRCA1-mutated mouse mammary tumors has been shown to result in resistance to the PARP inhibitor olaparib as measured by cellular growth and tumor relapse (PMID: 23103855).

TYK2 fusion proteins generally involve the fusion of the C-terminal end of TYK2 with the N-terminal of the fusion partner. These fusion proteins generally retain the TYK2 kinase domain while losing activity of the pseudokinase domain that functions to negatively regulate kinase activity, ultimately resulting in increased TYK2 kinase activity. These fusion protein are typically found in patients with B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. In vitro, cell-based studies expressing various TYK2 fusion proteins demonstrate that they are activating as shown by increased downstream pathway activation and cell proliferation (PMID: 25349176) (Abstract: McEachern, et al. Abstract #2063, 106th Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research, 2015. http://cancerres.aacrjournals.org/content/75/15_Supplement/2063).

The TYK2 E957D mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 and murine bone marrow cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased TYK2 phosphorylation, downstream signaling activation, IL-3 -independent growth, and increased proliferation as compared to wildtype TYK2 (PMID: 23471820). In vitro studies suggest that TYK2 E957D is sensitive to various JAK inhibitors as measured by cell viability and decreased downstream signaling (PMID: 23471820).

The TGFBR1 N45S mutation is located in the ligand binding domain and has been found in families with multiple self-healing squamous epithelioma (MSSE). Expression of this mutation in HEK293T cells showed reduced phosphorylation of TGFBR1 effector genes, including the SMAD proteins, in a reporter assay compared to the wildtype (PMID: 21358634, 23358096).

The TYK2 R425H mutation lies in the FERM domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is neutral as measured by IL-3 -independent growth comparable to wildtype TYK2 (PMID: 23471820).

The TYK2 G36D mutation lies in the FERM domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased TYK2 phosphorylation, downstream signaling activation, and IL-3 -independent growth compared to wildtype TYK2 (PMID: 23471820).

The TYK2 R1027H mutation lies in the kinase domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased TYK2 phosphorylation, downstream signaling activation, and IL-3 -independent growth compared to wildtype TYK2 (PMID: 23471820).

The TYK2 V731I mutation lies in the JH2 domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased TYK2 phosphorylation, downstream signaling activation, and IL-3 -independent growth compared to wildtype TYK2 (PMID: 23471820).

The TYK2 S47N mutation lies in the FERM domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in Ba/F3 cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased TYK2 phosphorylation, downstream signaling activation, and IL-3 -independent growth compared to wildtype TYK2 (PMID: 23471820).

The U2AF2 Q190_K195del mutation is located in the RNA recognition motif of the protein. This mutation has been found in myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloid neoplasms (Abstract: Xingxing et al. Abstract# 6900, ASH 2022. https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/140/Supplement%201/6900/487186/Mis-Splicing-Due-to-Somatic-U2AF2-Mutations-in). Transcriptome analysis and in silico analysis of samples from patients with Q190_K195del mutant myeloid neoplasms demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by aberrant alterative splicing compared to samples without Q190_K195del (Abstract: Xingxing et al. Abstract# 6900, ASH 2022. https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/140/Supplement%201/6900/487186/Mis-Splicing-Due-to-Somatic-U2AF2-Mutations-in).

UB5R amplification results in overexpression of the protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer and is co-amplified with MYC. Expression of UBR5 is activating as measured by reduced cell proliferation upon UBR5 knockdown in cervical cancer and breast cancer cell lines (PMID: 32029551).

The MYH9-USP6 fusion protein results from a chromosomal rearrangement that fuses the promoter region of MYH9 with the coding region of USP6. This fusion has been identified in nodular fasciitis (PMID: 21826056). Screening of primary mesenchymal tumors and cell lines demonstrates that MYH9-USP6 is activating as measured by transcriptional upregulation of USP6 in MYH9-USP6 expressing samples compared to control (PMID: 21826056). In vivo xenograft studies of nude mice overexpressing USP6 demonstrate that USP6 upregulation is activating as measured by tumor growth with clinical and histological features resembling human nodular fasciitis (PMID: 21826056).

The CNBP-USP6 fusion protein, also referred to as ZNF9-USP6, results from the chromosomal translocation t(3;17)(q21;p13) and fuses the promoter region of CNBP with the coding region of USP6. This fusion has been identified in aneurysmal bone cysts (PMID: 15735689). cDNA expression profiling of aneurysmal bone cyst and non-aneurysmal bone cyst samples demonstrate that CNBP-USP6 is activating as measured by transcriptional upregulation of USP6 in CNBP-USP6 expressing samples compared to control (PMID: 15735689). In vitro studies with HT-1080 cells overexpressing USP6 demonstrate that USP6 upregulation is activating as measured by increased tumor cell invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 35926707).

The TGFBR1 S241L mutation is located in the kinase domain and has been found in as a germline variant in patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (PMID 16596670, 16791849, 16928994). This residue is highly conserved and modeling experiments suggest that this mutation impedes kinase function, however further studies are required to validate the function of this mutation (PMID: 16791849).

The COL1A1-USP6 fusion protein results from the chromosomal translocation t(17;17)(p13;q12) and fuses the promoter region of COL1A1 with the coding region of USP6. This fusion has been identified in aneurysmal bone cysts (PMID: 15735689, 32157177). cDNA expression profiling of aneurysmal bone cyst and non-aneurysmal bone cyst samples demonstrate that COL1A1-USP6 is activating as measured by transcriptional upregulation of USP6 in COL1A1-USP6 expressing samples compared to control (PMID: 15735689). In vitro studies with HT-1080 cells overexpressing USP6 demonstrate that USP6 upregulation is activating as measured by increased tumor cell invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 35926707).

Amplification of USP6 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. In vitro studies with HT-1080 cells overexpressing USP6 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased tumor cell invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 35926707).

The USP8 S718P mutation occurs in the 14-3-3 binding domain of the protein (PMID: 25675982). Expression of the USP8 S718P variant in HeLa cells results in enhanced protein stability of EGFR and activated downstream signaling (PMID: 25675982). Cell lines expressing USP8 S718P had abolished activity of USP8 due to loss of 14-3-3 binding, as evidenced in biochemical assays (PMID: 25675982).

The USP8 S718del mutation occurs in the 14-3-3 binding domain of the protein (PMID: 25675982). Expression of the USP8 S718del variant in HeLa cells results in enhanced protein stability of EGFR and activated downstream signaling (PMID: 25675982). Cell lines expressing USP8 S718del had abolished activity of USP8 due to loss of 14-3-3 binding, as evidenced in biochemical assays (PMID: 25675982).

The USP8 C748A mutation is located in the cysteine box of the protein. This mutation changes the catalytic cysteine residue of the protein to an alanine, rendering the protein catalytically inactive (PMID: 16120644).

The YAP1-SS18 fusion protein is a result of chromosomal translocations fusing exons 1 through 7 of YAP1 to the C-terminus of SS18, retaining YAP1's transcriptional enhancer factor and WW domains. This fusion protein has been identified in cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma (PMID: 29099951). In vivo studies with mice expressing this fusion protein demonstrated the YAP1-SS18 fusion is activating as measured by tumor formation compared to mice expressing wildtype YAP1 and wildtype SS18 (PMID: 32675324).

The USP8 P720R mutation occurs in the 14-3-3 binding domain of the protein (PMID: 25675982). Expression of the USP8 P720R variant in HeLa cells results in enhanced protein stability of EGFR and activated downstream signaling (PMID: 25675982). Cell lines expressing USP8 P720R had abolished 14-3-3 binding, as evidenced in biochemical assays (PMID: 25675982).

YAP1-MAMLD1 fusion has been identified in distinct molecular subgroups of supratentorial ependymomas (ST-EPN) (PMID: 25965575). Genetically engineered mice expressing this fusion protein developed severe neurological symptoms. Tumors harvested from these mice primarily expressed the YAP1-MAMLD1 fusion in the nucleus (even when phosphorylated at serine 127, a modification that retains YAP1 in the cytoplasm), suggesting constitutive activation of YAP1. These transformed tumor cells demonstrated oncogenic potential when transplanted into immunocompromised mice (Abstract: Pajtler, K. et al. Abstract EPN-30, Neuro-Oncolgy 2016 http://neuro-oncology.oxfordjournals.org/content/18/suppl_3/iii37.1.full.pdf+html).

Fusions of YAP1 generally arise from the chromosomal translocation of the N-terminus of YAP1 and the C-terminus of the partner gene (PMID: 23737213, 25965568). Experimental studies suggest that YAP1 fusions are sufficient to drive tumorigenesis in xenograft animal models (PMID: 24553141).

The YAP1 R331W mutation is located in the transactivation domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 26056182, 27449093). In vitro studies with A459 cells overexpressing this mutation demonstrate YAP1 R331W is activating as measured by increased colony formation and invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 26056182).

The YAP1-TFE3 fusion protein is a result of chromosomal translocations fusing exons 1 through 7 of YAP1 to the C-terminus of TFE3, retaining YAP1's transcriptional enhancer factor and WW domains and loss of the canonical Hippo pathway regulation. This fusion protein has been identified in epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (PMID: 23737213). In vivo studies with mice expressing this fusion protein demonstrated the YAP1-TFE3 fusion is activating as measured by tumor formation compared to mice expressing wildtype YAP1 and wildtype TFE3 (PMID: 32675324). Preclinical studies of the fusion protein demonstrate that YAP1-TFE3 is activating as measured by aberrant constitutive nuclear localization of the fusion protein, promotion of anchorage-independent growth, increased cellular proliferation and promotion of tumorigenesis and metastasis compared to wildtype (PMID: 33913810).

YES1 amplification results from the gain of extra copies of the YES1 gene on chromosome 18p11.YES1 amplification leads to increased expression of YES1 protein (PMID: 28416483), phosphorylated Src family kinases (SFKs), phosphorylated Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP1) (PMID: 29875142) and sustains mTOR pathway activity (PMID: 31166114). YES1 amplification is found in various cancer types, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), esophageal squamous cell carcinomas, head and neck, bladder, and other cancers (PMID: 11756219, 31166114, 31391186). YES1 amplification has been found in patients with NSCLC whose EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas progressed on EGFR inhibitors (PMID: 28416483, 29875142). In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate that YES1 amplification in NSCLC cell lines results in sensitivity to the SFK inhibitor dasatinib as measured by decreased cell proliferation and invasion and reduced tumor growth in a xenograft model upon drug treatment  (PMID: 31166114). YES1 amplification in an EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma cell line results in resistance to all three generations of EGFR TKIs (erlotinib, afatinib, osimertinib) as measured by continued growth upon drug treatment in cell viability assays (PMID: 29875142, 28416483). YES1 amplification has also been associated with resistance to HER2-inhibition with Trastuzumab in HER2+ cancers (PMID: 32572172, 28158234).

The ACKR3 N127D mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 N127D demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased degradation of CXCL11 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29180449).

Amplification of ZNF217 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. ZNF217 amplification has been identified in breast cancer, ovarian cancer and prostate cancer (PMID: 22728437, 22139760, 27768596). In vitro studies with HO-8910 cells overexpressing ZNF217 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and migration compared to vector control (PMID: 25031722). In vivo studies with mice overexpressing ZNF217 also demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by aberrant tumor growth compared to vector control (PMID: 25031722). Preclinical studies with cancer cell models expressing amplified ZNF217 demonstrate sensitivity to triciribine, as measured by inhibition of tumor growth, and resistance to doxorubicin, as measured by sustained cellular growth (PMID: 22728437, 16203743).

The ACKR3 D7N mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in malignant melanoma (PMID: 27433843). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 D7N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL11 compared to wildtype (PMID: 27875312).

YAP1 amplification has been identified in lung cancer, cervical cancer and thyroid cancer (PMID: 24810989). In vitro studies with YAP1-silenced EKVX, CaSki and RO82 cell lines demonstrate YAP1 overexpression is activating as measured by decreased cellular proliferation, migration and anchorage-independent growth after silencing (PMID: 24810989).

Truncation mutations of ACKR3 typically occur in the C-terminal region of the protein and cause protein dysfunction. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing C-terminally truncated ACKR3 demonstrate that these mutations are inactivating as measured by the impaired recruitment of β-arrestin, the inability to degrade CXCL12 or CXCL11, impaired localization and reduced ERK1/2 activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 22457824, 22300987).

The ACKR3 D141N mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 D141N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL12 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29180449).

The ACKR3 D179N mutation is located in the ECL2a domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 D179N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL11 and CXCL12 compared to wildtype (PMID: 27875312).

The ACKR3 R142A mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 R142A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL12 and CXCL11 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29180449).

The ACKR3 N127S mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 N127S demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL12 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29180449).

The ACKR3 Y143A mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 Y143A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL12 and CXCL11 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29180449).

The YAP1-FAM118B fusion protein is a result of chromosomal translocations fusing exons 1 through 7 of YAP1 to the C-terminus of FAM118B, retaining YAP1's transcriptional enhancer factor and WW domains. This fusion protein has been identified in supratentorial ependymoma and NF2-wild type meningioma (PMID: 33480048, 33074854). In vivo studies with mice expressing this fusion protein demonstrate the YAP1-FAM118B fusion is activating as measured by tumor formation compared to mice expressing wildtype YAP1 and wildtype FAM118B (PMID: 32675324).

The ACKR3 K206D mutation is located in the ECL2b domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 K206D demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL11 and CXCL12 compared to wildtype (PMID: 27875312).

Amplification of ACKR3 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in breast cancer and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 17898181, 24074251). In vitro studies with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells overexpressing ACKR3 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cell migration and invasion and upregulation of TGF-β1/Smad signaling and Akt phosphorylation compared to wildtype (PMID: 31792315).

The ACKR3 D275N mutation is located in the ECL3 domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 D275N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL11 and CXCL12 compared to wildtype (PMID: 27875312).

The ACKR3 N127K mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 N127K demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased degradation of CXCL12 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29180449).

ACTG1 truncation mutations can form several forms of C-terminally truncated ACTG1 protein. Knockdown of ACTG1 in the SH-EP neuroblastoma cell line was shown to be oncogenic and inactivating as centrosome amplification was enhanced and prometaphase/metaphase was delayed, resulting in the mitotic inhibitor paclitaxel to induce mitotic arrest of the cancer cells (PMID: 21908715, 26697841).

The ACKR3 Y315A mutation is located in the transmembrane domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing ACKR3 Y315A demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding affinity and degradation of CXCL12 and CXCL11 compared to wildtype (PMID: 29180449).

The APLNR T44S mutation is found in the extracellular domain of the protein. This alteration was identified in a melanoma patient who failed T-cell based immunotherapy (PMID: 28783722). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, expression of this mutation in APLNR knockout melanoma cells resulted in resistance to T-cell mediated cytolysis (PMID: 28783722)

The APLNR C181S mutation is found in the transmembrane domain of the protein. This alteration was identified in a melanoma patient who failed T-cell based immunotherapy (PMID: 28783722). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, expression of this mutation in APLNR knockout melanoma cells did not result in resistance to T-cell mediated cytolysis compared to other APLNR mutants (PMID: 28783722).

The APLNR P292L mutation is found in the transmembrane domain of the protein. This alteration was identified in a melanoma patient who failed T-cell based immunotherapy (PMID: 28783722). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, expression of this mutation in APLNR knockout melanoma cells did not result in resistance to T-cell mediated cytolysis compared to other APLNR mutants (PMID: 28783722).

The ARID3A P268A mutation is located in the ARID domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 15456761).

The APLNR G349E mutation is found in the transmembrane domain of the protein. This alteration was identified in melanoma and lung patients who failed T-cell based immunotherapy (PMID: 28783722). While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, expression of this mutation in APLNR knockout melanoma cells resulted in resistance to T-cell mediated cytolysis (PMID: 28783722)

The ARID3A Y330A mutation is located in the ARID domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 15456761).

ARID3A truncation mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. Loss of ARID3A in embryonic kidney cells, mouse embryonic fibroblasts and in a transgenic mouse model resulted in the bypass of cellular senescence, increased cellular plasticity, and development of in vivo teratomas compared to wildtype (PMID: 24511468, 20680960).

The ARID3A F317A mutation is located in the ARID domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 15456761).

The ARID3A W299A mutation is located in the ARID domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in vitro demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding compared to wildtype (PMID: 15456761).

ARID4A truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations have been found in microsatellite-instability high colorectal carcinomas (PMID: 24382590). ARID4A deletion in a transgenic mouse model resulted in a myeloproliferative disease that progressed to leukemia (PMID: 18728284).

The ATP1A1 L100_I104del mutation is located in the N-terminal ATPase cation transporting domain. This alteration has been identified in aldosterone-producing adenoma (PMID: 23416519). In vivo studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes expressing ATP1A1 L100_I104del demonstrate that the alteration is inactivating as measured by loss of K+-stimulated pumping, resulting in membrane depolarization and voltage-gated Ca2+ channel activation (PMID: 23913004).

ARID4B truncating mutations can produce several forms of C-terminally truncated proteins. These mutations have been found in microsatellite-instability high colorectal carcinomas (PMID: 24382590). While these mutations have not yet been functionally characterized, heterozygous deletion of ARID4B in combination with deletion of ARID4A resulted in the development of acute myeloid leukemia in a transgenic mouse model (PMID: 18728284).

The ATP1A1 G99R mutation is located in the N-terminal ATPase cation transporting domain. This alteration has been identified in aldosterone-producing adenoma (PMID: 24082052). In vivo studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes expressing ATP1A1 G99R demonstrate that the alteration is inactivating as measured by loss of K+-stimulated pumping, resulting in membrane depolarization and voltage-gated Ca2+ channel activation (PMID: 23913004).

Amplification of ATP1A1 has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer, breast cancer, glioma and melanoma, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 17471453, 28529692, 18300910, 19243476). In vitro studies inhibiting ATP1A1 expression in HT-144, G-361, C-32 and SKMEL-28 melanoma cell lines demonstrated ATP1A1 overexpression is activating as measured by reduced tumor growth upon ATP1A1 inhibition. Tumor cells expressing amplified ATP1A1 demonstrated sensitivity when treated with ATP1A1 inhibitor UNBS1450 and antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (PMID: 26334094, 19243476).

The ATP1A1 V332G mutation is located in the E1-E2 ATPase domain. This alteration has been identified in aldosterone-producing adenoma (PMID: 23416519). In vivo studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes expressing ATP1A1 V332G demonstrate that the alteration is inactivating as measured by loss of K+-stimulated pumping, resulting in membrane depolarization and voltage-gated Ca2+ channel activation (PMID: 23913004).

The ATP1A1 E960_A963delinsS mutation is located at the C-terminal ATPase cation transporting domain. This alteration has been identified in aldosterone-producing adenoma (PMID: 28484360). In vivo studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes expressing ATP1A1 E960_A963delinsS demonstrate that the alteration is inactivating as measured by loss of K+-stimulated pumping, resulting in membrane depolarization and voltage-gated Ca2+ channel activation (PMID: 23913004).

The ATP1A1 L104R mutation is located at the N-terminal ATPase cation transporting domain. This alteration has been identified in aldosterone-producing adenoma (PMID: 23416519). In vivo studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes expressing ATP1A1 L104R demonstrate that the alteration is inactivating as measured by loss of K+-stimulated pumping, resulting in membrane depolarization and voltage-gated Ca2+ channel activation (PMID: 23913004).

The ATP6V1B2 Y371C mutation is located at the ATP binding interface of the protein and is a recurrent alteration in follicular lymphoma (PMID: 30720463, 28064239, 26691987). Expression of the Y371C alteration in HEK293T and lymphoma cell lines resulted in the activation of autophagic flux as determined by the expression of the autophagosomal marker LC3-II (PMID: 30720463).  Treatment of cell lines with an autophagy inhibitor resulted in the accumulation of LC3-II levels in mutant cell lines (PMID:  30720463). In addition, lymphoma cell lines with ATP6V1B2 mutations had activated the mTOR signaling pathway, altered lysosomal amino acid sensing, and reduced proton pump function (PMID: 30720463). Lymphoma cell lines expressing the ATP6V1B2 Y371C mutation demonstrated enhanced growth and in the context of leucine starvation (PMID: 30720463). These data suggest that the ATP6V1B2 Y371C mutation may be sensitive to therapeutic strategies targeting autophagy (PMID:  30720463).

The ATP6V1B2 R400Q mutation is located at the ATP binding interface of the protein and is a recurrent alteration in follicular lymphoma (PMID: 30720463, 28064239, 26691987). Expression of the R400Q alteration in HEK293T and lymphoma cell lines resulted in the activation of autophagic flux as determined by the expression of the autophagosomal marker LC3-II (PMID: 30720463).  Treatment of cell lines with an autophagy inhibitor resulted in the accumulation of LC3-II levels in mutant cell lines (PMID:  30720463). In addition, lymphoma cell lines with ATP6V1B2 mutations had activated the mTOR signaling pathway, altered lysosomal amino acid sensing, and reduced proton pump function (PMID: 30720463). Lymphoma cell lines expressing the ATP6V1B2 R400Q mutation demonstrated enhanced growth and in the context of leucine starvation (PMID: 30720463). These data suggest that the ATP6V1B2 R400Q mutation may be sensitive to therapeutic strategies targeting autophagy (PMID:  30720463).

ATXN2 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of the protein. In vivo studies with ATXN2 knockout transgenic mouse models demonstrated that the loss of ATXN2 is inactivating as measured by impaired protein synthesis rates and mTOR signaling (PMID: 25721894).

ATP6V1B2 truncation mutations occur throughout the protein and result in ATP6V1B2 haploinsufficiency. Truncating ATP6V1B2 mutations are found in patients with dominant deafness-onychodsytrophy (PMID: 24913193). In vivo studies with ATP6V1B2 knockdown transgenic mouse models demonstrated loss of ATP6V1B2 is inactivating as measured by impaired lysosome acidification and development of dominant deafness-onychodystrophy syndrome compared to wildtype (PMID: 24913193). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing ATP6V1B2 R506*, a truncation mutation, also demonstrated truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by decreased ATPase hydrolysis and aberrant lysosome acidification compared to wildtype (PMID: 24913193).

The ATXN7 Q30R mutation occurs in the polyQ tract of the protein that is commonly expanded in neurodegenerative disorders (PMID: 28584132). Expression of the ATXN7 Q30R variant in Nthy-ori cells, a T-immortalized human follicular thryoid line, in the context of the HRAS G12V mutation resulted in increased profileration compared to controls (PMID: 28584132). Mutations in the polyQ of ATXN7 may result in enhanced aggregation of ATXN7-associated complexes; however, the exact role of this variant requires additional functional studies. (PMID: 25755283).

The RAD51C-ATXN7 fusion protein is a result of chromosomal translocations with RAD51C exons 1 through 7 and ATXN7 exons 6 through 13. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and breast cancer (PMID: 27296891, 21980511). RAD51C-ATXN7 fusion protein expression is suggested to be inactivating as measured by association with the loss of FANCD2 DNA repair foci in human colorectal tumors expressing the fusion (PMID: 27296891).

The ATXN7 P40Q mutation occurs in the polyQ tract of the protein that is commonly expanded in neurodegenerative disorders (PMID: 28584132). Expression of the ATXN7 P40Q variant in Nthy-ori cells, a T-immortalized human follicular thryoid line, in the context of the HRAS G12V mutation resulted in increased profileration compared to controls (PMID: 28584132). Mutations in the polyQ of ATXN7 may result in enhanced aggregation of ATXN7-associated complexes; however, the exact role of this variant requires additional functional studies. (PMID: 25755283).

The ATXN7 P42_P43insP mutation occurs in the polyQ tract of the protein that is commonly expanded in neurodegenerative disorders (PMID: 28584132). Expression of the ATXN7 P42_P43insP variant in Nthy-ori cells, a T-immortalized human follicular thryoid line, in the context of the HRAS G12V mutation resulted in increased profileration compared to controls (PMID: 28584132). Mutations in the polyQ of ATXN7 may result in enhanced aggregation of ATXN7-associated complexes; however, the exact role of this variant requires additional functional studies. (PMID: 25755283).

The BACH2 T817A mutation is located in a predicted phosphorylation site in the BACH2 protein. In vitro experiments demonstrated that this mutation is likely neutral as measured by phosphorylation and downstream signaling comparable to wildtype (PMID: 28461702).

The ATXN7 Q39P mutation occurs in the polyQ tract of the protein that is commonly expanded in neurodegenerative disorders (PMID: 28584132). Expression of the ATXN7 Q39P variant in Nthy-ori cells, a T-immortalized human follicular thryoid line, in the context of the HRAS G12V mutation resulted in increased profileration compared to controls (PMID: 28584132). Mutations in the polyQ of ATXN7 may result in enhanced aggregation of ATXN7-associated complexes; however, the exact role of this variant requires additional functional studies. (PMID: 25755283).

The BACH2 L24P mutation is located in the BTB/POZ dimerization domain of the protein. The mutation has been found as a germline mutation in BACH2-related immunodeficiency and autoimmunity (BRIDA) syndrome (PMID: 28530713). In vitro experiments demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by decreased protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 28530713).

The BACH2 S521A mutation is a predicted phosphorylation site in the protein. Expression of the mutation in 3T3 cells resulted in reduced phosphorylation, loss of nuclear localization, altered PI3K/S6 signaling, and reduced viability (PMID: 28461702).

The BACH2 T519A mutation is located in a predicted phosphorylation site in the BACH2 protein. In vitro experiments demonstrated that this mutation is likely neutral as measured by phosphorylation and downstream signaling comparable to wildtype (PMID: 28461702).

BACH2 truncating mutations can form C-terminally truncated BACH2 protein. BACH2 is located on chromosome 6, band q15, a region frequently associated with deletions in ALL and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. It was noted that BACH2 expression was significantly diminished in mouse models of C-REL-/- Eμ-Myc lymphomas. Even among Eμ-Myc mice with wildtype C-REL, those expressing lower levels of BACH2 had an earlier onset of lymphomas. BACH2 was also shown to be important for tumor suppression of pre-B lymphoblastic leukemia by mediating the negative selection of pre-B cells that failed to undergo proper maturation. However, one study showed that BACH2 was also shown to be important for tumor immunosuppression because xenograft models using B16 melanoma cells in BACH2 knockout mice had slower progression rates than those in wildtype mice (PMID: 23852341, 26522720, 11746976, 26731475).

Amplification of CACNA1D typically results in the overexpression of the protein. CACNA1D amplification has been identified in prostate cancer (PMID: 36949059). In vitro studies with LNCaP cells overexpressing CACNA1D demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and CaV1.3-mediated Ca2+ signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 36949059).

The BACH2 E788K mutation is located in the cytoplasmic localization domain of the protein. The mutation has been found as a germline mutation in BACH2-related immunodeficiency and autoimmunity (BRIDA) syndrome (PMID: 28530713). In vitro experiments have demonstrated that this mutation is likely inactivating as measured by aberrant cytoplasmic aggregation and reduced protein expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 28530713).

BRSK1 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with BRSK1-knockout MDA-MB-231 cells demonstrate that loss of BRSK1 is inactivating as measured by reduced CDKN1B expression and loss of cell cycle arrest compared to mock cells (PMID: 25036402).

Amplification of CAD typically results in the overexpression of the protein. CAD amplification has been identified in breast cancer, glioblastoma and prostate adenocarcinoma (PMID: 33186350, 31391321, 21982950). In vitro studies with colo320DM and IMR32 cells overexpressing CAD demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 16155188).

The CHD4 R877W mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic B-cell leukemia and melanoma (PMID: 31697823, 24265153). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is pathogenic and disrupts protein function (PMID: 33981601).

The CHD4 X34_splice mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in uterine endometrioid carcinoma (PMID: 23550210). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is inactivating and leads to loss of DNA binding, functional remodeling and ATPase activity (PMID: 33981601).

The CHD4 E139del mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in hemangioblastoma and salivary gland mucoepidermoid carcinoma (PMID: 25589003, 27340278). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation results in nonsense mediated decay (PMID: 33981601).

Amplification of CHD4 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. CHD4 amplification has been identified in colorectal cancer, uterine serous carcinoma and oral cancer (PMID: 33994851, 23359684, 28683324). In vitro studies with PC-9 and H292 cells overexpressing CHD4 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and migration compared to vector control (PMID: 32228507). Other in vitro and in vivo studies with knockdown of CHD4 in CHD4-overexpressing ovarian cancer cells demonstrate suppression of cellular migration and invasion and prevention of disease progression following CHD4 knockdown (PMID: 36681835).

The CHD4 R572* mutation is located in the chromodomain 1 of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 27149842). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is inactivating and reduces DNA binding function (PMID: 33981601).

Truncating mutations of CHD2 typically result in the loss of protein function. CHD2 truncating mutations have been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 26031915). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing truncating mutations of CHD2 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by defective association with active chromatin and loss of colocalization with acetyl histones H4Ac and H3K4me compared to wildtype (PMID: 26031915).

The CHD4 L1215P mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain on the C-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in mixed endometrium cell carcinoma (PMID: 23104009). In vitro nucleosome binding, ATPase and nucleosome remodeling assays of CHD4 L1215P demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced ATPase activity and nucleosome remodeling activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 29844320). Mutations that affect the nucleosome remodeling function of CHD4 are predicted to contribute to tumorigenesis through prevention of nucleosome deacetylation and altering nucleosome positioning to allow for repression of tumor suppressor genes and activation of oncogenes (PMID: 29844320).

The CHD4 H1151R mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in uterine serous carcinoma (PMID: 23104009). In vitro nucleosome binding, ATPase and nucleosome remodeling assays of CHD4 H1151R demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced ATPase activity and nucleosome remodeling activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 29844320). Mutations that affect the nucleosome remodeling function of CHD4 are predicted to contribute to tumorigenesis through prevention of nucleosome deacetylation and altering nucleosome positioning to allow for repression of tumor suppressor genes and activation of oncogenes (PMID: 29844320).

The CHD4 H1196Y mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain on the C-terminal region of the protein. In vitro nucleosome binding, ATPase and nucleosome remodeling assays of CHD4 L1215P demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased nucleosome remodeling activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 29844320). Mutations that affect the nucleosome remodeling function of CHD4 are predicted to contribute to tumorigenesis through prevention of nucleosome deacetylation and altering nucleosome positioning to allow for repression of tumor suppressor genes and activation of oncogenes (PMID: 29844320).

The CHD4 L912V mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in uterine serous carcinoma (PMID: 23104009). In vitro nucleosome binding, ATPase and nucleosome remodeling assays of CHD4 L912V demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced ATPase activity and nucleosome remodeling activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 29844320). Mutations that affect the nucleosome remodeling function of CHD4 are predicted to contribute to tumorigenesis through prevention of nucleosome deacetylation and altering nucleosome positioning to allow for repression of tumor suppressor genes and activation of oncogenes (PMID: 29844320).

The CHD4 R1162W mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer and endometrioid carcinoma (PMID: 22722193, 23104009). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is pathogenic and disrupts protein interaction with ATP (PMID: 33981601).

The CHD4 R975H mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic B-cell leukemia and colorectal cancer (PMID: 36050548, 26416732). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is pathogenic and disrupts protein function (PMID: 33981601).

BRSK1 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with BRSK1-knockout MDA-MB-231 cells demonstrate that loss of BRSK1 is inactivating as measured by reduced CDKN1B expression and loss of cell cycle arrest compared to mock cells (PMID: 25036402).

The CHD4 R877Q mutation is located in the ATPase motor domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic B-cell leukemia and skin basal cell carcinoma (PMID: 25207766, 26950094). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is pathogenic and disrupts protein function (PMID: 33981601).

CMTR2 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing truncated variants of CMTR2 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by reduced or loss of MTase activity compared to full length CMTR2 (PMID: 24402442).

The CMTR2 D235A mutation occurs in the RNA methyltransferase domain of the protein (PMID: 21310715). In biochemical studies, CMTR2 D235A is unable to methylate RNA molecules in vitro, suggesting this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 21310715).

The CHD4 K119del mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer and melanoma (PMID: 22810696, 24265153). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation results in nonsense mediated decay (PMID: 33981601).

The CMTR2 K275A mutation occurs in the RNA methyltransferase domain of the protein (PMID: 21310715). In biochemical studies, CMTR2 K275A is unable to methylate RNA molecules in vitro, suggesting this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 21310715).

The CMTR2 K117A mutation occurs in the RNA methyltransferase domain of the protein (PMID: 21310715). In biochemical studies, CMTR2 K117A is unable to methylate RNA molecules in vitro, suggesting this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 21310715).

The COL2A1 G1170S mutation is located in the collagen triple helix repeat of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 22810696). In vivo studies with mice expressing COL2A1 G1170S demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of COL2A1 expression and accelerated chondrocyte hypertrophy compared to wildtype (PMID: 30854241).

The CRBN R419* mutation occurs in the last exon of the protein. Expression of CRBN R419* in HEK293T cells demonstrated that the mutation is inactivating as measured by enhanced autoubiquitination and degradation in biochemical assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 23983124). The CRBN R419* mutant protein still assembles in the E3 ligase complex; however, the variant has decreased stability (PMID: 23983124).

Truncating mutations in CRBN that occur in the C-terminal domain have been shown to inactivate its function (PMID: 29370161). The CRBN gene codes for the protein cereblon which is a component of the cullin ring E3 ubiquitin ligase complex and the target for thalidomide (of the IMiD family), used in the treatment of multiple myeloma (PMID:24166296). Cereblon has been found to activate the protein synthesis machinery by negatively regulating AMP kinase (PMID: 24993823). Decreased cereblon expression has been associated with resistance to IMiD-based therapy, and truncating mutations in CRBN have been proposed as a plausible mechanisms of resistance (PMID: 24166296). However, truncating mutations in CRBN are extremely rare in this setting (PMID: 29718735)

The EWSR1-CREB1 t(2;22)(q33;q12) fusion usually involves exon 7 of EWSR1 and exon 7 of CREB1 (PMID: 24320889). This fusion has been identified in various soft tissue neoplasms including Angiomatoid Fibrous Histiocytoma and Clear Cell Sarcoma (PMID: 19801966, 21822206, 25364450, 24320889). In each case the transactivation domain of EWSR1 is fused to the DNA binding domain of CREB1, potentially increasing the activity of CREB1. However, further characterization studies of the fusion protein are needed.

CTR9 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. Truncating mutations of CTR9 have been identified in Wilms' tumor (PMID: 29292210). In vivo studies with yeast expressing truncated variants of CTR9 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of binding with PAF1c compared to full length CTR9 (PMID: 30228257).

The CTR9 R201C mutation is located in the tetratricopeptide repeat domain of the CTR9 protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma, among others (PMID: 30228257). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to PAF1, an RNA polymerase II binding protein, compared to wildtype (PMID: 30228257).

COL2A1 truncating mutations occur throughout the gene and typically result in loss of protein expression. Truncating mutations of COL2A1 have been identified in Stickler syndrome and spondyloperipheral dysplasia (PMID: 7487609, 20179744, 15316962). In vitro studies with patient-derived RNA samples expressing truncating mutations of COL2A1 demonstrate that the mutations are inactivating as measured by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of COL2A1 (PMID: 17721977, 18023161).

The CTR9 R98W mutation is located in the tetratricopeptide repeat domain of the CTR9 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely neutral as measured by binding to PAF1, an RNA polymerase II binding protein, compared to wildtype (PMID: 30228257).

The CTR9 A220T mutation is located in the tetratricopeptide repeat domain of the CTR9 protein. This mutation has been found in lung adenocarcinoma, among others (PMID: 30228257). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to PAF1, an RNA polymerase II binding protein, compared to wildtype (PMID: 30228257).

The CTR9 P164S mutation is located in the tetratricopeptide repeat domain of the CTR9 protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma, among others (PMID: 30228257). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased binding to PAF1, an RNA polymerase II binding protein, compared to wildtype (PMID: 30228257).

Amplification of CUL4 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. CUL4 amplification has been identified in lung cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer and ovarian cancer (PMID: 34119472, 22422151, 24305877). In vitro studies with H460, A549, LNCAP, C4-2, CWR22, 22RV1, MCF10A and MDA-MB-468 cells overexpressing CUL4 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and malignant cellular transformation compared to vector controls (PMID: 28576144, 25413624, 28223829). Preclinical studies with ovarian cancer cells and lung cancer cells overexpressing CUL4 demonstrate resistance to cisplatin, doxorubicin, docetaxel, gemcitabine and erlotinib as measured by decreased cellular apoptosis and sustained cellular proliferation (PMID: 25413624, 26503734, 30718461).

The DDB2 R273H mutation is located adjacent to the WD40 domain of the protein. In vitro studies with Hi-Five insect cells expressing DDB2 R273H demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of DNA-binding activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 33276309).

The DDB2 K244E mutation is located in the WD40 domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HeLa cells expressing DDB2 K244E demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by defects in chromatin association compared to wildtype (PMID: 33276309).

CY19A1 amplification is an event that has been identified in ER+ breast cancer previously treated with adjuvant aromatase inhibitors (PMID: 28112739). In vitro studies with MCF7 breast cancer cells expressing CYP19A1 amplification demonstrated that CYP19A1 overexpression is activating as measured by increased aromatase activity and estrogen-independent ERa binding to target genes compared to wildtype (PMID: 28112739). CYP19A1 amplification is suggested to confer resistance to aromatase inhibitors in ER+ breast cancer due to promotion of local autocrine estrogen signaling (PMID: 28112739).

EGR1 truncation mutations generally reduce the expression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in patients with acute and chronic myelogenous leukemia (PMID: 29050203). In vivo studies with EGR1 knockdown mouse models demonstrate that loss of EGR1 is inactivating as measured by development and aggressiveness of BCR-ABL-driven leukemia compared to wildtype (PMID: 29050203).

DDB2 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. DDB2 truncating mutations have been identified in patients with xeroderma pigmentosum (PMID: 32530099, 12812979). In vitro studies with patient-derived cells expressing truncated variants of DDB2 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by deficient UV-damaged DNA binding activity and repair compared to vector control (PMID: 12812979).

ECT2L truncation mutations occur throughout the gene. These mutations have been identified in patients with T-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemias (PMID: 22237106). These mutations have not been functionally characterized.

Amplification of DDX5 typically leads to the overexpression of the protein. DDX5 amplification has been identified in breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 22750847, 26212035). In vitro studies with NCI-N87, KATO III, H520, A549 and HCT116 cells overexpressing DDX5 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 28216662, 26212035, 22750847). In vivo studies with mouse xenograft models overexpressing DDX5 also demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased tumor growth compared to vector control (PMID: 28216662).

The SLC45A3-ELK4 fusion protein results from a fusion between exon 1 of SLC45A3 fusing with exon 2 of ELK4. This fusion protein has been identified in prostate cancer (PMID: 19293179). In vitro studies with LNCaP cells expressing SLC45A3-ELK4 demonstrate that the fusion is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and cell cycle progression compared to vector control (PMID: 28716526).

EP400 truncation mutations occur throughout the gene and result in loss of protein function. Truncating mutations in EP400 have been identified in immortalized murine embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cell lines with concurrent inactivation of TP53 (PMID: 24670820). In vitro studies with PRM-depleted Eu-myc B cells demonstrate that truncated EP400 is likely inactivating as measured by aberrantly spliced EP400 transcripts resulting in loss of EP400 expression, reduced cell viability and increased apoptosis compared to full transcript EP400 (PMID: 25970242).

Amplification of ELK4 typically results in the overexpression of protein. ELK4 amplification has been identified in gastric cancer, glioma and breast cancer (PMID: 34663788, 21846680, 16457699). In vitro studies with HGC-27 cells and xenograft mouse models overexpressing ELK4 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion and tumor growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 34372882).

Amplification of EPHB4 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. EPHB4 amplification has been identified in breast cancer, lung cancer and esophageal squamous cell cancer (PMID: 16816380, 31934189, 31885720). In vitro studies with SKBR3 cells and ZR75 cells overexpressing EPHB4 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular survival and tumor growth compared vector controls (PMID: 16816380).

The EPHB4 P881S mutation is located in the intracellular linker region adjacent to the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung cancer (PMID: 26073592). In vitro studies with H661 cells expressing EPHB4 P881S demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26073592).

The EPHB4 A742V mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung cancer (PMID: 26073592). In vitro studies with H661 cells expressing EPHB4 A742V demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26073592).

The EPHB4 G723S mutation is located in the kinase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung cancer (PMID: 26073592). In vitro studies with H661 cells expressing EPHB4 G723S demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26073592).

The EPHB4 P381S mutation is located in the first extracellular fibronectin III repeat region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung cancer (PMID: 26073592). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is likely oncogenic (PMID: 26073592).

The EPHB4 A230V mutation is located in the extracellular linker region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung cancer (PMID: 26073592). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is likely neutral (PMID: 26073592).

The EPHB4 A371V mutation is located in the first extracellular fibronectin III repeat region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in lung cancer (PMID: 26073592). In silico analysis suggests that the mutation is likely neutral (PMID: 26073592).

Amplification of ERC1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. In vitro studies with A549 and HEK293T cells overexpressing ERC1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased NF-kB and proinflammatory gene activation as well as promotion of cellular migration and invasion compared to vector control (PMID: 37252973).

Recurrent translocations involving EPOR are found in patients with B-acute lymphoblastic leukemias (B-ALL) (PMID: 26859458, 28972016). EPOR fusion proteins lead to overexpression of the C-terminal of EPOR, resulting in truncation of negative regulatory domains (PMID: 28972016). In hematopoietic assays, expression of truncated EPOR leads to enhanced JAK-STAT signaling, hypersensitivity to EPO, and sensitivity to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib (PMID: 28972016).

Amplification of ETS1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. ETS1 amplification has been identified in ovarian cancer and prostate cancer (PMID: 11297247, 23064684). In vitro studies with MDA-MB231 cells and MCF-7 cells overexpressing ETS1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, invasion and migration compared to vector control (PMID: 24706481, 21444677, 22971289). Preclinical studies with breast cancer cell lines overexpressing ETS1 demonstrate resistance to vincristine, docetaxel, doxorubicin and paclitaxel as measured by sustained transactivational activity (PMID: 20392592).

Truncating mutations in ESCO2 can occur throughout the entire gene and are generally inactivating (PMID: 18411254, 16380922). ESCO2, a cohesion factor involved in sister chromatid cohesion, is a tumor suppressor gene required for successful cell division (PMID: 527250). Germline mutations resulting in the inactivation of ESCO2 have been identified in patients with Roberts syndrome and SC phocomelia, a spectrum of hereditary disorders characterized by multiple organ defects, variable degrees of limb and craniofacial abnormalities as well as higher risk for tumor development (PMID: 3568444, 16380922). Studies in zebrafish models have shown that inactivating mutations in ESCO2 result in premature chromosome separation, with resulting chromosomal scattering, genomic instability and aneuploidy (PMID:26044958, 21637801). Patients with ESCO2 germline inactivating mutations also display defective DNA damage repair (PMID: 30508616).

The gene T73S mutation is located in a disordered region of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in posterior fossa group A (PFA) ependymomas (PMID: 29909548). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by increased activity of the Polycomb Repressive 2 (PRC2) Complex compared to wildtype (PMID: 29909548).

The gene Y184C mutation is located in a disordered region of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in posterior fossa group A (PFA) ependymomas (PMID: 29909548). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by increased activity of the Polycomb Repressive 2 (PRC2) Complex compared to wildtype (PMID: 29909548).

The gene I88F mutation is located in a disordered region of the gene protein. This mutation has been found in posterior fossa group A (PFA) ependymomas (PMID: 29909548). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by increased activity of the Polycomb Repressive 2 (PRC2) Complex compared to wildtype (PMID: 29909548).

Amplification of FRS2 typically results in the overexpression of protein. FRS2 amplification has been identified in ovarian cancer, bladder cancer and osteosarcoma (PMID: 25368431, 30755618, 30001240). In vitro studies with ovarian cancer cell lines overexpressing FRS2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased anchorage-independent growth and MAPK signaling activation compared to vector control (PMID: 25368431).

The FES L334P mutation is located in the second coiled-coil domain of the protein. In vitro studies with TF-1 cells expressing FES L334P demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by kinase activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 11509660).

The FES L145P mutation is located in the first coiled-coil domain of the protein. In vitro studies with TF-1 cells expressing FES L145P demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased kinase activity, cell attachment and cell spreading compared to wildtype (PMID: 11509660). Preclinical studies with COS-7 cells expressing this mutation demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with TAE684 as measured by loss of autophosphorylation and microtubule association (PMID: 22520759).

The FOXF1 S2F mutation occurs in the DNA binding domain of the protein (PMID: 31199666). Mice engineered to express the FOXF1 S2F mutation exhibited a lung development phenotype similar to that found in patients with alveolar capillary dysplasia with misaligned pulmonary veins (ACDMPV). This alteration inhibited the interaction of STAT3 with FOXF1 and reduced the ability of FOXF1 to bind chromatin (PMID: 31199666).

The GAB1 Y83C mutation occurs in the N-terminal pleckstrin homology domain of the protein (PMID: 22751113). Expression of the GAB1 Y83C mutation in mammary epithelial cell lines resulted in a more fibroblast-like cellular phenotype (PMID: 22751113). Cell lines engineered to express this mutation demonstrated increased EGF independent signaling, modest enhancement of ERK signaling, and altered branching morphogenesis (PMID: 22751113), suggesting that this mutation is gain-of-function.

Truncating mutations of GATA4 typically results in the loss of protein function. In vivo studies with GATA4-deficient mice demonstrate that loss of GATA4 is inactivating as measured by increased tumor growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 35017504).

The GAB1 T387N mutation occurs near the GRB2-SH3 domain binding site of the protein  (PMID: 22751113). Expression of the GAB1 T387N mutation in mammary epithelial cell lines resulted in a more fibroblast-like cellular phenotype (PMID: 22751113). Cell lines engineered to express this mutation demonstrated increased EGF independent signaling, modest enhancement of ERK signaling, and altered branching morphogenesis (PMID: 22751113), suggesting that this mutation is gain-of-function. Biochemical analyses determined that the T387 residue is a likely phosphorylation site that is important in negative feedback regulation (PMID: 22751113).

Amplification of GAB2 has been found in various cancer types including breast cancer (PMID: 19881546, 21748818, 19881546), ovarian cancer (PMID: 25852062, 24385586) and melanoma (PMID: 19509136 ), among others. GAB2 amplification results from focal gains of the GAB2 gene on chromosome 11q14 (PMID: 19881546). Overexpression of GAB2 in a variety of cell types resulted in increased ERBB2 and EGFR signaling with enhanced growth and invasive properties (PMID: 26754532,     26657155, 21996746, 21118992, 19342374). Murine models engineered to overexpress GAB2 resulted in enhanced tumor growth and metastasis in several cancer types (PMID: 17310989, 16369543).

Deletion of GATA4 typically results in the loss of protein expression. In vivo studies with GATA4-deficient mice demonstrate that loss of GATA4 is inactivating as measured by increased tumor growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 35017504).

gene is a linker histone (H1) of the B family. Truncating mutations in gene are predicted to lead to loss of the H1 linker histone, which is associated with cellular senescence (PMID: 17158953). Mutations in gene have been identified in follicular and diffuse large B-cell lymphomas and are thought to be involved in epigenetic deregulation in these tumors (PMID: 24435047, 26473533).

Amplification of GATA6 typically results in overexpression of the protein. GATA6 amplification has been identified in esophageal adenocarcinoma, pancreatic cancer and cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 33300112, 27325420, 33060563). In vitro and in vivo studies with QBC939 and RBE cells overexpressing GATA6 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cellular proliferation compared to vector control (PMID: 33060563).

Amplification of GPC3 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. GPC3 amplification has been identified in hepatocellular carcinoma (PMID: 33384879, 12824919, 36165051). In vitro studies with hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines and tissue samples overexpressing GPC3 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased expression of various growth signaling molecules, including MMP2, MMP14, FGFR1 and IGF1R, compared to GPC3-knockdown cells (PMID: 20653060). In vitro studies with NIH3T3 cells overexpressing GPC3 also demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, colony growth and IGF1R and ERK phosphorylation compared to GPC3-knockdown cells (PMID: 18413366).

HIRA truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with HIRA- and Fh1-deficient mouse epithelial cells and xenograft models demonstrate that loss of HIRA is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and tumor initiation and growth compared to the Fh1-deficient control (PMID: 36269833). In vitro studies with HIRA suppression in breast cancer cell lines also demonstrate that HIRA deficiency is inactivating as measured by induction of dormancy pathways and increased cellular survival through induction of stress-inducible transcription factors NRF2, MITF and ATF3 compared to wildtype (Abstract: Drapela et al. Abstract# 65, AACR 2023. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/83/7_Supplement/65/722615/Abstract-65-HIRA-is-a-master-regulator-of-the).

HIRA deletion mutations result in either downregulation or the complete absence of protein expression. Downregulation of HIRA has been identified in hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma (PMID: 36269833). In vitro studies with HIRA- and Fh1-deficient mouse epithelial cells and xenograft models demonstrate that loss of HIRA is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and tumor initiation and growth compared to the Fh1-deficient control (PMID: 36269833). In vitro studies with HIRA suppression in breast cancer cell lines also demonstrate that HIRA deficiency is inactivating as measured by induction of dormancy pathways and increased cellular survival through induction of stress-inducible transcription factors NRF2, MITF and ATF3 compared to wildtype (Abstract: Drapela et al. Abstract# 65, AACR 2023. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/83/7_Supplement/65/722615/Abstract-65-HIRA-is-a-master-regulator-of-the). Preclinical studies have demonstrated HIRA-deficiency may confer chemotherapy resistance in ovarian cancer models (Abstract: Yasukawa et al. Abstract# LB281, AACR 2023. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/83/8_Supplement/LB281/725464).

Truncating mutations of HLA-C result in reduced HLA-C protein expression. Loss of HLA-C has been reported as a common characteristic of malignant cells and has been proposed to enable tumor cells to escape from cytotoxic T-lymphocyte surveillance (PMID: 15546342); however, this has yet to be functionally validated.

The KBTBD4 R297delinsPRR mutation (also cited as KBTBD4 R313delinsPRR) is located in the Kelch repeat domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, it has been identified as the sole alteration in several pineal parenchymal tumors of intermediate differentiation (PPTID) and is recurrent in Group 3 medulloblastomas (PMID: 30877433, 28726821). Structural studies suggest that this insertion may disrupt the substrate-binding interface of the protein (PMID: 28726821).

Translocations involving IL3 and IGH are found in patients with B-precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemias, typically presenting with eosinophilic proliferation (PMID: 29424254, 3546615, 30207070). The resultant fusion protein pairs the IL3 promoter with regulatory enhancers from the IGH locus, leading to upregulation of IL3 (PMID: 29424254, 2114933). Activation of IL3 expression is predicted to increase serum IL3 levels, promoting hypereosinophilia and cellular proliferation (PMID: 25382309). IGH rearrangements are predicted to occur due to failed V(D)J recombination in immune cells (PMID: 20018760).

The KBTBD4 P295delinsPP mutation (also cited as KBTBD4 P311delinsPP) is located in the Kelch repeat domain of the protein. While this mutation has not been functionally characterized, the mutation has been recurrently found in group 4 medulloblastomas (PMID: 28726821). Structural studies suggest that this insertion may disrupt the substrate-binding interface of the protein (PMID: 28726821).

Amplification of KEL typically results in the overexpression of protein. KEL amplification has been identified in acute erythroleukemia (PMID: 35140839). In vitro studies with K562 and HEL cells overexpressing KEL demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion compared to vector control (PMID: 35140839).

The KLF5 E419Q mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutant is a hotspot and has been found in lung squamous cell carcinomas and lung adenocarcinomas (PMID: 28963353). Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells demonstrated that this mutation increases the number of DNA binding sites recognized by the protein and increases activation of its target genes compared to wildtype KLF5 as measured by integrated ChIP-Seq and RNA-Seq assays (PMID: 28963353). Expression of this mutation in cancer cells also resulted in increased cell proliferation compared to wildtype KLF5 (PMID: 28963353).

The KLF5 E419K mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutant is a hotspot and has been found in cervical cancer, bladder cancer and lung adenocarcinomas (PMID: 28963353). Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells demonstrated that this mutation increases the number of DNA binding sites recognized by the protein compared to wildtype KLF5 as measured by ChIP-Seq (PMID: 28963353).

The KLF5 S303P mutation is located in the phospho-degron domain of the protein. This mutant is a hotspot and has been found in colorectal cancers (PMID: 28963353). Expression of this mutation in human cancer cells demonstrated that this mutation significantly increases the stability of the protein compared to wildtype KLF5 as measured by a cycloheximide chase assay (PMID: 28963353).

The KLF5 P301S mutation is located in the phospho-degron domain of the protein. This mutant is a hotspot and found in colorectal cancer, uterine cancer and lung adenocarcinomas (PMID: 28963353). Expression of this mutation in human cancer cells demonstrated that this mutation significantly increases the stability of the protein compared to wildtype KLF5 as measured by a cycloheximide chase assay (PMID: 28963353).

Truncating mutations of IRF2 typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with TM3 cells and NIH3T3 cells expressing truncated variants of IRF2 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of DNA binding and reduced transcriptional activity and repression compared to full length IRF2 (PMID: 11058120, 10586038).

The KLF5 D418N mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutant is a hotspot and has been found in bladder cancer and lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 28963353). Expression of this mutation in human fibroblast cells demonstrated that this mutation increases the number of DNA binding sites recognized by the protein compared to wildtype KLF5 as measured by ChIP-Seq (PMID: 28963353).

The KLF5 P304A mutation is located in the phospho-degron domain of the protein. This mutant is a hotspot and has been found in colorectal cancers (PMID: 28963353). Expression of this mutation in human cancer cells demonstrated that this mutation significantly increases the stability of the protein compared to wildtype KLF5 as measured by a cycloheximide chase assay (PMID: 28963353).

The CLIP1-LTK fusion joins multiple coiled-coil domains of CLIP1 upstream of the full LTK kinase domain. This fusion has been found in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (PMID: 34819663). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that the CLIP1-LTK fusion protein is constitutively activated as measured by cell viability assay and kinase activity compared to other activating LTK mutations (PMID: 34819663). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this fusion is sensitive to the ALK inhibitor lorlatinib as measured by decreased cell viability and kinase activity compared to untreated cells (PMID: 34819663). One patient with NSCLC harboring the CLIP1-LTK fusion demonstrated a good clinical response to treatment with lorlatinib (PMID: 34819663).

LMNA amplification typically results in the overexpression of the protein. Amplification of LMNA has been identified in various cancers, including cervical cancer, prostate cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (PMID: 32896989). In vitro studies with prostate tumor cell lines overexpressing LMNA demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, colony formation, migration and invasion compared to LMNA-knockout cells (PMID: 22301279).

The MERTK R758C mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was identified as a germline mutation in a patient with pheochromocytoma (PMID: 26700204). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing MERTK R758C demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by sustained ERK phosphorylation after stimulation with MERTK ligand GAS6 and nutrient starvation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26700204).

The MERTK R758H mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. This mutation was identified as a germline mutation in a patient with pheochromocytoma, recurrent and metastatic paragangliomas and medullary thyroid carcinoma (PMID: 26700204). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing MERTK R758H demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by sustained ERK phosphorylation after stimulation with MERTK ligand GAS6 and nutrient starvation compared to wildtype (PMID: 26700204).

The NFE2 R284H mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with myeloproliferative neoplasms (PMID: 30755419). In vitro assays and expression of this mutation in CB3 cells demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as shown by reduced binding to DNA and reduced transcriptional activity compared with wildtype NFE2 (PMID: 30755419).

The NFE2 R272Q mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with de novo acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 30755419). There is conflicting functional data for this mutation.
