While in vitro assays demonstrated that this mutation does not alter DNA binding compared to wildtype NFE2, expression of this mutation in CB3 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as shown by reduced transcriptional activity compared to wildtype NFE2 (PMID: 30755419).

The NFE2 C283R mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with de novo acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 30755419). In vitro assays and expression of this mutation in CB3 cells demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as shown by reduced binding to DNA and reduced transcriptional activity compared with wildtype NFE2 (PMID: 30755419).

The MERTK Y754F mutation is located in the tyrosine kinase domain of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing MERTK Y754F demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by the inability to phosphorylate ERK compared to wildtype (PMID: 26700204).

C-terminal truncating mutations of NFE2 result in truncated variants that are unable to bind to DNA and lack transactivation activity. These mutations are found in patients with myeloproliferative neoplasms and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (PMID: 30755419, 23589569). Truncating mutations in this range are classified as type Ib NFE2 mutations, which are NFE2 mutations that lack DNA binding and enhance wildtype NFE2 activity (PMID: 30755419). Expression of C-terminally truncated NFE2 protein in mice showed that truncating mutations in this range are activating as measured by enhanced transcriptional activity and stability of the wildtype NFE2 protein and progression from myeloproliferative neoplasms to AML (PMID: 30755419, 23589569). The AML resulting from NFE2 truncation in these mice demonstrated acquired chromosomal aberrations and TP53 mutations similar to those observed in human AML (PMID: 30755419, 23589569).

The NFE2 K287R mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with de novo acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 30755419). In vitro assays and expression of this mutation in CB3 cells demonstrated that this mutation does not alter DNA binding and increases transcriptional activity compared to wildtype NFE2.

The NFE2 Q7Tfs* mutation is located in the transactivating domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with de novo acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 30755419). This mutation abolishes expression of the full-length NFE2 protein and instead allows for expression of a shorter, 350-amino acid isoform. Expression of this mutation in CB3 cells demonstrated that this mutation is likely activating as measured by increased transcriptional activity compared to wildtype NFE2 (PMID: 30755419).

The NFE2 R273W mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with de novo acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 30755419). There is conflicting funtional data for this mutation. In vitro assays and expression of this mutation in CB3 cells demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as shown by reduced binding to DNA and reduced transcriptional activity compared with wildtype NFE2 (PMID: 30755419). However, expression of this mutation in BaF3 cells demonstrated that this mutation increased IL-3 dependent proliferation with or without coexpression of JAK2 V617F (PMID: 30755419).

The NFE2 R219Q mutation is located in between the transactivating and DNA binding domains of the protein. This mutation has been found in patients with de novo acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 30755419). In vitro assays and expression of this mutation in CB3 cells demonstrated that this mutation does not alter DNA binding and increases transcriptional activity compared to wildtype NFE2 (PMID: 30755419).

The NADK I90F mutation is found in the N-terminal domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in a mouse model and in a functional CRISPR screen demonstrated that it is activating as measured by increased kinase activity, enhanced substrate availability and increased tumorigenesis in a mouse model of pancreatic cancer comapred to wildtype (PMID: 26806015). Structural modeling of this alteration demonstrated that the NADK I90F mutation may increase the dimer interface of the protein, which likely contrinutes to enhanced substrate availability and kinase activity (PMID: 26806015).

Amplification of MERTK typically results in the overexpression of the protein. Overexpression of MERTK has been identified in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (PMID: 33239426, 35728303). In vitro studies with MCF10A cells overexpressing MERTK demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by enhanced motility, increased efferocytosis and upregulated PD-L1 expression compared to empty vector control cells (PMID: 25074939). Preclinical studies with MCF10A cells overexpressing MERTK demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with soluble recombinant TAM ecto-domains as measured by reduced efferocytosis (PMID: 25074939).

The CD74-NRG1 fusion protein pairs the N-terminus of CD74 and the cytosolic EGF-domain of NRG1 (PMID: 24469108). The N-terminal MHC domains of CD74 are predicted to replace the transmembrane domains of NRG1 III-β3, the NRG1 isoform implicated in CD74-NRG1 fusion-positive IMA patients (PMID: 24469108). Translocations involving CD74 and NRG1 are recurrent in patients with invasive mucinous lung adenocarcinoma (IMA) (PMID: 24469108, 29515761, 25501131, 25531467, 30988082). Wildtype NRG1 III-β3 functions as a membrane-bound ligand that activates ERBB signaling; the CD74-NRG1 protein allows for membrane stabilization and activation of NRG1 (PMID: 12648463, 25501131). Fibroblast cell lines engineered to express the CD74-NRG1 fusion have increased ERBB2/ERBB3 heterodimer formation, activated PI3K-AKT signaling, and increased transformation ability in colony formation assays (PMID: 24469108). In addition, lung cancer cell lines expressing the CD74-NRG1 fusion protein were sensitive to treatment with ERBB-targeted kinase inhibitors in proliferation and signaling assays (PMID: 24727320). An IMA patient treated with afatinib, an ERBB-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor, achieved progression-free survival of 6.5 months, an improved response over patients without the fusion (PMID: 29169524).

The resultant NRG1 fusion proteins typically pair an N-terminal transmembrane component with the cytosolic EGF domain of NRG1 (PMID: 29802158, 24469108). A number of NRG1 N-terminal fusion partners have been identified including CD74, SLC3A2, ATP1B1, SDC4, SARAF, and APP, among others (PMID: 29802158, 28950338, 24469108). NRG1 III-β3 is the NRG1 isoform that has been implicated in these oncogenic fusion proteins; resultant fusion proteins likely leverage the membrane binding of the N-terminal partner to stabilize NRG1 III-β3 for subsequent processing (PMID: 29802158, 24469108). Translocations involving NRG1 are recurrent in patients with invasive mucinous lung adenocarcinomas (IMA) and pancreatic cancer (PMID: 24469108, 29515761, 25501131, 25531467, 29802158, 28950338, 30988082). In preclinical assays, overexpression of NRG1 fusion proteins results in increased ERBB2-ERBB3 heterodimer formation, enhanced proliferation, and increased PI3K-AKT signaling (PMID: 24469108, 29802158) which can be inhibited clinically with antibodies directed at HER2, such as MCLA-128 (PMID: 31685488). NRG1-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma and pancreatic cell lines were sensitive to treatment with ERBB-targeted kinase inhibitors, suggesting that ERBB-mediated signaling is a driver in these cancer subsets (PMID: 24727320, 29802158). In addition, five patients with NRG1 rearrangements have achieved clinical responses to afatinib treatment, including two patients with IMA, two patients with pancreatic cancer and one patient with metastatic cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 29169524, 29802158, 28950338). In a Phase II clinical trial, patients with pancreas cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and other solid tumors harboring NRG1 fusions exhibited a response to zenocutuzumab, a bispecific antibody targeting NRG1 fusion signaling in NRG1 fusion-positive (NRG1+) cancers, while tumor regression was observed in 25 of 33 patients and confirmed investigator (INV) assessed responses were seen in 9 of 33 patients (ORR 27%; 90% CI, 15;43) (Abstract: Schram et al. Abstract # 3003, ASCO 2021. https://ascopubs.org/doi/abs/10.1200/JCO.2021.39.15_suppl.3003).

The ATP1B1-NRG1 fusion protein pairs the N-terminus of ATP1B1 and the cytosolic EGF-domain of NRG1 (PMID: 29802158). The N-terminal transmembrane domain of ATP1B1 is predicted to replace the transmembrane domains of NRG1 III-β3, the NRG1 isoform implicated in ATP1B1-NRG1 fusion-positive patients (PMID: 29802158). Translocations involving ATP1B1 and NRG1 are recurrent in patients with pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma and lung cancer (PMID: 28950338, 29802158, 30988082). Wildtype NRG1 III-β3 functions as a membrane-bound ligand that activates ERBB signaling; the ATP1B1-NRG1 protein allows for membrane stabilization and activation of NRG1 (PMID: 27626312). Pancreatic cell lines engineered to express the ATP1B1-NRG1 fusion have increased ERBB2/ERBB3 heterodimer formation, activated MAPK-ERK and PI3K-AKT signaling, increased proliferation, and enhanced transformation in xenograft assays (PMID: 29802158). In addition, pancreatic cell lines expressing the ATP1B1-NRG1 fusion protein were sensitive to treatment with afatinib, a pan-ERBB kinase inhibitor (PMID: 29802158). Two patients with ATP1B1-NRG1 fusions, including one patient with metastatic cholangiocarcinoma and one patient with pancreatic cancer, had substantial clinical responses to afatinib treatment (PMID: 28950338, 29802158). This fusion protein was identified in two patients with KRAS wildtype advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. One of these patients was treated with the EGFR-family kinase inhibitor afatinib and saw a significant response with a delay in disease progression for 5.5 months (PMID: 31068372).

The SLC3A2-NRG1 fusion protein pairs the N-terminus of SLC3A2 and the cytosolic EGF-domain of NRG1 (PMID: 27626312). The N-terminal transmembrane domain of SLC3A2 is predicted to replace the transmembrane domains of NRG1 III-β3, the NRG1 isoform implicated in SLC3A2-NRG1 fusion-positive IMA patients (PMID: 27626312). Translocations involving SLC3A2 and NRG1 are recurrent in patients with invasive mucinous lung adenocarcinoma (IMA) (PMID: 27626312, 29959202, 30988082). Wildtype NRG1 III-β3 functions as a membrane-bound ligand that activates ERBB signaling; the SLC3A2-NRG1 protein allows for membrane stabilization and activation of NRG1 (PMID: 27626312). Fibroblast and cancer cell lines engineered to express the SLC3A2-NRG1 fusion have increased ERBB2/ERBB3 heterodimer formation, activated PI3K-AKT signaling, increased transformation in colony forming assays, and enhanced invasive properties (PMID: 27626312, 29959202). In addition, lung cancer cell lines and murine xenograft models expressing the SLC3A2-NRG1 fusion protein were sensitive to treatment with ERBB-targeted kinase inhibitors (PMID: 24727320, 29959202).

The PIGA R412* truncating mutation results in the loss of the C-terminal tail of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human bone marrow cells demonstrated a decrease in GPI anchor protein, leading to decreased proliferation, aberrant synapse formation and abnormal membrane depolarization (PMID: 28441409).

The APP-NRG1 fusion protein includes the EGF-like domain of NRG1 and the transmembrane domain of APP.  While this fusion protein has not been functionally characterized, other fusions with NRG1 have been shown to be activating, suggesting that this fusion is likely activating (PMID: 24469108, 29515761, 25501131, 25531467, 29802158, 28950338). This fusion protein was identified in a patient with KRAS-widltype advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma who responded to treatment with the EGFR-family kinase inhibitor afatinib (PMID: 31068372).

PIGA deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with PIGA-deficient JY5 cells demonstrate that loss of PIGA is inactivating as measured by reduced expression of GPI-anchored proteins compared to wildtype (PMID: 24706016).

Amplification of PIK3C2B typically results in the overexpression of the protein. PIK3C2B amplification has been identified in glioblastoma (PMID: 14655756). In vitro studies with human lung carcinoma cells overexpressing PIK3C2B demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased talc-induced cell death and IL-6 secretion, which are known cellular events that can drive fibrosis, compared to wildtype (PMID: 31513749).

Deletions in PPP2R2A are found in various cancer types, including prostate, ovarian, and non-small cell lung cancers, among others (PMID: 21872824, 23087057, 25879784, 31349904, 27531894). The loss of PPP2R2A activity results in reduced PP2A phosphatase activity and altered activity of PP2A target proteins (PMID: 27531894). In addition, reduced PPP2R2A activity has been associated with altered DNA damage responses and increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents (PMID: 32522823, 23087057).

Amplification of PRCC typically results in the overexpression of the protein. PRCC amplification has been identified in non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 16322280). In vitro studies with NCI-H358 and A549 cells overexpressing PRCC demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cell proliferation, colony formation, anchorage-independent growth, migration and invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 30900418). In vivo studies with PRCC-silenced mouse xenograft models also demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by reduced tumor growth compared to PRCC-overexpressing mice (PMID: 30900418).

The PPP2R2A E83* mutation is found in the central region of the protein. This alteration has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) blast cells (PMID: 27531894). Expression of this mutation in AML blast cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by loss of PPP2R2A protein, reduced PP2A phosphatase activation, and activation of the AKT signaling pathway in biochemical and cell growth assays (PMID: 27531894).

PPP2R2A truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. The loss of PPP2R2A activity results in reduced PP2A phosphatase activity and altered activity of PP2A target proteins (PMID: 27531894). In addition, reduced PPP2R2A activity has been associated with altered DNA damage responses and increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents (PMID: 32522823, 23087057).

PIGA truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with PIGA-deficient JY5 cells demonstrate that loss of PIGA is inactivating as measured by reduced expression of GPI-anchored proteins compared to wildtype (PMID: 24706016).

Truncating mutations of PRKDC typically results in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with PRKDC-knockdown A549, H23 and HBEC3 cells demonstrate that loss of PRKDC is inactivating as measured by increased malignant transformation and reduced DNA repair activity compared to vector control (PMID: 31055244).

The DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion occurs as a result of an in-frame fusion event that joins the first exon of DNAJPB1, a gene that encodes a heat shock 40 protein family member, with exons 2 to 10 of PRKACA (PMID: 24578576). This fusion event gives rise to an expressed fusion protein that is pathognomonic to fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma (FL-HCC), a rare type of liver cancer that affects children and adolescents (PMID: 25122662) and that is enriched with cancer stem cells with endodermal stem cell traits (PMID: 26437858). The DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion constitutively activates PRKACA as demonstrated by association with the PKA-substrate CREB even in the absence of stimulation with forskolin (PMID: 25122662).

Deletion of PRKDC typically results in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with PRKDC-knockdown A549, H23 and HBEC3 cells demonstrate that loss of PRKDC is inactivating as measured by increased malignant transformation and reduced DNA repair activity compared to vector control (PMID: 31055244).

The PTPN1 M282L mutation lies in the proline-rich domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cell lines has demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased phosphatase activity and increased downstream JAK-STAT signaling (PMID: 24531327).

Amplification of PRKDC typically results in the overexpression of the protein. PRKDC amplification has been identified in breast cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (PMID: 31513357, 25480831). In vitro studies with MCF-7 cells overexpressing PRKDC demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and deregulation of mitosis and damage response compared to PRKDC-knockdown control (PMID: 31513357).

The PTPN1 R156* truncating mutation lies in the catalytic domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cell lines has demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased phosphatase activity and increased downstream JAK-STAT signaling (PMID: 24531327).

The PTPN1 Q9* truncating mutation lies in the first exon of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cell lines has demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased phosphatase activity and increased downstream JAK-STAT signaling (PMID: 24531327).

The PTPN1 V184D mutation lies in the catalytic domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cell lines has demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased phosphatase activity and increased downstream JAK-STAT signaling (PMID: 24531327).

Expression of truncated PTPN1 mutants in HEK293 cells and knockout of PTPN1 in a human lymphoma cell line demonstrated loss of PTPN1 is activating as measured by increased JAK/STAT signaling (PMID: 24531327). Knockout of PTPN1 in mouse models has been shown to accelerate lymphomagenesis and induce myeloproliferative disorders (PMID: 16267035, 28111468).

The PTPN1 A69V mutation lies in the catalytic domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cell lines has demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased phosphatase activity and increased downstream JAK-STAT signaling (PMID: 24531327).

The PTPN1 M74L mutation lies in the catalytic domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human cell lines has demonstrated that it is inactivating, as measured by decreased phosphatase activity and increased downstream JAK-STAT signaling (PMID: 24531327).

Truncating mutations in PTPN13 result in loss of protein function. In vivo studies have demonstrated that truncation of PTPN13 results in increased growth and invasiveness of breast tumors in mice that lack the PTPN13 catalytic domain compared to wildtype (PMID: 31938048).

Amplification of RANBP2 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. In vitro studies with Hep3B and HepG2 cells overexpressing RANBP2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to vector control and RANBP2-knockdown (PMID: 34298689).

The RELN R2290H mutation occurs in the arginine-amino acid-arginine (RXR) motif. This alteration has been identified as a de novo variant in Autism Spectrum disorder (PMID: 28419454). Expression of this variant in 293T and HeLa cells results in reduced Reelin secretion. The RELN R2290H mutation also resulted in increased expression of protein disulfide isomerase A1, an ER-chaperone protein, resulting in an altered ER-stress response (PMID: 28419454).

The RELN R1742Q mutation occurs in the arginine-amino acid-arginine (RXR) motif. This alteration has been identified as a de novo variant in Autism Spectrum disorder (PMID: 28419454). Expression of this variant in 293T and HeLa cells results in reduced Reelin secretion. The RELN R1742Q mutation also resulted in increased expression of protein disulfide isomerase A1, an ER-chaperone protein, resulting in an altered ER-stress response (PMID: 28419454).

RELN deletions have been identified in patients with neurological disorders, including psychiatric disorders, and are predicted to result in a truncated protein (PMID: 30158644). Murine models engineered to express a RELN deletion of exons 52 to 58 exhibit abnormalities in social behavior and motor learning as well as reduced expression of GABAergic markers (PMID: 30158644). In addition, C-terminal RELN deletions have been associated with reduced binding to RELN receptors and regulation of receptor specificity (PMID: 28123028).

The RELN R2290C mutation occurs in the arginine-amino acid-arginine (RXR) motif. This alteration has been identified as a de novo variant in Autism Spectrum disorder (PMID: 28419454). Expression of this variant in 293T cells, HeLa cells and neurospheres result in reduced Reelin secretion. The RELN R2290C mutation also resulted in increased expression of protein disulfide isomerase A1, an ER-chaperone protein, resulting in an altered ER-stress response (PMID: 28419454).

The REST N290Y mutation is found in the DNA binding domain of the protein (PMID: 26551668). This mutation was identified in a patient with Wilm's tumor, a childhood kidney cancer (PMID: 26551668). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by increased transcription of the REST target gene SCG2 in a qPCR assay compared to wildtype REST (PMID: 26551668).

The RELN R1742W mutation occurs in the arginine-amino acid-arginine (RXR) motif. This alteration has been identified as a de novo variant in Autism Spectrum disorder (PMID: 28419454). Expression of this variant in 293T and HeLa cells results in reduced Reelin secretion. The RELN R1742W mutation also resulted in increased expression of protein disulfide isomerase A1, an ER-chaperone protein, resulting in an altered ER-stress response (PMID: 28419454).

Truncating mutations in REST are found in several cancer types, including colorectal cancer and Wilm's tumor (PMID: 26551668). qPCR experiments testing the ability of mutated REST to repress the transcription of target genes demonstrated that truncating mutations found in Wilms' tumor patients result in increased target gene transcription, suggesting these alterations are inactivating (PMID: 26551668). In addition, a truncating mutation found in colorectal cancer was shown to increase PI3K signaling (PMID: 15960972).

Expression of this mutation in human bone marrow cell lines demonstrated it is neutral as measured by apoptosis, cell growth and colony formation comparable to wildtype ROBO1 (PMID: 26608094).

The ROBO1 R922H mutation (also cited as ROBO1 R886H) lies in the extracellular fibronectin-type III domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human bone marrow cell lines demonstrated it inactivates the tumor suppressor function of wildtype ROBO1 as measured by decreased apoptosis, increased cell growth and increased colony formation compared to wildtype ROBO1 (PMID: 26608094).

The ROBO1 T1260A mutation (also cited as ROBO1 T1160A) lies in the intracellular conserved cytoplasmic I domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in human bone marrow cell lines demonstrated it inactivates the tumor suppressor function of wildtype ROBO1 as measured by decreased apoptosis, increased cell growth and increased colony formation compared to wildtype ROBO1 (PMID: 26608094).

The ROBO1 E280* mutation is located in the extracellular region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma (PMID: 35615148). In vitro studies with RBE and HCCC9810 cells expressing ROBO1 E280* demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and angiogenesis compared to wildtype (PMID: 35615148).

ROBO1 truncating mutations can occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with RBE and HCCC9810 cells expressing a truncated variant of ROBO1 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and angiogenesis compared to wildtype (PMID: 35615148).

SAMHD1 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with SAMHD1-knockdown THP-1 cells demonstrate that loss of SAMHD1 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, increased G1/G0 phase cell population, increased dNTP and reduced apoptosis compared to vector control (PMID: 27183329).

The SAHMD1 R366H mutation is located in the GTP binding region of the protein. Expression of the SAMHD1 R366H mutation as recombinant protein demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by decreased dNTPase activity compared to wildtype SAMHD1 (PMID: 27071091).

Truncating mutations of RPL5 typically result in the loss of protein function. RPL5 truncating mutations have been identified in uveal melanoma (PMID: 32415113). In vitro studies with HeLa cells expressing truncated variants of RPL5 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by accumulation of 32S and 12S pre-rRNA compared to wildtype (PMID: 19061985).

The SAHMD1 V133I mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. Expression of the SAMHD1 V133I mutation as recombinant protein demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by decreased dNTPase activity compared to wildtype SAMHD1 (PMID: 27071091).

The SAHMD1 A338T mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. Expression of the SAMHD1 A338T mutation as recombinant protein demonstrated it is inactivating as measured by decreased dNTPase activity compared to wildtype SAMHD1 (PMID: 27071091).

The SAMHD1 D137N mutation is located in the dNTPase region of the protein. In vitro studies with HT-29 (Cas9-SAMHD1) cells expressing SAMHD1 D137N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and loss of apoptosis compared to wildtype (PMID: 35949607).

The SETD3 M1_E242del mutation is located in the SET domain of the protein. Expression of a SETD3 protein lacking the SET domain in NIH3T3 cells demonstrated this mutation is inactivating as measured by increased colony formation compared to wildtype SETD3 protein (PMID: 23065515).

The SLFN11 E669Q mutation occurs in the Walker B ATP hydrolysis domain of the protein (PMID: 29395061). In a leukemia cell line, expression of the SLFN11 E669Q mutant protein did not render cells sensitive to cisplatin and did not induce a replication block, suggesting that this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 29395061).

Amplification of SETD3 has been identified in liver cancer (PMID: 28442573). In vitro studies with liver cancer cells overexpressing SETD3 demonstrate SETD3 amplification is activating as measured by increased proliferation, colony formation and xenograft formation (PMID: 28442573).

The SMARCA2 R1159Q mutation occurs in that ATPase domain of the protein. SMARCA2 R1159Q alterations predominantly occur as heterozygous alterations in patients with Nicolaides-Baraitser syndrome (PMID: 22366787). Human embryonic stem cells engineered to express this mutation had impaired differentiation to neuronal precursors (PMID: 31375262). Expression of the SMARCA2 R1159Q mutation resulted in enhancer reprogramming, with enhanced SMARCA2 binding at altered enhancer locations. This epigenetic reorganization led to aberrant targeting of SMARCA4 to chromatin and activation of astrocyte gene expression programs (PMID: 31375262).

SLFN11 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with SLFN11-knockout DMS114 and Li-7 cells demonstrate that loss of SLFN11 is inactivating as measured by increased unfolded protein response, global protein ubiquitylation, endoplasmic reticulum stress and protein aggregation compared to wildtype (PMID: 33863777). Preclinical studies of SLFN11-deficient cells have demonstrated sensitivity to ATR inhibition and resistance to PARP inhibition (PMID: 27708213, 29395061).

SLFN11 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with SLFN11-knockout DMS114 and Li-7 cells demonstrate that loss of SLFN11 is inactivating as measured by increased unfolded protein response, global protein ubiquitylation, endoplasmic reticulum stress and protein aggregation compared to wildtype (PMID: 33863777).

Truncation mutations of SPRTN usually occur in the C-terminal region and typically result in loss of protein function. In vitro studies with HeLa cells expressing C-terminally truncated SPRTN variants demonstrate that truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by decreased DNA binding affinity and loss of proteolytic activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 27871366).

SMARCA1 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. SMARCA1 deletion has been identified in gastric cancer (PMID: 34736517). In vitro studies with SMARCA1-knockdown melanocytes and gastric cancer cell lines demonstrate that loss of SMARCA1 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular growth, migration and invasion compared to control cells (PMID: 25462860, 22508985).

Expression of the SMARCA2 K755R mutation resulted in enhancer reprogramming, with enhanced SMARCA2 binding at altered enhancer locations. This epigenetic reorganization led to aberrant targeting of SMARCA4 to chromatin and activation of astrocyte gene expression programs (PMID: 31375262).

The SPRTN Y112A mutation occurs in the SprT metalloprotease domain of the protein (PMID: 27871366). In biochemical experiments, SPRTN E112A was unable to resolve protein-DNA crosslinks and demonstrated hypersensitivity to crosslinking agents (PMID: 27871366, 27852435).

The SPRTN Y117C mutation occurs in the SprT metalloprotease domain of the protein (PMID: 25261934, 27871366). In a rescue experiment, expression of SPRTN Y117C in 293T cells depleted for wildtype SPRTN resulted in the inability to resolve stalled replication forks and a defect in cell cycle progression (PMID: 25261934). In biochemical experiments, SPRTN Y117A was unable to resolve protein-DNA crosslinks and demonstrated hypersensitivity to crosslinking agents (PMID: 27871366, 27852435).

Amplification of STAT4 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. STAT4 amplification has been identified in ovarian cancer and lung cancer (PMID: 28114283, 30987235). In vitro studies with hypoxia-exposed A2780 cells overexpressing STAT4 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and cellular invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 33636177).

Truncation mutations of SMARCA2 can occur throughout the gene and typically result in loss of protein function. In vitro studies with HeLa cells expressing C-terminally truncated SMARCA2 demonstrate that truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of nuclear localization and inability to induce interferon-stimulated genes compared to wildtype (PMID: 29848589).

Translocations involving TRB are found in patients with pediatric and acute T-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) (PMID: 28671688, 23033986, 19841179) and precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) (PMID: 15470492). In the fusion oncoproteins, the promoter and enhancer regions of TRB typically recombine with various C-terminal partners, resulting in activation of the fusion partner (PMID: 28671688, 23033986). Recurrent TRB rearrangement partners include NOTCH1, TLX1, TLX3, TAL1, HOXA, among others, and rearrangement leads to their aberrant overexpression (PMID: 23033986, 19841179). TRB rearrangements commonly require another mutational event to drive tumor progression and coordinate leukemic transcriptional programs (PMID: 19841179).

Translocations involving TRA are found in patients with pediatric and acute T-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) (PMID: 28671688, 26917488, 9407948). In the fusion oncoproteins, the promoter and enhancer regions of TRA typically recombine with various C-terminal partners, resulting in their activation of the fusion partner (PMID: 28671688). Recurrent TRA rearrangement partners include the transcription factors TLX1, TLX3, and TAL1, among others, and rearrangement leads to their aberrant overexpression (PMID: 28671688, 9407948).

Amplification of TAF1 typically results in the overexpression of protein. TAF1 amplification has been identified in prostate cancer and non-small cell lung cancer (PMID: 20181722, 36368153). In vitro studies with non-small cell lung cancer cells overexpressing TAF1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased TGFβ1 activation, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, cellular proliferation, migration and invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 36368153).

Recurrent TRD rearrangement partners include HOXA and NKX2-5, among others, and rearrangement leads to their aberrant overexpression (PMID: 23033986, 19841179). TRD rearrangements commonly require another mutational event to drive tumor progression and coordinate leukemic transcriptional programs (PMID: 19841179).

Translocations involving TRG are found in patients with acute T-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias (PMID: 11972513, 15470492, 18245528). Recurrent TRG rearrangement partners include HOXA and TLX genes, among others, and rearrangement leads to their aberrant overexpression (PMID: 11972513, 15470492, 18245528). TRG rearrangements commonly require another mutational event to drive tumor progression and coordinate leukemic transcriptional programs (PMID: 15470492).

The TRIP13 R354* occurs in the AAA+ ATPase domain of the protein (PMID: 28553959). Expression of this variant in HCT116 cells had a comparable effect to TRIP13 knockout, including early mitotic exit as evidenced in cell cycle studies (PMID: 28553959).

Amplification of TRIM27 has been identified in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, breast cancer, renal cell carcinoma, colorectal cancer and ovarian cancer, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 31719796, 33251042, 34284744, 23342271, 29767249). LoVo cell-derived xenograft studies in nude mice modeling colorectal cancer demonstrated that TRIM27 overexpression is activating as measured by decreased cell proliferation and metastasis following TRIM27 inhibition (PMID: 29767249). Treatment with the AKT inhibitor LY294002 demonstrated sensitivity in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma cell lines overexpressing TRIM27 as measured by suppressed cell proliferation and upregulation of cellular apoptosis (PMID: 31719796).

This alteration is commonly found with loss of heterozygosity of the other WIF1 allele (PMID: 17171686, 18828159) suggesting it may be a loss of function alteration.

In vitro luciferase reporter assays with ZBTB7A C387F demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced GLUT3 and PFKP transcriptional repression compared to wildtype (PMID: 26455326).

The ZBTB7A T403N mutation is located in the zinc finger domain of the protein. In vitro luciferase reporter assays with ZBTB7A T403N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced GLUT3 and PFKP transcriptional repression compared to wildtype (PMID: 26455326).

The ZBTB7A S22R mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. In vitro luciferase reporter assays with ZBTB7A S22R demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by GLUT3 and PFKP transcriptional repression comparable to wildtype (PMID: 26455326).

The ZBTB7A K424N mutation is located in the zinc finger domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute lymphoblastic T-cell leukemia (PMID: 28671688). In vitro luciferase reporter assays with ZBTB7A K424N demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced GLUT3 and PFKP transcriptional repression compared to wildtype (PMID: 26455326).

Truncating mutations of ZMYM3 occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing truncated variants of ZMYM3 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by abrogated interaction with the RNase H2 complex compared to wildtype (PMID: 30889214).

The ZBTB7A G562D mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. In vitro luciferase reporter assays with ZBTB7A G562D demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by GLUT3 and PFKP transcriptional repression comparable to wildtype (PMID: 26455326).

The ZNRF3 P103A mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in solution-based in vitro assays demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased binding to RSPO1 compared to wildtype (PMID: 22575959).

ZNRF3 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with miR-146a-mediated ZNRF3 silenced MG-63 cells and HOS cells demonstrate that loss of ZNRF3 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and colony formation compared to control vector and miR-146a knockout controls (PMID: 29088784).

ZNRF3 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. These mutations have been identified in adrenocortical carcinoma and osteoblastoma (PMID: 25490274, 24236197). In vitro studies with miR-146a-mediated ZNRF3 silenced MG-63 cells and HOS cells demonstrate that loss of ZNRF3 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and colony formation compared to control vector and miR-146a knockout controls (PMID: 29088784).

AJUBA truncation mutations are found in several cancer types including head and neck and esophageal cancer (PMID: 25839328). Esophageal cell lines engineered to express patient-associated AJUBA truncation mutations resulted in increased proliferation, invasion and migration in functional assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 25839328). AJUBA expression is downregulated in tissues from patients with truncating AJUBA mutations, suggesting that these alterations are inactivating (PMID: 27172796).

ALDH2 truncation mutations can occur throughout the protein and typically result in the loss of protein expression. Loss of ALDH2 mutations have been identified in lung adenocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and esophageal cancer (PMID: 31071657, 28027570, 16822169). In vivo studies with ALDH2-deficient mice demonstrate loss of ALDH2 is inactivating as measured by increased oxidized mitochondrial DNA copy number following chronic carbon tetrachloride and ethanol administration compared to wildtype mice (PMID: 3127990).

Truncation mutations of ATRIP occur throughout the gene, and have been identified in breast cancer and ovarian cancer (PMID: 24448499). In vitro studies with CV1720 cells expressing a premature stop codon in exon 12 of ATRIP demonstrate ATRIP truncation in inactivating as measured by reduced expression of ATRIP and loss of ATR–dependent G2/M cell cycle arrest (PMID: 23144622).

Amplification of ANKRD26 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. In vitro studies with patient-derived megakaryocytes overexpressing ANKRD26 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased MAPK/ERK pathway signaling and thrombopoietin/myeloproliferative leukemia virus oncogene (TPO/MPL) signaling (PMID: 36626254).

ATRIP loss is an alteration identified in myeloma and ovarian cancer (PMID: 26282654, 19737971). In vitro studies with ATRIP-depleted lens progenitor cells demonstrated loss of ATRIP is inactivating as measured by replicative stress, DNA damage accumulation and TP53-dependent apoptosis (PMID: 33110058). Treatment with the ATR inhibitor RP-3500 is predicted to be synergistic with ATRIP loss as measured by a genome-wide CRISPR screening that identified loss of ATRIP as a target alteration for sensitivity to this inhibitor (PMID: 34911817, 30532030).

ALDH2 deletion mutations have been identified in head and neck carcinoma, esophageal cancer, lung adenocarcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma (PMID: 31071657, 28027570, 28257851, 16822169). In vivo studies with ALDH2-deficient mice demonstrate loss of ALDH2 is inactivating as measured by increased oxidized mitochondrial DNA copy number following chronic carbon tetrachloride and ethanol administration compared to wildtype mice (PMID: 3127990).

The ANKRD26 K1300N mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 19657110). In silico analysis suggest that the mutation is deleterious (PMID: 19657110).

The ALDH2 E487K mutation, also known as ALDH2*2, is located on exon 12 of the gene. This mutation is a polymorphism that has been identified in gastric carcinoma, esophageal cancer and colon cancer (PMID: 22320964, 24334570). The ALDH2 E487K mutation demonstrates a semi-dominant-negative effect on wildtype ALDH2 due to structural alterations impairing the formation of the ALDH2 homotetramer complex (PMID: 20062057). In vivo studies with ALDH2 E487K knockin mice treated with chemical carcinogens demonstrate the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased DNA damage response in hepatocytes, liver injury and development of hepatocellular carcinoma compared to wildtype mice (PMID: 26150517).

ADHFE1 amplification results from the gain of extra copies of the ADHFE1 gene on chromosome 8q12.3 and leads to overexpression of protein. These mutations have been identified in breast cancer (PMID: 29202474, 30250890). In vitro studies with MCF7, MCF10A and MCF12A cells overexpressing ADHFE1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased MYC expression and accumulation of D-2-hydroxyglutarate and mitochondrial ROS leading to cellular dedifferentiation compared to wildtype (PMID: 29202474).

BAALC amplification is an event correlated with poor patient prognosis and is frequently reported in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 11707601, 20535151). BAALC gene amplification in patients with AML highly correlates with the expression of MN1, an oncogene implicated in leukemogenesis (PMID: 17494859). In vivo studies with mice transduced with patient-derived bone marrow cells containing high BAALC levels demonstrated leukemogenesis induction through BAALC blocking ERK-mediated monocyte differentiation, thus preventing myeloid differentiation (PMID: 21869843). High BAALC expression in patients with cytogenetically normal-AML and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents a chemoresistant phenotype (PMID: 20065290).

The BCOR-CCNB3 gene fusion results from the fusion of the 3' end of the BCOR gene to the 5' end of the CCNB3 gene. This fusion occurs primarily in undifferentiated sarcomas and shows a high male predominance, as the fusion occurs on the X chromosome. Ectopic expression of the fusion or the fused part of CCNB3 in NIH3T3 cells leads to aberrant expression of CCNB3 and increases the number of cells in S phase (PMID: 22387997, 25360585, 29300189). This fusion has been confirmed by FISH and RT-PCR in multiple small clinical studies. A comparative gene-set enrichment and pathway analysis between BCOR-CCNB3-positive sarcomas and tumors lacking the fusion showed that genes involved in morphogenesis and development, specifically of the skeletal system, were strongly represented in the BCOR-CCNB3-positive subgroup, as demonstrated by the overexpression of homeobox genes. Activation of the WNT and Hedgehog signaling pathways was also significantly upregulated in the BCOR-CCNB3-positive subgroup (PMID: 22387997).

CHTF8 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with knocked down CHTF8 in yeast cells demonstrated that loss of CHTF8 is inactivating as measured by the loss of disjunction in meiosis II, leading to sister chromatid cohesion defects (PMID: 15226378, 11389843).

The CTDNEP1 L72H mutation is located in the NIF (NLI interacting factor-like phosphatase) domain of the CTDNEP1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased phosphatase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 36765089).

CHTF8 loss is an alteration frequently identified in renal and prostate cancer, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 12477976). In vitro studies with knocked down CHTF8 in yeast cells demonstrated that loss of CHTF8 is inactivating as measured by the loss of disjunction in meiosis II, leading to sister chromatid cohesion defects (PMID: 15226378, 11389843). Treatment with the ATR inhibitor RP-3500 is predicted to be synergistic with CHTF8 loss as measured by a genome-wide CRISPR screening that identified loss of CHTF8 as a target alteration for sensitivity to this inhibitor (PMID: 34911817, 30532030).

CTDNEP1 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. CTDNEP1 truncating mutations (frameshift, nonsense and splice) or low CTDNEP1 expression levels have been found in patients with MYC-driven medulloblastoma, an aggressive tumor with a poor prognosis. In vitro studies in medulloblastoma (MB) cell lines have demonstrated that loss of CTDNEP1 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, stabilization of MYC and activation of MYC signaling pathways upon knockdown of CTDNEP1. Additionally, depletion of CTDNEP1 in neural stem/progenitor cells in an in vivo MB tumor model led to the formation of aggressive MB tumors while no tumors formed in control mice. Additionally, CTNEP1 depleted tumors had strong expression of MYC and higher proliferation rates as assessed by immunohistochemical characterization compared to control cells (PMID: 36765089).

The CTDNEP1 R158A mutation is located in the NIF (NLI interacting factor-like phosphatase) domain of the CTDNEP1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased ability to dephosphorylate its substrate, lipin-1, compared to wildtype (PMID: 38776370).

The CTDNEP1 E70S mutation is located in the NIF (NLI interacting factor-like phosphatase) domain of the CTDNEP1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased ability to dephosphorylate its substrate, lipin-1, compared to wildtype (PMID: 38776370).

The CTDNEP1 D67N mutation is located in the NIF (NLI interacting factor-like phosphatase) domain of the CTDNEP1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased phosphatase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 36765089).

The CTDNEP1 D69N mutation is located in the NIF (NLI interacting factor-like phosphatase) domain of the CTDNEP1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased phosphatase activity compared to wildtype (PMID: 36765089).

Truncating mutations of DDX41 can occur throughout the gene and typically result in the loss of protein function. These mutations have been identified in acute myeloid leukemia and myeloid neoplasm (PMID: 26712909, 36322930). In vivo studies with zebrafish expressing truncated DDX41 demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by increased hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell proliferation compared to wildtype (PMID: 33651979).

Deletion of CTDNEP1 typically results in loss of protein expression. Low CTDNEP1 expression levels have been found in patients with MYC-driven medulloblastoma, an aggressive tumor with a poor prognosis (PMID: 36765089). In vitro studies in medulloblastoma (MB) cell lines have demonstrated that loss of CTDNEP1 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, stabilization of MYC and activation of MYC signaling pathways upon knockdown of CTDNEP1. Additionally, depletion of CTDNEP1 in neural stem/progenitor cells in an in vivo MB tumor model led to the formation of aggressive MB tumors while no tumors formed in control mice. Additionally, CTNEP1 depleted tumors had strong expression of MYC and higher proliferation rates as assessed by immunohistochemical characterization compared to control cells (PMID: 36765089).

The DDX41 R525H mutation is located in the helicase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in acute myeloid leukemia (PMID: 27174803, 26712909). In vitro studies with cord blood cells, THP-1 cells and K562 cells expressing DDX41 R525H demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of ATPase activity but leads to decreased cell cycle progression, decreased cell growth and suppressed MDM2-mediated RB degradation compared to wildtype (PMID: 27174803). In vitro studies with mouse primary hematopoietic progenitor cells demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by increased R-loop formation and DNA damage, but leads to decreased cellular proliferation as compared to wildtype (PMID: 36229594). Other in vitro studies with DDX41-knockout HeLa and THP-1 cells expressing DDX41 R525H demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by decreased  ATPase activity, dysregulation of cyclic GMP-AMP synthase activity and increased type I interferon expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 35613581).

Amplification of ALDH1L2 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. ALDH1L2 amplification has been identified in glioblastoma and colorectal cancer (PMID: 35565854, 20498374). In vitro studies with MTHFD1L-knockout and MDA-MB-468 293T cells overexpressing ALDH1L2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by glycine-independent cell growth (PMID: 30500537). Other in vitro studies with U251 glioblastoma cells overexpressing ALDH1L2 also demonstrate amplification is activating as measured by reduced tumorsphere formation following ALDH1L2 knockout (PMID: 35565854).

ECSIT amplification results in the overexpression of the protein. In vitro studies with MDA MB-231 cells overexpressing ECSIT demonstrate that ECSIT overexpression is activating as measured by increased cell proliferation, migration and invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 35571656). Other in vitro studies with 293 cells overexpressing ECSIT have also demonstrated that ECSIT overexpression is activating as measured by increased NF-kB activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 10465784).

The DKK1 E232K mutation occurs in one of two cysteine-rich domains in the protein (PMID: 22000856). Expression of this mutation in WNT reporter assays demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased luciferase activity compared to wildtype DKK1 (PMID: 22000856).

The DKK1 W206E mutation occurs in one of two cysteine-rich domains in the protein (PMID: 22000856). Expression of this mutation in WNT reporter assays demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased luciferase activity compared to wildtype DKK1 (PMID: 22000856).

The DKK1 K226E mutation occurs in one of two cysteine-rich domains in the protein (PMID: 22000856). Expression of this mutation in WNT reporter assays demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by luciferase activity comparable to wildtype DKK1 (PMID: 22000856).

The DKK1 H229E mutation occurs in one of two cysteine-rich domains in the protein (PMID: 22000856). Expression of this mutation in WNT reporter assays demonstrated that it is likely neutral as measured by luciferase activity comparable to wildtype DKK1 (PMID: 22000856).

The DKK1 F234K mutation occurs in one of two cysteine-rich domains in the protein (PMID: 22000856). Expression of this mutation in WNT reporter assays demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased luciferase activity compared to wildtype DKK1 (PMID: 22000856).

The ECSIT V140A mutation is located in the PPR repeat motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in extranodal natural killer/T cell lymphoma (PMID: 29291352). In vitro studies with SNK6 cells expressing ECSIT V140A demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased NF-kB activation compared to wildtype (PMID: 29291352).

Truncating mutations of ERCC1 typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with ERCC1-knockout primary human fibroblasts demonstrate that loss of ERCC1 is inactivating as measured by hypersensitivity to UV-C irradiation, suggesting dysregulation of the nucleotide excision repair pathway (PMID: 33315086).

EIF2B1 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vivo studies with EIF2B1-knockout yeast demonstrate that loss of EIF2B1 is inactivating as measured by loss of EIF2B localization and the inability to regulate the integrated stress response compared to wildtype (PMID: 33334879).

Deletion mutations of ERCC1 typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with ERCC1-knockout primary human fibroblasts demonstrate that loss of ERCC1 is inactivating as measured by hypersensitivity to UV-C irradiation, suggesting dysregulation of the nucleotide excision repair pathway (PMID: 33315086).

The ECSIT T419C mutation is located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. In vitro studies with SNK6 and NKYS cells expressing ECSIT T419C demonstrate that the mutation is activating as measured by increased TNF-a and IFN-y production and upregulation of NF-kB signaling genes compared to wildtype (PMID: 29291352).

The FBXW2 E269K mutation is located in the WD-40 substrate binding domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in H1299 cells demonstrated that it is likely activating as measured by decreased ability to down-regulate the target protein SKP2 by western blot, increased cell growth in a clonogenic assay, and increased tumor growth and proliferation index in a xenograft model compared to both wildtype and vector controls (PMID: 28090088).

The FBXW2 G258W mutation is located outside of a known functional domain. This mutation has been found in lung cancer (PMID: 28090088). Expression of this mutation in H1299 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as its ability to suppress cell growth is comparable to wildtype (PMID: 28090088).

The FBXW2 D30Y mutation is located outside of a known functional domain. This mutation has been found in lung cancer (PMID: 28090088). Expression of this mutation in H1299 cells demonstrated that it is likely neutral as its ability to suppress cell growth is comparable to wildtype (PMID: 28090088).

Amplification of FGF2 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. FGF2 amplification has been identified in colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer and prostate cancer (PMID: 27007053, 14522896). In vitro studies with osteoblastic ROS 17/2.8 cells overexpressing FGF2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation compared to vector control (PMID: 12898525).

The FBXW2 S84C mutation is located in the F-box domain of the protein. Expression of this mutation in H1299 cells demonstrated that it is inactivating as measured by decreased ability to down-regulate the target protein SKP2 by western blot, increased cell growth in a clonogenic assay, and increased tumor growth in a xenograft model compared to wildtype (PMID: 28090088).

Amplification of FGF1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. FGF1 amplification has been identified in ovarian cancer and colorectal cancer (PMID: 17538174, 34552869). In vitro studies with B-CPAP and CAL-62 cells overexpressing FGF1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular invasion and metastasis compared to vector control (PMID: 36952626).

FGF7 amplification typically results in the overexpression of the protein. FGF7 overexpression has been identified in urothelial carcinoma, ovarian cancer and fusion-positive rhabdomyosarcoma (PMID: 25623741, 38491511, 34850536). In vitro studies with cancer-associated fibroblasts overexpressing FGF7 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion compared to cancer-associated fibroblasts treated with anti-FGF7 (PMID: 38491511).

Amplification of FGF5 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. FGF5 amplification has been identified in renal cell cancer, prostate cancer and breast cancer (PMID: 11454700). In vivo studies with nude mice overexpressing FGF5 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and tumor growth compared to FGF5-knockout mice (PMID: 31372048).

Amplification of FGF8 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. In vitro studies with HSC-3 and HSC-4 cells overexpressing FGF8 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cell proliferation, invasion and migration compared to vector controls (PMID: 33649301).

Amplification of FGF9 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. FGF9 amplification has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 26916220, 32104224, 24334956). In vivo studies with mice overexpressing FGF9 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by tumor growth and metastasis compared to vector control (PMID: 34438248).

FOLR1 is amplified in various cancers and most often leads to increased levels of folate receptor α (FRα) (PMID: 36508886, 36402875). In addition to acting as a membrane-bound folate transporter, unbound FRα can act as a transcription factor that upregulates the expression of other transcription factors related to stemness such as Fgfr4, Hes1, Oct4, Sox2, and Klf4 (PMID: 36508886, 23243496, 27300003). Knockdown of FOLR1 in cell lines with high FRα expression results in decreased cell proliferation, further supporting that FOLR1 amplification is oncogenic (PMID: 23144806, 25816016).

Amplification of FOLH1 typically leads to the overexpression of the protein. FOLH1 amplification has been identified in prostate cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma and colorectal cancer (PMID: 10397265, 31289613, 19716160). In vitro studies with human umbilical vein endothelial cells overexpressing PSMA demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and invasion compared to the negative control group (PMID: 33748101).

EIF2B1 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vivo studies with EIF2B1-knockout yeast demonstrate that loss of EIF2B1 is inactivating as measured by loss of EIF2B localization and the inability to regulate the integrated stress response compared to wildtype (PMID: 33334879).

Amplification of FOXN4 typically results in the overexpression of protein. FOXN4 amplification has been identified in lung adenocarcinoma (PMID: 34155000, 33447073). In vitro studies with PC9 and HCC827 cells overexpressing FOXN4 demonstrate that amplification is likely activating as measured by downregulation of EGFR expression, a commonly observed phenotype in transformed small cell lung cancer, compared to vector control (PMID: 34155000). Preclinical studies with lung adenocarcinoma cells observed upregulation of FOXN4 following treatment with osimertinib (PMID: 34155000).

Amplification of HDAC2 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. HDAC2 amplification has been identified in breast cancer, pancreatic cancer and colon cancer (PMID: 28560068, 34903606, 24948597). In vitro studies with A549 cells overexpressing HDAC2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and inhibition of apoptosis compared to wildtype (PMID: 22492270).

The HSD17B2 G160R mutation is located in an unknown functional domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer (PMID: 18372405). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing HSD17B2 G160R demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein expression and transcription activity comparable to wildtype (PMID: 18372405).

Truncating mutations of HSD17B2 occur throughout the protein and typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with various prostate cancer cell lines expressing truncated HSD17B2 isoforms through alternative splicing demonstrate that HSD17B2 truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by increased protein degradation compared to full-length HSD17B2 (PMID: 30228209).

The ERCC1 R156W mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. In vitro studies with primary human fibroblasts expressing ERCC1 R156W demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced protein expression, increased chromosomal breakage and reduced nucleotide excision repair activity (PMID: 33315086).

Truncating mutations of HTATIP2 commonly occur in the NADPH-binding domain of the protein. These alterations have been identified in colon carcinoma and small-cell lung cancer (PMID: 10611237). In vitro studies in RAT1a cells transfected with truncated HTATIP2 transcripts demonstrate truncated HTATIP2 is inactivating as measured by increased antiapoptotic activity caused by the transcript’s short hydrophobic carboxyl terminus (PMID: 10611237).

The HSD17B2 A111D mutation is located in the NAD+ binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in breast cancer (PMID: 18372405). In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing HSD17B2 A111D demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by reduced protein stability compared to wildtype (PMID: 18372405).

Loss of HTATIP2 has been identified in hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, colon cancer, gliomas and small cell lung cancer, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 27418384, 18972434, 24037692, 17097132, 19798571, 26718891, 9174052). In vivo studies in a HTATIP2 knockdown A549 cell line demonstrate loss of HTATIP2 is inactivating as measured by increased tumor growth and tumor metabolic plasticity (PMID: 32545251). Treatment with multikinase inhibitor sorafenib is suggested to have reduced sensitivity in tumors with loss of HTATIP2 expression (PMID: 32545251).

Truncating mutations in ING1 typically occur in the PHD finger and lead to loss of protein function. In vitro studies have demonstrated that loss of ING1 contributes to neoplastic transformation and leads to increased migration and invasion in breast cancer cells (PMID: 10545957, 24962136). In vitro studies in melanoma cells have demonstrated that deletion of the PHD finger domain leads to decreased DNA repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 15201991).

The ING1 N260S mutation is located in the PHD zinc finger domain of the ING1 protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 15201991). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by decreased DNA repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 15201991).

Amplification of ID1 results in the overexpression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in pancreatic cancer, gastric cancer and glioblastoma (PMID: 31582374, 22245935, 31292163). In vitro studies with hepatocellular carcinoma cells overexpressing ID1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased MYC signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 32705157). ID1 overexpression is suggested to be sensitive to treatment with AURKA inhibitor VX689 and MYC inhibitor 10058‑F4 as measured by decreased metastasis and drug resistance following treatment in hepatocellular carcinoma cells (PMID: 32705157). In vitro studies with ID1-positive U251 glioblastoma cells treated with the neuroleptic drug pimozide resulted in the inhibition of ID1 expression and increased sensitivity to treatment with temozolomide chemotherapy (PMID: 31292163).

INTS6 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with ectopic expression of INTS6 in androgen-independent PC3 and DU145 cell lines demonstrated that loss of INTS6 is inactivating as measured by colony growth suppression following INTS6 re-expression (PMID: 19906297).

The ING1 R102L mutation is located in the Sin3-associated polypeptide 30 (SAP30) interacting domain of the ING1 protein. This mutation has been found in melanoma (PMID: 15201991). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by decreased DNA repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 15201991).

INTS6 loss is an alteration identified in non-small cell lung carcinoma, prostate cancer and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (PMID: 10467397, 19906297, 12527901). In vitro studies with ectopic expression of INTS6 in androgen-independent PC3 and DU145 cell lines demonstrated that loss of INTS6 is inactivating as measured by colony growth suppression following INTS6 re-expression (PMID: 19906297).

FZR1 loss is an alteration identified in colorectal cancer, melanoma and glioma, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 18535175, 28174173, 18662541). In vitro studies with FZR1-depleted human primary melanocytes demonstrated loss of FZR1 is inactivating as measured by upregulation of BRAF and phospho-ERK from lack of premature senescence (PMID: 28174173). Treatment with the ATR inhibitor RP-3500 is predicted to be synergistic with FZR1 loss as measured by a genome-wide CRISPR-screening that identified loss of FZR1 as a target alteration for sensitivity to this inhibitor (PMID: 34911817, 30532030).

FZR1 amplification is an event reported in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and multiple myeloma (PMID: 28143883, 27655696). In vitro studies with specific knockdown for FZR1 in U266, OPM-2, KMS-18, JJN3, HS-5 and Phoenix GP multiple myeloma cell lines demonstrated FZR1 is activating as measured by reduced cell viability and tumor growth arrest (PMID: 27655696). Knockdown of FZR1 in multiple myeloma cell lines and patient-derived primary multiple myeloma cells demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with the topoisomerase inhibitors etoposide and doxorubicin as measured by significant reduction in cell viability (PMID: 27655696).

Amplification of IQGAP1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. IQGAP1 amplification has been identified in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, gastric cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma (PMID: 11289714, 29846864, 20530982). In vitro studies with bronchial epithelial cells overexpressing IQGAP1 demonstrated that amplification is activating as measured by upregulation of c-MYC and cyclin-D1 compared to negative control groups (PMID: 18625219).

Amplification of KAT7 results in the overexpression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in breast cancer and gastric cancer (PMID: 35868058, 36724120). In vitro studies with patient-derived gastric cancer cells overexpressing KAT7 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cell growth, migration and invasion compared to normal expression (PMID: 35868058).
Truncating mutations in KDM5D result in loss of protein function. In vitro studies have demonstrated that truncation of KDM5D results in increased DNA damage as compared to wildtype (PMID: 35132955).

Truncating mutations in KLF2 occur throughout the protein as frameshift indels and nonsense mutations (PMID: 25428260, 25283840). Truncating variants that delete 1-3  zinc finger domains have a reduced ability to suppress NF-κB transcriptional activity, as evidenced in reporter assays in lymphoma and 293T cell lines (PMID: 25428260, 25283840). In addition, the expression of KLF2 truncating mutations failed to regulate the activity of NF-κB in response to a variety of stimulants that initiate TNF-receptor, TLR (toll-like receptor), canonical and non-canonical NF-κB pathways, suggesting a defect in binding of KLF2 to DNA (PMID: 25428260).

The KLF2 A291V mutation occurs in the first zinc finger domain of the protein (PMID: 25428260, 25283840). This variant had a similar ability to suppress NF-κB transcriptional activity compared to wildtype KLF2, as evidenced in reporter assays in lymphoma and 293T cell lines (PMID: 25428260). In addition, the KLF2 A291V mutation was found to co-occur with other KLF2 mutations in the same lymphoma patient sample, suggesting the KLF2 A291V mutation alone is not sufficient to be tumorigenic (PMID: 25428260).

The LRP5 R154M mutation is found in the first β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 17052975). This alteration is found in patients with high bone mass disorders (PMID: 17052975). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by a decreased interaction between LRP5 and SOST, a WNT antagonist, likely boosting downstream WNT signaling (PMID: 17052975).

LGR5 amplification is an alteration frequently reported in various cancer types, including basal cell carcinomas, hepatocellular carcinomas, colorectal tumors and ovarian tumors (PMID: 16575208, 18688030). In vitro and in vivo studies overexpressing LGR5 in SiHa and HeLa cells and in nude mice demonstrated LGR5 is activating as measured by increased cell proliferation and tumor growth (​​PMID: 25193857). Treatment with Wnt/beta-catenin signaling inhibitor tegavivint in patients overexpressing LGR5 with recurrent or refractory solid tumors, including lymphomas and desmoid tumors, is currently being evaluated in a phase I/II clinical trial (NCT04851119).

The KLF2 C274Y mutation occurs in the first zinc finger domain of the protein (PMID: 25428260, 25283840). This variant has a reduced ability to suppress NF-κB transcriptional activity, as evidenced in reporter assays in lymphoma and 293T cell lines (PMID: 25428260). In addition, the expression of KLF2 C274Y failed to regulate the activity of NF-κB in response to a variety of stimulants that initiate TNF-receptor, TLR (toll-like receptor), canonical and non-canonical NF-κB pathways, suggesting a defect in binding of KLF2 to DNA (PMID: 25428260).

The LRP5 N198S mutation is found in the first β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 17052975). This alteration is found in patients with high bone mass disorders (PMID: 17052975). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by a decreased interaction between LRP5 and SOST, a WNT antagonist, likely boosting downstream WNT signaling  (PMID: 17052975).

The LRP5 G171V mutation is located in the first β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 17052975, 15143163). This alteration is found in patients with high bone mass disorders (PMID: 17052975). Murine models engineered to express this mutation had a substantial increase in bone mass, a phenotype consistent with LRP5 activity (PMID: 12817748).

The LRP5 T253I mutation is found in the first β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 17052975). This alteration is found in patients with high bone mass disorders (PMID: 17052975). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by a decreased interaction between LRP5 and SOST, a WNT antagonist, likely boosting downstream WNT signaling (PMID: 17052975).

Truncating mutations of LRP5 typically occur at the multiple tandem repeat regions of the protein and result in dysregulation of the protein signaling pathways. These mutations have been identified in breast cancer (PMID: 19158955). In vivo studies with a mouse xenograft model expressing truncated LRP5 variants demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of β-catenin signaling regulation and increased tumor growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 19158955).

The LRP5 W199A mutation (also cited as LRP5 W781A) is found in the third β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 17052975). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by a decreased interaction between LRP5 and DKK1, a WNT antagonist, likely boosting downstream WNT signaling (PMID: 17052975).

The LRP6 W767A mutation is located in the third β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 22000855). Expression of this mutant in 293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by a decreased interaction with DKK1, a WNT antagnonist, leading to increased WNT activation in luciferase reporter assays compared to wildtype (PMID: 22000855).

The LRP6 Y875A mutation occurs in the third β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 22000855). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased responsiveness to the WNT3A ligand compared to wildtype (PMID: 22000855).

The LRP6 R739G mutation occurs in the second β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 22000855). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased cell surface expression and WNT signaling compared to wildtype (PMID: 22000855).

The LRP6 S488Y mutation occurs in the second β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 24427284). Expression of this mutation in HUVEC cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased cell surface expression, decreased WNT signaling and reduced cellular proliferation and invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 24427284).

The LRP6 Y706A mutation is located in the third β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 22000855). The LRP6 M877A mutation occurs in the third β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 22000855). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased responsiveness to the WNT3A ligand compared to wildtype (PMID: 22000855).
