The LRP5 D111Y mutation is found in the first β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 17052975). This alteration is found in patients with high bone mass disorders (PMID: 17052975). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by a decreased interaction between LRP5 and SOST, a WNT antagonist, likely boosting downstream WNT signaling (PMID: 17052975).

MBD4 truncation mutations typically occur in the methyl-CpG binding domain and result in impaired protein function. These mutations have been identified in MSI-high colon cancer (PMID: 10545939, 10637515). In vitro studies with MSI-high human colorectal carcinoma cells expressing a truncated MBD4 transcript demonstrate that MBD4 truncation mutations are inactivating as measured by the dominant negative impairment of DNA repair and the subsequent increased mutation frequency compared to full-length MBD4 (PMID: 17285135).

Translocations involving MEF2D and SS18 are found in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 27507882, 27824051). Typically, the N-terminal of MEF2D containing the DNA binding domain is fused in-frame to the C-terminal of SS18, resulting in truncation of the SSXT N-terminal domain (PMID: 27824051). Gene expression analyses in patients with MEF2D fusion proteins demonstrate reduced WNT-signaling, suggesting an altered transcriptional activity (PMID: 27507882). The MEF2D-SS18 oncoprotein confers lymphoid self-renewal in hematopoietic assays as well as activation of HDAC9 expression, demonstrating that the protein mediates leukemogenesis (PMID: 27824051, 27507882, 29408457).

Translocations involving MEF2D and FOXJ2 are found in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 27507882, 27824051). Typically, the N-terminus of MEF2D containing the DNA binding domain is fused in-frame to the C-terminus of FOXJ2, resulting in truncation of the N-terminal domains (PMID: 27824051). Gene expression analyses in patients with MEF2D fusion proteins demonstrate reduced WNT-signaling, suggesting an altered transcriptional activity (PMID: 27507882). MEF2D fusion proteins confer lymphoid self-renewal in hematopoietic assays as well as activation of HDAC9 expression, demonstrating that the protein mediates leukemogenesis (PMID: 27824051, 27507882).

MAL2 truncation mutations typically occur in the MARVEL domain of the protein and produce N-terminally truncated MAL2 proteins. In vitro studies with yeast two-hybrid screening assays with N-terminal truncated MAL2 transcripts demonstrate that the mutation is inactivating as measured by loss of D52-like protein interaction compared to wildtype (PMID: 19175940).

Translocations involving MEF2D and DAZAP1 are found in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 27507882, 27824051). Typically, the N-terminus of MEF2D containing the DNA binding domain is fused in-frame to the C-terminus of DAZAP1, resulting in truncation of the RNA recognition domains (PMID: 27824051). Gene expression analyses in patients with MEF2D fusion proteins demonstrate reduced WNT-signaling, suggesting an altered transcriptional activity (PMID: 27507882, 27824051). The MEF2D-DAZAP1 oncoprotein confers lymphoid self-renewal in hematopoietic assays as well as activation of HDAC9 expression, demonstrating that the protein mediates leukemogenesis (PMID: 27824051, 27507882, 15744350, 17898785).

Translocations involving MEF2D and HNRNPUL1 are found in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 27507882, 27824051). Typically, the N-terminus of MEF2D containing the DNA binding domain is fused in-frame to the C-terminus of HNRNPUL1, resulting in truncation of the SPRY and AAA domains (PMID: 27824051). Gene expression analyses in patients with MEF2D-HNRNPUL1 fusion proteins demonstrate reduced WNT-signaling, suggesting an altered transcriptional activity (PMID: 27507882). The MEF2D-HNRNPUL1 oncoprotein confers lymphoid self-renewal in hematopoietic assays as well as activation of HDAC9 expression and altered B-cell differentiation programs, demonstrating that the protein mediates leukemogenesis (PMID: 27824051, 27507882, 30171027).

MIDEAS deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with MIDEAS-knockout U2OS cells demonstrate that loss of MIDEAS is inactivating as measured by increased mitotic chromosome misalignment compared to vector control (PMID: 32591534).

The MLH3 W1276R mutation is located in the C-terminal dimerization domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in colorectal cancer (PMID: 12702580, 16981255). In vitro studies with Sf9 cells and 293T cells expressing MLH3 W1276R demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein stability and mismatch repair comparable to wildtype (PMID: 18521850). Although in vitro studies of MLH3 W1276R demonstrate that the mutation does not contribute to mismatch repair deficiency, it is suggested that in vivo studies with MLH3 W1276R alongside other mismatch repair mutations would demonstrate that the mutation may contribute to compound pathogenicity (PMID: 18521850).

Translocations involving MEF2D and CSF1R are found in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (PMID: 27507882, 27824051). Typically, the N-terminus of MEF2D containing the DNA binding domain is fused in-frame to the C-terminus of CSF1R, resulting in deletion of the N-terminal immunoglobulin (IgG) domains (PMID: 27824051). Gene expression analyses in patients with MEF2D-CSF1R fusion proteins demonstrate increased tyrosine kinase signaling. In addition, patients with Ph-like ALL have demonstrated sensitivity to imatinib (PMID: 27507882, 25207766). The MEF2D-CSF1R oncoprotein confers lymphoid self-renewal in hematopoietic assays as well as activation of aberrant B-cell differentiation programs, demonstrating that the fusion protein mediates leukemogenesis (PMID: 27824051, 27507882).

Truncating mutations of MLH3 typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with COS7 cells expressing truncated MLH3 variants demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by the inability to interact with the DNA mismatch repair complex and increased microsatellite instability compared to wildtype (PMID: 10615123).

Amplification of MAP3K21 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. MAP3K21 amplification has been identified in breast cancer and melanoma (PMID: 30552384, 24849047). In vitro studies with MCF10A cells overexpressing MAP3K21 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion compared to wildtype (PMID: 30552384).

The LRP5 E721A mutation is found in the third β-propeller domain of the protein (PMID: 17052975). Expression of this mutation in 293T cells demonstrated it is likely activating as measured by a decreased interaction between LRP5 and DKK1, a WNT antagonist, likely boosting downstream WNT signaling (PMID: 17052975).

MIDEAS truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with MIDEAS-knockout U2OS cells demonstrate that loss of MIDEAS is inactivating as measured by increased mitotic chromosome misalignment compared to vector control (PMID: 32591534).

The MLH3 Q24E mutation is located in the HATPase domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (PMID: 11586295). In vitro studies with Sf9 cells and 293T cells expressing MLH3 Q24E demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by protein stability and mismatch repair comparable to wildtype (PMID: 18521850). Although in vitro studies of MLH3 Q24E demonstrate that the mutation does not contribute to mismatch repair deficiency, it is suggested that in vivo studies with MLH3 Q24E alongside other mismatch repair mutations would demonstrate that the mutation may contribute to compound pathogenicity (PMID: 18521850).

Although in vitro studies of MLH3 E1451K demonstrate that the mutation does not contribute to mismatch repair deficiency, it is suggested that in vivo studies with MLH3 E1451K alongside other mismatch repair mutations would demonstrate that the mutation may contribute to compound pathogenicity (PMID: 18521850).

The MYBL1-NFIB fusion protein is a fusion between the 5' end of MYBL1, including the negative regulatory domain, and the 5' end of NFIB. This mutation has been found in adenoid cystic carcinomas (PMID: 29149504, 26631609). Expression of this fusion in HEK293T cells demonstrated that it is activating as measured by significant increase in reporter gene activation as compared to wildtype transcripts (PMID: 26631070).

The NHERF1 K172N mutation is located in the PDZ2 domain of the NHERF1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by increased cellular proliferation and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 24012959).

The NHERF1 A190D mutation is located in the PDZ2 domain of the NHERF1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by increased cellular proliferation and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 28011475).

The NHERF1 E43G mutation is located in the PDZ1 domain of the NHERF1 protein. This mutation has been found in breast cancer (PMID: 26977012). In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by increased cellular proliferation and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 26977012).

Amplification of ONECUT2 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. ONECUT2 amplification has been identified in prostate cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma and small cell lung cancer (PMID: 25788493, 26547929, 34155000). In vitro studies with A549 cells and xenograft models overexpressing ONECUT2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by tumor growth and metastasis and increased cellular proliferation and invasion compared to vector control (PMID: 31882655).

Amplification of NQO1 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. NQO1 amplification has been identified in gastric cancer, breast cancer and colon cancer (PMID: 34168410, 27966538, 25885439). In vitro studies with RKO and MDA-MB-231 cells overexpressing NQO1 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased HIF-1α signaling and tumor growth compared to vector control (PMID: 27966538).

Truncating mutations in NHERF1 lead to loss of protein function.  In vitro studies have demonstrated that truncating mutations in the C-terminus of NHERF1 are inactivating as measured by inhibition of pseudopodia formation involved in the migratory process in ovarian cancer cells (PMID: 28684865).

The NHERF1 D301V mutation is located outside of a known functional domain of the NHERF1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by increased cellular proliferation and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 24012959).

Amplification of PHF19 leads to the overexpression of the protein. These alterations have been identified in multiple myeloma, plasma cell leukemia and glioblastoma (PMID: 31383640, 30323224). In vivo studies with a KRAS G12D, P53 null-driven hepatocellular carcinoma mouse model mice overexpressing PHF19 demonstrate that amplification of PHF19 is activating as measured by increased tumorigenesis and metastasis compared to wildtype (PMID: 25955388). Preclinical studies with L-363 cells overexpressing PHF19 demonstrated sensitivity to treatment with dual EZH2 and EZH1 inhibitor UNC1999 as measured by reduced cell proliferation upon drug treatment (PMID: 31383640).

Amplification of POU2F2 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. POU2F2 amplification has been identified in lung cancer, gastric cancer and liver cancer (PMID: 33832481, 26019213, 14576340). In vitro studies with A549 and H1299 cells overexpressing POU2F2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion compared to vector control (PMID: 33832481).

Amplification of POU3F4 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. Amplification of POU3F4 has been identified in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and neuroendocrine prostate cancer (PMID: 19307926, 31371344). In vitro studies with prostate cancer cells overexpressing POU3F4 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular differentiation compared to controls (PMID: 31371344).

POU3F2 amplification typically results in the overexpression of the protein. Amplification of POU3F2 has been identified in glioblastoma, small cell lung cancer and melanoma (PMID: 2216722, 23530560, 32632141, 7478537). In vitro studies with MDA-MB-231 cells and hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines overexpressing POU3F2 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, invasion and migration compared to wildtype (PMID: 36797433, 31920461). Preclinical studies with breast cancer cells overexpressing POU3F2 demonstrate radioresistance as measured by sustained cell survival following irradiation (PMID: 36797433).

The PRPF8 A687P mutation is located in the PROCN domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 24781015). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the corresponding somatic yeast mutation PRPF8 N760P demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by cell growth and splicing assay results comparable to wildtype (PMID: 24781015).

The PRPF8 G1750E mutation is located adjacent to the PRPF8 domain IV core of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 24781015). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the corresponding somatic yeast mutation PRPF8 G1822E demonstrate that the mutation is likely neutral as measured by cell growth and splicing assay results comparable to wildtype (PMID: 24781015).

The PRPF8 M1307I mutation is located in the U5-snRNA binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 24781015). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the corresponding somatic yeast mutation PRPF8 M1379I demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by loss of second-step cell growth suppression in splicing assay results compared to wildtype (PMID: 24781015).

PRPF8 truncation mutations occur throughout the gene and result in the loss of protein. In vivo studies with zebrafish expressing truncation mutations of PRPF8 demonstrate that PRPF8 truncation is inactivating as measured by impaired myeloid differentiation, accumulation of aberrantly spliced spliceosome transcripts and cell death compared to wildtype (PMID: 23714367).

The PRPF8 V1015N mutation is located in the RNA recognition motif of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 24781015). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the corresponding somatic yeast mutation PRPF8 V1088N demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by loss of second-step cell growth suppression in splicing assay results compared to wildtype (PMID: 24781015).

The PRPF8 H1875R mutation is located in the PRPF8 domain IV core of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 24781015). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the corresponding somatic yeast mutation PRPF8 H1947R demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by loss of second-step cell growth suppression in splicing assay results compared to wildtype (PMID: 24781015).

Truncating RAD17 mutations occur throughout the gene and have been identified in various cancer types (PMID: 26437225). In vivo N-terminal truncation of RAD17 in mouse embryonic stem cells demonstrated that RAD17 truncation is inactivating as measured by hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents and impaired homologous recombination (PMID: 15297881).

The PRPF8 E1292K mutation is located in the U5-snRNA binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 24781015). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the corresponding somatic yeast mutation PRPF8 E1364K demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by loss of second-step cell growth suppression in splicing assay results compared to wildtype (PMID: 24781015).

The PRPF8 D1598Y mutation is located in the U6-snRNA binding site of the protein. This mutation has been identified in myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 24781015). In vivo studies with yeast expressing the corresponding somatic yeast mutation PRPF8 D1670Y demonstrate that the mutation is likely inactivating as measured by loss of second-step cell growth suppression in splicing assay results compared to wildtype (PMID: 24781015).

PSMB2 amplification is an event frequently reported in chronic leukemia and hepatocellular carcinoma and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 32933107, 29780166). In vitro studies with HeLa cells overexpressing PSMB2 demonstrated that amplified PSBM2 is activating as measured by suppressed homologous recombination and DNA double-strand break repair in cells (PMID: 21660142). Amplification of PSMB2 in N-87 and AGS cell lines also demonstrated that it is activating as measured by upregulation of proteasome activity and cell proliferation, and suppression of apoptosis (PMID: 36110152). Overexpression of PSMB2 in HeLaG1 cell lines demonstrated increased sensitivity to treatment with camptothecin (PMID: 21660142).

RAD17 loss is an alteration frequently identified in various tumor types (PMID: 17657792, 26437225). Somatic conditional alleles of RAD17 in HCT116 cell lines demonstrate loss of RAD17 is inactivating as measured by chromosomal stability loss, replication disruption and frequent internal DNA damage (PMID: 12672690). Treatment with the ATR inhibitor RP-3500 is predicted to be synergistic with RAD17 loss as measured by a genome-wide CRISPR screening that identified loss of RAD17 as a target alteration for sensitivity to this inhibitor (PMID: 34911817, 30532030). Treatment with CHK1 inhibitor AZD7762 and WEE1 inhibitor MK-1775 is predicted to be synergistic with RAD17 loss in tumors as measured by a synthetic lethal interaction in a yeast model (PMID: 26437225).

Truncation mutations of PTPN14 typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with HEK293 cells expressing truncated transcripts of PTPN14 lacking linker regions demonstrate that truncating mutations are inactivating as measured by loss of YAP1 binding, the inability to translocate YAP1 to the cytoplasm from the nucleus and the inability to inhibit anchorage-independent growth compared to wildtype (PMID: 22948661).

RNAseH2A amplification is an event frequently identified in various cancers, including glioma, ER-positive breast cancer and kidney cancer (PMID: 27176716, 32509219, 29843367). In vitro studies with silenced RNAseH2A in U85 and U251 glioma cells have impaired cell proliferation, clone formation reduction and increased cell apoptosis (PMID: 27176716). In vivo studies with nude mice demonstrate RNAseH2A amplification is activating as measured by tumor size reduction following RNAseH2A inhibition (PMID: 27176716).

REV3L loss is an alteration identified in various cancers, including colon carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer and gastric cancer (PMID: 18622427, 15617831). In vitro studies with REV3L-depleted HeLa, U2OS and 293T/17 cell lines demonstrated loss of REV3L is inactivating as measured by accumulation of chromosomal aberrations, but with no significant effect on cell growth and viability (PMID: 20028736). Other in vitro studies inhibiting REV3L in lung, breast, mesothelioma and colon tumor cell lines demonstrated loss of REV3L is activating as measured by suppression of colony growth with accumulation of persistent DNA damage (PMID: 22028621). Treatment with the ATR inhibitor RP-3500 is predicted to be synergistic with REV3L loss as measured by a genome-wide CRISPR-screening that identified loss of REV3L as a target alteration for sensitivity to this inhibitor (PMID: 34911817, 30532030). Loss of REV3L is suggested to synergize with alkylating agent cisplatin based on in vitro studies with knocked down REV3L H1299 cells demonstrating sensitivity to treatment (PMID: 26165320). Treatment with irreversible pan-HER inhibitor dacomitinib synergizes with loss of REV3L as measured by dacomitinib-resistance cells, FADU and MSKQLL2, demonstrating sensitivity following REV3L inhibition (PMID: 26790612).

The RNAseH2A R280G mutation is located on the RNase H type-2 domain, and has been identified in skin cancer (PMID: 30273559). In vitro studies with site-directed mutagenesis in Rosetta-2 cells demonstrated this alteration is inactivating as measured by a decrease in nuclease activity toward DNA duplexes containing single ribonucleotides (PMID: 30273559).

The RNAseH2A V133M mutation is located on the RNase H type-2 domain, and has been identified in intestinal cancer (PMID: 30273559). In vitro studies with site-directed mutagenesis in Rosetta-2 cells demonstrated this alteration is inactivating as measured by a decrease in nuclease activity toward DNA duplexes containing single ribonucleotides and RNA/DNA hybrids (PMID: 30273559).

The RNAseH2A P158S mutation is located on the RNase H type-2 domain and has been identified in skin cancer (PMID: 30273559). In vitro studies with site-directed mutagenesis in Rosetta-2 cells demonstrated this alteration is inactivating as measured by a decrease in nuclease activity toward DNA duplexes containing single ribonucleotides and RNA/DNA hybrids (PMID: 30273559).

REV3L amplification is an event identified in various cancers, including glioma, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and cervical cancer (PMID: 19289490, 26752104, 18593951). In vitro studies with amplified REV3L in SiHa, HeLa, ME180 and MS751 cervical cancer cells demonstrate REV3L overexpression is activating as measured by upregulation of G1 phase to S phase transition, leading to increased cell growth and tumor colony formation (PMID: 25781640). REV3L overexpression demonstrated resistance against treatment with cisplatin as measured by attenuated cisplatin-induced apoptosis in treated U251MG and U87MG glioma cell lines (PMID: 19289490).

The RNAseH2B E202* mutation is located at the C-terminal of the protein in the RNAse H2 complex component domain. The RNAseH2B E202* mutation is inactivating as measured by in vivo studies using mice with an RNAseH2B E202* mutation demonstrating significant DNA damage accumulation, loss of RNAse H2 function, reduced cell proliferation and embryonic lethality (PMID: 22579044).

RNAseH2B truncating mutations occur throughout the gene, and have been infrequently identified in various types of cancer, including ovarian cancer (PMID: 33353557). Truncating mutations result in RNAseH2B inactivation as measured by in vivo studies using mice with an RNAseH2B E202* mutation demonstrating significant DNA damage accumulation, loss of RNAse H2 function, reduced cell proliferation and embryonic lethality (PMID: 22579044).

RNAseH2B loss is an alteration frequently identified in various cancers, including cervical cancer, intestinal carcinoma and prostate cancer, and is associated with poor patient prognosis (PMID: 29642758, 30273559, 35179959). In vitro studies with RNAseH2B-inhibited prostate cancer cell lines LNCaP, C4-2B, 22Rv1, PC-3 and DU145 demonstrated loss of RNAseH2B is inactivating as measured by impaired DNA damage repair and increased cell proliferation (PMID: 35179959). Treatment with the ATR inhibitor RP-3500 is predicted to be synergistic with RNAseH2B loss as measured by a genome-wide CRISPR screening that identified loss of RNAseH2B as a target alteration for sensitivity to this inhibitor (PMID: 34911817, 30532030). RNAseH2B deletion synergizes with PARP inhibitors olaparib, rucaparib, talazoparib and veliparib as measured by in vitro studies with RNAseH2B knockout C4-2B and 22Rv1 cells demonstrating sensitivity to treatment (PMID: 35179959). Sensitivity to PARP inhibition is lost when cells are both RNAseH2B null and RB1 null, however, treatment sensitivity is restored if cells are additionally BRCA2 null (PMID: 35179959).

The RPS15 P131S mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 26466571). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RPS15 P131S demonstrate that the mutation switches function as measured by defective mRNA translation and metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis compared to wildtype (PMID: 30181176).

Amplification of RIOK2 results in overexpression of the protein (PMID: 36518977). RIOK2 amplification has been detected in multiple cancer types, including ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma, adrenocortical carcinoma and renal clear cell carcinoma (PMID: 36518977). Knockout of RIOK2 in tongue squamous cell carcinoma cells with RIOK2 amplification leads to decreased protein synthesis and decreased cell proliferation demonstrating that amplification of RIOK2 is likely oncogenic (PMID: 36661680).

The RPS15 H137Y mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 26466571). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RPS15 H137Y demonstrate that the mutation switches function as measured by defective mRNA translation and metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis compared to wildtype (PMID: 30181176).

The RPS15 S138F mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 26466571). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RPS15 S138F demonstrate that the mutation is switches function as measured by defective mRNA translation and metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis compared to wildtype (PMID: 30181176).

The RPS15 G132S mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RPS15 G132S demonstrate that the mutation switches function as measured by defective mRNA translation and metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis compared to wildtype (PMID: 30181176).

The RPS15 T136A mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 26466571). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RPS15 T136A demonstrate that the mutation switches function as measured by defective mRNA translation and metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis compared to wildtype (PMID: 30181176).

SLIT3 truncating mutations typically result in loss of SLIT3 protein expression. In mice inoculated with hepatocellular carcinoma cells, SLIT3 downregulation via slit3-shRNA activates the G1/S phase transition, inhibits apoptosis and activates the GSK3β/β-catenin pathway demonstrating SLIT3 loss is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29859044).

Amplification of RPS15 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. In vitro studies with KYSE30 and KYSE450 cells overexpressing RPS15 demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion compared to RPS15-knockout cells (PMID: 37264021).

The SQSTM1-NUP214 fusion protein involves the N-terminus of SQSTM1 combined with a short C-terminal fragment of NUP214. This mutation has been found in adult T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 20851865). Expression of this fusion in HeLa cells and in mice demonstrated that it is activating as measured by the recruitment of CRM1, nuclear export proteins and nucleoporins to aggregate nuclear bodies that inhibit nuclear protein RNA export (PMID: 27613868, 32343715).

The STAT1 Q463H mutation is found in the DNA binding domain of the protein (PMID: 28011069). Expression of this mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted in decreased phosphorylation and reduced transcriptional activity in reporter assays (PMID: 28011069).

The STAT1 G250E mutation is found in the DNA binding domain of the protein (PMID: 28011069). Expression of this mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted in decreased phosphorylation and reduced transcriptional activity in reporter assays (PMID: 28011069).

The STAT1 E157K mutation is found in the coiled coil domain of the protein (PMID: 28011069). Expression of this mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted in decreased phosphorylation and reduced transcriptional activity in reporter assays (PMID: 28011069).

The STAT1 T385M mutation is found in the DNA binding domain of the protein (PMID: 25288569). This alteration was identified in patients with Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis Disease, a disorder in which patients acquire persistent infections due to deficient immune responses. Expression of this mutation in EBV-transformed B-cells or HeLa cells resulted in increased STAT1 phosphorylation following interferon stimulation largely due to defects in STAT1 dephosphorylation (PMID: 25288569).

SLIT3 deletion results in loss of SLIT3 protein expression. In mice inoculated with hepatocellular carcinoma cells, SLIT3 downregulation via slit3-shRNA activates the G1/S phase transition, inhibits apoptosis and activates the GSK3β/β-catenin pathway demonstrating SLIT3 loss is likely oncogenic (PMID: 29859044).

SFRP1 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vivo studies with SFRP1-knockout cancer stem cells and mice demonstrate that loss of SFRP1 is inactivating as measured by increased tumorigenic potential, earlier tumor initiation and upregulation of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness, proliferation and metastasis compared to wildtype (PMID: 31928951).

The STAT1 R274Q mutation is found in the coiled coil domain of the protein. Expression of the R274Q mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted in increased phosphorylation in response to interferon, with levels consistent with other STAT1 gain-of-function mutations (PMID: 31114772, 28011069).

The RPS15 G134R mutation is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. This mutation has been identified in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (PMID: 26466571). In vitro studies with HEK293T cells expressing RPS15 G134R demonstrate that the mutation switches function as measured by defective mRNA translation and metabolic reprogramming toward aerobic glycolysis compared to wildtype (PMID: 30181176).

SFRP1 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vivo studies with SFRP1-knockout cancer stem cells and mice demonstrate that loss of SFRP1 is inactivating as measured by increased tumorigenic potential, earlier tumor initiation and upregulation of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness, proliferation and metastasis compared to wildtype (PMID: 31928951).

The STAT1 K278E mutation is found in the coiled coil domain of the protein (PMID: 25288569). This alteration was identified in patients with Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis Disease, a disorder in which patients acquire persistent infections due to deficient immune responses. Expression of this mutation in EBV-transformed B-cells or HeLa cells resulted in increased STAT1 phosphorylation following interferon stimulation largely due to defects in STAT1 dephosphorylation (PMID: 25288569). A patient with this mutation was also found to have reduced CD4+IL17A+ Th17 cells compared to normal controls as well as dampened interferon production (PMID: 25288569).

The STAT1 Y701C mutation is found in a canonical phosphorylation site of the protein. This germline mutation was found in a family with several individuals with multifocal osteomyelitis, a disorder that results in susceptibility to myobacteria infections (PMID: 23585529). Expression of the Y701C mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted loss of phosphorylation in response to interferon, suggesting that this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 31114772, 28011069). This alteration functioned as a dominant negative for IFN-gamma activity in patient-derived CD14 monocytes (PMID:  23585529).

The STAT1 T437N mutation is found in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This germline alteration was identified in a family with history of lympadenopathy and nodulcar lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) (PMID: 31114772). Expression of the T437N mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted in increased phosphorylation in response to interferon, with levels consistent with other STAT1 gain-of-function mutations (PMID: 31114772). Monocytes, NK cells, and T cells expressing the T437N mutation demonstrated a delay in STAT1 dephosphorylation (PMID: 31114772).

The STAT1 G384D mutation is located in the DNA binding domain of the protein. This alteration was identified in patients with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis disease (PMID: 25288569). Expression of this mutation in EBV-transformed B-cells or HeLa cells demonstrated that STAT1 G384D is activating as measured by increased STAT1 phosphorylation following interferon stimulation compared to wildtype (PMID: 25288569). A patient with this mutation was also found to have reduced CD4+IL17A+ Th17 cells compared to normal controls as well as dampened interferon production (PMID: 25288569).

The STAT1 T437I mutation is found in the DNA binding domain of the protein. Expression of the T437I mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted in increased phosphorylation in response to interferon, with levels consistent with other STAT1 gain-of-function mutations (PMID: 31114772).

The STAT2 R510* mutation is located in a linker domain of the protein. This mutation was found in a family with increased susceptibility to viral infection (PMID: 28087227). Expression of this alteration in COS-7 cells resulted in depletion of phosphorylated STAT2 is response to interferon alpha stimulation, suggesting that this mutation is loss-of-function (PMID: 28087227).

Amplification of TIGAR typically results in the overexpression of the protein. TIGAR amplification has been identified in colon cancer, breast cancer and glioblastoma (PMID: 23726973, 21820150, 22887998). In vitro studies with U2OS cells overexpressing TIGAR demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased reactive oxygen species and decreased autophagy compared to wildtype (PMID: 19713938 ). In vivo studies with xenograft mouse models overexpressing TIGAR also demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by decreased cellular proliferation and increased apoptosis following knockdown (PMID: 31799200).

Translocations involving the regulatory units of TRA and TCL1B are found in patients with T-cell acute lymphocytic leukemias and T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) (PMID: 9407948, 24825865, 10077617). TRA-TCL1B fusions result in the recombination of N-terminal TRA promoter and enhancer regions in frame with the open reading frame of TCL1B (PMID: 9407948), leading to activation of TCL1B. While TRA-TCL1B fusions have not been studied in functional assays, the fusions are predicted to behave similarly to TRA fusion to family member TCL1A. In preclinical studies, overexpression of TCL1A results in the activation of AKT, a downstream effector of T-cell receptor signaling (PMID: 17890451). TRA-TCL1A likely hyperactivates TCR signaling, leading to oncogenic AKT signaling (PMID: 17890451).

The TLE1 S289A mutation is located in the serine/proline rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity in luciferase-based reporter assays compared to wildtype TLE1 (PMID: 19956621).

The TLE1 S298E mutation is located in the serine/proline rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity in luciferase-based reporter assays compared to wildtype TLE1 (PMID: 19956621).

The TLE1 S286A mutation is located in the serine/proline rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity in luciferase-based reporter assays compared to wildtype TLE1 (PMID: 19956621).

The TLE1 S286E mutation is located in the serine/proline rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity in luciferase-based reporter assays compared to wildtype TLE1 (PMID: 19956621).

The TLE1 S289E mutation is located in the serine/proline rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity in luciferase-based reporter assays compared to wildtype TLE1 (PMID: 19956621).

TLE1 is located in the 9q region that is commonly deleted in acute myeloid leukemia which is associated with t(8;21) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (PMID: 18258796, 27636548). Knockdown of TLE1 expression cooperates with AML1-ETO to promote proliferation and survival in AML cell lines (PMID: 18258796). In addition, loss-of-function screens targeting all genes on the 9q deleted region found that loss of TLE1, or the family member TLE4, promoted transformation in human myeloid cells (PMID: 18258796).

Amplification of TNFSF13 leads to overexpression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in breast cancer and multiple myeloma (PMID: 18366696, 30135465, 25750171). In vitro studies with TNFSF13-knockdown in SW480 cells demonstrate inhibition of cell adhesion, migration and invasion, suggesting that activation of the gene is oncogenic(PMID: 19573525).

TLE4 is located in the 9q region that is commonly deleted in acute myeloid leukemia which is associated with t(8;21) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (PMID: 18258796, 27636548). Knockdown of TLE4 expression cooperates with AML1-ETO to promote proliferation and survival in AML cell lines (PMID: 18258796). In addition, loss-of-function screens targeting all genes on the 9q deleted region found that loss of TLE4, or the family member TLE1, promoted transformation in human myeloid cells (PMID: 18258796).

The STAT1 K673R mutation is found in the SH2 domain of the protein (PMID: 28011069). Expression of this mutation in U3C osteosarcoma cell lines resulted in decreased phosphorylation and reduced transcriptional activity in reporter assays (PMID: 28011069).

The SFRP1 C140Y mutation is found in the Frizzled cysteine-rich domain of the protein (PMID: 22927647). This mutation has been found in glioblastoma (PMID: 22927647). Expression of the SFRP1 C140Y mutation in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased ability to inhibit WNT-transcriptional activity in luciferase assays compared to wildtype SFRP1 (PMID: 22927647). In addition, expression of this variant in IMR-90 cells demonstrated decreased promotion of senescence compared to wildtype SFRP1 (PMID: 22927647).

Amplification of TRIB3 typically results in the overexpression of the protein. TRIB3 amplification has been identified in breast cancer, renal cell carcinoma and gastric cancer (PMID: 31844113, 30745845, 27573078). In vitro and in vivo studies with knockdown of TRIB3 in TRIB3-overexpressiong A549 cells demonstrate decreased cellular proliferation, invasion and tumor growth following knockdown suggesting that TRIB3 overexpression is oncogenic (PMID: 23632994). Other in vitro studies with renal cell carcinoma cell lines overexpressing TRIB3 also demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, migration and invasion compared to negative control lentivirus (PMID: 30745845).

Amplification of UBE2A generally results in the overexpression of the protein. These mutations have been identified in ovarian cancer, breast cancer and melanoma (PMID: 26679603, 12640129, 24891954). In vitro studies with MCF10A cells overexpressing UBE2A demonstrate that amplification is activating as measured by promotion of multinucleated cells, centrosome amplification, multipolar mitotic spindles, aneuploidy and anchorage-independent growth compared to normal expression (PMID: 11929833).

The TLE1 S298A mutation is located in the serine/proline rich domain of the protein. Expression of this variant in 293T cells demonstrated that it is likely inactivating as measured by decreased transcriptional activity in luciferase-based reporter assays compared to wildtype TLE1 (PMID: 19956621).

UBTF internal tandem duplications (ITDs) are located in the high mobility group box domain of the UBTF protein. These mutations have been found in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome (PMID: 36448876, 37085611, 35176137, 37236968, 38426285). Expression of these mutations in cord blood CD34+ cells demonstrated that they are activating as measured by increased colony growth as compared to wildtype (PMID: 35176137). In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that these mutations are sensitive to SNDX-5613, a menin inhibitor, as measured by reduced tumor growth and myeloid differentiation (PMID: 37890156).

The TNFSF13 G67R mutation is located in the extracellular domain of the protein. This mutation has been identified in bile duct adenocarcinoma (PMID: 25526346). In silico analysis suggests that TNFSF13 G67R is likely activating and damaging through the introduction of a new furin cleavage site (PMID: 12730512).

UCHL1 overexpression is observed in many cancer types and is correlated with 1q21 amplification in multiple myeloma (PMID: 26513019). In urothelial bladder cancer (UBC) tissue samples, UCHL1 is significantly overexpressed at the mRNA and protein levels and is associated with a less favorable prognosis (PMID: 37815895). Knockdown of UCHL1 in UBC cell lines results in decreased cell proliferation and colony formation, while UBC cells with UCHL1 amplification demonstrate enhanced tumor cell expansion (PMID: 37815895). High UCHL1 levels are also associated with significant overexpression of Ki67 and PCNA at the mRNA and protein levels (PMID: 37815895).

The XRCC1 R194W mutation is located outside of a known functional domain of the XRCC1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is neutral as demonstrated by colony formation similar to wildtype when exposed to the alkylating agent MMS (methyl methanesulfonate) (PMID: 15781218).

XRCC1 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with XRCC1-knockout HeLa cells demonstrate that loss of XRCC1 is inactivating as measured by impaired DNA repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 35778544). In vivo studies with XRCC1-knockout mice also demonstrate that loss of XRCC1 is inactivating as measured by increased DNA damage breakage compared to wildtype (PMID: 14642568).

The XRCC1 R280H mutation is located outside of a known functional domain of the XRCC1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is inactivating as demonstrated by sensitivity to the alkylating agent MMS (methyl methanesulfonate) comparable to XRCC1 loss of function mutations and decreased growth after MMS exposure compared to wildtype (PMID: 15781218).

XRCC1 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with XRCC1-knockout HeLa cells demonstrate that loss of XRCC1 is inactivating as measured by impaired DNA repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 35778544). In vivo studies with XRCC1-knockout mice also demonstrate that loss of XRCC1 is inactivating as measured by increased DNA damage breakage compared to wildtype (PMID: 14642568).

The XRCC1 R339Q mutation is located in the BRCT 1 domain of the XRCC1 protein. In vitro studies have demonstrated that this mutation is neutral as demonstrated by colony formation similar to wildtype when exposed to the alkylating agent MMS (methyl methanesulfonate) and similar DNA repair compared to wildtype (PMID: 11909950).

The EWSR1-YY1 t(14;22)(q32;q12) chromosomal rearrangement leads to a fusion protein with the transactivation domain of EWSR1 and the DNA-binding domain of YY1 (PMID: 23630070). This fusion is found in mesothelioma (PMID: 23630070). Further studies are needed to characterize the effects of the gene fusion on YY1 activity and the oncogenicity of the fusion protein.

The ZBTB20 G419V mutation (also cited as ZBTB20 G346V) is located in a central sumoylation site of the protein. This alteration is an autism risk variant. Expression of this variant in cortical pyramidal neurons results in increases in the basal dendritic compartments, with implications for neuronal function (PMID: 30281617).

The ZBTB20 P46R mutation is located in the N-terminal region of the protein. This alteration is an autism risk variant. Expression of this variant in cortical pyramidal neurons results in decreased dendritic spine length, with implications for neuronal function (PMID: 30281617).

The ZBTB20 A693V mutation (also cited as ZBTB20 A620V) is located in the C-terminal region of the protein. This alteration is found in a subset of patients with intellectual disabilities. Expression of this variant in cortical pyramidal neurons results in reduced apical dendritic length, with implications for neuronal function (PMID: 30281617).

ZFP36L1 truncating mutations typically result in the loss of protein function. In vitro studies with ZFP36L1-knockout SW620 cells demonstrate that loss of ZFP36L1 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and cyclin D expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 29426877).

ZFP36L1 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with ZFP36L1-knockout SW620 cells demonstrate that loss of ZFP36L1 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation and cyclin D expression compared to wildtype (PMID: 29426877).

Truncating mutations of ZFP36L2 can occur throughout the protein and have been identified in bladder cancer (PMID: 33397444). In vivo studies in HeLa cells transfected with full-length, C-terminal and N-terminal fragment transcripts of ZFP36L2 demonstrated truncation of the C-terminal of ZFP36L2 is inactivating as measured by transcript instability and reduced protein degradation (PMID: 29449217).

ZFP36L2 loss is an alteration identified in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 20622884). In vivo studies with double knockout ZFP36L2 and ZFP36L1 mice demonstrated that loss of ZFP36L2 with ZFP36L1 loss is inactivating as measured by impairment of thymic development and onset of T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID: 20622884).

Amplification of ZFP36L2 has been identified in gastric cancer and low-grade glioma (PMID: 31048690, 35910229). In vitro studies in SNU-719 and NCI-N87 gastric cancer cells demonstrated that ZFP36L2 overexpression is activating as measured by increased colony growth formation (PMID: 31048690).

The ZFP36L2 G145* frameshift mutation is located in the N-terminal of the protein. In vitro studies in HeLa cells expressing ZFP36L2 G145fs* demonstrated the G145fs* alteration is inactivating as measured by protein instability, impaired cell viability and loss of cell cycle regulation (PMID: 29449217).

ZNF750 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. Loss of ZNF750 has been identified in esophageal cancer, cervical cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and lung cancer (PMID: 27819679, 31148199, 30563911, 29760388, 29216641, 28608921, 27749841, 25839328). In vitro studies with ZNF750-silenced KYSE180 and KYSE140 cells demonstrate that loss of ZNF750 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, invasion, migration and colony formation compared to vector control (PMID: 32042337).

ZNF750 deletion mutations typically result in the loss of protein expression. In vitro studies with ZNF750-silenced KYSE180 and KYSE140 cells demonstrate that loss of ZNF750 is inactivating as measured by increased cellular proliferation, invasion, migration and colony formation compared to vector control (PMID: 32042337).
